en: The First Chapter of the Jñānapāda in the Śrī Pādmasaṃhitā.
The sages, inhabitants of Kaṇva’s hermitage, began to question the sage Kaṇva as he sat in his hermitage, seeking to know the action that leads to the highest good. 1.1. Ṛṣis.
"O venerable Kaṇva, the Vedas, along with their limbs and sub-limbs, have been studied by me from you in full detail,
as well as the treatises concerning their meaning exactly as they are. Yet,
though these have been studied, they do not lead to liberation."
The reason for this must also be heard from you; there is no other way.
Kaṇva said: "O sages, listen all of you to what was heard by me previously."
Having approached the sage Saṃvarta,
who was like another sun and blazing with splendor, he saluted him and asked about this very matter.
While all the great seers were listening, Saṃvarta himself, the omniscient one, [spoke].
To me, who was desirous of hearing, Saṃvarta replied exactly as it was:
"All the Vedas have been studied by me, along with their limbs, sub-limbs, and in full detail."

The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, along with the Vākovākya, have been heard by you; in all of them, all the deities are seen. In others, they are seen as independent, and no fruit other than heaven is observed.
Various treatises and systems of logic have been established,
yet I do not see anywhere a means that results in liberation.
Moreover, we have heard that even for him [the Buddha], the Veda alone is the authoritative source.

"Even though I reflected upon it with my mind, I did not attain certainty. (1.9) Thereupon, being deeply despondent and with a heart thus tormented, I reached Siddhāśrama and worshipped Brahmā. (1.10)
I performed most severe austerity; thereupon Prajāpati, being pleased, came into my presence himself along with the ṛṣis and the deities. 1.11 Brahmā.
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever dwells in your mind.
O best of the twice-born, for those who seek boons, the sight of me is a granter of boons. Thus spoke Saṃvarta.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, I replied with palms joined:
"May pure knowledge arise within me, free from doubt and free from confusion, by which path of knowledge I may cross over the suffering of saṃsāra. (1.13)
Thus addressed, the God of gods, laughing, spoke this:
"O Brahmin, listen; I shall declare the flawless means for attaining perfection."
For the twice-born, the Śruti alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good.
Since, by constantly worshipping Hari with the mantras of the Śruti,
one attains the ultimate liberation (kaivalya) and shall not wander again in this world.
"O Blessed One, by what scripture is the Supreme Deity propitiated? Of what nature is the Supreme Deity, and what is the procedure for his worship? (1.17)
Brahmā [received] the Vaiṣṇava teaching, which is pure, flawless, and destructive of sin;
it was enjoined by the Primeval God for the benefit of all the deities.
"Endowed with four quarters and bestowing the fruits of the four aims of life—
by means of that scriptural injunction, propitiate Keśava.
The eminent sage Kapila heard that scripture from me.
"But by my command, go from here to Pātāla, which is near that place.
Having said this, the blessed Brahmā vanished right there.
Once again, I performed austerities for the purpose of going to Pātāla.
Entering Pātāla, which was protected by nāgas, by the power of my asceticism,
I saw there the Lord of Nāgas seated in comfort, surrounded by his attendants.
Prostrating like a staff upon the ground before Kapila Viṣṇu, I said:
"I am Saṃvarta, returned from Jambūdvīpa; be gracious to me!
Know me, O Blessed One Viṣṇu, as one who has arrived by the command of Brahmā."
That which is sought by the great seers through knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct—
that which utterly destroys existence— is fully known by you.
[Save] me, who am deeply afflicted and submerged in the shoreless ocean of saṃsāra.
"Save the afflicted one, O Blessed One, with supreme compassion, O All-pervading Lord!
For there is no other who knows this path, the means for liberation, except you.
Thus addressed, the divine Kapila, through the grace of the Lotus-born [Brahmā], [responded].
Beholding the lotus standing at his side, Kapila, becoming gracious, spoke this:
"O Padma, O lord of the serpent kings, [you have become] the cause for the destruction of rebirth."
"You have heard the entire Mahopaniṣad from my own mouth. Now let this Saṃvarta, who has mastered the Vedas,
proclaim in its entirety that supreme knowledge among all knowledges which rests directly upon the God."
It is the sattvic [state] born from the act of propitiating the God of gods,
which is constantly sought by those seeking liberation and is difficult to attain. —
Saṃvarta.
I shall relate to you in its entirety that great scripture which was spoken by the high-souled Kapila, known as Padma, as he spoke thus;
it consists of one and a half crores of verses and was heard from Keśava by Brahmā.
Brahmā gave five hundred thousand [verses] to Kapila;
Kapila, in turn, gave one hundred thousand to Padma;
and Padma gave them to me in a number of ten thousand verses.
Because this was taught by Padma, it is therefore called the *Pādmasaṃhitā*.
O Prajāpati, in this [text] is the primordial dharma that yields liberation as its sole fruit.
By means of that very same primordial dharma, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, [attained his status].
They propitiated Mahādeva, Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme.
And the Śruti declares: "The sacrifice is to be worshipped by means of the sacrifice.
Thus, those wise ones who worship, having established themselves in this primordial dharma.

They go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu, from which there is no return. While all human beings were thus acting as seekers of liberation, there occurred a great destruction of creation; the hellish earth became overgrown with grass.
All were devoted to the five-fold ritual time, and all were permeated by the Blessed One. No men worshipped or meditated upon anyone else except Nārāyaṇa,
O great sage, while the Dharma of the Kṛta Yuga was thus prevailing.
Brahmā himself, the creator of the world, approached Nārāyaṇa and praised Hṛṣīkeśa with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā. Having prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, he remained silent.
O Blessed One, why do the worlds not follow your eternal teaching? O Brahmin, has your authority been usurped by the Rākṣasas? (1.41)
"Or having attained his station, why do the gods not practice austerity?
Thus addressed by the God of Gods, the Lotus-born Brahmā replied.
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, while you are awake for my welfare, all is well with me at all times and in every respect.
Nevertheless, O Lord of Gods, I shall speak; [for those who are] faithful and have conquered their senses.
Abiding in this great secret, all human beings perform sacrifice;
they go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu, which is free from rebirth.
There is neither heaven nor hell, nor both birth and death.
Addressed as "Saṃvarta" by Brahmā, the god Hari himself, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
looked toward Rudra standing at his side and spoke.
"O Śaṅkara, you who are our deity, please compose six types of tantras that are mutually contradictory, exactly as they are. (1.47)
Furthermore, through many incarnations such as the Fish and others,
I shall re-establish upon the surface of the earth the scriptures composed by you—
scriptures that yield abundant and wonderful fruit with little effort and are easily accessible.
And in this sixfold treatise, demonstrate the cause of its stability.
(1.49) Viriñci shall be the authority for the composition of the Yoga-śāstra, and Kapila shall be the authority for the creation of the Sāṃkhya. (1.50)
Assuming the form of a Buddha, I compose the Buddha-scriptures,
which are expert in concealing knowledge, as well as the knower, the known, and the fruit.
Assuming the form of an Arhat, I then teach the scripture of the Arhats.
"Indeed, the scripture named Pāñcarātra was previously composed by me. Now, create three other scriptures— the Kāpāla, the Śuddhaśaiva, and the Pāśupata—
for the purpose of deluding the worlds."
"The treatises composed by me and expounded by you shall remain in the world until the dissolution of all beings, by my command.
"So be it," they all replied, bowing down to Hari.
Then Brahmā, having accomplished his purpose, departed for his own abode together with the gods,
while Saṃvarta was honored by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, Cāraṇas, and others.
O Sage, from that time forth, the Śaiva and other scriptures became equal to the Pañcarātra;
by the command of Hari, they spread throughout the world, circulating unrestrainedly through the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu.
The Śaiva and other traditions are also established here and there.

As for the other five, they themselves disparage even the *Pañcarātra*, which is not defective, simply because it was created by the Īśvaras; for that very reason, they seek to disparage it. (1.57–1.58)
When the heretics have been repelled, those fallen and evil-minded ones develop an inclination toward rationalist arguments through the illusory powers of Viṣṇu;
they become atheists and revilers, tormented by diseases.
They are born and they die, and they are even cooked in the hells;
others dwell in the heavens, their minds defiled by illusion.
And those who are excluded from [true] illusion cross the ocean of existence.

"Having churned all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, the exponents of Brahman declare that meditation on the nectar of Nārāyaṇa is the highest. Among all castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the best; and among those in the stages of life, the ascetic is the most excellent."
Just as the Gaṅgā is foremost among sacred fords and Acyuta is foremost among deities,
so too is the Pañcarātra praised above all scriptures.
He who worships Hari according to the rules prescribed in the Pañcarātra [attains the highest goal].
Having attained supreme isolation (kaivalya), he shall not wander again in this world;
that man obtains an imperishable fruit—of this there is no doubt.
His ancestors, who perform auspicious deeds, dwell in heaven.

They are honored even in the world of Brahmā; what need is there to mention the ocean of hell? Whatever oblation (havya) or ancestral offering (kavya) is given with Vaiṣṇava mantras becomes inexhaustible, and by that the ancestors and deities are satisfied.
The ancestors clap their hands and the grandfathers dance,
when in their lineage is born a high-minded Vaiṣṇava who has taken refuge in Vāsudeva according to the rules prescribed in the Pāñcarātra.
With all disturbances entirely dispelled by meditation on the nectar of Nārāyaṇa,
this scripture should be given to a disciple who is free from malice,
who seeks liberation, and to no one else whatsoever except by chance.
It should be given to one who is devoted to the three Vedas, and it should be studied like the Veda;
so said Kaṇva [regarding this scripture known as the Mahopaniṣad], O Great-minded One.
How does this designation "Pañcarātra" circulate in the world? Saṃvarta said:
Other five scriptures, even though they are great, are disregarded (or treated as nights). || 1.71 ||
In his presence, that designation prevails in the world.
Just as the host of moons and stars does not shine at all during the day, so too the other five do not shine in his presence. (1.72–1.73)
Just as nights come to an end when the sun is blazing,
so too do all other things perish in his presence.
This scripture is purifying, destructive of sin, and the destroyer of worldly existence.
For those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra and caught in the snares of karma,
the fourfold division of Tantra— consisting of the Ṛgveda and the others— is like a great ship that delivers one across the sea of existence.
Just as the Veda is divided into four parts by the designations of the Ṛgveda and the others,
so too the Pañcarātra is fourfold according to the distinctions of its doctrines.
And just as the single [Veda], beginning with the Ṛgveda, is divided into many branches, [so is the Pañcarātra].
Likewise, each established tenet (siddhānta) differs according to the difference between its proponents;

and scholars declare that the term "established tenet" (siddhānta) is etymologically significant (*anvartha*). Those wise ones who are the established authorities in treatises such as the Mīmāṃsā— 1.78 — [they are the ones whose views constitute the tenets].

"Because they have authority at the end of those [others], it is designated as the Siddhānta. (1.79) This is the definition of the divisions of the Siddhānta: "But that which has the Single Form as its primary focus is called the Mantra-Siddhānta."
That which has the four forms as its primary focus is designated as Āgama;
it is called Siddhānta by the wise, being renowned in the world as the second [system].
And that which has the nine forms as its primary focus is called Tantrasiddhānta.
Wherever the procedure for worship is directed toward a four-faced or three-faced deity, that shall be considered a different Tantra; this Tantra is thus fourfold.
The four [deities], Vāsudeva and the others, have likewise been described previously.
Nārāyaṇa, Hayagrīva, Viṣṇu, Nṛhari, and Sūkara—[these are the forms].
There is a fault in the mixing of Tantras;
one should not, however, cause mutual confusion among the Siddhāntas.
If, through confusion and by causing a mixture [of rites], the king and the kingdom perish.

(1.84) One who knows the divisions of the Tantras should perform every ritual action by means of that very path of established doctrine through which the acts of plowing and so forth were performed. (1.85)
That other tantra would be desired [as such], for all [tantras] bestow all fruits.
Among them, this system of mantra-siddhānta is designated as the "Lotus" (Pādmasaṃjña).
Siddhāntas are recorded as being manifold according to the distinction of each individual speaker.
The summary and the detailed exposition of the tantras have been made manifest in the Siddhānta by those perfected in mantra, out of a desire for the welfare of disciples;
indeed, Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of all the tantras. || 1.87–1.88 ||
For the sake of favoring his devotees, he himself caused it to be heard;
the listeners were the various manifestations of his form, the sages, and the Grandfather (Brahmā).
And the purpose of the scripture is liberation, which is difficult to attain through natural means.

The subject matter is the supreme propitiation of the Blessed One. The relationship is also accepted by the wise as being characterized by the means and the end to be achieved. This Tantra has its root in the Śruti and is authoritative, like the Kalpasūtras.
In every creation, by the command of the God of gods, she remains unbroken like a wish-fulfilling gem or the variegated Kalpa-tree in this world;
she bestows everything desired upon supplicants, even without their seeking it out.

The scripture known as the Pañcarātra, however, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life. For those addicted to other scriptures, their practice is merely a waste of time, or else it yields some other trivial result that is rejected by the wise.
"Those who, abandoning Vāsudeva, worship another deity, go to hell; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Truth, truth, and again truth—raising my arm, I declare it! (1.95)
There is nothing superior to the Vedic scriptures, nor is there any deity higher than Keśava.
Therefore, O sage, worship the Lord of Gods according to this very injunction.
"O best of Brahmins, how many divisions of the Tantras are there, and what are their names? I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is great. (1.97)
We have heard in the Purāṇa, O Kaṇva, that there were one hundred and eight Saṃvartas in the past;
hear now their names as they are told by me. (1.98)
The Pādma, the Padmodbhava, the Māyāvaibhava, the Nalakūbara,
the Trailokyamohana, the Viṣṇutilaka, and the one called Parama;
the Nāradīya, the Dhanadīya, the Vāsiṣṭha, and the one named Pauṣkara.
The Viśvasaṃhitā [contains] Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and the one called Satya; the Māhendrasaṃhitā [contains] the one called Ananta, the Mahīpraśna, the Śrīpraśna, Puruṣottama,
and the Tattvasāgara known as the Pañcapraśna.
The Vāgīśa, the Sātvata, the Draviṇa called Śrīkara, the Sāṃvarta, the Viṣṇusadbhāva, the Siddhānta preceded by Viṣṇu,
the Viṣṇutantra, the Kaumāra, and likewise the Ahirbudhnya-saṃhitā.
The *Īśvarasaṃhitā* contains the *Viṣṇuvaibhavika*, the *Saura*, and the *Saumya*.
The *Mūlasaṃhitā* consists of the *Anantākhyam*, the *Bhāgavatam*, and the *Jayākhyam*.
The *Śaunakīya* contains the *Puṣṭitantra*, and the *Dakṣasaṃhitā* contains the *Mārīcam*.
The Aupendra, Yogahṛdaya, Hārīta, Pārameśvara, Ātreya, Māndara, Viṣvaksena, that which is called Auśanasa,
Vaikhānasa, Vihangendra, Bhārgava, and Parapūruṣa.
The Yājñavalkya, the Gautamīya, the Paulastya, the one called Śākala; the Jñānārṇava, the Jāmadagnya, the Yāmya, the one named Nārāyaṇa;
the Pārāśarya, the Jābāla, the Kapila, and the one called Vāmana.
The Jayottara, the Bārhaspatya, the Jaiminīya, that called Sātvata,
the Kātyāyanīya, the Vālmīki, the Aupagāyana-saṃhitā,
the Hairaṇyagarbha, the Āgastya, the Kāṇva, and that called the Bodhāyana.
The Bhāradvāja, Nārasiṃha, Gārgya, and Uttarapūrva;
the Śātātapa, Āṅgirasa, Kāśyapa, and that called Paiṅgala;
the Trailokyavijaya, Yoga, Vāyavīya, and Vāruṇa.
The *Kṛṣṇa*, the *Āgneya*, and the *Mārkaṇḍeya-saṃhitā*;
the one called *Mahā-sanatkumāra*, the *Vyāsa*, and the *Viṣṇu-saṃhitā*;
the *Mārkaṇḍeya-pāriṣada*, and the *Brahma-nārada-saṃhitā*.
The dialogue between Śuka and Rudra called Umāmāheśvara;
and those called Dattātreya, Śarva, Vārāhamihira,
Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Vāmana, Kalki, and Rāghava.
The one known as Prācetasa—these are remembered as the one hundred and eight [tantras].
These names of the tantras have been declared by me, O Great-minded One. Indeed, many tantras are understood as distinct means for liberation.
Thus has the Tantra been fully declared as a scripture by the wise. The man who constantly recites the names of the Tantras is liberated from all sins and goes to the eternal Brahman.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Descent of the Scripture," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
[Now begins] the second chapter.
Saṃvarta said: "O Padma, lord of the serpent kings, you have heard what occurred in the past;
if you have favor toward me, I am to be instructed in that tantra."
Śrī Padma said: O brahmin-sage, I shall proclaim that Tantra which is renowned throughout the world,
endowed with the four quarters of knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct.
This secret, marvelous, and divine [teaching], which I heard from Kapila,
is concise yet of great significance, and it bestows grace for all spiritual accomplishments. Brahmā heard it from Keśava in its full extent of one and a half crores [of verses].
Therefore, this tantra has been extracted like nectar from the ocean.
First, the complete *vijñāna* (knowledge) is taught as the introduction to creation;
after that, *yoga*, then *kriyā*, and immediately following that, *caryā*.
The meaning of the word "consciousness" (vijñāna) is the consciousness that is the knowledge of the Blessed One; liberation is said to arise from that knowledge.
This is the primordial form of the Blessed One.
Devoid of beginning, middle, and end, without increase or decrease, and immutable;
eternal, incomparable light, eternally satisfied, and stainless;
possessing all forms yet formless, beyond darkness, and imperishable. (2.6–2.7)
By the power of that cause, from that eternal [source] there emerged [a form] with two hands and one face, resembling pure crystal,
possessing a radiance equal to thousands, hundreds of thousands, millions, and tens of millions of suns and moons.
Situated in the center of a circle of rays, marked with weapons such as the discus,
his chest adorned with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, resplendent with a forest garland,
and decorated with a crown, necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments.
He who wears yellow garments, who is gentle, the primordial and eternal form—
he is to be known as Vāsudeva, from whose mouth all that is to be created proceeds;
he is to be constantly meditated upon by yogins on the seat called the heart-lotus.
The wise behold that eternal, supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
From Vāsudeva was then born another named Vāsudeva,
having one face and four arms, characterized by weapons such as the discus.
Holding the discus for maintenance, the lotus for creation,
the Pāñcajanya conch for liberation, and likewise the mace for reabsorption;
with the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem upon his chest, he is adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
Dark as a peacock’s neck and clad in his natural yellow garment,
that Blessed Lord Vāsudeva— the bestower of creation, preservation, end, and liberation—
divided himself in two for some unknown purpose.
Of those two, one is Vāsudeva, resembling pure crystal;
the second is Nārāyaṇa, with a luster like a dark blue cloud.
From that Vāsudeva comes Saṅkarṣaṇa, and from him [comes] he known as Pradyumna.
From Pradyumna, Aniruddha arose; all these [four] possess four arms.
Vāsudeva is proclaimed as the commonality of qualities such as knowledge;
when there is a variation in the six qualities, the forms will be described in sequence.
O Brahmin, he who is called Saṅkarṣaṇa would be superior in knowledge;
Pradyumna would be superior in strength, and Aniruddha in sovereignty.
And from these four forms, twenty-four forms arise.
O Brahmin, they are born in succession, just as one lamp is lit from another lamp.
All of them have four arms and hold the lotus, conch, discus, and mace;
they arise from Vāsudeva, the primordial god, and likewise from Keśava.
O best of the twice-born, Nārāyaṇa and Mādhava were born from Saṅkarṣaṇa;
and from him [Saṅkarṣaṇa] were born Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana. These three were born, and from Pradyumna came Trivikrama.
Vāmana and Śrīdhara—these were born, O best of sages. From Aniruddha, O observer of noble vows, Dhṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and Dāmodara were born; thus, these twelve portions were produced.
From Vāsudeva, from Saṅkarṣaṇa,
from Pradyumna, and likewise from Aniruddha— each named after those [preceding ones]—
there arose, in succession from those four, the Supreme Persons (puruṣottama).
Adhokṣaja, Nṛsiṃha, and Acyuta are considered the fourth.
From those very four, these were born in due order:
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and he who is known by the name Kṛṣṇa.
From Vāsudeva, the primordial god, the eightfold form was born:
the first form is Brāhmī, and the second is Prājāpatyā Vaiṣṇavī;
the third is Divyā, the fourth is Ārṣī, the fifth is Mānuṣī, and the seventh is considered to be Āsurī.

O Brahmin, among those forms, the tenth was Paiśācī, the last; from the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha), the Fish and the others were born in due order. From Vāsudeva, the Fish, the Tortoise, and the Boar were born.
Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma the son of Jamadagni, and likewise Saṅkarṣaṇa were born; from Pradyumna was born the mighty Rāghava;
from Aniruddha arose Kṛṣṇa and Kalki—these are the ten forms.
From Saṅkarṣaṇa was born the true Puruṣa, originating from Pradyumna;
and from Aniruddha was born Acyuta, the enlightened one who deludes the three worlds.
Daśārha, Śauri, and the Lord of the waters, Vāsudeva, were born [from him]. (2.33–2.34)
From Saṅkarṣaṇa come Hayagrīva, Śaṅkhodara, Nṛkesarī,
the primordial Vaikuṇṭha-mūrti, Mukunda, and Vṛṣākapi;
and right there, from that same Saṅkarṣaṇa, comes Ādivarāha.

The powerful serpent Ananta was born with a thousand hoods. At the time of the manifestation of his form, these weapons such as the Sudarśana discus and ornaments such as the crown were born together with him.
Likewise, the goddesses, Śrī and the others, having assumed distinct forms,
were born from the divine mark Śrīvatsa itself, which possesses every excellence.
Garuḍa, the lord of birds and the best among the powerful, became his vehicle.
From the forms of Vāsudeva and the others, the form of the Vedas was born.
And from the feet of Aniruddha, Kumuda and all the other lords of beings appeared by the thousands, together with their attendants.
From Aniruddha, who possesses a wondrous form with a thousand heads, feet, hands, and eyes,
the world was born from his very own limbs in due order:
from his mouth came Indra and Agni, as well as the Vedic meters and the six Vedāṅgas.
From his head the sky was born, from his eyes the sun, and from his mind the moon;
from his ears the quarters of space, from his navel the ether, and from his feet the earth came into being.
From his out-breath (prāṇa) arose the wind, from his in-breath (apāna) death, and from his body hair the clouds.
The divisions of time, such as the *truṭi* and so forth, as well as time itself, arose from his intellect;
likewise, trees and medicinal herbs issued forth from the pores of his skin.
From him were born many sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
The fourfold order of castes arose, respectively, from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet. Having thus created the entire world, Hari, the Lord who bears the universal form,
remains seated upon the infinite throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, in the city called Śvetadvīpa, fashioned of gold,
he is served by various yogins,
as well as by the gatekeepers beginning with Caṇḍa and the attendants beginning with Kumuda.
Attended with joy by Viṣvaksena and the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa),
he has the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, possesses eternal splendor, is unconquerable, perpetual, and immutable.
As Aniruddha, he protects the world through his own portions, such as Indra and the other gods.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Differentiation of the Manifestations of the Divine Forms," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the third chapter.
O best of the twice-born, the creation of Brahmā from the lotus shall now be described.
Nārāyaṇa created the waters, and there indeed was the great ocean.
Durgā, born from a portion of Aniruddha, possessing a form of illusion and highly enchanting,
produced a banyan tree within that great tree which was a form of illusion.
Within that great tree, the glorious and ancient Padmanābha was born from a portion of Aniruddha.
Having withdrawn the worlds, the Supreme Person went to his bed of leaves; there,
upon the navel-lotus of that Man lying on a serpent-couch, was the creation of the Four-faced One.
From his navel arose a golden egg, the womb of a lotus.
That egg, consisting of the five elements, was pure and beyond the reach of thought;
in the center of that expanding egg was a lotus of white radiance.
Extending to a thousand petals and adorned with filaments within,
it was joined in the center by a pericarp— an extraordinary cause of creation.
Within that, Padmanābha created the four-faced Creator.
The lotus posture is the seat of Brahmā because the lotus appeared first;
for other gods as well, the lotus is desired as their seat.
The Lotus-born himself created Sanandana and the others for the purpose of creation;
yet at that time, those sons of Svāyambhuva did not set their minds upon creating. (3.8)
They all became yogis, free from passion and devoid of envy. When those great-souled ones were thus indifferent toward the creation of the world, Rudra was produced from the wrath of Brahmā.

A great wrath arose in Brahmā, capable of consuming the three worlds. Then, from his forehead, which was inflamed with anger and furrowed by a frown, Rudra emerged, possessing a radiance like the fire at the end of an eon.
Possessing a great body with the form of half-man and half-woman, the majestic one divided his own body and fashioned both man and woman. From that couple were born millions of Rudras.
All are four-armed, fierce, three-eyed, and hold tridents in their hands.
Among them, O best of Brahmins, the eleven Rudras are remembered as the foremost;
by Marīci and the others, the creation of the world was accomplished.
Even after observing that the creation by Rudra was futile, Brahmā, the creator of the world,
again mentally fashioned six other [sages], beginning with Marīci.
By them, this entire triple-world, including all things moving and stationary, was created.
Having thus created this world, the four-faced one, whose source is the lotus, Brahmā entered into supreme meditation, contemplating the cause of his own being. (3.16)
As he meditated, there appeared before him a mass of splendor,
possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns and resembling a flash of lightning;
in its midst was the Best of Men, clad in pure yellow garments.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, with four arms;
marked with the Śrīvatsa, having a serene countenance, and resplendent with the Kaustubha gem;
adorned with shimmering ornaments such as a crown and necklaces.
Seeing that best of men, the lotus-born one reflected:
"This indeed is the supreme deity, the lord of the entire world.
No other person standing superior to him is to be seen. (3.20)
He began to ask him various questions regarding his doubts:
"O Supreme Person, who are you, a man of such most wonderful appearance? Are you Brahmā?"
"Reveal yourself to me, who am desirous of knowing you. Thus [spoke Arjuna].
The Blessed Lord [replied]: "I am the creator of all worlds, the ancient, supreme Puruṣa."
"Know me to be without beginning, middle, or end, immovable and eternal;
know me to be the cause of the entire world, and let there be no doubt in you regarding this. I stand here as the dispeller of your doubt."
O Brahmā, I am blessed, I am favored, my desires are fulfilled, and I am eternal.
There is nothing to be known that you do not know, and there is no duty to be performed that remains undone. (3.25)
"There is nothing unattained that remains to be attained in the three worlds.
For what reason, then, do you urge people to create the world? Tell me. (3.26) —The Blessed Lord said:
"I sport solely through the creation, destruction, and protection of all the worlds for no reason whatsoever.
Thus [ends] the Jñānapāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
The third chapter, titled "The Manner of Creation by Brahmā and Others";
the fourth chapter: Brahmā.

In what form do you ordain [the world], in what form do you protect it, and in what form do you strive to withdraw it? My desire to hear this is growing. (4.1) Among the infinite powers for the purpose of creation, four are primary.
O Four-faced One, infinite powers were created by the Blessed Lord through his mind alone;
among them, four principal forms, beginning with Viṣṇu, have been specified. (4.2)
Among these, three have the sphere of saṃsāra as their domain, while the fourth bestows liberation.
The three consisting of rajas, sattva, and tamas have the sphere of saṃsāra as their domain; but the fourth, called Ānanda, bestows both enjoyment and liberation. (4.3)
The qualities useful for creation and so forth:
"By means of the quality of rajas, I create the world with its moving and non-moving beings;
I protect it by means of sattva, and I dissolve it by means of tamas. (4.4)
Abiding in my own self which is bliss, I myself, called Vāsudeva,
liberate from saṃsāra those who worship me alone.
I create, protect, and destroy this world through these three forms beginning with Brahmā.

For those free from desire, liberation from bondage occurs through Vāsudeva in his form as the Supreme Self, across the ocean of existence. I release from their bonds those who worship me while being free from desire.
Among the four [forms] beginning with Viṣṇu, the Vāsudeva form is said to be the primary bestower of liberation; among these four, he is declared to be the Supreme Person.
Because he effects liberation, he is called Vāsudeva.
But others, such as Brahmā and the rest, possess views that are harmful to [liberation from] saṃsāra. (The nature of those in saṃsāra and their measure.
Brahmā.
Who is the transmigrating person? What are his higher and lower states? Who is the liberated one, for whom the two states—the higher and the lower—no longer exist? (4.9) —The Blessed Lord.
He who experiences pleasure and pain caused by merit and demerit is a transmigrating being; that which is beyond those measures is said to be the state of becoming Brahman.
For one who possesses those supreme measures, there would be the state of a stationary thing, equivalent to non-existence.
The wise say that one who has the nature of liberation, who has transcended the latent impressions of saṃsāra, who is released from the bonds of karma,
who is self-satisfied, and who is indifferent, is liberated.
For that which is eternally of a single form, no measure whatsoever exists.
Who among them enter into saṃsāra, and who go to nirvṛti?
"O Blessed One, there is indeed curiosity; please speak the truth exactly as it is regarding the bondage to and liberation from saṃsāra.
Thus [asked] the illustrious Lord.
One who performs Vedic action with a desire for its fruit is bound;
one who performs action without desire is not bound.
Knowledge that is merely sensory, dependent upon the eyes and other faculties, is worldly.
He is bound by the supreme deity; he whose knowledge [is such] is liberated.
O Puruṣottama, what difference is there between you and the liberated soul, Brahmā?
"Tell me this, O Blessed One, if it is not too secret, O Lord:
the distinction between the liberated self and the Supreme Person. Thus [asked] the Blessed Lord.
"These beings are indeed myself; there is no difference whatsoever therein.
Just as I abide, so too do the liberated embodied ones. — Brahmā, 4.17.

What are those causes that bind the person? They are the causes consisting of karma. They are the ones who cause persons, bound by the fetters of karma, to wander about. (4.18) These are the causes of bondage.
The Blessed One has previously described action as being threefold, proceeding indeed through the three qualities— sattva and the others— both individually and collectively. (4.19)
"By that [ignorance], O best of gods, men of former conduct enter into saṃsāra— this is exactly what you are asking me. Thus spoke Brahmā.
How does the union with these qualities arise for a person?
And how is a person, being liberated, released from the bonds of karma? (4.21) Through the influence of sense objects, there occurs both union with and separation from the three qualities.
O Blessed One,
those qualities of a person which follow the attributes of the body come into being and cease to be through the power of their objects. (4.22)
A question regarding the nature of the object:
"O Maheśvara, who is this object said to be for men? Brahmā [replied].
Through connection with which these qualities arise, and through which they cease to exist—
this is the definition of the objects of experience,
as taught by the Blessed Lord.
O Brahmin, primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇā), is known as the object of the embodied soul.
Through union with it, a living being is bound; through separation from it, he is liberated.
The Puruṣa eternally knows Prakṛti, whose essence consists of the three qualities.
And that [tamas], once produced, constantly gives rise to various forms of sleep and lethargy.
Overpowered by this sleep, he himself forgets his true nature;
this is held to be the bondage of men. What more do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Liberation from Saṃsāra for Those Seeking Release," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrī Pādmasaṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
[Now begins] the fifth chapter.
By what cause does the union of Brahmā with Prakṛti arise?
Tell me this, O Blessed One; it is a secret difficult for me to obtain. (5.1)
O Brahmin, the cause of the primordial union of Puruṣa and Prakṛti is the Illusion (Māyā) of the Blessed Lord, which is beginningless and indestructible.
This very [nature] binds the person through its form of the qualities (guṇas).
Through the grace of the Blessed One, there is separation from nature;
without my grace, there is no cessation for anyone.
"As long as I do not become pleased, Māyā remains difficult to overcome.
Brahmā spoke these words as the basis for the favor of the Blessed One, whose desires were already fulfilled.
What is the basis for the grace of the God whose desires are fulfilled?
I do not know the cause of that; tell me its basis. (5.4) Śrī Bhagavān:
"Those who follow the boundaries established by me for the social classes and the stages of life—
toward them my grace is great.
Therefore, for men caught in the cycle of worldly existence, there is never [liberation] without my grace."
"Understand, O Lotus-seated One, that there is nothing else that brings about the supreme good.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Supreme Person, I know [this]."
"I consider you alone, O lotus-eyed one, to be the creator of the worlds, from whom the worlds arise and into whom they go at their dissolution.
O Blessed One, I wish to know this in its entirety; please explain it to me."
The Description of Creation, etc.:
Both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are my two forms, which are difficult to transcend. Having entered into this pair, I agitate them by my will. (5.9)
Nature (prakṛti), O Brahmin, consists of the three qualities (guṇas); it is beginningless and indestructible.
Presided over by the Puruṣa, it brings forth both the immobile and the mobile.
Furthermore, from that [nature], whose essence is the equilibrium of the qualities, when presided over by the Puruṣa...
The Great Principle (mahattattva) was born, characterized by the threefold qualities (guṇas).
From that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arose; its three modes are traditionally taught as the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Bhūtādi. Thus it is threefold.

From the *vaikārika* ego, which is characterized by *sattva*, the five organs of perception were born; furthermore, from the *taijasa* ego, which is characterized by *rajas*, the five organs of action were produced; and then, from the *bhūtādi* ego, which is characterized by *tamas*, [the elements arose].
The subtle element of sound came into being, and that produced space.
Likewise, from space came the subtle element of touch, and from that wind was born.
From wind came the subtle element of form, and from that fire was born. (5.14–5.15)
From fire, which possesses only the quality of taste, water was produced; likewise, from water, the subtle element of smell arose, and from that mere smell, earth was born.
Space has sound as its sole quality, while wind possesses the qualities of sound and touch.
Likewise, sound, touch, and form are declared to be the qualities of fire.
Sound, touch, taste, and form are recorded as the fourfold qualities of water;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the five qualities of earth.

Having been created with diverse powers and existing separately, they were unable to produce progeny without a union; therefore, they themselves united. Impelled by Pradhāna and Puruṣa, those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas [proceeded].

O lotus-born one, from the navel of Padmanābha—who is a portion of myself—this egg was produced; from that, you became the source of the universe. Thus, at the beginning of creation, the entire world arose from primordial nature (prakṛti).
O Lotus-seated One, at the end of the eon, he dissolves back into primordial nature itself.
O Lord, I believe the universe was created by you and is sustained by you;
you alone, in the form of Time, withdrew it at the end of the kalpa.
Now, O Acyuta, tell me that knowledge which grants the perfection of Brahman,
by knowing which there is no further birth, death, or bondage to worldly existence. (5.23) [The Twofold Nature of the Knowledge of Brahman]
The Blessed One said: "Knowledge is declared to be of two kinds: that which is called sattva and that which consists of action (kriyā).
The accomplishment of that which is called sattva through that which is called action is infallible. (5.24)
O Lord, tell me first what kind of knowledge consisting of action that Brahmā is,
by practicing which I shall attain that which is called sattva and bestow the perfection of Brahman.
The characteristic of knowledge consists of the activity of the being;
the Blessed Lord has declared that action is twofold: namely, restraint (yama) and observance (niyama).
From those two, one certainly attains that which is called *sattva*—namely, knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
(5.26) In Brahman, that which is called *sattva* is non-different from knowledge; through knowledge, the object of knowledge is attained.
From knowledge comes liberation in the Supreme Self, the supreme bliss, O Lotus-born One. (5.27)
O Lord of the gods, you previously explained to me the correct means for attaining Brahman;
now, tell me the characteristics of Brahman.
The characteristic of Brahman is that the Blessed Lord is Brahman, whose characteristic is bliss, whose form is sound, and who is changeless.
Untouched by afflictions and the like, inactive, free from conceptual construction,
beyond dualities, uninterrupted, self-cognizable, stainless,
extremely subtle, independent, spontaneous, self-luminous, and beginningless. (5.29–5.30)
Infinite, inexhaustible, peaceful, beyond illustration, without increase,
eternal, one, ever-blissful, of the nature of consciousness, all-pervading, supreme,
liberated from coming and going, the all-powerful Lord called Vāsudeva.
The source of all beings, the Lord, the Supreme Person;
eternally pure by nature, waveless, undisturbed, boundless, transcending the qualities (guṇas), yet possessing qualities and granting all desires. || 5.32–5.33 ||
It is not to be cultivated by those of inferior character, yet it is unexpectedly to be studied and meditated upon by those seeking liberation; it is a marvel beyond the reach of speech and mind.
It is the embodiment of the sixfold qualities, possessing all powers, and is both self-supported and the support of all that rests within it.
The Lord of beings, the creator of beings, the Being who stands beyond darkness;
distinct from primordial matter (pradhāna) and nature (prakṛti), he is the object of experience, the unimpeded enjoyer,
transcending the means of knowledge and cognition, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere.
With hands and feet on all sides, standing pervading everything,
situated both outside and inside, all-pervasive, and transcending all systems;
the unborn, the syllable Om, the unmanifest, the auspicious one whose nature is the root mantra.
It is an illusory form, yet distinct from illusion; eternally satisfied, subtler than the subtlest;
greater than the greatest, yet vast and gross; incomparable, soft, and radiant; formless, yet embodied; powerful, a mass of consciousness, and free from affliction.
"Beholding thus the Supreme Brahman with the supreme eye of knowledge,
the mortal ever engaged in yoga attains the highest state.
(5.40) Thus ends the Jñānapāda in the Śrī Pādma-saṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
The fifth chapter, named "The Characteristics of Brahman";
the sixth chapter, "Brahmā."
The form of Brahman is said to have hands, feet, and so forth everywhere;
even though it is formless, explain all of that to me exactly as it is.
6.1 This is the definition of the Blessed One’s state of having hands, feet, and so forth everywhere.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded by the Supreme Self;
therefore, that state of being the hand of all is said to be His characteristic. 6.2
The Lord is traditionally held to protect [the world] simultaneously, eternally, and from all sides, joined with the Supreme Being through specific places and times;
having gone upwards, downwards, and across, he illuminates the universe.
Just as the sun is so described, he is called "all-seeing" (viśvataścakṣus) because the entire multitude of objects stands before him from every side;
therefore, O Lotus-seated One, that Brahman possesses faces on all sides (viśvatomukha).
Just as all the organs of perception depend upon the head as the supreme part,
so too the Lord, being the locus of all knowledge, should be known as the one who has all things as his head.
He is both far and near, as well as concealed and otherwise.

He hears the collection of sounds; therefore, he is "all-hearing" (sarvataḥ-śravas). Just as fire, though distinct from a mass of iron, appears as if non-distinct, so too [the Self], existing outside the manifest, remains enveloping the manifest.
Just as a reflection situated within a stainless mirror is seen therein,
so too would there be the unmanifest form of the All-pervading Lord.
O Four-faced One, consciousness dependent upon the senses [perceives] forms and other objects.
For this reason, the Blessed One is called "all-knowing" by the wise.
Because of his union with the Supreme Self through supreme greatness,
the pervasive nature of Viṣṇu, the Lord, is declared by the learned.
The Lord’s beginninglessness follows from His being unborn, and likewise His endlessness;
because He is beyond the perception of all, He is called "non-existent" by men.
O Brahmin, He is not an object of cognition, just as fragrance in a flower and such things [is not perceived by the blind].
Though unbound by the three qualities, he remains among them as if bound. Just as clear water rests upon lotus leaves,
so does the One remain, pervading both the interior and exterior within the great ocean.
Just as a submerged jar exists both within and without the water,
so too is the unity of the two selves— the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) and the Supreme— enjoined by the Śruti.
The multiplicity of this Knower of the Field is perceived due to the diversity of bodies.
Just as there is only a single reflection appearing in various mirrors,
so too is it with this field (kṣetra), which is a collection of the five elements beginning with the gross (bhūta).
The wise know that living being (jīva) who is situated therein as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), designated as "the Supreme" (para).
The wise perceive with the eye of knowledge Viṣṇu, who is incomprehensible to the intellect, indistinct, situated beyond the manifest, and higher than the highest;
yet they do not know that imperishable one, the object of knowledge, due to ignorance.
The movement of another's body and so forth does not cause delusion [regarding the Self],
just as the notion that "the space within a jar is moving" arises when the jar is being carried, yet in reality there is no difference at all between the Supreme and the individual soul. (6.19–6.20)
Just as no distinction in time can be perceived among the piercing of a thousand lotus petals one after another due to their extreme subtlety,
even so this Supreme Self is proclaimed to be atomic by name.
The ignorant perceive Him as dwelling far away, though He is always situated within the lotus of the heart.
Just as the one Lord wind remains pervading the entire sky,
so too does the Unborn One Himself abide, permeating the entire universe of moving and non-moving beings.
Just as the sun, having risen, is capable of emitting and withdrawing its rays,
so too is Hari the Lord capable of creating and destroying the entire universe.
Being a mass of consciousness, he illuminates both his own domain and that which is other.
Just as a lamp illuminates both itself and objects such as cloth,
so too Hari, though devoid of colors such as white and the like,
illuminates [all things] because he is endowed with the six qualities— knowledge and the rest— which are not found elsewhere.
The Blessed One has been described by the wise as the Supreme Self, pervading the universe;
like clarified butter in curd, oil in sesame seeds, and sweetness in molasses and the like,
He is essentially non-different from the substance, yet remains there in an incorporeal form.
Because of its capacity for being perceived, it is seen; yet that which is seen is not truly seen.
Though unborn, formless, the inner self of all, and the Supreme Person, He has entered the path of perception through the power of the contemplation of the wise.
Among all things, both moving and unmoving, who are they that know that Brahman which abides pervading everything, which is formless, non-differentiated, and self-realized? (6.30)
"O Blessed One, tell me truly by means of knowledge how those who have been initiated according to the rules of the Pañcarātra cross over Viṣṇu’s Māyā.
Śrī Bhagavān:
Those who, having received initiation in the maṇḍala according to the path taught in the Pañcarātra,
perform the worship of Viṣṇu with the sixteen-syllable vidyā,
and as supreme teachers propitiate Him according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures— 6.31.
In the lotus of their hearts, the Supreme Person manifests directly;
they cross over Viṣṇu’s Māyā, while other people do not.
"Brahmā has directly realized the reality; what is its characteristic and of what nature is it?
O Blessed One, if you have favor toward me, let all of this be told."
The Blessed Lord, whose true nature has been meditated upon, exists as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, consisting of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
Devoid of coming and going, subtler even than the subtle;
most vast, honored as the supreme reality whose form is ultimate bliss;
free from increase and decrease, all-pervading, and consisting of pure consciousness.
The reality whose nature is Being (sadrūpa) is to be known through the Praṇava, beyond ratiocination, and established by valid means of knowledge;
thus do yogis always contemplate this reality within their hearts.
Its threefold nature consists of its gross and other forms.
Its form is said to be threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme.
Regarding the characteristics of the gross and the others:
the gross is to be known as "with parts" (sakala), while the subtle is "with parts and yet without parts" (sakalaniṣkala). (6.37)
But the supreme form of the Supreme Self, O Lotus-born One, is indeed partless (niṣkala);
the form consisting of a thousand heads and so forth is the qualified (sakala) form.
The form that is both qualified and partless shines like a mass of radiance.
Its form consists of truth, consciousness, and bliss, and it is designated as partless (niṣkala).
Regarding the description of nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikṛti):
both nature and transformation are the very essence of the Supreme Self.

The aggregate of qualities such as truth and the rest is *prakṛti* (primordial nature), while the *puruṣa* (spirit) known as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the transformation (*vikṛti*). Therefore, this world, consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*),
arises from *prakṛti* when it is presided over by the Supreme Self.
Presided over by him, she brings forth the entire world consisting of conscious beings;
and by his command alone, she also withdraws all of that.
That Supreme Self, Nārāyaṇa,
is the one and only supreme deity, endowed with manifold powers;
he performs both creation and dissolution, and he is remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
Just as the inhabitants of a city enter through various gates from different directions, and just as men enter into the Supreme Person,
so too do the practitioners always enter within by means of the supreme knowledge.

For one whose impurities have been burnt away by meditating on the nature of Brahman— distinguished by qualities such as a golden luster— in the *brahmarandhra* and other locations, there is the attainment of Brahman;
[the text describes] the Supreme Person, golden-hued, situated in the midst of the circle of light.
Yogins meditate upon Him who is seated upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
and possessing four arms— within these locations:
the aperture of Brahmā, the middle of the eyebrows, the navel-cakra, and the hollow of the throat.
Contemplating [the light] at the tip of the tongue and in the middle of the palate, those who have restrained their senses,
having burnt away the karma performed in previous births, go to the eternal.
(6.47) This is the description of the attainment of Brahman even for others who perform actions free from desire.
Devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, dedicated to the five daily observances,
perfected in the eightfold yoga, and meditating upon the twelve-syllable mantra—
mortals who take refuge in Vāsudeva are solely intent on Vāsudeva.
And those whose sins are entirely purified go to the eternal Brahman.

(6.49) The determination of the non-difference containing difference between the liberated self and the Supreme Self, illustrated by an example: Just as the streams of rain, falling separately from the cloud in the sky, [merge into one].

Just as [rivers] attain oneness upon the earth, so too do yogis [attain oneness] in Brahman. (6.50) Just as the water of rivers, though diverse in its various forms and characteristics, does not differ from the water once it has entered the ocean, (6.51) so it is with the yogis in Brahman.

In the very same way, O Four-faced One, liberated souls abide in the supreme Brahman through a state of oneness, so that they may attain its same world (sālokya). This secret has been declared in the Niṣads and the Upaniṣads.
"Yoga has been revealed to you by me, O Lotus-born One.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Means for Attaining Brahman," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrī Pādmasaṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
The Seventh Chapter:
The Question Concerning the Cause for the Arising of Knowledge, the Means to Attaining Brahman; [The Teacher] Brahmā.

"If you have favor toward me, let the cause for the arising of that knowledge which is the means to attain Brahman be told in its entirety. (7.1) This is the description of the arising of the knowledge of Brahman in one whose mind has been purified by desireless actions (*niṣkāma-karman*).
The Blessed One [says]: "For him whose consciousness has become stainless through the acts of propitiating the Blessed One, there arises a state free from external coloring. (7.2)
The dissolution of beginningless ignorance occurs through the limbs of yoga, beginning with restraint (yama):
purity, sacrifice, austerity, the practice of self-study, celibacy, moderation in diet, silence, and control of the senses. (7.3)
Non-violence, fasting, bathing, and resorting to sacred fords;
detachment from wife and children, avoidance of unwholesome food, lack of passion, service to the elderly, forbearance, friendliness, and compassion. (7.4–7.5)
Aversion toward the wives and property of others, devotion to the scriptures, and detachment from objects of enjoyment— by these means of purifying the mind,
knowledge becomes turned inward; through that, they know that supreme state.
Having attained which, men— freed from birth and death and devoted to action— do not return,
[this is] the description of the cause of the soul's transmigratory existence at the arising of knowledge and realization.
O Four-faced One, I shall now explain the cause of saṃsāra:
having performed actions consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, beings fall under the power of māyā and,
taking up a body as a locus for experience, they are born through the continuous flow of those various karmas.
Regarding liberation and worldly existence, the predominance of knowledge and the predominance of action, respectively, are the causes;
O Four-faced One, men of restrained senses experience either suffering or happiness, and that cycle of rebirth has karma alone as its cause.
Liberation from that cycle of existence occurs for the self when knowledge predominates;
however, when action predominates, that very cycle arises again without restraint.
That [cycle], which is the cause of saṃsāra, is destroyed by knowledge of action.
When karma, the cause of saṃsāra, is exhausted, liberation follows immediately.
It is certain that saṃsāra is established as having karma as its cause;
and a person, rendered helpless by ignorance, performs karma of his own accord. (7.12–13)

The three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are indeed the threefold group that constitutes knowledge; they function both collectively and individually. It is by means of these alone that one performs action, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (7.14)
Through these three, the various types of sleep arise, caused by karma.
This very thing is called ignorance (*avidyā*) and illusion (*māyā*) by the best of the learned.
Sleep consisting of pleasure arises from *sattva*; that which is crowded with activity arises from *rajas*.
From *tamas* arises that which is called delusion (*mohinī*); by these [qualities], the person, driven out and lacking self-control, performs actions that cause rebirth within *saṃsāra*.
This is an elaboration of the meaning already stated.

The mind, endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and the rest, when applied to the five elements and divided fivefold, produces manifold activities. When the mind, possessed of the quality of *sattva*, becomes established in the earth element, [it performs its functions]. (7.17–18)

At that time, a man performs such actions as digging the earth; likewise, when the moon is in the constellation Ārdrā, he should engage in activities for the protection of men. When the moon is in the constellation Rohiṇī, there is injury to living beings and the intent to hunt.
When the heart is situated in *tamas*, there is cutting and likewise piercing,
as well as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), subjugation, the seizing of others' property, and so forth.
When it is situated in *sattva*, O Four-faced One, there is water-sports and drinking water in the waters.
Helpless, a man performs such acts as crossing rivers;
he plunges into and sinks within a wooden trough of water due to passion (rajas), and likewise builds embankments across the ocean and so forth, or crosses by means of his own arms. 7.22

When the mind is established in *tamas*, a person always effects release on the shore of a body of water, or falling into a well or a chasm. When the mind is established in *sattva* within its own radiance (*tejas*), there is the vision of the sun, the moon, and other such luminaries.
When the *rajas* quality has arisen, there is acuity, a sensation of heat, and the sight of jewels, gold, and the like;
one stands up with a sword in hand, kills deer, and strikes others violently with fists and clubs. (7.25)
When the mind is situated in *tamas*, there is a longing for red flowers and the like;
when it is situated in the quality of *sattva* within the breath, there is swift movement and dancing;
and when it is situated in *rajas*, it performs the actions of singing and prattling.
When the mind is situated in the quality of darkness (tamas), there appear visions such as riding elephants or horses, as well as ascending upwards;
when the mind is situated in the quality of passion (rajas), there is the climbing of palaces and the like.
When the mind is situated in the quality of goodness (sattva) within the space of the heart, it perceives that which is without appearance and without support.

O Queen, that movement which is seen while awake continues to manifest even during sleep when the darkness of the mind persists; yet one who has been bitten by a snake does not perceive pleasure or pain in the body. (7.29–7.30)
Thus, under the sway of Māyā and joined with the three guṇas, a person performs manifold actions; through those very actions, the person goes to their abode.
Having entered into saṃsāra, he also undergoes birth and destruction.
When the eternal Supreme Self is well-disposed with favor, then one who is liberated from illusion, disciplined in yoga, and has conquered the senses,
attains through higher knowledge the Supreme Brahman, which is characterized by bliss.
An explanation of the cause for the soul's conjunction with or separation from the three qualities:
"O Brahmā, how does such conjunction with or separation from these qualities occur?"
O Lotus-seated One, these three qualities of the Supreme Person exist or do not exist through the conjunction and disjunction of Māyā.
Māyā, which never departs and is eternal, dwells perpetually within me.
All beings, having fallen under the sway of māyā, wander about deluded by ignorance—
even Brahmā and the others, let alone the gods and such, O Lotus-Seated One.
Through the grace of the Blessed One, the cessation of *māyā* occurs;
through my grace, that which is dependent on me comes to an end.
By means of *māyā*, beings are bound; those who conquer it are liberated. (7.37)
An Investigation into the Cause of the Blessed One’s Grace:
"O Blessed One, by what cause was your grace toward the perfect Brahmā produced?"
"I do not know the cause for that; tell me that as it truly is.
The Blessed One replied: "Faith, devotion, and meditative absorption have been perfectly dedicated to me."
The cause [of liberation] occurs through the method seen in the scriptures, and not otherwise.
(7.39) For all those who are to be liberated, a triad of causes has been declared; without these, other people wander in saṃsāra, under the sway of māyā. (7.40)

Having understood that my forms as incarnations were created from my own mouth for the purpose of quelling unrighteousness and for the increase of dharma and desire, there is a fixed determination regarding the specific objects of faith, devotion, and meditative concentration. (7.41)
Many things are worthy of being understood; among them, one should practice three.
That form of the Supreme Self which is liberated from all aspects is difficult to discern and is beyond the scope of these qualities, such as faith and the rest.
"O Brahman, the cause of liberation has been indicated; what more do you desire?
[Thus spoke] Brahmā, who established that the conscious and the unconscious have a single, non-different cause.
It is observed that both the insentient and the sentient are created as form.
Is that creation of a single origin, or is there a difference in the origins of these two? (7.44) — Śrī Bhagavān.
The form of that Supreme Self is undivided, one, and unmanifest;
it exists both undivided and divided, like clarified butter within curd.
At times, by the will of the Puruṣa, the unmanifest becomes manifest.
From that unmanifest (avyakta), the Great One (mahat) was born; from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) arose.
From the ego-sense, the mind (manas) was born, and from that, the five subtle elements (tanmātra-pañcaka). O Lotus-born One, the eleven organs (indriya) were likewise produced. 7.46–7.47
Immediately following that, the five great elements beginning with earth [are described];
thus has the creation from both the insentient and the sentient been illustrated.
Through the influence of the three qualities (guṇas), there arises the state of being superior, inferior, or intermediate.
By these three qualities alone, beings are born as superior, inferior, or middling according to the influence of their causes; I shall describe them to you in due order. 7.49 Their essential nature:
Among those dispositions, O Four-faced One, that which consists predominantly of *sattva* is the most excellent;
that which consists predominantly of *rajas* is middling; and that which abounds in *tamas* is the lowest.
(7.50) [The worship of dispositions characterized by supreme *sattva* is the means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.]
In this regard, worship performed with dispositions characterized by a predominance of *sattva* is pleasing to me;
their fruit shall be either worldly enjoyment or liberation, according to their desire.
However, for those possessing dispositions of *rajas* and *tamas*, the fruit is perishable.
Those twice-born who perform sacrifices with a predominance of *rajas* dwell in heaven,

but their stay is characterized by a return [to this world]. And for those who perform sacrifices with a predominance of *tamas*, there is the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*) until that merit is exhausted.
Their residence is upon the earth, and at the end [of their merit], they undergo transmigration within the world of mortals.
Those dominated by tamas worship yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, and the like;
having dwelt in a terrible hell, they shall take birth among mobile creatures and other such beings.

Only those who sacrifice to the Blessed One attain the fruit characterized by non-return; those devoted to the dharma of sacrifice return again and again, but those established in my worship do not return even to this day. (7.55)

The worlds situated below, extending up to the abode of Brahmā, arise; those who dwell in my world, however, transmigrate no further anywhere. Therefore, O Brahmin, remaining always established in the state of pure being, devote yourself to me.
The threefold nature of food:

it is taught that the food of those endowed with the qualities of *sattva* and the others is of three kinds. Those foods that are unctuous, sweet, and pleasing to the heart abide in the first quality (*sattva*).

Those who abide in the middle quality find food consisting mostly of bitter, sour, and salty flavors to be dear to them. Those who abide in the lowest quality find food that is flavorless, stale, foul-smelling, long-kept, and leftover to be a source of pleasure.
From *sattva* comes sleep consisting of happiness; from *rajas*, sleep crowded with activity.
For one in whom *tamas* is the predominant quality, there is sleep day and night. (7.60) The threefold destination of those established in *sattva* and the other qualities.
For one established in *sattva*, there is upward movement; for one in whom *rajas* predominates, there is stability in the middle;
and for those characterized by *tamas*, there is downward movement—thus is the threefold destiny of the three types of beings.
Virtues such as knowledge and the like belong to one who is devoted to *sattva*.
In that regard, *sattva* is luminous and unobscured due to its purity.
Truth, knowledge, austerity, silence, fortitude, purity, tranquility, and forbearance—these and other such qualities residing in *sattva* bring about auspiciousness. (7.62)
Egoism and the like are the qualities of one established in rajas;
egoism is said to be threefold: pride, anger, and hypocrisy.
These are the qualities of the rājasa type, while those of the tāmasa type are now described.

"O Four-faced One, backbiting and the like are the qualities of one established in *tamas*; backbiting, censuring others, sleep, laziness, cruelty—these and other such qualities are said to be governed by *tamas*. (7.64)
When rajas and tamas have dissolved through the increase of sattva, there is the attainment of knowledge and so forth, as the other two qualities have subsided;
when sattva has increased, superior and abundant discernment arises. (7.65)
By that, one attains the supreme state, which is difficult to reach by nature;
having attained which, they do not return to this world of suffering.
Abiding in purity while casting off the body, they go to the eternal worlds.
O Four-faced One, for a person established in *rajas* who has dissolved [into the source], there is birth in a great family;
but for a person established in *tamas* at the time of dissolution,
there shall be repeated births in lowly and deluded wombs.

At the end, as one abandons the body, whatever objects the self remembers regarding its connection to the body, the person attains those very states by the power of such mental cultivation (bhāvanā). Thus have the various destinies of men been described.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Specific Gatis," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Mahopaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
[Now begins] the eighth chapter.
The inquiry into the nature of consciousness, means, and ascetic practice: Brahmā has proclaimed both the means of consciousness and ascetic practice.
"O Blessed One, what is that austerity like? Or rather, let it be told to me.
(8.1) [The Blessed One explains] the threefold nature of austerity, beginning with verbal austerity.
Austerity is considered to be of three kinds, arising from speech, mind, and body.
Worshiping the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity; straightforwardness;
non-violence; and celibacy—this is declared to be bodily austerity. (8.2)

Speech that is intent on favoring others, truthful, and beneficial to living beings, as well as the practice of Vedic study—this is vocal austerity (vācika-tapas). Furthermore, constant contentment through reflection on Brahman and self-restraint are also included. || 8.3–8.4 ||
Purity of being and gentleness are declared to be mental austerity;
furthermore, it is divided into three types—sāttvika and so forth—as correctly performed by men who possess faith and do not desire fruits. (8.5)
That austerity should be known as *sāttvika*, for it brings about true knowledge.
Austerity performed for the sake of gaining honor, respect, and worship is *rājasa*. But that austerity which consists of the destruction of others and the like is *tāmasa*.
That karma is of two kinds, and it is certainly not the cause for the arising of consciousness.
[8.7] An exposition of the causes of creation, the locus of dissolution, and the duration of maintenance;
Brahmā.
From what does the origin of the worlds arise, and where is their destruction held to occur?
O Blessed One, tell me for how long is their duration? The Blessed One replied:
Prakṛti, having entered [the state of equilibrium], gives birth to the manifest universe, including all things moving and stationary;
everything dissolves back into that very same source, and its duration lasts for the lifespan of Brahmā. (8.9) [The measure of the lifespan of the Four-faced One.]
A period called a thousand yugas constitutes a day and night for Brahmā; by that measure, his lifespan is one hundred years. In a single day of Brahmā, there are fourteen Manus.
During that day, there are fourteen Manus;
the duration of one Manu is proclaimed to be sixty-nine [units of time].
O Brahman, when the subsequent Brahmā has dissolved into the prior Brahmā, [the cycle concludes].
This dissolution called Mahat is proclaimed, O Four-faced One,
as the intermediate dissolution;
the intermediate dissolutions arise at the conclusion of the days.
Through those various creators, there is an unceasing cycle of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, and again the great dissolution;
time revolves like a wheel, and there is never any rest.
O Brahmā, what is the nature of primordial matter (prakṛti), O Lord, and how does it give birth to this world?
Tell me everything in its entirety, O Blessed One, O Creator of beings.
An Exposition on the Essential Nature of Prakṛti:
O Four-faced One, [I shall explain] the nature of sattva and the other guṇas, which exist in forms that are neither deficient nor excessive.

The withdrawal of the qualities (guṇas) is called "Prakṛti" by the wise. Presided over by the Blessed One, she is the source of the world; though insentient herself, she is the unmanifest womb of the universe.
The eternal one gives birth to the entire universe by the command of the Supreme Self.
Undivided and yet divided, she exists like clarified butter within curd.
The Blessed Lord named Saṅkarṣaṇa [resides] in that very Prakṛti as those progenies.
At the end of Brahmā’s day, Rudra withdraws [the world] at his will;
at the beginning of the day, he creates the entire world and its creatures once again.
Brahmā himself, the creator of the worlds, acts just as before and in due order.
Thus have the processes of creation and dissolution been correctly described by me.
[Now, regarding] Brahmā’s sovereignty consisting of the eight qualities: what is that which a devoted person [attains]?
What kind of *sāyujya* (union) does the wise practitioner attain?
Having obtained complete sovereignty, by what means does one return from it?
[This is] the description of the sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) beginning with *aṇimā*.
The Blessed One [attains] atomization and magnification; moreover, whatever extent he desires,
he obtains that much— whether it be heaviness or lightness.
By means of that lightness (*laghimā*), a person attains whatever is desired;
he travels even to a distant land in a mere instant.
Just as the cotton of the *śālmali* tree is light, so too is his body.
Because of that weightiness of his body, it cannot be lifted up, as if it were a mountain.
He engages in food and recreation according to his desire;
by mere volition alone, O Lotus-Seated One, all beings are brought under his control.
And they enter the bodies of others at will;
by these very eight [attainments], they dwell as they desire.
Should they forget me, being deluded by pleasant sleep, [they would fall].
Simply by the flow of devotion to me, people become carriers of the counter-current;
they are born again into the lineages of great and virtuous beings,
and they may worship me once more, desiring spiritual perfection.
By my grace, they are liberated from this censured birth.

O Four-faced One, liberation is threefold according to its distinctions— through union (*sāyujya*) and so forth— and it is also fourfold through the distinctions of difference, non-difference, and their mixture.

Liberation is declared to be of three kinds; in its distinct form, it is characterized by service (kiṅkaryalakṣaṇā). Just as in these worlds, O men, the supreme activity of Hari is liberation, so too in Vaikuṇṭha is that of the Supreme Lord.
In this world, liberated souls who are composed dwell near him as virtuous servants, always intent upon his grace.
There is non-dual liberation; there shall be ultimate oneness between the Supreme and the individual soul.

For one whose meditation on the identity of the self consists of the thought "I am that," there occurs the attainment of oneness between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme Self; this is liberation. But according to the Siddhānta, which is of a mixed nature, [liberation is attained] by remaining in the state of difference through worship and other such means.
Having gratified the supreme deity, one who is then disciplined and composed attains oneness with the supreme Self— the mass of consciousness— through concentrated discernment;
that is said to be liberation, characterized by union (*sāyujya*).

The attainment of the eightfold qualities beginning with *aṇiman*—so difficult for men to obtain—is sovereign power (*aiśvarya*); or liberation (*mukti*), which consists in the attainment of supreme bliss, is what is desired. Both of these, as well as liberation itself, are produced within the Supreme Self.
O Acyuta, Brahmā has joined many principles together with numerous scriptures regarding the inquiry into reality.
When meditative cultivation has been performed in due order upon all those principles,
there arises a single-pointed concentration (*samādhi*) which is the supreme knowledge of the scriptures;
by means of that, one gives birth to that Brahman, which is therefore considered superior to them.
"Tell me how all men attain the principles (tattvas).
"The fifty-one principles," said the Blessed Lord.
"O Four-faced One, I shall briefly describe the forty-one principles as the very forms of the Supreme Self.
Unmodified contemplation upon them leads to supreme accomplishment."
Therefore, those [topics] must be explained; grasp them from their cause.
First is the Unmanifest (avyakta), then the Intellect (buddhi), and after that the Ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti).
Then the five subtle elements (tanmātra) and the eleven [senses] are said to follow in sequence.
O Lotus-seated One, the five elements beginning with earth,
as well as Māyā, Kāla, Kalā, Rāga, and Vidyā, arise from these in succession; Nanda, Mahānanda, and Mahāvidyā are likewise proclaimed.
Kṣetrajña, Śiva, Brahmā, and thereafter Puruṣa;
Satya, Acyuta, Ananta, Viṣṇu, Sarva, Nirvṛti, Viśva, and Puruṣa—these two are declared to be Parameṣṭhin. (8.43–8.44)
By name they are Aniruddha, Pradyumna, he who is called Saṅkarṣa�ṇa,
and Vāsudeva— these four, O Four-faced One, [plus] forty, ten, and one.
Then all this was proclaimed, wherein the moving and the unmoving were produced.
Its manifestation consists of forms; who is capable of naming them all?
Even the Lord of Speech is unable to utter every one of them here in their entirety.
Thus has this sequence of names for the principles been described to you.
"Yogins who cultivate the principles through conceptualizations and through meditative absorptions,
constantly practicing yoga, attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the Jñānapāda in the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
The eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Specific Austerities";
the ninth chapter,
"The Determination of the Nature of the Cosmic Egg."
Brahmā, having crossed the ocean of ignorance and reached the further shore of knowledge,
said: "Now let the fourteen worlds be described to me."
O Supreme Lord, there is a desire to know [you] both in form and in name—
wherein the Blessed One is established, what his measure is, and what his form is like. (9.2)
Who would be capable of describing in full detail that entire universe with hundreds of mouths, O Four-faced One?
Or who is able to comprehend it, or who is capable of sustaining it?
I shall tell you all that in brief, so that you may understand it:
the measurement of the earth is fifty koṭis of yojanas, and the ground is square.
It is vast in all directions, extending for a full ten million yojanas.
There are seven islands here, and as many oceans;
they all rest upon the earth like a finger-ring.
The seven islands shall now be described by their names; listen as they are told in order: Jambū, Plakṣa, Kuśa, Krauñca, and Śākadvīpa as the next. (9.7)
O Four-faced One, the seventh is named Śālmalīpuṣkara.
I shall describe the seven oceans in their proper sequence and according to their true nature:
first the salt ocean and the sugarcane juice ocean, and immediately after that the *maireya* ocean.
Ghee, curd, milk, and then water purified from that [source] are the other [substances].
9.9 The dimensions of the continents and oceans, as well as the measurement of Jambūdvīpa within the middle region of the earth, are now described.

Immediately following that, extending for a hundred thousand yojanas in width on all sides, is the salt ocean; and next to it is an island of equal extent. Each successive one is double the length and breadth of the preceding.
O Four-faced One, the remaining continents and oceans [are as follows]:
one should further divide the continent known as Jambū into nine parts.
[This is] the specific arrangement of Meru.
In the middle portion of Meru, the height is measured at one hundred thousand [yojanas];
sixteen thousand yojanas are submerged within the earth,
while the remaining portion shines forth.
Above the earth is Mount Meru, which extends across the summit;
it measures thirty-two thousand yojanas and is situated perfectly in the center of the earth-lotus like its pericarp.
With its hundreds of thousands of peaks, each extending for a hundred *yojanas* and having a circumference of that same number,
I shall describe its subsidiary mountain ranges in due order; listen attentively to it.
To the south of Meru are three mountain ranges of the regions:
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, and Niṣadha are to its south. O Lotus-born One, these three have been declared to be the mountains of the regions.
The first region is called Bhārata-varṣa;
