after that, the one named Kiṃpuruṣa; and immediately following that is Harivarṣa.

To the north of Mount Meru are three mountain ranges of the regions; these are the Varṣa-mahīdharas in successive order: Nīla, the one called Śveta, and Śṛṅgin. Furthermore, there are three regions by name. (9.19)
The three delightful regions— Hiraṇmaya and likewise Uttarakuru—
are said to be six regions in total, each equal in extent. (9.20)
The middle continent is known as Ilāvṛta, measuring nine thousand yojanas; in its center, Meru is said to be situated. There, extending four directions from Meru, it is six thousand yojanas wide.
And there are three thousand mountains there,
adorned with the form of buttresses, rising ten thousand yojanas high;
these are the names of the directional mountains.
Mandara is in the eastern direction, Gandhamādana in the southern;
that which is named Vipula presides over the western quarter, and Supārśva over the northern. Thus, there are four trees in the four directions.
In those directions, four trees stood as lofty as banners:
the *kadamba* tree, the *jambu*, the *pippala*, and the banyan (*vaṭa*).
Each of them was one thousand and one *yojanas* in height.
O Lotus-Seated One, the power of the Jambu tree shall give its name to this continent;
its fruits, as large as elephants, fell upon the surface of the rocks.

The excellent river that carries their essence shatters into a hundred streams; it is called Jāmbūnadī. Those who dwell on its banks, having drunk its essence, are freed from old age, death, wrinkles, and gray hair.

They conceive of the golden splendors known as Jāmbūnada; such is the excellence of the Kalpa. O Four-faced One, the specific location of the regions of Bhadraketa, Māleya, and Ilāvṛta is declared to be the region of Bhadrāśva, situated to the east of Meru.
The western one is named Ketumāla; between these two regions, Ilāvṛta is declared to be the center, as previously described. In the four directions are four gardens.
To the east of Meru is the Caitraratha forest, to the south is Gandhamādana,
to the west is Vaibhrāja, and to the north is the Nandana forest.
There are four lakes.
First is Lake Aruṇoda, and beyond that is Mahābhadra;
Śītodaka lies to the west, while Mānasa is to the north.
Thus have the lakes fit for the enjoyment of the gods been described to you.
On each of the four sides of Meru, there are five Kesara mountains;
Śīta, Mukunda, Kurarī, Mālyavat,
and the one named Vaikaṅka— these are the five eastern Kesara mountains.
Both Trikūṭa and Uṅgira, as well as the serpent named Kūṭala,
and Niṣadha on its southern side— these are the Kesara mountains of equal extent.
Then there are Śikhivāsa, Vaidūrya, Kapila, and Gandhamādana.
O Brahmin, Jāruthi is the fifth; Kesaras are the five mountains.
Śaṅkhakūṭa is well-known, as is Ṛṣabha;
the serpent is known by the name Haṃsa, and likewise Kālāja-naprabha.
In the north are twenty-five Kesara mountains;
in the center of Meru’s summit is the settlement of Brahmapurī,
measuring thirty-two thousand yojanas.
On the middle portion of the summit of Mount Meru,
a city four and ten thousand yojanas in extent has been fashioned; it is like the pericarp of the mountain-lotus of the Creator.
In the intermediate directions and the eight cardinal directions all around the city of Brahmā,
there are the cities of the world-protectors; the cities of the world-protectors such as Indra and others are situated in the east and the other directions.
In its breadth and length it measures one hundred yojanas;
the city is Mādhonī by name, and is indeed like Amarāvatī,
crowded with a thousand gate-towers, gates, walls, and defensive beams.

The city of Agni is Tejovatī; to the south is the city of Yama, Saṃyamanī; the city of the Rākṣasas is Rakṣovatī; and then there is Śuddhavatī, the city of Varuṇa. The city of Vāyu is known as Gandhavatī, while that of Soma is Mahodayā by name.
She is said to be glorious upon the lands of Mount Kesarācala.
Before the various forms of the Blessed One, there are well-adorned [shrines];
in the four directions lies the division of the Gaṅgā.
Having pierced the lunar orb, Gaṅgā— the birthplace of the Blessed One’s feet—
falling from heaven toward every quarter, flows near the city of Brahmā and divides herself spontaneously into four streams in the four directions.
The Sītā, the Alakanandā, the Sucakṣu, and the Bhadrā—
these are the four distinct names corresponding to the four directions, O Four-faced One. The river Sītā, flowing through the sky, emerges from the eastern mountains.
It flows out through the eastern region known as Bhadrāśva;
then, having entered the mouth of the ocean by way of the southern route,
it passes beyond the Bhārata-varṣa from the Saptamukha mountain.
Having entered that river Alakanandā, which purifies the three worlds,
Sucakṣus herself again from the western mountain Ketumāla crosses over the region and reaches the ocean,
just as a woman approaches her husband.
The Bhadrā river flows from the northern regions toward the Uttarakurus;
having crossed the ocean, it goes to the lord of rivers. This is the arrangement of the world-lotus's divisions.
Mālyavat and Gandhamādana extend as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha mountains.
Between them stands Mount Meru, like the pericarp in the center of a lotus.
[There are the regions of] Bhārata, Ketumāla, Bhadrāśva, and that known as Kuru.
The petals of the world-lotus extend beyond the boundary mountains;
Hemakūṭa and Niṣadha stretch from south to north.
Kailāsa and Gandhamādana are to be known as the two boundary mountains.
The two great oceans to the east and west are eighty *yojanas* in extent;
they touch the mountains Pāriyātra and Niṣadha at their limits,
and they lie respectively to the west and northeast of Meru.

The triple-peaked Jārudhi and Varṣaparvata are mountain ranges situated to the north of Mount Meru, reaching from the eastern to the western great ocean. Because of the infinity of mountains, their specific locations are not described in detail.

The inner valleys of the mountains are frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*, as well as by other merit-makers—such as *daityas*, *dānavas*, and *kiṃnaras*. For these earthly paradises have been created; they are difficult for those of evil deeds to attain.
For the sake of protecting the world, the Blessed One dwells in Bhadrāśva and other regions;
Hayagrīva, the embodiment of knowledge, himself resides in Bhadrāśva.
The forms of Viṣṇu dwell in the various continents and on the boundary mountains.
They dwell there, distinguished by various forms, for the sake of protecting the world.
O Lotus-born One, what is the purpose of establishing regions such as Kiṃpuruṣa as lands of enjoyment? Regarding those regions such as Kiṃpuruṣa and the rest, [what is their significance]? 9.61

The subjects are forever free from affliction; likewise, there is neither sorrow nor fear, neither thirst nor hunger, neither hatred nor the wasting away of their lifespan. They live for twenty-two thousand years.
In those regions there is no earthly lifespan, nor does rain fall from the sky.
There is no god [to ordain it], no division of seasons, and no time characterized by the divisions of the ages;
O Four-faced One, the time of the Kṛta age prevails forever.
The entire Dharma has four feet, and meditation itself is the worship of Hari.
Wherever there are mountains and rivers, and wherever there are cities,
there are many villages where people are always devoted to their own duty.
The Brahmins and the kings, intent on protecting the subjects,
remained established in their respective duties; thus the four castes were maintained,
and likewise the four stages of life (āśrama) persisted exactly as prescribed.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Dimensions of Jambūdvīpa and Other Continents," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrī Pādma Saṃhitā within the Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the tenth chapter.
(Description of Bhāratavarṣa) The Blessed One [traversed] from the southern ocean up to the Himālaya mountains.
This land is Bhāratavarṣa; it is the earth of men who perform actions.
Its extent is said to be thousands of yojanas.
Here, men must perform action that yields the fruits of heaven and liberation.
The Sahya, Mahendra, Malaya, Śuktimat, the one named Ṛkṣavat,
Vindhya, and Pāriyātra— these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvata).
For an action performed right here, the fruit is hell.
In all other ages, only the fruit is enjoyed.
Here alone are established the four stages of life (āśramas) and the four social classes (varṇas); here occurs the manifestation of the four ages, beginning with Kṛta.
Mortals who desire the fruits of the world beyond perform charity, sacrifice, and austerity here; they worship Puruṣottama, the Lord of Sacrifice.
That land of Bhārata is the most excellent, esteemed among all lands.

Those wise ones who seek the fruits [of their actions] desire birth in the lands of karma. Likewise, in this [world], the Supreme Person dwells within thousands of divine abodes, and there are holy rivers by the thousands.
There are more than a hundred villages, cities, and towns;
and in the six other continents, there are indeed seven regions (varṣas).
O Brahmin, in each of these, there are seven principal mountain ranges (kulaparvatas).
The distinctions of the social classes (varṇas) and the stages of life (āśramas) are established there.
[This concludes] the description of Puṣkaradvīpa;
in the final Puṣkaradvīpa lies the Mānasottara mountain.
In its center, it shines like a bracelet; its height is now described.
Its elevation is fifty thousand yojanas, and its width is exactly the same, as if dividing the island [of Jambūdvīpa]. || 10.11–10.12 ||
O Brahmin, that best of mountains stands encompassing two circular regions;
both the interior and the exterior of the mountain are equal in extent.
Furthermore, upon its summit are the abodes of the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
Furthermore, their cities exist as before, and their names also remain as they were. There are also separate cities for other gods;
O Brāhmaṇa, there are innumerable cities in Puṣkara.
The ocean outside Puṣkara is filled with sweet, clear water; by it that continent is surrounded, just as the others are by the oceans beyond them. (10.16) Description of the Lokāloka Mountain.

Outside the sweet-water ocean, the entire earth is made of gold; and beyond that, O Brahmin, is the Lokāloka mountain made of refined gold (tapanīya). The whole terrestrial world is square like a sāla tree.
As he stands enveloping all, his height is one *yojana*,
and his width is likewise; on his head and everywhere else,
the Supreme Person himself remains through infinite manifestations of form.
Herein are also the groups beginning with Kumuda, as well as the weapons beginning with the discus;
the two goddesses Mahī and Lakṣmī; Viṣvaksena, the king of birds;
and the stations for the various forms of Viṣṇu and his attendants.
O Four-faced One, there are many other beautiful places here and there; however, the sun does not illuminate its further side with his rays,
for darkness, having enveloped that mountain slope, remains stationed on the outside.
And that mountain Lokāloka, moreover, encircles [the world] on all sides.
Immediately outside the great shell of the cosmic egg,
this earth is measured at five hundred million yojanas.
"Along with the shell of the cosmic egg, including the continents, oceans, and mountains—by her all this world is sustained; therefore she is remembered as the Sustainer (Dhātrī).
Thus ends the Jñānapāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Extent of the World of the Earth";
the eleventh chapter:
the description of the subterranean regions (atala) and others, preceded by a restatement of what has been said.
The Blessed One said: "O Lotus-seated One, this expansion of the world of mortals has been described. Now I shall speak truly of the seven worlds below. 11.1
Aṭala is the first world; the second is called Vitala;
know that the third is Nitala, and the fourth should be known as Gabhastimat.
The fifth is named Mahātala, and Sutala is declared to be the sixth.
Know that Pātāla is the seventh, and each of these is elevated by ten thousand yojanas; in these regions, beginning with Atala,
dwell the Dānavas, Daityas, Kāleyas, and likewise the serpents.
Even in heaven, there are no such enjoyments as those found in the netherworlds (atala) and below—
food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, and drinks that are most delicious and of superior quality;
nor are there the delightful palatial grounds, groves, and rivers.
And there are hundreds of nāga maidens, beautiful in all their limbs.
When darkness is destroyed day and night by the blazing net of jewels,
neither the sun nor the moon is ever sought after by the people there.
The joy experienced by those dwelling there is not found even among those who have liberated their souls;
for whatever object they desire to enjoy is seen to be already present before them. Indeed, nothing at all is ever sought after by those intent on such enjoyment.

In the seven nether worlds, beginning with Atala, the Rākṣasas, Daityas, and Dānavas— who are devoted to enjoyment— experience pleasures eight times greater than those in heaven. They are neither poor, nor afflicted by disease, nor emaciated, nor distressed.
There are hundreds of vast subterranean abodes on every side.
In the seventh, known as Pātāla, Viṣṇu, possessing a thousand hoods and named Kapila,
resides, protecting the regions beginning with Talātala.
Together with all his attendants in that great, splendid city,
Viṣṇu remained there, having assumed a dark form; he is the exceedingly powerful one known as Śeṣa, presiding over the seven netherworlds beginning with Atala.
Adorned with a thousand hoods and illuminating the quarters with his jewels,
he is known in the world by wise great seers as Ananta.
Upon his head, the entire earth is borne like a garland.
Weakening the gods, Daityas, and others by his own splendor—
wearing a diadem and garlands, with beautiful brows and eyes rolling from intoxication,
clad in blue garments yet possessing a fair body, he was like Mount Kailāsa.
Bearing the plow and the pestle as weapons that shatter the Daityas,
he was being constantly served by Vāruṇī, who offered him food;
from whose mouths at the end of the kalpa, Śiva Saṅkarṣaṇa [emerges].
The fire of poison emerges to destroy the entire world;
it remains worshipped by all the inhabitants of the netherworld (pātāla).
No one is able to describe its qualities, even with hundreds of mouths.
When he stands shaking his head with pride, then the entire surface of the earth, with its mountains, oceans, and forests, trembles.
Who could endure it? Who could fully describe his strength?

Beneath the serpent with its remaining hoods is the tortoise, upon whom the fire of time rests. O Lotus-seated One, he is unbearable, matted with thousands of flames. Below him is the supporting power, the body of Viṣṇu.
Immediately thereafter, there arises for this [being] the shell of the egg;
these have been described as the planes of the fruit of merit-forming karma. Now, the planes of the fruit of demerit-forming karma are being described.
Beneath the earth and below the waters, the regions known as the hells (naraka) are recorded. First among them is Raurava, followed immediately by Mahāraurava;
then Taptaputtalikā, Kumbhī, and the impalement on a stake (śūlāropaṇa) are proclaimed.
The needle-point and the razor, the sword and the cleaver on one side;
the boar, the oil-pot, the great flame, and the heating; the sword-leaf forest, the stench-bearing river, and the tigers, lions, wolves, and other beasts.
A heated pillar to be devoured by dogs, a silk-cotton tree in golden bloom,
rivers of blood with water of saliva, and likewise cutting with spears—
these and other such fruits, they say, are for those who have performed evil deeds.
I have described this direction of the innumerable hells;
the most wicked beings who have fallen into them experience the fruit [of their deeds].
O Brahmin, there is no exhaustion of karmas without various distinct experiences.
The fire of knowledge thoroughly reduces all actions to ashes;
for those who have attained the science of yoga, there is neither heaven nor hell.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Measurement of the Worlds Beginning with Atala," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
[Now begins] the twelfth chapter.
The description of the nature of the worlds beginning with Bhuvaḥ:
Brahmā has described the extent of the earth and the seven worlds beginning with Talātala.
The hells have thus been described; now, O Blessed One, let the form and the measurement of the worlds beginning from the earth be told to me. The Blessed One [replied].
O Brahmin, as great as the earth is in its extent and circumference, so great is the terrestrial realm in its extent and circumference;
[this is] from the measurement of the distance between the earth and the sun.
Above the earth, at a distance of one hundred thousand yojanas in the sky,
the sun stands, illuminating the world with his own fierce rays;
the Blessed One, having mounted a chariot extending many yojanas in width.
On the left side of the chariot, one divine wheel is established;
seven horses, who are the seven meters (chandas), draw this great chariot.
And Aruṇa himself acts as the charioteer, driving all the horses.
Upon the summit of Mount Mānasottara is the track of the chariot,
which is the cause for the division of the dawns and the succession of days; it is remembered as the supreme path for yogis in the total destruction of the afflictions.
Those seeking liberation travel by this path to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The sun neither rises nor sets; it faces everyone everywhere.
The rising and setting of the sun are considered merely the appearance and disappearance of its light.
Wherever the sun is seen by people, that is traditionally considered its rising for them;
wherever it goes out of sight, there is the perception of its setting among men.
In the forenoon, the continuous rays of the sun become abundant.
But afterwards they become short until they are no longer visible;
except for the city of the Dhātu on Mount Meru,
the rays of the sun fall sideways, upwards, and likewise downwards on all sides.
Furthermore, those who protect him as he departs after having gone to the assembly hall of Brahmā do not suffer any stumbling elsewhere due to that splendor of Brahmā;
such is Bhuvarloka.
The space between the earth and the sun is declared to be the region of Bhuvaḥ; there,
the Vidyādharas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, along with the Dānavas,
dwell joyfully in their respective cities.

The other planets are situated between the Sun and the Pole Star (Dhruva). From the position of the Sun, the position of the Moon is said to be one hundred thousand [yojanas] away; above that, the constellations (nakṣatras) abide in their respective order.
It is said that the station of Mercury lies three hundred thousand [yojanas] above;
Uśanas, however, remains situated two hundred thousand [yojanas] beyond that,
and Bhauma (Mars) always stands having traversed those same [two hundred thousand] yojanas further.
The Guru remains at that same distance;
Saturn stays above him at that same measure; and beyond that, the son of the Sun (Saturn) is situated at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas] for each subsequent step.
O sages, the stars are situated further upward in the same sequence of hundreds of thousands.
There are more than a thousand sages who dwell above, moving ever upwards.
Beyond that, Dhruva is established in a station difficult for even great seers to ascend;
it is a great wheel with twelve spokes, two rims, and two hubs.
There are three [seasons] that abide in his spokes at the ends of the months;
likewise, the twelve signs beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces are situated in the spokes.
There are twelve months, beginning with Caitra, and likewise those beginning with spring.
The six seasons, the transits, the equinox, and the two solstices; the two fortnights, white and black, and the divisions of the yugas and years;
the divisions of time beginning with the *truṭi*—these are well-established as the spokes of the wheel. (12.21–12.22)
The Pole Star (Dhruva) is fixed in the center of the navel; the zodiac signs revolve clockwise, while all the planets move counter-clockwise—such is their motion.
Dhruva is like a lump of clay situated in the middle of a potter’s wheel.
All the hosts of luminaries always revolve around Dhruva.
The world of the sun (Suvarloka) is the region situated between the sun and Dhruva, known by the name Svarga.
In those celestial chariots dwell the gods individually;
they are innumerable, eternally satisfied, and possess bodies composed of light.
For them, the water of the Gaṅgā is to be enjoyed, as are the flowers of the divine trees.
Wealth was known as wish-fulfilling gems and women as celestial nymphs;
the Siddhas and others dwelt in those cities free from all affliction.
There, the Blessed One, in the form of Upendra, was ever seated.
By his own splendor, he protects the gods and others dwelling in heaven.
The three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar—are recorded as having fifteen lakhs [of yojanas].
Beyond that is Maharloka, extending for ten million yojanas.
Ten crores of sages dwell there, beginning with Sanandana.
Following that is the description of Janaloka and the others; Janaloka extends for two crores [of yojanas].
Immediately following that is Tapoloka, situated at eight hundred million yojanas;
Satyaloka, moreover, is three times as extensive.
Above that, the city of the Dhātu (Brahmā) stands, extending for three hundred million yojanas.
O Lotus-seated One, the sages describe that world of Brahmā as being one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, with palaces and gate-towers made of *sāla* wood;
it is the realm of Viṣṇu situated within the circle of primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The wise know that to the north of the world of Brahmā lies the world of Viṣṇu; the distance between these two worlds is said to be one hundred thousand yojanas. [Beyond that is] the world of Śiva.

In that very interval, O Four-faced One, the world of Śiva is situated in the southern direction; in it, Śiva himself resides. Above [this], in ascending order, are the five worlds of the Blessed One.
Having ascended ten million *yojanas* above and standing before [the world],
the Lord, the Soul of All, extends three times that distance upward.
Therein dwells the imperishable Lord himself, whose nature is cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Hari, the soul of the universe and the creator of the universe, remained within that very measure of pride.
But the Puruṣa-soul stood before the four-cornered measurement;
having transcended one corner above, he was situated behind five.

That blessed Lord Parameṣṭhin, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, eternally occupies that fivefold seat of Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu, who consists of the five powers, [resides] within that space measuring ten million yojanas.
He dwells together with Śrī and Bhūmi, served by Vainateya; the shell of the cosmic egg forms his wall, and above it, at a height of ten million yojanas, he remains aloft.
O Lotus-seated One, its density is equal to ten million [times that of the previous];
it should be known as a pure, golden egg, which is most wonderful. It consists of seven coverings.
By this shell of the cosmic egg, all the worlds are completely covered.
These worlds are situated one above the other like wood-apple fruits,
and they are surrounded by water of a corresponding superior magnitude.
Just as the egg is enveloped by water, so too is that [egg] by fire;
it is likewise enveloped by wind, and that by space.
One should know that all these increase tenfold each time, and that space is enveloped by the Great (Mahat).
And that Great One (Mahat) is the primary [evolute] of Pradhāna; it is enveloped by Tamas.
Beyond that limit, no further enumeration exists.
It is the cause of the entirety [of existence], the supreme Prakṛti of Tamas.
Regarding the number of those eggs, O Brahmin, there are thousands and tens of thousands of such eggs;
what is the use of saying more? Their number cannot be told.
Nārāyaṇa’s pervasion both within and without:
Nārāyaṇa stands pervading all those cosmic eggs;
and within them also dwells the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, who is all-pervasive. (12.48)
And standing outside, he remains beholding everything like a witness.
Beyond the great darkness are the four worlds of the Vyūhas, worlds extending for many yojanas.
There are four [emanations] in succession, presided over by the four;
I shall describe them in order through their manifestations. Aniruddha is remembered as the supreme; after them comes Pradyumna, and the one called Saṅkarṣaṇa.
After that, O Lotus-seated One, is the one called Vāsudeva known as Vyūha;
immediately following him is the one called Vāsudeva known as Vibhava;
and then there is the beginningless Vāsudeva, who successively presides over those two worlds.
Beyond that, the world of Nārāyaṇa is situated near it;
the distance between each of these is said to be ten million yojanas,
and their exceedingly beautiful extent is exactly that much as well.
The world of Vaikuṇṭha stands outside of those worlds, where the unborn Lord resides;
the beginningless one, known as Vāsudeva, shines within a pavilion of jewels.
Seated together with Śrī and Bhūmi upon the divine throne of the remaining enjoyments,
he is surrounded by those eight powers, such as Vyāpti and the rest,
who serve him closely with chowries in their hands.
He was being served by the attendants, Senaśa and others, and also by the weapons such as the discus, all bowing down; he was attended by those established in the stages of proximity and so forth,
and by liberated Siddhas who, knowing the five times of the day, had entered into the state of servants.
He was constantly being worshipped by many who were perfected in the eightfold yoga, absorbed in the Lord,
who knew the true meaning of the Pañcarātra, and who remained ever-satisfied in his presence. || 12.58–59 ||

O Brahmin, this direction has been described as it truly is by great-souled ones who have reached the culmination of their duties remaining under the Lord; it is for those fortunate ones who dwell therein,
both within the worlds and outside the cosmic eggs.
The full extent is not even mentioned, for it is difficult to grasp for those such as you.
Having extracted the mere essence from everywhere, this conclusion for the sake of others has been set forth.
Brahmā’s manifestation of gratitude: Brahmā is the knowledge of the Blessed One by which some ignorance is destroyed. 12.62
The darkness of ignorance has been destroyed, and that great knowledge has been revealed;
and all my doubts have vanished through your grace, O Blessed One.
Thus is the purity of the tradition of the knowledge as it was spoken.
The Blessed One gave this most secret knowledge, called Padma, to Brahmā;
and Brahmā, in turn, introduced it to Kapila according to its true nature.
The great seer Kapila also gave that knowledge to you exactly as it is; thus it has come down through the succession of the lineage.
Out of a desire to show favor toward you, he bestowed this supreme knowledge of the established doctrine.

"O Blessed One, this most secret and wonderful [knowledge] consisting of the Blessed One has been declared. This knowledge, which is most profound, should not be told to one who is an unfit vessel for the knowledge of the Blessed One, nor to one who is excessively arrogant."
It should not be given to one who lacks devotion, nor to one who is base, nor again to one who does not wish to listen;
it should not be imparted to one who has not been initiated, nor to an ungrateful person, nor to a sinner;
likewise, it must not be told to an atheist or to a heretic.
Not to one of low caste, nor to a slanderer, nor to one of evil nature;
nor indeed to one who has not been initiated, nor to one devoted to external scriptures;
nor ever to one who is envious, nor to one who has abandoned right conduct.
The description of the worthy recipient must be told to one who is humble, pure, and a celibate student;
likewise to one who is desirous of hearing, serene, observant of vows, and self-controlled.
To one who dwells in a hermitage, who is turned away from worldly existence, who seeks liberation; likewise, to one who desires to know the ritual practice proclaimed in the Pāñcarātra;
to one of good character, grateful, upright, and of upright intellect.

I joyfully imparted this *Saṃhitā* of Saṃvarta to one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), who is of noble birth, and who is an ascetic— a member of the three twice-born classes.
One should not teach it, nor instruct it, nor speak of this knowledge to an enemy.
Kaṇva, having first restated what was said, described the fruit of studying the *Saṃhitā*:
"O disciples, all that has been heard from the mouth of Saṃvarta has been told. (12.74)
That consciousness has been explained by me to you in its entirety;
and I shall also instruct you in Yoga, if you have a desire to hear it there.
He who, established in his observances, studies this *Pādma* Saṃhitā, [attains the highest goal].

He goes to the world of Brahmā; he is not born here again. (12.76) For one who is well-restrained, reciting even a single verse, or half a verse, or a single quarter daily, the desired fruit stands in the palm of his hand. (12.77)
The twelfth chapter, which is a portion concerning knowledge (*jñāna*), has been proclaimed in the *Pādma-tantra*;
having extracted its essence and condensed it from the vast ocean of tantras.
Even disciples who are desirous of hearing [it] [should listen] with a serene inner self.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Extent of Bhuvarloka and the Other Worlds," in the Jñānapāda of the Śrī Pādma Saṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra;
the Jñānapāda is completed.
The first chapter, on Brahmā, in the Yoga-pāda of the Śrī Pādmasaṃhitā.
O Blessed One, O Ocean of Compassion, O Supreme Person, the highest good for a wise person engaged in yoga has been proclaimed; O Puruṣottama,
if it is still to be heard by those like me, let that yoga be explained once more.
"If there is favor toward us who are devoted,
[then please explain] the two-fold nature of yoga," [said the disciples to] the Blessed One.
O Four-faced One, that binding of an undisturbed mind to some object is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and it partakes of two kinds. [Now follows] the definition for each of these two divisions.
The constant binding of the mind to those very actions prescribed as "this must be done" is called the yoga of action (karmayoga).
But that which is the constant binding of the mind to the goal of the highest good is [yoga of the mind].

That should be known as the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga), which is auspicious and brings about all perfections. When the mind is established in these two types of yoga, characterized as described above, they together constitute the means to liberation.
He goes directly to the supreme good, characterized by liberation.
Regarding the definition of the limbs of yoga: restraint (yama) and the others are the limb of the former [concentration], while dispassion (vairāgya) and the others belong to the latter.
There are eight yogas beginning with *yama*; *yama* is characterized by non-violence and so forth.
(1.7) Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, uprightness, forbearance, fortitude, moderation in diet, and purity—these are the ten *yamas*. (1.8)
Furthermore, *niyama* (observance) is said to consist of austerity (*tapas*) and so forth;

its characteristics include austerity, contentment, faith in the scriptures (*āstikya*), charity, worship of Hari, listening to the established doctrines, modesty, and the recitation of mantras (*japa*). 1.9.6–7.

Now, all the postures beginning with the svastika are described. Having placed both knees toward the northeast, the two soles of the feet together—this is declared to be the svastika posture. (1.10–1.11)
Placing the right ankle on the left side of the suture and the left ankle on the right side— that posture is called *svastika* by the wise.
Furthermore, having placed both feet upon the thighs [and grasping] the two big toes...
One should take hold of each respective seat with both hands in a crossed manner.
Among all seats, the bound lotus posture (baddha-padmāsana) is known to be most highly honored;
it is performed by placing one foot upon the other thigh while remaining motionless.
That which is called the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), which destroys the masses of sins,
is as follows: having pressed the perineum with the two ankles in reverse order,
and having extended the hands over the knees, this is the posture preceded by the lion (siṃhapūrvaka).
Placing the two ankles below the scrotum on both sides of the perineum,
and having firmly secured the feet with both hands—
this posture should be known as Bhadrāsana, which destroys all sins. (1.16–1.17)
Having placed the left ankle on the right side of the back,
and likewise having placed the other ankle on the other side of the back,
that posture which is like a cow’s mouth is desired as the *gomukhāsana*. (1.18)

Pressing both the perineum and the sides with the two ankles in reverse order, this posture is declared to be *muktāsana*. Likewise, placing the left ankle upon the penis and the other [right ankle] in the same manner [upon the other side], [this is another form]. (1.19–1.20)
Or, having placed the feet upon the ankles, it becomes the *muktāsana*. Alternatively,
having firmly supported the earth with the palms of both hands and placed the elbows at the sides of the navel like a peacock, [one remains in that posture].
"By raising both the head and the feet, the mayūrāsana (peacock posture) is prescribed.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Various Postures," in the Yogapāda of the Śrī Pādmasaṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
The Second Chapter: Purification of the Channels; The Blessed Lord.
Restrained by the *yamas* and *niyamas*, as well as by the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅgas*) and postures (*āsanas*),
one who is well-disciplined performs breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) once the purification of the channels (*nāḍiśuddhi*) has been achieved.
(2.1) The measurement of the body, according to one's own fingers, is ninety-six finger-breadths in length.
The vital breath (prāṇa) extends twelve finger-breadths beyond the body. One who,
through yoga, makes the wind residing in the body— by means of the fire produced from the body itself— either diminished or equalized, is considered a knower of Brahman.
Within the body is the seat of fire, possessing the luster of molten gold;
it is triangular for bipeds, square for quadrupeds,
circular for birds, and hexagonal for aquatic creatures.
Within that [body], for those born of sweat, there is an eight-cornered fire, Vaiśvānara, blazing like a lamp;
joined with prāṇa and apāna, it digests food.
It is said that food is of four kinds within the body.

Two finger-breadths above the *apāna* and below the penis on the left side is the center of the body for humans; for quadrupeds, it is the middle of the penis, O Lotus-born One; and for all others, it is the middle of the belly. (2.7)
The location of the *kanda* within the body of humans is nine finger-breadths from the center.
It is four finger-breadths in height and four finger-breadths in length;
for animals, both bipeds and quadrupeds, it is egg-shaped.
The middle of that [body] is indeed desired as the torso, and its center is held to be the navel.
Therein they speak of a twelve-spoked wheel, with the months as its spokes;
and within each of those twelve, there are the twelve forms beginning with Viṣṇu.
There, by my own power of illusion (māyā), I cause the wheel that stands there to revolve.
O Lotus-Seated One, the living being (jīva) revolves among its spokes in succession,
just as a spider moves within the cage of its web.
He who moves mounted upon the vital breath (prāṇa) cannot exist without that [breath].
Above that, at the level of the navel, is the seat of Kuṇḍalinī, situated transversely and upwards;
she consists of the eightfold primordial nature and is coiled eight times.
Constantly [observing] the movement of the breath and the blazing of the fire as they truly are,
one should remain forever having completely restrained [the breath] at the side of the *kanda*;
likewise, one should gaze with the mouth toward the opening of the *brahmarandhra*.
And at the time of yoga, impelled by the wind together with fire,
she vibrates within the space of the heart in the form of a serpent, intensely radiant.
Then, through the mouth of the wind, the wind itself proceeds via the suṣumṇā.
Situated in the middle of the bulb (kanda), the channel Suṣumnā is well-established. Resembling the fiber of a lotus stalk, straight, and extending upwards,
it reaches as far as the aperture of Brahmā, shining like lightning and possessing a tube-like form.
The Vaiṣṇavī is the channel of Brahman, the path for attaining Nirvāṇa;
Iḍā and Piṅgalā are situated to its left and right respectively.
Iḍā, arising from the *kanda*, extends as far as the left nostril.
From there, Piṅgalā rises as far as the other nostril;
Gāndhārī and Hastijihvā, along with two other channels,
are situated in front and behind it, facing the left and right eyes respectively.
From that very source arise the two glorious *pūṣā* channels;
the *alambuṣā* extends from the base of the anus to the limit of the right ear. The *kuhū* channel is downward-facing and extends as far as the end of the penis.
The *keśinī* extends from the *kanda* down to the big toe;
these ten principal channels are said to originate from the *kanda*. From them arise many other channels, both gross and subtle. (2.23–2.24)
"Seventy-two thousand are coarse, O Lotus-born; but the subtle ones cannot be numbered at all, for they are of various kinds with coarse roots.
Just as on the leaf of an ashvattha tree, both the subtle and the coarse are spread out."
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna,
as well as nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya—
these ten vital winds (prāṇas) move within the ten channels (nāḍīs). (2.26–2.27)
Among those, the pentad beginning with prāṇa is primary, and within that, two are most important;
or rather, prāṇa alone is supreme, for it sustains the individual self (jīvātman).
Its locations are the middle of the mouth and nose, the heart, and the region of the navel.
"The big toe," O Lotus-Seated One, "is thus the locations of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
The apāna moves, O Brahmin, in the anus, penis, thighs, and knees;
the samāna is established as all-pervading throughout all the limbs. (2.29–2.30)
Udāna resides in all the joints, as well as in the feet and hands;
vyāna is located in the ears, the anus, the ankles, the shoulders, and the throat.
The five winds, beginning with Nāga, are situated in the skin, bones, and other parts.
The water and food situated in the stomach are processed by the fire of the tongue;
the vital breath (prāṇa), located within the middle of the stomach, separates them one by one.
Through such activities as these, the prāṇa maintains its presence within the body.
The apāna wind effects the discharge of urine and other such substances;
the activities of the prāṇa, apāna, and other vital breaths are performed by the vyāna wind.
The body situated within is sustained by the udāna wind.
The *samāna* wind always performs the nourishment and other functions of the body.

*Nāga* produces belching and other such actions; *kūrma* effects the closing of the eyes and so forth; *kṛkara* is the agent of sneezing; and *datta* performs the functions of sleep and the like. (2.35–2.36)
O Dhanañjaya, the splendor and other qualities of a dead body have been described;
likewise, O Lotus-seated One, having understood the different channels, the different vital airs, the very locations of those vital airs, and their various movements— 2.37.
"One should strive for the purification of the channels by the method that will be described.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Channels," in the Yoga Section of the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The Third Chapter:
The Procedure for Breath Control (Prāṇāyāma), by the Blessed Lord.
A member of the three twice-born classes, engaged in the worship of Vāsudeva, should practice the disciplined conduct prescribed for his own varṇa and appropriate to his stage of life (āśrama);
having sought out a secluded place free from all disturbances, [he should perform his practice].
There, upon a beautiful wooden seat prepared with *darbha* grass, clothing, a black antelope skin, and so forth— complete with the substances required for the limbs of yoga—
he sat at a height of one *tāla*, measuring two *tālas* in total.
Having sat upon a seat suitable for subjugation, such as the *svastika* posture or another according to one's preference,
facing east, with the body properly straightened and the mind composed,
one should fix the gaze on the tip of the nose without touching the teeth with the teeth. (3.4)
Placing the tongue against the palate and keeping both arms relaxed,
with the neck slightly contracted, he should bind himself in the yoga-mudrā and perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with his hands according to the prescribed rule.
The definition of *prāṇāyāma* is the emptying, filling, and retention of the breath; likewise, the emptying [again]—the distressing of the breath by these four—is declared to be *prāṇāyāma*. (3.7)
With the right hand alone, one should press the nostril;
one should fill the interior with air through the *iḍā* and retain it within oneself (*kumbhaka*).
Then, one should gradually expel the breath outward through the *piṅgalā*.
One should fill the abdomen with air through the *iḍā* for thirty-two measures;
then again for sixteen measures, and finally for sixty-four measures, one should fill the body with the vital wind like a completely full pitcher. (3.9–3.10)
All the channels are filled with the vital air (mātariśvan);
when this is accomplished, O Brahmin, the ten winds move about as the very fruit of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The lotus of the heart also clearly becomes fully blossomed.
Through the filling [of breath] and likewise through the retention (kumbhīkaraṇa), it remains facing upward;
however, that lotus is turned downward when it has grown into the hollow of the throat.
His [penis] is like a palm tree, endowed with eight petals,
resembling a plantain flower, and possessing a luster equal to moonstone.
At the two twilights and at midnight, one should perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).

By practicing this for even a single day, one is liberated from all sins. What is the use of many other teachings? Those devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) have shaken off all evils by the completion of three years.
O Brahmin, after three years, a man devoted to *prāṇāyāma* beholds even me situated within the lotus of the heart;
he becomes a yogi perfected in yoga, a conqueror of the vital breaths and a master of his senses.
One who eats little and sleeps little shall become radiant and strong;
having transcended untimely death, he shall attain a long life.
He for whom perspiration arises during the practices of breath control (prāṇāyāma) is the lowest.
That in which there is a trembling of the body during the middle breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) is declared to be middling;
that in which there is a rising of the body is declared to be the highest.
In the lowest [level], there is the destruction of diseases and sins; furthermore, in the middling [level]...
Furthermore, in the highest [grade], there shall be the destruction of evil diseases and great afflictions.
(3.20) One has little urine and little excrement, a light body, and moderate eating;
with senses subdued and a sharp intellect, one knows the three times and possesses self-mastery. (3.21)
For one who, having abandoned exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), performs only the retention of breath (*kumbhīkaraṇa*),
there is nothing in the three worlds that is difficult to attain.
The diligent practitioner [should focus] on the root of the navel, the tip of the nose, and the big toe.
Always holding the vital breaths with the mind during the periods of the twilights,
the yogi shall become free from all diseases and devoid of fatigue.
By fixing [the breath] upon the navel-center, there shall be the destruction of diseases of the abdomen.
By fixing [the breath] on the tip of the nose, there is indeed long life and lightness of the body;
by holding it on the big toe, O Lotus-born One, the wind [is mastered].
Having drawn in the wind and drinking it at the tip of the tongue, one is free from fatigue and burning heat.
When the *brāhma-muhūrta* has arrived, one should draw in the breath with the tongue and drink it; within three months, great perfection of speech shall arise for the practitioner,
and by practicing for six months, there shall be the destruction of even great diseases.
Wherever the wind is held within a limb afflicted by disease or other ailments,
through that very concentration on the vital air (marut), one attains health in those respective parts.
By the concentration of the mind alone, the breath becomes stabilized.
The determination of the steadiness of the mind:
O Lotus-seated One, the cause for the stabilization of the mind is now stated.
Having withdrawn the senses from their objects, one should remain composed. (3.29)
Drawing the *apāna* upward, one should hold it above the bladder (3.30).
Binding the sense organs, such as the ears and so forth, with both hands according to the proper method,
the mind of the practitioner comes under his own control through the path previously described (3.31).
When the mind is touched by the conquest of the vital air, that very air is indeed always established under one's own control;
the prāṇa flows alternately through the two nostrils. (3.32)
The vital breath flows for three *nāḍikās* through the southern opening of the *śaṅkhinī*, and for that same duration it moves through that [opening] of living beings;
and again for that same amount of time, it flows continuously through the northern [opening].
Thus, by practicing in this sequence with the vital breath, the person who has conquered the breath,
being composed and inward-turned, should discern the divisions of time— day and night, fortnight, month, season, solstice, and so forth. (3.34–3.35)
Even by the non-perception of the throbbing of one's own limbs, such as the big toe and so forth,
through these omens (*ariṣṭa*), one should know the exhaustion of one’s own life.
Having known this, the best among those who know yoga should strive for the attainment of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*).
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Abodes of the Five Elements," in the Yoga-pāda of the Śrī Pādma-saṃhitā, within the glorious Śrī Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the fourth chapter.
On the Determination of Omens:
"O Blessed One, what are the omens of death, and how does the exhaustion of life occur through them?"
O Blessed One, you are indicated as the cause for cutting through this doubt regarding the various types of omens. 4.1a-riṣṭaprakārāḥ śrībhagavān.

If the throbbing in the big toe of the foot or the big toe of the hand ceases for one, the end of his life shall occur after one year. Likewise, if the throbbing in the wrist or the ankle ceases for one...
The duration of his life shall be six months.
For one who experiences throbbing in the elbow, the duration is three months;
likewise when throbbing is perceived in the armpit, the genitals, or the sides.
If the light [of the eyes] is like that of a firefly, his life lasts for half a month;
when the sound of digestion is heard, his life lasts for ten days;
when the light is like that of a firefly, his life lasts for half that time.
In the vision of the tongue, one's own stay [in this world] lasts for three days.
In the vision of the tip of the nose, death occurs in two days; there is no doubt at all.
These are the things to be done immediately after the knowledge of the *ariṣṭa* (signs of death).
Having seen such omens of death as these, one who seeks the cause of their cessation should apply himself to the supreme good, devoted to recitation and meditation;
[this concludes] the two methods of withdrawal.

That performance of daily obligatory rites within the self by means of the mind is to be understood as withdrawal (pratyāhāra), when practiced as a limb of yoga; or rather, it is the fixing [of the mind] upon the vital points among the eighteen varieties [of such rites]. (4.8–4.9)
Drawing [the breath] from one place to another is intended as *pratyāhāra*.
There are eighteen vital points (*marmasthāna*):
the big toe, the ankle, and likewise the middle of the calf; 4.10.
The middle of the thighs, the base [of the thighs], the anus, the heart,
the penis, the center of the body, the navel, the hollow of the throat,
the root of the palate, the root of the nose, and the sockets of the eyes.
The space between the eyebrows, the forehead, and then the head; furthermore,
the root of the two ears— O Lotus-born One, these are the vital points (marmans) characterized by meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
The fixing of the mind upon these five elements within the body composed of the five elements— that which is practiced by one disciplined in the restraints (yama) and other virtues—
is *dhāraṇā*, and it is the cause for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. (4.13–14)
Regarding the division of the locations of the five elements within the body:
the region from the knees down to the feet is held to be the location of earth; it is characterized by a predominance of bile, is quadrangular, and marked with the sign of a thunderbolt. (4.15)
Five ghaṭikās should be measured there, having applied the wind [element];
above that, O Four-faced One, is the place of water, extending to the root of the thighs,
shaped like a half-moon, white, and marked with a lotus.
One should contemplate the breath, having mounted it upon the limb for ten *nāḍikās*. The region from the navel to the center of the body is declared to be the locus of fire;
there, the fire is the color of vermilion, marked with three corners, and consists of fifteen [units]. 4.17–4.18.
One should contemplate the channels, having made the breath steady and held it through kumbhaka;
for that is indeed the station of the wind, from the navel up to the tip of the nose.
There, the elemental wind is smoke-colored and powerful, like the shape of a sacrificial altar.
One should contemplate by means of *kumbhaka* alone, having fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the wind;
for twenty *ghaṭikās*, from the nose up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmabila*).
There, in the station of space, is the ether (*nabhas*), possessing a luster like crushed collyrium.
Having ascended the wind [breath] through retention (*kumbhaka*) with effort,
the yogi should meditate upon Aniruddha-Hari, adorned and four-armed, within the *viśvabhara* portion of the body; he should worship Him for the sake of liberation from worldly existence.
The yogi of exalted intellect should fill the water-element with Nārāyaṇa;
in the fire-element, Pradyumna; thereafter, in the air-element, Saṅkarṣaṇa; and in the space-element, he should worship Vāsudeva as the Supreme Self. (4.23–4.24)
For one who applies himself to practice, there is no doubt that its attainment will occur before long.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Abodes of the Five Elements," in the Yoga-pāda of the Śrī Pādma-saṃhitā, within the illustrious Śrī Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the fifth chapter.
Having first assumed the posture of yoga and placed his joined palms at the region of the heart, the Blessed One displayed the characteristic mudrā of meditative concentration.
Fixing his gaze on the tip of the nose and placing the tongue against the palate,
not touching tooth with tooth, with his body erect and composed,
he should then withdraw the collection of sense-faculties by means of purified awareness.
The contemplation of Vāsudeva— the supreme Self,
who is both with form and without form— upon the lotus-seat of one’s own heart,
is that meditation which they always praise as bestowing the fruit of liberation.
The yogi who, through the practice of breath retention (kumbhaka), meditates upon Vāsudeva for the duration of a single watch as the fruit of his meditation,
destroys the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes. (5.4)
The locations of the states such as waking and the rest begin from the root of the navel and extend as far as the region of the heart.
One should know that the waking state resides in the heart, while the supreme dream state is located in the throat.

One should perceive deep sleep as situated in the middle of the palate, the fourth state (turya) as located between the eyebrows, and the supreme Brahman beyond the fourth (turyātīta) in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). Beginning from the states of waking and proceeding up to the interior of the aperture of Brahmā— 5.6–5.7.
Therein, the fourth state (turiya) is the arising; at the end of the fourth, Viṣṇu is spoken of.
One who is thus disciplined should meditate upon the nature of the auspicious object of meditation within the utterly pure sky. 5.8
Or one should meditate upon Adhokṣaja, who possesses the brilliance of ten million suns, who is eternally risen,
who sits within the lotus of the heart, and who has a universal form—
adorned with manifold shapes and endowed with many abodes. (5.9)
Endowed with many arms and adorned with various weapons,
the god assumes manifold forms— tranquil, fierce, and with uplifted arms;
he is covered with many eyes and possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
For the meditating yogi who maintains this, all ignorance perishes;
for consciousness is the imperishable light situated in the center of the heart-lotus,
shaped like a kadamba bud, and beyond the mandala that ends with the fourth state (turya).
Infinite, consisting of bliss, consisting of consciousness, luminous, and all-pervading;
like a lamp in a windless place, with the radiance of an uncut gem—
for the yogi who meditates upon this, liberation rests in the palm of his hand.
Whatever form indeed belongs to the god of universal form— whether it be gross,
subtle, or otherwise— the object appears directly to the yogi who meditates upon it while beholding it within the lotus of the heart.

Even the fruits such as *aṇimā* and the rest are entirely [attained]; what need is there to mention others? Samādhi is the unity of both the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*parātman*).
That should be known as *samādhi*, which accomplishes the goals of the virtuous.
Established in meditation with the thought, "I myself am the supreme Brahman," this is the method of concentration.
Becoming firm and like a pillar, he never again perceives sense objects.
Just as water entering the ocean, that motionless reservoir,
abandons its restless nature, so too the individual soul (jīva) dissolves away.
For the yogi established in samādhi within Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme self,
the means for aspiring toward the highest reality quickly sets in motion a longing for that supreme reality. (5.20)
I shall explain that method; listen, O Lotus-Seated One:
[one should worship] Hari with the supreme cognition of the Self within the twelve-syllable [mantra], upon a well-characterized wheel-lotus drawn on ground where the sun does not shine.
Seated upon a very wide kusha-grass mat on top of that,
the yogi, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) during the bright fortnight or the northern solstice,
should first restrain the breath as before.
Having kindled the fire situated in the center of the body until it blazes intensely,
one should meditate upon the eternal Brahman residing within the lotus of the heart—
resembling a thousand flashes of lightning and like the wind at the end of an eon. (5.24)
Having made his own consciousness consist of that [mantra], he should burn the entire body of the elements with the rays of that fire. Having burned it, perceiving the true nature of the mantra,
he should slowly meditate on himself seated like the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) within a liberated egg.
Even while contemplating that mantra-body— which is always composed of light, consisting of consciousness, all-pervading, and having the nature of sound— as it gradually matures,
one should then, by oneself, gradually restrain that which is unstable.
For one who has attained Brahman, there is no returning;

the yogi attains Brahman and shall not wander again in this world. (5.28) This is the conclusion of the subject matter explained, as well as the determination of the fruit for the qualified aspirant and so forth.

Thus, O Lotus-seated One, has this essence of yoga been declared for those who are constantly devoted to ritual action, whose souls are terrified of saṃsāra, and for my initiated devotees who approach me. 5.29. This is to be spoken to those who draw near.
This merit-bestowing yoga, which removes existence and grants the accomplishment of all goals—
whosoever, permitted by their teacher, studies it, goes to the supreme state.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Definition of Yoga," in the Yoga-pāda of the Śrī Pādma-saṃhitā, which is part of the Śrī Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the Kriyā-pāda of the Śrī Pādma-saṃhitā.
The First Chapter: Brahmā’s question to the Blessed One concerning the path for the ignorant regarding knowledge and yoga. Brahmā.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace:
knowledge and yoga have been heard of by us as bestowing the fruit of liberation in their entirety.
O God, those who are ignorant of these two never possess the qualification for them at any time.
And for ignorant devotees and for men who desire [liberation], as well as the goal for those seeking heaven and other such fruits—
by whatever means the fruit of nirvāṇa, or heaven and so forth, or anything else comes to be,
you ought to instruct us in that straightforward means.
If you have favor toward me, another thing must be said:
O Madhusūdana, tell me what means there is for worshipping you.
(1.4) [It is taught that] the worship of the Lord’s image in specific locations brings about all spiritual accomplishments.
The Blessed One,
having properly fashioned [the image] from wood, metal, stone, or other materials,
and having installed it in my place according to the path prescribed by the scriptures.
"O Lotus-seated One, worship me according to the procedure that shall be described.
Therefore, hear now the ritual procedure beginning with the plowing of the ground and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
I shall explain the method by which I may quickly be propitiated."
Those men who have studied the sciences, who have previously heard the scriptures,
and who are devoted to the yoga of knowledge— they worship me;
as do other devotees, though they lack such learning, yet possess great abundance.
Success arises without delay for those who establish me in my proper place;
for this knowledge and yoga, which are pure, are the sole cause of liberation.
Indeed, by establishing me in my place, a person attains the state of pure being (*sattva*).
He who, having established me in his dwelling, worships me himself—
his success is not merely his own, but also that of those who dwell in the vicinity of that place.
Therefore, O Brahmin, a person should establish me in this spot with all their soul.
The twofold nature of the locations:
two kinds of locations have been declared, distinguished by the categories of accomplished (*siddha*) and unaccomplished (*asiddha*). [Now follows] the exposition of the accomplished location.
At the base and the summit of mountains, on the banks of rivers and at their confluences,
on the seashore, on sandbanks, in lakes, at sacred fords, and in forests—
these are the places fashioned by Viśvakarman known as the seats of the Siddhas.
If I have been installed there by gods and others according to the prescribed rite,
then a place such as a city or other site constructed by humans is my unestablished shrine (asiddhāyatana). // 1.14 //
Know that the abode of the unaccomplished is caused by residing in villages and the like;
it is the form of a sacrificer who is faithful, orthodox, devoted, and possessed of an abundance of wealth and grain. (1.15)
One who possesses great energy, is pure, skillful, grateful, and free from greed—
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born in the natural order (anuloma)—
know him to be a patron (yajamāna) endowed with all these qualities.
The characteristics of the teacher to be chosen are as follows:
one who knows the Pañcarātra, is tranquil, has exerted effort in the Siddhāntas, is born of the lineage of the Blessed One, pure, free from greed, and devoid of pride and hypocrisy. (1.17)

The wise man should first choose as his preceptor that devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata) who is sinless, upright, free from disease, and possessed of unshakable faith in the Supreme. [This concludes] the examination of the ground.
On an auspicious day, the preceptor and the patron, together with an astrologer,
should first examine the omens for the establishment of a village or other settlement.
When the omens are auspicious, the wise man should begin the construction of the village and so forth.
The preceptor, who is an expert in the Pañcarātra, should perform all the rites beginning with the examination of the ground together with the chariot-maker, following the prescribed sequence.
[This concerns] the classification of the ground into the "excellent lotus" and other types.
The stages (*bhūmi*) are of four kinds: Supadmā, Bhadrakā, Pūrṇā, and Dhūmrā. I shall now teach you their characteristics in due order.
The Supadmā stage [is characterized by the fragrance] of campaka, agallochum, camphor, kadamba, tilaka, and arjuna [trees].
Covered with betel-nut trees, coconut palms, *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses,
filled with lotuses and water-lilies, auspiciously sloping toward the east and north—
that ground which is surrounded by water is celebrated as "Supadmā" (the Excellent Lotus).

The ground was auspicious, situated beside rivers and the ocean, and frequented by those seeking sacred fords; it was thickly covered with milk-exuding trees and crowded with fruit-bearing trees. (1.25)
Endowed with gardens and groves, covered with creepers and shrubs,
where there are sacrificial trees, *kuśa* grass, *kāśa* grass, and indeed fields of rice—
that land situated near underground water is known as *Bhadraka*.
The Pūrṇā ground is characterized by horse gram, neem, niṣpāpa, kodrava,
and śyāmaka; it is situated on the side of a mountain or rests upon a mountain peak.
Land that has insufficient water is proclaimed as "full" [of defects].
The "smoky" land is infested with barley, bamboo, and the like, and is filled with *snuhī* and *śleṣmātaka* plants.
Intermingled with *vibhītaka* and *arka* trees, hard and filled with gravel,
abounding in crows, hawks, and vultures, crowded with jackals and wolves, and endowed with saline soil and the like— that [land] is proclaimed as "Smoky" (*dhūmrā*). (1.29–1.30)
The distinction between the fruits of the Supadmā and other stages is as follows:
the Supadmā stage bestows peace; the Bhadrakā stage bestows happiness;
the Supūrṇā stage bestows nourishment; and the Dhūmrakā stage brings about decay. (1.31)
The examination by filling the excavated earth:
one should dig a pit in the ground one cubit deep and of corresponding width; then, one should fill it with that very same earth up to the height of the knees. (1.32)
If it is superior, the ground is excellent; if it is level, it is middling;
if it is deficient, one should know it to be inferior. A wise man should avoid such ground. (1.33) Sowing seeds upon the site of the dwelling.
Having sown seeds of rice, mung beans, barley, and so forth upon the ground,
the examiner should test whether it is fertile or otherwise;
[he should observe] where a sprout arises within three nights from the earth.
One should know that [the ground] is excellent after five nights,
middling after seven nights, or inferior if the sprout is not visible;
one should avoid inferior ground and establish [the site] on either of the other two.

Even a lowly site may sometimes be worthy of acceptance if there are kuśa grass, palāśa trees, and deer upon it; know that such a place, O Lotus-seated One, is praiseworthy despite its inferiority. 1.37

Know that the examination of the ground is performed by means of its color and other qualities; by its taste, a sweet earth is excellent, one with a pungent nature is middling, and one with other tastes is inferior—thus understand it according to its flavors. (1.38)
The best ground is white in color; the middling is yellowish-red;
the inferior should be black—this is the characteristic of the ground. 1.39 The offering of oblations.
Accompanied by a chariot-maker who is skilled in the sciences of architecture, proficient in practical crafts, and adept in the Pañcarātra system,
the Ārcāya priest should first perform the supreme *praveśabali* offering.
The preceptors, together with the patron, [should proceed] to the boundary of the site,
accompanied by dances, instrumental music, and musical instruments, as well as by reciters of auspicious verses,
full water-pots, and lamps provided with banners and parasols.

Having circumambulated [the site] clockwise by Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with knowledge, learned in the Vedas, and possessed of great erudition, and having performed rites for well-being with mantras,
one should offer oblations in all directions, starting from the east, throughout the cardinal and intermediate points.

The twice-born man should diligently offer oblations with milk-rice at the station of Brahmā to the spirits, piśācas, rākṣasas, sons of Diti, the planetary deities (grahas), the nāgas, and others as well.
Having offered the bali, one should then recite this mantra:
"May the bhūtas, piśācas, nāgas, asuras, rākṣasas, and grahas—
may they all depart, satisfied by the bali, each to their respective place."
"I shall duly prepare a place for the gods and the twice-born.

With the weapon-mantra, one should scatter everywhere white mustard seeds that have been consecrated and have fulfilled their purpose, for the sake of the divine Vāsudeva, who is the self of all beings."
Having performed the sacrificial offering (bali) according to the scriptures, one should also cast the lines;
one should then place the foundation stones there at all the intersections of the lines.
1.49 The conceptualization of the Vāstu-puruṣa.
One should place the Vāstu-puruṣa with his face downward and his head toward the east;
with both hands and feet extended, he is conceived as being situated in the corners.
Having thus meditated upon and worshipped the Puruṣa conceived as the Vāstu, [one should proceed].
On its southern side, one should perform the Vāstuhoma.
Having kindled the fire upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should offer five upaniṣadic oblations of ghee,
or a thousand, or even a hundred, for the pacification of the site (vāstu).

One should personally offer fuel-sticks of Apāmārga, Śamī, and Khadira, respectively, for the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas. Having offered one hundred and eight oblations separately with the two root mantras, one should proceed.
One should offer a hundred oblations of *caru* with the mantra of the Lord of the Site (*Vāstunātha*).

Then, having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should cast the sacrificial offering (*bali*) for Indra and the other deities in the eight directions according to their respective [mantras]. In this same manner, one should prepare the site for a village and so forth.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Acceptance of the Village," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the second chapter.

I shall now describe to you the characteristics of the villages and so forth, as well as their essential nature and their divisions, which bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life in due order. 2.1
Regarding the different designations for the dwelling places of the castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas:
"The place where Brāhmaṇas reside is called a *grāma* (village); its other name is recorded in tradition as an *agrahāra*. (2.2)
Likewise, the residence of Kṣatriyas is called a *pura* or a *nagara*;
the residence of Vaiśyas is a *pattana*, and also a *malikākulam*. These are the various names for the locations of villages.
The *daṇḍaka*, the *svastika*, the *prastara*, the *prakīrṇaka*,
the *saṃdhyāvarta*, the *patāka*, the *padma*, and the *śrīpratiṣṭhita*—
these are the varieties found in villages and other places; hear now their defining characteristics.
If the village of Daṇḍaka extends from east to west and from north to south to whatever extent it may be,
and its streets are arranged like a staff, then it is called Daṇḍaka.
Having made the Svastika-grāma with its front facing east and north, one should again create two pathways;
then, facing southward, there is an exit from the eastern pathway.
Facing west, one should exit by the southern [gate];
facing north, one should exit by the western [gate];
then, facing east, one should exit by the northern path (saumyavīthī).
In this manner, the village named Svastika is conceived;
and in exactly this same way, the emergence of all villages and so forth, such as Prastaragrāma, occurs.
(2.9) Prastaragrāma.
If there are two, four, five, six, or seven rows facing north,
combined with three facing east, it is proclaimed as the *prastara* [arrangement],
known as the *prakīrṇaka-grāma*.
With its eastern and northern ends joined by three streets,
this "scattered" (prakīrṇaka) layout should be known as the means for accomplishing one's intended purpose.
This is the Nandyāvarta village.
In the east, south, west, and likewise in the north,
as well as at the exit of the village, the arrangement is prescribed in the four directions.
By means of the thirteen [units] and so forth, each path (vīthī) shall be successively greater by one.
The *nandyāvarta* consists of five [rows] joined with five [cells] facing east.
The group of banners (*patākagrāma*) increases by one each with eighteen, and likewise by five.
With six [lines] facing north, there should be a banner; with six facing east, there is the Padmagrāma.
Of the twenty-three rows, the first five face north.
A village of lotuses (*padmagrāma*) is described as being joined with seven [streets] facing east;
a village established in glory (*śrīpratiṣṭhitagrāma*) consists of twenty-eight streets, both facing east and north.
When it is joined with eight [lines] facing east, it is called "established by Śrī.
Thus, the division of the building sites for villages and so forth has been declared in eight ways in brief.
Having divided the village and so forth into five parts, one should discard one part on the outside.

Furthermore, one should know that there are four types of portions therein: the divine (brāhma), the celestial (daiva), the human (mānuṣa), and the demonic (paiśāca); among these, the divine portion is [the first]. (2.17–2.18)

In the divisions of the earth beginning with the divine (daivika), one should arrange the celestial abodes (dhiṣṇyas); and in the human (mānuṣa) division, one should arrange the houses of the twice-born.
In the demonic (paiśāca) division, one should arrange the celestial abodes in the eight directions and in the center.
The distinction of the locations for the depositing of the embryo according to the division of villages and so forth is as follows:

the placement of the embryo in a village should be made in the center prior to the installation of the twice-born; however, in ancient cities and in fortified towns (pattana), it should be done in the direction of Indra (the east).
Thus has the placement of the embryo in the northern direction been described.
The substances to be deposited in the vessel containing the embryo are:
minerals, metals, gems, a bulbous root, a seed, and likewise earth.
Having placed [the materials] in a vessel made of iron, wood, or even clay,
having fasted, being pure, and having bathed while wearing new lower and upper garments,
one should perform the *garbhādhāna* ceremony when the proper hour (*muhūrta*) has arrived at night. (2.22)
Having taken the vessel, one should thereafter remember one's own self as Hari.
Having meditated upon the goddess Earth, one should utter this mantra;
it is the mantra for requesting the Earth.
O beloved bearer of all beings, adorned with mountains for breasts,
O Goddess clothed by the ocean, take up this embryo;
may there be protection for the deposited embryo.
Then, having properly filled the pit on all sides with earth,
one should vigilantly perform protection for five nights or three nights;
[this is] the teacher’s fee.
One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) with faith to the teacher who has established the agrahāra— either one hundred *niṣkas*, or half of that, or even half of that again.
It is traditionally taught that in the case of cities and other such locations, the sacrificial fee should be two or three times a *niṣka*.
After the depositing of the embryo, the twice-born should be lodged in the house;
once the depositing of the embryo has been performed, one should subsequently lodge the twice-born in the house at the site of the deity Vāstu.
The wise one should duly install the deities of the site (vāstudevas) in their proper sequence.
For the installation of the fivefold form of Hari in a village or similar location, the five great sacrifices (pañcayajña) and other rites become fruitful;
therefore, one should install Hari in his fivefold form in the center of the village.
In this way, this fivefold sacrifice of the Brahmins attains its fulfillment.
For the sake of the success of the four stages of life (āśramas), one should worship either the fourfold form,
or the single form that encompasses all purposes, in the center of the village.
One should have the Lord Acyuta fashioned as either a yogin or a possessor of enjoyments;
one should worship him whether he is seated, reclining, or standing.
The bed of enjoyment of the God of gods is proclaimed to be the creator of the universe.
One should not worship the dissolution, nor the bed of enjoyment, nor the body of Narahari; one should not worship the son of Jamadagni,
nor the god who bears the universal form, nor the son of Jamadagni.
The difference in results arises from the different directions of the gates:
O Sage, the eastern gate bestows happiness; the western gate increases prosperity;
the northern gate bestows wealth; and the southern gate grants liberation.
The determination of the locations and doors for Bhāskara and the others:
one should designate the location of Bhāskara in the northeast (Aindra) with a western door;
one should designate the location of Madana in the southeast (Pāvaka) with a western door.
To the south of the Subrahmaṇya [shrine], there should be the dwelling for the eastern gate.
To the southwest, one should arrange the eastern gate for Vighnarāja;
in the west, one should install Viṣṇu, standing together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
One should visualize him as seated, endowed with splendor, or indeed mounted upon Garuḍa; one may likewise imagine him bearing the universal form (viśvarūpa) or reclining upon a couch of enjoyments.
One should fashion him facing eastward, while the temple of Viṣṇu is situated to the west.
In the west, however, the wise one should likewise arrange the place for Śrī;
or else, he should designate the place for Durgā in the northwest, facing the east.
And in the north, he should designate the place for the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), together with Jambhala and others.
One should designate the station of Īśvara in the northeast, either between Soma and Īśāna, or between Indra and Īśāna; one should not conceive of it elsewhere.
And one should place Mahāmoṭī in the southeast, situated at a great distance from the village.
And in the southwest, the Teacher is situated at a greater distance from the village;
and on the northern side of the village, situated somewhat further away,
should be the Mātṛ-sthāna, where all those goddesses face north.
The house should be situated in the northeast, or not too far from the Mothers' [shrine],
or in the southeast, or toward the northwest (between Vāyu and Soma).

There is a prohibition against building houses, temples, and so forth at the points where the cord falls, the trident-mark, the intersection of the threads, the junctions of the watches of the day, and the like.
In all places where a rope descends, at tridents, and at the joints of threads,
one should not establish a divine shrine, especially at the front of the pathways.
Furthermore, houses should never be constructed there by one who desires the prosperity of their lineage.
If, through negligence, one should perform [the rites] among them, there would be the destruction of the village and so forth.

(2.45) The worship of Hari in the midst of the village, along with the ritual application of mantras and so on, serves as the expiation for all omissions— whether there be a lapse in the mantra, a lapse in the ritual action, or in rites such as those for the gods (*havya*) and ancestors (*kavya*).
His expiation shall be the worship of Hari in the midst of the village.
Regarding the specific fruits of worshipping the retinue of Bhāskara and the others:
by propitiating Bhāskara, no disease arises in the village.
Through the worship of Kāma, the qualities of good fortune, gentleness, and beauty [are attained].
Through the worship of Guha, malevolent spirits and the like do not afflict men.
Through the worship of Vighnarāja, all obstacles are destroyed. (2.47–2.48)
One should worship Viṣṇu in the western quarter (Vāruṇī), who bestows the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
one should constantly worship the goddess Durgā for the increase of longevity. Through the service of Kubera, there shall be an abundance of wealth and grain.
Through the worship of Śiva, all men shall become possessed of knowledge.
Through the worship of Moṭī, no calamity shall befall children.
And through the worship of the Teacher, the inhabitants of the village shall prosper.
By the constant worship of the Mother, the Piśācas will never cause affliction.
One should not install Hari between a city wall and a jasmine vine; one should not place Hari in the middle of either the city or the jasmine vine. (2.52)

Among those born of anuloma unions, there is a prohibition against worshipping Hari; one should not worship Hari among those born of anuloma unions in the context of the household deity (vāstu). There is also a prohibition for Śūdras and others regarding the deity of the dwelling place.
For Śūdras and those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), there is neither a consecrated site (vāstu) nor a presiding deity.
If, through lack of discrimination, a king were to allow this, both the kingdom and the king himself would perish.
