This is a prohibition against the ritual preparation of sites and deities for the purpose of village festivals and the like.
One should not designate the deities of the site (vāstudeva) for the purpose of a festival for the gods in a village or similar location.
For those who are independent do not designate their own limbs as if they were separate from the possessor of the limbs;
[if they were so designated], they would become hostile toward the subjects and the kingdom.

In all the intermediate spaces, as well as in all the cardinal and intermediate directions, the wise man should cause the temple of the Blessed One to be built for the forms of Keśava and others, and likewise for the Fish-incarnation and others, throughout the village and other areas.
One should not gaze upon a village, nor at one who is fierce, nor at one with raised fierce weapons;
likewise, one should not look at the son of Jamadagni, nor at a man-lion, nor at the bed of dissolution, nor at a bed of enjoyment, nor indeed at a place of enjoyment. (2.57–2.58)
One should cause the Bhogāsana, the bed known as Sṛṣṭi, and the vehicle endowed with ritual action (kriyā) to be constructed everywhere. However,
within a village, there is a prohibition against the installation (nyāsa) of the Trident-bearer (Śūlin).
One should not establish a shrine for the trident-bearing God within a village;
otherwise, the village will perish before long, as will the king and the kingdom.
Therefore, one should place the Lord of Umā at a great distance from villages and other such settlements.
According to the distinction of deities, there is a distinction among worshippers;
having thus established the deities of the directions, the worshipper should perform the worship in due order.
For Viṣṇu, [the worship] should be performed by the Bhāgavatas alone who are devoted to the Pañcarātra.
Worship should not be performed by those who worship ordinary deities or mothers;
rather, the worship of Śiva should be performed by those who know the Śiva-śāstras and by Śiva-dvijas.
The worship of the Sun should be performed by the best of the twice-born, the Soma-pās. (2.62–2.63)

The twice-born Śivadvija should worship Madana, Gaṇanātha, and Subrahmaṇya; he is considered a Brahmin worthy of being a priest for the worship of Dhanada and the others. A true devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavata) himself should always worship the goddess Durgā.
The worship of the Mothers should likewise be performed by those who know it, as well as by the Pāraśavas.
The potter should always worship the Teacher and Mahāmoṭī. The goldsmiths and Ambaṣṭhas should have their dwellings established within the village.
One should establish within the village those skilled in the arts of goldsmiths and Ambaṣṭhas;
for others, such as those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), one should provide a dwelling outside the village.
In the eastern direction, there shall be the settlement of those who follow the natural order (*anuloma*) among the ritual performers (*karmiṇ*).
For all those who follow the inverse order (*pratiloma*), their placement is prescribed toward the south and other directions.
Even beyond the guilds (*śreṇī*) and at a great distance, the *caṇḍālas* are traditionally held to dwell in the southwest (*nairṛta*).
In general, the cremation ground is located far to the north of the village, near a body of water;
for the twice-born, there is a specific location within the cremation ground.
On the southern bank of the lake, there shall be a cremation ground for the twice-born. For all those born in the natural order (anuloma), cremation takes place on the eastern and other banks;
for others born in the inverse order (pratiloma), they know the directions to be the east and so forth [in reverse].
In this manner, one should fashion a village, a city, or even a family;
such a person attains liberation and is not born here again.
Those mortals who assist with material goods or through their mental disposition [attain the same].
Those lords of the earth who protect villages and other settlements as ordained dwell in the heavenly world for the duration of a kalpa.
They attain incomparable fame and reside upon the vault of heaven.
And those men who cause agitation are born into the wombs of dogs.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Layout of Villages and Other Settlements," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Mahopaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra tradition.
Chapter Three:
The Procedure for Constructing Temples.
O Brahmin, I shall describe for you the construction of a temple; listen to that.
Having reached the ground previously described, one should perform the consecration of the site for the purpose of plowing, preceded by the entry-offering (praveśabali). 3.1
Having circumambulated the ground clockwise, one should utter this mantra:
"O Yakṣas, Piśācas, and Nāgas who always dwell here—may you all depart elsewhere; I am preparing a place for Viṣṇu."
Then, one should scatter white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*) that have been consecrated by the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) in every direction.
As before, one should perform the *vāstu-homa* as well as the *vāstu-bali*.
Regarding the oxen, there is a distinction of colors according to the classes [of the patrons], such as Brāhmaṇas and farmers.
Then the Bhāgavata preceptor should plow the ground with a plough.
A Brāhmaṇa should be the sacrificer; the ox should be white for a Brāhmaṇa, red for a Kṣatriya, yellow for a Vaiśya, and black for a Śūdra.
If the aforementioned colors cannot be obtained, however, they may be tawny or even fair;
the two bulls should be considered large, red-colored, and powerful.
One should wash their hooves, horns, and so forth, and adorn them with gold and other ornaments.
There is a variety of ploughs and yokes according to the social classes of the cultivators: a plough and a yoke made of *pālāśa* wood are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
those of a Kṣatriya should be made of *nyagrodha* wood, and those of a Vaiśya and a Śūdra should be made of *plākṣa* wood. (3.7)
The Nyagrodha and Pippala trees should serve as the two plow-shares for all [classes].
For all castes indeed, the Kuśika [plow-handle] should be made of gold;
their yoke-tie, moreover, should be silver or copper, according to the order [of the castes]. (3.8–3.9)
Kuśa grass, vīraṇa grass, and kāśa grass—these may be used for bowstrings, ropes, and the like made from them;
one may likewise have a plough and a threshing post fashioned from the same material.
This is the equipment for the limbs of a farmer. (3.10)
Having bathed, wearing new garments and a turban, pure and self-possessed,
adorned with garlands and unguents, and provided with an upper garment and finery,
the preceptor himself, being thus decorated, should then wash the [disciple's] feet.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma), and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules,
he should then begin the cultivation after being authorized by the best of the twice-born;
the yoking of the pair of ploughs and so forth should be done with a mantra, preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Having had the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) proclaimed by Vaiṣṇavas who are most skilled in mantras,
one should fasten the yoke to the shoulder of the bull with the Root-Vidyā;
and with that same Vidyā, one should fasten the plow to the yoke.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, standing facing the east, he should have [the image] drawn;
and he should cause drums, kettledrums, conchs, and other instruments to sound in all directions.
O Brahmins, let them recite the Śākunika Sūkta, which bestows peace upon all.
And one should meditate upon me in the lotus of the heart with the eye of the form of the Vidyā.
One should fashion a staff and a carriage from trees such as the *pālāśa*. This is the procedure for plowing.
Having taken up the goad, one should then press down with *huṃ phaṭ* and so forth.
O Brahmin, facing east, one should first plow the ground with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), and the second plowing of the site should be done with the *Puruṣasūkta*. (3.17–3.18)
The third [plowing] is with the Viṣṇu-sūkta; the fourth with its Gāyatrī;
the fifth is recorded as the plowing with the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka.
The sixth, the plowing of the ground, should be performed with the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
The best of instructors should plow the seventh [line] with the Bhūmisūkta.
O Lotus-seated One, the furrow (sītā) should follow the clockwise sequence;
likewise, one who knows the Pañcarātra should plow from south to north.
At that time, the supreme guide should examine the signs;
the satisfaction of the guide’s mind at that moment will lead to well-being. (3.22)
Know that destruction occurs through the opposite of these conditions for both the temple and the sacrificer:
when the oxen lie down, when the yoke and other parts break, when there is a reversal of order, when an error is made regarding the Brahmin, and likewise upon the appearance of an ill omen. (3.23)
If the thread is cut while the meaning remains, the death of the master is certain.
If it is cut during the third part, there will certainly be an upheaval in the kingdom;
even if it is cut during the fourth part, it is said that the performer shall suffer a fall.
In the event of an ill omen, one should perform a pacification rite with the five Upaniṣads by offering oblations of ghee one hundred times;
all those defects will be stilled, and the performer shall not encounter misfortune. (3.26)
The preceptor, acting as the sacrificer, should feed the Brahmins with wealth;
he, surrounded by great effort, should level the ground and perform the sowing of seeds upon that tilled earth. (3.27)
Having prepared separate basins provided with water-channels,
one should sow seeds such as rice, barley, and so forth therein.
The field should be irrigated daily with a great quantity of water.
And one should diligently provide protection until the stage of full ripening.
When it is ripe, one should harvest that field and bring the herds of cattle there;
this is the result of the increase or decrease of the fruit.
When the fruit is great, that abode of Hari shall endure for a long time;
but when it is small, the presence of Hari in the palace will last for a shorter time.
When devoid of fruit, the abode will have its wealth and grain completely exhausted.
There, one should feed a thousand or even a hundred Brahmins;
after they have eaten, one should give wealth, such as cows and other gifts, to those Brahmins. (3.32) This is the purification of the ground.
One should sprinkle the ground with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the five Upaniṣads;
or, using spades or digging tools, one should dig into the earth as far as water is reached, extending as wide as the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa). 3.33.
O Lotus-Seated One, one should dig a pit as deep as a staff's length,
or in proportion to the defects of the site, even when constructing the height of the temple;
if husks, charcoal, or similar items are found, a propitiatory rite (śānti) must be performed.
When the ground is being dug up, if ashes, charcoal, husks, and so forth are found,
or if malevolent beings are encountered, such as the sight of worms, insects, and the like,
the preceptor should perform a fire offering with ghee and other substances for their pacification. (3.35–3.36)
One should give gold and other wealth to Brahmins according to one's ability.
Upon obtaining jewels and such, there shall be prosperity;
by seeing jewels and such, one’s abode shall always be filled with abundance. (3.37)
The procedure for establishing the fire-pot and so forth:

having dug the pit and performed the external oblation on a square sacrificial mound outside the pit, the preceptor, having established and kindled the fire, should perform the rite with clarified butter. (3.38)
Furthermore, with the root mantra and the Puruṣasūkta, one should offer oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru),
guggulu resin, sesame, and nīvāra grain using the root vidyā-mantra.
Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should cast śāli rice into the pit.
Around the jars [should be placed] grains of rice wrapped in threads, cloth, and so forth.
The jars are said to be made of iron, but in their absence, they may be earthen.
Having fashioned the Ādhāraśakti out of gold, one should place it inside the jar.
Thereafter, one should deposit seeds into the central jar,
all types of metals in the eastern jar, and all minerals in the southeastern jar.
One should place earth from sacred bathing sites in the southwestern jar, and again in the western jar.
One should fill the pitcher of the wind [quarter] with honey, and that of the fire [quarter] with ghee.
In the pitcher of the lord of wealth (northeast), one should place jewels; in the pitcher of the northeast (or center), earth from a mountain;
and likewise, one should place earth from a field of śāli rice in the central pitcher.
Standing facing the east, one should cast into [the vessel] earth from a termite mound that has arisen in a lake that never dries up, as well as the bulbs of blue lotuses and other such plants;
likewise, one should place iron and gems, and a bundle of *darbha* grass.
One should also place [the vessel] with a shallow bowl and worship it in due order.
Upon the central jar, one should set another jar;
having fashioned a tortoise and the Fire of Time (Kālāgni), one should deposit gold therein.
Having placed the third jar, one should pour the form of Ananta into it;
for the fourth, the support of the earth, one should place a pot on top.
Having filled those jars with scented water, one should worship them.

One should fill it with sacred earth from a pit that has not been defiled by impurities, and also with sand; one should fill it up to the top with water. Having made it firm with the feet of elephants, one should fill it again with water.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Ploughing," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the Pāñcarātra.
[Now begins] the fourth chapter.
The Question on the Means for Averting Obstacles:
O Janārdana, when a temple or a village and so forth is being commenced...
"O Blessed One, tell me how there may be peace for those Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Dānavas who create obstacles.
Is the pacification of obstacles achieved through the worship of the Blessed One in the temple of a child?"
The wise one, having first constructed a house for the child, should worship me there;
by that, all those who create obstacles will certainly be pacified. (4.2)

And a village or similar settlement is completed without obstacle in a very short time. [The construction of a child’s house and so forth should be done] either between Indra and Īśāna, or between Soma and Īśāna.
Either between Indra and Agni, or between Agni and Yama;
between Yama and Nirṛti, or between Nirṛti and Varuṇa;
between Varuṇa and Vāyu, or between Vāyu and Soma. (4.4–4.5)
According to their preference, one should determine the site for these [temples] with respect to the location;
one should know that the house for the children (the temple) should measure seven, five, or three cubits.
It should be constructed in the direction from the base of the main edifice toward the east.
One should likewise conceive of the door of the *bālālaya* in that very same place.
Regarding the measurement of the image to be worshipped in the *bālālaya*:
the image in the *bālālaya* may be made of metal, stone, or wood.
It has four arms bearing the divine weapons—the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus.
(4.8) The height of that image is traditionally held to decrease by five finger-breadths, while it increases by twenty-three finger-breadths. (4.9)
Whatever form brings happiness to the sacrificer, that should be [the form] of the deity.

In the incarnations beginning with the Fish and others, starting from the ritual manuals (*kalpa*), it should likewise be so in the temple; even in the childhood abode (*bālālaya*), the four-armed Viśvarūpa should be present.

One should arrange either a vehicle within a vehicle, or even its placement [therein]. Having consecrated that image in water, one should then consecrate it in the pavilion; this is the preparation of the altar.
In the center of the foundation of the temple, or in a divine portion,
the Guru, having constructed an altar three cubits high and provided with three tiers of girdles, at the clear dawn during an auspicious moment, [should proceed].
One should place the image of the Child upon the altar with the root mantra;
having established Hari there, one should assign the mantra according to the prescribed rite. (4.14) The Petition to the Blessed One.
The best of preceptors should pray for the presence of Hari in the child’s chamber from the very foundation until the time of the final dissolution:
"O Blessed One, please accept worship in this abode of the child."
"Subduing the lineage of Daityas who cause obstacles to the primary abode. Having thus requested the arrangement of the retinue and having bowed, one should fashion the retinue.
At the door, one should assign Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, as well as Kṣetrapāla and Khageśvara;
one should also assign Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas) to their respective directions.
One should worship Seneśa in the northeast corner and Gaṇeśa in the southwest.
A wise person should worship the bodiless deities upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
As for the measurement of the mound, the mound should be one cubit in size and provided with three girdles (*mekhalā*). (4.19)
Having made it either circular or square, one should perform worship there;
one should worship all the hosts beginning with Kumuda upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha).
One should perform everything from the hoisting of the banner until the conclusion of the flower sacrifice in the temple of Bāla.
Having established [the deity] in this manner, the wise one should perform a great festival at the conclusion;
it should begin with the hoisting of the banner and end with the flower sacrifice.
Alternatively, he may perform the festival for a single day in the temple of the Child.
If there is an image of the Child made of iron, one should perform the festival with that very [image].
The daily, occasional, and optional rites should take place in the temple of the Child;
in the absence of a festival image, one should perform the festival with the image of the Child alone.
If the image is not for the sake of a festival, the festival itself would be performed with a child [image] alone.
Regarding the prohibition of the fourth bathing during a festival with a child image:
"In that case, one should not perform the installation, nor likewise the fourth bathing. (4.24)
Regarding the distinctions of the *ālaya* as superior and so forth, the chariot-maker should begin the construction of the *ālaya* together with the master builders;
the primary type is a house made of stone, while the middling type is made of brick and similar materials. (4.25)
One should know that [a shrine] made of wood is inferior, while one made of clay is said to be rejectable;
there is a distinction between those constructed with accumulated materials and those not so accumulated, due to the combination of various substances such as stone, both single and multiple. (4.26)

The bound [structure] may be either accumulated (*sañcita*) or unaccumulated (*asañcita*), or indeed "well-accumulated" (*upasañcita*). That which is conceived by means of a single substance from the base up to the pinnacle should be known as the best; that is the accumulated. When there is a pair of substances, it is unaccumulated. (4.27)

That which is made of clay, wood, and so forth, is called the middle dwelling; that which is constructed with stone and wood like a womb (garbha) is declared to be the lowest abode, for there is a fault in the construction of such a residence.
One should avoid stones or timber containing a living embryo for the construction of a temple;
if one were to use such materials, the patron would undoubtedly become afflicted with disease.
Furthermore, there is an even greater fault in taking stones and other materials from the dwelling of another deity.
One should not take stones or other materials belonging to the abode of another deity.
By building a residence with such materials, one destroys one's own lineage;
one is cooked in a terrible hell and is reborn among the wombs of dogs.

Even stone and such materials taken from monasteries, wells, or tanks are unfit to be accepted; he who does so is cooked in a terrible hell and is born poor. (4.32) Likewise, wood, stone, or bricks from the temple of Vāsudeva [are forbidden].
Having taken [the property], the builder of the temple becomes a vessel for nothing but suffering;
in turn, he shall go to the most terrible and exceedingly dreadful hells.
In those sufferings, that man is cooked perpetually, turn after turn.
Regarding the fruit of constructing a temple with wealth acquired through just or unjust means:
"The sacrificer obtains inexhaustible fruit by building an abode for Hari with wealth accumulated through righteous means; of this there is no doubt. (4.35)
The fruit [of their actions] is consumed by the asuras with wealth acquired through unjust means;
having viewed them as equal to water, and having placed the primordial nature upon the earth, one should view it as equal to water. (4.36)
Having placed the first plank upon that [foundation] with the eye of the scriptures,
and having made it firm with mortar, one should ensure its levelness with water. (4.37) [This concludes] the arrangement of the pedestal and so forth.
Having constructed the *upapīṭha*, the supreme *adhiṣṭhāna* should be placed above it;
or even without an *upapīṭha*, the arrangement of the *adhiṣṭhāna* may be made.
Alternatively, one should first fashion the *adhiṣṭhāna* as the sole base.

One should construct the base (pāda), the platform (prastara), the neck (grīvā), and likewise the pinnacle (śikhara) in their proper sequence, as far as necessary for the layout of the floor-plates (talaka) until they are satisfied;
these constituent parts should be designed starting from two stories up to twelve stories.
In a two-storied temple,

one should fashion the foundation, the base, the plinth, the pinnacle, the hall, the structural arrangement, the cage-like lattice, the upper floor, the altar, the neck, and the spire in successive order. (4.40–4.41)
The first [measurement] for the *tritala* and other celestial palaces (*vimāna*) extends up to ten stories;
having thus conceived [the proportions] as prescribed in the scriptures, one should apply them to others as well.
The limbs of the eighteen-fold abode [are as follows].
The *upāna*, the *jagatī*, the *kumuda*, and likewise the *paṭṭikā*;
the *kaṇṭha* and the *paṭṭikā*, as well as the *caraṇa* and the *talottara*;
the *haṃsamālā*, the *kapota*, the *prati*, and the *prativedikā*.

The wise one, having first completed the construction on a cloth or similar surface, should then fashion the neck and the pinnacle (śikhara) in sequence with eighteen parts, extending to the top of the dome (sthūpī) of the temple, or according to the requirements of the patron. 4.44–45.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Construction of the Śikhara," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra;
[now begins] the fifth chapter.
Regarding the examination of the directions:
the Blessed One should first examine the eastern direction according to the method prescribed in the scriptures.
The rule for the doors and so forth is desired according to the division of directions such as the east;
the installation of the *śaṅku* (stake) involves a stake one cubit long, or indeed twelve finger-breadths.
One should place a straight and auspicious staff made from a milky tree, with a circumference equal to the thumb,
in the center of the site of the temple by means of the root-mantra.
One should then draw a mandala all around it, measuring twice the size of the *śaṅku*.
At the edge of the mandala, one should mark the shadow of the gnomon in the forenoon and afternoon.
Having fixed two points, one should draw a thread situated from east to west.
The distance between the two points should be taken as the body of a tortoise, with its mouth at one end and its tail at the other.
When the thread has been thus leveled,
one should write the first word "uttarādi" (beginning with the north) as the boundary-thread (*sīmāsūtra*) that was previously established toward the north.
One should likewise write the boundary-thread in the eight directions according to the proper rule.
One should construct it measuring three, five, or seven cubits, or even more according to one's desire;
one should arrange the layout of its lines for the prosperity of the village site.
Then, by means of rotation, one should bring the directional line to form a perfect square.
One should perform the installation of the gnomon in the eight directions according to the rule. (5.8) At the time of installing the gnomon, one should observe the omens;
if they are auspicious, one attains success, but if they are inauspicious, one should perform a rite of pacification. (5.9)
Regarding the description of the architectural form of a palace:
one should construct a palace of four types—quadrangular, perfectly circular, oblong quadrangular, or oblong circular. (5.10)
The postures for standing and sitting are square and circular;
they may be oval, well-rounded, or even oblong and square. (5.11) One should likewise arrange the bed there in a form that is multiform.

The wise man should there fashion the Lord of the lords of gods, who has transcended the world (lokakrānta). In this manner, the learned one should cause the temple to be built according to the proportions of the image;
the measurement of the residence of Viṣṇu shall be by means of an odd number of cubits.
Indeed, beginning from one cubit up to ten cubits, one should construct the temple of Hari using an odd number of cubits;
or, for one desiring liberation, it may be even, while for one desiring worldly enjoyment, it should be odd. (5.13–5.14)
Having measured out the dimensions according to the desires of others, up to twelve stories in height and in accordance with their wealth,
one should have a celestial mansion (vimāna) constructed there according to the prescribed rules.
Having done this, one who knows the science of architecture should begin with the first brick;
as for the varieties of bricks, bricks are said to be of three kinds: made of stone, wood, or clay. (5.16)
According to the requirements of the temple structure, there is a distinction regarding the first brick:
in temples made of stone, the first brick shall be stone;
when constructing a dwelling with wood, the first brick shall likewise be of that same material. (5.17)
In a temple made of bricks, one should use well-baked bricks;
likewise, in a fire-altar (dhiṣṇya) built with unbaked bricks, the first brick is the same.
In a structure composed of both stone and bricks, the first brick should be a stone.
In the case of a structure joined with bricks and wood, the first brick is called the *iṣṭakā*.
Regarding stone, there is a distinction based on gender and so forth, as well as its specific application;
in the place where the stones are collected, it should be preceded by the perfuming (*sādhivāsa*) ceremony.
Having gathered the stone there, one should examine its gender, whether masculine and so forth.
(5.20) With a masculine stone, [the structures] from the footwear up to the stupa should be made; likewise, with a neuter stone, one should make the crowning stone (*mūrdhaśilā*). (5.21)
There is loss in accepting an image that possesses defects;

an image should be accepted as being like wood—free from defects and possessing excellent qualities—if it is not made with the prescribed characteristics, whether out of greed or even through ignorance. (5.22)
The destruction of the king and his kingdom is certain for both the one who acts and the one who causes it to be done.
Now I shall fully explain the procedure for bricks made of clay; indeed, I shall describe the rule for bricks in the case of those made of clay. (5.23)
Having reached the place indicated by the chariot-maker,
the guide should there offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter into the blazing fire with the root mantra,
and furthermore, eight oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Nṛsūkta.
One should offer fuel-sticks while reciting the root mantra; likewise,
one should further perform oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) for the attendants of Viṣṇu,
as well as for the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), the spirits (bhūtas), and the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) himself.
For the deities, the sages, and likewise for the host of gods,

the wise man, having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*, using mantras according to their respective characteristics and ending with *svāhā*, should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
And in the four directions, beginning with the east, one should perform the offering of the *caru* oblation with this mantra ending in "namas," in due order,
for Viṣṇu’s attendants and for all beings. (5.29)
Having likewise offered [oblations] to the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) and to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla),
one should then cast away the fire; thus, when the initial oblation and other rites have been performed,
the rule for the construction of the bricks is fulfilled.
The potter, facing east, should prepare the clay, earth, and bricks there.
Regarding the nature of the bricks as masculine and so forth, and their application,
their classification is prescribed according to the division of masculine gender and the rest.
Where the line is straight or odd-numbered, that brick is masculine;
where the line is transverse or even-numbered, that brick is feminine.
A brick without a line, or one with a line at the tip or at the two corners, is neuter. (5.32–5.33)
A masculine *iṣṭakā* is not prescribed for the *garbhādhāna*;
one should perform the foundation (*pīṭhikā*) beginning with the *garbhādhāna* using a feminine *iṣṭakā*.
A wise man should construct the temple (*prāsāda*) using a masculine *iṣṭakā*.
Regarding the measurement of the bricks:
the best should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length;
furthermore, the middling should be eighteen finger-breadths in length, and the smallest sixteen finger-breadths.

The width should be half the length, and its thickness is desired to be half of that. The bricks for the covering should have a width equal to their length; one should determine the measurement of such bricks according to the nature of the ground.
One should know this measurement of the brick as the *mahīmāna* (great measurement); now the *alpamāna* (small measurement) is being declared.
The width is desired to be equal to the width of the base of the temple (*prāsādapāda*). (5.38)
The wise one should fashion bricks with a length that is twice their width;
in this same manner, the measurement for stones and timber applies to structures made of wood and stone. (5.39) These are the qualities of bricks.

Well-baked, resonant, resembling a ripe bimba fruit in color, very firm, even, and uniform in hue—such a brick is praised as the first and most beneficial; other bricks are to be rejected. (5.40) Bricks to be avoided.

O Brahmin, one should avoid bricks for the commencement of a temple that are associated with an inauspicious time-circle, or those that are broken, cracked, crooked, or fissured. This is the number of the first bricks for both divine and human dwellings.
One should place four initial bricks in a temple for the deities;
for the dwelling of mortals, one should arrange five initial bricks.
In a structure built of baked bricks, the first brick should be a baked one.
In the fire-chamber constructed with the first layer of bricks, the first [rite] must not be otherwise.
For the purpose of consecrating the bricks, there is the offering of sprouts, the placement of the water-pot, and so forth;
one should first offer the sprouts during the rite of consecration (*adhivāsana*).
In one of the four directions, specifically in the eastern quarter,
he should construct a water-shed adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and provided with sixteen pillars;
there, he should prepare an altar seven *alā* long and one cubit high.
Then, having placed a pedestal in the center made of three *bhāras* of *śāli* rice,
one should fashion it either circular or square, O Four-faced One, according to one's preference.
The medium size is prescribed with two [parts], and the inferior with one.
One should place the jar, wrapped with threads and the like, upon a pedestal of grain.
One should then set eight jars around it in the eight directions.
To the north of that jar, which is filled with water, the preceptor [should proceed].
One should prepare a grain-seat (*dhānyapīṭha*) of that same measure;
half of it filled with rice, and half of that with sesame seeds.
It should be strewn thickly with *darbha* grass and adorned with a new cloth.

Having thus performed the consecration of the bricks for that purpose, the supreme preceptor should first bathe the bricks and then place nine water-pots upon a well-prepared pedestal of rice, one in the center and one in each of the eight directions.
One should pour clarified butter into the central jar, milk into the eastern one;
curd into the southeast, molasses into the southern, and likewise into the southwest;
the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or fruit juice into the western and northwest jars.
Having placed fragrant water in the north, iron-water in the northeast, and honey in the auspicious [east],
and having wrapped it with a new cloth, one should worship it;
this is the consecration by bricks.
Having placed the bricks upon the pedestal, one should bathe them with water-pots in due order.
First, one should bathe them with milk and ghee while reciting the *Sāman* hymns;
thereafter, one should bathe them with milk, and then bathe them with sugarcane juice while reciting the mantra "madhu vātā."
One should bathe [the image] with water containing fruit using the *phalinī* hymn;
one should bathe it with molten metal water using the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra;
then, one should bathe it well with curd using the *dadhi krāvṇa* Yajus formula.
One should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) with the mantra beginning "pañcavāruṇikā" (5.57).
One should bathe it with scented water using the mantra "gandhadvārā" (5.57).
One should perform the honey-bath with the mantra "madhuvātā" (5.58).
With the *sāman* chant "dhṛtasāmnā," one should indeed bathe [the image] with clarified butter;
then, one should wrap each [image] individually with a new cloth and encircle it with *darbha* grass.
Having taken hold of all the bricks, one should place them upon the bed.
One should perform the fire-oblation for the purpose of acceptance,
and fully adorn the arches, the pitchers at the gates, and the banners.
In the central pitcher, the four-faced Supreme Self is to be invoked.
One should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Viṣṇu in the other eight jars.
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) or rice with jaggery (gulodana) into the great jar.
One should prepare the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in either the eastern or the northern direction.
Or, having brought fire to a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should offer oblations with fuel-sticks and other materials;
one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds, and flowers separately one hundred and eight times each.
One should then offer oblations with the root mantra and the hymn (sūkta), and furthermore, the sacrificial porridge (caru).
The preceptor should touch all the bricks with the clarified butter from the *saṃpāta* oblation.
He should bind them with the *homasūtra*, with *pratisara* threads, and with the *astra-mantra*,
or alternatively with other materials such as cotton or silver, according to his means.
One should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the mantra of Svapnādhipati.
For the examination of dreams and their meaning, the sacrificer should lie down together with the preceptor.
Upon seeing an evil dream, one should abandon the construction of that house;
but if the dream is auspicious, one should begin the building without delay.
On the following day, at an auspicious moment, the preceptor, having laid the bricks, [should proceed].
And the best of instructors should cause those well-consecrated bricks to be brought into the palace from the storage place for the bricks,
located to the south of the prepared entrance.
One should cast those [bricks] below the base of the pillar and cause musical instruments and the like to be sounded.
Having had the *svastika* recited and having satisfied the Brahmins with wealth,
there is this specific distinction regarding the laying of the bricks for both the abodes of gods and humans.
In the temple of the gods, one should place the bricks in a clockwise direction, beginning with Indra and ending with Soma;
however, for the abode of humans, one should place them from the middle to the end using the root mantra dedicated to the deity in the human dwelling. (5.70–5.71)
The laying of the bricks is performed with the Śrīsūkta; the presiding deities of the bricks are the Goddesses.
They possess four forms, but in human [practice], they have five forms.
Their base is toward the south and west, and their tip is toward the east and north.
If there is an inequality in the placement of the sandals, a loss of bricks will occur;
if the placement of the bricks becomes uneven, it results from the sandals being placed unevenly. If this occurs through delusion or ignorance, it is caused by the fear of such irregularity.
Therefore, one should first cast bricks resembling sandals.
Regarding the examination of the pit filled with water and whirlpools:
having first worshipped Ādideva, one should fill the pit with water.

When the pit has been filled to the brim with various kinds of gems, grains, metals, and flowers, one should examine the whirlpool of water. A clockwise rotation is auspicious, whereas a counter-clockwise rotation is inauspicious.
If the water placed in a chasm should dry up immediately, there will be the ruin of the temple, the sacrificer, and others;
even that temple already begun shall not reach completion. (5.77)

Either the sacrificer dies, or there will be a calamity for the kingdom. When such inauspicious omens occur, [the result] will likewise be inauspicious; but when they are auspicious, the result will be good.
For the success of an undertaking depends upon the satisfaction of the mind.

The satisfaction of the guide’s mind always brings about all prosperity; likewise, his dissatisfaction would bring about calamity. In the case of ill omens, there should be propitiatory fire-offerings and other rites.
In all cases of ill omens, the preceptor should perform oblations for the sake of pacification;
he should feed Brahmins and give gold according to his capacity.
He should also cast the bulbous root of the blue lotus (*utpala*) or the red lotus (*aravinda*) into a pit.
With the earth from a sacred bathing place and from a field of rice paddies,
one should fill that pit with the root mantra and cover it.
[This concludes] the sacrificial fee for the preceptor and the others.
The king should give a teacher’s fee consisting of one hundred *niṣkas*;
for all others as well, the minimum should be ten *niṣkas*.
Having thus established those very foundation bricks in their proper places, [he should proceed] as before.
O Brahmin, for the sake of pacification, the wise man should perform oblations and have a celestial mansion constructed.
Regarding the fruit of constructing a temple for the gods:
merely by the resolve, "I shall build a temple for the gods," [the merit is attained].
Evil accumulated over hundreds of births is destroyed instantly within the body.
(5.85) If a mortal begins the construction of a temple but dies before completing it, he still enjoys the full fruit of a completed house. (5.86)
Therefore, a lord should construct a temple for Viṣṇu according to his wealth;
for as many bricks as are used for the edifice,
for that many many years shall the builder dwell even further upon the vault of heaven, highly honored.
For those who obstruct the access to a temple, there is punishment;
even for stealing [the materials], one is cooked in hell for all eternity.
Even if one has playfully drawn a temple or a pavilion upon the ground, [it is a grave offense].
A person of deluded intellect who should erase it goes without doubt to a terrible hell.
Therefore, O Lotus-Seated One, one should not disturb what has been established as a sacred site;
for those who assist in the purpose of building a temple, there is the attainment of the supreme state.
"Those mortals who assist [the devotee] through the actions of mind, speech, and body,
they too go to the abode of Viṣṇu, from which there is no return.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad within the venerable Pāñcarātra.
The fifth chapter, titled "The Rule for the First Brick";
the sixth chapter [begins with] the Blessed Lord.
O Brahmin, listen as I shall describe the procedure for the ritual depositing of the embryo (garbhanyāsa).
One should first take earth in sequence from ten locations:
from a mountain, a lake, a sacred bathing place (puṇyatīrtha), an anthill, and the dwelling of a crab; [and likewise] from a confluence, a temple, a pond, a cow-pen, and a forest.
Then, the clay produced from these—namely, from a river, the tip of a bull’s horn, an elephant’s tusk, the ocean, and a plow—is praised;
as is that from kumuda, aravinda, kaśeru, and utpala. (6.2–6.3)
One should also collect these five tubers of the blue lotus:
realgar, yellow orpiment, collyrium, black lead, and saurāṣṭra; as well as gorocanā, red ochre, and mercury.
Having taken the elements and jewels— diamond, lapis lazuli, pearl,
crystal, topaz, conch shell, ruby,
and furthermore moonstone and sapphire— one should collect these nine.
He may take nine kinds of new grain: *śāli*, *nīvāra*, *kaṅku*, *priyaṅgu*, sesame, *māṣa* beans, green gram (*mudga*), barley, and bamboo seeds;
as well as gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead.
Having brought together all these— a golden tortoise, and golden conch and discus— one should place them in a vessel containing the embryo-substance. Then,
having set the vessel upon a heap of grain, one should wrap it with a cloth.

Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, and then having brought fire to either a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or a consecrated mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and kindled it, one should likewise offer clarified butter and fuel sticks with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra dedicated to Viṣṇu as the deity.

Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should collect the remaining clarified butter. With the *narasūkta*, one should offer sixteen oblations of *caru* to Indra and the other world-protectors, as well as to the various realms.
From the mountains and from the oceans, and likewise from the Ādityas;
from the Vasus and the Maruts, and immediately thereafter from the Ṛṣis;
from the Vedas and all the Śāstras, and likewise from the Purāṇas.
Immediately thereafter, one should offer oblations separately to the nāgas from the netherworlds and the cardinal directions,
to the hosts, to all beings, and likewise to the lords of men,
and to all the planets, ending each with "svāhā. (6.14–6.15)
One should offer oblations to them with sacrificial porridge mixed with sesame seeds and clarified butter;
having collected the residual drops of the clarified butter, one should sprinkle them upon the vessel containing the embryo.
The placement of the embryo must take place specifically at night.
The preceptor should perform the depositing of the embryo during the night itself,
at an auspicious moment endowed with a favorable lunar mansion, a favorable fortnight, and a favorable *karana*,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, along with those reciting auspicious texts.
Accompanied by the chanting of the Vedas by the best of the twice-born and by the sounds of hand-claps and shouts,
he should then take the vessel, circumambulate the temple,
and enter the inner sanctum properly together with the brahmins.
Beginning from the side of the door on the right-hand side, the specification of the location for the deposition of the *garbha* according to the various classes of deities and others is as follows:
for the gods, the deposition of the *garbha* is recommended upon the molding (*paṭṭikā*). (6.20)
For Brahmins, [the throne] is on a slab with ivory tusks; for kings, upon a white lotus;
for Vaiśyas, indeed upon a lotus; and for Śūdras, upon the earth.
(6.21) In the case of a reversal of high and low [status], there is an undesirable result.
If it is placed too low, there will be constant suffering; if too high, there is the destruction of wealth.
If it is at the door, it certainly causes loss of one's position; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with great effort, it should be well-concealed in the middle of the wall.
The ritual procedure for the casket of the deposited embryo:
having fashioned a casket from the primary metal according to the measure of a palm, it should be provided with nine cavities and endowed with the prescribed ritual rules. (6.24)
In the absence of that [stone], it should be made of wood and provided with a covering over a pit;
having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should purify it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). This is the method of meditation.
Meditating upon the entire circle of the earth, together with its mountains, islands, and oceans—
supported by the elephants of the quarters and resting upon the crest of the lord of serpents, Śeṣa—
one should fix in the mind the auspicious, dark-green earth, measuring two cubits.
One should cause her, who has bathed after her menses and is adorned with ornaments, to conceive a perfect embryo;
having meditated upon oneself as Keśava, adorned with all ornaments, as the locus for the depositing of earth, water, and the other elements.
Having taken clay from the ocean, one should circumambulate it clockwise.
One should place the clay from a mountain in the east, likewise that from a sacred ford (tīrtha) in the south,
that from a river in the western part, and likewise that from a lake in the north.
One should place clay from a crab in the southeast, clay from an anthill in the southwest,
clay from a plow in the northwest, and clay from an elephant's tusk in the northeast;
one should also place clay from the horns of a bull at the site of Brahmā.
The *kanda-utpala* should be in the eastern direction, the *kaumuda* in the northern direction;
the *nīlotpala* in the western direction, and the *kāśerava* in the northern direction.
The *pādma* should be in the Brahma-place; thereafter, one should deposit the minerals.
In the east, realgar; in the south, yellow orpiment;
in the western quarter, collyrium; in the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the north), lead;
in the southeast, saurāṣṭra; in the southwest portion, and in the northwest, yellow pigment (rocanā).
Gairika is in the northeast, mercury in the center, and in the station of Brahmā;
the diamond is in the east, lapis lazuli in the south, the mani-gem in the west,
topaz in the quarter of Kubera, and crystal should be in the southeast.
In the southwest, there is pearl; in the northwest, likewise the moonstone (*candrakānta*);
in the northeast, the great sapphire (*mahānīla*); and in the center, the ruby (*padmarāga*). There shall be rice seed in the east, and likewise wild rice (*nīvāra*) in the south.
Kaṅgu grain for the western direction, priyaṅgu for the lord of wealth (Kubera), and likewise jvalana (fire) [for the southeast];
māṣa beans should be in the region of Nairṛta, tila and mudga in the region of Māruta;
veṇudhānya in the northeast, and barley should be in the place of Brahmā.
Having placed gold in the eastern quarter, silver in the south, and copper in the west, one should cast [the vessel] facing north. Tin should be placed in the southeast,
bell-metal in the southwest, and likewise in the northwest.
One should place a golden tortoise in the northeast, a cinnabar [object] made of gold,
and a wheel of Jāmbūnada gold in the center, using the root mantra;
this is the mantra for the meditation on the Earth-deity.
Then, having meditated upon the goddess Mahī, one should utter this mantra:
"O beloved bearer of all beings, adorned with mountains for breasts, clothed by the ocean—O Goddess, take up the embryo. (6.42)
The Procedure for Filling the Chasm:
Having spoken thus, one should then fill the chasm with cow urine, cover it according to the prescribed rite, and ensure its stability with plaster. (6.43)
The teacher’s fee: one should give a fee to the teacher according to the number of items previously mentioned.
Protection of the fetus.
If there is a miscarriage of the fetus, one should perform protection on all sides;
thereafter, one should perform an expiation as previously prescribed for ill omens.
There is a fault in constructing villages, palaces, and so forth, without the ritual placement of the embryo (garbhanyāsa).

If one should construct a village or even a palace without first performing the ritual placement of the foundation (garbhavinyāsa), that dwelling or site will quickly go to ruin. Therefore, at the very beginning, one should perform the rite for the foundation of both the building and the site using gold.
The rule for the length and breadth of the temple (dhāman):
one cubit is the minimum, while a hundred cubits is recorded as the maximum;
one story is the minimum, while twelve stories is the maximum. (6.47)
O Lotus-Seated One, the height should be twice the width, the floor should correspond to that height, and the elevation should be constructed according to one's wealth;
such is the rule for the Lord’s reclining and other postures on structures with from one to twelve floors.
The resting place of the Creator God is ordained on the first level;
the seat joined with Śrīdhara shall be on the second level.
Likewise, the standing posture is on the third, and the vehicle is desired on the fourth.
In the fifth [day] there is the Yoga-sleep; in the sixth, the Bhoga-seat.
In the seventh there is the Yoga-station; in the eighth, the Tārkṣya-vehicle.
In the ninth is the Bhoga-sleep; in the tenth, there would be the Bhogas.
"In the eleventh [stage] there is stability; in the twelfth, one possesses the universal form (viśvarūpa).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Deposition of the Embryo" (garbhanyāsavidhāna), in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, within the glorious Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
The Seventh Chapter: The Rule for the Foundation; The Sub-Pīṭha.
The Blessed One said: Below [the base] there should be a pedestal (upapīṭha) which supports the foundation;
it is for the sake of beauty, for protection, or indeed for the sake of height. (7.1)
The height of the pedestal (upapīṭhaka) should be equal to the base (adhiṣṭhāna), or half of it, or three-quarters;
or it may be one-quarter, one-third, one-and-a-half parts, or one-and-a-quarter parts;
or it may even be made double or triple [the height of the base]. // 7.2 //
Having divided the height into ten parts, by increasing it by one part,
the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be one-fifth [of the height]; its projection outward from the temple wall shall be one,
one and a half, two, or three daṇḍas.
The *adhiṣṭhāna* may be either circular or square, with its base outside the [inner] foot.
It is considered to be of three types according to the distinctions of the *vedī*: the *vedībhadra*, the *pratībhadra*, and the *subhadra*. (7.5)
In the height of the altar-base (vedī), one part is for the auspicious plinth (bhadra); a staircase is said to occupy two parts.
Above that, one part is for the lotus (padma), half a part for the projection (kṣepaṇa), and five parts for the remainder.
The neck should be half [of the height], the lotus one part,
the *vājana* the remaining parts, and the *upapīṭhaka* one-eighth of a part.
Alternatively, it should be made with six components, provided with arms above and below.
Vedibhadra is declared to be of two kinds, suitable for all types of mansions;
likewise Pratībhadra and Anīdṛk, [constructed] with portions of eleven and twelve parts respectively.
In the one-third, one-ninth, and one-eighth [divisions], one should join it with two parts.
In the height consisting of twenty-seven parts, from the base of the world up to the top,
there should be the pedestal (pādukā), the lotus (paṅkaja), the fillet (kampa), the throne (pīṭha), and the upper lotus (ambuja).
The section beginning with the *kapotapālikā* (dovecot) is called the *prativājana*;
this is known by the name *pratibhadra*, endowed with all ornaments.
In the pair [of pillars], there are two parts of the axle-measure (*akṣa*) and one part of the quarter-measure (*kāṣṭha*), along with parts of the eighth and sixteenth measures.
One should join here [the elements] with three parts, two parts, and one part respectively:
the pedestal (pādukā), the lotus (paṅkaja), and likewise that which is separated by the liṅga;
then the upper base (vājana), the neck (kaṇṭha), the upper limit (uttarānta), and the pigeon-eave (kapotaka).
The *āliṅgāntarita* and the *ūrdhva* [are two types]; and the *prati* is indeed the *ūrdhvavājana*.
The *pratibhadra* is of two kinds; from that, the *subhadra* has one additional part.
In its height, which consists of twenty-one parts, two parts are for the birth-mould and likewise for the lotus;
half a part is for the neck, half a part for the lotus, and two parts for the fillet (vājana).
Half a part is for the [upper] half, and likewise for the fillet (kampa); thus the neck is said to consist of eight parts.
One part for the upper section, half a part for the lotus, and three parts for the pedestal;
half a part for the upward projection—this is known by the name Subhadraka.
Two parts for the base, one-third for the lotus, and one part for the neck.
With two [parts] there is a *vājana*, with one a *kampa*, and with eight parts the neck (*gala*);
with one part a *kampaka*, with two a *vājana*, and with one part a *kampa*.
Thus, the *subhadra* is said to be of two kinds, endowed with all ornaments.
It should be adorned with lions, elephants, sea-monsters, beasts of prey, spirits, and the like;
each face should have a fish-mouth, and the western face should be mounted by a child.
One should imagine this on every temple, whether it is worthy or unworthy.
The wise describe that which is devoid of growth in each and every limb as the abode named Sūkara; one should employ it in the secondary seat (upapīṭha).
This is the remainder of the procedure for the secondary seats.

The *upapīṭhaka* (sub-base) should be made here twice as high as the height of the image's pedestal, or equal to it, or one and a half times, or half, or one-third; this should be provided with its own minor members,
or equal to or half of that, and it shall be the *ājana*.
O Kamalāsana, this has been declared as the *upapīṭha* in brief. Now,
for the sake of the perfection of the temple, I shall describe the various *adhiṣṭhānas*.
The base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be one-third of the pillar's height in measurement.
One-eighth of the pillar's height shall be the projection for the base and its fillet (kampa).
The length of the pedestal (pada) and the height of the floor (tala) should be equal to the excellent base.
Or even less than a *vitasti*, or else six *aṅgulas*;
thus it is divided in three ways for the support of the halo and its movement.
Above that, one-eighth part is for the support of the color and its movement.
The foundation of the "section on the shoes" (upānavarga) is here recited as the "shoes" (upāna).
The twelve components are:
the shoe, the lotus of the world, the throat, the tremor, and the band.
The *nidrikā* should be like a closed lotus bud, and the shoulder should be concealed;
in this manner, one should arrange the twelve limbs during the binding and securing of the feet.
The *pādabandha* and the *pratibandha* are the two types based on the root of the womb (*yonimūlaka*).
Because it binds the feet (*pādānām*), it is called *pādabandhana*; because one should obstruct with clarified butter (*vṛta*), it is intended as *pratibandhana*. (7.29–7.30)
That which is to be cut should be bound at its base; that which is not to be cut should be firmly secured.
One should cause that limb to be cut all around, but one should not cause it to be half-cut. Cutting of a limb is declared auspicious, while half-cutting brings fame.
The *homa* sacrifice should be performed with the binding of its feet; the counter-measure against paralysis is the suppression [of the affliction].
One should not allow the site of the obstruction to be cut;
if one were to do so, one would incur faults such as the destruction of the entire lineage. (7.32–33)
The enclosure wall, the gate-tower, and the gateway should have their foundations cut according to rule;

thus one should cause the prescribed method for the path to be executed in accordance with the *Vāstu-śāstra*. [The width of the threshold is as follows: 7.34. The width of the *upāna* (the base molding).

That sacrificial altar (upāna) is fivefold in form, extending outward by one, one and a half, two, two and a half, three, and four cubits [from the center]. (7.35) Thus the sacrificial altar has five types of shapes for the exit of the oblation.
One *daṇḍa*, two *daṇḍas*, half of a half, and three-quarters; or that same measure of a *daṇḍa* according to the measurement of the *homāyā*;
and whatever stands above the *prakṛti* according to the measurement of the *homāyā*. (7.36–7.37)

O Lotus-born One, one should construct there a sacrificial altar for the Vimānādhāra-homa, with many pillars raised high and sunk into the ground to that same measurement. First, the wise man should have the foundation for the birthplace constructed there.
The presiding seat for the deities should be forty [units] in size;
this presiding seat should be constructed with materials such as stone,
and the lotus-bond and other such designs should be applied to the presiding seat.

I shall describe the foundations for the *padmabandha* and other [architectural forms], preceded by their ornaments. That supreme foundation for the assembly hall may be adorned with various lotus petals; it may be less than a *vitasti* in height, or even as low as six *aṅgulas*.
Thus, it is divided into three parts: the base, the pedestal, and the capital;
and above that, the capital, the pedestal, and the shaft should each be one-eighth [of the total height].
One should calculate the height as having nine bases, beginning from the base.

Half of the foot [pillar] is the height, while the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is sixteen [parts]. Half of the plinth (upāna) is its height; from the lotus comes the square [base], and one part is the support for the fillet (paṭṭika); the remainder is the raised lotus.
The central pitcher (madhyakumbha) shall be two and a half parts, and the upper lotus (ūrdhvapadmaka) one and a half parts.

The interval between the shoulders (skandhāntara), however, shall be two parts; from the first [pitcher], it is divided by two parts. Each individual base (prativājana) is one part; this is known as the lotus-band (padmabandha).
The foundation and the height [of the temple] shall consist of fifteen parts.
The first part shall be one part, while the *jagatī* (pedestal) shall be five parts.
The *kumuda* (fillet) shall be a fourth part, and the *skandha* (plinth) shall be two parts. The *aṃśaka* (moulding) shall be one part. (7.46–7.47)
O Lotus-born One, this is celebrated by the name *pratibandha*, having two parts for its height and one part for the *vājana*;
its base has a height of twenty-three parts. (7.48)
The height of its pedestal (upadhāna) is two and a half [parts]; the jagatī should be five and a half [parts].
The height of the kumuda is five parts; the upper fillet (uparipaṭṭikā) is one part.
The height of the neck (grīva) is three parts; the kampas and the nidrā are each two parts.
The *kapotasadana* (dove-cot), highly honored among architectural members, is [one] part;
the *upāna* (plinth) is one part, while the *jagatī* (pediment) is seven parts.
The *vapraka* (rampart) should be six parts, and the *vetra* (staff) one and a quarter parts.
In the same manner, the recessed height is two parts, and the height of the *pratī* is one and a half parts.
Each *vājana* is one part, joined with twenty *bhāgas*. The *pratīmukha* is made of *kāri* material and is as long as a *nāgavaktra*.
This *pratibandha* [pediment] is suitable for all types of beings by name;
with two parts it serves as the base (*upapāda*), and with seven parts it becomes the *jagatī*.
With six parts, the height of the *kumuda* [fillet] is formed, along with the well-rounded edge of the drip (*dhārāvapra*).
The *āliṅgāntarita* [type of arch] consists of two [units], while its half would be increased by one.
Half of that is the *pratimukha*, adorned with all its constituent parts and embellished with lions, sea-monsters (*makara*), serpents, creepers, and leaves. (7.55–7.56)
The front [of the arch] should have a makara-mouth joined with the makara-banner;
from the mouths of the makaras and elephants emerge hosts of serpents and vidyādharīs.
The remaining portion should be provided with a molding (vājana) and endowed with the tips of filaments (kesara).
It is joined with one twenty-first part and possesses various recesses (pratikrama).
Then, the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) consists of fifteen parts;
the *janman* is half a part, and the *jagatī* is four parts. (7.58–59)
The pitcher (kumbha) should be three parts in height, joined with a garland-band (srakbandha), a lotus-band (padmabandha), and a fillet-band (vedibandha).

Above that, the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) should be three pādas high, joined with a lotus-band. Likewise, the height of the fillet (paṭṭikā) is two parts, and the height of the counter-projection (pratiruc) is two parts.

One should make the *vājana* half [the size], and the *ardhapatta* half a part; this is known by the name Padmabandha, which grants supreme fearlessness to the gods. For the measurement of the base should indeed be twenty-two steps.
One should make the fillet with one part, and the lotus should be made with two parts;
the upper fillet should be of that same measure, and the base (jagatī) should consist of six parts.
The height of the kumuda should be four parts, and above it, there should be a fillet of one part.
The neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be three parts; the upper fillet (*uparipaṭṭikā*) half [of that].
One should make the upper lotus (*ūrdhvāmbuja*) half [a part], and the great fillet (*mahāpaṭṭa*) three parts.
The lotus above should be half [a part], and one should fashion the *kampa* (molding) as half [a part].
One should apply this "obstruction" (pratibandha) by name to all the chambers;
it consists of two types, the sacrificial obstruction (homastambha) and the fixed obstruction (pratiṣṭambha), each having a length equal to the foot [of the structure].
One should arrange the sacrificial obstruction above the base (tala) of the primary structure.

Above the *pratistambha* and the *prati*, the *uttarānta* and the *prapādaka* [should be constructed]. (7.67) Their height shall be half the length of the base (*pāda*), according to the measurement of the foundation (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The specific measurement shall be as declared for the production of particular features. (7.68)
The height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be measured by six, eight, or nine parts respectively;
it should consist of one part of the sun (sūrya) according to the measurement of ten parts for the binding (bandha).
The line for the [corner] mark (aṅkasūtra) should be one part according to the seventh measurement.
The remaining portion shall be the length of the legs, or the neck may be measured according to the seventh proportion. In a temple, palace, assembly hall, or pavilion,
there should be a penthouse (agraharbhyaka) consisting of five units or four units.
Then, that temple should be constructed according to the measurement of its foundation;

in a temple or an assembly hall, it should be according to the measurement of the base. However, in a human dwelling, it must not be made [according to that], for it would cause the destruction of both the builder and the patron. (7.72)
The binding of the feet and the binding of the hands—these two types of binding are prescribed.
This [binding] is to be performed in a temple; it is not to be performed in a human dwelling.
It is declared that the exit for the sandals consists of four staffs and three staffs.
Half of three *daṇḍas*, two *daṇḍas*, two and a half, and one are said [to be the measures];
thus, the number of directions outside the base is determined by the steps as they emerge from the *homa*. The width of the base step is such that the front step is wider.
The height of each respective terrace should correspond to its respective width.
One should divide the projection of the plinth (upāna) into three parts;
having set aside one part on the outside, the wise man should have a rampart (vapraka) constructed there. // 7.76–77 //
Likewise for the *kumudapaṭṭa*, and likewise for the insertion of the neck;
[the measurements are] two *daṇḍas*, three *daṇḍas*, one and a quarter *daṇḍas*, one and a half *daṇḍas*,
and one and a quarter *daṇḍas* plus a half-*daṇḍa* in width.
Thus has the characteristic of the consecrated site been described in many ways.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Consecrated Site," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
The Eighth Chapter:
The Procedure for Vimānas, by the Blessed Lord.
Now I shall describe the classification of the celestial palaces (vimānas) along with their characteristics;
since their classifications are infinite, only a small portion will be demonstrated.
And these palaces are distinguished by the difference in their floors and foundations.
The Vaijayantaka vimāna consists of the neck and the head; if these two are circular, it is the Vaijayantaka,
also known as Śrīviśāla.

If it is thick at the base and fine at the tip—wondrous!—with a large nostril in the front portion and very small nostrils in the three other directions; and if there is a set of four cupolas on the nose, both on the temple and on the pavilion; [then it is auspicious]. (8.3)

That Puṣpaka chariot was circular and elongated, honored for its firm splendor; it possessed side-projections and a pinnacle, was endowed with beauty and luxury, and likewise featured a central *bhadra* projection of that same kind.
That which is called Śrīviśāla is said to have eight sides and to provide a secure foundation.
Furthermore, the square Śrīkara, provided with sixteen supports,
is this Puṣpaka vimāna, which is highly honored among all vimānas.
The *kesara* [shoulder] together with the *bhadra* [chest] is in the middle; the *mastaka* [head], *karṇa* [ear], and *kaṇṭhara* [neck];
the *koṣṭhaka* [thorax], the limbs of the *bhadranāsa* [beautiful-nosed face], and the well-rounded *gala* [throat] and *mastaka* [head]. (8.7)
This celestial chariot Kesara is adorned with every ornament;
it is beautiful to behold, with faces turned toward every direction, and its head possesses two or three eyes.
The frontispiece is shaped like a *karkarī* (water-pot), provided with a circular inner chamber;

at its mouth is a great nose, and the temple (*vimāna*) belongs to both [the *śikhara* and the *stūpa*]. There is a pair of *stūpīs*, or perhaps an odd number, resembling a nose on the three directions.
Whether it be circular, oblong, or well-rounded, this [vessel] shall be known by the name Sudarśana;
likewise, its base, neck, and head should be in the form of a svastika or square.
It is endowed with four peaks and provided with four courtyards;
its summit in the cardinal directions is adorned with great spires,
and it is embellished with various wonderful paintings, including arches, altars, and auspicious motifs.
This is declared to be the *svastika* configuration, highly honored among celestial chariots (*vimāna*).
That very same [structure] is called *sauṣṭhika* when it is vast and beautiful, yet its compartments (*koṣṭhaka*) are both depressed and elevated. (8.13)
This vast and beautiful mountain, joined with an inner terrace,
consists of one part, two parts, three-quarter parts, and one-quarter part [of the total height]. (8.14)
In a two-storey vimāna and similar structures, the base, the entablature, the neck, and the head are divided into two parts; however, when the rise of the base consists of nine parts,
it is provided with an intermediate entablature and endowed with gabled halls.
It is endowed with various ornaments and adorned with various verses.
The mountain is said to be the celestial chariot (vimāna), most highly honored among all chariots;
it is Mandara itself, circular, with its base as the altar, its peak as the neck, and its summit as the jar.
It has eight peaks, is provided with four halls, and possesses seven or eight spires; it has a central courtyard and an exit, with two or three pillars and eight [other features];
it is endowed with a complete neck and head, and is furnished with peaked gables and storehouses.
O Lotus-seated One, this celestial chariot, joined with various pedestals and adorned with various feet,
whether square or perfectly round and endowed with many hubs,
is called Mandara by name. (8.19–8.20)
That very [structure] is the Svastibandha; at its peak, there are four half-cells (sārdhakoṣṭhaka),
joined with a square top and provided with four kūṭas.
Joined with various foundations and endowed with many stories,
with thousands of turrets— or half that, or even a quarter—
this [structure] shall be known by the name Svastibandha, adorned with diverse architectural members.
That very auspicious and well-constructed chest is provided with internal cross-beams;
the neck is slightly recessed for a necklace, and the nose is formed by nine or eight [parts].
This auspicious [structure], when joined with various ornaments, is desired;
that same [structure] at the summit, however, is called *pāñcāla* if it consists of one and a half *koṣṭhakas* and is devoid [of further ornamentation]. // 8.24 //
This [structure] joined with eighty-four [parts] is desired as the Pāñcāla style.
That same [style], when having eight facets, is called Viṣṇukrānta; it consists of the altar (vedi), the neck (kaṇṭha), the pinnacle (śikhara), and the pitcher (ghaṭa).
On the summit are eight great peaks; this one is named Viṣṇukāntaka, and it is most auspicious,
being devoid of the intermediate ridges found among the other peak-halls.
That [structure] is four times longer and square;
likewise, the altar (vedi), the corner (karṇa), the pinnacle (śikhara), and the pot (ghaṭa) are elongated.
Equipped with three cupolas (stūpī), this is known by the name Sumaṅgala.
If that very same forest is long and circular, with a sacrificial altar for its belly and a head,
and is endowed with all its constituent parts, it is considered a "forest-palace. (8.29)
The Puṣkara [temple] is half a unit more than the Tāra in length, square in shape, provided with two corners, a pinnacle, and endowed with a window and a front hall. 8.30
The Vimāna style is declared to be the Puṣkara, honored among all types of palaces; it is captivating, quadrangular, and provided with a circular base and a circular inner sanctum. (8.31)
Adorned with all ornaments, this [palace] named Manohara belongs to Kubera;
it should be square, and its inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) must not be narrow.
If the dome is circular from its base, the turret is beautiful, the upper chamber is round,
the foundation is elongated, the neck is hexagonal, and the head [is likewise],
and it is endowed with all ornaments, it is known by the name Kauberakāntaka.
The Bhadrakoṣṭa [throne] is joined with various pedestals and adorned with various feet;
it is beautified by the svastika-binding posture of those seated upon the feet.
Joined with many courtyards and adorned with various ornaments,
equipped with many windows and provided with many cupolas,
this [palace] named Bhadrakoṣṭha was long and quadrangular. (8.35–8.36)

That same [structure] is a *vṛttakūṭa* when it is circular; likewise, with circular pinnacles (*karṇakūṭa*) and circular tops (*karṇaśiras*), and provided with four noses (*nāsī*), this becomes a *vṛttakūṭa*. (8.37)
That very [structure] is the Koṣṭhabhadra;
it is eight parts longer than its width, square, with corner-pinnacles, and likewise with corners extended and a circular top. // 8.38 //
One should know this Koṣṭhabhadra to be honored in all palatial dwellings; it is likewise Śrībhoga when it is circular, possessing a pedestal, corners, a spire, and a finial.
The remainder is designated as before; it is desired by the name Śrībhoga. When circular, it is called Puṣkara, provided it is endowed with many nostrils. (8.40)
This Puṣkara is said to be joined with many palm trees, adorned with various ornaments, and equipped with supports for the celestial palaces; it has hanging lattices. (8.41) Lambapañjara.
Leaving the water and land behind, it extends upward, being elongated and square;
likewise, it possesses corner-turrets and a pinnacle, is endowed with four noses,
is joined with supports for the celestial palaces (vimāna), and is provided with many stupas.
It is said to be joined with various decorative elements and featuring hanging lattices;
it brings victory and is adorned with various *masūraka* motifs, pillars, altars, lattice-work, and archways.
Adorned with various ornaments and variegated with diverse paintings;
[it has] a base with a pedestal, a simple frame, and a lintel joined in the shape of a svastika, decorated with nose-ornaments. // 8.44–8.45 //
Long and square, joined with many stories and featuring various theatrical performances— this, known by the name Vandika, brings victory. (8.46)
That very same [temple], with its neck and head formed by the four corners of the Vedas, was adorned with various other ornaments such as pillars and altars made of *masūraka* stones;
it is called by the name Vandika, the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The Saubhadra [hall] had a long-sided courtyard and a hall-shaped pinnacle with all its sides extended;
it was joined with many stories and endowed with three stupas.
Alternatively, one equipped with four stupas or endowed with four *nāsīs* is to be known as *saubhadra*, provided it is devoid of a *varṣasthala* and possesses a *kamalamaṇḍala*.
The base is square, and the neck is likewise square;
above the neck it is shaped like a water-pot (kumbha) and joined with many stories.
This celestial palace (vimāna) of the Lord is to be known as the "Lotus-Mandala."
The nose is at the mouth, occupying one-third of the great cloth (mahāpaṭṭa) of the forehead;
the hundred-eyed [face] touches the sides, and the three-tiered canopy should be supported there. 8.52
This Indubhadra by name is highly honored in the dwellings;
it is white at its extremity,
endowed with bands, lotus-garlands, and white cane-staffs, and possessed of lattice-windows.
The courtyard is of four types and is provided with a *śukanāsa* (frontal pediment).
It is square, with a large *nāsikā* (central projection) at its front containing a *candraśālā*.
[The proportions] are by one, five, half-five, and half-four parts, respectively, from the bottom.
By name it should be Dhavalikānta, joined with a lotus-base;
it is gentle,
surrounded by a square ground, and topped with an eight-sided [structure].
Above that, it is circular and endowed with the sequence previously mentioned;
it is named Saumya, and being common [to all], its pinnacle bears the "neck-peak" (kaṇṭhakūṭa), and it is the Lalitabhadra.
The ear-ornament, appearing well-rounded, shaped like a neck, and adorned with earrings,
is joined with a crest; it is known by the name Lalitabhadra and is called Vyāsa.
The long-hermitage [posture] has its base in the *vyāsa* meter and is characterized by the binding of power (*śaktibandhana*).
The mountain-meter is elongated; the lotus-binding, however, consists of a rounded neck as well as a head.
That which has five squares for the feet and so forth, with both aggregated and non-aggregated [syllables],
whose limbs are both assigned and unassigned, and which is called the *śailacchandas*,
is the *madhye bhadra*.
This very [type of] temple, broad and possessing a head-piece (*śiras*), brings victory.

However, one that has low walls and high pinnacles, or is quadrangular, octagonal, or circular, and is provided with many nose-projections (*nāsikā*) at its base, middle, and top, [is also auspicious]. 8.60–8.61
The central sanctuary with a circular interior is known by the name Bhadra;
this is called the Śrīmacchanda, while the Śriyaśchanda has a square inner hall. (8.62)
This very [mandala] is the Yogānandana; if it has three sides, its head and neck are shaped like branches,
its mouth-end is elevated, and the rest has circular ears.
That which has a back joined with a horse, with its hair and forearms appearing fatigued, and possessing a perfectly rounded head, is called the Haṃsatāraka, the Delight of Yoga. (8.64) Haṃsatāraka.
With a neck possessing sixteen long peaks and sixteen nostrils,
endowed with ease and delicacy, and possessed of sixteen peaks;
having the shape of a jar and a symmetrical form, with its throat shimmering from the protrusions of its ears.
The neck has a six-cornered summit; it is named Haṃsatāraka.
The Māhendraka [roof] has an elongated tip-shape; the hall (śālā) and the head-hall (śiraḥśālā) are at each opening.
The back [of the temple] with two moon-chambers is called Mahendraka by name; the Sūryakānta is square,
joined with square limbs, and has a square *masūraka*.
The ninth [section] is thirteen units long; it is shaped like a short circle and a mandala.
At the entrance of the hall, at the front, the back, and on its sides, there are eight nostrils;
the neck-mass is adorned with twenty-four nostrils.

This [posture] is called *sūryakānta*; it has a rounded and elongated head and neck, is a locus of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), possesses solar grace (*sauramya*), extends to the sides and the ends of the feet, is moderate, and features an upward-pointing lattice-work (*ūrdhvapañjara*). (8.70)
It is said to be the abode of auspiciousness; by name it is Śeṣa, as previously described.
It possesses noble essence, consists of ten parts, has four parts, and is extensive with the narrative of Vyāsa.
It is square and possesses many verses, with [a structure] at the mouth of the hall at each opening;
it is endowed with two great nostrils, and at the mouth there is a fourfold group of eight;
the head is upon a lotus-seat, and the path resembles a lotus-earring.
Twenty-two *dvārīkā*s, accompanied by *nidrā* and *anidra*, [are used];
