two parts and four parts for the increase, with the root of the long hall (*dīrghāśrama*). As previously stated, it is square and joined with a *śālāpañjara*.
It is joined with one hundred and twenty [spikes];
facing east, beginning from the middle, another peak is as previously described.
This, however, is noble in substance, long, circular, and solid.
The Vijaya [mandala] is joined with seven and a half octagons at the bottom and four rectangles;
it is brilliant, blazing, and possesses eight circular mandalas on the square ground.
The *ardhāra*, the neck (*grīvā*), the pinnacle (*śikhara*), and the "yoke-nose" (*yuganāsika*)—
these constitute the one called *vijaya*, which is endowed with six, seven, half, and half parts respectively;
it is the *amalāṅga*.
The pure form has four and a half [units], with a neck and head consisting of eight sides within four squares;
it is joined with twelve squares and eight smaller squares.
It is endowed with eight upper lattices and possesses eight peaks on its nose-like projections. It is complete with many stories and is known by the name Vimalākṛti.
The great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) shall be the womb (garbha), while the upper frieze (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) shall be half a cubit in height.
Having fashioned a seat from frogs appearing as *dhārikā* bricks,
it was provided with twelve chambers and eight *sauṣṭika* sections;
with distinct penthouse-halls, it had a neck formed by door-arches and pinnacles.
Above that, the cage-like structure (pañjara) is eight [units] high, and the pure temple (vimāna) is one hundred and twenty [units].
It is perfectly circular with a peaked neck (śikharagrīva), possessing eight "doves' noses" (kapota-nāsikā).
On the four corners, which exceed half [the width], the floor is fashioned in an auspicious shape.
For this is the stainless abode, to be established in three ways with a stainless form:
Śrīdhara [is placed] at twenty-one parts, or at thirteen parts, or at eight parts within the twelve-part [mandala].
The womb should be thirty-two or thirty *aṅgulas* in length and four *aṅgulas* in width;
it should be two *aṅgulas* longer by half an *aṅgula*, with its nose shaped like a *karkarī* vessel.
Likewise, all its limbs should be properly positioned, having the form of a *śālā* house and provided with a head.
Having eight peaks, possessing great nostrils, and joined with a cage-like hall—
this is called Śrīdhara; it bestows prosperity upon embodied beings and is as pleasing as the moonstone.
With a shape that is thus long and rounded, and with a nose made like a water-pitcher (karkarī),
all else being as previously described, this is known as the *candrakānta* face;
it is established as the seat of prosperity (*śrīpratiṣṭhita*).
In every opening was the face of the assembly hall, and from its head it possessed two eyes;
the pleasant countenance became like a water-jar, provided with circular inner chambers.
Within the circular and elongated celestial palaces, there was a large nose upon the face.
Behind the nose [of the structure], it is also provided with three stupas;
its floor plan is square, it possesses a circular inner sanctum,
it is well-rounded with the shape of a pinnacle, and it is endowed with five noses.
Or, when nine parts are joined with eight, it is called the Śrīpratiṣṭhita.
In the Mahānāsī, there should be four pure svastikas joined with the *śālā* and *pañjara*.
That [temple] was four-sided and joined with a half-[dome], with its spire rising upwards (8.91).
It was well-constructed with well-proportioned members, featuring four sets of stairs,
and was provided at the entrance with a *kapotamūla* molding and a banner (8.93).
The interior was joined with stone slabs and endowed with elevated structures;
the center of the palace featured large, dark-blue cornices situated at the corners,
and the top of the palace was equipped with halls, latticed windows, and gables.
When it is provided with four sets of stairs arranged in the form of a *nandyāvarta* through groups such as the *adhiṣṭhāna*, along with projections, recesses, and ornaments,
and is endowed with many floors, it is called the *śuddhasvastika*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Classification of Temples," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the ninth chapter.
The Blessed One [taught] the procedure for the temple, including the vesara style.
It is of three types: Nāgara, Drāmiḍa, and Vesara.
The Nāgara style is designed as square, beginning from the stūpa-shaped pinnacle and the ears. (9.1)
That which measures eight cubits is called Dhāmāyata, or else Nāgara;
Drāmiḍa measures ten cubits, while Dhiṣṇya is six cubits or else elongated. (9.2)
That which is called Drāmiḍa has been described; furthermore, there is the Vṛtta, the Vṛttāyata, and the Vesara known as Vesarākhya. Thus, it is held that [the meter] is of three kinds. 9.3
The Ritual for the Topmost Brick:
O Brahmin, listen now as I shall explain the ritual for the topmost brick.
Prior to the construction of the temple, one should first cause a water-shed (prapā) to be built in the east, just as before. 9.4

In the center of that, one should construct an altar (vedikā) endowed with all ornaments, made of the same materials and of the same form as the first bricks previously fashioned. It is prescribed that the four head-bricks (mūrdheṣṭakā) should likewise be made of those same materials and be of that same form.
For the purpose of the ritual bath, one should perform the consecration of the jars and bathe [the image] as before; then, one should place those jars upon heaps of grain.
One should properly worship the door-jars, the banners, and the archways.
One should set up a great jar and, having invoked [the deity] therein, perform worship.
(9.7) A fire-offering (homa) in the four directions of the altar is prescribed as before; likewise, one should arrange a peace-offering (śāntihoma) in the eight directions of the sanctuary. (9.8)
O Lotus-born One, being purified, one should wrap the bricks with threads as before;
having placed twenty-five jars upon heaps of grain,
they should be filled with jewels, gold, and other precious substances, and wrapped in threads and cloths.
The preceptor, with the eye of the scriptures, should worship [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Regarding the preceptor’s observances:
having fasted, being pure, bathed, and wearing new garments and rings.
There, having spread out darbha grass, he whose senses are subdued should lie down.
Likewise, the one who places the bricks on the head—pure in soul, fasting, and with senses conquered—should do so together with the preceptor and the patron of the sacrifice. (9.11–9.12)
He should dwell right there upon the *darbha* grass, meditating on the Supreme Person (*paramapūruṣa*).
In this manner, he should perform everything at night exactly as prescribed, without omission,
during the rites of the brick-bath and the installation of the fire.
When the next day has dawned, during a clear and pure *muhūrta*, the self-possessed Guru,
having lifted all the jars, should bathe [the disciple] with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
The Guru should then bathe them again with the water contained in the great jar (*mahākumbha*).
Having worshipped with the root mantra, one should encircle it with a new cloth.
Then, taking all the bricks, the well-adorned officiating priests,
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, should circumambulate the temple.
They should place all of them upon the ground above the pavilion;
there, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited.
Facing the east and with a well-composed mind, he shall be the one who places the bricks on the summit.
Meditating on the god Nārāyaṇa within the lotus of the heart, one should mutter the *praṇava*.
One should lay down all the bricks, following the sequence starting from the east.
For women, *śūdras*, and others, the establishment of the fire is performed without mantras.
Women, Śūdras, and those born in the natural order (ānuloma) should perform the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) in silence.
O Brahmin, in the rite concerning bricks, persons afflicted with sinful diseases, outcasts (patita), and those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) are to be excluded.
One should avoid mortals by exerting effort during the rite of laying the head-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā).
Having prostrated with his head upon the ground, the patron (yajamāna) should again honor the preceptor (guru).
With garments, wealth, grain, cattle, land, and likewise gold;
he should give the five-fold ornament, as well as male and female slaves; and a vehicle—whether elephant or horse—as well as an umbrella and sandals. (9.21–9.22)
And he should offer everything to that teacher without hesitation;
he should satisfy the chariot-makers and gratify the artisans with clothing, food, wealth, and grain. (9.23)
The Ritual for the Finial Peg:
O Lotus-Seated One, I shall now describe the finial peg. The finial peg is desired to be made either of metal or of wood. (9.24)

The pinnacle (stūpikā) and the pin (kīla) should be equal to the foot of the upper story, measured by its width and length; this [pin] should be one finger-breadth at its tip. The [stūpikā] should be equal to the neck of the pavilion (vimāna-kaṇṭha), being either one-and-a-half or double [that measure].
The different forms of the *kīla* are thus declared to be fourfold; the *stūpikākīla* is said to be the most excellent.
One should fashion it as curved, or quadrangular, or pentagonal.

The number of stakes varies according to the type of celestial palace (*vimāna*); in a circular palace, they are circular, and in a square one, they are likewise square. For those desiring the state beyond rebirth (*apunarbhava*), there should be a pair of stakes for the pinnacle (*stūpikā*).
For the others, the arrangement of the stūpikā and the kīla should be odd;
it may be up to twenty even, or nineteen odd.
This applies to the square, the hexagon, the octagon, and the circle.
The stūpikā-kīla should be thus; it bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
Regarding the consecration of the kīla, there is this distinction:
having fashioned the stūpikā-kīla in this manner, one should perform the consecration. 9.30
All the rites, beginning with the ritual bathing and ending with the rite of installation, should be performed as in the case of the crown-brick; however, a specific rule is now prescribed.
Then, once the stake has been installed, the wise practitioner should stand upon the top of the celestial chariot.
One should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) and deposit the nine jewels into the pit.
From the east to the center and the end, one should place the seed-syllables of the elements along with their corresponding metals.
Having cast these into the pit, one facing east [should erect] the stūpa-base (*stūpī*) while reciting the root-mantra.
The master-ornament,
the master, adorned with the fivefold ritual attire, should establish the stūpa, [adorned] with necklaces, sacred threads, bracelets, armlets, and finger-rings. (9.34)
Adorned with these five-fold ornaments and provided with an upper garment,
one should immediately make the cavity of the stūpa-dome firm with plaster.
There is a fault if the stūpa is crooked.
A stūpa-pillar should be set upright; if it is crooked, it brings many faults.
Regarding the material of the stūpa-pillar, the results vary: one made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise wood. (9.36)
Each preceding [initiation] yields great fruit, while each subsequent one yields little.
A teacher’s fee (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given, consisting of gold in the quantities as previously specified.
The crest-jar (*śikhākumbha*) may be made of gold, silver, or even copper.
One should install it immediately at an auspicious moment in either a bronze or an earthen vessel;
its shape should correspond to the sanctuary— circular if the sanctuary is circular, and polygonal if it is polygonal.
One should fill the pinnacle-vessel with various jewels and metals.
The top of the jar should be made in the shape of a bud or even like a lamp-flame;
it should be beautiful and pleasing to the heart, and beneath it, a lotus flower.
At Śūlabheda, on the head of Mahānāsa, one should establish either a discus or a trident, made either of iron or of wood; it should be so. (9.41)
On the floor of the celestial palaces (vimāna), one should visualize the deities who are to be imagined; on each floor of the palaces, one should arrange the gods in the various directions:
Indra in the east, or Kumāra in the south, and the Lord of Umā (Śiva) [in the north]. 9.42
Or Dakṣiṇāmūrti in the south, or Nṛhari Hari in the west,
or Śrīdhara likewise in the north, or Brahmā or the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
or else Ādivarāha in the east, and likewise Narahari.
From him, the god Śrīdhara [arose], and from him, Hayaśiras is remembered.
Alternatively, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa— these four may be in the eastern and other directions— or else he is the Supreme Puruṣa.
Satya is in the south, Acyuta in the west, and Ananta in the north;
or alternatively, Vāsudeva and the others may be placed in the directions starting from the east in sequence. Śrīdhara is in the eastern sector, and likewise Varāha in the south.
One should place Nṛsiṃha in the western part and likewise Ananta in the north.

Regarding the deities of the celestial chariot (vimāna), their arrangement is identical to that of the permanent image (dhruvabera); when the permanent image is situated [in the center], the forms (mūrtis) are likewise situated in the cardinal directions.
Likewise, when [the principal deity] is seated, they should be seated; when he is reclining, both [postures] may occur.
When the principal deity is mounted on a vehicle, they should be mounted on vehicles or standing;
or, in the case of the Universal Form (viśvarūpa), it should be the same, or they may be four-armed while standing.
Indra and the other gods of the quarters always remain seated;
likewise, those very same deities reside in palaces made of stone, and in palaces born of rock, the deities of the quarters are likewise born of rock. (9.50)

Having performed the preliminary consecration with water and having consecrated it within the pavilion, one should station it during an auspicious moment; then one should apply a coating of colored powders to the directions.
One should place tridents in the directions upon a temple made of bricks.
Having performed the ritual consecration with water and having thus consecrated it, one should install [the deities] in sequence.
Regarding the procedure for applying the colors:
having prepared the three substances, one should perform the application of the colors.
The plastering should be performed with the same pigment that is prescribed for a particular [deity] in the scriptures.
If there is a transposition among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, a mixture of castes occurs.
Regarding the wall sections of the deities, there are various options such as half-paintings and so forth.
And all those situated on the wall sections are seated upon lotus-thrones (padmaviṣṭara).
All of them may be made with half-painting (ardhacitra), or they may exist by means of the appearance of painting (citrābhāsa).
In a [panel] joined with a single nose (nāsā), one directional form (diṅmūrti) is desired. 9.54–55.
He may have four arms or two arms, with a gentle countenance and a smiling face.
In a temple lacking a nose (nāsikā), the directional form (diṅmūrti) is prohibited;
in a temple lacking a nose, even the directional form is not desired.
According to the distinction of their celestial chariots (*vimāna*), there is a distinction in the forms of the directions: in a square, oblong, or circular abode, they likewise appear as circular;
these are Vīrasena, Suṣeṇa, Vīranātha, and Subhadraka. (9.57)
In the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast,
these attendants of Viṣṇu, who bear the temple upon their arms and possess terrifying faces,
are to be installed within the square and elongated abode provided with two nostrils.
To its south and north,

two men with full water-jars should be placed, holding conch shells and curved objects, their hands touching the curtain; at every level of the celestial chariot, gods and Vidyādharas are said to reside.
Dancing in many ways and holding flutes, lutes,
and drums, other species such as Kinnaras and Uragas are likewise to be imagined;
my incarnations everywhere and their deeds are to be so conceived.
One should fashion rows of swans and likewise garlands of living beings upon the pigeon-colored [sections],
both on the pigeon-colored parts and on the lower levels. 9.62 One should arrange a row of swans and similarly a garland of elemental beings.
Gazing at one another's faces, various beings moving through the sky stood still; others with distorted countenances danced upon the rafters,
above the necks, below them, and in the corner spaces.
One should fashion Garuḍas and lions, either reclining or standing; their stated height should be as high as the neck or even as high as the feet. (9.65)
The height is desired to be either one and a half [parts] or three-quarters; no other height is prescribed.
One should arrange the deities residing beneath the base within that base in their proper sequence.
In the southeast is the elephant-faced one; or else, to the south, is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, served by sages and seated beneath a banyan tree. In the west is Viśvarūpa, and in the north is Kamalāsana.
The wise practitioner should install the goddess Vasudhā in the northeast;
or else, as before, he should visualize all the deities of the directions.
Furthermore, on the lower pedestal, one should likewise place the previously mentioned deities in their respective directions.

Alternatively, one should fashion manifestations accompanied by that narrative; this is the method for preparing the nectar (*sudhā*) using three kinds of substances: stone, sugar, and *takra*-nectar.
Having ground [the powder] with water decocted from the three myrobalans (triphalā), and having diligently moistened it once, twice,
or thrice with the waters of khadira, arjuna, śālmali, and milky trees,
one should properly prepare it in a pit thoroughly saturated with water.
Having poured the decoction over it, and then again with the mixture [of the previous ingredients],
and having boiled it intensely once more with those juices of processed molasses (*guḍapāka*),
one should smear the *dhāma* in due order according to its three types, beginning with the thick.
In this way, that constructed temple shall indeed endure for a long time.
Regarding the three types of plastering:
one should first grind stone, gravel, and sugarcane-juice into a fragrant powder.

While that powder is being ground, one should add double the amount of sand. If it is ground once, it is called "coarse"; if ground twice, it is known as "fine"; and if three times, it should be understood as the sequence of application beginning with the coarse. (9.75)
Then, one who possesses the eye of the scriptures should perform the conceptualization of the five colors and adorn [the image] with those five colors.
One should decorate everything from the sandals up to the stūpa with gold and other precious materials.
One should decorate the temple of Viṣṇu with pearls, gems, golden garlands, and networks of small bells, according to one's available wealth. Thus,
in the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, in the section on ritual practice (*kriyāpāda*).
The ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Topmost Brick and the Conception of the Deities of the Mansion";
the tenth chapter,
"The Conception of the Locations and Other Attributes of the Retinue Deities."
The Blessed One should construct a wall all around for the purpose of establishing an entourage, for the beauty of the temple, and for its protection. (10.1)
Description of the Walls of the Inner Mandala and Other Enclosures: They know the first wall to be named the inner mandala;
after that is the inner moat, and immediately following is the middle moat. (10.2)
And immediately following that is the fifth, called *maryādā*, which is "great.
These five are square and provided with a *khalūrikā*.
Furthermore, there are five divisions in the tantras, and the final one is the *candrikā* ground.
O Lotus-seated One, one or two *bhūvalīs* should be fashioned at the end.
One should fashion the fivefold pedestal consisting of the sandals and so forth;
its staff is said to be half [the length], and its height is declared to be three-quarters of that.
Once that consecration has been performed, a series of pillars is established;
they say the intervening space is the earth, known by the name of the inner circle (antarmaṇḍala).
It may be five cubits, four cubits, or two cubits, according to one's desire.
In the midst of this inner enclosure, there was a cluster of five palaces;
the measurement of the height of the halls and the intervals between them, as well as the ground space between those pillars, was [as follows].
It should be increased successively by one, two, three, or four cubits.
The height of the *sāla* [roof-structure] should be equal to the great nose (*mahānāsa*) of the temple, or it may be level with the top of the neck, or even commensurate with it. (10.8–10.9)
The *sāla* (hall) should be joined with the *upapīṭha* (sub-base); the staff (*daṇḍa*) is three times the height [of the base].
They know the height of the *sālās* to be four, five, or two *daṇḍas*.
Above the *sāla*, there is the arrangement of Garuḍa and other figures.
And above the sal trees, a lion or even a garuḍa should be diligently fashioned upon the flagstaff on all sides. (10.11) This is the procedure for the half-pavilion.
At the top of the temple, an ancillary half-pavilion (ardhamaṇḍapa) should be constructed;
when the sanctum (dhāman) is divided into four parts, it may be one quarter, or even a half,
three-quarters, equal to the sanctum, or half of that half, according to one's preference.
It should be double [the size], or four-faced, or according to the dimensions of the palace;
one should have a half-pavilion constructed with a length of one cubit, two cubits, or three cubits, or four cubits, or five cubits.
The space between those two should be made one *tāla*, or equal to the length of the hand;
the staff should be one and a half [units] or double, or even without it.
In a smaller *ardhamaṇḍapa*, this is the prescription for the location of the exit.
In the case of an inferior half-maṇḍapa temple, the exit is prescribed on both sides;
furthermore, there should be side-paths both in front and behind.
For a temple provided with a pedestal-base, there should be four gate-towers (gopuras).
If the temple is provided with a pedestal (upapīṭhaka), there should be four gate-towers (gopura).
In front of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), at its midpoint, there should be a spacious circular pavilion.
It may be raised to a height equal to, or greater than, the main structure, according to one's desire.

The measurement of the length of the two circular pavilions (maṇḍapa) is one, two, three, four, or five cubits; the space between them is prescribed as the interval, and the projection on both sides is recorded [as the width]. (10.18)
Rows of steps should be constructed on both sides as well.
In temples, they should be in pairs, six aṅgulas in height, and of the same width;
or both [height and width] may be two aṅgulas.

On both sides of the staircase, one should place elephants; furthermore, one should fashion elephant trunks on the sides of the staircase for those that are thicker. Alternatively, one may fashion a chariot-wheel [ornament] or a side-mounted elephant.
Prohibition against constructing a wall over a door or a window:
"One should never construct a wall over a door or even a window;
for by building such a wall, there occurs the destruction of the lineage, ruin, or disease. (10.22)

The determination of the intervals between the windows, such as the palm-tree supports and the plow-shaped brackets, should be half, three-quarters, or even one-quarter [of the width] of the half-pavilion;
or the interval between the intermediate spaces may be equal to that. (10.23)
One should reduce the width on both sides of that central space;
one may also reduce it by one cubit, one palm-span, or half of that on both sides as well.
It may be provided with pairs of pillars, or otherwise, it may have a rhythmic structural arrangement (*tālabandha*).
One may fashion it in the shape of a plough, or it may be without either [of these];
or it may be square and elongated, with four doors facing the four directions.
Or there may be a window; however, one should not construct a wall-enclosure on the pair [of sides]. (10.25–10.26)
The length and width of the pavilion— whether measured internally, externally, or both— should be such that the length of the pavilion is an odd number according to its measurement. (10.27)
O Lotus-born One, the width of the pavilion is prescribed as sixteen cubits when it is symmetrical, or thirteen cubits when it is asymmetrical;
alternatively, it may be equal to the main temple or half the size of the pavilion.

O Lotus-seated One, the length of the pavilion is prescribed as half or even a quarter of that [length of the shrine], or it may be equal to the shrine itself; or it may be one and a half, double, or one and a quarter times the length of the shrine, while its width is likewise determined. 10.29–10.30.
It may be equal in size to the root-abode (mūlālaya) or one palm-span greater;
it is provided with features such as a base-platform and endowed with all ornaments.
It is furnished with various dramatic performances and is devoid of internal pillars.
They say the height of the pavilion should be equal to half its width;
or, O four-faced one, that height of the pavilion may be greater. Alternatively, there should be an exit on the side with stairs facing east or south.
One who is learned in the treatises on the arts should fashion the walls at the corners;
above that, one should arrange a stone-binding or a plow-shape.
Regarding the corners, there is an option for the placement of either Garuḍa or a lion.
O Lotus-seated One, one should place a Garuḍa or a lion in the corners;

or one may construct an assembly hall there according to one's available wealth. Regarding the enclosure wall, there is an option for the construction of four gate-towers (gopuras) in the four directions.

One should construct gate-towers (gopura) on the four sides of the enclosure wall; alternatively, they may be placed at the front and back of the temple, or one may be constructed at the front alone. This concludes the description of temples with two stories and more.
The best [type of temple] among those with two stories and so forth is endowed with twelve tiers (*tala*);
one should fashion the crown-brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*) and the pinnacle (*stūpikā*) in sequence as before.
The directional deities (*diṅmūrti*) shall be as before, and Garuḍa and the others shall be as before.
Regarding the construction of walls for the pavilions according to the distinctions of superior and other measurements, there should be pavilions on all sides within all the enclosures.
They know a pavilion measuring twenty-six *dhanus* to be the best.
They know a pavilion measuring eighteen *dhanus* to be of medium size;
they declare a pavilion of twelve *dhanus* to be inferior.
Alternatively, one may construct the assembly pavilion according to the number of cubits previously mentioned.
One should know that ten cubits is the best [size], eight cubits is the middling,
six cubits is the lowest, and three cubits is the small.
One should construct its wall on the back, extending from south to north.
There, one should construct a staircase provided with eight pillars;
below it, one should make a long hall equipped with a canopy for the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
All the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) should face the east and be situated within all the enclosures.
One should construct all the assembly pavilions facing every direction;

everything, beginning with the purification of the ground, should be done as in the commencement of a temple. Having performed this, one should likewise prepare the "elephant-nail" (hastinakhā) and the pavilion.
The method for the placement within the interior of the pavilion:
"In the ritual of the pavilion, the placement within the interior (garbhanyāsa) should be in the southeast corner;
however, when a gate-tower (gopura) is being constructed, it is prescribed for the southern direction."
Regarding the arrangement of the pair of door-panels and so forth for the gate:
having installed a pair of door-panels at each gate so that they are firm, they may be made of iron or wood, and decorated with horses and other such figures. (10.46)
The teacher, together with artisans, should remove the northern part made of stone or wood;
having had it carved by a chariot-maker or a carpenter, he should quickly wash it all over.
Then, after having a proclamation of an auspicious day made, at a beautiful moment, the teacher [should proceed].
The chariot-maker, together with artisans, should place [the frame] above the door;
he should fashion four cross-beams, or likewise do so with stone.
Having washed the cross-beams and the door-panels with water consecrated by the five Upaniṣads—
Having wrapped [the image] in a new cloth, one should place it upon heaps of grain.
One should perform the worship of the great jar as previously prescribed by the scriptures.
Having done so, at the clear dawn, during an auspicious moment, the Guru [should proceed].
Having placed iron and other materials into the pit, one should have them fashioned together with the artisans;
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should smear it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Immediately thereafter, one should install the deities with water from the great jar (*mahākumbha*) using a *kūrca* grass-bundle.
Upon the door-panel, the deities to be visualized are as follows:
Śānti below, Vāgdevī to the right, Śrī above, and Rati to the north;
thus they are placed in order upon the four door-frames.
On the southern door-panel, one should establish Viśvadhṛk, the leader of beings;
on the northern door-panel, one should establish the powerful Viśvavaktra.
One should then sprinkle the incarnations situated there with one's own vidyā-mantra.
The Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas dwell within the bamboo poles;
the thirty-three gods reside in the iron shafts, and the Rishis in the wedges. Furthermore, the Lord of Beings (Bhūtanātha) is established upon the door-panels.
The Creator of the Universe (Viśvabhāvana) should be established upon the door-panel and the threshold.
Having thus meditated upon [the deity] within the water of the pitcher, one should install all the deities.
One should give the teacher’s fee (*ācāryadakṣiṇā*), numbering a *niṣka*, as previously prescribed.
Regarding the ritual procedure for making the door golden:
it is prescribed that the door may be made of gold, silver, copper, or wood; each preceding material among these is conducive to greater fruit for men. (10.59)

A door-panel made of wood, when adorned with gold, is worshipped by the gods. The construction of pillars and pedestals, as well as the placement of jewels within the pillars upon the foundation stones, is to be performed as previously described. 10.60

One should not place small pots upon them in the position of Brahmā; rather, those [pots] should be prepared with a well-fixed upper support, complete with a rim and other such features. Afterwards, one should mount the balance and secure it with bricks and similar materials.
Then, O Brahmin, one should perform the foundation-binding (talabandha) according to one's wealth;

or alternatively, one may construct the canopy over the sacrificial post (yūpa) in accordance with the scriptures. Furthermore, the assignment of the gatekeepers, such as Caṇḍa and others, is to be determined according to the specific directions.
Canda and Pracaṇḍa are to be placed at the door of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha),
standing on the right and left sides, dressed as sages and accompanied by their wives;
they are either terrifying with faces made formidable by fangs, or they are bearers of staffs.
Separated from their beloveds, hideous, radiant with crowns and caskets,
and bearing conchs and discs upon their heads,
they stood at the two gates of the inner enclosure (*antaḥmaṇḍala*) of the *sāla* grove.
"Jaya and Vijaya must be installed at his gateway (gopura).
In this same manner, gateways are desired for the others in the four directions.
At the eastern gate of the inner enclosure (antarhāra), there shall be the two who bear the lotus and the mace."
One should place the bearers of the sword and the bow at the southern gate;
one should place the bearers of the thunderbolt and the mace in the western direction, O Brahmin; and the bearers of the noose and the goad should be stationed in the northern direction.
Within the Madhyāntarhāra-sāla, in the directions starting from the east and proceeding in order, there are Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, then Bhadra and Subhadra,
Kṛtānta and Asuravidhvaṃsa, and Kubera and Akṣakubera.
Likewise, in the eastern and other directions, one should construct the boundary walls, the salas, and the gate-towers;
Durjaya and Prabala should be made, as well as Viśvabhāvana and Puṣkara.
Saṃbhava and Prabhava should be Suśobhana and Subhadraka.
At the gate of the lowest enclosure, starting from the east, are Kumuda and the others:
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita. (10.72–73)
Two by two, eight [deities] should be arranged at each door according to the prescribed rite;
all the attendants of Viṣṇu, surrounded by armies numbering in the tens of millions,
with staffs in hand, having deformed eyes, and adorned with crowns shaped like baskets.
Adorned with hoods, bracelets, and garlands, their eyes curved with frowns,
they guard the entrance with hands and feet crossed;
the wise one should establish the kitchen in the fourth enclosure.
Whether in the first enclosure, or in the second enclosure,
or even in the third enclosure, according to the suitability of the location, this is the instruction regarding the site of the training ground (*khalūrikā*). (10.77)
Its location is prescribed either between Indra and Agni or in the southeastern quarter;
it is provided with a threshing floor and, in the center, joined by a courtyard.
It is divided into square and rectangular sections, extending eastward and ending at a stone boundary.

One should prepare a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) between the fire and Yama for the daily oblation (*nityahoma*), provided it is joined with pairs [of stones] measuring one cubit (*hasta*) or with a long oven (*dīrghaculya*); this is the place for baking cakes (*apūpa*).
The place for baking cakes is between the southwest (Nairṛta) and the south (Yāmya).
The place for storing fruits, black pepper, and so forth— one should deposit the fruits between Nirṛti and Varuṇa.
One should fashion a door facing west between the positions of Vāyu and Varuṇa.
The placement of Marīci and the others should be between Vāyu and Soma;
the location for liquids such as clarified butter should be in the middle between Śarva and Śacīpati.
The examination of the site regarding the washing of rice, the exit for smoke, and the location of the well:
The washing of rice and other grains, the well—whether internal or external—and the paths for the exit of smoke should always be in pairs and curved. (10.83)
The bathing area, the place for betel-leaves, garments, flowers, and the inner apartments, as well as the dining hall for those who eat alone, are situated thus:
the bath-house is in the south, the betel-plantation house in the southwest, the storehouse for garments in the west, and the flower-pavilion in the northwest. (10.84)
In the north, one should establish the dining area for those who are exclusively devoted; in the northeast, the treasury;
and in the outer enclosure, the place for storing grain, umbrellas, and other such items. One should also place the granary in the southeast.
To the south of the Lord of Umā (Śiva) should be the slaughter-house, and the cow-shed;
in the third enclosure, the place for umbrellas and such items should be in the southeast (Vibhāvasu).
The placement of palanquins and so forth should be in the east (Indra), and water should be located in the west (Varuṇa).
During a festival, the sacrificial ground for the worship of the gods should be located between Soma and Īśāna;
or it may be between Indra and Īśāna, or in the middle between Agni and Sureśa (Indra),
or between Yama and Agni— one should construct the sacrificial pavilion for the festival in one of these places.

Sarasvatī presides over the place of standing, while Vāyu presides over the place of instrumental music. When there is a contraction of space, the method of arrangement may, in some cases, occur even in the absence of the aforementioned enclosures. (10.89)
The procedure for constructing water reservoirs such as wells and tanks:
a well may be made in the western, northern, or even the northeastern direction;
or one should construct a well wherever there are natural springs of water.

One should cause a great embankment to be constructed in the eight directions as appropriate; outside the enclosure wall there should be a long pond, and monasteries for ascetics and others, and there should be a long pond situated outside all the enclosure walls. (10.91)
A monastery (maṭha) should be established outside for ascetics who are devoted to hearing the scriptures and those distinguished by the study of the Vedas, as well as for others;
and dwellings should also be constructed for those who remain there taking refuge in the deity.
The description of the garden and so forth:
one should construct a dwelling all around the garden and the flower grove. (10.93) This is the definition of the single-layered enclosure.
Listen to these attendants for one who is joined with a single enclosure:
the King of Birds (Garuḍa) should be envisioned here facing the principal image.
One should also construct his abode in front of the dance-hall.
In the northern hall of the gopura, Ravi faces the temple;
in its southern hall, one should install Sudhāṃśu.
Kāma is in the southeast, Brahmā in the south, and Gajānana should be in the southwest.
In the western direction is Ṣaṇmukha, Durgā in the north-west, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) in the north;
Śaṅkara is in the north-east, and likewise Kṣetrapāla should be there. One should place Viṣvaksena in the space between Soma (the Moon) and Īśa (Śiva).
On the southern courtyard are the Seven Mothers, and Śrī is in the southwest (nairṛta).

The world-protectors, Indra and the others, are to be worshipped in their respective directions on the courtyard. There should be a sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭhaka) inside or outside the gateway (gopura).
In the specific temple known as Antarhāra,
it is said that the two persons, Sūrya and Acyuta, are to be installed in their respective places.
Likewise, in the second enclosure (āvaraṇa), Sūrya and Candramas are to be envisioned.
Hayagrīva should be placed in the position of Smara; Saṅkarṣaṇa in the position of Vidhi; Varāha in the position of Vighnarāja; Pradyumna in the position of Śarajanman;
Ananta should be in the place of Kātyāyanī; and Aniruddha in the seat of Nara.
If there is a lion-man (Nṛkesarin) on the Śāṅkara [section], then Indra and the other deities should be worshipped in due order in their respective positions upon the pedestals in the courtyard.
[These are] the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, the wielder of the conch, the wielder of the sword, and the wielder of the club.
The wielders of divine weapons— the Sārṅgin, the Padmin, and the Vajrin— are to be worshipped.
Regarding the positioning and so forth of the deities of the retinue,
those whose places have been mentioned elsewhere are situated in the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
All those retinues in the second [enclosure] are to be known as previously described.
But in the middle, within the *sāla* grove, on both sides of the main gate, the twelve Ādityas are to be worshipped; in the center are Manmatha and Vedhas.
The Vasus should be worshipped in front of the architect of obstacles;
in the middle, between the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) and Gaṇeśa, the hosts of Pitṛs are to be honored;
and the Viśvedevas and Maruts are to be propitiated between Guha and Durga.
The Seven Sages (Saptarṣis) are to be worshipped between Durgā and Kubera.
The eleven Rudras are recorded as being between Kubera and Īśāna;
and right there, on the front courtyard, are the Kṣetrapālas, Kumuda and the others.
O Lotus-seated One, those eighteen who are among the Gaṇas should be honored at the site of the pedestal for Indra and the others, and they should be stationed within the boundary-enclosure;
furthermore, those excellent attendants [should be placed] upon the surface of the courtyard ground.
Upendra and the others are to be worshipped in the directions starting from the east in due order:
Upendra, Prākṛta, Puṇya, Puṣkara, Viśvabhāvana,
Asuraghna, Kṛtānta, and Bhūtanātha is remembered as the eighth.
Within the great boundary, those who are middling among the Gaṇas should be made into retinues; Viśva and the others [should be placed] among Vāsava and the rest.
The deities are to be worshipped in the courtyard.
I shall describe in due order those who are to be worshipped in the courtyards:
Viśveṣī, Viśvakṛt, Viśva, Viśvātmā, Viśvalocana,
Viśvapāda, Viśvabhuja, and likewise Viśvakarmakṛt.
The Ādityas and the other eighteen groups—I shall describe those eighteen groups as they are proclaimed in sequence; understand them:
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Sādhyas, and likewise the Maruts.
The Viśvedevas, the ancestors, the mothers, and the household deities;
Aṅgiras, the two Aśvins, and the hosts of female deities;
the lords of the worlds, the Vāstu-deities, and the lunar mansions as attendants. (10.116–10.117)
The lords of the principles (tattvas) are proclaimed as the highest,
as are the Siddhas, the Ṛṣis, the Nāgas, the Asuras, and even the Rākṣasas;
likewise the Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Saurabheyas, and Guhyakas.
The Gandharvas and Apsarases, as well as the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), mortals, and the Rohiṇyas— these groups are known as the intermediate ones. Furthermore,
the Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Kūśmāṇḍas, and Pramathas [are also among them].
Skanda, the Bālagrahas, and the terrifying Taitalas;
the Kinnaras, Vetālas, and likewise the Apasmāras;
the Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, and Cārikās.
And the Mohinīs among all [the classes] are proclaimed to be the lowest.
Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Vidhātṛ, Mitra, Varuṇa, Bhaga, Vivasvat, Pūṣan, Savitṛ, and likewise Ravi; 10.123–10.123.
Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu—these twelve are declared to be the sons of Aditi:
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala, Pratyūṣa, and Prabhāsa; these are the Vasus of tranquil luster.
Mṛgavyādha, Śarva, Nirṛti, Dhvaja, Ekapāt,
Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and likewise Yavasa,
Sthāṇu, Bhava, and Kapālin— these are remembered as the eleven Rudras. (10.125–10.126)
Three-eyed and resembling Rudra, they wear crowns of matted hair: Āvaha, Vivaha, Udvaha, Saṃvaha,
Nivaha, Anuvaha, and likewise Pravaha.
These seven Maruts are proclaimed; they are the seven who split the mountains. Time, Ravi, Rudra, Agni, and likewise Water—these five are declared to be the groups known as the Sādhyas.
Rudra, Agni, Savitṛ, Viṣṇu, and the Viśvedevas are recorded as the hosts of gods;
likewise Kavyavāḍ Anala, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman;
as well as the Agniṣvātta Pitṛs, the Somapas, and the Barhiṣads.
These are declared to be the seven groups of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas), honored by the worlds:
Kratu, Dakṣa, the one called Kālaka, Vasu, Satya, Śuci, Ruci, Purūravas, and Dhruva; these are remembered as the Viśvedevas.
The two Aśvins are celebrated as both Nāsatya and Dasra; they are gods who resemble one another and were born from the jar of nectar. [Then follow:
Ravi, Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Guru, Śukra, and Śanaiścara.
Rāhu and Ketu are likewise mentioned as being conjoined; thus, the nine grahas have been described.
Śakra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna—these eight are proclaimed as the guardians of the world (lokapālas). 10.134–10.135
Brahmā, Marīci, Atri, Vivasvat, Pṛthivīśvara,
Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, and Savitraka;
Rudra, Rudrajaya, Indra, and likewise Indrajaya.
Īśa, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Bhānu, Satya, Bhṛgu, and Antarikṣa were in the east;
likewise Agni, Pūṣan, Kṛśānu, Bṛhatkṣatra, and Yama. (10.137–10.138)
Gandharvī, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are in the south;
likewise Pitṛ, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, and Puṣpadantaka;
Varuṇa, Bhṛśa, Āpa, Cakṣuṣmān, and Manojava.
Roganātha, Mṛtyanta, Bhallāṭa, and Soma;
Aditi and Vāstunātha—these are remembered as the hosts of Vāsudeva.
Agni, Vāyu, Prajāsakta, and the four Aṅgirasas are likewise remembered.
They abide in two forms: in the form of sages and in the form of gods.
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Vighnā—these three are the household deities.
Thus, these eighteen classes have been declared, categorized as middling, superior, and inferior.
The superior and middling [attendants] are esteemed among the retinues;
the inferior retinues are proclaimed to be in the abodes of Rudra and similar places.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Conception of the Deities of the Retinue and Others," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the eleventh chapter.
The ritual for the materials of the image and so forth:
thereafter, the venerable Lord explains the ritual for the material of the representation.
Whatever material this image is made of, that is said to be manifold.
(11.1) The specification of the six materials, beginning with gems:
gems, metal, stone, clay, wood, and crystal.
The six substances from which images are said to be made are the primary materials.
One should have an image fashioned with gems, foremost among them rubies, complete with all its limbs; or one may worship an image that is half-finished, or even one that is entirely plain.
The description of the fruits of the aforementioned substances:
All gems produced from precious sources are faultless and bestow the fruits of all desires.
Gold, silver, and copper are recognized as the three types of metal. (11.4)
An image made of gold brings about all prosperity;
wealth, fame, victory, and wisdom are the fruits of silver.
Through the worship of an image of udumbara wood, there shall arise intelligence, peace, and good fortune.
Regarding the fourfold nature of stone:
"O Brahmin, stone is of four kinds according to the distinctions of color, such as white and so forth.
A white stone is for a Brāhmaṇa, while that of a Kṣatriya is pale-red. (11.6)
The yellow for a Vaiśya and the black for a Śūdra are the primary [colors], as previously described.
A Brāhmaṇa may have four, a Kṣatriya three, and a Vaiśya two;
there should be only one for the fourth [caste]. This is stated to be the secondary rule.
The supreme stone [is marked with] the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and spear; sandalwood, garlands, a lion, an elephant, a deer, a boar, kusha grass, and a water-pot. 11.9
Where the śrīvatsa, chowrie, umbrella, banner, fish, and birds,
as well as sesame seeds, rice grains, and sand, are seen upon the stones,
those [stones] are auspicious and bestow prosperity upon the sacrificer and the king.
The method for examining internal defects in stones, wood, and so forth: Stones containing an embryo must be rejected, for the embryos remain situated within.
Listen now to this method by which they can be detected.
Having ground together buffalo butter, powdered ram's horn,
and the powder of *kuruvinda* (red pepper), one should smear it with cow’s milk upon a stone or wood; thereby,
the manifestation of the interior [contents] shall occur.
If furrows are seen, as well as circular whorls,
and if there is a faint sound within them, or even warmth upon touch—
there are clearly embryos in those [plants]; one should carefully uproot them.
In a pale-red mandala, one should point out red sands;
in a white lotus, white sands situated within the form of the embryo;
and in a glossy, tawny-colored [mandala], a tortoise situated there.
In the color of a pigeon it is gaulī; in the madder-red color, lohitadardura;
in the white color like foam, however, it is śukla; in the reddish-yellow, it is kacchapa.
In the saffron-yellow color, however, the yellow one, barṣābhū, is situated.
In a womb of color resembling white gold, one sees a small bird;
in a color like black iron, a lizard situated within;
and in a molasses-colored [womb], a stone-firefly, while in one resembling honey, [one sees a similar object]. 11.18–11.19
Upon a complexion like that of a spotted deer, he saw a scorpion; upon one resembling a sword, a grasshopper; playfully, upon a dark and rough surface, a piece of foam;
upon a tawny one, a mouse; and upon a black one, a black snake; and upon one resembling young grass, [he saw] a [white] insect.
A wise man should extract everything from such a fish-shaped embryo according to the distinction of colors within the mandala, and he should remove it with effort;
just as one fashions an image from wood or stone using the interior of the embryo.
Whether out of ignorance or greed, a sacrificer who acts with haste destroys his own kinsmen root and branch;
both the king and the kingdom perish, as does the one who established them. (11.23)
Once the inner sanctum has been constructed, the preceptor should subsequently perform oblations for the sake of pacification (śānti).
He should feed the Brahmins and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to his own capacity.
[This concludes] the application of the female, male, and neuter stones in the case of images and the like.

If one should respectfully fashion an image from cool stone, Hari—the bestower of boons—becomes manifest in person, present, and prosperous. Stone is said to be of three kinds: female, male, and neuter.
If, upon cutting, a sound arises resembling the ringing of a bronze bell at the center of the head region, and if it resembles the sound of bronze at the base,
where there is a sound like that of a palm-clap, that stone belongs to a man.
A stone that is slightly deficient in sound due to some flaw is called *sādhama*.
A stone devoid of resonance, however, is declared to be *napuṃsaka* (neuter).
An image should be fashioned from a male stone (*puṃśilā*), while the pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be made from a female stone (*strīśilā*).
The placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) should not be performed upon a stone slab; rather, it should be done according to the sequence [of the ritual].
For the construction of goddesses such as Śrī and others, a female stone is best;
for the footstool, a male stone should be used, while the placement of jewels is performed on a neuter stone.

A cool stone is Saumya; that which belongs to Viṣṇu yields great fruit. A hot stone is Āgneyī; that which belongs to Rudra becomes the seat of disease. That which is known as Saumya is of a fearless nature, while the Brāhmī stone brings about creation.
That stone which is cool during the hot season and becomes very hot at the arrival of the clouds,
being pure and of a single color, is fit for the making of an image. However, a stone that is variegated with many mixed colors always brings about disease.

One should take a stone for an image from mountains that are well-known for their sites of stone acquisition and their fruits; or a stone found on the ground is praised, but one that is censured is never acceptable. 11.34.

That land which is filled with flowering groves and surrounded by reservoirs is to be known as Vāruṇī; the stones found there grant all desires. That region where the water is to the north and the great field is to the south [is also Vāruṇī].
And where milky trees are found nearby, that ground is considered to belong to Mahendra;
the stone situated there is always highly esteemed as a bestower of nourishment.
To its southeast are the *kāśmarya* and *khadira* trees, and others.

The jhallikā, ṭiṭṭibha, vulture, boar, wild beasts, and so forth [are found there]. || 11.38 || Where this [earth] becomes fiery due to the very small amount of water contained within it, the stone produced there possesses little power and is therefore not approved. || 11.39 ||
Where trees such as the *vibhītaka* grow, where predatory beasts are ever-present,
where water and grass have been abandoned, and which is overgrown with thorny trees;
and upon that wind-swept ground lies a stone that bestows desolation.
Places where stone is to be avoided include the banks of rivers, the shores of lakes, a site of ashes, a crossroads,
a village, a cremation ground, an anthill, and a place afflicted by salt water.
On ground that is impure, frequented by Śabaras, Caṇḍālas, and the like;
crowded with heaps of gravel, devoid of grass, and lacking water;
and near a temple, scorched by wind, sun, and fire. || 11.42–11.43 ||
In such a location, all stones should be avoided, for if they are taken, they bring misfortune.
Stones that are to be accepted are found in a meritorious field, in an auspicious region, and in a place densely filled with sacred trees.
In a place filled with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass and water, frequented by black deer,
strewn with lotuses and water-lilies, and dense with fields of rice;
crowded with *hintāla*, *pūga*, *punnāga*, and coconut trees.
In a region crowded with ascetics, a stone may be taken.

Having thus distinguished what is to be avoided and what is not, and having examined the merits and defects, as well as the different regions, the various types of ground, and likewise the different forms of the Liṅga. || 11.46–11.47 ||
One should select an auspicious stone that possesses distinct colors such as white and the like;
the time for taking the stone is during auspicious lunar mansions, lunar days, and weekdays favorable to the patron.
Accompanied by favorable omens such as those of birds,
and endowed with supreme faith, both the patron and the preceptor,
together with the chariot-maker and groups of master builders, [proceeded].
Having first fed the Brahmins and had them recite blessings such as *svasti*,
he should cause a large water-shed (*prapā*) to be constructed at the site where the stone is to be installed.
Having performed the rite of sowing sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) there, he should remain celibate and subsist on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*).
The preceptor, remaining pure, should dwell there together with the patron.
One should place a load of śāli rice upon that altar-platform in the middle of the water-shed;
therein he should set down a great pitcher wrapped in thread, cloth, and other materials.
Having placed a *kūrca* grass-bundle and covered it with fresh shoots of the *aśvattha* tree,
and having arranged [the vessel] enriched with jewels and metals according to the mantra of the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*),
one should place jars wrapped with thread in its eight directions.
One should place the *vardhanī* vessel at the side of that very *mahākumbha*,
and one should scatter consecrated *siddhārtha* seeds in all directions with the *astra-mantra*.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should then display the *cakra-mudrā*.
Then, having displayed the mahāmudrā and bowed with the añjali-mudrā,
the preceptor should then invoke the omnipresent deity using the mūrti-mantra;
having established [the deity] in the great jar, he should worship him in due order.
One should worship the King of Mantras with the *vardhanī* vessel in the eight jars;
thereafter, one should offer the images of Viṣṇu and the others, and present the supreme food (*paramānna*).
One should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) in the four directions, either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a ritual mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should offer fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood, flowers, fruit, clarified butter, and sprouts,
each separately one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
and likewise, one should offer oblations of *caru* with the *Nṛsūkta* separately in each of the four sacrificial pits.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the eastern pit to the forest deities,
as well as to the mountains, the boulders, the peaks, and the waterfalls there;
likewise to the oceans, the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the great forest trees.
O Lotus-born One, he likewise [offered] those born from a womb, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouts;
indeed, all beings with mantras dedicated to their respective deities,
ending in "svāhā," along with the vyāhṛtis, until the final full oblation.

The preceptor should offer an oblation (bali) to the spirits with these substances: parched grain, powdered turmeric, parched rice, cakes, and curd-mixed gruel. One hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter should be offered to the Lord of Dreams.
With musical instruments and likewise with the chanting of the Veda, one should cause proclamations to be made everywhere throughout the night.
Having fasted and slept upon a bed of *darbha* grass, pure and with a restrained mind,
the self-possessed man should mutter [the mantra] one hundred and eight times to the Lord of Dreams.

If, while sleeping, one should see a mountain blazing brightly in a dream, a stone should be taken immediately in the morning; if it is not seen, one should perform a rite of pacification. This applies likewise if it is difficult to see or if other previously mentioned ill omens arise.
At that auspicious moment, the most excellent of preceptors should gaze upon the stone:
"May the yakṣas, piśācas, nāgas, and others who dwell here constantly all depart; may Hari ever abide here. (11.68–69)
Having said this, one should place there those who have attained mastery through mantras and have accomplished their goals;
and one should offer an oblation to the spirits in every direction with all the mantras.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited, one should touch the stones with the Puruṣasūkta.
Having offered the *arghya* with the root mantra, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
In accordance with the dimensions of the temple, the master masons should quickly lay down the measuring lines;
the stone-cutters should then carve the stones according to the command of the chariot-maker.
Determining suitable and unsuitable stones based on the irregularity of their veins:
one with a vein running toward the south bestows peace; one with a vein toward the east grants victory;
one with a vein toward the west brings prosperity; and one with a vein toward the north bestows nourishment. (11.73)
One should avoid [the stone] whose head faces a corner, for if one were to do so, it would cause the destruction of the lineage.
This is the rule for bringing the stone: the head of the stone should face the direction opposite to that of the temple’s entrance. (11.74)
If there is an inversion [of the foundations], calamity will soon befall the sacrificer, the king, the kingdom, the site, the dwelling, and all others.
Likewise, if the base portion of the stones should be on top, [the same result follows].
If the head portion [of the stone] should fall downward, there will be ruin for both the king and the kingdom.
One should bathe the extracted stone with water from a large jar,
and with water from jars dedicated to Viṣṇu and others, while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
One should sprinkle the stone again with water from the *vardhanī* vessel.
This is the procedure for the stone suitable for an image of the goddess Śrī and other deities;
for the purification of the images of these goddesses, one should perform the preparatory consecration (*adhivāsana*) separately.
One should worship the goddess Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, in the central pitcher;
having worshipped the eight goddesses in due order in the eight pitchers,
and having performed the fire-oblation and other rites as before, there shall be a stone slab for the image.
If, O goddesses, the [boundary] stones are set up by a woman or a stone out of negligence,
or if they are possessed by great greed, they may destroy the subjects within their own domain; therefore,
at that very moment, auspicious surrounding stones must be taken up.
One should perform the collection of the stones with their respective mantras in due order.
Having properly taken up that stone and placed it upon carts and other vehicles,
the architects, following the tradition of the chariot-makers, shall lead it to the temple site.

They should perform the consecration according to the scriptures, endowed with the characteristics prescribed therein. Whatever ritual for the collection of stones has been described outside the temple,
one may instead perform all of that— including the rites beginning with the germinating of seeds— within the temple.

Know that even a stone taken for another purpose becomes pure through renewed consecration, because it is permitted to be taken again after having been formally relinquished according to rule, due to an inability to complete the task for which it was first taken. (11.85)
The time for collecting timber is considered auspicious during the eight months beginning with Kārttika; however, the collection of stone is deemed auspicious in all months. (11.86)
The description of the woods suitable for construction:
sandalwood, aloe-wood, kāśmarya, yellow sandalwood, kesara, khadira, kurava, and likewise asana. (11.87)
Madhuka, devadāru, jasmine, bilva, and likewise śamī;
śāka and panasa, as well as kadamba and tilaka;
nameru, phalinī, surabhi, and likewise campaka.
The *śiṃśupā*, *kṣīrikā*, *sāla*, *bījaka*, and *kuruvindaka*;
the *tiniśa*, *candana*, *cūta*, *tamāla*, *sarala*, and *arjuna*;
the *kuṭaja*, *karakelī*, *saptaparṇa*, and *madhuṣṭhila*. (11.89–11.90)
The *varaṇa*, the *nicula*, the *punnāga*, the *khadira*,
and the *rājavṛkṣa*— these are declared to be suitable for making images;
they must be full of heartwood, dense, and free from all defects.
An image should never be fashioned from these [forbidden materials].
I shall now describe the woods that must be avoided and the trees that must be shunned; listen to them.
Dried out by themselves and burnt by themselves, broken down and with their bark stripped away;
crooked, riddled with woodworms, hollowed out, and inhabited by birds;
constantly frequented by the lowest of men such as Caṇḍālas and those born of inverse unions (pratiloma).
Those who dwell in trees, those stationed at shrines, as well as those presided over by deities; those dwelling in cremation grounds, those on roads, and those near temples;
those dwelling by wells, those by tanks, and those who are deformed—these are to be avoided.
If one should, through negligence, fashion an image from trees that are forbidden,
both the maker and the one who commissioned it shall perish along with their lineages.
Even regarding the gathering of wood, the rule is exactly the same as for the selection of stone.
In a place where timber is gathered, the ritual consecration (*adhivāsana*) is performed as before;
all the fire-oblations (*homa*) should be performed according to the rules, just as when gathering stone.
The limbs of the trees, such as the sprouts and so forth, are [treated] as before. || 11.97–11.98 ||
The best of teachers should offer oblations into the eastern fire-pit;
he should wash the base of the tree with a cloth and then cover that spot with darbha grass while reciting the root mantra.
And having offered oblations with the twelve forms, beginning with the Fish, in their proper sequence,
he should thereafter worship the tree with the *vyāhṛtis*.

"By virtue of my past actions, I have assumed this stationary form; I choose it as the image of Viṣṇu for you, which brings about all prosperity. Therefore, depart from this state of being stationary and attain a divine, unsurpassed form."
"Enjoy abundant pleasures through the grace of Vāsudeva;
O tree, I do not harm you, but I release you from birth.
Having addressed [the tree] with this mantra, one should wrap it with a protective thread.

Other matters not mentioned here should be performed at night, like the taking up of the stone. Regarding the cutting of trees, the preceptor, having bathed at dawn and being pure, should give the instruction on the time, direction, and so forth during an auspicious moment.
One should cut down a tree with an axe while facing east, identifying oneself with the Self (ātman).
Then, having received permission from his teacher, the chariot-maker should cut the tree;
there is a difference in the result depending on the direction in which the felled tree falls.
A tree fallen toward the east or the north brings prosperity.
One should fashion the *bimba* with the trunk and a branch, and perform its consecration; likewise, one should fashion the *pratimā* with the trunk and a corresponding branch.
Having meditated upon Hari situated there, one should sprinkle him with water from a pitcher;
one should sprinkle all around with water from a jar while reciting the root mantra.
O Lotus-seated One, one should give a sacrificial fee to the guru as before.
The chariot-maker is authorized to fashion the image;
having brought the wood to the temple, he should have the chariot-maker construct an image of most wonderful form according to the measurements of the sanctuary. (11.109)
Having established the dwelling, the residence, and so forth, and having set up the tree on the ground,
one should perform everything outside in the forest according to the ritual rules;
this is the fault in creating an image from an unprepared tree.

If one should, out of delusion, fashion an image with unrefined [materials] according to the aforementioned procedure, it will lead only to misfortune. Therefore, that which is made with the materials as specified brings about prosperity. (11.111–112)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Stone and Wood," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
The Twelfth Chapter:
The Procedure for the Dimensions and Other Attributes of the Primary Image of the Blessed Lord.
Now I shall fully explain the measurement of the height of the principal image (mūlabera),
or the measurement of the width of the inner sanctum (garbha), or else the length of the door;
or the measurement of the base of the temple (prāsādapāda), or even the measurement in cubits (hasta).
The measurement of the sacrificial post may be equal to the height of the patron, or otherwise;

one should fashion an image of Dhruva that is favorable to the village and other settlements. This concerns the measurement of the image and its various classifications, such as the superior and so forth.
O Four-faced One, an image that is equal in height to its internal width is the best;
an image one-ninth part less than that is middling;
and an image one-fifth part less is proclaimed as the lowest.
Having divided the width of the womb into seven parts, one should omit two;
the height equal to the remaining portions would be excellent, O Lotus-born One,
while the middling is with three parts of five threads, and the smallest with two.
The best [height] is one and a half times the height of the door; furthermore, the middling is one-quarter more than that. The smallest should be equal to the door itself;
having divided the door into sixteen parts, it is reduced by one, two, or three parts respectively.
Thus, for the feet and so forth, there are respectively superior, middling, and inferior [measures].
The height of the *kautuka* (marriage canopy) when standing is declared to be five cubits for the best, three for the middling, and one for the others. 12.8.
Having divided the width of the sanctum (garbhagṛha) into three parts, there are two [types]:
the best [is] with five parts, the middle with three parts, and the smallest with half [of that]. || 12.9 ||
Or, when seated, it is best if it is equal to the width of the womb;
the middling is one-ninth less than that; the lowest is said to be one-fifth less;
and the excellent is six-sevenths [of the womb-width]. || 12.10–12.11 ||
The middle [height] is indeed sevenfold by three [units], and the smallest is threefold by two;
for one standing at the doors and so forth, the sequence of height while seated is as follows:
the best is seven cubits when seated, while the middle is five.
I shall describe the measurement for the form of the bed, as well as the height of the bed itself;
having divided the length of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) into sixteen parts once more. || 12.13 ||
Having set aside four parts from the head and two likewise from the feet,
there is an excellent elevation for one lying down by means of the remaining tenth part.
Having divided the length into eight parts, having omitted two at the head and at the sides...
One part [of the length] from the feet, and by the remaining portion, the middle [part];
having divided the total length into seven parts, two at the head and one from the feet—
having omitted these, the shape of one lying down is formed by the remainder.
Alternatively, having divided the width into four parts, one should set aside one of them.
With the remainder doubled, there shall be the maximum height for one lying down;
having done so, with a fifth part [of that], there shall be the middling height for one lying down.
The lowest height for one lying down should be equal to the measurement of the womb's width;
the highest elevation for one lying down should be double the measurement of the door.
The middle height should be one and a half times that measure, and the final (highest) should be one and a quarter times that measure.
Just as the sequence beginning with the *uttama* [size] has been proclaimed in relation to the door,
so too should it be for the *dhruvabera*, whether it rests upon a pillar or another support;
these are excellent when measuring seven, five, or three cubits respectively.
Just as with the seat, the measurement for the chariot is established in its universal form.
Having divided the inner sanctum (garbhageha) into three parts, the upper portion shall be the best. When that [sanctum] is divided into five parts, the middle portion shall be the medium one.
The lowest [type] consists of half a *garbha* by measure; this is the rule common to all.
Now, the rule for the measurement of the form according to the suitability of the patron (*yajamāna*) and others is being described.
O four-faced one, one should convert the obtained portion into finger-breadths for the temple;
this is the rule for finger-breadths.
Regarding that, I shall now declare the rule for finger-breadths—listen attentively to it.
The five types of finger-breadths (aṅguli) are declared; these modes are described in sequence:
measure (māna), intermediate measure (mānāntara), unit (mātrā), the fist (muṣṭi), and likewise the body (deha).
Listen now to the definitions of these divisions according to the order that will be explained.
The subtle particles of dust that spread within those rays of the sun which reach the path of the window are called *paramāṇus*.
Eight of those are equal to one hair (*keśa*); eight hairs are equal to one nit (*līkṣā*); and eight nits are equal to one louse (*yūka*).
Eight of those *yavas* are declared to be one *aṅguli*.

Among these, the superior *aṅguli* consists of seven *yavas*, while the middle is six *yavas*; the inferior is said to be five *yavas*. This constitutes the *mānāṅgula* (the finger-breadth as a measure).
The measurement of an *antara-aṅgula* is formed by eight barley grains placed crosswise;
or, the *antara* measurement may be three *śāli* grains placed straight.
[This is] in the middle of the middle finger of the teacher’s right hand.

The long interval between the two joints is declared to be one *mātrā-aṅgula*. One should divide this into four parts; one such part is known as a *muṣṭyaṅguli*. This is the measurement for the length of the marriage-thread (*kautuka*).
Having divided whatever is the length of the *kautuka* into ten parts,
and then having divided one of those parts into twelve, the height of the image should be one of those [twelfth] units; this is based on the *mahāmāna-aṅgula*.
The measurement in finger-breadths for palaces, altars, and so forth, as well as for the palaces themselves, may be made using that very unit or by another measure;
furthermore, this is the rule for altars, pedestals, palanquins, chariots, and the like. (12.34)
The measurements for the sacrificial implements should be made using the *mānāntara-aṅgula* and not by any other;
furthermore, one should make the tools for the sacrifice using the *mātrā-aṅgula*.
The components for the fire-oblation (*homa*), such as the *sruva* ladle and others, depend on the *kuṇa-muṣṭi-aṅgula*.
The measurement of the limbs of the image should be determined by the same *dehalabdha-aṅgula* (finger-breadth obtained from the body);
one should fashion the limbs of the image using that very *dehalabdha-aṅgula*. It has been declared that the image is to be worshipped with as many divisions of parts as there may be.

The division of the dimensions of villages and other such entities is by means of the *mānāṅgula* (measuring finger) alone; their measurement is performed using that *mānāṅgula*. Having taken that as the finger-measure, one should then apply it to income, expenditure, and so forth, so that whatever may be auspicious for the village and other entities may come to pass. (12.37)

That shall now be explained, O Brahmin; let it be understood. Having made the obtained portion into finger-units, one should then increase that finger-unit by eight and likewise decrease it by the number twelve.
The remainder should be known as *aṅgula*; one should increase it by nine through expenditures (*vyaya*) and decrease it by ten. The remainder is designated as *aṅgula*.
Income brings all auspicious results, while expenditure brings only slight auspiciousness.
O Lotus-Seated One, when adverse and contrary [planets] occupy the villages and other divisions, there is loss;
with three [planets] there is growth, and with eight there is destruction. The remainder is declared to be the source (yoni). The eight starting from the banner (dhvaja) are the gains (āyas).

The banner, the smoke, the lion, the dog, the bull, the donkey, and the elephant—these are said to be wombs; among them, that which possesses auspicious characteristics is auspicious. The banner, the lion, the elephant, and the ox are auspicious wombs that bring about prosperity.
For the births of those who smoke, those born of donkeys, and dogs are indeed unfavorable.
Regarding the method of calculating the lunar mansions and so forth:
it increases by eight during growth and decreases by twenty-seven.
That which remains is declared to be the "residue" (*śiṣṭa*); it is auspicious for villages and the like.
When increased by nine or decreased by seven, the residue is in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Those days are auspicious if they are gentle (*saumya*), while the cruel ones (*krūra*) bring about fear.

In the case of increase, [the result] is by four and nine; in the case of decrease, the remaining portion is the subtracted fraction. The thief, the one capable of enjoyment, the fortunate one, the king, the impotent, the well-guided, the beloved, and the long-lived—these are declared to be the lords of the signs.
The definition of the tāla, dhanus, krośa, and so forth: A measurement of twelve *mānāṅgulas* is considered to be that which is called a *tāla*.
Two *tālas* are said to be a *hasta*, and eight of those are called a *dhanus*. (12.48)

That same *daṇḍa* with its yoke-pole is one *krośa*; five hundred of those [make] four *krośas*, which is a *gavyūti*; and that [gavyūti] multiplied by four is a *yojana*. [This applies] to the village, the sacrificer, the king, and the countryside.
If the Āya and other [proportions] are favorable, the images grant all accomplishments.
This Āya and so forth should be understood as being based on the primary image (mūlabera);
it does not apply to the limbs of [subsidiary] images, whether they are made of metal or otherwise.
Faith is to be understood as residing in the images and likewise in the temple pavilions;
now, in this context, the various measurements such as the *prastha* and the specific limits of those measures are being stated. 12.52
Four *vrīhis* make one *kuñja*; eight of those are called a *mañjiṣṭha*.
One hundred and sixty of those make a *niṣka*, and eight *niṣkas* make a *phala*.
Five *phalas* make a *kuḍupa*, and four times that amount makes a *prastha*.
One should know that four of those [kuḍavas] make an āḍhaka; two of those are called a śiva.
Two of those are declared a droṇa; two of those would be a khārī.
Three of those khārīs are declared a bhāra as a measure of weight.

By this measurement, the ghee and other substances are to be measured. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Determination of Proportions Consistent with the Fixed Image," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
The Thirteenth Chapter:
The Procedure for the Installation of the Śūla, by the Blessed Lord.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the installation and other rites for the Śūla, including the rules concerning its form, dimensions, and so forth, according to whether it belongs to the same or a different species. Solid woods such as sandalwood and others that are dense [are recommended]. (13.1)
Having accepted [the request] as before, the supreme guide should take it;
if the trident is made from a single individual tree of that species,
one should know that it is excellent, but if it has many joints, it is middling.
O Lotus-seated One, if that [liṅga] is made of various materials, it is considered inferior.
However, having had it carved by artisans and removed from its core, one should have the trident fashioned from the essence; its measurement is now described.
The height of the auspicious banner is said to be one hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths,
while the length of the bamboo staff is stated to be sixty-two.
Its base, tip, and middle are to be expanded in that respective order.
Those [four] measures of four finger-breadths each, together with three and a half [of those],
and six barley-corns— thus the circumference at the base shall be measured at sixteen finger-breadths;
likewise, the circumference in the middle shall be fifteen finger-breadths.
O Lotus-seated One, its circumference at the tip should be fourteen finger-breadths;
the breast-rod (vakṣodaṇḍa) should be thirty-four finger-breadths in length.
It should be four finger-breadths in width and sixteen finger-breadths in measurement [at the other end].
The crest should have either two or three points, resembling the bud of a *kiṃśuka* flower.
The length of the staff-like arm should be twenty-five finger-breadths;
its base should be three and a half finger-breadths wide, and its middle portion should be broader than that.
O Four-faced One, its tip should be two, three, or two-and-a-half finger-breadths;
the forearm should be twenty finger-breadths long, plus two barley-corns.
