The width at the base, middle, and tip should be two or three finger-breadths.
One should know that there are three and a half finger-breadths [in height] respectively.
The hollow at the base of the arm and the tip of the forearm and upper arm should be made in pairs; the lower arm is also to be fashioned in this manner.
The length of the ritual staff (kalpadaṇḍa) shall be measured at sixteen finger-breadths;
its width in the middle shall be four finger-breadths,
and its circumference in the middle is proclaimed to be sixteen finger-breadths.
The length of the side-staff (pārśvadaṇḍa) should be made thirty-two finger-breadths;
the circumference of the side-staff is measured at four finger-breadths.
Furthermore, the hip-staff (kaṭīdaṇḍa) has two prongs, and the chest-staff (vakṣodaṇḍa) is likewise fixed by rule.
The length of the upper staff, measured correctly from the sides of the two [lower] staves, should be twenty-one finger-breadths; the staff should be equal in height to the shank-staff.
The width at the middle, the tip, and the base is recited in sequence as follows: [12, 8, and 4 finger-breadths respectively].
Three finger-breadths, three and a half, two and a half, and four finger-breadths [are the measures].

(13.18) The base of the shank is three finger-breadths; the interval is two and a half finger-breadths; and there, the width is considered to be three times two finger-breadths (six finger-breadths). (13.19)
The hollow at the base of the thighs should be two finger-breadths wide and six barley-corns deep;
one should fashion a pair [of sockets] at the ends of the upper and lower parts of the thighs.
One should fix the bamboo staff so that it is set low in the middle of the chest and the hips.
The measurement of the tridents has been declared; now the enumeration of the tridents is being stated:
the number of tridents consists of the bamboo staff, the waist staff, and likewise the chest staff.
The four staff-like arms, the forearm likewise,
and the staff-like shank— these are the thirteen staffs of the trident;
one should join them as appropriate and must not leave any part hollow.
A wedge should not be inserted by craftsmen during the work on the spire;
they prescribe a bamboo staff reaching either to the edge of the crown or to the top of the head.
Alternatively, the wise man should fashion it so that it reaches down to the base, ensuring stability as required.
One should perform the firm binding of the stakes with an iron band.
Regarding the varieties of the stake-pole, such as iron and others:
the stake-poles should be made of iron, or otherwise, if one has the means.
The base of the bamboo is desired to be four-cornered, its middle part eight-sided, and its tip perfectly round;
the spikes may be round or otherwise. The portion of the bamboo stem measured from the neck downward shall be straight. (13.26–13.27)
Above, as appropriate, the four faces should be slightly curved;
the position of the bamboo staffs for the images should be according to their respective proportions.
The staffs of the chest and the waist should have their tips slightly curved.
Having made the base of the staff-like arms and thighs depressed according to the crest-line (yathāśikha),
the face should be one and a half [units] from the crown, or twice the length of the trident;
the width of the base of the head-ornament (mauli) should be three finger-breadths or three barley-corns.

When there is a bed for the goddesses, the distance from the base of the principal image (mūlabera) to the end of the arms should be three barley-corns (triyava), three finger-breadths (tryaṅgula), or measured at three and a half finger-breadths;
otherwise, in the case of a trident or when on a vehicle and so forth, it may extend to the tip of the nose.
When Brahmā is lying down, the height [of the liṅga] is desired to extend as far as the chin;
otherwise, it is held to extend to the knees or to the limit of the arms.
For those accompanied by Bhṛgu and the others, it is said to extend to the limit of the arms.
The preliminary consecration of the waters for the tridents and so forth,
as well as the consecration of the waters themselves, the installation in the pavilion,
the fire sacrifice, the worship of the pitcher, the worship of the gateway, and the satiation of the Brahmins. || 13.34 ||

Purification, drying, and so forth for the *śūla* [defects] are taught to be like the *bimba* [image]. Having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) at night with a concentrated mind, one should not do so during the day. On the following morning, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the site and likewise offer the ritual gift (*bali*) to the site-spirits.
One should purify the inner sanctum; one should cleanse the inner sanctum by means of sweeping, smearing with plaster, and so forth.
One should gradually strike the measuring-line that has been sprinkled with sandalwood water.
The lines run eight toward the north and likewise eight toward the east;
there are forty-nine squares, free from excess or deficiency.
This is the rule for the division of the portions designated as "Brahmin" and so forth.
The middle portion is for the Brāhmaṇas, while the portion between that is for the deities (daivika).
The third is intended for humans, and the fourth is considered the portion for the Piśācas.
Worship should take place on the pedestal in the Brāhma portion, and the [deity's] presence should be established in the Daiva portion.
In the human [class], there should be attendants; in the fourth, weapons.
In the divine [class], one should rely on something human, and there should be a seat.
For the divine and human [classes], a bed is prescribed; for the piśāca [class], a vehicle is desired.
The divine goddesses should be situated on his left side, whether he is seated,
lying down as appropriate, or even mounted upon a vehicle; likewise,
the threads [of the ritual] should face northward.
One should likewise lay down ten threads facing north;
from that, there will be eighty-one squares facing east.
The central square is the portion for the Brāhmaṇa, and the one immediately following it is for the Devas.

The third is for the ancestors (paitṛka), the fourth is for humans (mānuṣa), and the fifth again is for the Piśācas; thus one should designate the portions within the womb-chamber (garbhamandira). This describes the division of the Brahma-portion and others for single-liṅga, multi-liṅga, and other types of shrines.
The rite for a single image is prescribed for the Brahma-portion, while that for multiple images is for the Daiva-portion.
In both the Daiva and Mānuṣa sections, two seats are desired.
One should cause a bed to be made in all three: the Daiva, Mānuṣa, and Pitrya portions.
In the Paiśāca and Mānuṣa [yantras], the mounting of both is prescribed. (13.46) If there is a reversal of the stated positions, an undesirable result occurs;
when there is a reversal of the stated positions, the king and the kingdom perish.

Therefore, those who desire supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) should establish [the mantras] in the aforementioned sections. Having established the four grounds for placement according to one's desires, one should again place them in the central square.
One who desires liberation should worship the God in the [highest] station;

if there is a desire for divine enjoyments, in the one immediately following that; if seeking progeny, in the human station; and if desiring cattle and so forth, in the Paiśāca station—in this manner, according to the sequence of the stations.
Regarding the measurement of the width of the palace door:
having divided the width of the palace door into three parts, one should take the middle part and divide it into seven; then, five of those parts [should be set] to the south.
The Brahma-line has been cited as that which must be avoided in the adjacent section;
in the Brahma-section, there is a prohibition against walls, pillars, and the like.
A wise person should not construct walls, pillars, or similar structures upon the Brahma-line. (13.51)
If one should perform [the rites] out of ignorance, a great transgression would occur;
in that case, there should be a single-liṅga image made of stone upon the Brahma-thread.
Or else, it may be made from those three materials: gems, metals, or wood and clay.
A painting with many components is desired as being "half-painted" (*ardhacitra*) when it possesses a semblance of form.
The creation of all forms—whether standing, sitting, or reclining—by means of substances such as gems and the like, brings about supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) and does not cause any fault. (13.53–54)
Regarding the procedure for the depositing of the *garbha* in the sanctum:
then, in that portion of the sanctum, one should dig the earth as previously described to a depth of one cubit; right there, one should place the *napuṃsaka-śilā*.
There, upon the stone slab, one who is instructed should gradually deposit jewels together with metals, seeds, and minerals, or even without them; having performed this,
he should make it firm with the female stone (mortar) using lime and other materials.
Having fashioned a chest made of iron, or else one should deposit jewels within it.
This very placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) is prescribed to be situated at the base of the feet;
one skilled in the placement of jewels should perform it behind the others.
Regarding the variation in the form of the footstool:
that footstool may be either circular or square;
it should be placed upon a stone image or upon a stone slab. (13.59)
In the proper place, upon the stone slab, one should fashion a half-spike with two perforations;
likewise, one should construct a pedestal above the stone using bricks. Its height and width should be according to the measurement of the ground portion.
The footstool should be one-eighth of the door's width, or else one-eighth of the pedestal; it may be circular or square, according to its dimensions. (13.61–13.62)
One should fashion a lotus upon both a circular and a square base;
this is the rule for standing images, while for seated ones it should be double that amount.
For reclining images, the height should be equal to the length of the statue.
Alternatively, one may construct a lotus-seat (*padmapīṭha*) or the like using the finger-breadths obtained from the body;
it should be twelve finger-breadths in height and twice that (twenty-four) in width,
provided with twenty-five petals, or else with sixteen.

It should be provided with twelve petals or indeed with eight; the length of the petals shall be determined by the measurement of the foot. Then, it should be joined with an upper covering and endowed with fewer petals.
In the center, provided with a pericarp and having the form of a slightly blossomed lotus—
this is declared to be the seat (*viṣṭara*) for that which stands in the divine portion.
The measurement of the altar (*vedikā*) is according to the distinctions such as the single image (*ekabera*) and others.

Having divided the length in that manner into three parts, one should construct the altar (*vedi*) as one part; or alternatively, having divided it into four, one should fashion it with a fourth part. This is the height of the bathing altar, which may be circular or oval.
Whether square, oblong, hexagonal, or octagonal,
it should be joined with a base and a waist-band, measuring twelve finger-breadths [in height].
Its stalk should be as long as four finger-breadths.
Its mouth, shaped like that of a sea-monster, was twenty finger-breadths wide; from that,
the stalk rose slightly slanted and upward,
and above that altar-base was a rim four finger-breadths thick.
O Lotus-seated One, one should cause it to be raised to such a height that its width conforms to the altar,
or else the entire structure may be in the form of a lotus.
There are various types of water conduits according to the distinctions of the deity’s face and other features.
For a deity facing west, the water-channel should likewise face east;
for one facing south, it should face north.
The channel should be made to face east; no other rule is prescribed.
The procedure for the water-channel:
a water-channel should be constructed so that it reaches as far as the opening situated outside.
One should cause a stream of water to fall into the pit by means of elephant trunks and other such devices.
One should construct a pit, either circular or square, made of stone and other materials,
which is beautiful and deep, situated outside that temple;
this is the procedure for the seated image.
I shall describe the measurement for one seated upon the lion-throne:
the height is thirty-six finger-breadths measured by the fingers of the body itself, and its length is twice that, with eight lions [supporting it]. (13.77–78)
Supported by four of them, his faces were like those of a lion;
the remainder of his body was human-like and endowed with four arms.
With two hands he bore a seat, and with two others he joined his palms in reverence at his heart.
One should construct a seat adorned with jewels, or provided with lions alone, or equipped with elephant legs; there is no other rule. This is the procedure for the bed of enjoyment.
O Lotus-seated One, I shall describe for one lying upon a bed of enjoyment:
it should be circular and elongated as appropriate, and likewise formed into three circles,
with five or seven coils turning clockwise.
The circle of enjoyment (bhogamaṇḍala) has a height of four tālas measured by the fingers of the body;
it is said to be greater by three fingers at the top than at the base,
or else its enclosures (valaya) are as previously described, being doubled by three.
From that point onwards, each successive part is slightly higher than the last.
It is said that the best [image] is endowed with nine, seven, or five odd-numbered hoods; the middling and the inferior are likewise distinguished by these numbers.
The height should be three *tālas*, and the middle fruit [of the hood] should be six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The intervals between the hoods should be eight finger-breadths,
and those hoods themselves should be made concave, decreasing successively by five, four, and three [finger-breadths].
The width of their middle hood increases sequentially by finger-breadths (aṅgula).
O Four-faced One, its hoods on the sides are thirty-two finger-breadths wide,
and they are also extended by twenty, five, four, and two finger-breadths respectively.
The remaining two hoods of the serpent are twenty finger-breadths in width;
in all the others as well, a reduction should be inferred in due order.
The face is like that of a cat, adorned with fangs.
With a great jewel placed upon its head and endowed with sharp horns,
one should gradually lower its face until it reaches the tip of the crown;
from the neck to the top of the hood, the height should be four *tālas* and ten *aṅgulas*.
Alternatively, they prescribe such a height for the couch:
when the height of the threshold and the door-step is divided into three parts,
the height of the *bhogamaṇḍala* (the seating area) is desired to be one part.

Or one may construct the *bhogamaṇḍala* for the enjoyer using a fourth part [of the area]. Its height is prescribed to be like that of a seat of enjoyment or a bed of enjoyment; it should be well-rounded and elevated at the back of the God of Gods.
Just as a circle of hoods is beautiful, so too is a parasol;
it should be twenty finger-breadths high above the crown of the deity’s head. There may be a square or elongated pedestal, or else a couch.

An altar seat (*āsana*) measuring only one *padma* (twelve *aṅgulas*), provided with the previously mentioned feet and proportioned according to the *upadhāna* and other measurements, is prescribed for the Universal Form (*viśvamūrti*). This concludes the description of the vehicle, the seat, and the form.

Beneath the vehicle of Garuḍa, a lotus seat is prescribed. Upon that, one should place the Lord of Birds, joined with half the body of the god [Viṣṇu], the mighty-armed Garuḍa, upon whom Acyuta stands mounted. || 13.97–13.98 ||

One should fashion the deity and arrange the seats for those in the standing and other postures; this is the procedure for installing the consecrated *śūla*. Then, when an auspicious moment has arrived, the most excellent of teachers [should proceed]. (13.99)
Having removed the spikes that had been consecrated by the Adhvaryu priests,
and having circumambulated the sacred site while sounding the music of trumpets,
he should place the spikes in the pit according to the prescribed ritual for the depositing of jewels.
The procedure for the fivefold consecration consists of installation (sthāpanā), re-installation (sthāpana), as well as re-establishment (saṃsthāpanā),
dismissal (prasthāpanā), and consecration (pratiṣṭhā); this is known as the fivefold consecration.

That which is the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) in a [fixed] place is proclaimed as *sthāpanā*. That which is said to be the consecration on a seat is equal to *asthāpanā*. And that which is the consecration on a bed shall be *saṃsthāpanā*. || 13.102–13.103 ||
The installation that is performed upon a vehicle is called *prasthāpanā* by name;
that which is for an image on a pedestal is proclaimed as *karmārcā*. Whatever ritual action is prescribed for that [image] is celebrated as *pratiṣṭhā*.

According to the distinctions of Parameṣṭhin and the others, the preceptor should install the trident; he should install the trident of Parameṣṭhin in a standing posture, install that of Puṃs in a seated posture, and likewise that of Viśva in a reclining posture. (13.105)
In every way, however, the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) becomes a vehicle through cessation (*nivṛtti*).
Having likewise established the trident of the Goddess upon the placement of jewels in due order,
one should [establish] the tridents of the deities beginning with Brahmā by means of their respective mantras (*vidyā*).
The installation of the wall-śūlas:
having thus established the śūlas, one should fix the wall-śūla.
One should perform this for the peak and the sides of the back of the structure.
Having thus described [the procedure] for one who is seated, it is now stated for one who is lying down:
For one lying on a bed with a painful piercing sensation, one should place a bamboo staff vertically while the patient remains facing upwards;
one should have this bamboo staff placed between the divine and the human [ends]. (13.108–13.109)
On the back and the sides, at the peak [of the altar], one should place the *śayānādhāraśūlaka*.
One should fashion two *śayānādhāra* spikes facing upwards and standing erect.
Between the divine and the human [spaces], one should place the *śayitādhāraśūlaka*.
A wise person should install the *ādhāraśūla* on the bed or the ground;
for others, one should have it installed against the wall. In the absence of an *ādhāraśūla*, there is an excessive lack of divine presence (*sānnidhya*).
When the installation is performed everywhere without the pain of the foundation-crack (ādhāraśūla),
the granting of boons and the presence [of the deity] certainly become superior;
[this applies to] the sprinkling of the great jar (mahākumbha) and so forth.
Then, with water from the great *kumbha* and other jars, one should sprinkle the installed tridents with the root-vidyā using a bundle of *darbha* grass;
this is the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*).
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teacher so that the teacher may be satisfied;
one should cause ten niṣkas of gold, or half of that, to be given.
To all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) as well, one should cause ten niṣkas to be given.

At that time, having summoned the chariot-maker, the best of the twice-born [the priest] should send him away and the sacrificer should gratify him abundantly with wealth. (13.116) [This is] the appointment of the potter.

The chariot-maker should employ a potter who is skillful, tranquil, free from disease, and untainted in all the tasks prescribed by the scriptures. In his absence, he may employ a Pāraśava, at least until the completion of the journey.
An expert should perform everything according to the procedure taught by the chariot-maker.
There is a fault in uprooting a fixed stake;
one should not uproot a fixed stake, for in its removal there is great danger.
It certainly comes to pass for both the one who performs the act and the one who causes it to be performed; of this there is no doubt.
(13.119) If a limb is displaced, the sacrificer will surely suffer the loss of that limb. However, when the stake is properly established, the result is auspicious.
"Merely by the installation of the *śūla*, the patron obtains great fruit—
whether human or divine— even if [the rite] has not been fully completed.
Thus ends the section in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The thirteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installing the Śūla";
the fourteenth chapter,
"The Procedure for Constructing the Image."
O Lotus-Seated One, I shall now describe the fashioning of the image of the Blessed Lord; having bound the joints of the spikes firmly with a strip of iron. (14.1)
One should smear all the spikes on every side with the eight-fold binding;
one should wrap them with ropes, making them firm and free from gaps,
just as the body is bound by many veins.
The nature of the spikes, ropes, and so forth, consists of bones and veins:
the spikes are bones, the clay is flesh, the ropes are veins, and the cloths are skins.
(14.3) Applying uncooked clay results in an auspicious fruit.
O Four-faced One, one should perform the plastering with unbaked clay;
one should avoid using baked clay for the image, whether in a private home or even in a temple.
Unbaked clay yields all fruits, whereas baked clay brings many defects.
The construction of the image using only clay:
one should fashion the image with clay alone, or else with three substances.
When the earthen mold is filled according to the ritual, [the image] is complete with its primary and secondary limbs.
In a vessel made of three substances, smeared with clay and likewise with *kaṅka* gravel,
one should cover the entire body with a cloth and apply a coating of color.
[Next,] the locations for excellent clay:
In a field of merit, on a riverbank, in a forest, or even on a mountain,
one should take earth that is complete and free from all defects,
which has not been trodden upon by the lowly and is devoid of sacred shrines, cremation grounds, and the like.
Having gathered all the bark of the Khadira, Udumbara, Aśvattha, Nyagrodha, and Arjuna trees suitable for the Kalka, one should place them in water for one month. (14.9)
One should mix clay with water that has been kept for a month and knead it;
having placed this in new vessels and covered them carefully,
one should set the vessels in the shade so that they are not touched by wind or other elements.
The procedure for the substances to be added as a paste:
three parts of *dhātukī* and six times that amount of *harītakī*;
and twelve varieties of *dhātrī*, making those parts twenty-one in total.
O Lotus-seated One, having let it soak for the duration of one month,
the wise man should then mix that clay with the three myrobalans (triphalā) in a vessel. 14.12
In the shade, one should mix that [earth], which is not overly dried out, with nineteen types of clay—
those to be described as originating from sacred fields and other such places. (14.13) These are the nineteen clays.
In a field of merit, on a riverbank, a mountain, a sandbank, or a lake;
at a waterfall, a confluence, a cow-pen, a temple, or likewise on two shores;
in a field of rice, a natural pool, or on the horns of a bull or an elephant.
From earth ploughed by a boar, from an anthill, and likewise from the dwelling of a crab,
as well as from a lotus pond and a large oblong pool— one takes nineteen measures of clay;
such is the measure of the clay and the proportion for the powder.
One should mix the previously mentioned clay with handfuls of fine earth.
Then, one should again mix it with the powders of the three myrobalans (triphalā) in the proportions previously stated,
along with one-third part of powdered brick-dust and sugar.
With river-born smooth pebbles and powdered portions of earth, one should mix fragrant substances such as sandalwood,
saffron, *koṣṭha*, *śrīveṣṭa*, and yellow sandalwood.
One should powder guggulu, dried turmeric, yellow orpiment, realgar, tamāla leaves, and these [other] substances such as sandalwood.
With those powders, using twenty-one parts of soft earth and an equal amount of sand, [one should prepare the mixture].
One should mix fine clay with a fourth part of *kapittha* juice;
having mixed the clay with powdered metals and gems,
one should add the oily substances and liquid ingredients for blending.
With honey, oil, curd, milk, and ghee, each measuring one *śukti*,
and mixed with linseed oil (*atasī-taila*), one should again mix the clay.
This is the consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the prepared clay.
Having thus placed the consecrated clay into a new vessel,
and having covered the jar with a new cloth,
the best of preceptors should place the earthen vessels among grains of rice and worship them with the root mantra.
One should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter, reciting the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
the wise person should then offer the *caru* oblation verse by verse with the *Puruṣasūkta*.
One should sprinkle that clay, placed in a vessel, with the residual clarified butter from the oblations.
Having consecrated the clay according to the rule, either immediately at the time of consecration or at night,
the procedure for the application and the knowledge thereof [are as follows].
At an auspicious moment, during the *bimba*-muhūrta, the Guru should smear clay [upon the image].
He should smear it up to the crown of the head and the neck with the *vyoma-vidyā*.
From the neck down to the navel, he should smear it with the *vāyu-vidyā*.
One should smear [the area] from the navel down to the waist with the Fire-mantra (vahnividyā). One should smear from the waist down to the knees with the Water-mantra (vārividyā).
One should smear from the knees up to the waist with the Earth-mantra (bhūmividyā).
One should smear [the body] from the navel to the throat with the *śvasana-vidyā*;
one should smear from the navel to the end of the secret place with the *śikhividyā*;
and one should smear from the secret place to the knees with the *vāri-vidyā*.
One should smear [the body] from the knees down to the feet with the Earth-vidyā.
This is the instruction regarding the vidyās for the smearing with clay for the goddesses and others,
as well as for Śrī and the other goddesses, and likewise for Brahmā and the others.
At this time, one should perform an anointing according to the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the teacher so that he may attain satisfaction.
[This includes] the wrapping with ropes and so forth.

Having subtracted from the measurement of the image that which is the measurement of the core, one should divide it into eight parts. Among those, one should wrap three parts with cords for the virtues;
one should coat three parts with clay, and two parts with cloth, resin, and sugar.
One should again mix fine coconut husk with the second [layer].
Then, in due order, one should fashion the dimensions of the face, arms, thighs, and chest,
as well as the arrangement of the channels.
One should wrap the image of Viṣṇu with threads made from the *nāḍīs*— namely the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*— which are white, yellow, and reddish-brown respectively.
Having repeatedly cut fine strips of coconut bark and clay, [one should apply them].
One should mix that third [ingredient] and apply it during the initial drying.
Having fashioned a handle complete with a finger-guard, one should bind it with iron;
then, having formed a spiral for the ear, one should fix it in place with iron.
One should nourish the body while avoiding any cracks or holes.
Regarding the procedure for applying clay and coarse sugar:
one should apply the clay with the hand and the coarse sugar with a brush. (14.38)
Having ground the powders of *kaṭuśarkara* and *triphalā* with alkaline water (*kṛṣitāmbhas*),
one should form them into the shape of cakes and dry them in the sun. Then,
one should grind those balls again with the juice of *kapittha*.
Having done this four, three, or five times, one should grind it again;
mixing cotton-wool with the juice of *kapittha* and water,
one should grind it until it becomes as thick as an arm when held in both arms.
Regarding the preparation of the flour for the effigy:
if it should fall during the grinding while being lifted up, one should gently stroke it with a brush once it has been well-ground. 14.42
Then, with the tip of a small basket, one should smear the limbs that have been anointed;
when all the limbs are completely covered,
one should firmly wrap them with a cloth made of cotton, which is strong and free from hair and other such defects.
Having placed [the items] upon heaps of grain and caused [the preceptor] to recite benedictions once more,
one should accomplish purification with grain and worship with the Vāyu-vidyā.
One should indeed offer oblations of sacrificial wood and clarified butter one hundred times with the root mantra.
One should offer sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Puruṣasūkta.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should cover [the image] with a cloth and apply [pigments].
Then, one should prepare [the colors] using the very same sugar that was on that cloth.
An application of white clay mixed with the juice of *kapittha* [is used]. (14.47) Regarding the procedure for the application of color:
thereafter, one should perform the application of color by those who are experts in the technical treatises of the artisans.
White, yellow, red, green, and black—
these five colors are the presiding deities of the colors of earth and the other elements.
The best minerals are said to be those, while the middling ones are those derived from trees.
Those born of such unions are base; now hear of the other threefold knowledge (traividyam), as well as the threefold combination of caste (varṇa), non-golden [caste], and refinement (saṃskāra).
This threefold combination of caste is proclaimed in the scriptures.
The "pure" (śuddha) castes are thus described; one should have them perform those [tasks] like kings.
Those castes which, in their imitation, are generally devoid of purity are called "subordinate" (anuvarṇa); I shall now describe to you the mixed (saṅkīrṇa) ones.
White, red, yellow, and black—thus it is fourfold;
furthermore, there are four mixed types, each of which is traditionally held to be twofold.
White and *valarkṣa* are said to be the two kinds of white.
That which has the luster of a conch shell, cow’s milk, or a *kunda* flower is designated as "white" (*śukla*). That which has the luster of a pearl, crystal, or the moon is designated as "valarkṣa.
Furthermore, the red variety is described through its distinctions as "aruṇa" (dawn-red) and "śoṇa" (crimson).
That which resembles the blood of the hibiscus is considered *aruṇa* (dawn-red) because of its red color;
that which resembles the *kiṃśuka* or *aśoka* flowers is designated as *śoṇa* (crimson).
Green and yellow likewise constitute two types of *pītavarṇa* (yellowish-brown).
That which resembles realgar and yellow orpiment is called green (harita).
That which has the luster of turmeric and saffron is designated as yellow (pīta).
Dark (śyāma) and black (kṛṣṇavarṇa) are two types of the black color (kṛṣṇavarṇa). || 14.57–14.58 ||
That which has the luster of *dūrvā* grass or emerald is designated as "dark-green" (*śyāma*).
That which resembles sapphire is "black," and is proclaimed to be of black color.
Red mixed with white is called "tawny" (*babhru*).
Black mixed with white is proclaimed as *karāla*;
black mixed with yellow is designated as *kāla*.
White joined with yellow and black is declared to be *karbura*.
In this way, one should apply the castes born of mixture through the process of inclusion and exclusion.
This summary of the castes has been stated; by means of them, as prescribed, one should perform the sequence for the conceptualization of the forms. 14.62.
The Procedure for the Conceptualization of the Forms.
The first [layer] is a wooden framework; the second is a wrapping of rope; the third is a coating of clay; the fourth is the binding of fibers;
the fifth would be a wrapping of rope, and then again with the bark of the coconut.
The sixth is mixed clay; the seventh is the wrapping with cord.
The eighth is the application of gravel; the ninth is the joining of the cloth.
The tenth is declared to be the ornamenting; and beyond that is the eleventh.
The twelfth application of color is specified as a white coating;
these twelve are prescribed for the making of the image, O Lotus-born One. This concludes the limit for the drying of the coatings.
In due time, by means of mere rain, the substance dries up and not otherwise;
for a dried image according to the prescribed rite, its lifespan extends for a thousand years, accomplished over twelve months. (14.67)
With two [units] the lifespan would be ten thousand; with three, it is established as one hundred thousand.
Nourishment by gold alone brings radiance to all the social classes (varṇas).
Whether depicted in a painting, on a cloth, on a wall, or even on a wooden panel—
The application of colors has been fully described, as well as the origin of the substances.
According to the distinction of the ages (yugas), a difference in color for the forms is prescribed;
that is, a difference in color for the forms is ordained based on the specific age.
In the Kṛta age Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person, is white; in the Tretā age he is ruddy; again in the Dvāpara age he is yellow; and in the Kali age he is dark as a rain-cloud.
The god Saṅkarṣaṇa is red, and Pradyumna has the luster of gold.
Aniruddha is said to be dark-complexioned throughout all four ages, beginning with Kṛta;
Keśava is the color of gold, while Arjuna has a complexion like that of a white lotus.
Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned; Mādhava has the luster of crystal; Govinda resembles the filaments of a lotus; Viṣṇu is thus described. Madhusūdana is said to resemble a reddish lotus.
Trivikrama resembles a peacock; Vāmana is like the rising sun. Śrīdhara has the luster of a white lotus; Hṛṣīkeśa has the brilliance of lightning.
Padmanābha is dark-complexioned, with the hue of the bandhūka flower.
Dāmodara— these twelve beginning with Keśava have been declared;
they are the colors of the twenty-four forms,
which are the colors previously described for the forms beginning with Vāsudeva.

That very Puruṣottama, who resembles pure crystal, is to be known as the form of the four [deities] beginning with Vāsudeva, as well as of those born from them. Adhokṣaja is dark-complexioned, and Nṛsiṃha is like gold in appearance.
Acyuta is of yellow color; Janārdana is exceedingly red;
Upendra is said to be dark-blue; Hari is remembered as resembling yellow;
Kṛṣṇa has the appearance of a black cloud—these are the twenty-four forms.
The colors of the goddesses beginning with Śrī are as follows:
Śrī has the luster of gold on a touchstone; Bhū is dark-complexioned; Sarasvatī has the brilliance of white lotuses; Prīti has a form resembling the color of a dark-blue lotus.

Kīrti should be red; Śānti is said to have the luster of crystal; Tuṣṭi should be yellow; and Puṣṭi is remembered as being dark—these are the goddesses [of the Matsya and other incarnations]. (14.81) [The colors of the forms beginning with the Fish.]
The Fish is like crystal; the Tortoise resembles gold;
the Boar is dark-hued, or perhaps has the form of a black bear;
Nṛsiṃha has the luster of the moon's color; and Prahlāda has the radiance of gold.
Vāmana is like a dark-blue cloud, and Mahābali is black in complexion;
Jāmadagnya has a golden luster, and Rāghava has a dark-complexioned form;
Bharata is dark in color, and Lakṣmaṇa has the radiance of gold.
Śatrughna has the luster of red; Sītā has a form resembling gold; Māṇḍavī has the luster of red; Ūrmilā has a dark-blue radiance;
Śrutakīrti has white limbs; and Hanumān has the brilliance of gold.
Aṅgada has the luster of red; Sugrīva is golden-yellow;
Guha has the appearance of blue; Vibhīṣaṇa is black in color;
Nīla is said to resemble sapphire; and Jāmbavān has the brilliance of gold.

Bala shall be like milk in color, and Revatī is red; Kṛṣṇa shall be dark as a rain-cloud, and Rukmiṇī has the luster of gold. Satyabhāmā shall be dark-complexioned, and Kalkī is recorded as being like blood in hue.
The colors of Ananta, Garuḍa, and the others are as follows:
Ananta is like milk in appearance, or else has a form resembling gold;
Garuḍa is like refined gold, and Brahmā is similar to gold.
Viṣṇu is said to resemble a dark-blue cloud, and Rudra resembles blood.
Hayagrīva should be like a red goat, and Senānī has a dark-complexioned form.
Caṇḍa should be red in color, and Pracaṇḍa resembles white.
Jaya is yellow, and thereafter Vijaya is dark-blue; Padmī is like a lotus, Gadādhara is golden, Kṛṣṇa should hold a sword,
Śārṅgadhārī is gold-colored, and Vajradhara is considered to be white.
Śyāma should hold a pestle; Pāśadhṛk has the luster of gold.
Kṛṣṇa holds a goad; Dhātṛ possesses a body of reddish-yellow hue.
Vidhātṛ is white; Bhadra and Subhadra indeed have a ruddy complexion.
Kṛtānta is dark blue and red; he is remembered as the destroyer of the gods.
Kubera’s eye should be yellow, while Kubera himself bears a red body. Sambhava is declared to be dark blue, while the first [of the series] resembles red.
Suśobhana shall be dark-complexioned, while Subhadra possesses a white complexion.
Kumuda has the luster of white, Kumudākṣa resembles fire,
Puṇḍarīka is said to be white, and Vāmana has a dark form.
Śaṅkukarṇa should be red; Sarvanetra has a dark luster;
Sumukha is said to be dark-blue; and Sapratiṣṭhita is red-hued.
The Sun is red, the Moon is white, Mars is red, and Mercury is white.
Bṛhaspati has a golden luster; Śukra is white; Śanaiścara is black. Rāhu is copper-colored, and Ketu is said to be black.
Kāma is red; the elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa) is white; and the six-faced one (Kārttikeya) is red.
Durgā is dark-complexioned; Dhanada and Kṣetrapālaka have a golden luster.
Nīla is dark-blue; Brāhmī has a golden luster, and Māheśvarī should be red.
Kaumārī has a reddish complexion, and Vaiṣṇavī has a dark-blue radiance.
Vārāhī has a dark-blue complexion, and Indrāṇī has a dark form; Cāmuṇḍā has a red complexion, and Vīrabhadra has a reddish luster;
Jyeṣṭhā is blue, Indra is dark, and Agni has a reddish radiance.
Yama is Kāla; Nirṛti is Nīla; Śyāma is Pracetas;
Vāyu is Dhūmra; Indu is white; Rudra is said to be red. Puruṣa is Śyāmala; Acyuta is remembered as having the luster of gold.
The collection of colors for the Vasus is white,
red, yellow, dark, blood-red, and white-lustred;
brown and yellow are the colors of the Vasus beginning with Dharā.
The collection of colors for the ancestors (pitr̥s) is as follows: red, white, radiant yellow, dark, white, and reddish-white; this sequence of colors for the ancestors has been declared. 14.106.
Babhru is also a color of the ancestors, thus it has been described in order.
The collection of colors of the Maruts is as follows:
smoky, red, yellow, dark-blue, white, ruddy, and black.
This is the color of the seven Maruts declared in their proper sequence.
The collection of the colors of the seven sages is declared in order to be golden, dark, yellow, black, red, white, and dark-blue. (14.108)
Red, yellow, white, dark-blue, red-yellow, and white-black:
this is remembered as the sequence of colors for the retinue beginning with Viśva.
These are the colors of the Ādityas.
Red, yellow, ruddy, dark, white, tawny, and variegated;
green, white, crimson, and like the kunda flower—
this is recorded as the sequence of colors for the twelve Ādityas.
A summary of the complexions of the apsarases:
they are white-complexioned, golden-complexioned, dark, and with a golden luster;
red, black, and yellow—such is considered the form of the apsarases.
The colors of the Rudras are crimson, green, blue, white, dark-complexioned, yellow, black, tawny, reddish-brown, pale-red, and black. (14.113)
This description of the eleven Rudras has been proclaimed;
as for the two Aśvins, the Aśvins are ruddy and yellow, and Mārkaṇḍeya should be likewise.
The colors of Nārada, Bhṛgu, and the others are as follows:
Nārada is crystal-white, Bhṛgu is yellow, Dakṣa is likewise dark, Manu is red, Sananda is dark-brown, and Kanaka is golden. (14.115)
Sanatkumāra is yellow, and Hāhā is red;
Hūhū is yellow, while the Kinnara Tumburu is dark blue. Śuka is red, Kiṃpuruṣa is dark blue, and Citrasena should likewise be dark blue.
Viśvāvasu is said to be yellow, and Madhu is honey-colored (madhuvārṇaka).

Kaiṭabha is said to be dark blue (śyāmala); as for any color not mentioned, it should be understood [according to context]. Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, within the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Mahopaniṣad* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Description of the Deities," and the fifteenth chapter,
"The Specification of the Sthitā and Other Mūrtis."
The Blessed One said: "Now, therefore, I shall describe the various types [of images] situated in statues and so forth:
standing, seated, and likewise mounted upon vehicles. (15.1)
These three are said to be of two kinds, distinguished by enjoyment (*bhoga*) and yoga.
For one who is lying down, the two previously mentioned bring about the dissolution of all things.
O Lotus-seated One, there are two others for the one lying down, which consist of four divisions.
Each one is divided into two or three types— superior, inferior, and middling.
Among these, the superior is the *bhogamūrti* (enjoyment form),
wherein the Lord stands amidst divine enjoyment, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Together with Śrī and Bhūmi, they stand at the sides of the pedestal of worship;
Sananda and Sanatkuṃāra stand with their palms joined in reverence,
rising on their left knees while remaining supported by the others.
The wise one should have both of those [deities] placed at the front of both feet;
such is the seat on the ground adjacent to the side of the pedestal for worship (arcanāpīṭhikā).
On the southern and northern sides of the wall, [one should place] Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
Behind them, on the right and left sides, one should place Puṣpavanta;
likewise, one should place Sananda and Sanaka leaning against the wall,
wearing the attire of youths and standing with their left feet extended.
Bending his right foot and raising his right hand,
he held a blossoming lotus with its stalk upon the palm of his left hand;
Sanaka and Sanandana, however, were positioned differently than described.
The sun and the moon should likewise be depicted according to the sequence of hands and feet;
the fly-whisks, fans, the white umbrella, and the pearls should be placed on the wall,
and one should create a radiance on the side of the wall endowed with the proper characteristics.
One should place a banyan tree behind him against the side of the wall;
and on the front side of the wall, one should place Rati and Śānti,
O Four-faced One, fanning that god with two chowries.
The Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, Garuḍa, and likewise Nārada,
as well as deities and sages, reside in that abode;
one should know that, O Lotus-seated One, it is the supreme place of enjoyment.
The middle form is that of enjoyment;
the Lord of Birds is in the place of the Earth, and the Earth is on the seat of Sanaka.
At the end of the seat of Mārkaṇḍeya are the two manifestations, Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
And where the others previously mentioned reside, that is the middle place of enjoyment; the inferior form of enjoyment is the four-armed God stationed together with Śrī and Dhara. || 15.16 ||

The right hand is in the boon-granting gesture (varada), and the left is either in the lion-ear (siṃhakarṇa) position or resting upon the root of the thigh; the two others hold the conch and the discus. Brahmā and Īśāna are present with their respective vehicles, while everything else is as previously described.
That place where there is the lowest [form] is declared to be the station of enjoyment (bhogasthāna). There, the station of yoga (yogasthāna) is characterized by the supreme form:
the Lord accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Beside the pedestal for worship are Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu;
everything else is as previously described, and that is the supreme station of yoga.
The central form is the embodiment of Yoga.
Nārada is in the place of Brahmā, and Khageśvara is in the place of Śiva;
on the sides of the pedestal for worship are Brahmā and Īśāna with palms joined in reverence.
All else is as previously described; that is the middle [arrangement] in the station of Yoga.
The inferior form of Yoga is the four-armed deity; he may be in the divine portion of Brahmā, or otherwise,
his right hand may display the gesture of fearlessness, the gesture of granting boons, or the gesture of welcome.
Or else, resting upon the root of the left thigh, it may have a sprout;
or it may be in the form of a mace-mudrā, while the other two hands hold the conch and the discus.
Devoid of Brahmā, Īśāna, and the others, that lowly state is the "Yoga-saṃsthiti."

The form seated upon the seat of enjoyment (bhogāsana) is the most excellent there; thus the classification of the postures has been declared. Now, the seated posture is described: seated together with Śrī and Bhūmi, he rests upon a lion-throne.
Brahmā and Īśāna should be placed at the sides of the wall, or alternatively, seated in comfortable postures (sukhāsana). One should likewise depict Bhṛgu and Nārada at the two sides of the wall.
Beside the pedestal for worship (arcanāpīṭhikā), Rati and Śānti should be shown with palms joined in reverence.

Behind [the deity] are the moon and the sun, and everything else as previously described. That is the exalted seat of enjoyment (bhogāsana); seated upon the lion-throne, the central [deity] is seated.
Having placed the goddess Śrī upon his left lap, the four-armed one embraces her with his left hand, or else the Earth as previously described;
or there may be Brahmā and Īśvara, depicted half-visible on the two sides of the wall.
Pūjāśikha and both Bhṛgu and Nārada should be depicted on either side.
Both Dakṣa and Manu stand behind with chowries in their hands;
behind them, in the middle seat, are the moon, the sun, and the rest.
The junior queens were seated; Brahmā and Īśa were on the two sides of the wall with the two Sahadevīs;
and Rati and Śānti stood by the side of the wall holding fly-whisks.
That is the lowest seat for enjoyment; now the yoga-seat is described.
Among those, the yoga-seat is best when one is seated comfortably upon a lion-throne, with Brahmā and Īśa on either side of the wall.
Rati and Sarasvatī, both fanning with white whisks, are on either side of the pedestal for worship; Śrī and Bhūmi stand with palms joined in reverence.
Behind them are the moon, the sun, and others; this is the supreme yogic seat.
In the Āsīna-yoga, he is seated comfortably upon a central lion-throne, with Brahmā and Īśvara on the two sides of the wall;
Śrī and Mahīdevī are seated, standing with chowries in their hands.
On the side of the pedestal for worship (arcanāpīṭhikā), Śrī and Bhūmi are depicted with palms joined in reverence;
likewise, Dakṣa and Manu are on the side of the wall with palms joined.
Behind them are the moon, the sun, and so forth; in their midst is the central seat.
Seated comfortably upon the lion-throne in a solitary place, the four-armed God, having cast aside his entire retinue including the moon, the sun, and other attendants, sat alone. (15.37)
Whether in the divine or the Brahma portion, that yoga posture is considered low;
the remaining posture there is the best.
Now I shall describe that remaining posture correctly; listen and understand it as it is. 15.38
The body of the serpent is well-rounded, coiled in a circle, and threefold;
the head, however, is slightly oval and elongated, held raised up.
There, together with Śrī and Bhūmi, he sits comfortably upon a seat.
Rati and Sarasvatī are the two [deities] on the sides of the seat of worship;
all of them have their palms joined in reverence. This is the supreme Śeṣāsana; the middle [form] is in the Śeṣāsana.
The four-armed Lord sits enthroned, his beloved resting upon his left lap;
Mārkaṇḍeya and the Earth are at the sides of the seat of worship,
while Bhṛgu and Nārada stand holding white chowries.
Behind [the central seat] are the seats for the moon, the sun, and so forth; the remaining one is the middle seat.
The lowest is the remaining seat where the goddess Śrī is seated; on both sides of the worship-pedestal [are the seats for the two goddesses]. 15.43
Brahmā, Vasudhā, and the god Dharma whose banner is a bull stood before the Lord; the illustrious Mārkaṇḍeya stood with palms joined in reverence.
Behind them were the moon, the sun, and others, while Śeṣa occupied a lower seat.

The supreme among beds and seats has been declared; the various types of remaining seats have also been mentioned. Now hear the classification of the bed: [it is] a bed upon the coils of Ananta, prepared with soft coverings.
Upon the pillow at the side of his head, and likewise at the side of his feet—
resting his body upon this head, the eternal Supreme Self extended his two feet, which were easy to bear, across the laps of the two goddesses.

The two goddesses, Rati and Śānti, with palms joined in reverence, should be placed on a comfortable seat beside the pedestal of worship, gazing at the lotus-face of the God. One should likewise visualize Indra and the other deities at the sides of his feet and upon the wall.
On the back wall, however, one should depict Śaṅkha and others together with their bodies.
On the wall beside the head of the deity, one should arrange the forms of Brahmā and the others, as well as Sanandana, Sanaka, and the rest, in the same order as before.
Before the god, on the wall, were Hāhā and Hūhū,
as well as Citrasena and Citraratha, both intent on the performance of dance and song;
[there were also] maidens born in the world of Viṣṇu and those originating from the world of Brahmā.
Maidens born in the worlds of Rudra and others, endowed with various graceful charms;
Tumburu, Nārada, Garuḍa, and likewise the Kinnaras; and great sages above, playing upon lutes and other instruments. || 15.52–15.53 ||
By means of a variegated form, all [deities] provide excellent enjoyment upon the bed;
on the bed, they are of middling quality when located on the head, the sides, and at the base of the arms.

Rati and Śānti are at the side of the foot [of the deity], and Sanatkumāra and Sanaka are on the sides of the worship-pedestal when it is a comfortable seat touched by the feet. With half-ornamentation, they are situated on the wall; however, the middle [type] has a bed of enjoyment (bhogaśayyā).
Śrī shall comfortably carry the low couch with her two lotus-hands;
and Rati and Vasundharā shall remain by the side of the pedestal for worship.
On a bed depicted in a painting on a wall, the enjoyment would be inferior.
On a sleeping couch, the yogic posture (yogāsana) is superior; there, on a couch of infinite enjoyment, one has renounced all possessions.
Having resorted to yoga, the Supreme Person himself lies down;
marked with the Śrīvatsa, with a serene countenance, and resembling a dark blue cloud, he has two arms—this is declared to be the supreme yoga-sleep. (15.58–59)
On the bed of yoga, he is attended by Vainateya seated at his side;
he has four arms and is devoid of all other retinues. (15.60)
O Four-faced One, that is called the middling yoga-bed;
the inferior yoga-bed consists of being accompanied by two arms and having abandoned all possessions. (15.61)
Beside the pedestal for worship, Śrībhūmi stands with palms joined in reverence.
Now hear of the inferior yoga-bed; as for the bed of withdrawal (saṃhāra-śayana), it is the supreme.
Reclining upon a bed of infinite coils, adorned with an infinite circle of hoods,
the eight-armed Lord has his face furrowed with a frown;
he bears a single, terrifying countenance made formidable by its fangs.
With a terrifying sound as deep as the roar of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution,
emitting from within the fire fanned by the breath of his mouth—
this, the wise declare, is the supreme bed of withdrawal.
In the bed of dissolution, he has a middle face with fangs baring its jaws, eyes crooked with a frown,
four arms, and is adorned with a mace, a sword, a conch, and a lotus.
On the side of the pedestal for worship, the two Śrīkhagendras have their hands joined in añjali;
the middle fingers are contracted [to form] the bed (śayyā), while the little fingers form the reclining posture (śayana). Listen:
the little fingers constitute the reclining posture of withdrawal (saṃhāra-śayana).
With his beautiful face adorned by locks of hair and clusters of curls,
resembling a dark blue cloud with a green lotus in its center—
this was the supreme bed of creation.
On the wall surrounding the bed of creation in the four directions, one should paint the ocean;
and on the side of the wall adjacent to the bed, at a height of four tālas, one should depict Brahmā facing upwards from the navel of Nārāyaṇa.
Four-faced and four-armed, endowed with a crown of matted locks;
with his two principal hands joined in the gesture of reverence (añjali),
he stands displaying the yoga-mudrā with his other two hands, O Four-faced One.
With his two upper arms raised, he holds a rosary and a water-pot;
he rests upon a lotus, seated in the svastika posture.
Behind the head of the God, one perceives Śrī, marked by his very glance.
Raising the left knee and standing firm on the right,
with the right hand holding a flower and the left hand bestowing wealth,
[he should be placed] beneath the Ananta-bed on both sides of the worship pedestal.
One should depict Nārada and Sanaka with palms joined in reverence toward the human [form],
while the goddess Earth should be shown touching the feet at their sides.
Above the oceans, one should place Śaṅkha and others, endowed with bodies.

On the back wall of the deity, however, using the finger-breadth obtained from the *deha* measurement, one should [depict] those bearing weapons such as the conch, with a height of twenty-four finger-breadths;
namely, the five weapons: the conch, the discus, the mace, the sword, and the bow. || 15.76–15.77 ||

One should fashion Śaṅkhādhāra as being two cubits tall, having the form of a man, with his head marked by his own emblem, possessing a protruding belly, and white in luster. One should further fashion Cakradhara as red in color, with rolling eyes.
Gadādhara has a massive body, round eyes, and a yellowish luster.
Strīveṣā, however, holds a sword, possesses beautiful breasts, and has a dark-blue radiance.
Śārṅgadhṛk has the brilliance of gold, a large body, and a protruding belly.
Vainateya is golden-hued and adorned with a circle of wings;
these others are clad in various bodices and wear diverse garments.
They have faces made terrifying by fangs and eyes curved with knitted brows.
Wearing crowns and adorned with all ornaments, they ran toward both Madhu and Kaiṭabha; some brandished their left hands while others held clenched fists. || 15.82-15.83 ||
On the sides below the feet, one should have Madhu and Kaiṭabha fashioned;
they are dark as honey, massive-bodied, resplendent with crowns and baskets,
standing knee-deep in the ocean, and brandishing swords and staffs as weapons.
With mouths formidable with fangs and eyes crooked with frowns,
they were scorched on all sides by the flames of fire from the mouths of the infinite serpents;
terrified, they fled, struck by fists as hard as thunderbolts.
On the eastern wall of the temple, one should depict the manifestations:
Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Kīrti, Rati, Śānti, and Sarasvatī;
holding clusters of flowers in their hands and fanning with white chowries.
Above all of them, however, one should fashion a row of clouds;
and above the clouds are the gods and likewise the sages,
as well as Indra and the other guardians of the directions, and the seven staff-bearing sages.
All of them stood with their upper garments arranged and their palms joined in reverence;
Viṣṇu and Rudra, both four-armed, stood at the head and at the side.
One should depict [the deity] on the wall in front of the Lord, above the path of the clouds.
The Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, as well as Kinnara and Tumburu,
and all the hosts of Apsarases who are ever devoted to dance and song,
were present there upon that delightful couch of Ananta, prepared as before.
Four-armed, dark-complexioned, bearing the conch, discus, and mace;
wearing yellow garments, gentle, with eyes reaching as far as his ears;
and upon his right arm, he placed his crown with the palms of his fingers extended.
Having placed the end of his turban-band [on the ground] and with one arm extended,
the Lord lay down like a king, glancing slightly toward the door;
all those previously mentioned were situated on the wall in painted form.
The wise say that this is the supreme bed for creation;
the middling bed for creation is one who is dark-complexioned, of tender form, and endowed with two arms. (15.96)
Behind [the deity], on the shoulder and the side, and in the east, Padmā is established;
one should represent Brahmā in a painting on the side of the wall.
Sanaka and Mahī should be placed on the two sides of the pedestal of worship.
The remaining [elements] should be represented with half-painting; the *sṛṣṭiśayyā* (creation-bed) is middling,
while the *kanīyasī sargaśayyā* (minor creation-bed) is for Śrī, the Earth, and the spirits beneath the ground on the sides of the pedestal.
One should depict Brahmā on the side of the wall as a painted image:
endowed with two arms, four-faced, Padmanābha, the cause of the universe, lying asleep in the midst of the ocean of dissolution. || 15.99–15.100 ||
By mere appearance, the inferior creation-bed situated within the wall [is perceived].

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Varieties of Postures for Remaining Seated and so forth," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the sixteenth chapter.
Regarding the characteristics of the form mounted on a vehicle therein, this supreme distinction of the Blessed Lord as mounted on a vehicle is now being demonstrated.
[He saw] Vainateya, golden-hued and adorned with a circle of wings,
possessed of a dark-tipped beak, and decorated with ornaments of lordly serpents;
having mounted upon his shoulder, he drew up his left leg and extended his right.
The Lord, endowed with eight arms, extended his foot,
holding in his right hands a discus, a lotus,
a sword, and arrows, while bearing a conch, the Kaumodakī mace, a shield, and a bow with his other hands.
On the back wall, at its side, [one should depict] the celestial tree (suradruma) with its parasol.
On the two sides of the wall, Nanda and Sanaka, as well as the Moon and the Sun;
and if the gods are present, they should be depicted standing, mounted upon their respective vehicles.
On the side of the pedestal for worship, one should depict the illustrious Mahi and Mahī with palms joined in reverence; likewise, on the wall surfaces,
one should have the gods, asuras, sages, nāgas, siddhas, vidyādharas,
gandharvas, apsarases, and clouds fashioned.
All [of these] are joined with a painting; mounting the vehicle is the most excellent.
The middling form consists of making the deity four-armed, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having placed upon his left lap the goddess Rati, who resembles a pomegranate,
who holds a noose and a goad, and whose eyes are overwhelmed with passion;
one should likewise fashion Śrī and Bhūmi on either side of the pedestal for worship.
Nārada and Bhṛgu, holding chowries, should be placed on the wall;
one should arrange Prīti, Sarasvatī, and Śānti in the southern regions.
One should likewise place Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, and Kīrti on the left wall.

With flower-clusters in their hands and fanning with white whisks—this is the procedure for all [the deities] either by half-painting or by mere outline. Now hear, O Four-faced One, about the middling and the inferior mounting of the vehicles. || 16.11-16.12 ||
The inferior form has four arms and large eyes, with a luster like that of crushed collyrium;
and with his two principal hands, he holds the Śārṅga bow and the five arrows.
Holding a conch and a discus with his two upper hands and the other two,
he bore [her] who resembled molten gold, resting upon his left lap,
as if sprinkling everything on all sides with the nectar-water of her loveliness.
One should place Rati and Śānti on either side of the pedestal for worship— with the right hand holding a flower and the left hand bestowing wealth—
depicted in painted form upon the wall; [one should also observe] the mounting of a low vehicle.
The Universal Form (Viśvarūpa) is the supreme form therein;
O Lotus-born One, listen as I describe the Universal Form:
it has two feet, one neck, and four faces in the four directions. (16.17)
Above the mouth of Vāsudeva are the mouths of all the gods;
above the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa are the mouths of all the ṛṣis;
and above the mouth of Pradyumna are those of the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas.
Above the face of Aniruddha are the faces of the Nāgas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras.
These and other faces should be fashioned with devotion according to their respective magnificence; O Four-faced One, they must be made capable by those who are discerning.
And above the faces, one should fashion an exceedingly beautiful crown, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, appearing simultaneously;
it is joined with many arms and adorned with many weapons.
The deities on the wall-surfaces were worshipped by Brahmā and Rudra;
all were fashioned in painting. That supreme one is Viśvarūpa, while this is the middle form.
If all the aforementioned walls are decorated with half-painting (*ardhacitra*), one should place Sananda and Sanaka on the two sides of the pedestal for worship.
The central figure should be Viśvamūrti; now hear also about the inferior [type]. (16.23–24)
The lowest [form] is Viśvamūrti;
by mere appearance, the two goddesses are situated on the wall, established upon the seat of worship;
and Vāsudeva is eternal, endowed with four arms.
Holding the mace and the lotus with his two principal hands— the left and the right—
and the conch and the discus respectively with his other two hands raised above;
or else, the right hand may be displayed as the boon-granting (*varada*) or the fear-dispelling (*abhaya*) gesture.
Without the mace, his left hand rests upon the region of his hip;
he may have two arms or many arms, and likewise be endowed with many faces;
or he may be white in color, the eternal Vāsudeva.
Thus Nārāyaṇa is beginningless and resembles a dark blue cloud;
now the characteristics of the twenty-four forms will be described. (16.29)
The lotus, conch, discus, and likewise the staff are said to be the weapons of Keśava’s arms in successive order from left to right;
Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the bearer of the conch, lotus, mace, and discus.
Mādhava, whose weapons are the discus, conch, and lotus, should be accompanied by the mace.
Govinda should bear the discus, staff, lotus, and conch as his weapons; Viṣṇu should hold the mace, lotus, conch, and sword, as should Madhusūdana.
Trivikrama should be depicted holding the discus, conch, lotus, and staff;
Vāmana should hold the lotus, staff, discus, and conch;
Śrīdhara should have the mace and lotus in his hands and likewise hold the lotus.
Together with the discus, mace, and conch—listen now to Hṛṣīkeśa.
Bearing the weapons of the mace, discus, lotus, and conch, he whose navel is a lotus is the lotus-navelled one;
Dāmodara is remembered as the bearer of the lotus, discus, water-lily, and mace.
The twelve forms are the bearers of the lotus, conch, mace, and discus;
these are remembered as bearing the Kaumodakī mace, the conch, the discus, and the lotus.
Vāsudeva is the source of the universe; now hear concerning Saṅkarṣaṇa.
[One should meditate on] the four-armed [Pradyumna] holding a mace, a conch, a lotus, and a discus.
Pradyumna holds a discus and a conch, along with a staff and a lotus; Aniruddha is four-armed, holding an enemy (sword), a staff, a lotus, and a water-lily in his hands.
Puruṣottama is remembered as holding a mace along with a discus, a lotus, and a water-lily;
Adhokṣaja is remembered as bearing a lotus-stalk, a conch, and a discus. Nṛsiṃha is remembered as bearing a discus, a water-lily, a mace, and a conch.
Acyuta has four arms, holding a staff, a lotus, an enemy [of the lotus], and a conch.
Janārdana has four arms, holding a lotus, a discus, a conch, and a staff.
Upendra is adorned with the weapons of a conch, a staff, an enemy [of the lotus], and a lotus.
Hari, seated upon a lotus, shall hold the conch, discus, lotus, and staff as weapons;
Kṛṣṇa, four-armed, shall have the conch, mace, lotus, and discus in his hands.
Starting from the right hand, one should arrange them in a clockwise direction.
The wise one [should know] the bodily marks and the weapons, such as the conch and others.
Vāsudeva, Padmanābha, Nārāyaṇa, and Janārdana—
among these there is no difference in color, nor is there any distinction in their weapons.
All twenty-four forms should be depicted wearing yellow garments and adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, the Kaustubha jewel, ornaments, and forest garlands.
If they are intended for the sake of worldly enjoyment, one should install them on the wall together with the two goddesses.

Those desiring liberation should, in the absence of those two, duly install the eightfold forms beginning with Brahmā according to the prescribed rules during sitting, standing, sleeping, traveling, and other activities. 16.46. [The eightfold forms beginning with Brahmā.]
I shall describe the eight supreme forms; among them, the Brāhmī is praised as the first.
The second is the Prājāpatyā, while the third is considered the Vaiṣṇavī.
O Four-faced One, the fourth is the Daivī, followed by the Ārṣī form.
The sixth should be known as human, while the seventh form is that of the Asuras;
another is the form of the Piśācas—the characteristics of these are now described. (16.49) [The Brāhmī form:]
The first [form] has eight arms and possesses a luster like that of molten gold.

Among the arms, the primary one on the right grants boons; the other three on the right are equipped with a discus, a sword, and an arrow. On the four left hands, they are likewise equipped with [the remaining weapons].
O Four-faced One, one should depict him holding a conch, a mace, a shield, and the Śārṅga bow;
the God wears yellow garments and is adorned with a forest garland,
and he is worshipped by the great seer Marīci and by Bhṛgu.
Belonging to Prajāpati, he has the luster of the color of a conch, jasmine, or the moon; he is clad in yellow garments, possesses four arms,
holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and is resplendent with the gesture of granting fearlessness.
Wearing a forest garland, gentle, and well-worshipped by Sanaka as well as by Sanatkumāra— this is the Vaiṣṇava form of Prajāpati.
Gentle as a mass of crushed collyrium, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
the Lord wears yellow garments and is adorned with a forest garland.
His right hand is the bestower of boons, or likewise the giver of welcome and fearlessness.
With his left hand resting upon his hip, he stands together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
Even by Nārada and Bhṛgu, this Vaiṣṇava form was worshipped; it is divine.
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus, with four arms,
dark-complexioned, wearing yellow garments, and adorned with a forest garland—
worshipped by Brahmā and Rudra— this shall be the divine form.
The Ṛṣi’s [consort] resembles pure crystal, wears yellow garments, and has four arms;
she holds the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) in her right hand and carries a conch, a discus, and a mace. || 16.59 ||
The form of Āruṣī is marked with the Śrīvatsa, has a serene countenance, is adorned with a forest garland,
and is worshipped by Sananda and Sanaka;
she is the human form.
Now the human form is described, O Lotus-seated One:
in the divine portion of the square and long abode, one should establish the gentle [deity] holding a conch and a discus, resplendent with a crown, possessing two arms. (16.61)
One should fashion the goddess Śrī on the right side of the god;
on his right side, one should have Balabhadra made,
and on the right side of Balabhadra, one should also have Pradyumna made.
One should fashion Aniruddha on the left side of the god;
on his left side, O four-faced one, one should place Sāmba.
On the right wall one should place Brahmā, and on the left, the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa).
Those [images] standing in a standing posture are prescribed for a standing [deity], and the same applies when it is seated.
The ritual image (karmārcā) may have four arms or even two arms;
however, all the representative images (pratikṛti) used for festivals (utsavārcā) must have four arms.
The human ritual for Vāsudeva has been declared in brief. The demoniac form is black, with one face and four arms. (16.67)
With a face formidable with fangs and eyes curved by a frown,
she holds an arrow and a bow in her two principal hands, while above them are a discus and a conch;
one should draw [the deity] holding the Śārṅga bow reaching to the forehead and an arrow in hand.
Extending from the navel to the end of the waist-thread, it is endowed with three folds;
this is the primordial form of the Piśācī, namely Khaḍga and Kaumodakī.
The principal [form] grants boons and fearlessness, is black in color, and has two hands;
its face is formidable with protruding fangs, and its eyes are curved with a frown.
And all eight forms are adorned with every ornament.
With the Śrīvatsa mark and Kaustubha gem upon their chests, and adorned with forest garlands—
the fruit of the installation of these [images] is that the installed form of Brahmā leads one to the state of becoming Brahman. (16.72)
Through the Prājāpatya consecration, one increases greatly in progeny;
at the end, one attains the station of Prajāpati—of this there is no doubt.
A Vaiṣṇava image that has been installed will indeed bestow liberation before long.
The divine [form] bestows the fruit of divinity and grants the fulfillment of all desires.
The form of the Ṛṣis certainly leads to the attainment of the state of a great Ṛṣi;
it will also grant him the power of both cursing and favoring.
A human form will soon lead to great fame,
and the perfection of sovereignty over the three worlds shall endure for all time.
By propitiating the demonic form of the Rākṣasas, the sons of Diti, [one attains this].
They attain sovereignty over all beings, beginning with the Bhūtas. Even when performing worship in the form of a Piśāca, the Piśācas, Asuras,
and Rākṣasas all become submissive and grant the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Viśvarūpa and Others Mounted on Vehicles," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā within the glorious Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the seventeenth chapter.
Description of the Matsya and other forms:
The characteristics of the ten forms of the Lord, beginning with the Fish, are now being described.
They are indeed slightly thick, variegated, and endowed with various faces.
Therein is the form of the Fish, and the body of the Fish is sixteen finger-breadths in length.
One should fashion the so-called "fish" [mark] with a width of ten finger-breadths;
having made the trident in the shape of a fish, it may be made of stone, metal, or wood,
or else one may make it with half-painting or even with a painted image.
One should depict the ocean on the wall and fashion various paintings and so forth;
one should draw the five weapons on the wall and fashion the parasols and other ornaments.
This has been respectfully honored by both Nārada and Manu.
The images [of Viṣṇu], such as those made of metal or stone, have gentle faces and four arms;
they may be seated or standing, bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
[Also] the Tortoise-form (Kūrmamūrti).

O Lotus-seated One, one should fashion the form of the Tortoise like a tortoise. The Lord, resembling molten gold, twelve finger-breadths in width, made of stone, clay, or wood, should be installed upon a lotus pedestal.
One should depict the churning of the Ocean of Milk either in a sketch or in a half-painting,
showing Mount Mandara, the best of mountains, upon the back of the lordly tortoise;
and on its southern side, the eternal Vāsudeva.
The Teacher of the World has placed his hand upon the peak of Mount Mandara;
on the left side of that mountain, Brahmā together with Śaṅkara [are stationed],
while the Asuras and Rākṣasas seize the eastern portion of Vāsuki.
The hosts of deities seize the tail portion of Vāsuki.
The images [of Viṣṇu] such as Karmārcā have gentle faces and four arms;
this is the Varāha form.
The manifestation of Viṣṇu as the Great Boar is now described:
up to the neck he is like a man, while his facial creation is like that of a boar;
he has four arms, bears the conch and the discus, and possesses the luster of crystal.
He should place [the image] on the divine thread-line in a horizontal position, either wearing yellow garments and a crown, or having a dark complexion;
however, a bed or a vehicle for Varāha is not desired.
One should install a single-formed image bearing the conch, discus, and mace;

likewise, on the seat, it should have that same form, but in the Brahma-position (the center), it should be straight. However, in a divine location, one should certainly not make it with straight limbs.
Having lifted up the goddess Earth at the elbow of his left hand,
and supporting her waist with his right hand,
the god— marked with the Śrīvatsa and wearing a diadem— began to smell the breast of the goddess.
With palms joined in reverence, the goddess Earth— dark-complexioned and slender-waisted— should be visualized standing before the god while he stands, O Lotus-born One;
likewise, when he is seated, the Earth-goddess should be seated with flowers in her hands.
Having established [the image] on the left side of Hari in his boar-form,
the Earth-goddess (Vasundharā) should be placed upon the god’s left lap;
she should be embraced with his left hand, her face gazing up at him.
The images for the worship of karma and so forth may be either seated or standing;
they have the face of a boar together with the Goddess, or they have gentle faces and four arms. [This is] the form of Nṛsiṃha.
There, a certain form of Nṛsiṃha is displayed in many ways:
a lion’s face with a wide-gaping mouth and fangs;
terrifying, with knitted brows, three eyes, and radiant with a crown.
Like another limb of the man himself, he had four arms raised with weapons;
he was clad in a red tunic, resplendent with the Śrīvatsa mark,
resembling pure crystal, and adorned with the conch and the discus.
Seated properly upon his seat in the full-lotus posture,
he extended his two principal hands with fingers spread over his knees;
their nails were as formidable as thunderbolts, and they were placed upon his divine thighs.
If the rite for a single deity is performed, [the deity] may be either seated or standing.
O Lotus-seated One, if he is standing, he holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands;
or else, in the divine portion, he is seated upon a lion-throne.
Seated together with Śrī and Bhūmi in the bound paryaṅka posture,
or else, having firmly placed one right foot upon the surface of the earth,
he sits comfortably on a broad and firm seat with the other [foot].

Alternatively, having extended the knees upward and raised them above the knees, one should extend the left hand and make the other hand into the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*). Then, having placed the right [hand] below the knee, one should likewise remain on the seat. (17.29–17.30)
Standing in his divine portion as before, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
one should likewise visualize Nṛsiṃha endowed with eight arms;
in his right hands, he holds a discus, a sword, an arrow, and the gesture of fearlessness.
One should depict the *pāñcajanya* conch, the mace, and the *śārṅga* bow in his left arms.
Likewise, one should extend one left hand over the knee,
or else arrange both arms over the two knees.
Alternatively, Narasiṃha is praised as having sixteen arms;
[he holds] a discus, a sword, an axe, a trident, an arrow, and likewise a goad in his right-hand regions, and likewise in the others. 17.34 [He also holds] a thunderbolt.
One should place the conch, shield, mace, spear, Śārṅga bow, noose, and javelin [in the hands],
and position the remaining two hands as before upon the two knees;
one should place the left knee upward and the other below it.
On the lap of the God of gods was his enemy Hiraṇyakaśipu,
whose chest had been torn open by [Viṣṇu’s] claws, and who was tawny with flowing blood;
he was crowded with a multitude of veins formed from the mass of that blood.
And one should perform the ritual on the right side, while elsewhere it is for Śaṅkara;
one should also have Prahlāda and Garuḍa fashioned at the two sides there.
But in the independent Narasiṃha [tantra], one should have the action-images (karmabimba) fashioned.
One should have [the image] made with four arms, seated or standing well-composed in every respect; it may be accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, or even without them.
For rituals, worship, and so forth, the image should have a gentle countenance and four arms.
Regarding the form of Vāmana,
they describe the form of Hari as Vāmana in many ways:
Vāmana has a dwarf-like appearance, is dark-complexioned, and holds a staff.
Two-armed, adorned with a girdle and a string of beads, and of beautiful form;
wearing a loincloth and a deerskin, the Lord;
wearing a sacred thread, with locks of hair marked by the side-locks of a youth.
With his left foot slightly bent and standing straight with the right,
he was begging the earth with his right hand;
he was adorned, possessed of a beautiful form, and remained in a posture of sitting or reclining.

Alternatively, O Lotus-seated One, one should visualize [Viṣṇu] mounted upon Garuḍa. If the rite of a single image is performed, he should be installed in the station of Brahmā; however, if the rite of multiple images is performed, he should be depicted as intent on traversing the three worlds.
One should fashion Viṣṇu in the divine portion, endowed with eight arms,
or four arms, or even provided with many arms.
On his right side, however, one should place Vāmana, who has a dwarf-like form.
To his right was Bali, the lord of the Daityas, holding a water-pot,
the giver of the three worlds, accompanied by his domestic priest in the assembly hall;
and on his left side was the king of birds, who slew Śukra with his fist.
On the left wall, above, is the Creator (Brahmā) stationed,
intent on washing the left foot of the advancing God;
