[and there is] the Gaṅgā, arising from the water of that foot, flowing through the sky.
And with his left index finger,
he pointed toward his own uplifted left foot, which was exceedingly tall and dark, clad in yellow garments,
and bearing a conch, a discus, a mace, a sword, a bow, a noose, and other weapons.
And having depicted Jāmbavān on the wall intent upon beating the drum,
and the hosts of gods and sages standing with their palms joined in reverence;
then, having fashioned the image of Karmādi with four arms upon the wall— 53–54.
The form of Bhārgavarāma shall now be described; one should fashion the image of Bhārgavarāma as seated, with two arms, peaceful, and wearing a crown of matted hair. (17.55)
Holding an axe and a bow with an arrow in his two right hands,
he was golden-hued and resplendent with divine splendor;
his chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa, and he wore a sacred thread and an upper garment.
One should visualize the Lord standing in the position of Brahmā as having a single form;
or, in the divine position of the multi-formed [Lord], one should visualize the Goddess on the left. And the ritual image (karmārcā) may have four arms, being equal to that of Paraśurāma.
Endowed with the three postures and the thirty-two auspicious marks,
one should fashion the son of Jamadagni as four-armed and four-faced;
he should hold the conch and discus and carry the Śārṅga bow and arrows, just as before.
Now the characteristics of Śrī Rāma’s form— of Rāma, the descendant of Raghu— will be described:
he has three bends in his body, two arms, is beautiful, dark-complexioned, and wears a crown.
One should meditate on Him who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and has a serene luster, or as the four-armed Rāma, standing upright with His right foot [firmly] placed and the other slightly bent,
holding a bow made of horn and arrows.
One should raise the left hand, holding a bow, up to the edge of the forehead;

the right hand, holding an arrow, should reach the space between the brows. The measurement of the face, including the *gola* (the frontal protuberance), should be made equal to the measurement of the waist-belt.
There should be a space between the clenched fist and the waist-string;
with the other two hands, one should hold a conch and a discus.
The face is turned slightly to the right, while the middle of the torso is turned to the left.
A fracture on the right side of the hip is considered to be a minor fracture;
[the body] has a shell-like neck and a broad chest—these are thirty-three excellent marks.
It is five parts long, four parts short, five parts subtle, and six parts elevated.
Seven things that are red, three that are deep, and three that are broad are praised.
(17.67) The two arms, the distance between the eyes, the jaw, the nose, and the space between the breasts—these five long features are praised. (17.68)
A slender neck, genitals, back, shanks, and fingers are praised when they are short;
likewise, the joints of the fingers, hair, teeth, nails, and skin should be fine.
O sinless one, these five have been described by me as the qualities of slenderness.
The armpits, the belly, the chest, the nose, the shoulders, and the forehead—this is declared to be the sixfold protuberance (*ṣaḍunnata*). Now hear of the seven red parts (*saptarakta*):
the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and the eyes, beginning with the corners and including the nails, are red.
The palate, tongue, lower lip, and upper lip—these seven are known as the "seven reds.
A deep voice, a profound nature, and a deep navel are praised as the "three depths.
The chest, head, and forehead are proclaimed as the "three broads."
One should thus fashion Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, endowed with these characteristics, bringing happiness to the entire world, and possessed of the threefold pride;
this is the manner of depicting Lakṣmaṇa and the others.
One should have Lakṣmaṇa depicted on the left, endowed with his characteristic marks;
likewise, on the right side, the goddess Jānakī, arisen from the altar;
and on the right wall, Bharata along with Śatrughna and Vibhīṣaṇa.
With Śatrughna, Aṅgada, and Hanumān likewise on his left—
such is the arrangement of the retinue for him who stands in the divine portion.
Having seated him upon the auspicious throne (bhadrāsana), he has laid aside his bow along with its arrow.
The right hand should be in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), while the left should be in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*).
Jānakī, however, should be seated comfortably on the right side,
and Lakṣmaṇa should stand on the left side with his hands joined in reverence (*añjali*).
Or else, one should imagine him reclining upon a costly couch;
behind him, at the side of his head, Jānakī should be seated comfortably.
All others, including Lakṣmaṇa and the rest, are to be depicted as before, standing against the wall.
Or else, he may be mounted upon the vehicle of the Son of the Wind (Hanumān), carrying his bow and arrows.
In the ritual of the single image (ekabera), however, one should depict Rāghava standing in the abode of Brahmā,
bearing his bow and arrow, and endowed with all the auspicious marks.
Alternatively, one should make the right hand the "giver of fearlessness" (abhayada) or the left hand the "giver of boons" (varada), with the hand touching the hip, according to one's preference.
On the southern and northern walls, the retinue [should be depicted] as before.
One should assign the region of the earth up to the end of Rāma’s [form] to Bharata; Lakṣmaṇa should extend to the edge of the cheek or even to the chin;
and Śatrughna should extend to the middle of the throat. All of them are equipped with bows and arrows.
The *bhaṅga* and other [ornaments] should likewise be provided with hair-ties (*keśabandha*);
their height should be double the width of the face, or one and a half times that. Their hair-ties should be present, though they are otherwise devoid of the *śrīvatsa* mark.
One should imagine the left hand holding a staff and the right hand placed upon the arm of the Queen, as Bharata is in his state of independence;
and Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa likewise, just as Bharata is in his state of independence.
Bharata shall be dark-complexioned, Lakṣmaṇa golden-hued,
and Śatrughna radiant with a red complexion, endowed with auspicious marks.
Māṇḍavī shall be the wife of Bharata, while Ūrmilā shall be the wife of Lakṣmaṇa.
O Lotus-Seated One, Śrutakīrti shall be the queen of Śatrughna.
Sītā should be depicted like Śrī, endowed with many auspicious marks,
wearing a basket-shaped crown and a head-veil, and accompanied by children.
Holding a lotus bud in her left hand,
with her right arm resting upon the region of her thigh; or else,
holding a lotus in her left hand which rests upon the region of her thigh.
Holding the fastening of her red bodice with her left hand, Sītā was golden-hued; Māṇḍavī had the luster of a pale-red lotus;
Ūrmilā had a dark complexion; and Śrutakīrti had a white radiance.
O Four-faced One, the goddesses should be depicted with well-arranged hair;
Hanumān should be made in human form, resembling gold.
He stands with his body slightly bent, his great tail curved at the tip.
Having covered the mouth with the hand— using the right one and not the other—
and having concealed the area of the garment, one should arrange it so as to be tied with hair, standing in a humble manner; its height shall now be described.
The height of Rāma’s arm may be one-third of his total stature,
or half, or even a quarter, according to one's means;
[one should fashion] Sugrīva in the form of a monkey, with a height equal to Rāma’s arm.
One should fashion [the figure] golden-brown, wearing a crown, standing with palms joined and holding a cane, adorned with necklaces and other ornaments;
[he should be] Angada, in the form of a monkey, elevated to half the height of Rāma.
With palms joined in reverence, holding a cane, a razor, and a crown,
his hair was bound up; he possessed the luster of the bandhujīva flower,
a massive body, and was formidable with the brilliance of black iron.

One should fashion [the image] with a face formidable with fangs, eyes curved by a frown, red eyes, and adorned with a crown; standing with palms joined in reverence, its height reaching up to the arms of Rāma. || 17.101–17.102 ||
To Guha, the gentle lord of the Niṣādas, who stood with palms joined in reverence,
who resembled a dark blue rain-cloud, and who was as tall as Rāma himself, [Rāma said]:
"Both independence and dependence shall belong to the descendant of Raghu."
Whether he be in celestial enjoyment or in the Brahma-abode,
if Rāghava is said to be independent while situated in the womb, then the four-armed one is conceived in the womb as seated upon a lotus.

Subsequently, for the sake of beautifying the celestial chariot (vimāna), this other [image] was fashioned; it is independent of Rāghava and should be used for making images for rituals and other purposes. One should fashion others resembling him—Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the daughter of Janaka.

One should [visualize them] together on a single lion-throne, adorned with radiance; or alternatively, O Four-faced One, one may make them four-armed. For the worship of the rites and so forth, one should arrange the doorkeepers independently on both sides of the entrance.
And Nala was on the right side, while Jāmbavān was likewise on the left;
Jāmbavān had a complexion like the color of gold, and Nala possessed a radiance equal to that of white. Both held daggers and staffs in their hands and were clad in fine, auspicious armor.
Having made Nīla the commander-in-chief, one should establish him in the position of Viṣvaksena;
or else Guha should be stationed there, or Viṣvaksena himself. Mārutī (Hanumān) should be fashioned in front of Rāma, in the pavilion at the entrance.
Or, as before, one may arrange the attendants for Garuḍa;
now the characteristics of the form of Balarāma—of Rāma Balabhadra—are being described. 17.112
Then, one should visualize him as two-armed and white in his divine form,
holding a pestle and a plough in his right and left hands respectively;
or alternatively, with his left hand placed upon his hip.
Or else, one should meditate on the Lord who grants protection from the fear of the south, having four arms with uplifted weapons;
holding a plow in his right hand and a mace as a weapon in his left,
clad in blue garments, and bearing the conch and the discus.
One should visualize the goddess Revatī either to the left of the one wearing a crown with bound hair, or to the right according to one's preference;
she may wear a small casket-shaped crown or bear her hair in a braid.
"Black [in color] in dependence and independence, just as before.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Fish and Other Forms," in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The eighteenth chapter:
The Blessed Lord as the Form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
Now, the manifestation of Kṛṣṇa, the descendant of Yadu, is described:
the Lord stands upon a lion-throne, possessing the three-fold bend (tribhaṅga) and endowed with auspicious marks,
accompanied by Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
With his left foot slightly bent and the other well-placed, he was wonderful to behold—
dark as a rain cloud, large-eyed, clad in yellow garments, and four-armed;
with his left lotus-hand resting upon the right arm of the Goddess.
With the tips of the hands facing downward and aligned with the line of the navel,
it is beautiful with the playful fists touched by the left and the other hand;
that hand reaches as far as the waist-string, while the two hands are raised upward.
One should fashion [the deity] holding a conch and a discus, or with two arms as previously described (18.5).
One should arrange him upon the divine portion, marked with the Śrīvatsa, possessing a serene luster, most excellent, radiant with a crown, or even wearing locks of hair tied up (18.6).
One should place Rukmiṇī on the right side and Satyabhāmā on the left;
or else, one may arrange the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa) in the place of Satyā.
Or [the Lord] may be depicted seated comfortably upon a throne together with the two goddesses.
With his left hand granting boons and his right hand bestowing fearlessness;
or else, he may lie down like a king upon a highly adorned couch,
or even upon the bed of the lord of serpents, decorated with a great palanquin.
Behind [the Lord], at the side of the crown, the wise man should have Rukmiṇī fashioned;
Satyabhāmā should be intent on massaging his feet.
Or else, two goddesses should be shown massaging his lotus-feet with their hands.
Mounted upon Tārkṣya, four-armed, and bearing a bow and arrow with his two principal hands,
and a conch and discus with his other two, O Four-faced One,
he should be depicted as having four arms with Satyabhāmā seated on his left lap.
One may visualize the Lord as having two arms, mounted upon and departing with the King of Birds (Garuḍa), according to one's preference;
or one may conceive Him as performing the role of Arjuna’s charioteer,
seated in the chariot with four arms, holding both the whip and the reins.
With his principal left hand and his right hand,
he proclaimed the supreme knowledge to the humbled one who bears the monkey-banner;
and with his other two hands, he held the Lord who wields the conch and the discus.
O Lotus-born One, one should depict him wearing a crown, with large eyes, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, having two arms, and with his hair tied up;
and Pārtha should be shown with palms joined in reverence, bowing low, holding an arrow, a quiver, and a bow.
One should visualize the dark-complexioned Kirīṭin (Arjuna) stationed upon his chariot;
or one may depict Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, in his universal form (Viśvarūpa);
or Kṛṣṇa, the Lord who follows the cows, situated in Vṛndāvana.
With his left foot slightly bent and the other standing straight,
he was moving along and singing most wonderfully on the flute;
glancing slightly toward his left side, which was adorned with a flower-ornament.
Adorned with a forest garland woven of various flowers,
and decorated with the beautiful plumage of peacocks and ornaments of calf-tethering ropes,
it was frequented by gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas.
Having placed the *kadamba* garland at midday, it was established; or else,
it stood in reverse, with the left foot straight and planted,
while the other [right] foot stood touching the back part [of the body] with its forepart.
It was surrounded by cows with their calves, deer, and birds;
it was frequented by sages, gods, gandharvas, kinnaras, and others;
or else, it was the lord of serpents, Kāliya, endowed with five hoods.
In front, he had the form of a man, and at his back, the form of a serpent;
with palms joined in reverence, difficult to overcome, he stood treading upon [the demon's] head.
With his left foot he grasped the tail, and with his left hand [he held him].
The wise one should cause [the deity] to dance with his right hand granting fearlessness;
or else, having fashioned earrings, he should perform a wondrous dance while the queen of the Naga king begs her own husband for alms.
He should depict the Goddess standing by his side with trembling body and palms joined in reverence;
or else, he should depict the Teacher of the World situated in the center of the circle of the Rāsa dance,
holding the tips of the hands of the two goddesses who stand at his sides.
He was dancing, surrounded by many thousands of cowherd girls;
he danced for the sake of fresh butter, standing with his left leg straight,
having raised his right foot, or even in a reversed position.

One should fashion the left hand so that its height reaches as far as the chin; with the right hand, one may depict either the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*) or the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*), according to preference.
Furthermore, the boon-granting hand is desired to be positioned between the breasts and the navel.

Whatever form was assumed by Kṛṣṇa, the lord of the Yādavas, for the sake of sport— that very form should be fashioned and worshipped by those seeking prosperity. If one intends to establish the rite of a single image (ekabera), one should install it in the station of Brahmā.
One should fashion images such as those made of clay or other materials like the heroic descendant of Raghu;
one should place them upon a pedestal together with Rukmiṇī and Satyabhāmā.
Rukmiṇī should have the luster of gold, while the other, Satyā, should be dark-complexioned.
She may wear a small basket-shaped ornament on her head, or a crown, or else she may have her hair braided and secured.
Satyabhāmā should hold a lotus in her right hand;
she may rest the other two [hands] upon her thighs, or otherwise.

O Lotus-Seated One, the arrangement of the aforementioned limbs should be conceived; even in her childhood state, that Goddess should be visualized according to the prescribed rite. (18.37) [This is the form of Kalkin.]
Now I shall describe the incarnation of the great-souled Viṣṇu as Kalki:
he has tawny beard and wide-open eyes, a reddish complexion, and a horse for his vehicle;
he has two arms, wears a hide garment, and carries a sword and a shield.

One should fashion a vehicle for the Piśāca [deity], adorned with a crown of matted locks and resplendent with the splendor of Brahmā; it should be situated in the divine portion. Alternatively, one may fashion a four-armed form, holding a sword and a shield in the two primary hands.
One should never represent Hari as holding a shield and a sword on his seat with the two other hands that bear the conch and the discus; rather,
one should fashion the pair of hands as bestowing fearlessness and granting boons.
The reclining form of that high-souled Kalki-Viṣṇu is not prescribed [for this].
If one should arrange the rite for a single image (ekabera) in the station of Brahmā,
one should arrange both the seated and standing forms in the divine portion.
On his right side, one should arrange Yājñavalkya as the domestic priest (purohita),
and Nārada on the right flank; on the wall-surfaces,
one should fashion the deities as mobile images, and the twice-born ones as four-armed figures.
One should imagine two arms as granting fearlessness and bestowing boons;
in the four-armed form, the conch and discus should be in the other two. This is the general characteristic of the ritual image.
One should fashion images made of metal, such as ritual icons (*karmabimba*), with chests marked by the *śrīvatsa* and adorned with either matted locks and crowns or diadems;
these are the festive images (*kautuka*) for the various partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāra*) of Viṣṇu, beginning with the ritual icons.
They may be fashioned with four arms or two arms according to one's preference;
the forms of Varāha and others are measured by ten *tāla*s.
One should likewise arrange the external and internal retinues.
Just as it is for the Primordial Form (Ādimūrti), so there is no difference whatsoever. One should fashion the Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa image, endowed with eight arms.
Alternatively, he may have four arms, adorned with weapons such as the conch and the discus;
in his two left hands, he grants boons or holds a lotus,
and in his other two hands, he displays the gesture of fearlessness or the discus.
The form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa is indivisible: on the right side of the body is Viṣṇu, and on the left is the lotus-bearer;
the left side has full breasts, while the other bears the Śrīvatsa mark. (18.52)
The left side is desired to be golden-hued, while the right side is dark;
he may be depicted as seated, reclining, or even mounted upon Garuḍa— such is the form of the Sacrifice (Yajñamūrti).
Or one may visualize the God standing; therefore, hear [the description] of Him in the form of the sacrifice:
three-headed, three-footed, four-horned, and four-faced;
with seven arms, equal to the merit of recitation, and adorned with a forest garland.
The primary right hand is in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), while the other is the granter of boons (*varadamudrā*).
His five other hands are adorned with weapons such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
There are various forms consisting of one, two, three, and more [faces or arms].
Vāsudeva is the single form, or else he is the supreme Nārāyaṇa. Those two constitute the dual form; Satya and Acyuta-Puruṣa constitute the triple form;
and Vāsudeva along with Saṅkarṣaṇa would constitute the fourfold form.
Listen to the five forms of him who possesses five forms: Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Satya, Acyuta, and likewise Ananta and Vāsudeva, the Supreme Person (Puruṣa).
He who possesses six forms is the Lord of Food, the Lord of Power (Śaktīśa), and the conqueror of Kālanemi.
Trailokyamohana and Yajñavarāha are the fifth;
Śaṅkhodara and Nṛsiṃha are the [seventh]—thus the seven forms are now declared. The four forms beginning with Vāsudeva have been described previously. (18.59–18.60)
Pūṣan and the others, as well as the three [others], are declared to be the seven forms;
likewise Hayagrīva, Mukunda, Babhru, and Vṛṣākapi; Śauri, Dāśārha, Vaikuṇṭha, and Puruṣa.
He is declared to have eight forms; now the nine forms are described. The four previously mentioned are Vāsudeva and the others, as well as Nārāyaṇa, Hayagrīva, Viṣṇu, Nṛhari, and Sūkara.
The six lords beginning with Anneśa are declared to be the forms of Vāsudeva and the others;
there are four [more], and the ten-fold form consists of these ten primary forms.
There may be an eleven-fold form, and the twelve-fold forms have been proclaimed.
The four and twenty forms have been described previously. Now,
the ritual procedure for the consecration of the five forms,
the installation of the five forms, is being proclaimed.
The wise one should install the image [of Vāsudeva] in the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) along with the two [attendants].
Alternatively, he should place Puruṣa in the divine or Brāhma portion outside in the eastern direction,
Satyamūrti in the south, and likewise Acyuta in the west.
To the north, one should place the deity named Ananta, whether mobile or immobile;
within the sanctum, Vāsudeva shall be present among the four forms as previously described.
One should install Saṅkarṣaṇa in the southern direction on the exterior.
And Pradyumna in the western direction, and Aniruddha in the northern.
O Lotus-seated One, one should arrange these previously mentioned forms facing whichever respective direction they occupy.
One should construct either a door or a window, but one should not fashion a wall [in that place].
[The image] should be endowed with a conch, a discus, and a mace, with its primary hands granting protection.
Thus ends the [section] in the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, in the section on ritual practice (*kriyāpāda*).
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Different Forms";
the nineteenth chapter:
"The Procedure for the Measurement of the Form-Icons of the Ritual Actions and Other Deities."
In this regard, the venerable Lord now describes the method for the various types of images, such as those made of clay or other materials.

The worship of the ritual action (karmārcā), the worship of the festival (utsavārcā), and likewise the worship of the offering (balyarcā); the worship of the bath and the pilgrimage site (tīrtha) together, along with the worship of the sleep and the awakening—these six types of images should be fashioned; among them, the [first] would be the most excellent for worship.
With three [images], the middle one is to be known; with the first, the last [one] would be [the middle].
This rule for the many-bera [temple] has been told, O Lotus-seated One. [This is] the measurement for a single bera.

However, the ritual image (karmārcā) and the bathing image (snapanārcā) are not desired [to be of the same size] as the permanent image (dhruvabera). When the height of the permanent image is divided into ten parts, the height of the ritual image is one part. (19.4)
It may be one-twelfth, or it may be one-sixteenth;
or it may be by an eighteenth part, or even a twenty-fourth part. Or else, its height is determined in relation to the finger-breadths of the great image. || 19.5–19.6 ||
It may be twenty-four finger-breadths, or eighteen finger-breadths,
or sixteen finger-breadths in measure, or it may be twelve finger-breadths;
or it may be eight finger-breadths, or six finger-breadths in height.
Or it may be four finger-breadths in measure, or according to the *mānāṅgula*;
the measures of the fingers mentioned previously should be made according to one's preference. This is the measurement for the forms used in the *bali* offering and so forth.
The representation of Balitīrtha and the ceremonies for the Lord’s lying down and rising have been described.
O Lotus-seated One, the height of the ritual image (karmārcā) has been stated;
the height of the action-image (karmabimba) is three times that of the remaining two.
For the purpose of the bathing festival (snapanotsava),
one should divide the height of both images into three or four parts;
in one part, one should fashion the height of the *nalas* for the festive image (*utsavakautuka*).

O Lotus-seated One, the measurement for the *karma-kautuka* [image] should be one-third or one-fourth of that of the festive image (*utsava-arcā*). This is the sequence for the Brahma-image and others;
however, in the case of a single-liṅga (*ekabera*), it should be half of that, or indeed one-fourth.
Alternatively, the height of the festival image (utsavārcā) may be one-third [of the main image];
the ritual image (karmārcā) is to be made exactly like the stationary, mobile, or seated image,
just as the permanent image (dhruvabimba) was fashioned according to the rules for the stationary, mobile, or seated types.

In that same manner, there would be the ritual image (*karmārcā*) and so forth; however, when the permanent image (*dhruva*) is lying down, one may either stand or sit. O Four-faced One, the ritual image and the others are of a standing form, while the image for the daily festival (*nityotsava-bimba*) is indeed of a standing form.
The image for the perpetual festival should be established everywhere.
Having divided the measurement of the pedestal of the stationary image into three parts for the purpose of the worship, one should fashion the lotus with one part. || 19.16 ||
The circular seat, provided with five components such as sandals and the like, brings happiness;
it is quadrangular, captivating to the mind, with its length equal to its width, fashioned with a third part [of the circumference], and marked by two auspicious light-crests. (19.17)
Having divided the height of the pedestal into three parts, one should fashion a lotus with one part;
it should be provided with twelve petals or eight, according to preference,
and likewise endowed with upper petals, with a broad pericarp in the center.
One should not construct a lotus that is joined with a pedestal, shaped like a slightly blossomed lotus,
measuring one cubit in height and having petals extending [to that length], or a simple lotus,
or even a simple pedestal, nor should one ever make it hollow.
This construction of the pedestal for one standing has been described.
Regarding the measurement of the pedestal for one sitting: it may be long, circular, square, or rectangular.

The lotus should have a height equal to half the statue’s height, or even one-third of it; it should possess many petals with a broad pericarp in the center. [The deity’s] right foot is not bent, while the other hangs down below.
The Lord sat upon the seat as previously described, O Lotus-seated One;
one should visualize a lotus with a hanging foot-rest.
[This is] the arrangement of Śrī and Bhūmi.
One should arrange the goddess Śrī on the right and Dharā on the left of the Lord;
the sixfold group of images, beginning with Karma, should always be accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi. This is the alternative arrangement for the seated positions of the goddesses Śrī and Dharā.
The two beloved ones may sit together on a single seat, or separately;
contracting the left foot, one should let the other hang down.
Śrī and Dharā sit otherwise; when the Lord stands, they likewise stand.
One should fashion the halo (prabhā),
whether circular or oval, in accordance with the proportions of the image;
it should be made beautiful, for the halo is considered to be a mass of radiant energy.
The measure of the stalk (*kāṇḍa*) should be two finger-breadths, and the field of the flower (*puṣpakṣetra*) half of that.
The field [of the next part] should be half a finger-breadth, and the stalk follows in that same sequence.
Furthermore, there is a cane-staff (*vetra*), and above it are situated those garlanded with flames.
The flames should have an interval of half a finger-breadth and likewise possess five crests,
or three crests as appropriate, beautified by a clockwise curl.
Within the radiance, one should visualize forms such as the Fish and others.
One should arrange either an even or an odd number [of images] for each section;
or else, the ten incarnations, beginning with the Fish and Keśava, [should be placed].
On both sides and at the back of Prabhā, one should fashion a handle with a peg.
When the image is mounted on a vehicle or similar support, the archway-radiance (toraṇaprabhā) must be fashioned;
for the sake of stability, one should insert a supporting frame both inside and outside.
Regarding those [images] with the radiance of a reflection, they are indeed made of metal;
one should fashion either the reflected image or the seat of the radiance out of metal. (19.33) This is the procedure for the construction of a metal image.
Having melted beeswax, one should fashion an image with it.
Having placed a heap of grain there, one should place sesame and rice upon it.
One should then draw a wheel and a lotus, and strew *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing toward the east.
Having spread a new cloth over it, he should place the image upon it.

Afterwards, the preceptor should offer oblations into the fire with flowers, sacrificial fuel-sticks, parched grain, and clarified butter— one hundred and eight times each— while the head of the image is directed toward the east.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra and again with the *Nṛsūkta* using the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Having thus performed the sacrifice according to the rule, the preceptor— wearing a garland and adorned with golden ornaments—
should sprinkle the image, which is the sequence of the principles (*tatva*), with the residual clarified butter (*saṃpātājya*).
One should meditate there during an auspicious moment and worship with the root mantra (mūlavidyā).
While performing the rite, one should honor the preceptor and satisfy him with abundant wealth;
one should likewise fully satisfy learned Brahmins with great riches.

The master sculptor should fashion the image with the permission of the chariot-maker; he should have that auspicious image made according to the standards of measurement, dimension, and proportion. Then, he should apply a coating of clay in accordance with the treatises on craftsmanship.
Having taken gold, silver, copper, and pure, excellent iron— the various forms of metal—
one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon a heap of grain as previously described.

And the preceptor should perform the oblations as before, according to the prescribed sequence. Then, having prepared pure metal acquired by righteous means, the master craftsman should fashion the image by the method taught in the scriptures.
One should likewise fashion an image of the Supreme Self out of iron;
he goes to the supreme abode, from which there is no return.
(19.44) If there is a deficiency in the hands or other limbs of the image, a propitiatory rite (śānti) must be performed.
If there is a deficiency in the hands, feet, or other limbs of the image, one should perform a rite of pacification (*śānti*).
Through acts such as giving gifts and performing fire-oblations (*homa*), the preceptor (*ācārya*) shall then bring about peace.
Furthermore, the master craftsman (*sthapati*) should restore the missing parts.
The definition of *citra*, *ardhacitra*, and *citrābhāsa* is as follows:
it is threefold—namely, *citra*, *ardhacitra*, and *citrābhāsa*.
Among these, that in which the limbs are clearly visible is called *kautuka*. (19.46)

O Four-faced One, all that which is variegated on every side should be known as such. However, when the limbs beginning with the hands can be clearly seen in one part of the chest but not in the other part, that is considered a half-painting (ardha-citra). || 19.47–19.48 ||
A form that is fashioned by means of colors such as white and so forth,
appearing as a painted image on a wall or similar surface, is declared to be *kautuka*.
It is said that the best [type] is *citra*, while the middle is called *ardha*.
Know that the reflection [of the deity] is the lowest [type], whether it be in a temple or a private dwelling.
If the primary image (dhruvabimba) cannot be obtained, one should install [a substitute] according to the sequence from best to worst.
This concerns the measurement of images in terms of *tāla* and other units.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the measurement of the image (pratimā),
according to the distinctions of the number of tālas ranging from one up to ten,
preceded by the manifestation of their forms, beginning with the "excellent" (uttama) and so forth.
Having divided whatever the measure of the image may be into ten parts,
and then having divided one of those parts into twelve, a single part therein is known as an *aṅgula*.
Having divided an *aṅgula* into eight parts, a single part therein is known as a *yava*.
The arrangement of the limbs and minor members is according to that same measurement of finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Here, the measurement of twelve finger-breadths is called a *tāla*;
this *tāla* of twelve finger-breadths is proclaimed as the primary one.
Two finger-breadths (aṅgula) should be known as a *golaka*, which is designated as a *kala*;
one finger-breadth is a *mātrā*, and a *bhāga* consists of four *mātrās*.
O Lotus-Seated One, these are the *tālas* categorized as superior, inferior, and middling.
They cut [the proportions] by numbers starting from one up to ten.
The eternal Vāsudeva is measured by ten tālas;
Brahmā and Īśa are nine and a half tālas, and the other deities are nine tālas.
Know that the qualities beginning with Kumuda stationed at the doors are four *tālas* in height;
likewise, humans and the seven classes of *piśācas* and others are eight *tālas*.
Know that the hunchbacks are six *tālas*, while the dwarfs are five *tālas*.
The Bhūtas are four *tālas* in height, and the Kinnaras are likewise three *tālas*.
Fishes should be known as two *tālas*, and the Pannagas at one *tāla*.
Ten *tālas* shall consist of one hundred and twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgulis*).
The best is twenty [tālas], the middle is sixteen, and the lowest is remembered as nine tālas; however, that which is one hundred and twelve is the best,
one hundred and eight is the middle, and one hundred and four is the lowest.
One hundred *tālas* is the best, while ninety-six is the middling;
that which is reduced by four is proclaimed as the lowest, consisting of eighty *tālas*.
In other cases, such as those beginning with seven *tālas*, the sequence starting from the highest is to be inferred accordingly.
If it should be four [tālas] less four [aṅgulas] respectively by finger-breadths,
one should understand that the threefold division mentioned previously applies there.
In the best of the ten-tāla proportions, the face measures twelve and a half aṅgulas.
They declare the middle [measurement] to be one-half of a finger less [than the best].
Each of the others is also less by half a finger.
For the *dhruvā* [drum], the best *tāla* is used; for the *arcā*, the middle should be used.
O Lotus-seated One, you are the lowest among all your attendants.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Division of the Palm [Measurement] for the Manufacture of Metal Cast Images," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, within the glorious Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Chapter Twenty.
Regarding the procedure for the measurement of the image,
the venerable Lord shall hereafter proclaim the supreme measurement of the image.

Measurement (māna), weighing (pramāṇa), and measuring by capacity (unmāna)—thus measurement is threefold. Measurement is the measure of height; weighing is considered to be the measure by balance. And that which is horizontal and vertical is here called measurement (pramāṇa).
In that regard, the measurement of the proportions of the image, from the head down to the feet in successive order, is now described. First,
based on the body obtained [in the previous calculation], it is measured with one hundred finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
One should fashion the image according to the measurement of twenty-four [finger-breadths].
The *uṣṇīṣa* is measured at one finger-breadth, and the hairline is considered to be three finger-breadths.
Starting from that hairline down to the end of the eye-line, it is measured at thirty-six barley-corns (*yava*).
Likewise, it should extend to the end of the nostrils, and similarly down to the chin.
Thus, O Four-faced One, the measurement of the face, beginning from the hairline,
consists of one hundred and eight barley grains up to the parts of the chin.
The neck is desired to be half an aṅgula, and the throat three and a half aṅgulas.
Starting from the line of the hiccough up to the heart, it is situated in the mouth;
from there down to the navel, it is sixteen and a half aṅgulas.
From that point [the navel] up to the end of the penis, the elevation is desired to be the same;
from the base of that [penis] down to the knees, it is three less than thirty fingers (twenty-seven).
The circumference of the knee-joint is desired to have an elevation of four fingers.

The *akṣānta* is said to be below the knees and equal in measure to the thighs. Then follows the height up to the end of the *tāla*, measured at four finger-breadths; according to the honored system, there are ten body-fingers (*dehāṅgula*) in one *tāla*.
Having thus divided them, those [proportions] have been stated; now hear the sequence for the middle [type]:
the face is thirteen finger-breadths, and its three locations are each one finger-breadth.
The measurement of the thigh is declared to be twenty-six finger-breadths in height.
In the same way, the height of the shanks is equal to that [of the face], and the other [parts] are equal to the latter.
In the inferior ten-tāla system, the face is considered to be one hundred yavas;
the three regions [from the navel to the top of the head] should be of the same measure, and the thigh should be two hundred yavas.
The shank is equal in height to that [the knee]; the other parts are considered equal according to the primary measurement.
O Lotus-seated One, the length of the foot is one hundred and twenty barleycorns;
the big toe should be four finger-breadths (vedas) wide, and the index finger (tarjanī) should be equal in length to it.
The middle finger is held to be thirty-one barley-corns in length;
the ring finger should be thirty barley-corns, and the little finger three finger-breadths.
The heel, moreover, should be four finger-breadths and joined with five barley-corns.
The *hikkā* [of these two] is the lower arm; the fingers are twenty-seven [finger-breadths].
From there, to the end of the wrist (*maṇibandha*), it is twenty-six finger-breadths long. Furthermore, from the wrist, the palm is joined with the width of a barley grain.
The length up to the base of the middle finger is measured at fifty barley grains (yava).
Then, the thumb is five fingers long; the index finger is likewise extended, being six barley grains longer in length; and the middle finger is six fingers long. (20.19–20.20)
The ring finger is also considered to be six barley-corns long;
it is equal to that [middle finger] up to the point where the nail meets the flesh, and it is balanced by the thumb and little finger.
The length of the nail is one finger-breadth, while the remaining [fingers] are measured at six barley-corns.
The *bāhu* and the *upabāhu* should each be four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length.
The neck (*kaṇṭha*) should be four barley-corns (*yava*) high, and the stalk (*nāla*) five finger-breadths long.
The phallus (*liṅga*) should be five finger-breadths in height, while the scrotum (*muṣka*) should be four finger-breadths.
Immediately following that, the forehead has a width of eight and a half finger-breadths;
it is shaped like the crescent moon and has a width of twelve finger-breadths. Then, the distance between the two ears is thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
The width of the chin below that [the neck] should be ten finger-breadths;
it should be full, measuring two and a quarter finger-breadths, and its shape should be like a bow.
The width of the neck at the base, middle, and top should be in progressive sequence.
The distance between the two arm-pits below the *hikkā* (the point where the heart is located) should be nine fingers, or likewise eight, or seven and a half fingers.
It should be four *yava*s in width and forty fingers in length.
The width between the armpits is three finger-breadths and twenty-five;
the measurement for the distance between the breasts is eighteen finger-breadths,
and the middle of the abdomen is declared to have a width of sixteen finger-breadths.
The hips are held to be eighteen finger-breadths, while the lower abdomen is desired to be three finger-breadths; the width of the hip region is twenty-five and a half finger-breadths,
and the width of the root of the thighs is thirty-two and a half finger-breadths.
The tip is desired to be one finger-breadth, and the middle part two and a half finger-breadths.
The width at the base of the *liṅga* is declared to be two finger-breadths;
the base is three finger-breadths wide, and the middle part is again increased by half [a finger-breadth].
The width of his scrotum is thirty-two barleycorns;
the middle of his thighs is eleven finger-breadths wide;
O Lotus-Seated One, its base is ten finger-breadths wide.
The circle of the knee is nine finger-breadths [in height], and its side is shaped like a half-moon.
The base is nine or eight [finger-breadths], the middle part should be [eight], and the top of the shank is seven and a half.
The portion of the shank (nalaka) is broad by four and a half finger-breadths.
The width at the base of the foot is three finger-breadths plus four barley-corns;
the middle part is five and a half finger-breadths, and the tip is six and a half finger-breadths.
The base [of the hand] is seven and a half finger-breadths, while the two arms are seven finger-breadths each.

The part of the forearm [the *prakoṣṭha*] has an equal width at the middle and the tip. Furthermore, it is described as being seven and a half units wide at the base (*mūla*), four and a half units wide in the middle, and four units wide at the tip of the wrist (*maṇibandha*). || 20.37–20.38 ||
The palm is likewise remembered as being five and a half finger-breadths [in length];
the width at the base of the thumb is two finger-breadths,
and the middle finger is six barley-corns [in length], while the tip of the fist is measured by a single finger-breadth.
The width at the base of the index finger is measured by nine barley grains.
Its middle is said to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) and its tip seven barley grains;
the base of the middle finger is ten barley grains, its middle nine barley grains.
The tip is said to be one finger-breadth (aṅgula), while the other [the base] is equal to the index finger;
the base of the little finger is eight barley-corns (yava), and that of the middle finger is seven.
The width of the nails is six barley-corns less than the length from the tips, minus one-quarter of a finger-breadth.
In the center of the palm, a line rises from the base of the middle finger.
Starting from the base of the little finger, the line should extend toward the middle finger;
it must be drawn by the wise between the middle and index fingers.
Starting from the base of the thumb and ending at the tip of the index finger,
a line should be drawn between those two [thumb and index finger] lines, extending to the base of the index finger,
according to the scriptures by a craftsman skilled in the treatises. (20.45)
The width of the forehead should be two and a quarter finger-breadths (sapādadvyaṅgula). Below that, the two eyebrows should be fashioned, measuring forty barley-corns (yava) in length;
they should be one barley-corn wide in the middle, with tips like the points of barley-awns and resembling the shape of a bow.
The space between those two is nine barley-corns wide and eighteen barley-corns long;
the length and width of the pupil of the eye is said to be one barley-corn.
The white circle (the sclera) is one finger-breadth wide, and [the black circle] is the black orb (the iris).

The light is one *yava* in measure; in its center, it is equal to a *yava*. Within that, however, the gaze is the size of a louse (*yūka*). Furthermore, the eyelashes above, joined together, measure three and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) or ten *yavas*.
The eyelids are one yava in length and half that in width;
there are eighty eyelashes, curved at the tips and black.
The distance between the two eyes is two aṅgulas, and the same is the distance from the center of each eye to its outer corner.

The width of the ear should be forty barley-corns and two finger-breadths (aṅgulas). The length of the ear above [the opening] is four and a half finger-breadths. The stalk (nāla) measures five finger-breadths, while its width is six barley-corns.

Behind it, the *nālī* is four barley-corns [in width]; and the *caturmukha*, equal to the *nālī*, is situated like the *karṇapippalī* of the ear. The central cavity of the *śravaṇa* and the *pippalī* is four barley-corns [in depth].
The *gallapātra*, shaped like the *karṇapippalī* with three openings, is likewise positioned.
The binding should have a hole three finger-breadths wide and as high as the cord for the eyes. The width at the base, middle, and tip of the nose is stated in sequence to be one finger-breadth,
one finger-breadth, and two and a half finger-breadths plus four barley-corns respectively.
The base is elevated by one finger-breadth; the middle part is elevated by that plus half a finger-breadth;
and the tip is elevated by two finger-breadths from the base and two finger-breadths from the middle. Its hollow is six barley-corns wide, and the middle of its cavity is four barley-corns wide.
The width of the side of the nostril is proclaimed to be two barley-corns;
its height is half a finger-breadth, and the nose is like a sesame flower.
The length of the upper lip is desired to be four and a half finger-breadths.
Its width is half a finger-breadth, and its length is at most one and a half finger-breadths;
its breadth is one finger-breadth, and its rim is considered to be one barley-corn.
The chin and the lips are each measured at ten barley-corns in both width and length.
The ankle should have the height of the toes of the foot and be like the surface of a mirror.
The two [canine teeth] should have broad and symmetrical parts, resembling royal teeth and measuring four barley-corns.
Thirty-two teeth should be fashioned according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
The tongue should be six finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths in width;
the neck is marked with three lines, and the position of the breasts is measured from the line of the *hikā* (the junction of the neck and chest).
The circumference of each breast is eleven finger-breadths, and the circular area of the nipple is two finger-breadths.
The nipple, situated in the center of the breast-circle, should be four *yava*s in size. The navel-cavity is desired to be four *yava*s deep and spiraling to the right;
the eye-socket is one and a half *aṅgula*s in circumference and half an *aṅgula* in height.
From the crown of the head to the end of the hair at the back is eleven finger-breadths;
from the crown of the head to the end of the hair on the side is a measure of twelve finger-breadths.
One should know that the distance between the two ears is thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
At its base, middle, and top parts, the back of the neck is, respectively,
nine and a half finger-breadths wide, then nine,
and then eight; below that is the position of the hump.
That hump [of his] was four barley-corns in length, height,
and breadth; the distance between his shoulders across the back was thirty-six finger-breadths,
and the space between his armpits was twenty-six finger-breadths.
O Brahmin, the width of the middle of the back is seventeen finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The two sides of the hips are likewise twenty-five finger-breadths wide;
the width of the hip region should be twenty-six finger-breadths.
The middle of the hump and likewise the waist measures thirty-six finger-breadths;
its buttocks are two finger-breadths high, and the space between them is one finger-breadth.
The base of the breasts is one finger-breadth, and the distance between them should be seven finger-breadths.
The width at the top [of the thighs] should be three finger-breadths;
from the roots of the thighs, the width should increase in sequence to four and a half, thirty-one, and likewise twelve finger-breadths. (20.73–74)
The knee should have a width of eight fingers,
and the middle of the shank should be eight and a half fingers wide;
the lower part of the shank (nālikā) should be four fingers, and the ankle (gulpha) should be four fingers with an additional four barley-corns.
The width of all [the hands] is considered to be three times [their height], and they are held to be capable of withstanding [weight].
The right hand should be in the gesture of granting fearlessness or granting boons;
the tips of the fingers of that hand should be made level with the line of the breasts.
O Lotus-born One, there should be an interval of twelve finger-breadths between those two;
in the middle of the thumb and forefinger, there should be a lotus with its stalk.
On the palm of the hand that grants boons, one should draw the shape of a lotus.
In the principal left hand, which is turned downwards, one should fashion an auspicious mace (gadā).
It should be four tālas in length, thick at the base and slender at the tip, and straight.
Its base-joint should be three aṅgulas wide, and its tip-joint one aṅgula wide.
The other [arm] is two and a half finger-breadths [long], while the middle of the mace is four finger-breadths;
the right side of the waist and the space between the two hands should be two finger-breadths.
One should make the hand on the right side touch the waist, except for the mace.
One should raise the boundary line high, with both hands holding weapons.
The distance between the middle of the two forearms should be eight finger-breadths;
the middle part is measured at ten finger-breadths, and the measurement at the tip is known as the mouth.
With the two thumbs raised upward together with the ring fingers, he is bent;
likewise, he holds a lotus with the index and middle fingers,
as well as the circular Sudarśana disc, measuring twelve finger-breadths.

The protective field is eight finger-breadths [in width], and the hub of the wheel is two finger-breadths; likewise, there should be a rim for the felloe endowed with four flames. On both sides of the nave, there are flames beautified by three-pronged whirls.
The height [of the conch] should be one and a half or two finger-breadths, and its width should be more than half a finger-breadth;
the spokes should be equal to a barley-corn or equal to the pupil of the eye.
A conch with six flames is desired to have eight, twelve, or six spokes.
Its width is eight finger-breadths and its length is twelve finger-breadths.
It is endowed with a clockwise curl at the tip of the flame of the conch and the discus;
it should be level with the hairline or equal to the line of the eyes.
Above the knees, there should be a space of one and a half finger-breadths;
between the shanks, a space of two finger-breadths is recommended.
The middle of the two eyes should be three finger-breadths, and the distance between them should be seven finger-breadths.

The distance between the two big toes is declared to be nine finger-breadths (navāṅgula). When standing upright on the bed, the right foot is straight, while the other is bent; the distance between them is twenty-seven finger-breadths.

The distance between the two big toes and the middle of the ankles is held to be four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula). The space between the knees is said to be fifteen and a half finger-breadths (sārdha-sat-tridaśāṅgula). One should place the right hand from the top of the head down to its tip.
O Lotus-seated One, one should extend the left hand down to the knee;
one should fashion a lotus in the right hand and a mace in the left hand.
O Four-faced One, the image is distinguished by these three postures.
Indeed, by means of non-bending, equal bending, and even extreme bending—
at the crown of the head, the center of the forehead, the tip of the nose, the middle of the mouth, and the throat;
in the center of the chest, the navel, and to the left of the middle of the penis.
One should hang the string without bending it at the shoulder, six finger-breadths from the elbow, on the left side, and between the two ankles; a statue that deviates from this is considered flawed.
It may be less than the stated measurement of the statue by three finger-breadths.
The thread reaching the crest-jewel, with its middle filled on the left,
[is placed] on the left forehead, in the left crocodile-mark, and on both eyes;
if one should let it hang at the navel, in the middle, and between the two ankles.
That [line] is distinguished by being level, while this one is deficient by four finger-breadths.

[The lines] are located on the crown, the left [side], and the forehead; for the left-eyed [deity], they pass through the middle of the mouth and likewise the navel; for the right-eyed, they pass through the middle of the right ankle.
The cord should be suspended in this manner; otherwise, it is considered to be "excessively bent.
This image is deficient by five finger-breadths compared to the previous measurement. An excessively bent posture for one reclining is recommended for [the images of] Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
O Four-faced One, I shall now describe, in due order and according to the truth, the measurement of the crown and other ornaments that are innate to the deities.
The crown should have a length of twenty-four finger-breadths, or fifteen finger-breadths; it should be capable of withstanding [pressure] at its base, middle, and tip respectively,
measuring thirty, seven, two, and one finger-breadths [in width].
In its center and in the four directions, one should arrange those [sections] filled with finger-breadths;
and one should beautify it with great jewels, with a single crest-jewel at the front.
One should fashion the hair-binding with a height of fourteen finger-breadths.
The base-band of the crown should be two finger-breadths wide;
its tip should be one finger-breadth, and the crest-jewel three finger-breadths.

One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus below the crest-jewel; it should be twice the size of the two spheres and adorned with various other colors. On the back part of the head, there should be a head-wheel (*śiraścakra*) shaped like a wheel.
Alternatively, one may fashion a lotus devoid of flames according to one's preference.
From the center, one should construct a circular band and an elongated sphere; its stalk should be two finger-breadths wide and as long as the sphere.
One should fashion a *makara* with the height of a sphere (*golaka*) and a length of eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
From its mouth, a garland of beautiful flowers should emerge like a crescent moon.
One should hang a flower for the ear and an ear-garland two finger-breadths long.
One should fashion a necklace three finger-breadths in width, with a cord for binding the ends at both tips;
it should be adorned with pearls in the middle and embellished with a great gem.
Furthermore, one should depict the Śrīvatsa mark, one finger-breadth in size, upon the right side of the chest.
And in the middle of that triangle, which is one and a half cubits [in size], is the wonderful Śrī, whose abode is the lotus; she is two cubits tall, holding a rising lotus,
and endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in her other two hands.
One should fashion her adorned with all ornaments, including a crown, necklaces, and armlets. The width of the swing at the front should be five finger-breadths long;
the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) should be threefold and should extend around the navel.
One should fasten the upper garment with a binding one finger-width wide;
it should be broad at the middle for two fingers, while the ends should be one finger-width wide. Adorned with ornaments such as strings of pearls, it shall be decorated with all types of jewelry.
One should join the marvelous waist-band with the eye-band;
one should fashion a pearl necklace and an armlet that appear as if filled out,
seven finger-breadths in width and adorned with various jewels.
The beads should be one finger-breadth in width and two fingers long;
one should fashion three such beads and fasten them with a cord for binding the eyes.
One should provide ornaments made of all kinds of jewels and three bracelets.
Adorned with bracelets having a circumference of one finger-breadth,
they wore golden rings set with single gems;
their circumference should be two or even three barley-corns.
One should not adorn the middle finger with rings at all.
The waistband, adorned with jewels, should have a width of three finger-breadths;
in its center, there should be a sea-monster (*makarī*) five finger-breadths in length.
The face should have fangs four finger-breadths wide and curved;
the eyes should be round and accompanied by a frown. One should fashion pearl necklaces emerging from the mouth, and arrange three such strings reaching down to the ankles.
One should fashion an anklet with three bands, two finger-breadths in circumference;
likewise, one should make a *nūpura* adorned with a network of small bells.
And there should be a yellow garment reaching to the ankles, hanging down at the sides.
One should fashion a forest garland (*vanamālā*) resplendent with various flowers;
it may consist of various gems, or even be made solely of lotuses.
Of wondrous form, it should hang from the ear down to the feet.
Alternatively, one should suspend upon the chest a clear gem resembling a *vallikā* flower, four finger-breadths in length, shining like the Kaustubha and radiant with the luster of a thousand suns,
which is as pure as the interior of the womb of Lakṣmī.
The rule for forms and ornaments has been fully demonstrated.
Indeed, it is not possible for you, let alone for other craftsmen, to recreate my form or my deeds in their entirety. (20.131–132)
"Nevertheless, having examined the scriptures and having reflected upon that scripture with those who know it,
one should fashion the image exactly as it is, free from deficiency or excess.
Thus ends the [chapter] in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The twentieth chapter, titled "The Measurement of Images," and the twenty-first chapter,
"The Measurement of the Forms of Goddesses such as Śrī."
The Blessed One then states the procedure for the creation of the goddesses beginning with Śrī: by which measurement of proportions, such as the ten-tāla system and others, they are fashioned. (21.1)

O Four-faced One, the deities Śrī and the others should be fashioned according to the proportions of the goddesses; this should be done with a *tāla* that is neither more nor less than that, but equal to it. Whatever the number, whatever the identity, and whatever the measurement of the trident-shafts for Śrī and the others may be, [they should correspond].
Those [flutes] are said to be of that same measure; now they shall be described in order.
O Four-faced One, a bamboo staff is five tālas in length;
its width at the base is three aṅgulas along with six barley-corns.
In the middle it should be three finger-breadths wide, and again three and a half finger-breadths at the tip;
fourteen finger-breadths in the middle and fifteen finger-breadths at the base. At the tip of the bamboo staff, the circumference should be thirteen and a half finger-breadths.
The staff should be fashioned by artisans as either square or well-rounded.
The chest-staff (vakṣodaṇḍa) is twenty-seven finger-breadths in length;
its middle width is three finger-breadths plus six barley-corns.
The circumference [of the base] is ten fingers together with five fingers;
at its tip, one should fashion two [protrusions] like the bud of a *kiṃśuka* flower.
The root of the arm is desired to be twenty-four fingers in length.
Its base width is prescribed as three and a half finger-breadths;
its middle width is three finger-breadths, and its tip should be two finger-breadths.
Its forearm [length] is eighteen finger-breadths from the base. || 21.9–21.10 ||

The width at the middle of those two base-prongs should be three finger-breadths, and it should be four barley-corns thick; at the tips of those two, the width should be two finger-breadths, and there should be a hollow in the base-prongs. The length of the waist-staff should be fifteen finger-breadths.
Its width at the middle is three finger-breadths together with six barley-corns.
Its circumference at the middle should be fifteen finger-breadths;
the circumference of the shaft at the sides is proclaimed to be six finger-breadths.
One should apply the two side-sticks for pains in the waist and the chest.
A chest-spike (uraśśūla) is said to be twenty-six finger-breadths in length;
its base-width is three finger-breadths, and its tip should be two finger-breadths.
The middle part of the trident should be two finger-breadths wide and four barley-corns thick;
one should fashion the leg-trident with a length equal to that of the main trident. There should be a hollow at the base of both, and their tips should be joined as a pair.

For those whose circumference has not been stated, it is held that the height shall be three times [the width]. Having prepared the thirteen types of *śūla* according to the previously mentioned measurements,
one should perform all the rites, such as the ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsa*), just as in the consecration of a Śrī-liṅga.
Whether in the case of independence or dependence, preceded by the placement of the jewels,

one should install the trident and other [emblems], along with the wrapping of cords and so forth, as before. One should perform everything up to the application of the coating of colors, according to the measurements as they are demonstrated.
Having established a height of one hundred and twenty finger-breadths, it is described as follows:
the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) measures one finger-breadth, and the head should be three finger-breadths.
From the end of the eye-line, [the distance to the ear] is four finger-breadths plus three and a half barley-corns.
O Lotus-Seated One, from the junction [of the nose] to the end of the nostril-flap is likewise [four finger-breadths].
From the flap inward to the chin is four finger-breadths plus one-quarter;
the neck should be four finger-breadths in measure, and from there [downward] is the region of the heart.
The measurement from the end of the breast-line is said to be thirteen finger-breadths;
from there down to the limit of the navel, it should be fifteen finger-breadths.
The hips are six finger-breadths in width, and the vulva is three and a half finger-breadths.
The measurement of the hips should be three and a half finger-breadths,
and the length of the thighs is twenty-five and a half finger-breadths; the shanks are equal to that,
and likewise the knees and the distance down to the soles of the feet are three and a half finger-breadths.
Its width is eight finger-breadths and its length twelve finger-breadths;
it is marked with a clockwise curl at the tip of the flame of the conch and the discus.
It should be level with the hairline, or else equal to that [measurement] by means of a thread.
With a space of one and a half finger-breadths, there should be two *guñjā* seeds at intervals of two finger-breadths.
They declare that the distance between the shanks is twenty barley-corns;
the middle of the eyes is three finger-breadths, and that of the breasts is seven finger-breadths.
The distance between the two big toes is said to be nine finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
Beyond the axle [of the foot], the big toe is three finger-breadths long;
the second toe (tarjanī) is half that length plus two finger-breadths, with an additional barley-corn (yava).
The two others are respectively diminished by one *yava* each;
the measurement of the heel and the sides should be four *aṅgulas*,
and the ankle should likewise be measured at twenty *aṅgulas* in length.
From the end of the *hikka* line downwards, the lower arm (*bāhu*) measures eighteen and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The forearm (*prakoṣṭha*) should be six finger-breadths in length.
Likewise, the remaining middle finger (*madhyamā*) is fifteen and a half finger-breadths.
The measurement of the head should be ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and its width should be eight finger-breadths.
The forehead should be eighty barley-corns (yavas) in length at the front;
immediately following that, the measurement is desired to be eighty-eight barley-corns.

The length of the ear should be measured at thirty-two barley-corns; likewise, the upward length of the stalk above the pippalī-joint is considered to be two barley-corns. The width of the base of the stalk should be equal to six barley-corns.
The tip [of the neck] is four barley-corns; the base of the neck is six finger-breadths.
The shoulder-joint is five and a half finger-breadths at the tip and two finger-breadths thick.
Below the ends of the *hikkā*, the base of the arms is thirty-two finger-breadths.
The circle of the chest between the two breasts is eighteen finger-breadths in extent,
correctly demarcated by fifteen finger-breadths;
its width is nine finger-breadths, and its height is likewise.
The distance between the breasts is desired to be twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width.
O Four-faced One, the diameter of the dark circle (the navel) is two finger-breadths;
however, the circumference of the middle of the abdomen should be thirty-three finger-breadths.
The circumference at the middle of the hips is fifteen and seven (twenty-two) finger-breadths;
the circumference at the middle of the waist is twenty-one finger-breadths;
and likewise, the girth at the roots of the thighs should be thirty-six finger-breadths.
The circumference of the thighs should be thirty finger-breadths;
the circumference of the knees is likewise twenty-four finger-breadths;
and the circumference of the shanks is held to be twenty-one finger-breadths.
The circumference at the middle of the shaft and the shanks is twenty-two and a half finger-breadths;
the tip of the shanks should be eleven finger-breadths.
The circumference of the circular rim of the axle-hole is also eleven finger-breadths.
The circumference of the axle should be one finger-breadth; it is considered to be capable of bearing a medium load.
The tip of the palm should be six finger-breadths long, with a height of four finger-breadths.
The width of the thumb should be two finger-breadths, and the forefinger should be one finger-breadth wide.
The other fingers, starting from the middle one, are successively shorter by one barleycorn (*yava*).
The width of the thumb nail is proclaimed to be three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
The index finger should be shorter by a quarter [of a finger], and the others are successively raised by one barleycorn.
The middle part of the arm should be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and the root [of the arm] three more than that.
Including the base of the forearm, it should be fifteen finger-breadths;
from the middle to the end it should be twelve finger-breadths, and the wrist nine finger-breadths.
The palm is desired to be one and a half *tāla*s in width;
the base of the thumb is one and a half *aṅgula*s, the nail is one *aṅgula*,
and the protruding part is said to be three *yava*s, provided with two joints.
The width of the index finger (tarjanī) shall be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) together with one-eighth of an aṅgula.
The middle finger (madhyamā) is desired to have a width of one and a quarter aṅgulas;
the remaining four fingers are to have three joints and a width of seven or eight barley-corns (yava).
From the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) to the end of the hair at the side should be ten finger-breadths (*daśāṅgula*).
Starting from the end of the hair at the side, the two eyebrows should be two and a quarter finger-breadths apart.
The eyebrow should be six finger-breadths long, with the middle part like a barley grain (*yava*) and the ends like a louse-egg (*yūkā*).
The space between the eyebrows is nine barley-corns wide, and the eye is three finger-breadths long.
The pupil should be known to be one finger-breadth in length and width;
the black portion [of the iris] is one finger-breadth less than that, and the light [of the pupil] is the size of a louse.
Surrounding the black disc is a white circle one finger-breadth wide;
in the center is an eye, one finger-breadth in extent, shaped like a winnowing basket or a fish.
Its upper eyelashes are three and a half fingers long and extend one finger-breadth in width.
The other [eyelid] is three finger-breadths in length, and its width is measured as one barley-corn.
There are eighty curved eyelashes, numbering one hundred;
the distance between the two eyes is two finger-breadths, and the root of the nose is one finger-breadth.
Whether broad or high, the middle [of the tube] should be one and a half finger-breadths;
the tip should be two finger-breadths or one and a half, and the hollow should be six barley-corns.
The middle of those two [ends] should be four barley-corns, and the side of the joint (*puṭa*) should be four barley-corns.
From the outer corner of the eye to the root of the ear, the distance is considered to be forty barley-corns (yavas).
The width of the ear is two finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and the opening is four barley-corns.
The upper lip is four and a half finger-breadths in length.
The lower lip is one *aṅgula* in width and one *aṅgula* in length;
the chin is two *aṅgulas* in width and two *aṅgulas* in length. It is adorned with a crest (*āpīḍa*) joined to the nose and provided with a basket-shaped crown (*karaṇḍamukuṭa*).
She wore a central gem-ornament, armlets, and three bracelets;
she was adorned with a jeweled bodice, a girdle, flower-patterned garments, and breast-bands;
she was graced with anklets and embellished with every kind of ornament.
Standing at the right side of the Lord, having cast aside her modesty,
she indeed holds a blossoming lotus with her left hand,
while the lotus of her other hand rests upon the region of her thigh.
Alternatively, the two hands may have the luster of refined gold. On the seat, the right hand bestows fearlessness (*abhaya*) and the other bestows boons (*varada*);
or else, there may be a lotus on the right, while the left is marked with a bracelet.
This is the procedure for [the form] dependent on another; now it is described as it is for the independent [form]:
she has four arms, holding a lotus with her two lower hands, or else holding a conch and a discus with her two principal hands, and bestowing boons.
One should visualize the goddess named Vasundharā, who bestows fearlessness, wears a crown of matted locks, is free from all fear, possesses two hands, and has the luster of gold;
she grants protection with her right hand and bestows wealth with her other hand.
Holding a pomegranate fruit in her left hand, or else bearing the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāratna), she is seated upon a golden lion-throne;
she is adorned and has her left foot touching a jar of treasure.
Likewise, one should visualize the goddess Mahī standing there, taking refuge in the shade of a *kalpaka* tree;
she is on the left side, two-armed, with a dark complexion,
devoid of breast-bands, and lacking earrings and hair-ornaments.
Standing firmly on her left foot, with the other slightly bent,
she holds a flower in her right hand and possesses a pure smile;
her left hand rests upon the region of her thigh, and she is fully adorned.

They know the *Śrītanu* [form] as being with an upper garment (*sottarīya*) according to the requirements; in its independence, however, it is [described differently]. The *Yogalakṣmī* is the *Śrīvatsa*, while the *Bhogalakṣmī* is on both sides;
the *Vīralakṣmī* is indeed the remainder, with a separate arrangement for the abode.
The goddesses Rati, Sarasvatī, and Tuṣṭi are to the right of the God.
Rati resembles vermilion; Sarasvatī has the luster of crystal;
Tuṣṭi resembles yellow orpiment; and they possess ornaments and other attributes like those of Śrī.
This rule applies when [the deity] is dependent on another; however, the rule for when [the deity] is independent is now stated:
Rati and the others have four hands. Of these, the two primary hands of Rati should display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while the other two hold a noose and a goad. (21.78–79)

Sarasvatī’s two principal hands are such that the right is marked with the *jñāna-mudrā*, while the left holds the book of higher knowledge (*vijñāna-pustaka*). In the lowest [pair], she holds a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) in the left hand; all [the deities] beginning with Vajra are situated on the right.
And as before, Tuṣṭi’s primary [emblems] are the conch and the lotus, while the secondary ones are the conch and the lotus.
Kīrti, Prīti, and Śānti are stationed on the left side of the Lord;
their left feet should be well-placed, slightly bent by the other [the right].
Others, holding flowers, have their left [hands] resting upon the region of the thighs.
Kīrti is desired to have the luster of crystal, while Prīti has a blue luster.
Śānti has the appearance of a dark-green hue, and all are adorned with every ornament.
This rule applies when [the deity] is dependent; it is also as before when [the deity] is independent.
When the god is standing, the goddesses remain standing, or they may sit according to their preference.
Likewise, even when he is seated, they should be so in the case of independence on a lion-throne.
All of them are praised when seated in the *padmāsana* or the *svastikāsana*.
Padmā should be in the *padmāsana*, while Śrī should be upon a lion-throne (*siṃhaviṣṭara*). On the petals of the lotus, starting from the east, are the forms of Vāsudeva and the others.
Furthermore, on the petals beginning with the southeast (āgneya), there are four white elephants.
Below, at the sides of the feet, are Śaṅkha and Padma, the lords of the treasures (nidhi), as well as two Lambodarās,
both standing while gazing at one another's faces.
The goddesses Earth and the others are situated outside in the eight directions;
then Indra and the other guardians of the directions are stationed outside the goddesses.
In the four enclosures, there should be four women holding canes in their hands.
"The women stood there, adorned with all their ornaments.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Image," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrī Pādmasaṃhitā within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
The Twenty-second Chapter:
Description of the Form, Color, and Other Attributes of the Retinue; by the Blessed Lord.
O Four-faced One, [I shall describe] the form, the color, as well as the attire, the hand-gestures (hasta-mudrā),
and likewise the number of hands according to their respective applications;
or else, I shall explain the retinues exactly as they are.
Hayagrīva—
four-armed Hayagrīva, resembling pure crystal,
horse-faced, wearing a crown, and clad in a lower garment and upper shawl of washed cloth.
With one principal [hand] he grants boons,
while with the other [right hand] he holds a book of wisdom; and in his two lower hands,
he carries a rosary and a conch shell, being most beautifully adorned.
One should visualize him in the form of a man, infinite and wearing a crown, seated comfortably upon the coils of the serpent, with a canopy of hoods raised behind him;
he has four arms, possesses a white radiance, and provides shade with those uplifted hoods.
Alternatively, if the complexion of Ananta is proclaimed to be dark (śyāmala),
one should represent his principal hand as granting boons (varada) and his left hand holding a mace (gadādhara),
or else standing while leaning against the region of his hip.
With his two lower hands, he should hold a conch and a discus;
[he should be] Garuḍa, resembling gold in color and possessing a blue tip to the end of his nose.
With a broad chest extending to the left and right,
his face was formidable with fangs, and his eyes were curved with a frown;
he wore a crown shaped like a casket and was adorned with all manner of ornaments.
Wearing a variegated robe and adorned by the lords of serpents, holding a handful of flowers to his heart, he may be either standing or seated;
one of his two legs should be bent. || 22.10–22.11 ||
Behind him is another [deity], as appropriate, or there may be a lotus seat;
Sūrya, Mārtāṇḍa, two-armed, red in color, wearing red garments, and standing.
On his back, at the place of the head, was a large circular discus;
he wore a pair of lotuses in his two hands and was adorned with a crown.
Upon his broad chest was the great Syamantaka jewel.
Or he may be seated comfortably upon the image in an eight-petaled lotus; with the moon [at the center],
and the signs beginning with Aries on the lotus petals starting from the east.
One should visualize Soma as being served by two [attendants] holding white water-lilies;
and Kāma as resembling a red lotus, wearing garments of red flowers.
Holding a bow made of sugarcane and arrows of flowers with his two hands,
he has four arms and four faces, wears a crown of matted locks,
and bestows boons and fearlessness with his two primary hands, while the other two hands hold these implements.
Holding a water-pot and a rosary, seated in a comfortable posture—
Gajānana,
the elephant-faced one, four-armed, with a protruding belly and white radiance.
Wearing a crown with a basket-shaped ornament and a long sacred thread hanging down,
he holds a large fruit in his principal left hand;
with his other hand, however, he grasps a broken tooth.
With his other two hands, the Lord holds a noose and a goad;
he has six faces,
six mouths, four arms, and the luster of a pomegranate flower.
The two primary [hands] grant the boons and fearlessness, while the two secondary hands hold the spear and the javelin.
One should visualize her as dark-complexioned in luster with four arms,
respectively holding a mace, granting fearlessness, and bearing the conch, the discus, and the boon-granting gesture.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, crowns, anklets, and other ornaments—
