or else eight-armed Durgā— with her four right hands decorated with the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the arrow,
the trident, and the discus;
Holding a mace, bow, sword, and conch as her excellent weapons in her left hands;
or else, she may have twelve arms— the specific distinction being that she holds an axe and a trident in her right hands, and likewise a noose and a goad in her left.
The bell [is placed] on the five preceding [arms], or else [it is for] the twelve-armed [form].
Any weapon not mentioned should be assigned to another set of four arms;
or there may even be thirty-two hands, as it is taught that the weapons may be arranged as desired.
Then one should visualize the giver of wealth (Dhanada) as having a protruding belly and a large body;
he resembles molten gold, grants boons, and likewise holds a staff.
The attendants of Dhanada should be placed on his right side— namely Jṛmbhala and Maṇibhadraka—
and one should likewise place the Śaṅkha treasure (nidhi) on the left side.
Nalakūbara and Ambhojanidhi, as well as Śibi and Kuṇḍala;
Jṛmbhala is of a golden hue, Maṇibhadra has the luster of jewels,
and he who is named Nalakūbara is proclaimed to be of a dark complexion.
Śibi is adorned with earrings and is red; all of them bestow the boon of fearlessness.
Rudra is three-eyed, ruddy, and wears a crown of matted locks. || 22.31 ||
Four-armed, with a blue throat, adorned with a crescent moon,
clothed in a tiger skin, and decorated with all ornaments;
he stands with his two principal hands bestowing boons and fearlessness.
With his other two hands, he holds an axe and a deer;
the guardian of the field [worships] the four-armed guardian of the field, resplendent with a crown and a casket.
With a face made terrible by fangs and eyes curved with a frown,
he holds a staff in his left hand and displays the *tarjanī* (threatening) mudrā in his primary right hand;
in his two secondary hands, he holds a noose and a goad.
Viṣvaksena [worshipped] Viṣvaksena, who has four arms, a dark complexion, and wears a crown;
who has a protruding belly and grants fearlessness with his principal hand. || 22.36 ||
Standing with his right hand placed around his hip in a counter-clockwise direction,
he sits with his other two hands holding the conch and the discus;
or else, one may imagine the mace to be held in one of his two front hands.
Otherwise, one should fashion the *tarjanī* mudrā; or else, in the two right hands, one should place a mace in the primary hand and a conch in the secondary hand.
In the primary [left] hand, an *abhaya* [mudrā], and in the secondary, a discus; or otherwise, in the two hands.
Or [he may be] Viṣvaksena’s queen, holding a conch and a discus in her two principal hands, or bearing a razor and a staff, standing with her palms joined in reverence.
And one should place the goddess of Viṣvaksena on his left side, named Puṣpadharā, appearing like Kamalā. [22.41] The forms beginning with Brāhmī.
All the Mothers, beginning with Brahmyā, are the respective powers (*śakti*) of Brahmā and the other [deities];
they assume the forms, colors, weapons, and so forth of Brahmā and the others. (22.42) Vīrabhadra.
Vīrabhadra, in the form of Rudra, should stand behind them;
Vināyaka,
the Lord of Obstacles, should be in the eastern part, and his two arms should also be at their front.
Having placed it upon the shoulders of two female friends standing at his sides, he should remain there;
men with goat-faces stand at the side of the woman who is about to give birth, her face being like that of a goat. || 22.44 ||
Indeed, eight [beings] bearing divine weapons, their heads marked with their own respective emblems—
the wielder of the discus, the wielder of the mace, the wielder of the conch, the wielder of the sword, the wielder of the club,
the wielder of the śārṅga bow, the wielder of the lotus, and likewise the wielder of the thunderbolt— were human in form and possessed two arms.
The right hand is in the *tarjanī* (threatening) mudrā, while the left rests upon the hip.
The Ādityas are twelve in number; likewise, their forms and other attributes are like those of the Sun-god.
All the Vasus are two cubits in height and adorned with crowns and baskets;
the Pitṛs hold staffs and javelins, and these Pitṛs have two hands.
They hold staffs as weapons in their left hands, while their right hands grant fearlessness;
the Viśvedevas wear crowns shaped like small caskets, and the Viśvedevas are likewise [described].
The seven ṛṣis: "Atri, Bhṛgu, Kutsa, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama,
as well as Kāśyapa and Aṅgiras— these are remembered as the seven ṛṣis."
All seven Ṛṣis hold a book of knowledge in their hands;
elsewhere they are depicted wearing matted hair and crowns.
Adorned with divine splendor, the eleven Rudras are likewise remembered.
The attendants of Viṣṇu,
such as Kumuda and others, are the lords among Viṣṇu’s attendants;
they bear in their four hands the conch, the discus, and the mace.
In the south are those with the tarjanī mudrā, wearing yellow garments and crowns;
Upendra and the others,
as well as the group of eight beginning with Upendra, have two hands holding a discus and a conch.
Viśvā and the others have two arms, bearing maces, swords, and missiles;
they wear crowns with caskets and are adorned with all ornaments. (22.54) [The Aśvins]
The two Aśvins are identical and red in color, holding nectar jars,
wearing small caskets and crowns, possessing two hands, and being highly adorned.
(22.55) [Likewise are] Indra and the other guardians of the directions.
Śyāma is dark-complexioned, wears a crown, and has two arms; Vāsava holds a vajra in his right hand, rests his left hand upon his hip, and is adorned with all ornaments.
Jvalana, situated in the midst of a circle of flames, should have two arms.
The Giver of Boons has a spear in his hand and is radiant with a crown of baskets.
Vaivasvata is two-armed, wears a diadem, and has a dark complexion;
Nirṛti, who is fearsome to behold, holds a staff and grants protection from fear with his right hand.

With a face made terrible by fangs and eyes curved with a frown, his right hand holds a sword while granting fearlessness; he is radiant with a crown and a casket. Varuṇa is dark-complexioned, holding a noose in his [right] hand and bestowing fearlessness with his left.
Karaṇḍima, Kuṭa, Vāyu, Dhūmra, and Dvibāhuka;
the goad is in the right hand, while the left rests upon the hip.
These Maruts are equal to Vāyu, and Soma is desired to be like Soma.
Īśāna is to be conceived like Rudra; their respective vehicles are now described:
the vehicle of Brahmā and the others is the swan, that of Vidhātṛ is the bull, and that of Sūrya is the horse.
The makara is said to be the vehicle of Śūrpakārāti, the peacock of the spear-handed [Kārttikeya],
the lion of Durgā, and the mouse of Vighnarāja.
The man is the vehicle of Yakṣādhirāja, and the elephant of Śunāsīra.
The ram is the vehicle of Agni, and the buffalo is the vehicle of Kṛtānta. The Piśāca is the mount of Nirṛti, while the Makara is that of Varuṇa.
The deer is said to be the vehicle of Prāṇa, and it is the same for the Maruts as well.
Regarding the difference in measurement between the principal image and the retinue:
one should divide the height of the principal image into four parts;
from those, one should assign one part as the height for the retinue members. (22.66)
One should determine the height according to circumstance, whether by the *māna-aṅgula* or the *deha-labdha-aṅgula*,
as eight *aṅgulas*, or twelve *aṅgulas*,
or even double that.
O Four-faced One, your retinues are stationed in their respective places around the original image;
they sit upon its seat, and even on its bed, though there is no actual bedding—
whether sitting or standing, they move about according to their will.
Regarding the determination of the thickness and width of the body with hanging breasts:
it is said that the length should be five *tālas* and the thickness one *aṅgula*. One should make the width half the length, so that it is well-executed.
For the sake of achieving the proper curvature and straightness of the limbs of the image,
O Lotus-Seated One, one should fashion that half-remaining portion which hangs down, as well as the various cavities for the crest-jewel and other ornaments. (22.71–72)
One should oneself hang threads individually through those various apertures;
by means of them, one should ascertain the straightness of every limb without hesitation.
Thus, in the glorious *Pāñcarātra*, in the great *Upaniṣad*, in the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, in the *Kriyāpāda*.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Retinue";
the twenty-third chapter, "The Implements for Worship."
"O Brahmin, the means for propitiating the Blessed Lord, or its very characteristics, are now being described; listen to them in their entirety. (23.1)
One should prepare lamp-stands made of iron, four cubits in height,
or three, one, or two cubits high according to one's strength;
or they may be made of copper or silver, provided with pairs of oil-holders.

One should prepare the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, made either of gold or of other materials, adorned with lotus buds fashioned from streams of clarified butter, and arranged in pairs, or in large, many-sided, wide-circumferenced forms. (23.3–23.4)
In the absence of both [silver and gold], they may be made of pure copper,
or of any metal except for *paiśāca* iron, according to one's means.
The parts such as the wheels should have the appearance of full-blown lotuses in their centers.
One should also prepare inner vessels capable of being filled with substances measuring a *prastha* or more,
which may be of the nature of conch-shells or mother-of-pearl; likewise, one should provide offering vessels made of gold or other materials.
In the absence of both silver and copper, one should fashion vessels made of pure copper, circular in shape and proportionate to the quantity of the sacrificial materials.
A *darvī* ladle should be as long as the forearm, with its tip and base shaped like circles.
The water vessel should be made of gold or silver;
it may be round and long, well-rounded, or simply elongated,
with an auspicious interior capable of being filled with water measuring one *prastha*.
According to the measurement of the feet, there should be two auspicious sandals made of gold,
or else made of silver or copper, resembling the feet;
and their support, made of that same metal, should be circular with a lotus fashioned in the middle.
The vessel for holding water for washing the feet is marvelous:
it should be made of gold or silver, shaped like a lotus with three legs, or even of copper, provided it has a wheel-shaped base; such a vessel is purifying for the virtuous.
One should fashion a vessel for holding rinsing water from the finest metal, shaped like the pericarp of a lotus, of wondrous appearance;
it should be eight finger-breadths long, made of either gold or silver. || 23.14 ||
It should be six finger-breadths in length, or half of that in width;
it should be provided with twenty teeth on both sides,
or else with sixteen or eight teeth and three finger-breadths [in width].
A golden vessel for powdered collyrium, shaped like a man-deer, or perhaps in the form of a lion or even a swan;
it should have a hole at the top and a rod twelve finger-breadths in length. (23.17)
Or it may be made of gold, eight finger-breadths long and open at both ends.
Its mouth should be closed like a flower bud or a fruit, resembling a lotus;
it should be as beautiful as a mirror, or half that size.

It may be circular or made of bell-metal, inlaid with great jewels according to one's wealth; it may have feet or be without them, and its size may correspond to the measurement of the face. It may be made of gold, circular, or even of silver, which is purifying.
It should be one *aratni* in width and possess eight petals in the center. Within each lotus petal there should be a hundred apertures;
likewise, there should be a hundred [apertures] in the pericarp, the filaments, and the pedestals.
Furthermore, one hundred and eight petals from the edge to the center should be inlaid with great jewels; thus, the thousand-fold stream,
joined with eight streams, should be prepared for the consecration.
Or its measurement may correspond to the size of the image, ranging from one *tāla* up to nine *tālas*.
Now, O twice-born one, I shall briefly describe the characteristics of the banner (*patākā*):
the cloth should be eight *tālas* long or ten *tālas* long.

Having first fashioned a square of equal dimensions according to the method of measurement, using linen or cotton that is very smooth, beautiful in form, and variegated with various colors. || 23.26 ||
Having divided [the area] with the two diagonal threads, one should erase the eastern portion.
By means of the southern, northern, and western sections, one should lead it to a single white line.
Having prepared a staff on its western side, one should join it there.
Having the form of a blossoming lotus, pure and made of the finest metal,
it possesses a great cavity capable of holding water to the measure of one *āḍhaka*,
with a stream of water flowing from its hand-length [spout] and adorned by its side-measurements.
One should fashion another bathing vessel adorned with pearls;
or else, one resembling the shape of a conch with a water-pipe at its front,
a incense burner like a lotus, fashioned from gold or other precious materials.
The space between the hands should be three or two padas, not joined by a base;
the height of each foot should likewise be four aṅgulas.
Its construction should consist of many perforations and be natural.
Alternatively, it is adorned with a form resembling a blooming lotus; the moon is its stalk, well-established at the tip of the staff upon the feet,
while a lamp-vessel and a water-lily bud are likewise situated in the middle of the stalk.
The one most skilled in the arts should fashion that [lamp] with a base for the wick using even as many as a hundred, or exactly eight;
or twenty, or eight, or two, or ten;
or eight, according to his ability.
The bell, consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), should measure one cubit in height;
it should have the shape of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagolaka) and be made of Saurāṣṭra stone.
It should be turned downwards, with a width and height equal to that of a palm tree (tāla).
Having a shape like a lamp, with a sharp inner palate,
it should have a handle at the base of the palate and the king of birds well-positioned at the tip;
whether ending in a discus or a lotus, this is proclaimed as the bell (ghaṇṭā).
There are four other bells with leather thongs fastened to them, placed in each direction.
On this very bell, or according to one's means,
the rite of *nīrājana* is performed using a vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
It should be three *tālas* in length and width, circular, with a lotus in the center;
it may be nine, seven, five, three, or even one [in size].
The *balipātra* (offering vessel) should be four *tālas* [in height] and fashioned from materials such as gold.
Whether circular, square, or many-sided, according to one's preference;
or one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus in the center, or else one with sixteen petals,
or even one endowed with twelve petals.
A white parasol, released from its support, with a luster equal to the orb of the moon;
likewise, white parasols made of peacock feathers,
and many other parasols with golden handles, O Lotus-born One.
There were many auspicious and large fans,
as well as white chowries made of precious materials;
and fourfold sets of single-stemmed flowers, each serving as a fitting component of the worship.

O Brahmin, one should fashion a leaf-vessel from gold in the shape of a *nāgatilaka* flower; it should be one *aratni* in width, with a handle of the same measurement for its height, and an auspicious seat for worship one *hasta* in height.
Or else, it may be of lesser height, or according to one's wealth;
its width should be one cubit (*aratni*), with its length and proportions determined by that measure.
It may be provided with lion legs, or four elephant feet. (23.48–23.49)
Alternatively, it may have feet shaped like a tiger’s paw, adorned with gold and jewels;
it is square, decorated with a lotus designed in its center,
and provided with a pedestal, a rim, and side-arms.
Or else, one that is free from the wheel-marks on the path and polished by hands; or one made of gold, or fashioned from silver and other metals;
or one made of wood, inlaid with jewels, and fashioned with golden bands.
The bathing seat should be equal in width and height to those previously mentioned,
twice as long, fashioned with water-channels having mouths like crocodiles,
extending four finger-breadths [in depth], and adorned with the height of palm trees.

And one should fashion for him, as before, a most excellent and beautiful seat of ornaments, twice the length and width [of the previous], joined with the aforementioned feet, and adorned with gold and jewels. (23.54–55)

A seat for eating is said to be one-quarter less [in height], four *tāla*s in width, twice that in length, and two *aṅgula*s in thickness. A traveling seat (*yātrāsana*) is broad, measuring two cubits, with short legs.
Its stalk should be twice as long and as high as a palm tree.
One should fashion a door in the middle of the stalk of the vehicle-throne,
adorned with gold and jewels, and provided with an account of the descent [from heaven].

O Four-faced One, the seats made of metal should be as previously described; the one most skilled in craftsmanship should prepare those made of wood according to what is available. Furthermore, regarding the length, width, and height of these seats—

One should fashion [the throne] in accordance with the proportions of the image; this is the settled rule. One may also provide a palanquin or a chariot for the procession according to one's wealth, made of fine silk and colored white, black, red, or variegated.
One should also place banners resplendent with staffs made of gold upon the tips of the staffs; one should likewise arrange the vehicles of the gods,
or simply provide staffs made of *plakṣa* wood or bamboo.

One should prepare a water trough and a basin made of materials such as gold for the purpose of the deity’s consecration; these should be deep. One should also arrange various kinds of musical instruments, such as the lute and others.

One should have the bases for the vessels used for the *arghya*, *pādya*, and other offerings fashioned from materials such as gold, according to the size of the vessels. Thus ends the [section] in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Chapter Twenty-three: The Characteristics of the Implements of Worship.
Chapter Twenty-four:
The Characteristics of the Preceptor, the Planting of the Germinating Sprouts, and so forth.
The Blessed Lord said: O Brahmin, I shall describe the characteristics of a teacher exactly as they are.
First, he should be a learned Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to the Pañcarātra.

One should first choose a teacher who is free from all defects and a vessel for all virtues, for spiritual accomplishments depend upon him. He should be pure, with auspicious limbs free from deficiency or excess.

One who has auspicious hands, is learned in the scriptures, possesses good conduct, and is virtuous; a Brāhmaṇa devoted to dharma who is well-versed in the traditional lore and the Vedic meters, who knows the regulations for the five times of the day, is constant in performing those rites, and is patient. || 24.3–24.4 ||

The lord was one who had conquered his senses, possessed of splendor, and skilled in reasoning and refutation; he performed the six duties, knew the six paths, was learned in the six auxiliary sciences, and was free from greed. He was adept in the sixteen ritual depositions, gentle, and a knower of the various systems of established doctrine.
He was upright, compassionate, a knower of the Veda, truthful in speech, and esteemed by the virtuous.
He was an expounder of the scriptures, steadfast, noble, the first to speak, and sweet of tongue.
He was one who greeted others with a smile, possessed of the quality of goodness (sattva), and the most excellent among those who know the law.
Handsome, youthful, a debater skilled in disputations, with an intellect as sharp as the tip of a blade of kusha grass, tranquil, knowledgeable in ethics, and understanding of place and time;
free from envy, having conquered the pairs of opposites, and equal toward all living beings. (24.8)
Always remaining the same in both adversity and prosperity, he was of noble lineage;
he spoke measuredly, was devoted to meditation, and contemplated the twelve-syllable mantra.
He was intent on the propitiation of Mānasa and was dedicated to the Pañcarātra.
Independent, devoted to the elders, handsome, and a believer;
one who does not revile the Vedas, possessing all the traditional codes of conduct, and renowned;
free from all reproach and endowed with every auspicious mark.
One who knows the meaning of all the scriptures and has been initiated into the circle of the mandala—
whether he be a householder, a celibate student, or a forest-dweller—
shall be qualified for these [practices] provided he possesses the qualities as described.
Likewise, for the office of preceptor and for the office of officiating priest,
the diligent sacrificer, together with his guru, should select those very same brahmins who are endowed with all virtues and capable of carrying out the ritual acts. (24.14)
The *vaṭu* is described as being of four kinds: the youth, the equal, and the aged.
It is further said that there is a "divided" (*savibhāga*) type resulting from the proper division of two [of these]. One who is under sixteen years of age is designated as a *vaṭu*. (24.15–16)
A young man, one of equal age, or an elder—all are fit for the rite of daily worship;
however, in the occasional rite involving the ritual sprouts (sāṅkura), they are fit provided they are equal to or superior to the most excellent [preceptor].
At the proper time, the patron (yajamāna) should likewise give a cow, land, and gold.
And one should cause a coconut to be given to the preceptor at the beginning of the ritual.
O Brahmin, there should be sixteen officiating priests, or eight, or even four;
[the rite is performed] by the preceptor as prescribed and by the officiating priests as specified.
The diligent sacrificer should install Viṣṇu in the temple;
he attains all desires—of this there is no doubt.
Otherwise, if one of deluded mind should install Hari in the abode [in an improper manner], [he incurs misfortune].
He does not obtain the desired fruit, and he himself dies soon;
neither his abode nor his kingdom remains for long,
nor does the Blessed One dwell there, nor is he pleased by the sacrifice.
Neither the renunciant nor even the Brāhmaṇa possessing the aforementioned characteristics has the right [to perform sacrifices];
nor do the other three castes have the right to sacrifice.
Neither the Kuṇḍas nor the Golakas, nor others born of inverse unions (pratiloma), shall have such rights.
Those who are entitled to perform rituals are never outcasts (vrātyas), for they are indeed born from the womb of Brahman.
O Four-faced One, there is no entitlement for these people, nor for the Sūtas and others, in the offering of the ritual seed-sprout (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Prior to the rite of consecration, there should be the planting of sprouts.
O Brahmin, a ritual does not bear fruit without the planting of sprouts;
therefore, this must be done when rites such as consecrations are about to be commenced.
One should have the seeds sown according to the prescribed rule even beforehand for the sake of sprouting—
on the twelfth day, the ninth, the seventh, the fifth,
or on the third day prior to the day of the commencement of the rite.
One should sow [the seeds] in *pālikās*, in shallow bowls (*śarāva*), and in small jars (*ghaṭikā*). Sprouts are auspicious when grown in all three types of vessels.
The height of the *pālikās* and their opening should be one finger-breadth more than a cubit (*hasta*).
The opening should be sixteen finger-breadths in width and seven finger-breadths deep;
the width of the footstool below should be one finger-breadth.
The mouth should be shaped like a madana flower and resemble a lotus.
The length of the water-clocks (ghaṭikās) is proclaimed to be twenty-two finger-breadths.
These ghaṭikās should have five faces, and in their center is the shape of a jar;
their middle opening is six finger-breadths wide.
One should know that there are four [vessels] in the four directions, each measuring four finger-breadths;
their height is twenty finger-breadths and their width twelve finger-breadths.
Alternatively, one may understand the measurement of the shallow bowls (śarāva) according to the available wealth.
All [the vessels] may be made of gold and other metals, or even of clay, according to one's wealth.
There should be thirty-six *pālikās*, thirty-six *ghaṭikās*, and likewise thirty-six *śarāvas*; thus, there are one hundred and eight [in total].
The superior arrangement has been described; now the inferior arrangement is being stated:
sixteen vessels should be taken for each [deity], or even twelve;
or there may be eight, or four, shallow bowls, jars, and small pots.
For all purposes, there should be sixteen or eight *pālikās* according to one's capacity, or four; then, upon them, the auspicious sprouts are arranged.
In rites for humans (*mānuṣa*), an odd number of *pālikās* should be used, but in rites for the gods (*daiva*), they should be even.
The most excellent of teachers should construct a pavilion at the site where the seeds are to be sown, in a place that is auspicious, secluded,
and pleasing; it should have four doors on the four sides and be adorned with four faces.
Encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with strings of pearls,
it was spread with a canopy of fine linen, its floor smeared with cow dung,
and strewn everywhere with rows of lamps and unbroken grains of rice.
Having thus prepared a pavilion whose interior ground is decorated with white lime powder, one should take earth from there,
having washed the spade with water and covered it with a new cloth.
Then, having adorned either Viṣvaksena, or Vainateya, or even [another deity] with flowers, the preceptor should have them carried by the officiating priests;
or a carrier, mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant, a chariot, or a horse, should lead them.
Accompanied by umbrellas, banners, and flags, along with vessels containing sprouts,
and having proclaimed [the festival] on all sides with the three kinds of auspicious musical instruments,
together with devotees, followers of the Lord, ascetics, and sages—
Having gone forth, even while causing the students of the Ṛgveda to recite the Śākuna hymn,
he should go toward the distant eastern or northern direction and,
in a beautiful and pure place, dig up clean earth with a spade.
First, the Guru, having sprinkled the earth with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and touched it while reciting the Mahīsūkta, meditates with one-pointed mind; then,
having worshipped the Varāha-form of the Lord upon the ground with flowers.
Having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra and worshipped it with flowers,
one should face the east and dig into the earth with a spade while reciting the Kroḍa-vidyā.
One should take the soil into either a vessel made of iron or a vessel made of bamboo.
Having taken [the materials] with the root mantra and having wrapped them in a fresh cloth,
one should likewise take sand from a river and cow dung from a cow-pen as before, place them in a vessel, and cover them with fine cloths.
Having personally placed [the image] upon a vehicle, an elephant, or even a horse, the preceptor,
together with the officiating priests who recite the *Śākuna-sūkta*,
the *Śrī-sūkta*, and the *Bhūmi-sūkta*, should also cause musical instruments to sound.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, they should then enter the pavilion;
the preceptor and the guardians of the images should be dressed in new linen garments,
wearing upper cloths, well-adorned, with turbans and finger-rings.
With all their limbs perfumed, wearing garlands and polished earrings,
they had properly applied vertical sectarian marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) with white clay;
with purifying grass in hand, they were bathed and devoted to the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Having performed the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana), having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa), and having recited the mantras according to the rules,
they requested the goal for that purpose together with the patron;
then, having worshipped the Blessed One, the source of the world, according to the prescribed rite.
Having quickly sprinkled the field of the *pālikās* with pure water,
they should straighten the threads moistened with sandalwood paste in due order:
first, clearly twelve straight lines extending toward the east.
Likewise, one should arrange fifteen [vessels] with their tips pointing upward;
twelve each should be placed in the eight directions and in the center— namely, shallow bowls (*śarāva*), jars (*ghaṭa*), and small pots (*pālikā*)— making thus one hundred and eight.
The *pālikās* are placed in the south-eastern, south-western, and southern sectors;
the *ghaṭikās* in the western, central (Brahma), and eastern sectors;
and the *śarāvas* in the north-western, northern, and northeastern sectors, according to the prescribed rule.
One should first lay out nine threads extending from east to west;
there should likewise be twelve others for the bowls, jars, and small pots. Alternatively, one may arrange forty-eight threads.

There are exactly nine of two kinds, namely the thirty-six *pālikās* and so forth. Either there are nine extending eastward or six extending northward; or else there are twenty-four vessels extending eastward.

There are four other sūtras; in the twelve-fold arrangement, there are five in the first section on all purposes, and these two types [of arrangements] are both fivefold. Alternatively, sixteen *pālikās* may be situated around the moon and the water-pot.

Likewise, there may be twelve, eight, or four [pots] for each direction. In all cases, the placement of the Soma-pot is toward the west of the thread-vessels. Depending on one's capacity, the various divisions of the *pālikās* have been demonstrated.
O Four-faced One, having washed the shallow bowls, the water-jars, and the small offering vessels with the Viṣṇugāyatrī mantra,
one should tie *sahadevī*, *dūrvā*, and *aśvattha* sprouts around the necks of the vessels and so forth.
One should fill the openings of their holes with kuśa grass, kāśa grass, and other weeds. First, one should fill the holes with earth, then with sand;
finally, one should completely fill the hole from above with dried cow-dung powder.
Having placed at each foot either *pālikās* and the like, or *śālī* rice or even *vrīhi* rice—
whether an *āḍhaka*, a *prastha*, or half of that— or sesame and rice,
arranged either in a square or otherwise. (24.72)
One should first expand the circular diagram, and then sequentially place the *pālikā* vessels and so forth.
One should place them upon the grains at their respective positions with these mantras in due order;
the water-clocks (*ghaṭikā*) should be placed according to the prescribed location by means of the *pārameṣṭhyā* vidyā.
Immediately thereafter, facing either east or north, one should place the *pālikās* with the mantra called *puruṣa*, and the *śarāvas* with the *viśva-mantra*.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of these should be performed in sequence, starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna.
One should wrap all of them individually with garments while reciting the root mantra (mūlavidyā).
Or, if one has the capacity, one may cover each formation (vyūha) with cloth on top. Finally, in the western position of all, one should place the Soma-jar.
Having first wrapped a heap of grain with a new cloth as before,
one should place jewels into it when it is filled with scented water.
(24.78) Nīvāra rice, śāli rice, mung beans, śyāmāka, and priyaṅgu;
Having placed their seeds— barley, sesame, wheat, and whatever others are considered suitable for sacrifice— into a large, new vessel,
and having set that vessel upon his head to the accompaniment of the sounding of musical instruments, || 24.79–24.80 ||

Having circumambulated the temple, being well-composed, he should place the vessels for the *pālikās* and other items in the eastern region of that which is adorned with half a *droṇa* of *śāli* rice;
then, he should wash the various seeds of grain with milk.
Having covered [the vessels] with a new cloth, one should again perform the *puṇyāha* rite;
having caused the ten directions to resound with the sound of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments,
and having meditated upon the presiding deities of the *pālikās* and the others in their proper sequence.
Having meditated upon and worshipped according to the prescribed rite Ghaṭikānāṃ Vidhātṛ, Pālikānāṃ Janārdana, and Īśāna of the Śarāvas,
the preceptor [should likewise honor] the archways, the banners, and the pitchers at the entrances.
Having duly worshipped the *kumuda* and other groups [of deities],
one should worship the presiding deities (*adhidevas*) of the *pālikā* vessels and so forth in their proper order.
Then, having personally invoked Soma into the Soma-vessel, one should sacrifice to Soma.
Having offered the milk-rice as the sacrificial oblation, the knower of mantras should perform one hundred oblations with clarified butter,
as well as four fuel-sticks, using the root mantra. He should then perform the ritual with the *puruṣasūkta* until the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
One should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Soma mantra.
Having touched the *pālikās* with the remaining clarified butter from the oblation while reciting the Sparśa mantra,
one should pour that remainder of the sacrificial butter into the seed-vessel.
Having recited the Soma-mantra one hundred times with the permission of a Brahmin,
he should sow seeds in the *pālikās* and other vessels during an auspicious moment,
from the direction of Brahmā up to Īśāna, using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Other Vaiṣṇavas, approved by the preceptor, should remain established in meditation. They should silently scatter [the offerings], one should sprinkle with the water contained in the jars,
cover everything with lids, and then offer the bali-oblation in the cardinal directions.
One should offer oblations day and night to the guardians, Kumuda and the others;
one should worship Soma with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in that jar day and night.
One should protect the lamps that have been lit so that they do not go out.
The sacrificer, being diligent, should satisfy the best of the twice-born with desired betel leaves, flowers, and fruits,
and he should also satisfy his preceptor with wealth;
or he may immediately sow seeds of grain according to the prescribed rite.
One should sprinkle the sprouts with water infused with turmeric for their growth;
one should also constantly sprinkle the *pālikā* pots with water from the *soma* jar.
When the sprouts have turned yellow and likewise white, it is auspicious.
One should know that [the result] is auspicious when the shoots have grown straight, and inauspicious when they are the opposite.
(24.97) The teacher who first plants the sprouts for the sake of the ritual—he alone, and no other, even if he be wise, should perform the rite in its entirety. (24.98)
Or, with the permission [of the guru], his son or disciple may perform that rite;
or even the officiating priests (ṛtvij) may perform that ritual if the guru is unable to do so.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pāñcarātra.
The twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Depositing the Sprouts of the Characteristics of the Preceptor";
the twenty-fifth chapter: "The Requisites for Consecration."
The Blessed One said: Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
beginning with the determination of the primary time.
The northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is primary, while the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) is secondary.
The installation of the permanent image (dhruvabera) is desired only during the primary period;
however, the installation of the mobile image (jaṅgama) may take place during either the primary or the secondary period.
One should avoid performing the consecration in the months of Māgha or Bhādrapada; one should also avoid it when Jupiter or Venus has set, during the Vyatīpāta yoga,
on the day of a solar transit (saṅkrānti), on an unfavorable day, or during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
One should avoid [the performance of rites] on the sixteenth day both before and after;
likewise during an *aticāra* [transit], during the month of *māna*, and when joined with a pair of lunar nodes (*parvan*),
as well as during inauspicious conjunctions (*yoga*) and under the asterisms of Kāṇa, Sthūṇa, and Andha.
One should not form such conceptions regarding these and other censurable things,
nor toward the king, the kingdom, another village, or likewise the teacher;
nor toward the patron of the sacrifice, the sacrificial hearth, or anything auspicious and favorable.
On lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays that are auspicious, as well as on favorable moments (muhūrtas):
the first, second, fifth, and thirteenth;
the third, seventh, sixth, twelfth, and likewise the eleventh. (25.7–25.8)
The tenth and the full moon day in the bright fortnight are auspicious;
in the dark fortnight, however, these lunar days are proclaimed to be favorable up to the fifth.
In the three *uttarās*, in Revatī, Aśvinī, and Rohiṇī—
One should perform the installation of the deity Viṣṇu during the asterisms of Puṣya, Punarvasu, Hasta, and likewise Śravaṇa; this brings about prosperity.
Furthermore, [the installation should occur when] the Moon, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury [are favorable].
These are declared to be the auspicious planets for the purpose of installation. Alternatively,
on a Saturday or a Tuesday,
if Mars is situated in the third or sixth house from the ascendant, it portends good fortune for the installation.
In the second and third [houses], as well as in the fifth and sixth;
likewise in the seventh, the ninth, and again in the eleventh house—
there the Moon situated brings happiness, whereas it is not so when situated in the sixth, seventh, or tenth.
The Moon, when aspected by malefic planets, should be known as causing fear for one born under Bhārgava;
O Four-faced One, it is not auspicious during the guest-period or at other times. What need is there for much speaking on this matter with the astrologers? The Guru [Jupiter] [is likewise].
One should perform the installation of the God of gods at the auspicious time;
one should construct the pavilion for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in front of the temple.
One should construct [the pavilion] in the first enclosure, or in the second enclosure,
or even in the third enclosure, in a place that provides a suitable space;
one should fashion the pavilion in a desired location within the eight directions.
One should construct a pavilion ten cubits wide and as many cubits long, with four doors on the four sides. (25.19) [The Construction of the Fire-pit]
In the middle of that, there should be an altar five cubits long and one cubit high, constructed with square bricks;
then, all around it, there are sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
These should be either equal or unequal, at a distance of three tālas from the altar.
One should dig a square pit in the ground measuring twenty-four finger-breadths on each side. Around the excavated ground, which is equal in width and length,
one should fashion three brick girdles (mekhalās) two finger-breadths wide outside of that.
Or else, there may be four girdles below the base of the pit;
the base of the pit is twenty finger-breadths in height,
and its lowermost girdle is sixteen finger-breadths high.
The first [nostril] is equal in height to a palm tree; the middle one is eight finger-breadths high; and the other is raised by half of that. Their width is four finger-breadths.
Among all of them, the first is considered *sāttvikī*, and the middle one is regarded as *rājasī*.
The other [channel] should be known as tāmasī; the one other than that consists of the three guṇas.
At the western end, above the *prakṛti*, the yoni is fifteen finger-breadths long;
starting from its base, it becomes gradually wider.
It should be fashioned beautifully upon the girdle with measurements of ten, six, four, two, and one finger-breadth at the tip;
its arrangement should be like that of a vulva and it should resemble the leaf of a Pippala tree.
Sloping gradually and facing west, it is placed in front of the *kuṇḍa*.
In front of the *yoni*, there should be a stalk (*nāla*) four *aṅgulas* in length;
it is three *aṅgulas* wide at its base and six *aṅgulas* wide at its opening.
One should fashion it in the shape of a horn or place it in the direction of Yama (the south).
If the sacrificial hearth (yoni) should be facing north, the Hotṛ priest himself should face north;
or he may offer the oblation without [regard for] the hearth if he is in haste for liberation.
When measuring the pit (*kuṇḍa*) of two cubits or more, the girdles (*mekhalā*) and other features should be proportionate to that;
or, if the builder is in haste, the pit may have only a single girdle,
where half the pit and half the corner portion are both measured by that same [single girdle].
Starting from the center of the pit toward the southern direction, one should place the thread;
then, having positioned it in front and behind, one should rotate half of the thread.
By this means, the pit is manifested as being like a half-moon.
Whatever remains from half of the pit, and half of that [remainder] again,
as well as two [units of] half-pits— measured by that, a cord should be laid out lengthwise.
Having placed it in the center of that pit, one should fix it in all directions.
The pit should be circular, resembling a lotus in its arrangement.
One should fashion twelve or eight petals in the place of the girdle (mekhalā).
Having divided the pit into five parts, the outer portion should be twice as long [as the others].

Having placed the cord in the middle of the pit, one should then extend it to the ends of the two sides; by means of that, one should fashion a triangle. Having divided the pit into eight parts, one should increase it by one part.
Then, having grasped the center from both sides,
one should mark the six corners; having laid down six lines there, O Lotus-Seated One, the hexagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is formed.
Having divided the previously mentioned field into twenty-four parts,
one should subsequently place one part on the outside in every direction.
Having thus taken [the measurement] from the center and from the corner, one should subsequently mark it in those directions.
Then, through the conjunction of those threads, an eight-cornered figure clearly arises.
By means of the division into five corners, the laying down of the threads is prescribed;
one should lay down a fifteen-finger-breadth thread at each corner.
One should form the inner corners with eighteen finger-breadths;
one should lay down the thread for the eastern direction and drop [the cord] upon the five corners.
One should rotate the middle [cord], measuring ten finger-breadths, along an even line.

One should likewise fashion the *yoni* as ten finger-breadths in length, shaped like a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree. O Lotus-Seated One, the *mekhalā* (girdle) should be exactly the same shape as the *kuṇḍa*; one should fashion the *yoni* in all *kuṇḍas*.
With a *yoni*-shaped pit there shall be a *yoni*, and with a lotus-shaped pit, a lotus.
One should fashion a lotus in the center of the excavation for all the pits.
However, in the place for the petals previously mentioned, one should fashion spokes.
By that [measurement], there should be a wheel-shaped pit (cakrakuṇḍa), and indeed that very same [measurement] should be for a lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa).
Alternatively, O Lotus-born One, one may construct the pits according to the number of finger-breadths;
the bow-shaped pit (cāpakuṇḍa) should be in the eastern direction, and one should fashion the string (jyā) in the west.
A thread measuring twenty-four finger-breadths in both width and length,
when joined to form a square, is prescribed as a perfect square.
The bow should be sixty finger-breadths long, and the bowstring thirty-six finger-breadths.
In this manner, the *cāpakuṇḍa* shall be thirty-two finger-breadths;
furthermore, by means of a triple [measurement], one should clearly form a triangle.
Then, one should rotate a fifteen-finger-breadth cord from the center.

In this manner, the circular pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) is formed; the lotus-shaped pit (padmakuṇḍa) is likewise that very same [circular one], but with a lotus possessing a pericarp and petals. Indeed, the characteristic of the lotus is according to the measurement of the circle.
The procedure for the four sacrificial pits and so forth:
the pit on the ground to the east of the altar should be square;
one should know that the pit to the south is shaped like a half-moon.
In the western region, however, the shape is circular, while in the north it is lotus-shaped;
alternatively, it may be triangular—there one should arrange four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). Between the directions of Indra and Īśāna, there should be a lotus or a square.
In the rite of five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
there should be a lotus-shaped pit in the east and a triangular pit in the southeast;
O Lotus-seated One, this is the method for the arrangement of seven sacrificial pits.
It should be square in the eastern direction; in the direction of Agni, it should have the shape of a vulva (bhaga);
it should be bow-shaped for Yama, and six-cornered for Nirṛti;
it should be circular for Varuṇa, and five-cornered for Mātariśvan.
The triangle belongs to Naravāha; for Īśāna, it is an eight-cornered [octagon];
for the quadrangular pit, it is lotus-shaped in the eastern region.
This arrangement is prescribed for the nine pits in the rites involving the fires of the [nine] regions.
In the directions starting from the east, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be arranged in order among the fires:
square, then bow-shaped, circular, and that which possesses three corners.
This is the rule for the arrangement of four pits; however, the procedure for six pits is now described.
Having performed the four [preliminaries] as before, one should fashion the womb in the fire-quadrant;
there shall be a hexagonal pit in that direction for the half-eye.
In the case of eight pits, however, there are eight pits in the eight directions in due order.
Square, shaped like the female organ (bhaga), bow-shaped, hexagonal, circular,
pentagonal, triangular, and octagonal— these are the [eight] sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) that have been declared; or else, one may arrange three pits each in the cardinal directions.

One should fashion a lotus and a triangle on the two sides of the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) and in the four directions; there should be twelve [triangles] for the procedure of the fire, according to the number of the forms (mūrti). 25.66 The arrangement of the fires corresponds to the number of the forms.
In the consecration of five forms, one should arrange nine fires;
or five or seven fires in the case of four forms. One should arrange eight, six, or four fires for the Jātavedas.
Alternatively, O Lotus-Seated One, one may arrange twelve fires;
the Vītihotras may be in a single form, or otherwise they may be in pairs. [Then follows] the construction of the water-shed.
O Lotus-Seated One, one should prepare either a water-shed (prapā) or a large altar; or else,
one may construct a water-shed consisting of sixteen pillars,
and one should cover the interior of the pavilion all around with a curtain.
One should arrange four gates in the cardinal directions and construct a water-shed (prapā).
One should arrange a bathing pavilion in the northeast direction of that [shed].
And there, on its eastern side, there should be a bathing altar measuring one cubit.
It should be two cubits, or three cubits, or one cubit in height;
or else, it should be one palm in elevation, square, and beautiful. Furthermore, there should be a water-channel in the northern direction, sloping and pleasing to the mind.
For the purpose of the fire oblation (homa), one should prepare the sacrificial ladle (sruk) and the dipping-spoon (sruva), endowed with the proper characteristics;
the ladle may be made of Palāśa wood, Khadira wood, or even from another tree.
The artisan should fashion the sacrificial ladle (juhū) according to the ritual requirements, equal in length to its handle,
made of gold or other metals, or even of wood, and well-adorned;
O Lotus-Seated One, it may also be measured at two tālas plus one finger-breadth.

Having divided that [length] again into three parts, and having made the third part into two, one should further divide the upper portion into five parts by means of four [of those] parts. That shall be the tip of the *sruk* ladle; its base should be six finger-breadths in width.
One should fashion the top [of the head] as one finger-breadth, like the face of a boar;
with the remaining five parts, one should fashion the neck.
The neck is two finger-breadths in width on both its sides.
It should be half a finger-breadth deep, with its width and length equal to that;
one should completely discard the portion situated outside the line-drawing.
Below the neck, the remaining portion may be either circular or square.
In the center of that [altar], one should construct a pit whose length and width are equal,
circular, measuring one-third [of the altar's size], and of beautiful form.
The depth of the pit is declared to be equal to its width.
Having divided the area outside the pit into three parts, one should place the eight-petalled lotus in the first [section].
One should then divide the central portion into four;
in the first [of these], the abode of the lotus (the navel-maṇḍala) is to be fashioned.

With two middle portions, one should fashion a six-spoked wheel or double that; with the remaining portion, the arrangement of the rim (nemi) is made. When arranging the square, conch-shells are placed in the four corners.
The rim should be raised by four barley-corns, and the girdle should be four barley-corns wide.
Starting from the pit up to the edge, there should be a cavity for the clarified butter;
one should fashion the back portion so that it resembles the surface of a lotus.
It should be shaped like the back of a tortoise or square, provided with a pedestal;
its staff is said to be twice as long as that [pedestal].
Having divided that staff into eight parts, one should fashion it from the base portion.
One should fashion the base such that half [of the height] is below the jar and the remaining half above it as a lotus;
thus the stalk is established upon the lotus. Alternatively, even without a supporting base, the stalk is marked with three rings.
Alternatively, it may be circular or have sides equal to half that [diameter], and its tip should also be like a lotus;
it may be provided with three rings, and its handle should be one finger-breadth (aṅgula) in length.
The *sruva* ladle should be one cubit (hasta) in measure, and its tip should be two fingers-breadth in length.
It should be well-rounded like a *vāsikā* leaf-pouch and provided with two depressions.
(25.91) Each depression should be half an *aṅgula* deep and half an *aṅgula* wide; with the remaining one *aṅgula*, the spherical form is fashioned all around. (25.92)
On the back of the two testicles, there should be a central line raised by one barley-corn (*yava*).
On the neck, an odd-numbered ring (*ayugmavalaya*) raised by the measure of one barley-corn is auspicious.
The remainder shall constitute the shaft (*daṇḍa*), which should have the form of a *golāṅgūla* (a long-tailed monkey).
The base [of the ladle] should be two finger-breadths wide, made either of metal or wood.
For the sake of the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles and other implements, one must avoid wood that is cracked, infested with worms, split, dried out at the top, or hollow.
One should set aside a tree that has fallen of its own accord for the purpose of making sacrificial garlands and ladles;
however, if one were to take it up through negligence, a great fault would ensue.
[This applies to] the ornaments of the pavilion, the entrance, and so forth.
At the doors of the pavilion, there should be a set of four arches (toraṇas) made from the Aśvattha,
Udumbara, Vaṭa, and Plakṣa trees, starting from the east;
or, if these are unavailable, one may use a single tree as prescribed, or even a sandalwood tree.
The legs should be seven cubits long, or perhaps five cubits long;
the legs are of uneven lengths, and the fillet is half a cubit.
There are three spikes for each and every archway.
The tridents (śūla) shall be two tālas in height, and their circumference (nāha) shall be eight aṅgulas.
The base of the band (paṭṭikāpādanahana) shall be twenty-two aṅgulas; one should fashion the bases as either circular or square. || 25.99–25.100 ||
One should fashion a water-pot, a right-spiraling conch, a discus, a banner, a drum, a bow, and an elephant upon those [four] feet;
and one should likewise cause the eight auspicious symbols to be made upon the panels in their proper order.
Alternatively, [the seats] may be made of iron or from sacrificial wood according to one's wealth.
Each seat is twenty-two finger-breadths in length, half of that (eleven) in width,
and two finger-breadths thick, and is firmly established upon its respective pedestal.
There, upon the panels, one should draw the eight [emblems] beginning with the Śrīvatsa, each measuring eight finger-breadths:
the Śrīvatsa, the full pitcher, the kettledrum, the orb of the mirror,
the pair of fish, the conch, the discus, and the son of Kaśyapa (the tortoise).
Seated in the lotus posture, gentle, and twelve finger-breadths in length;
with the two sides expanded in accordance with that particular form,
one should imagine a lamp, a fly-whisk, and a parasol above his head.
One should construct a bathing pedestal made of udumbara wood in proportion to the size of the image,
as well as a pedestal for liberation through sight, and likewise a pedestal for the Lord of Waters and the Wind-god,
fashioning them according to the dimensions of the image without hesitation.
One should likewise prepare a seat for the officiating priests and for the preceptor.
One should fashion two sandals resembling feet from the sacrificial wood.
Likewise, one should prepare the secondary jar, the water-pot, the ritual vessel, and the large water-jar.
Lamp-stands, clarified butter and other such items, bathing materials in their entirety, sandalwood, fragrant substances, various garments,
sacrificial fuel, flowers, *kuśa* grass and the like, and various kinds of grain.
Having thus gathered gold, jewels, metals, and beautiful cows with their calves,
as well as other necessary materials, the best of preceptors, with an undistracted mind, should undertake the consecration according to the scriptures.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Requisites for Installation," in the Kriyāpāda of the Śrīpādmasaṃhitā, which is part of the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the twenty-sixth chapter.
Regarding the ritual for consecration:
what kind of consecration is considered appropriate for the all-pervading God of gods?
"O Blessed One, speak with certainty to me who am full of doubt. The Blessed Lord said: "Hari, though abiding as the Self of every class of beings,"
Through the potency of the mantra and likewise through the greatness of the establishing preceptor,
Hari himself dwells with excellence within the image. Therein, people petition Hari for all their desires without exception.
Therefore, this foundation exists on earth not in vain;
for just as fire, though it is burning, does not remain by pervading that which is burned,
so too is it seen to be born again from the friction of the fire-drills.
And he performs actions such as burning exactly as they are;
likewise, Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent and invisible to ordinary people,
is seen in an image through the power of the mantras of the officiating priests.

Therefore, having installed Viṣṇu with one's whole being, one should worship him in an image fashioned by artisans according to the path prescribed in the scriptures. This applies when the ritual image is placed upon a pedestal and set within a bed of gems and other precious materials.

And when the eyes have been opened, the most excellent of teachers, at the conclusion of the work, should examine everywhere all the limbs of the image— both gross and subtle— as well as all the well-executed features according to the treatises and as is appropriate for the pacification of all [obstacles].
The wise chariot-maker, having carefully examined [the materials],
and having satisfied the master craftsmen with wealth according to their merit,
[honored] the chariot-maker as well with various things that increase the joy of the mind.
When the artisans and the chariot-maker had thus departed,
and after the interior and exterior of the dwelling had been cleansed by sweeping and other means,
and the ritual of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) had been performed using kindled bundles of *darbha* grass; || 26.11–26.12 ||
When the enclosure wall, the pavilion, the temple, and the gateway have been purified by sweeping and other means,
and likewise sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then cause the Brahmins who are most skilled in the mantras to pronounce the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha).
Furthermore,
the preceptor, together with all the brāhmaṇas, should sprinkle everything both inside and outside the inner sanctum with *ṛc* verses that do not contain the word "water" (*abliṅga*),
and likewise with many lamps brightly lit with cow's ghee.
When the abode had been illuminated on all sides by incense such as black aloe-wood,
and perfumed with fragrant substances, with powdered lime and unbroken grains of rice,
and when the entire dwelling was further adorned with flowers and sprouts of dūrvā grass; || 26.16 ||

Then, in the afternoon, one should perform the *śānti-homa* (peace-offering). Whether there is a decrease or an increase in honor, measure, size, and so forth—all that which is difficult to discern is certainly pacified by the *homa*. (26.17–26.18)
The preceptor himself should offer one hundred oblations for each of the unhusked grains mixed with *śamī* sprouts, using the seven *vyāhṛtis*.
Likewise, he should offer sixteen oblations of the *caru* with the *Nṛsūkta*.
One should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the *pañcopaniṣad* mantra. Having thus performed the homa in the presence of the image, concluding with the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
the preceptor should thereafter perform the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) with this mantra.
Salutations to you, the Blessed One, Jātavedas, who possesses your own true form; to Nārāyaṇa, the rightful recipient of both oblations to the gods and oblations to the ancestors;
to the destroyer of the deities who are to be sacrificed to, the Self, the Supreme Self.
"O Lord, remain for a long time within this image for our welfare.
Having thus petitioned the god Adhokṣaja with palms joined and body bowed,
he [placed] the image upon a new cloth together with *darbha* grass, using the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
The preceptor should likewise provide an upper garment and offer it; as well as the water for honoring (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana), perfume, incense,
a lamp, and flowers— all with the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by [the name of] Viṣṇu.
One should offer everything to Śrī, Ādidevī, and the others with their respective vidyās;
likewise for the retinues beginning with Brahmā and other deities, each with their own vidyā.
One should bind the protective thread (kautuka) on the right hand with the root-vidyā.
In the same manner, having performed the consecration seven times with the Vidyā,
one should worship the God by binding [the image] with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā.
Then, for the purpose of accomplishing the preliminary dwelling of the shadow (chāyādhivāsa) before the God—
One should place a water trough or a cauldron made of iron,
or a vessel made of clay, whichever is available, for the collection of grain;
one should fill it with fragrant water that has the luster of pure crystal.
One should cast the *kūrca* consisting of twenty-eight *darbha* blades into the water,
worship Hari upon that *kūrca*, and meditate [upon him] with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Having recalled the sequence of reabsorption (*saṃhārakrama*), the preceptor himself [should cast] the *kūrca* into the water.
Having laid them down with their heads toward the east, one should display the *cakramudrā*.
For Śrīdhara and Rudra-Vedhas, the *kūrca* should be made with three *darbha* blades;
for the other drinkers of nectar (*amṛtāśinaḥ*), it should be made with twenty-five.
And one should place the protection-pitcher right there in the direction of Yama;
having wrapped it with two new cloths, as well as the water-jar with one.
One should worship Brahmā in the pitcher and Sudarśana in the water-jar.
One should place eight jars all around, wrapped in cloth;
they should have lids, be accompanied by cloths, contain gems, and be provided with *kūrca* grass-bunches.
One should worship the eight lords of the directions, beginning with Indra, within those eight [jars].
Then, having covered the image on all sides with a new cloth that wraps the entire body,
one should scatter white mustard seeds upon the ground while reciting the mantra "rakṣohaṇa" (O slayer of demons) to provide protection on every side.
He should set up many radiant lamps that shall not go out;
he should cause the sound of the Triple Veda to resound through Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
and having placed the mantra of the wheel in the settlement, the Guru should worship it.

One should exit from the sanctuary by way of circumambulation together with the image-keepers (mūrtipas). O Lotus-seated One, for that image for which the actual preparatory rite (*adhivāsa*) does not take place in water, this shadow-preparatory rite (*chāyādhivāsa*) has been prescribed.

The images made of wood, metal, or stone are of various kinds; for these, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in water is performed in this very manner. However, for images made of cast metal, it is performed prior to the water-consecration.
Having fashioned a cluster of lotuses, one should perform the consecration.
Having placed a circular mound of rice upon it, one should put rice grains on top;
half of that amount above, and half of that rice, one should scatter sesame seeds.
Having fashioned a lotus design upon sesame seeds and having spread kuśa grass over them,
one should place a new cloth with its fringes pointing eastward on top of them;
or else, having placed a pedestal there, whether it bears a lotus or is plain.
Having placed the gems and metals with the *gāyatrī* preceded by [the hymn to] Viṣṇu,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire one hundred and eight times.
One should also offer the *caru* oblation with the *Nṛsūkta* and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.
One should place the deity upon that pedestal and utter the mantra.
With the thought, "Supratiṣṭha," the preceptor should meditate mentally on the Teacher of the World;
immediately thereafter, he should recite the Sāman chant: "Pratiṣṭhito 'si" (Thou art established). || 26.47–26.48 ||
O Lotus-seated One, one should have the binding made firm by a master builder and open the eyes of the image according to the prescribed ritual.
Furthermore, one should satisfy the chariot-makers and others with great wealth.
Having performed a fire-oblation with *śamī* leaves and unbroken rice grains, and having anointed her with clarified butter using the mantra "ghṛtasnātā," one should rub her all over with powders,
wash her with warm water, and [wipe her] with *kuśa* grass and a new cloth.
One should wrap the image as before in the proper sequence;
the offering of the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the upper garment (*uttarīya*), and so forth, should be performed as previously.
Having sipped water (*ācamya*) and bound on the auspicious protective cord (*pratisara*), [one should proceed].
Then, having placed [the image] upon a chariot or other vehicle, the image-keepers (mūrtipās),
together with those skilled in Sāman chanting and other Brahmins,
should recite the excellent Rathantara and other such hymns, as well as the supreme Puruṣasūkta.
They should recite the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka and the Śākuna-sūkta in each direction, as well as the Rakṣoghna-sūkta;
[they should do so] with a white parasol and a white fly-whisk.
With parasols made of Chinese silk, with banners likewise made of peacock feathers,
with auspicious fans and various kinds of flags,
and with many sorts of musical instruments, dances, and songs on every side.
Accompanied by a great multitude of brahmins gathered from here and there, and having honored [the deity] with various royal services according to the prescribed rites,
one should lead the image around the village, the temple, and other sites in a clockwise direction.
The ritual procedure for the consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*):
Having reached the location for the water-consecration, one should lower [the image] from the palanquin or other vehicle onto a water-shed (*prapā*) or a lion-throne (*siṃhaviṣṭara*) near the water.
Having established [the image] facing east, or alternatively having established it facing north,
one should perform the ritual immersion in water in rivers, in oblong ponds, in lakes, or even in mountain springs,
or in clear water as well.
In a place with little water, at the edge of a cremation ground, or one defiled by salt water;
or in that which is astringent, pungent, or bitter, and defiled by froth;
or near a sacred tree (caitya-vṛkṣa), or likewise in a low-lying area frequented by others.
In saline soil, in soil covered with moss, or likewise in soil of a different color—
in such defective places as these, one should not perform the consecration of an image.
One should construct a water-shed in the middle of the water, provided with many pillars.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
furnished with canopies and banners, decorated with garlands of *darbha* grass,
endowed with strings of pearls, wreathed in flowers, and illuminated by lamps.

One should perform the ritual residence there with various kinds of fruits. First, after the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), the self-possessed preceptor, standing again by rivers and other waters, should dry the waters with the *puruṣasūkta* mantra.
Having burned [the obstruction] with the fire-mantra, which possesses a radiance equal to ten million moons,
one should meditate upon that *nivṛtti*-mantra. Then, by means of the waters emerging from that meditation— waters resembling nectar— one should once again fill the river and other such places.
In that water, having placed a new, auspicious, square, and spacious great seat (mahāpīṭha) provided with a covering and a pillow,
one should prepare the yoga-seat (yogapīṭha) upon it in the proper sequence.
Having worshipped the pedestal with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, being composed in mind,
one should thereafter worship the door, the archway, the water-pot, and so forth,
while the Brahmins together with the guardians of the images recite the Śākuna hymn.
Having taken the image from the edge of the shore,
the preceptor should then, recollecting the sequence of reabsorption, cause it to enter the water;
he should then lay the image down facing north with its head toward the east.
One should likewise immerse in the water the jars and other vessels, which have been wrapped in new cloth from the soles of the feet to the head, worshipped,
and placed on the bank in the same manner as before, following the proper sequence.
One should display the wheel-mudrā and display the protection-mudrā.
On the bank, one should cause the four kinds of musical instruments to be played, as prescribed by all authorities;
and the Brahmins should recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the Purāṇas.
They should invite [the deities] while they are not yet extinguished; one should even cause lamps to be lit.
From that time forward, one should not perform any acts such as bathing or drinking.
One should let them remain in the midst of water for one night or three nights.
One should practice dwelling in water for either a watch (yāma) or even half a watch;
one should perform this immediately at the time of installing the domestic image,
as well as during the preliminary consecration in water and the opening of the eyes.

O Lotus-seated One, the time for the consecration is not on a bed or a pedestal; the preliminary ritual (adhivāsa) should take place at dusk, and the laying down [of the image] at midnight. One should perform the final installation (pratiṣṭhā) during the day, at a moment prescribed by the scriptures.
In the absence of a river or similar body of water, the consecration of the image in water should take place.
Having drawn out a large quantity of water into a wooden trough or a cauldron,
it is performed as appropriate in another vessel made of clay or other materials.
"Or there may be an immediate immersion in water prior to the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Preliminary Consecration in Water," in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Śrīpādmasaṃhitā*, within the *Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad*.
The twenty-seventh chapter: The remainder of the ritual for consecration; the Blessed One.
Having thus consecrated the image according to the previously described method in the water,
on the following day when the night has turned to dawn, the chariot-maker shall have cleaned and properly adorned the pavilion and other structures.
When the chariot-maker had been gratified with wealth that gladdened the mind,
the preceptor and the guardians of the images, having accomplished their purpose and mastered their senses,
all donned new garments and wore the fivefold ornaments.
Bearing perfumes and garlands, auspicious, and clothed in upper garments and coverings;
adorned with the application of vertical *puṇḍra* marks, wearing turbans and polished earrings;
they were commanded by the patron with wealth consisting of both animate and inanimate property. || 27.4 ||
They should perform the determination of the Vāstupuruṣa and the Vāstu-homa so that the rite may become divine.
O Four-faced One, the one named Vāstu was born from the sweat of Bhārgava.
Proud of his own strength, he rushed forward to slay the gods. Though quickly struck by the gods on that ground and rendered overwhelmed,
Vāstuka remained with his limbs relaxed, yet he continued to hold onto his life-breaths.
One should place the Vāstupuruṣa with his face downward and his head toward the east,
having stretched out both his hands and feet which are positioned at the corners of the ground;
one should worship him with diligence so that the rite may become divine.
If the deity of the site (Vāstudeva) is not worshipped, the performed rite will become demonic.
One should draw the deity of the site on the ground on the right side of the pavilion;
having prepared a bundle of seven blades of darbha grass, one should place it there.
There, one should worship the Lord of the Site (Vāstunātha) in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should worship Aṃśumālin on the head of the deity of the site;
Jhaṣadhvaja at the base of the arm, and likewise Kumāra at the elbow.
One should place Vināyaka on the hand, the two Aśvin deities on the pair of feet,
Candra in the middle, Durgā on the two heels, the Mothers on the elbows,
Sthāṇu at the base of the arms, and me stationed in the heart.
One should worship the Brahman at the navel region and the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in their respective directions;
one should worship the Lord of the Field (kṣetreśa) on the northern side of the deity of the site (vāstudeva).
To the west, in the region of the Lord of the Site, the preceptor (guru) should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

Then, with clarified butter prepared from the five upaniṣads, the self-possessed practitioner should offer oblations either a thousand or a hundred times with fuel-sticks of śamī, apāmārga, and khadira wood,
using the root mantra repeated as many times as there are syllables in that mantra.
One should offer sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Puruṣasūkta;

one should also offer the porridge to the deities of the site (vāstudeva) once for each. Having likewise given an offering (bali) to the gods and to the lord of the field (kṣetrādhipati), [one should proceed].
O Lotus-seated One, the procedure for the Vāstu sacrifice has been declared for all occasions—at the commencement of a work, at its foundation, in the pavilion, and likewise in the dwelling.
In the pavilion, there should be sweeping, smearing with cow dung, and sprinkling. || 27.18–27.19 ||
Having adorned the surface of the ground with lime powder and unbroken grains of rice,
one should scatter white mustard seeds consecrated with the Astra-mantra in all directions.
People who are unworthy of the divine presence [should be excluded].
Those who are nihilists, those who have broken the bounds of propriety, those who revile the gods and Brahmins,
mortals afflicted with sinful diseases, the censured, as well as the slanderers;
those who are heretics, of base conduct, born in the inverse order of castes, and full of envy.
He should then banish from there those who are greedy, foolish, and ignorant.
He should wrap the pillars in that pavilion with new cloths,
spread out beautiful canopies, and adorn it with banners.

One should adorn the entire pavilion with strings of pearls, and with other fruits, flowers, and sprouts, as well as with ornaments of jewels and gold placed around the base of the sacrificial grass, according to one's means.
Having dug a pit two *tāla*s deep, one should install archways at the four directions— at the locations of the gates in the east and so forth— in due order:
an *aśvattha* archway in the east, and immediately after that, one made of *udumbara* wood.
To the west was the Nyagrodha tree, and immediately after that the Plakṣa;
[there were] dancers and singers, as well as lute-players and flute-players,
along with others skilled in instrumental music and likewise experts in the art of playing.
It was adorned on all sides and resounded everywhere with the chanting of the Vedas;
likewise, it was filled on every side with lamps and oil-lamps accompanied by sprouts,
and made fragrant with the incense of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Having thus properly constructed the pavilion, in the afternoon the Guru himself should raise the image from the water, as well as the primary jar and the other vessels; then,
having dismissed the deities from that [water], he should place that image upon a seat on the bank.
Having placed it facing the east, one should likewise wash it with water;
if it is made of metal, for the sake of purification, with the juice of *tintriṇī* fruit.
Then, having adorned it with beautiful garments, ornaments, flowers, and so forth, || 27.31–27.32 ||

Having placed that image upon a vehicle and having performed all the previous rites in their entirety, one should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion accompanied by auspicious musical instruments and the like;
one should then seat it upon a cushioned seat in the northern part of the pavilion.
The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should enter the inner sanctum.
If there is an extensive arrangement of many deities, this procedure is prescribed:
one should first remove the sacrificial grass (kūrca) that was previously consecrated from within that cavity.
The preceptor should remove the garments, ornaments, and garlands from the image;
then, having performed the opening of the eyes according to the scriptures,
he should show the eight kinds of grains, cows, and auspicious maidens to the permanent image (dhruvabera).

In this manner, according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, the teacher should perform the "unfolding" (unmīlana) of Śrī and the other goddesses with seventeen jars containing substances such as clay; he should then arrange the "shadow-bath" (chāyā-snāna) using a mirror together with a tuft of grass (kūrca).
The bathing of the goddesses, Śrī and the others, shall be performed separately with nine jars;
that of Brahmā and Īśa with seven jars; that of the Ṛṣis with five;
and that of the deities with three, or even with a single jar.
One should worship [the deity] with services such as garments, concluding with the lustration ceremony (nīrājanā).
Having placed upon the heart of the permanent image (dhruvabera) a light possessing the brilliance of a jewel,
the preceptor should apply the twelve-syllable mantra.
One should cover the image on all sides with cloths or blankets;
having done so for Śrī and the others, one should then depart from the temple and cover the effigy situated in the pavilion with blankets and other such materials.
Having placed a vessel made of either gold or silver, filled with one āḍhaka of grain,
in front of a heap of grain, one should fill it in due order;
one should then fill it with honey and clarified butter and cover it.
Furthermore, with a completely pure cloth and those two bowls,
one should worship the Sun in the east and likewise the Moon in the west;
with the mantra "madhu vātā," one should consecrate the clarified butter and other offerings.
The probe should be eight finger-breadths long and made of gold or silver.
One should place eight kinds of grain around the vessels,
as well as beautiful cows and maidens adorned with ornaments.
Having brought it, one should place it at the side and cause it to be proclaimed with the sounds of the Veda.
With a golden probe, its tip smeared with honey, one should scrape open the right eye;
the left eye with a probe smeared with clarified butter.
While reciting "That eye," the king’s wife should scratch his eye; then,
having removed the covering cloth, he should show him honey and clarified butter,
the eight kinds of grain, cows, and maidens standing before him.
One should present cows to the preceptor, saying, "May Govinda be pleased.
Likewise, one should give a pair of vessels, two sticks, and eight types of grain.
At the time of the opening of the eyes, one should cause it to be proclaimed with the sound of musical instruments.
One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor, consisting of wealth both animate and inanimate.
(27.52) One should bind the protective amulet (*kautuka*) upon the image according to the ritual procedure for the purpose of bathing;
