then, having raised that image with the root mantra, one should lead it forth. (27.53)
While the officiating priests and the Brahmins recite the Śakuna-sūkta,
he should place [the image] facing west upon a seat made of udumbara wood, situated on the ground within the bathing pavilion and covered with a linen cloth.
The preceptor, himself a knower of mantras, having personally recited the Bhadrādi-mantra and other such incantations,
stands facing north with nineteen portions of earth obtained from sacred sites and other auspicious places; he then anoints the image with that earth.
The preceptor, the guardian of the image, should recite this verse, "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," while using auspicious waters;
having recited "imaṃ me varuṇa," he should wash away all the ceremonial bonds and bathe [the deity] with the ritual jars.
Having placed [the image] before the deity, wrapped in thread and cloth,
one should set down water-pots filled with sprouts and accompanied by sacred grass (kūrca) upon heaps of grain;
then, reciting "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should perform the foot-washing and the ceremonial sprinkling.

The sprinkling with the *arghya* water is performed with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and likewise with the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the mantra "imaṃ me varuṇa. The sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is performed with the mantra "pavitraṃ te. (27.60)
One should perform the consecration with ghee while reciting the *sāman* "ghṛtasnāta";
one should perform the bathing with curd using the mantra "dadhi krāvṇa";
and the bathing with milk should be performed with the *sāman* known as *payovrata*.
The Guru should bathe [the disciple] with honey using the mantra "madhu vātā";
he should perform an ablution with decoction-water using the mantra "yajñā yajñā";
and an ablution with warm water using the verse "mā nas toke."
One should bathe [the deity] with water from a gem using the mantra beginning with "vaṣaṭ te viṣṇave";
with fruit-water using the *anuvāka* beginning with "phalinī";
and one should bathe [the deity] with metal-water using the "hiraṇyagarbha" mantra.
The bathing [of the deity] is performed with consecrated sprinkling waters using the mantra "śanno devīḥ";
then, with the mantra "gandhadvāram," one uses a pitcher of scented water;
and with the Sāman hymn "trātāram," one uses water mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata).
With a jar of barley-water, he should perform the rite using the three verses beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
and with the *Nṛsūkta*, he should consecrate [the image] at the end with pure waters.
He should also worship it with ritual services, such as the offering of garments and other articles.
One should prepare the bed upon the altar in the eastern or southern part;
first, one should sprinkle the altar with water using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Then, having spread out abundant darbha grass with its tips pointing either eastward or northward.
One should place five bhāras of śāli rice, equal in measure to a horse, upon them;
one should then scatter sesamum seeds over those. Having scattered either half as much again, or four-cornered, or circular [cakes], over them...
One should place a tiger skin upon the sesame seeds;
one should place a mattress adorned with a soft covering upon that.
And above the blankets, one should spread a linen cloth.
Likewise, colorful and white cloths [should be spread] upon it;
then, a very firm and smooth wooden platform, four cubits in length,
provided with four legs and rectangular in shape, [should be placed there].
Then, one should place a couch designated as a *khaṭvā* above that;
upon it, one should spread fine silk and a soft mattress, along with its various furnishings.
One should arrange colorful pillows and all the necessary components for the bed.
Having prepared a bed perfumed with fragrant scents such as musk,
covered with a spread of fragrant flowers, and adorned with various ornaments,
one should bring the deity and have him lie down upon it.
Accompanied by excellent and praiseworthy hymns such as the *Puruṣasūkta*, recited according to the rules by eminent Brahmins and other auspicious persons,
and with the sounds of musical instruments as before, the image-keepers and the Guru himself [proceeded].
Having raised the *kautuka* with the mantra beginning with "uttiṣṭha," they led it to the ground of the bed-altar outside the sacrificial pit in the prescribed manner;
then the Guru should slowly lay it upon the bed while performing a circumambulation from left to right.
Having recited "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and also "viśvataś cakṣuḥ," one should first [orient] the head toward the east, the face toward the south, or else toward the front of the temple;
or the head may be toward the southern direction— in this manner, the arrangement for the reclining is performed.
One should also cover the image with a woolen blanket or with garments,
reciting the hymn beginning with "The youth, well-clothed," O Four-faced One, on all sides.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the Aśvattha-arch in the east.

To the south, there should be an udumbara tree made of Yajurvedic wood, dedicated to Yama, having the form of an *ṛc* verse, dedicated to Indra, and named Suśobhana. To the west, there should be a nyagrodha tree dedicated to Soma and Varuṇa, belonging to the Sāmaveda, and named Subhadra.
The preceptor should worship the Plakṣa tree named Subandha in the north, known by the name Suhotraka;
it is designated as having Soma as its deity and belongs to the Atharvaveda.
Furthermore, he should worship the two banners situated at the sides of the door, which are called Ratna.
O Lotus-seated One, one should worship the illustrious gatekeepers;
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa are remembered as the two door-keepers in the east.
In the south are the two yellow banners, Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Vāmana.
Furthermore, one should meditate on the two gatekeepers at the western gate, who have the luster of sapphire and hold banners;
Śaṅkukarṇa and Sarvanetra likewise stand there with pale-white banners.
One should meditate on Sumukha and Supratiṣṭha as the two gatekeepers holding their banner-cloths.
One should place eight jars at the gates starting from the east—
two at each— with clothes, *aśvattha* sprouts, and lids;
and one should personally [place them] upon heaps of grain with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
Their names are told in sequence; listen to them:
Pūrṇa and Puṣkara shall be Ānanda and Nandana;
likewise Vīrasena, Suṣeṇa, Sambhava, and Prabhava.
One should place eight gems, respectively, into the jars:
ruby, coral, diamond, and lapis lazuli;
likewise topaz, sapphire, and emerald.
One should place all the pearls and crystals with the mantra.
One should worship separately the previously mentioned arches, banners, jars, and so forth;
and one should cover each of the arches individually with new cloths.
In the lotus petals starting from the east, O Brahmins, one should station those who are masters of the Ṛgveda,
the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda, as well as others who are experts in the Atharvāṅgirasa and have reached the further shore of the Vedas;
one should place those studying their respective Vedas in their corresponding directions.

The preceptor, being well-composed, should meditate upon the Lord Acyuta within his heart; and with the sounds of musical instruments such as the tūrya, he should cause it to be proclaimed everywhere. He should likewise place the image-pots, complete with lids and cloths, all around.
In the eight directions beginning with the east, [he placed] heaps of grain filled with pure water, containing *aśvattha* leaves and precious gems.
Within them were a conch, a wheel, a mace, a lotus, and likewise a banner.
One should place the Śrīvatsa, Garuḍa, and the tortoise made of gold [in the center].
Then, in the middle of the jars, one should place the eight auspicious symbols beginning with the Śrīvatsa;
thereafter, one should arrange the *pālikās* containing sprouts all around the altar.
One should invoke and worship the eight forms, beginning with Viṣṇu, in the jars;
then, one should place [the deity] of the great jar into a heap of grain in the north-western direction,
using a covered *droṇa* measure filled with scented water.
Furthermore, gold, gems, and so forth, covered with a pair of garments, should be placed there;
and beside it, one should set down a water-pot (galantikā) provided with a brush and pippala leaves, covered with thread and cloth, and equipped with a brush.

One should feed twelve or more Brahmins— who are embodiments of the Lord— with milk-rice (pāyasa) and with the sacred texts beginning with the Nigamas, using auspicious water contained in vessels provided with lids. (27.105)
The sacrificer, with a concentrated mind, should give sesame seeds, fine garments, gold, and cows as sacrificial fees to those who have finished eating; thereafter,
by the permission of the preceptor, the officiating priests should begin the fire-oblation.
One should fetch a fire-drill from an *aśvattha* tree that has grown from within a *śamī* tree;
then, having produced fire by friction, or having taken fire from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*),
or having taken common worldly fire, one should [proceed] with the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Having sprinkled [water] and meditated upon the divine fire, one should kindle it in the western pit (pratyak-kuṇḍa).
One should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) around the pits using handfuls of *darbha* grass.
From the other pits, one should transfer the burning fire to the western pit.
Having prepared the fire in front and having moved it to another pit,
one should meditate upon that respective deity seated upon a lotus in the midst of the fire:
Vāsudeva in the square [pit] and likewise Saṅkarṣaṇa in the bow-shaped [pit].

In a square [pit], one named Pradyumna; in a triangle, Aniruddha. When more than these [shapes] are conceived as sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa), whether in pairs or singly, the deities are to be worshipped exactly as previously described.
In the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east and proceeding in order, fuel-sticks (samidh) are prescribed for the trees *pālāśa*, *dūrvā*, *khadira*, *bilva*, and *audumbara*.
In the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (*āgneyī*), those originating from the *pippala* and *plakṣa* trees should be used.
Those originating from the *nyagrodha* tree as well as those from the *kāśmarya* tree [are used];
otherwise, *pālāśa* fuel-sticks are prescribed for the majority of preparations.
However, in the absence of what has been mentioned, *pālāśa* fuel-sticks are considered appropriate in all cases.
Four cows should be stationed at the southern gate, facing north—
Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Godā, and Yamunā in embodied form.
With their milk, one should perform the cooking of the sacrificial porridges (caru) as well as the oblations (āhuti).
First, one should cook an āḍhaka measure of śāli rice with milk in the southern fire using kṛsara; afterwards, [one should cook] that mixed with jaggery in the northern fire,
turmeric-rice in the eastern fire, and milk-rice in the other fires.
The fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed in sequence with fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), sacrificial porridge (caru), and seeds (bīja).
For each of these—beginning with the fuel-sticks—the oblation should consist of one hundred and eight offerings.
The seeds for the oblations, in their proper order, are sesame, rice, barley, and bamboo.
O Lotus-born One, sesame seeds should be used in the other sacrificial pits, or they may be used everywhere.
And the officiating priests, seated with their upper garments on and well-adorned,
should all offer oblations facing eastward according to the path instructed by the Guru.

While those officiating priests are offering oblations, the self-possessed preceptor should worship the supreme light, the dense and imperishable Hari, who is all-pervading; having invoked the infallible Lord with the root mantra into the great pitcher.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should worship with arghya and other offerings according to the Nigama and other scriptures.
And one should [visualize] the Sudarśana [discus] in the water-pot (karaka), resembling a thousand suns,
possessing a thousand spokes, and enveloped by a thousand flames.

Having invoked [the deity] with his own mantra, O Lotus-seated One, one should worship the image while it lies recumbent, having assumed the svastika posture. The preceptor, who is most skilled in the sequence of emanation and reabsorption, should sit there.
Having resorted to the process of withdrawal, he should dissolve that image composed of the elements;
then, established in its meditation, he should create it again by the very process of emanation.
He should offer oblations of clarified butter mixed with *kapittha* fruit into the eastern sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the sake of the principles (*tattvas*).
For each of the principles (tattvas), one hundred and eight oblations are prescribed;
or twenty-eight, or even eight, depending on one's capacity.
The homa of the principles, beginning with the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, is performed with their own names ending in "svāhā."
First, one should place the letter *ma*, which has the luster of crystal, representing the pervasive life-force (*jīva*).

Then, at the end of the oblation, one should project the *praṇava* (oṃ) onto the image. Thereafter, one should project the white letter *bha*, which is the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the life-force, as before.
One should place the syllable *ba*, which has the luster of crystal and represents the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), immediately [thereafter];

and the syllable *pha*, representing the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) with a pale-red hue, one should place in the heart. Likewise, the syllable *pa*, resembling white and black, representing the mind (*manas*), one should place in the heart.

The letter *na* is the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), appearing white, located in the ear; likewise, the letter *dha* is the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*), red, located in the skin; and the letter *ta* is the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*), black, located in the nose.

One should place the syllable *ṇa*, resembling the color of a pale red lotus, as the essence of the ears in the two ears; the syllable *ḍha*, with a luster like gold, as the essence of the skin upon the skin;
and immediately thereafter, the syllable *ḍa*, black in color, as the essence of the eyes in the two eyes.
O four-faced one, one should place the yellow letter *ṭha* on the tongue as the self of the tongue;
likewise, the black letter *ṭa* in the form of the nose as the olfactory faculty;
and the white letter *ñ* in the form of speech, one should establish in the support of speech.
One should place the red syllable *jhakāra* on the two hands as the self of action (*karmātmāna*);
one should place the red syllable *jakāra* on the two feet as the self of the feet (*padātmāna*).
And the placement of the red syllable *chakāra* is for the anus as its own self (*tadātmana*).
One should place the letter *ca*, gold-colored and having a deluding form, upon the organ of generation.
One should place the letter *ṅa*, representing the earth-element (*pṛthivī-tattva*), yellow in luster and square in shape,
at the end of the oblation, extending from the foot to the knee.
One should place the syllable *gha*, which is like the half-moon, identical in form to water,
and resembling crystal, at the end of the secret [place] above that. Then one should place the syllable *ga*, which is red, triangular, and like fire.
The supreme teacher should perform the ritual placement from the secret place up to the navel.
He should place the syllable *kha*, which has the form of an altar, is smoke-colored, and consists of the nature of wind;
having offered oblations, he should settle it above the navel and ending at the nose.
One should place the formless letter *ka*, which consists of the sky, food, and stone,

from the tip of the nose to the end of the head at the conclusion of the oblation; having thus performed the fire-offering of the principles (*tattva-homa*) and their ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should proceed immediately thereafter.
There should be the placement (nyāsa) of the ten vital winds, beginning with prāṇa, within the channels beginning with iḍā.

O Four-faced One, the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) should be performed according to the prescribed method upon the goddesses, such as Kamalā, who form the retinue of Brahmā and the others.

One should install the weapons, such as the Sudarśana discus, as well as the forest garland (vanamālā) and other ornaments, upon the various objects of worship belonging to the Wielder of the Śārṅga bow, using their respective mantras.
However, one should not perform the sixteen-fold installation (ṣoḍaśanyāsa) upon mobile images.
Of the Praṇava, the Vyāhṛtis, and the letters beginning with 'A';
of the constellations, time, and the solstices such as the northern course;
of the social classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, and of the Veda and its branches. || 27.149–27.150 ||
One should perform the placement of the deities, Virāj, the seasons, the qualities, the [three] constituents beginning with sattva, the forms, the powers, the six attributes,
and the sixteen worlds, in their proper sequence.
Having become composed of the letter *a* and the others, one should then [place] the *praṇava*.
One should place the letter *a*, which is the form of Viṣṇu, in the heart;
the letter *u*, which is the form of Brahmā, in the right part; and the final [letter], which is the nature of Śaṅkara, on the left.

Having gratified [the deities] with the oblation at the end, one should place the *praṇava* [at the top]. Then, the Guru should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the feet, the heart, and the head of the three *vyāhṛtis*, and should sequentially place the vowels beginning with *a*.

One should unweariedly perform the placement (nyāsa) of the letters beginning with *ya* upon the tongue, the mouth, the two eyes, the two ears, the nostrils, the row of teeth, the two lips, the face, and the palate. (27.155–156)
Having offered libations on the skin, the eyes, the nose, the tips of the teeth, as well as the ears,
the belly, the hips, the heart, and the region of the navel,
and finally on the organ of generation, the ritual placement (nyāsa) is prescribed by means of the oblation.

One should perform the placement five times on the fingers, the two shanks, and the two arms, beginning with the letter *ka*; such is the deposition of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*). [The channels are] Suṣumnā, Piṅgalā, Pūṣā, Hastijihvā, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Gāndhārī, Kāśinī, and Kuhū;
the vital breaths Prāṇa, Apāna, Samāna, Vyāna, and Udāna;
and the [five] winds Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya.
Alternatively, one should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa in this very manner:
having placed the letter *a* on the palate and the letter *ā* in the mouth;
having placed *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, and likewise *u* and *ū* on the two ears.
One should contemplate the vowels *e* and *ai* in the two rows of teeth, and *o* and *au* located in the two lips;
likewise, one should place *am* on the forehead and the syllable *aḥ* on the tongue.
Having assigned the letter *ya* to the skin, one should place the letter *ra* in the eyes.
One should place the syllable *la* on the nose, and the syllable *va* at the tips of the teeth;
having placed the syllable *śa* on the ears, likewise the syllable *ṣa* on the abdomen;
the syllable *sa* on the region of the hips, and the syllable *ha* on the heart.
The best of the twice-born should place the syllable *kṣa* at the region of the navel;
the *pa*-group is the first arm, while the *ta*-group is the second.
The *ṭa*-group and the *ca*-group are declared to be the two shanks.
O best of the twice-born, all the consonants of the *ka*-group should be understood as the fingers;
one should assign the constellations beginning with Rohiṇī to these [limbs] in due order:
in the heart, on the head, in the hair, on the forehead, and likewise in the mouth. (27.167–168)
In the nose, in the teeth, in the ears, in the two arms, in the two hands,
in the breasts, in the belly, in the hips, in the organ, and likewise in the scrotum;
in the anus, in the thighs, in the shanks, in the feet, and in the toes.
The sun and other planets, as well as the seven seers and Dhruva—
these he should place in the sky within the deity just as they are;
and the divisions of time from a *truṭi* up to the end of a *kalpa*, O Four-faced One.
The wise practitioner should appropriately assign the gross and subtle elements to the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of the deity; likewise, the Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes] should be assigned.
Rivers, wells, ponds, waters, and waterfalls should also be assigned.
The Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, should be established within the body of the Lord,
as well as their auxiliary limbs, the various treatises on their meaning,
and other deities whose faces are like those of the Four-faced One.
One should likewise place the principal sages and other powerful beings upon the deity; one should establish the entire triple world, with all its moving and unmoving things, [within him].
One should place the heavenly realm upon the head, and the moon and sun in the two eyes.

One should perceive the wind in the nose, the quarters of the sky in the arms, and those residing in the heart within the inner self; the sages and the ether [should be known] in the body, and the deities in the inner self.
The clouds are to be understood as the hair, and the stars as the ornaments. (27.176–177)
The mouth is fire, and likewise speech is Sarasvatī of pure syllables;
this, O Lotus-seated One, is called the Vairājanyāsa.
All sacrifices, such as the Aśvamedha and others, are [contained] therein exactly as they are.
In all the limbs of that Acyuta, who consists of the seasons,
the three qualities— sattva, rajas, and tamas— should be deposited;
immediately after that, the deposition of the ten forms beginning with the Fish (Matsya) should be performed.

The placement (nyāsa) of the goddesses, Śrī and the others, should be performed in due order; likewise, the six qualities beginning with *vijñāna* should be established through meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Similarly, the fourteen worlds should be placed in due order upon the feet and other limbs.
The Guru, who possesses the eye of the scriptures, should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs of the divine body up to the crown of the head according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus performed the sixteen-fold placement, he should carry out the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
Having offered one hundred oblations with honey into the eastern pit while reciting "bhūḥ," he should touch his feet with the remnants of the offering while reciting from "devasya bhuvaḥ.
Likewise, having offered oblations with milk into the southern fire, he should touch his belly.
Having offered oblations with curd into the western fire-pit, one should touch [the deity] with the mantra "Svaḥ.
Having offered oblations with clarified butter using the entire [mantra] into the northern fire,
one should touch the head and all the limbs of Hari with the residual drops.
Having himself offered oblations into that pit with jaggery, clarified butter, and honey, using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra, the Guru should touch his face with the residual drops from the ladle,
using water and the branches of the Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, and Bilva trees.

The image-keepers should properly sprinkle [the deity] with purifying mantras containing the word "water" (abliṅga), using water from the pitchers situated at the directions of the altar. Then the Guru should likewise sprinkle the corners of the altar with water from the pitchers using the Vaitasa branch and the Gāyatrī mantra.
This procedure has been proclaimed for [images] made of metal, wood, and stone.
However, in the case of a temple with many icons, one should perform the rites of dissolution, creation,
and so forth by entering inside [the shrine], concluding with the peace-offering (*śānti-homa*).
O Brahman, in the same way, the processes of dissolution and emanation occur within the retinues of Śrī and the others; likewise, it is so for Brahmā and the rest,
including the act of reviving and the placement of the *kṣetrajña*.
Having performed the worship with offerings such as the *arghya* and other services, one should worship Puruṣottama;
then, one should offer the four kinds of food with the *praṇava*.
This is prescribed for Brahmā and the others, as well as for Śrī and the other goddesses.
Whether he is seated or reclining upon a couch adorned with serpent-hoods,
the Guru should, according to the prescribed rite, fashion an infinite black serpent and bind it as a protective amulet (*kautuka*) at the primary amulet site (*mūlakautuka*).
Then one should cover the image with new cloths and the like;
having assigned the weapon-mantra (astramantra) at the door, one should offer a sacrificial oblation (bali) there.
This should be done for the retinues of Indra and the other deities who are to be established in their respective directions.
In each respective location on the secondary enclosure ground,

one should offer oblations into the fire— whether in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a ritual mound (*sthaṇḍila*)— in due order, using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) produced from the *palāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and *bilva* trees. (27.197–198)

The sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) should be of *audumbara* and *kāśmarya* wood, respectively. With these fuel sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), the Brahmins, observant of their vows, should perform one hundred and eight oblations (*āhuti*) in due order with the appropriate mantras.
Then, in sequence, [he recites] "trātāram" (the protector), "agne yad ulūkaḥ" (O Agni, what the owl...),
"āsane stha" (you are seated), and likewise "imaṃ me" (this mine) and other verses dedicated to Varuṇa;
and at the end of these mantras, he offers milk.
With the various mantras beginning with "tam īśānam," they should offer oblations to the deities such as Indra and others for the sake of the retinue, and they should also satisfy the Brahmins. Then,
having consecrated the pedestal (piṇḍikā), one should wrap it with a new cloth.
Having placed the metals, along with gems and mineral seeds, into a vessel,
one should wrap the vessel in cloth and bury it among heaps of grain.
One should bathe the images of Garuḍa and others with a new cloth.
One should cover it with a heap of grain and lay it down as before;
one should consecrate the seats for the deities of the directions for the sake of the offerings.
Having raised the image lying on the altar, one should place it in its own abode.
One should worship by offering the four kinds of food, beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having made the offering into the great vessel, one should then present the bali-oblation in the cardinal directions,
consisting of minced meat, powdered turmeric, parched grain, curd, and barley meal.
Having mixed the food for the offering with these [ingredients], one should recite these verses of the offering:
"May those beings who dwell in the eastern direction— both those primordial and those born of karma—
who desire the offering, accept this oblation with serene and well-pleased minds."
May those who dwell upon trees, on mountain peaks, and in the intermediate directions; those who abide on the earth and in the sky—they too shall accept this offering.
May the Vaināyakas, the Kṣetrapālas, and any others who desire the sacrificial oblation [accept it].
May Pūṣan and the other attendants accept this bali offering;
may Caṇḍa and the others, Kumuda and the others, and all those beings who dwell in every direction, come to this place and receive this bali.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra of Svapnādhipati,
one should bind a golden thread as a protective amulet on the right hand of the deity for the sake of accomplishing the rite of consecration, preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day.

Having worshipped the image of Bāli and its Śakti as well, the preceptor should invoke them into the great jar and deposit them upon heaps of grain. Then the guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into each and every sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
If the smoke of the fire-bearer possesses the fragrance of a lotus or a blue water-lily;
or if the smoke should be red, white, or yellow, it shall bring auspiciousness.
Furthermore, flames that curl toward the right certainly portend good fortune.
With the sounding of auspicious musical instruments and the chanting of Vedic hymns, the patron,
the preceptor, and those guardians of the images should spend the entire night sleeping on beds of *darbha* grass for the sake of dreams. 27.217–218ab.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Rules for the Bedding, the Consecration of the Image, and so forth," in the Kriyāpāda of the Pādmasaṃhitā within the glorious Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the twenty-eighth chapter.
The ritual for consecration is as follows:
then, when the morning has become clear and the orb of the sun is seen, the Blessed One—
On an auspicious moment, under an auspicious asterism, on an auspicious day and likewise on an auspicious lunar date,
one should begin the consecration of the God of gods at night when auspicious sights appear, without hesitation; and in the event of a bad dream, one should perform a rite for pacification.
One should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice once on the right side of the door;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there, one should enter the inner sanctum.
In its center, one should place that stone, which may be either square or circular.
One should prepare a pure pit, one cubit in length and likewise in width,

with four enclosures and a depression at the bottom. Then, with that same *gāyatrī* mantra, Viṣṇu [is worshipped] in the fire of the *vāstuhoma*, accompanied by offerings of sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and clarified butter.
The supreme preceptor should perform oblations for the sake of accomplishing the ritual placement of the jewels;
he should cast eight seed-syllables into the pits in the first enclosure:
barley, rice, flat beans, and millet.
Sesame seeds, mung beans, as well as wild rice and śāli rice; likewise,
diamonds and other precious gems were in the second enclosure—
diamonds, pearls, lapis lazuli, and coral.
One should place crystal, puṣyaka, and likewise the supreme moonstone,
as well as sapphire, in the directions starting from the east;
one should likewise place the minerals in the third enclosure.
Realgar, yellow orpiment, and collyrium immediately thereafter;
then black lead, tin, saurāṣṭra, and gorocanā; as well as red ochre—these eight metals are again in the fourth enclosure. (28.10–28.11)
One should place gold, silver, and likewise copper, as well as iron,
tin, and a tortoise fashioned from gold, into the pits;
along with a conch and a discus made of gold— this is declared to be the arrangement of metals (lohanyāsa).

One should place rice seeds, mercury, *brahmarāga*, and gold within the hollowed portion; then, one should firmly cover it with a "woman-stone" (*strīśilā*) while reciting the *Śrīsūkta*, and ensure its stability with lime (*sudhā*).
Thereafter, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited by Vaiṣṇavas who are most proficient in the mantras.
Within the lotus of the woman-stone (*strīśilā*), there should be the placement of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om);
the placement of the vowels should be in the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and the placement of the consonants on the petals.
On the petals are the eight Śaktis, and the ninth is in the region of the pericarp;
these are the Śaktis beginning with Vimalā:
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, and Yogā.
Prahvī, Satyā, and likewise Īśānā; Anugrahā is remembered as the ninth.
[28.17] One should perform the worship of the pedestal (piṇḍikā); afterwards, one should worship the pedestal (piṇḍakā) in due order with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having covered the pedestal, which possesses the form of Lakṣmī, with unwashed garments, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the weapon at the door, the Guru goes outside and,
for the sake of the bed and the sacrificial fee (*vedya*), should worship with water containing jewels.
Then one should release the deities residing upon the banner, the archway, and the pitcher;
having established the fire within the heart, one should lift up the great pitcher (mahākumbha),
as well as the eight pitchers of the forms (mūrtikumbha), the auspicious objects, the weapon, and the water-jar (karkarī).
Taking [the image], all the temple-keepers (mūrtipās) should proceed toward the temple.
With a continuous stream of dripping and flowing water rising up constantly,
one should sprinkle the path ahead with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having raised the deity from the elephant or other vehicle, the preceptor and all the others, including the image-bearers (*mūrtipāḥ*), should enter the temple by way of circumambulation,
accompanied by all auspicious items such as umbrellas, banners, and flags.
Amidst the resounding blasts of musical instruments and the chanting of the sacred voice of Brahman,

the Guru, together with learned Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas, those engaged in recitation, and the guardians of the images, should enter the inner sanctum while performing the ritual placement of the hands.
The preceptor should worship the deity at the entrance with offerings of water for honor (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth;
he should then cause the deity and the pedestal to enter within, circumambulating them. Having gone there when an auspicious moment (*muhūrta*) has arrived, he should install the imperishable Viṣṇu.

The preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should recite the *Sāman* "Pratiṣṭhāsi. Then, with the permission of the Guru, the image-keepers (*mūrtipās*) should recite the hymn "Ā tvāhārṣam" and the mantra "Dhruvā dyauḥ. (28.27–28)
The preceptor, standing in front, should establish Hari with everything [required];
he should place the image-pilaster (bimba-śaṅku) into the pit situated in the center of the pedestal.
He should observe the levelness of its position by means of a vertically suspended cord.
One should fill the hollow of the pedestal’s tube with the eight-fold binding substances:
lac, resin, guggulu, and molasses.
One should cook half of all these with oil over a gentle fire.
One should take equal parts of each of the following: powdered ghanasāra, beeswax, kuruvinda, red ochre, and likewise resin (sajjarasa).

It is prescribed that [the image] be cooked with oil together with the eightfold binding; having fixed it firmly with that, one should also have the auspicious day (puṇyāha) proclaimed. 28.33 Invocation (āvāhana).
Then one should invoke the God who is beyond darkness, the imperishable,
blissful, all-pervading, eternal, transcending space, and higher than the highest—
Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-powerful Lord, situated in the center of the circle of rays.
Having invoked Viśveśa with the root mantra,
the self-possessed Guru should contemplate that [deity] has entered within the image through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
He should then cause the Supreme Self, residing in the water-pot, to enter into the image.
Then the preceptor should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) with the root mantra;
he should request the presence of the deity and arrange for the retinue.
Having thus propitiated the deity, he should then offer milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having concealed the image with new garments or with a woolen blanket for three days,
one should fasten the door with a well-prepared panel for three days.
The celestial seers, the ancestors, the Siddhas, and likewise other divine beings worship the God for three days; at the end of the third night,
however, human beings should gratify the Brāhmaṇas with wealth, food, cattle, and other gifts.
When the fourth day has arrived, the ceremonial bathing is prescribed for the morning.
On that day, having raised the banner, one should commence the great festival.
O Lotus-seated One, this procedure has been described for the single-liṅga form.
If there is a rule for multiple vessels or a prescription for many vessels, the preceptor should bring forth the images of the deities, such as those of the ritual objects,
at that time, along with a large pitcher and the eight auspicious items.
Together with learned officiating priests and devoted followers of the Bhagavata,
the Guru himself, having lifted the vessel containing the weapon, should go in front;
he should then lead it into the temple by way of the stream of water.
No one should go between the image and the preceptor on the path. But when they have reached the doorway, one should offer water for the feet (pādya) at the auspicious object (kautuka).
This is the instruction regarding the placement of the ritual objects, the image, and so forth.
One should place the ritual image (karmārcā) upon the worship pedestal with the Nṛsūkta;
the images for festivals and other purposes should be placed on the two sides. One should install the ritual image in the Brahma-shrine, while the face-veil (mukhakautuka) is placed on the left.
The Guru should place the bathing image or the *tīrtha* image in the north;
the sleeping and rising images, as well as the offering (*bali*) image, in the south.
He should install images made of iron or other metals upon the desired grounds.
One should pour the water remaining from the stream into a shallow bowl; then,
with a continuous and unbroken stream the thickness of a reed,
one should perform a circumambulatory sprinkling all around with the Root Mantra.
Having placed jars upon heaps of grain, one should invoke Dharaṇī.
The preceptor, seated upon a lotus, should perform the invocation from the primary image into the ritual and other images when an auspicious moment has arrived. (28.50–28.51)

Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) before the primary image (mūlabera), having restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma) and purified the self, one should meditate upon the eternal Brahman. 28.52 The method of meditation.
Vāsudeva—the unborn, peaceful, radiant, and eternally manifest; without beginning, middle, or end; one, immovable, and steadfast;
a mass of consciousness, supreme bliss, beyond darkness, and imperishable.
Endowed with knowledge, power, strength, sovereignty, valor, and splendor; from head to foot, it is intangible and devoid of eyes, ears, and other such organs;
yet its hands, feet, and speech are everywhere, and its eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides.
Freed from coming and going, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
that consciousness is all-pervading, eternal, beyond the ether, and truly wondrous.
Within it, the world is the universal consciousness (*citsāmānya*), whose nature is the supreme root-mantra.

Having thus constantly engaged that Great Viṣṇu— who is Viṣṇu himself, consisting of bliss, and whose nature is the Praṇava— one should establish him within the mind; and having invoked Viṣṇu into the lotus of the heart, one should worship him in due order.
Having invoked [the deity] with the feminine mantra followed by the masculine mantra,
the Guru should then meditate upon Nārāyaṇa— the unborn, all-pervading Lord who is the source of light— as the universal self (viśvātman) within the seat held in his joined palms.
Having recited the *nivṛtti-mantra*, one should cause it to enter the image.

O Lotus-seated One, one should meditate upon it as having entered through the path of the *brahmarandhra* into the form of the image, pervading and remaining within its entirety by means of the mantra.
One should unite the powers residing in the *kumbha* with the Deity;
one should unite the power residing in the *mahākumbha* with the Deity;
and likewise those residing in the *mūrtikumbha*, as well as in the *bāla* and the *kautuka*. 28.62
One should unite that power with the deity through the form of the image;
one should close the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) of the image with the *tāra* (the syllable Om).
One should turn [the image] toward oneself by means of the *puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā*.
Having bowed slightly and then risen, the Guru should offer a welcome.
Regarding the varieties of ritual placement (nyāsa): thereafter, the preceptor should perform the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) using the root mantra.
The placement for stability (sthitinyāsa) should be performed during the state of stability; likewise, the placement for emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) on the seat.
On the bed, the placement for withdrawal (saṃhṛtinyāsa) is used if it is the bed of withdrawal;
O Lotus-seated One, the placement for emanation (sṛṣṭinyāsa) should be used on the bed of emanation.
The placement of stability (sthitinyāsa) is recommended during enjoyment, yoga, and sleep.
In the universal form (viśvarūpa), there is the placement of stability; when mounted on a vehicle, all three [placements] should be performed.
Alternatively, the placement of stability should be practiced everywhere, including on seats and so forth.
One should likewise sprinkle the goddesses such as Śrī and the deities such as Brahmā with water from the great jar (mahākumbha), using the *svapnavidyā* mantra.
[The ritual sequence consists of] emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), the placement of the creation (*sarganyāsana*), the ritual deposition (*nyāsa*), and the withdrawal of Rudra (*rudrasya saṃhṛti*).

The preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) for Śrī and the others, as well as for the rest; then, having lifted up the great pitcher,
he should at that very moment perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) with its water for Caṇḍa and the other deities as well.
The Guru himself should pour the remaining water upon the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Likewise, he should establish the fire in the kitchen hearth, in the sacrificial pit,
and in the cooking vessels, as well as the Gārhapatya fire, according to the path of the scriptures.
Having approached the presence of the deity, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff;
then, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite this verse.
Standing with palms joined in reverence together with the sacrificer, the Guru himself said:
"O God who is compassionate toward devotees, O fulfiller of the desired aims of your devotees! I pray to you, O Lord, out of a desire for your grace. (28.74)
"Be present for a long time in this place prepared by me with faith!
Be gracious, O God, Lord of Gods; accept my worship, O Consort of Indirā, for the sake of the village, the king, the kingdom, and the subjects."
"Grant nourishment, contentment, and likewise the supreme goal.
Having thus petitioned the God, the preceptor, who has mastered the Tantras,
[instructs] the surrender of all one's possessions to the Blessed One by the patron.
At the conclusion of the ritual offering of *madhuparka*, preceded by the permission of the preceptor,
one should give cows, land, gold, and so forth, according to one's means.
[One should offer this] into the right hand of the Deity, preceded by water, according to the prescribed rule.
With a head bowed in devotion, one should offer the articles of worship;
and one should place at the feet of the God one's self, sons, grandsons and so forth, wives, elephants and other vehicles, male and female servants, and all one's possessions. (28.79–28.80)
Just as the Lord is worshipped by a sacrificer with all his possessions, even with his life,
soul, and wealth when they are offered, so too should one always worship the Blessed Puruṣottama with all one's resources through the Bhāgavata.
The installation of the God of gods was performed by that former one, the supreme guide; by him alone, and even by his descendants though they may lack merit, must this worship be performed.
O Lotus-seated One, that very worship is what brings pleasure to the God.

The wise man should arrange the perfection of the abodes according to his wealth; or else, the sacrificer may arrange it solely according to his means. Whatever extent of the manifestation was initially planned, [he should maintain it accordingly].
One should bring about such prosperity even without causing any contraction [of resources].
In accordance with the prosperity of the deity, one should protect those who subsist upon the deity;
likewise, one should not cause distress to the devotees (bhāgavatas) or the attendants.

And at the conclusion of the deity’s consecration, one should cause it to be proclaimed in all directions with various kinds of musical instruments, and one should proclaim it with the sounds of Vedic recitation;
likewise, with various dances, songs, and manifold hymns of praise.
One should gratify the Lord of the Gods with various kinds of ritual services (upacāras).
Likewise, having offered the fourfold food according to the prescribed rite,
and having established the perpetual fire in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), [one should proceed].
Having offered oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, preceded by the *praṇava* and the root-mantra,
one should then offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then, having consecrated the offering-stands (*balipīṭha*) for each of the surrounding enclosures, one should install them in their proper order.
One should always offer oblations to them and to the spirits (bhūtas) in due order. When there is the provision of many vessels, however, one should not fasten the door with a bolt.
The celestial rishis, the ancestors, the Siddhas, and those of divine origin offer praise;
for three days they worship the God, and at the end of the third night,
human beings should gratify the Brahmins with wealth, food, cows, and other gifts.
When the fourth day arrives, one should arrange for the ceremonial bath;
this may be performed with either the three supreme [vessels] or the three intermediate ones. One should bathe the deity with these jars, and there shall be worship at four locations.

At the conclusion, one should hold a festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner. On that day of the consecration, the lord should worship the preceptor with gold flowers, new garments, and finger-rings.
With armlets, necklaces, and bracelets; with sacred threads and upper garments;
with fields, gardens, houses, and wealth; likewise with animate and inanimate riches; and with female and male slaves, as well as elephants, horses, palanquins, and so forth.

In these ways and by others as well, the self-possessed one should satisfy the guru. He should offer himself, his sons, and his grandsons to the deity, and likewise offer the supreme guru as mother, father, and kinsman.
Having regarded him as one's own kinsman and having prostrated before him again and again,
one thousand cows should then be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor;
or else, a fee of one thousand niṣkas is the most excellent of the excellent.
Half of that is to be known as the middling [fee], and half of that again is considered the lowest.
Alternatively, the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given is one hundred pieces of gold;
however, one who is unable may give ten niṣkas, or half of that, or even a quarter.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed according to one’s wealth;
whatever has been brought forth as an auxiliary to the rites of cultivation and so forth—
all that which is desired and remains after consumption shall become the property of the preceptor alone.
Likewise for all officiating priests who have studied the sacred scriptures (āmnāya),
for learned Brahmins devoted to Puruṣottama,
and for those established in the single path (ekāyana) whose selves are restrained by the twelve [rules]. || 28.104–105 ||
For ascetics devoted solely to Vāsudeva, for those who know the path of liberation, for those in the stages of life such as celibates and forest-dwellers,
and for other devotees of Viṣṇu who follow in this matter— 28.106.
And sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), consisting of cows, land, gold, and so forth, according to one's wealth, should be given to the members of the assembly who are fixed upon the asterism of Viṣṇu,
as well as to those who possess knowledge of the proper times and who perform dance, song, instrumental music, and the like.
One should provide satisfaction according to one's desire with wealth and garments as is appropriate.
Having brought a vessel made of gold or other materials,
the preceptor should wash it with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī and, by means of his own mantra, place it upon a heap of grain.
Having placed [the vessel] before the deity, one should fill it with fragrant water;
having consecrated it eighteen times with the eight-syllable mantra and twelve times with the six-syllable mantra,
one should invoke the omnipresent Lord who has entered into oneself by means of the five Upaniṣad mantras.
Having worshipped with the syllable *praṇava* using perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and other offerings,
he should then summon a pure artisan into the presence of the deity.
Having placed him facing the deity, bowing down and full of humility, [he should address him].
From that water consisting of half-and-a-half portions, having filled his hand with the arghya-water and a flower, one should then recite this verse:
"Without you, nothing belongs to me; likewise, who is there for you without me? (28.114)
Therefore, O Supreme Lord, be gracious so that you may make me your own;
for those whose feet have stumbled upon the earth, the earth alone is their support.
O All-pervading One, for those who have taken refuge in you alone, you alone are the shelter.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, whose mind was composed, the preceptor—
having uttered the twelve-syllable mantra at the lotus-feet of the Blessed One and having offered himself to the Maker preceded by water for honor and flowers— [proceeded].
Having offered himself to the Imperishable One, he should prostrate three times before the Lord;
being thus favored by Him, he should then go outside with his teacher. (28.118) [Guru-pūjā]
Having paid homage to the Guru, the God, with a mind that has accomplished its purpose,
he should place that Guru upon a vehicle preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
lead him around the village in circumambulation, and settle him in his own home.
The fruit of the installation of a deity:
he who should thus perform the consecration of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow,
O Lotus-seated One, goes to the supreme, imperishable abode.
He purifies twenty-one generations of his lineage.
But those men who, free from desire, install the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) in their home,
for them the fruit is characterized by non-return to worldly existence.
But for mortals who possess desires, characterized by return [to rebirth],
that particular heaven or other realm which is to be enjoyed is desired at the outset of each undertaking.
Expiation is considered for other sins, such as the killing of a Brahmin.
Those mortals who assist by means of actions of speech, mind, and body,
their fruit is held to be heaven and the like, characterized by return.
And in the case of the devis such as Śrī and others, [the fruit] is conceived together with the God.
If the two are situated separately, the rite of marriage should not be performed;
And just as that installation by devotees is remembered as "easily grasped" (sugrahā), [so too is this].
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installation," in the Kriyāpāda of the Pādmasaṃhitā within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Chapter Twenty-nine:
The Ritual for the Installation of the Ten Forms beginning with Fish, by the Blessed Lord.
Now, O Brahmin, the specific procedure for the installation of the ten forms beginning with Mīna— characterized by the ritual of invocation and so forth— is being described. 29.1 [The Form of Mīna]
With the *sāman* and with the *vāruṇa* hymn, which has the Supreme Person as its essence,
one should establish the flawless Vāsudeva in his fish-form.
Having invoked the Lord of Gods into that [image], the knower of mantras should perform worship.
Salutations to you, whose nature is the Fish, the protector of the Vedas;
to you who sport in the irresistible flood of waters of the ocean of dissolution.
[I worship you] with the Vāruṇa Sūkta as well as with the eight-syllable mantra.
Having placed the great jar, one should invoke Hari into it;
at the conclusion of the ritual, one should worship with the verse that is about to be recited:
"We pay homage to you, the Creator in the form of a tortoise."
To the sustainer of Mount Mandara, the bestower of joy upon the gods—
having established the form of Varāha, one should invoke Hari in the form of Vārāhī.
Salutations to you, the soul of the boar, the creator whose form is sacrifice;
O upholder of the earth, who sustains the entire world with the tips of your tusks—
Nṛsiṃha!
The best of preceptors should install the Lord in the form of Nṛsiṃha;
having invoked Janārdana with the *yuñjīta* hymn,
the best of preceptors should recite this *gādha* at the conclusion of the rite.
Salutations to the one who assumed the form of Nṛsiṃha, who displayed affection for his devotees, and whose chest split the asuras with his sword-like claws that resembled thunderbolts. 20.10 Vāmana.
Having established Vāmana with the *anuvāka* beginning "yuñjanti," the preceptor,
having invoked the Lord of Devas into him, should perform worship:
"Salutations to you, the enemy of Bala, who are the creator in the form of sacrifice."
To Vāmana, who deceived all men through his great illusion;
having established Janārdana as the son of Jamadagni by means of the Nṛsūkta.
Standing with palms joined in reverence and bowing low, he should worship with this verse:
"Obeisance to you, the Blessed One of fierce splendor, the slayer of the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times, who wields the battle-axe. (20.14)
Śrī Rāma should install Rāma together with Vaidehī and accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and the others, either at different times or perform the installation all at once. 29.15
Having installed Rāma according to the prescribed rite with the Puruṣasūkta,
one should worship Rāma, the scion of Raghu’s lineage, with this verse:
"Salutations to you, the Blessed One, the great-souled Rāghava."
Then, having installed the form of Rāma— who possesses great majesty in the destruction of the world's enemies such as Rāvaṇa— along with his retinue,
he further [installed] the sons of the gods beginning with Vāyu, headed by Hanumān.
Having worshipped each of those respective deities, he should install them in that very same manner;
for Vibhīṣaṇa and Guha are indeed distinct deities.
He should install both of them, who bring delight to Rāma, with the Viśva-mantra.
One should place Bharata in the east and Jānakī in the south;
Jāmbavān in the west and likewise Lakṣmaṇa in the north;
Sugrīva in the southeast corner, and Vibhīṣaṇa in the southwest.
One should place Nala in the northwest and Śatrumardana in the northeast;
the preeminent sages, beginning with Vasiṣṭha, reside in the second enclosure.
In the third enclosure, one should subsequently assign the world-protectors (lokapālas).
One should install Nīla or Guha there in the position of Viṣvaksena;
one should install Hanūmat in the place of the King of Birds (Garuḍa).
This specific distinction regarding the worship of Rāghava has been proclaimed.
Or else, having depicted the Lord of Birds or Hanumān, one should raise the banner;
this specific rule for the festival has been declared, O Lotus-Seated One.
— Balarāma.
The installation of Rāma and the son of Rohiṇī is as it was before;
however, there is a distinction in their attendance, which shall now be told—listen to it.
To the powerful Balabhadra, whose arms throb with the plow...
To you belongs the great earth like a root, by whom the head was uplifted. Śrī Kṛṣṇa [performed] the installation of the son of Vasudeva as Vāsudeva.
Salutations to you, Kṛṣṇa, the best of the Vṛṣṇis, the enemy of Madhu;
salutations to the slayer of the great asuras such as Kaṃsa, who were a burden to the earth,
and to the one who performed the establishing and marrying of Satyabhāmā and the other goddesses.
There is no difference whatsoever between Śrī and Bhūmi;
Kalki is proclaimed to be established as Kalki-Viṣṇu just as before.
At the conclusion of his work, he should pay homage with a verse in the form of praise:
"Salutations to you, the Blessed One, born into a lineage of brahmins, the destroyer even of barbarians and the cause of stability for the virtuous. (29.31)
The prohibition of the sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍaśanyāsa) regarding the Fish and other forms:
"The sixteen-fold placement is not desired for the ten forms beginning with the Fish, provided that for stone-made and other images, the method of painting is performed using colors. (29.32)
Having performed everything without exception as prescribed for the preliminary consecration of the water (jalādhivāsana) and so forth,
one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites once the work of painting has been completed,
provided that the installation of the ritual acts and the worship of the image occurs after the fixed icon (dhruvabimba) has been established.

For the different forms according to the various Siddhāntas, separate beds are prescribed; O Four-faced One, in the case of non-difference, the altar and the bed should be together. Furthermore, the sixteen-fold installation (ṣoḍaśanyāsa) is not prescribed for a mobile image made of metal.

One should perform the invocation from the primary image (mūlabera) into the ritual images (karmārcā) and so forth. O Brahmin, one should install the ritual image (karmārcā) to the south, while my festive image (kautuka) should be installed to the north; or the Guru may install the bathing image (tīrthasnāna-bimba) to the north.
One should install the image of [the Buddha] reclining and the image of [him] standing on the right;
one should place a worldly image made of metal upon the desired grounds.
Or else, one should install images of [the Buddha] walking on both sides of the door.
Or, for the purpose of consecration in a pavilion, they should face south;
O Four-faced One, this applies directly to those images that are unfit for immersion in water,
such as painted representations, those appearing in relief, or half-painted images, according to their respective types.
One should perform the dwelling in the shadow and the bathing upon the surface of a mirror;
on the altar, one should arrange the bed for the others by means of a bundle of kuśa grass.
One should arrange everything else that remains exactly as before.
The sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍaśanyāsa) is not desired, nor is the fourth ablution (caturthasnapana).
[He is] one who sleeps on a banyan leaf— that is,
one who sleeps upon the leaf of the great tree, the Nyagrodha, which consists of illusion (māyāmaya).
Now, the specific procedure for the installation of the deity is being described.
Having drawn the ocean above the door of the inner sanctum,
there, upon a leaf of the *nyagrodha* tree, [one should place] the deity in a tender form.

One should have Mārkaṇḍeya depicted with a youthful body, dark-complexioned, and lotus-eyed, lying down on the ground beside the feet of the Goddess. Thus, when the child is painted lying upon a child’s couch, [the rite is complete].
The self-possessed Guru should establish [the deities] according to the method described for the variegated manifestation.
During the installation, the two goddesses should be established simultaneously with the Lord, as before;
their resting together on the altar is simultaneous, but if there is a difference in time, it is separate.
The Kuṇḍabhedas:
the pit (kuṇḍa) in the east is shaped like a lotus, while that in the south is bow-shaped;
in the western part it is circular, and likewise in the north it is shaped like a womb (yoni).
The specific procedure for the pit has been described, as well as the ritual bathing of those two [deities] again;
one should worship Śrī and the others with the Śrīsūkta, and likewise Śrī the goddess and Bhū with the Bhūsūkta.
One should bathe them and also perform their worship; with those two, one should cause [the image] to lie down.
On the eastern archway, Balākinī is to be worshipped as the presiding deity (adhidevatā). Then, having propitiated Vanamālī and Vibhīṣikā there—
Śāṅkarī is the deity for the western door-pitchers in due order. One should worship the pair of deities, the installation and other rites,
first, and thereafter Śraddhā and Kānti.
One should worship the deities Kriyā, Sṛṣṭi, Kṣamā, Vṛddhi,
and Devatā upon the banners in the eastern and other directions as pairs of deities. Then, one should worship Dhṛti and Lajjā in front, followed by Jayā and the two Māyās.
Sāvitrī and Kṣamā, as well as the two— Śuddhā and Śraddhā— immediately thereafter; Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi,
these are the Śaktis who should be offered oblations in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east, according to the prescribed method.
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyā, Kīrti, Lakṣmī, as well as Sṛṣṭi, Prahvī,
Satyā, and Brāhmī— these are to be worshipped in the jars.
O lotus-seated one, one should worship the goddess Śrī in the great jar.
One should perform the remainder as before, excluding the sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍaśanyāsa).
For this is the rule when there is no independence; however, when there is independence, it is declared as follows:
whether in a village, a city, a town, or even a hermitage.
The abode of Śrī should be established facing the village and so forth; O Four-faced One, one should likewise arrange Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Sāvitrī, and Vāgdevī.
One should also fashion the deities of the directions in the four cardinal points of the temple.
In the corners, one may install either Vainateya or a lion according to preference;
or else, in the divine portion or the Brahma portion, one should establish the reflected image using stone or other materials,
and likewise install the attendant deities in order on the sides of the entrance.
One should place Caṇḍī and Pracaṇḍī on the two sides of the first gate;
then, at the door of the half-pavilion, Balākinī on the south;
and again, at the first northern gateway, Vanamālā.
On the right and left sides [of the second gate], one should place Vibhīṣikā and Śāṅkarī.
At the door of the second gopura, both the Śaṅkha and Padma Nidhis are located;
at the third gopura door, Nalakūbara and Jṛmbhala.
O Lotus-Seated One, at the fourth gateway, one should place Śibi and Kuṇḍala on the south, and Māṇibhadra on the north;
Jayā and Vijayā are the guardians of the western gate.
One should install Sumukhī in the place of Viṣvaksena, four-armed,
holding a staff in her right hand and making the threatening gesture (tarjanī),
while with the other two hands she holds a yellowish lotus.
One should place Vainateya in the pavilion at the front of the temple;
the arrangement of the retinue should be like that of the Primordial Deity (Ādimūrti). Such is the procedure for other goddesses as well when they are worshipped independently.
One should perform the fourth consecration and also a festival like that for the god.
The man who is thus an installer of the goddesses, Śrī and the others,
attains all desires and rejoices both in this world and in the hereafter.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Fish-Emblem and Others," in the Kriyāpāda of the Padmasaṃhitā within the glorious Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the thirtieth chapter.
The ritual for taking the hands of Śrī and the other goddesses:
Now, the Blessed Lord describes the ritual for taking the hands of the goddesses beginning with Śrī.
It generates all that is auspicious, destroys all suffering,
increases the lifespan of men, and accomplishes desired aims.
On the day specified, one should perform the offering of the sprouts.
When the day of the wedding has arrived and the auspicious moment (muhūrta) has come, the best of preceptors should tie the ritual thread (karmakautuka) separately for the god and the goddess.
Having dressed them in unwashed linen garments along with upper cloths, they should be fully adorned.
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin, one should lead it around the village in a clockwise direction;
then one should cause it to enter the wedding hall or the temple.
Having worshipped the deity with offerings such as the *arghya*, one should bring the fire onto the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Having brought the Lord into the inner chamber, one should seat him upon a throne;
having worshipped Hari there, one should clothe the Goddess in a new garment with the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ" and perform a circumambulation.
And one should adorn the goddess Śrī with flowers as well as ornaments.
(30.7) The Guru himself should unite the goddess with the God by means of the *praṇava*;
and he should give the goddess to the God, preceded by water, according to the prescribed rule. (30.8)
The sacrificer [offers] this unsurpassed Śrī, the golden earth together with cows and other riches, as described by her own lineage name.
Then, from the temple, he [leads forth] that goddess and the god, who have taken each other's hands.
Having led [the couple] to the wedding place, the Guru, facing the northern direction,
should perform the preparatory oblations (ādhāra-homa) and other rites in due order according to the path prescribed by the rules;
he should also offer sixteen oblations of fuel-sticks (samidh) with the Nṛ-sūkta.
With the *caru* and the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*, there should be twenty-four oblations.
Having offered clarified butter with the *Śrīsūkta*, if [the rites for] the Earth and [the deity] are performed simultaneously,
the rites beginning with the *aṅkura* (germinating seeds) must be performed separately for both.

O Lotus-born One, since it follows that both [the bridegrooms] would have a single agent [for the rite], one should nevertheless perform the wedding ceremony separately for each of them. While the ritual action may coincide at the same time, it should be performed as distinct acts through successive turns.
It should be divided according to the sequence [of the constellations] as appropriate;
or else, if the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) are distinct, the marriage ceremony may take place separately.
If the auspicious moments coincide, one should perform the rites in their proper order.
If the simultaneous marriage of Śrī and Bhūmi were to have different performers, even in that case the rule would be thus: for both [brides], there must indeed be a formal rite;
when the god performs the simultaneous marriage, there should be a single *pratisara* thread.
It may be performed either in a single fire or in separate fires according to one's preference;
the previous ritual procedure, such as the marking of the ground and so forth, need not be repeated if it has already been performed.
One should perform every action separately for each individual [deity].
One should perform the rite in succession for Śrī first and then for Bhūmi.
One should offer sixteen oblations of fuel-sticks with the root mantra;
there should be twenty-four oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Having again offered oblations of clarified butter with the Puruṣasūkta or the Bhūmisūkta,
and likewise having performed the oblation of parched grain (lājahoma) and the circumambulation of the fire in due order,
the preceptor himself [should consume] the entire remainder of the parched grain without exception.
Having offered oblations once with the *praṇava*, and then with the five *vāruṇika* [mantras],
with the five *upaniṣad* mantras, and with the twelve-syllable vidyā;
having performed everything up to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should satisfy the Brahmins.
One should worship the deity with the *arghya* and other offerings and perform the offering of clarified butter (*ghṛtāropaṇa*).
Taking all the items— clarified butter, *dūrvā* sprouts, sandalwood, and *śāli* rice—
in a vessel with both hands, all the members of the assembly [should do likewise].
Thinking, "May they cast [these] upon the limbs of the god and the goddess," [they perform] this auspicious rite.
Then, saying "Excellent ghee," they should sprinkle it on the feet;
saying "Very auspicious" on the waist, and likewise "Highly auspicious" on the head.
In this manner, they should cast all the items, beginning with the *dūrvā* grass, in successive order.
They should also present the *madhuparka* and utter the words, "I am [this].
Then, one should adorn the Lord of Lakṣmī with ornaments such as necklaces and the like.

One should also worship with garlands and ointments, as is appropriate. The sacrificer, bowing down, should give a cow to Hari, and he should give to the preceptor whatever is dear to himself, according to his wealth.
At the conclusion of the lustration rite (*nīrājana*), one should cast the ritual cakes (*piṇḍikā*) in the various directions;
furthermore, one should perform all other auspicious rites according to worldly custom. One should then cause the Lord, accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, to perform a circumambulation of the village.
Having placed the two goddesses and the god in the pavilion, one should treat them like a king.
At the conclusion of the offering of the great oblation, one should also feed the Brahmins.
Day after day, one should perform the festival preceded by ritual bathing.
On the fourth night, during the latter part of the night, one should perform the remaining oblation.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations consisting primarily of fuel-sticks, clarified butter,
and sacrificial porridge, using both the root mantras and the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
On the fifth day, one should anoint the Lord Hari with oil.
One should bathe the Lord, who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, according to the prescribed rites.
At the conclusion of the offering of the great oblation, one should hold a grand festival in the village.
There, one should worship [the Lord] daily in the temple together with Śrībhūmi.
Such is the marriage rite for the other goddesses as well.
The marriage of the goddesses beginning with Jāmadagnyā is performed according to the path of the Smṛtis.
The Ritual for the Consecration of Pavilions and Other Structures:
The ritual for the consecration of wedding pavilions and the like is now described.
[It may be performed] in front of, behind, or to the sides of the temple, according to one's preference.
One should construct an altar four cubits wide and one cubit high, which is beautiful to behold.
Around the altar, there should be eight or four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), along with arches,
gateways, water-pots, banners, and so forth, as before.
Having formed the directional forms and opened their eyes according to the ritual rule,
the Guru should bathe the Āśāmūrti and the celestial chariot (vimāna) in the mirror.
If the patron is a king, [he should likewise bathe] the vessels and the jars.
They should be made of gold, silver, or copper, or otherwise [of other metals], and not otherwise;
O Lotus-born One, when Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are the sacrificers,
the vessels may even be made of clay, according to the extent of one's wealth.
Then, one should cover the sacrificial hall with beautiful cloths that do not have hands [i.e.,
are not made by hand]. Having placed the loads of *śāli* rice as previously described in the middle of the altar,
one should place all the *taṇḍula* rice and sesame seeds in the quantities mentioned before.
And having placed a great golden jar above,
one should set down eight other jars made of the same material around it; and into each jar, one should place a measure of gold equal to a niṣka.
Having worshipped the nine gems within the threads and other materials as appropriate, one should place those eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalāni) therein;
then one should perform the offering for the image and present the oblation into the great jar.
The fourfold oblation, as well as other matters, are as previously described.
This is the method of meditating upon the limbs of the temple once that sanctuary has been purified by means of drying, plastering, and so forth.
One should meditate upon the abode of Ratnasthala, fashioned from molten gold.
Therein, one should also meditate upon the individual soul (jīva) as all-pervading and conditioned by that [abode],
as well as the intellect (buddhi) as the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and likewise the ego (ahaṅkāra) as the feet.
The feet [became] the footstone and the shanks; likewise, the womb-chamber became the belly.
The pillars became the arms, and the hips likewise became the girdle.
The tongue, the ears, the eyes, the nostrils, and the organ of generation [were formed].
The downward breath is the outflow of water, and the nose is considered the nostril.
The eye is the window, the neck is the neck, and from the neck come the shoulders and the cheeks.
The head is the jar, the flesh is the plaster, and touch is the nectar.

One should meditate on the bones as being within the stones, the sinews as the tips of the wooden beams and the banners, the manes and the beard as the hair [of the deity], and the abode as having the form of a person.
Having repeatedly offered oblations, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the powers (*śakti*) within the temple of Hari.
One should indeed deposit Pūrṇaśakti, who is known as Prakṛti, into the Upāna;
Śānti into the Jagatī; immediately after that, Pṛthivī into the Kumuda;
Vāgīśvarī into the neck; and likewise Mati into the fillet (paṭṭikā).
In the arrangement of the five limbs, the placement of Śakti is proclaimed;
in the twelve-limbed abode, one should place the Śakti known as Kīrti.
Furthermore, on the great fillet and on the neck, one should place Puṣṭi immediately thereafter.
One should place Mahī on the sacrificial altar (vedī) during the rite of strength (vājana), Tuṣṭi on the head, and likewise Sṛṣṭi on the feet;
Māyātmikā on the pigeons (kapota) and Mohinī on the garlands of elements (bhūtamālā). Thus is described the deposition of powers (śaktinyāsa) upon the twelve-limbed celestial chariot (vimāna).
Now the placement within the eighteen-limbed abode of Hari is described:
one should place Mahālakṣmī on the peak (kūṭa), and likewise Vasudhā on the other [limb];
the power of Earth (mahī-śakti) on the stone (śilā), and Atimohinī on the slab (prastara).
Svāhā is on the altar, Śrī in the abode; this is declared in the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa).
All rites, such as the fire-oblation for peace (śāntihoma) and so forth, should be performed as before.
And for all the deities of the directions, the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa) and so on is as previously described.
He should feed thousands or even hundreds of Brahmins according to his capacity,
and once they have eaten, he should give them wealth and other gifts. Furthermore,
on the panel of the celestial chariot, there should be twenty-five threads.
One should tie the protective thread (kautuka) in the four directions of the temple and cast [the offerings].
One should perform the sprinkling with the great jars, offer the oblation as before, and cause the sound of Vedic chanting to resound in all directions.
Then, at the time of dawn during an auspicious moment, the preceptor,
having lifted the great jar and led it around the temple in a clockwise direction,
placed the jar to the south with a concentrated mind.
Facing north, the Guru, O Four-faced One, having placed the Śakti residing in the water of the pitcher into the celestial chariot with the root mantra,
should sprinkle the deities of the directions with the waters of the pitcher using their respective mantras.

One should sprinkle the abode or dwelling place of other deities as well, according to the prescribed rule, with water from the ritual jars and with their respective Vidyās. One should first worship the temple and then the deities of the directions in their proper order.
When the foundation of the temple has been completed according to the rules,
one should give a hundred *niṣkas* to the preceptor, or half of that, or even a quarter;
and at the conclusion, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in accordance with one's wealth.
The patron, following behind, should give a thousand gold pieces as the excellent dakṣiṇā to the preceptor;
the middling gift should be half of that, and the lowest should be one-quarter;
he should also satisfy the image-makers with gifts.

One should satisfy the Brahmins and others as well with wealth, clothing, and other things that gladden the mind, as well as with food and the like. He who thus establishes a temple for Viṣṇu, free from desire for rewards, [attains the highest state].

Liberation stands in the palm of his hand; of this there is no doubt. But for him who, out of a desire for rewards, establishes a Vaiṣṇava temple, there shall be incomparable prosperity that transcends the path of all desires.

In the installation of the pavilion, however, having first constructed the altar and having performed the rites beginning with the purification of the ritual action (kriyāviśodhana) in their entirety,
the most excellent preceptor [should proceed] according to the path prescribed for the installation of the temple (prāsāda).
The pavilion, fashioned by Viśvakarman and adorned with all kinds of jewels,
is supported by many golden pillars embellished with various gems;
having meditated upon this, the Guru should perform the ritual installation of the Śaktis.
The *upāna* is considered to be Prakṛti, Śakti, Jagatī, Vasundharā,
Vaprā, Kriyā-śakti, and Vāgīśvarī;
likewise, Prīti, Kampa, Tuṣṭi, Kumuda, Paṭṭikā, and Kṣamā.
The pillar-base stone is Brāhmī; the pillar is Vaiṣṇavī. The bud is Kamalā-śakti; the northern one is held to be Śānti.
Rati is the crossbar (vājana), O Lotus-seated One, and she is my Māyā.
Kīrti is considered to be the row of bricks, as well as Kampa and Mohinī; Tulā, Padmā, Śānti, and Śakti are the rows of steps.
One should worship the archways (toraṇas) at the four doors of the pavilion.
O Lotus-Seated One, all the rites such as the peace-offering (śānti-homa) have been explained.
Then, at dawn, the Guru, having placed the Śaktis residing in the jars within that pavilion,
should then contemplate the pavilion in its pervasive form.

One should sprinkle with water from the jar those variegated objects that appear variegated and are situated there, using one's own mantra, after having performed the entire ritual placement (nyāsa) as before.
The patron should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor as before.
He who performs the installation of the pavilion for the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) enjoys abundant pleasures in this world and in the next,
and rejoices in the jeweled pavilion of the temple of the God of Gods.
The Ritual for the Consecration of the Assembly Hall and Other Structures:
The ritual procedure for the consecration of the assembly hall and other such structures is now described.
There is the Vāstu-sacrifice, the offering of oblations (bali), and the sprinkling with the five products of the cow. (30.87)
