The circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), as well as the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana),

the placement of the water-pot (kumbha), and the offering of oblations (āhuti) into the fire— all these should be performed at one time. Afterwards, one should sprinkle [the site] during an auspicious moment (muhūrta), or else perform everything immediately.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣi�ṇā) is proclaimed to be one hundred niṣkas or half of that;
O Four-faced One, the fruit for the performer is slightly less than before.
The consecration of a gate-tower (gopura) is no different from that of a temple.
Having performed the consecration of the wall so that everything is as it was before,
the Guru should sprinkle it with water from the ritual jar while reciting the Dharma-mantra. The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall be one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five gold niṣkas.
The construction and installation of the *balipīṭha* (offering pedestal) are now described.
The *balipīṭhikā* should have a length and width equal to those of the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), or it may be half that size, a quarter of that, or even five parts [of the same unit]. 30.92–93.
Or it may be one-ninth of the new [measurement], or it may be determined by the span of the hand;
the best is one cubit, or up to five, according to one's strength.
Its height should be twice its width, or three times, or even one-and-a-half times.
Alternatively, the height may be equal to the width; this is the arrangement of the five parts.
Adorned with garlands of pigeons, *bhūta*s, swans, and so forth, one should divide the width at the front into three parts, and with two of those parts, the lotus (*paṅkaja*) should be formed.
One should visualize Garuḍas or lions at the corners of the pedestal;
Vighnarāja is his father, and Kanyakā is also [his mother].
Their respective forms are traditionally taught to be located in the directions starting from the eastern quarter in due order.
Rows of steps should be constructed on both sides according to the height [of the structure].
The width of the gateway (gopura) door should be three or four times [the thickness of the wall];
outside and in front of the door, a sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) should be fashioned.

The preceptor should perform the entire sequence of rites, beginning with the *vāstuhoma* and concluding with the *śāntihoma*, in due order as for a temple. When the time of dawn has arrived during an auspicious *muhūrta*, the Guru—
One should sprinkle the pedestal with water from the pitcher using the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
One should also sprinkle the deities situated there using the self-mantra (ātmavidyā),
and one should sprinkle the pericarp as well using the "entire" mantra (samasta-ityādi-vidyā).
One should always request the presence of the eight [deities] beginning with Kumuda, together with their respective attendants, there preceded by mantras.
Having thus consecrated the pedestal, one should then perform the daily festival.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of at least one hundred niṣkas should be given to the preceptor.
He who thus establishes this supreme pedestal, which is the abode of Viṣṇu and all beings,
becomes liberated from all suffering and attains the highest state.
O Lotus-seated One, I shall now describe the consecration of the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha).
Its height is prescribed to be equal to the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra) on all sides.
Whether it be long or wide, in the center of the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra),
it is declared that [the height] should be seven parts out of ten parts of the total elevation;
or, when the elevation is divided into twenty-seven parts, [it should be seven].
The *pāduka* (base) should be known as two parts; the *jagatī* (plinth) is four parts.
The *kumuda* (corbel) should be known as three parts, and the *paṭṭikā* (fillet) should be one part.
The *karṇa* (corner) is said to be six parts, while the *gala* (neck) and *kampā* (molding) are each two parts.
The division here is by four parts, and the bamboo-strips (vaṃśas) are likewise;
the lotus flower is two and a half parts, and the pericarp of the lotus is one and a half parts.
Having understood this correctly, one should designate [the measurements] part by part.
It should be measured at three *hasta*s, or even more than three *hasta*s;
or it may be more than five *hasta*s, as prescribed for the *gopura*.
In the center, the *bhūta* should be fashioned according to the measurement of four *tāla*s.
One should cause this best [image] to be made seated comfortably and turned away;
let it be offered to Aniruddha, to Dṛṣad, and to Vatsara.
Likewise to Avaklptahasta and similarly to Cāmuṇḍa.
"To Nyāya," "to Varāya," and after that "to Udara";
likewise "to Udarabandhāya," and again "to the two Nāḍis";
and "Vasu" and "to the Vāstus," and again "to Vāstumuṣkāya."
"To Prajāpati," "To the singers," "To the buttocks"—thus [he says] again;
"To the pond," "To the bamboo," and "To those who bear the bamboo";
having said "To Prajāpati" and "O bold ones," [he offers] to the beings.
Reciting "To Śuka, to those dwelling in Śuka, from the thighs," let [the oblation] be offered; likewise,
"to the veins, to the ligaments of the bones, and to the mouths," and also "to the witnesses, from the roots of the knees, from the roots of the knees."
"From the ankles, from the heels, from the feet, or even from the soles;
from the toes, from the feet, and from the tips and soles of the feet;
from the sole and the upper surface of the sole—let it be offered with the words, ‘Svāhā to the skins!’"
Having offered oblations to Tvarasins, one should thereafter offer oblations, saying:
"To Romakūpa," "to the hairs of the body," "to Rasa," "to Rasada," "to Ratna," "to those who dwell in jewels," and likewise again to Medas.

One should offer oblations for the living soul (jīva) and for the dwelling place (vāstu), and again for the bones and marrow; furthermore, one should offer for those who dwell in intoxication (mattavāsin) and for the head (uttamāṅga).
One should also offer for the Creator (dhātṛ), for the elements (dhātu), and likewise for the forms of the elements (dhāturūpa).
One should offer oblations to the secondary elements, saying, "From the skin of the animal";
likewise, let the offering be made to the one of all forms, to the neck, to the giver of wealth, to the Self,
to the Lord of All, to Sacrifice, and to Puruṣa.
O best of the twice-born, the *pīṭha* should be constructed even without an *upapīṭha*.
Having first worshipped separately Āmoda, who consists of that element and is of the nature of the world,
[one should worship] Pramoda in the southern lotus, who consists of that element and is of the nature of fire.

The foremost [lotus] is in the western lotus; that consists of water. The upward-facing one is in the direction of the Moon (the north); that indeed consists of air. That which is above the instrument (karaṇa) is declared to consist of space.
The earth, the atmosphere, and heaven consist of the qualities of all beings;
O best of the twice-born, it is said that the Great Seat (Mahāpīṭha) is identical with that.
The width of the palace, which is described as being like a staff (daṇḍa),
begins from the main building and extends to six staffs,
or to ten, twelve, or up to fourteen staffs.
One should fashion the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) with sixteen or twelve [units],
or else the location for the pedestal is prescribed by another method:
in a temple with three, four, or five halls in its central courtyard.
The great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) should be constructed; its characteristics are now described.
Alternatively, the width of the pedestal may be one cubit (vyomahasta), which is the lowest;
two cubits is declared the middling; and three cubits is said to be the best.
The height should be equal to its width; the height [of the base] is seven, eight, or twenty-eight [parts].

The height of the *upāna* (the plinth) should be two parts, and the *jagatī* (the cornice) should be six parts. The height of the *kumuda* (the fillet) should be five parts, and the *kampa* (the recess) is said to be one part.
The portion for the neck is four parts, while the upward projection is one part of Śiva;
the great band (mahāpaṭṭī) is three parts, or specifically two parts.
The lotus portion is four parts, while the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) is two parts.
Alternatively, O best of the twice-born, the height of the *karṇikā* should be three parts;
the height of the lotus (*padma*) should be one part, and the great fillet (*mahāpaṭṭī*) should be two parts.
The height of the base (*upāna*) should be by the portion of Śiva (one part), and the remainder is exactly as before.

Or else, O Brahmin, fashion the emergence of the pedestal (pīṭha) as a square on the ground; the measurement above that is said to be the height of the pedestal, which is one part. One should perform the entry and exit according to the method prescribed for the base (adhiṣṭhāna).
O Padmatārā, the auspicious lotus should be made with a pericarp measuring either one-fourth or one-fifth [of the total],
shaped like a pedestal or having four corners;
it may be made of metal, stone, or even brick.
Upon the *aṃśa*, construct the height of the *pīṭha* along with the *upapīṭha* and the *upānaha*.
Above that, however, the *mahāpīṭha* should be described as being provided with its *udaya*;
O best of the twice-born, it may be made even without a *pīṭha* upon the *upapīṭha*.
The eye, the taste, the element, and one Veda with its parts;
the quality, the Veda, and the eye, like the measurement of a sandal;
likewise, one Veda and a quality, the ear, and one [unit] like the eye.
One should fashion a single cluster of qualities (or a single pedestal) according to the measurement of the *balipīṭha*,
in front of the *prabhava* [pillar], with dimensions corresponding to the temple itself.
In front of that, however, is the location of the door, which is the temple of Śiva containing that vessel.
All these [deities] are on the peaceful Vṛṣācala, to the left of the gateway;
now I shall describe the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), specifically the characteristics of the sacrificial pedestal.
The best [measurement] is equal to the height of the *liṅga*; half of that would be the smallest.

By taking nine parts between those two, the intermediate measurement is proclaimed. Alternatively, the height of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) may be the smallest, and the width of the base (*pīṭha*) [may be the largest].
That which has sixteen [units] in the middle is to be known as the *tattāra*; that is remembered as the most excellent *astra*.
That which is half of that is to be known as the inferior; between those two, when divided by eight, the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is ninefold, and its height should be equal to that.
Alternatively, the width of the pedestal (pīṭha) equal to the width of the door is said to be the lowest;
twice that is the middling, and thrice that is the highest.
Alternatively, half the height of the door is the smallest width for the pedestal.

The middle [measurement] is said to be three-quarters [of the height], while that which is equal [to the height] is the best. Between the inferior and the superior, the ninth measurement is proclaimed; the inferior width of the pedestal (pīṭha) has a height equal to the surface of the earth.
The middle [measurement] is said to be threefold; between those two, when divided by eight, the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is ninefold, and its width should be equal to that.
The maximum width is three cubits, while the minimum is one cubit.
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) is proclaimed to be known as having two types of middling [proportions].
Starting from twenty-five finger-breadths (aṅgula) and increasing by two finger-breadths at a time,
the width of the pedestal is proclaimed to extend up to eighty-one finger-breadths.
The width outside the *upāna* is proclaimed as the best;
the width outside the *jagatī* is proclaimed as the middling;
the width at the end of the *kumuda* should be made [the smallest], and is remembered as the lowest.
Or rather, according to the very sequence described for the *prāsāda*, there is the emergence of the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*).
In the emergence of the great pedestal, when [the height] is divided into forty-seven parts,
the height of the base-moulding (*jagatī*) is one mountain-part (seven parts), and the height of the lotus-base (*kumuda*) is seven parts.
The portion of Śiva should be trembling (kampamāna), and the portion of Indra should be the emergence of the neck (galodaya).
The height of the trembling part is the portion of Śiva, while the emergence of the lotus-base (ambujodaya) is equal to that.
The height of the pigeon-ornament (kapota) is four parts, and the height of the entablature (prastara) is two parts.
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be one and a half units, with the elevation of the lotus being six and a half units;
the height of the pericarp (karṇikā) should be one-fourth of that, and its width should be double that [height].
Alternatively, the height of the pedestal may be divided into five parts. || 30.159–30.160 ||
One part shall be the height of the altar (vedikā), one part the height of the kumuda;
the height of the corner (karṇa) shall be three parts, and the height of the fillet (paṭṭikā) half a part.
One part shall be the height of the lotus (kamala), and half a part the height of the pericarp (karṇikā).
Its width should be double that, or even one-quarter greater.
When the establishment of the kitchen has been performed, including the *vāstu-homa* and other rites,
one should install a single water-pot (*kumbha*) upon heaps of grain as previously described.
One should first offer fuel-sticks (*samid*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the root-vidyā.
Then, one should perform the ritual placement of the principles (*tattvanyāsa*) for the deities residing therein.
One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and likewise bestow sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Having washed the various parts of the body, such as the garments and so forth, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana).
Then, at the time of dawn, during an auspicious moment, the preceptor shall cause the fire to be placed upon the hearths with the mantra "agnim īḷe."
The attendants should cook the oblations, such as the *pācana* and others.
And one who possesses a sacred fire (*agnimān*) should establish the fire in the *kuṇḍa* for the purpose of the daily *homa*,
preceded by the mantra as previously mentioned and with the mantra recited first.
One should install the deities, beginning with Caṇḍa, in sequence using the water from the ritual jar:
Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the door, Kṣetrapāla and Khageśvara [at the other], and also the leader of the Gaṇas on the southern side of the door. (30.168–169)

Jṛmbhala, Maṇibhadra, Śibi, and Kuṇḍala [should be placed] on the northern side of the door and in the other quarters in due order. At the door of the palace, like the door itself, there is the arrangement of Lakṣmī and the others.
On the left and right of the *culī*, one should place *dharma* and *adharma*;
likewise, on the back and on both sides of the long *culī*, one should install the Creator (*vidhātṛ*) as well as the pair of *dharma* and *adharma*. One should also arrange all the vessels.
Having sprinkled [the items] with the Śrīsūkta after repeated recitation, one should also perform auspicious rites;
the patron should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor according to his capacity. [This concludes the section on] the fruit of constructing a kitchen and other such structures.
Likewise, O Four-faced One, there is the bathing hall, the pavilion for flowers and water, the chamber for preparing betel, the music hall,
and whatever other site belonging to the temple complex has been designed by the most skilled artisans.
The preceptor shall perform the entire range of rituals, beginning with the Vāstuhoma, according to the procedures prescribed in the scriptures and in the manner previously described.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee for the preceptor must be given in accordance with one's wealth.
When the consecration of a large pond, a well, or a tank is desired to be performed,
one should construct an altar on their western side as previously described,
containing the heart-pleasing presiding deity of water, fashioned from small materials.
There, the best of preceptors should bathe [the image] with jars made of iron, using mantras dedicated to Varuṇa as the deity; thereafter, he should place it upon the bed.
He should worship it in the great jar, or again, in all four together at one place.
One should offer oblations into the sacrificial pits with mantras dedicated to those respective deities, using clarified butter and other substances.
Furthermore, the Brāhmaṇas should recite the Vāruṇa hymns in all directions.
At an auspicious moment at dawn, the site should be beautified with water as previously described.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited,
the Guru, with a one-pointed mind, should at the conclusion sprinkle the filled tank and other sites with nectar-like waters.
There, he should pour the water from the great jar (*mahākumbha*) and that which belongs to Varuṇa.
One should cast aquatic creatures such as fish and those born of water, as well as iron [images], into that [water].
There, one should invoke the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā into the water with mantras.
When the Brahmins have eaten and have been gratified with offerings according to one's wealth, [one should proceed].
A fee of at least ten niṣkas should then be given to the preceptor.
He who constructs a tank or the like, or establishes a reservoir of water,
dwells for a very long time in the world of Varuṇa, eternally satisfied.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Marriage of Lakṣmī and Others and the Consecration of the Vimāna and Other Structures," in the Kriyāpāda of the Pādmasaṃhitā within the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the thirty-first chapter.
The Ritual for the Installation of Prabhā and Others:
The Blessed One states that the ritual for the installation of Prabhā and others will be described at a later time.
Having performed all the rites, such as the preliminary consecration in water (*jalādhivāsa*), according to the established procedure,
when the time for meditation arrives, the Guru himself should meditate thus:
[upon her] who is enriched by thousands of garlands of flames and resembles a mass of lightning.
Having meditated upon the radiance, one should touch [the disciple] with the clarified butter from the fire-oblation at the conclusion of the pacifying rite (śāntihoma).
At dawn, one should sprinkle [him] with the water from the ritual jar using the root mantra.
One should also join him during the auspicious moment (muhūrta) and cause a great festival to be held.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor according to one's means and with respect.
One should join the gods, goddesses, and others within the light (prabhā) according to the prescribed path;
he attains union (sāyujya) as well as all desired objects according to his wishes.
Having established the pedestal right there, the Guru should install the yogic seat (yogāsana).
Having offered oblations with the mantras in due order, such is the procedure for the installation of the lotus.
Furthermore, at the proper time, the Guru should join the pedestal and other components situated therein.
The person who thus prepares [the site] for the sake of the deities of the *pīṭhas* and so forth attains eternal consecration both here and in the next world.
[This applies to] the consecration of the bell and other such rites.
Having bathed the bell with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the prescribed mantras of the five Varuṇas, one should wrap it in a new cloth. Then,
having placed a load of śāli rice, along with sesame seeds and rice grains, upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), || 31.8–31.9 ||
Having placed a new cloth together with *darbha* grass upon that [altar] above,
and having laid the bell there, one should cover it with a new cloth.
Having worshipped a single water-pot, [one should place it] either in the pot or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

The preceptor should offer oblations with the *ghaṇṭā* mantra using fuel sticks and other materials. He should perform the rites of drying and so forth, and then meditate upon what has been described.
At the conclusion of the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), he should touch the [image] with the sacrificial clarified butter.
At dawn, one should sprinkle it with mantra-water preceded by the recitation of mantras.
Having thus consecrated the bell thoroughly, one should ring it in all ritual activities—
at the opening of the door, as well as when worship is about to commence.

The movement of the jewel [is prescribed] during the invocation, the offering of water (arghya), the bathing, the presentation of flowers, incense, and lamps; during the waving of lights (nīrājana), the removal of the curtain, the offering of food (naivedya), the oblation (homa), the bali-offering to the spirits, and at the rite of marriage. (31.14–31.15)
The eradication of piśācas and other malevolent spirits, the supreme gratification of Hari,
and the presence of the immortals— these result from the movement of the bell.
If it moves while un-consecrated, the movement of the village and its inhabitants will occur.
Furthermore, worship offered to another who is the Supreme Self would be fruitless.
(31.17) If one offers a bell to Hari, that man becomes renowned;
the consecration of the incense and lamp vessels is performed in the same manner as the consecration of the bell. (31.18)
The purification of drums and similar instruments with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) is praised;
this same purification is prescribed for all types of vehicles, such as chariots.
Purification by sprinkling with mantras is also desired for paintings and other such objects.
One should feed Brahmins everywhere and also cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be performed;
furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor according to one's means.
O Lotus-born One, the consecration of the rosary, the method of its consecration, its various types as they truly are,
and the entire fruit of recitation— all this is now being told.

One should have rosaries made from all kinds of gems, metals, and even the three types of crystal; or likewise from things produced in water or on land. For the rite of recitation (*japa*), beads the size of a joint of the finger-bone are considered the best.
O Lotus-Seated One, beads the size of the kernel of a dhātrī fruit are considered middling;
those the size of a jujube stone are known as the smallest.
A count of one hundred and eight beads is most auspicious.

Half that number is said to be the middle [count], while the final [count] consists of twenty-seven; with these, one should make a rosary. This jewel, made of gold, bestows heaven and liberation, and grants prosperity.
Silver bestows fame and wealth; copper brings about peace.
Recitation performed with beads of tin or gems brings even the yakṣas under one's control.
O Four-faced One, by means of a rosary of lead beads, one may bring the rākṣasas under one's power.
Likewise, one should afflict enemies with [beads] of bell-metal and bring them all under control.
With those of iron, the reciter may bring even spirits under his own power.
A crystal [bead] grants liberation to the one who recites, while the gem of the sun (sūryakānta) bestows everything.
Likewise, the beads may be made of crystal, or again, of lotus seeds;
the *putradīpa* grants sons, while the *indrākṣa* fulfills all desires.
Beads made of *vibhītaka*, *rudrākṣa*, or *nimba* are used for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).

A knot of *kuśa* grass is recommended for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). For one desiring a kingdom, [the rosary] made of lotus seeds ensures that his goal is certainly accomplished. A rosary of white lotus seeds, however, bestows the highest beatitude upon the one who recites [the mantra].
A conch-shell rosary bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; a pearl rosary bestows the fruit of liberation.
Thus, a rosary made of water-born gems yields such fruits for the one who recites the mantra. Having gathered the prescribed seeds—round and free from defects— [one should proceed].
Having washed it with the five products of the cow and with the knowledge of the five Vedāntas,
one should place it upon a triple-stranded golden thread that has been multiplied threefold,
or on a silver, linen, or hemp thread, provided it is free from hair and other impurities.
Just as when cotton is obtained, washed, and thoroughly purified,
[the beads] are joined to one another— back to back and face to face— with similar, auspicious gems.
With a thread or with gold, one should likewise fashion an interval in the middle;
then, upon those strung threads, a necklace in the shape of a bracelet should be fashioned.
Furthermore, one should fasten another, even larger, gem at the knot of the necklace.
The movement of that jewel known as Meru should be to the right.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) at the end, O Four-faced One, one should place the rosary within the interior of a lotus,
having smeared that rosary with saffron and other substances.
Having placed a load of śāli rice mixed with sesame and grain,
and having drawn a lotus-wheel there and spread out kuśa grass and cloth,
one should place a rosary upon it and cover it with a new garment.
One should perform the sacrifice in a water-pot (*kumbha*) provided with gold, cloth, and other offerings, reciting that mantra;
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in a single location, either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or even upon a leveled altar (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should offer eight hundred oblations of sacrificial wood (*samit*), cooked rice (*caru*), and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) while reciting one's own *vidyā*.
Having performed the drying and other [purificatory rites] through meditation, and having restored everything else as before,
one should meditate upon the Person situated in the center of that [lotus], standing with palms joined in reverence,
four-armed, with the luster of a reddish-brown bear, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Bearing a rosary in the form of a bracelet at the tip of his topknot,
the Guru should touch the rosary at the conclusion of the peace-offering (śānti-homa).
When the auspicious moment (muhūrta) has arrived, he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the principles (tattvas) according to the order of emanation.
Having first meditated upon that supreme power of Viṣṇu, which is non-different from the Supreme Self,
as resembling the sun in brilliance within the lotus of the heart,
one should then contemplate her as she slowly ascends from the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
Having invoked [the deity] with its own mantra over the rosary,
the preceptor, who knows the mantras, should sprinkle it with water from the pitcher using the root mantra.
He should then request the presence of the Supreme Self within the rosary.
May you take up residence here out of a desire to show grace to your devotees. Reciting this prayer with deep devotion over a rosary of *japā* beads,
one should meditate upon the Lord Janārdana holding that rosary there.
The Guru himself should place [the gift] into the hand of the disciple who is the patron;
having prostrated, the latter should receive it with his head, being composed in mind.
He should give the teacher’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā) according to his wealth, as one would offer knowledge.
At that moment, he should recite that vidyā with a rosary of beads. Since the Guru had previously established the mantra upon the rosary of Yama,
he should count that very mantra [with it] and never otherwise.
"If a man performs recitation out of delusion with a rosary that has not been consecrated at its end, he does not obtain any fruit whatsoever.
Thus [ends the section] in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Pādma-saṃhitā*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
The thirty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of the Radiance-Bell and Rosary";
the thirty-second chapter: "The Ritual for Domestic Worship."
In this regard, O Lotus-Seated One, I shall duly describe the installation of the household image, including the distinctions of metal, wood, and other materials, as well as the resulting fruits.
The image of the twice-born may be made of gold or silver;
or it may be made of brass, or it may be made of copper.
All images fashioned from metal bestow the fruits of all desires.
A wise person should not worship an image made of stone or wood in their own home.
An iron image is considered effective for subjugating piśācas and other spirits;
O Lotus-Seated One, a bronze image brings about eradication.
An image made of the three metals (triloha) conquers enemies; one made of lead brings about disease.
All images fashioned from jewels grant the fruits of all desires.
An image made of moonstone or crystal is considered to be gentle in nature.
The *mitramaṇi* stone is born from fire; others are of two kinds, born from crystal.
The white *sālagrāma* stone is lunar (*saumya*) and bestows lunar fruits.
The yellow-colored one is considered to bring prosperity (*śrī*), and the red one is held to grant desires.
The black stone always bestows nourishment, while the tawny stone always brings disease.
All stones originating from the Cakra mountain grant the fruit of liberation;
all stones born from the Cakra river are filled with divine forms.
O Lotus-seated One, they are marked by their manifestations beginning with the Fish, as well as by divine weapons and ornaments such as the Kaustubha gem; thus adorned,
they are to be worshipped by those who seek the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
All stones originating from the Svāyambhuva mountain and from the Cakrasaras river should be known as such.
In these, there is the eternal presence of the Supreme Self;
therefore, no ritual installation (pratiṣṭhā) is to be performed, nor the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites.
In whatever place the Śālagrāma stone is worshipped by those who are absorbed in the Lord,
within a distance of one *yojana* of that region, one who dies attains liberation.
Furthermore, the stones from Dvāravatī are equal to the Śālagrāma stones.
An image made of wood should be honored according to one's desire.
An image made of sandalwood, when worshipped, brings prosperity;
an image made of agalloch wood bestows the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation.
An image made of devadāru wood, when worshipped in one's home, bestows everything;
an image fashioned from bilva wood shall always bring about incomparable prosperity (lakṣmī).
One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) [should use] one produced from the brahma-tree.
An image made of *śamī* wood leads to heaven; one made of *nameru* wood shall be a giver of happiness.
An image fashioned from *udumbara* wood should be worshipped by those desiring food and other such things;
one fashioned from *aśvattha* wood should be worshipped in the temple by one who desires a kingdom.
An image fashioned from *nyagrodha* wood, when worshipped in every dwelling, brings about all things;
one made from *plakṣa* bestows the wealth of life and provides all necessary implements.
An image fashioned from *priyaṅgu*, when worshipped in the home, brings about prosperity and subjugation.

One should worship the straightforward ritual of worship, which consists of the lamp of sons, which brings about sons, and likewise grants liberation; it is joined with the accomplishment of mantras and other rites,
and like a Tamāla or Jāti flower, it brings happiness to all the worlds.

An *ārogyadā* [image] made of mango wood bestows sons and wealth; one made of *badarī* wood likewise grants these. O Brahmin, an image resembling a *panasa* fruit, when worshipped, grants many sons. A milky tree (*kṣīriṇī*) should be known as a giver of wealth, and a *saptalā* plant destroys suffering.
The *jātija* image bestows wealth; the *spandaja* is the cause of happiness.
O Brahmin, the *timija* bestows wealth, while the *kadamba* is the cause of knowledge. The *kurava* grants the fruit of nourishment, and the *tilaka* fulfills all desires.
They say that the *madhūka* tree bestows success, while the *asana* tree always brings prosperity.
The *jambu* tree grants nourishment, and the *punnāga* increases one's well-being.
The *roga* and *rājavṛkṣa* trees are beneficial, and the *khadira* tree destroys eye ailments.
An image made from a *nimba* tree is considered to cause enmity.
O Lotus-Seated One, an image made from *vibhītaka* or *śālmalī* is also prescribed;
likewise, an amulet fashioned from the root of the white *arka* tree uprooted by an elephant [is effective].
The Vaināyaka [image], which accomplishes all desired aims,
is measured for domestic worship according to the number of finger-breadths (mātrāṅguli);
it should not exceed one cubit (hasta) in measurement, nor be less than twelve finger-breadths.
In the home, a *kautuka* made of stone, wood, or other materials should certainly be worshipped.
The measurement of the images for the various castes is stated in sequence according to finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
An image measuring one cubit (*hasta*) may be worshipped in the home by those of previous births [the twice-born].
The image of a lord of the earth should be twenty-one finger-breadths;
that of a Vaiśya, nineteen; and that of a Śūdra, two less than that (seventeen), being inferior.
Likewise, an image that is half-painted or merely an appearance increases one's enjoyment in the home.
An image made of metal for one's previous birth should measure twelve finger-breadths;
that of a Kṣatriya should be nine finger-breadths, that of a Vaiśya seven finger-breadths,
and the image for the fourth caste (Śūdra) should be five finger-breadths in the home.
Whatever material the image is fashioned from, its radiance, pedestal, and so forth, are composed of that same substance;
or else, for an image of gold, there may be silver or even copper.
If the image should be constructed from a superior metal, [the other parts should likewise correspond].
Immediately thereafter, one should fashion the halo, pedestal, and so forth from copper.
In the case of an image made of the three metals, the halo and other parts may be made of gold;
however, for images made of gems or crystal, the halo and other parts [should be made of those same materials].

One should never worship the form of the Lord in the state of dissolution (saṃhāraśayana) at home; however, all other forms of the Blessed One may be worshipped according to the prescribed rule. The Lord should be worshipped together with Śrī and Bhūmi, or with Śrī alone.
One should always worship [the Lord] together with [the Goddess] with devotion, O Padmaniketana. Regarding the specification of the place of worship in the home:
it is taught that the place of worship in the house is in the north-eastern direction (māruti), and not otherwise.
The patron should worship the image in the temples as prescribed.
For the purpose of its consecration, he should honor the preceptor and bring him to his home,
or to a courtyard, a riverbank, or a well-honored field.
Having prepared four sacrificial pits (homakuṇḍa) around the altar,
or in a single one, the Guru should perform the rite of installation as before; first,
having offered the sprouts (aṅkura), he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in water.

One should also perform the opening of the eyes according to the previously mentioned method. [Then one offers] water for the feet (pādya), the arghya offering, water for sipping (ācamana), as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), curd,
milk, honey, astringent decoction (kaṣāya), warm water, and water infused with fruit.
O Lotus-born One, one should bathe [the deity] in this sequence with water for cleansing, water for sprinkling, jewel-water, iron-water, scented water, and barley-water,
using the *Nṛsūkta* as well as the verse beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."

The wise one should perform the ceremonial bathing with mantras according to the path previously described. The preceptor himself should personally carry out the rites for the bed and other such matters, as well as the entire cycle of activities, in accordance with the procedure for the great consecration (mahā-pratiṣṭhā).
At the site where the image is to be installed, preceded by the depositing of jewels and other rites,
when the auspicious moment (muhūrta) has arrived, one should place the desired stationary image in that location and then perform the invocation (āvāhana) and subsequent ceremonies.
If a mobile [form] is desired, one should perform the invocation and other rites upon the altar;
thereafter, one should stabilize it in its place according to the prescribed rule.
One should [place] Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa at the Valaja, and Kṣetrapāla at Khageśvara.
One should there visualize Vighneśa, Vāstunātha, or Durgā,
as well as Guha, Viṣvaksena, and the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
Then, urged by the preceptor, one should oneself prostrate on the ground like a staff.
The sacrificer should pray for that which he desires in its entirety:
"I am your servant, O Lord of Gods, together with my sons, attendants, and kinsmen.
Be present in my home, O Acyuta, for as long as my lineage shall endure. (32.50–51)

"Accept, O Blessed One, this worship offered by me according to my ability, though it be incomplete, out of your desire to show favor to your devotees. Having thus entreated the Lord of the Gods of gods in the presence of the preceptor, [he remained there].
One should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor according to the extent of one's wealth (32.53),
so that he may be satisfied, as was previously done for the officiating priests; and one should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability and give them a sacrificial fee as well (32.54).
Having installed [the image], the devotee should worship the God who is kind to his devotees.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, he is not reborn here after death.
Viṣṇu, when installed in a temple, nourishes his own lineage.

When Hari is installed in a temple, he nourishes the entire world. Having duly established the fourfold primary ornaments of Viṣṇu— the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha, the crown, and the garland of forest flowers— according to the prescribed rite.
Having first placed the Śrīvatsa upon a load of rice together with its cloth,
and having established the dissolution and the creation, the Guru should worship the great jar (mahākumbha) in a pit fashioned in the shape of a lotus using the Śrīvatsa mantra.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with fuel-sticks, parched grain, and sacrificial porridge.
Having performed the rite of pacification (*śānti*), one should deposit the principles (*tattvas*) that many times;
then, having sprinkled [the image] with water from the pitcher, one should touch it for a moment upon the chest of Hari.
One should cause [the image] to be installed, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of no less than three niṣkas should be given to the preceptor by the patron to increase his mental satisfaction.
[This is] the fruit of the preparation of ornaments for the Blessed One.

He who adorns the Lord of Gods with the decoration of the Śrīvatsa mark obtains eternal and supreme prosperity; there is no doubt in this matter. Having established the Kaustubha gem in its proper place according to its own mantra as before, [he attains the same].
At that moment, the most excellent preceptor should fashion Hari with that [material].
And the patron should present an auspicious sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru;
he who adorns the Lord of Gods with the Kaustubha gem attains prosperity.

Having placed a golden forest-garland (*vanamālā*), adorned with various jewels, upon the neck of Viṣṇu according to the prescribed method during an auspicious moment, the preceptor should hang it there; this brings all prosperity to men.
The sacrificer should also give a bountiful sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor.
And that man who adorns the Lord of Śrī with a garland of forest flowers attains all desires that are difficult to obtain; of this there is no doubt.
Having departed this life, he enjoys vast and imperishable worlds such as heaven;
with a mind endowed with devotion, he [receives] a crown made of pure Jāmbūnada gold, inlaid with jewels, as is fitting for the Slayer of Madhu.
Having established [the deities] with seventeen jars according to one's own mantra,
having placed them upon loads of śāli rice and wrapped them with a new,
unwashed cloth, one should again worship the jar, having invoked [the deity] with the mantra.
The Guru should perform oblations in the four directions with his own Vidyā-mantra;

and at the conclusion of the peace-offering (śāntihoma), having touched [the disciple] in the morning and sprinkled him with the water from the ritual jar (kumbha) using his own mantra, he should give the teacher’s fee (gurudakṣiṇā).
When the auspicious moment has arrived, one should bathe the Lord of Gods, who is seated upon a cushion of earth, like a king, after worshipping him with ornaments suitable for the ritual;
and [one should do so] while Brāhmaṇas learned in all four Vedas are present on every side.
While various musical instruments resounded in the four directions,
and while those bowing before the Lord of Gods praised Hari— who was accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi— with intense and diverse hymns of praise, they remained deeply bowed in devotion.
While other auspicious rites were being performed on all sides,
having offered oblations into the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in front as before with fuel-sticks and other materials,
[the officiants] stood at the four gates in the four directions, situated one cubit away from the fire.
The preceptors and the wise guardians of the image should place the crown upon the head of the deity with the five Upaniṣadic mantras;
they should also release a rain of flowers preceded by the sounding of musical instruments.
Having honored Hari with great services and with his preceptor,
and having given wealth to the Brahmins, he placed him— who was seated comfortably on a great throne—
upon a vehicle drawn by elephants and other animals, resplendent with a white parasol.
While being fanned on all sides with a white yak-tail whisk,
one should lead [the image] clockwise around the village and install it in the temple. Whoever would adorn the Lord with a crown and divine ornaments, [attains great merit].
He attains sovereignty over all the three worlds.
[He should worship] with ornaments made of gold, beginning with necklaces and ending with anklets,
which have been washed with scented water using the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra.
Having placed [the image] upon heaps of grain and performed a fire sacrifice (homa) with sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials,
the preceptor (deśika), having touched it, should recite the twelve-syllable mantra for an entire kalpa.
During that auspicious moment (muhūrta), he should adorn the Lord of Gods with that very vidyā-mantra.
He who adorns the Lord of Gods also attains his desires.
Now, the installation (pratiṣṭhā) of the five divine weapons, beginning with the measurement for the five weapons, shall be described.
O Lotus-seated One, the installation of the Cakra, which is the foremost among all [deities],
shall now be described— its measurement and its form;
it should be one cubit in extent, or seventeen finger-breadths.
It should be eighteen finger-breadths, or twenty finger-breadths,
or fourteen finger-breadths, or sixteen or twelve finger-breadths;
it should be equal in size to the face of the primary image, possessing a thousand spokes and being brilliantly radiant.
Or else it may have a hundred spokes, or be endowed with twenty-four spokes;
or twelve spokes, or eight spokes, or even six spokes at most;
or it may have a thousand flames, or six flames, adorned with a central hub.
Having fashioned a discus made of the three metals, complete with a hub and pedestal,
or bearing a crown and a basket,
one should visualize the Sudarśana as four-armed, wrathful, and with a face contorted by a frown.
One should visualize the Puruṣa with two arms; alternatively, he may have the right hand in the threatening gesture (tarjanī),
while the other touches his hip, and the two principal hands are joined in añjali,
as he stands firmly upon a lotus seat.
Having first performed the ritual acceptance (*adhivāsya*) in the water, then having placed [the deity] in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*),
and having laid [him] upon the bed, one should worship [him] in the jar (*kumbha*) with one's own mantra,
while meditating upon the exceedingly fierce Puruṣa, who has two arms and is clad in red garments.
The Guru should visualize such a seat of red fangs situated at the navel.
O Lotus-seated One, the guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ) should offer oblations of fuel-sticks and sacrificial porridge into the fire-pits in the four directions with the Cakra-mantra.
In one of the pits, having worshipped the archways and so forth in front as before,
one should then dry the wheel with the *śoṣaṇa* (drying) and other rites.
Having touched the parts beginning with the nave in sequence at the conclusion of the peace-offering (*śānti-homa*), [one should proceed].

At the auspicious moment (muhūrta), he should sprinkle [the vessel] with water from the pitcher while reciting his own mantra. Then the preceptor should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhāpana) of the other four vessels, beginning with the conch, in due order using their respective mantras.
A fee of at least ten niṣkas should then be given to the preceptor.
That wise man who, having fashioned the five weapons, installs them,
does not fear anything anywhere within the three worlds.
He enjoys extensive pleasures and rejoices in the third heaven.
Now the procedure for the installation of the gatekeepers, Caṇḍa and the others, is described:
first, the preliminary ritual of immersion in water, and likewise the ceremonial bathing in the pavilion.
The reclining upon the bed, the worship in a single jar,

and the fire-oblation in four pits— or in one pit, O Lotus-born One— likewise the ritual placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa), as well as the touching of the limbs during the propitiatory oblation (śānti-homa).
One should perform the sprinkling with water from the jar and with the Vidyā using one's own seed-syllable.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should also be given to the Guru according to one's means.
By installing Caṇḍa and the others, a mortal attains this very same form.
The installation of Vainateya and others:
regarding the installation of Vainateya, the specific details will now be stated.
Then, while offering oblations in the east with the Bṛhat Sāman, the Guru should meditate upon Satya.
In the south, one should invoke Suparṇa with the Sauparṇī Vidyā;
in the west, one should meditate upon Garuḍa in the fire-pit while offering oblations with the Rathantara Sāmans.
In the north, there is meditation on Tārkṣya, and the oblation is offered with the Gāyatrī and its own [mantra].
In front and above, the auspicious rite should be performed as before.
The consecrator of Vainateya attains proximity to him;
and the installation of the Sun-god should also be carried out according to the ancient tradition.
A certain distinction is now stated; understand it correctly:
the invocation is performed with one's own *gāyatrī*, and with that same [verse] the oblation is offered into the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*).
The installation is likewise performed with the *anuvāka* beginning with "bibhrāt" and with the *sāvitrī*.
The consecration with water from the pitcher using the root-mantra of the Sun—
the installer of that [image] shines in that world, freed from all sins,
just as [he would shine] before all the deities beginning with Brahmā. || 32.110–32.111 ||
Whether in cases of independence or dependence, the installation should be performed with their own respective mantras.
As for Durgā, the seven Mothers, and whatever other female deities there may be,
their consecration is distinguished by their own individual mantras, just like that of Lakṣmī.
Regarding the origin and installation of Viṣvaksena:
O Blessed One, from what cause did the birth of Viṣvaksena arise?
If you would grant me favor, please tell me how his installation is to be performed.
O Blessed One,
among all the doorkeepers, he who is the first, Caṇḍa—
In the war between the gods and the asuras, that powerful wielder of the staff himself,
impelled by his own nature, slew the Daityas for the sake of the gods.
Pleased with him, I granted him a form identical to my own.
[He granted] the sovereignty of Kumuda and the others, as well as unimpeded strength,
and the title "Viṣvaksena," which is appropriate for a commander-in-chief of all armies;
and [he received] the fourth part of all the food offerings presented by me.
"And in the place of Caṇḍa, I have established another who is exceedingly fierce.
Thus, O Brahmin, is his origin; he is to be installed in my presence, and his installation is to be performed with his own mantra, just as one's own [is performed]. (32.117–118)
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor as well as to the installer;
having performed the installation for each image, one should carry out the rite for the sake of the devotees.
Whether independent or dependent, [the image] should be fashioned from stone or other materials according to what is available.
With palms joined in reverence, gentle, whether standing or seated,
according to his caste, according to his form, and according to the duties of his stage of life,
he was established upon a lotus throne, bearing the appearance appropriate to his age.

One should have it fashioned by craftsmen so that it is endowed with the correct characteristics and well-examined; or else, one should construct a replica in accordance with the specific ritual action. First, having offered [the seeds], one should establish the sprouts on an auspicious day.
Odd-numbered *pālikās* should be prepared, excluding the *śarāva* and the *ghaṭa*.
From the commencement of the consecration (*adhivāsana*) onwards, the ritual procedure (*karmapaddhati*) is as before;
likewise the ritual service (*upacāra*), the fire offering (*homa*), the sacrifice of the jar (*kumbhayāga*), and the sprinkling (*secanam*).
After the Supreme Brahman has been worshipped with other well-consecrated mantras,
one should first worship the archways (toraṇas) and so forth, but not yet the altar or the water-pots (kalaśas).
At the auspicious moment (muhūrta), the best of preceptors should sprinkle them with the water from the pot.
If it is to be independent, the temple should be constructed without images of lions or the [eight] directions.
For the sake of attaining success in mantra, one should install an image of the initiating guru.
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the guru, and the brahmins should be gratified with offerings.
The gratification of Brahmins with wealth is unavoidable in every case,
as is the recitation for an auspicious day by the Brahmins and likewise the study of one's own Vedic texts.
Furthermore, there should be a heavy sacrificial fee for the preceptor, appropriate to the wealth of the patron.
One who is endowed with these qualities as described is not corrupted by anything else;
O Brahmin, there is no doubt in this matter regarding the establishment of the counter-embodiments (pratikāyas) and their daily worship with various kinds of ritual offerings.
The festival should also be performed, though excluding the hoisting of the banner;
there is no fire-offering, no ritual oblation, and no pilgrimage—such is the rule for independence.
But for devotees in a state of dependence, O Lotus-Seated One, there is the festival.
When the festival of the god has begun or has been commenced,
and when that ritual act has been performed, Janārdana is indeed pleased with the king,
the entire kingdom, the brahmins, and even the cows.
"When a festival has been performed, even greater prosperity arises.
Thus, O Brahmin, all the rites have been described to you as you requested.
Out of supreme compassion, what else do you wish to hear?
The conclusion of the scripture:
Saṃvarta said, "This Mahopaniṣad is a scripture endowed with the four Vedas."
Having condensed that which was heard from Kapila in one hundred chapters,
Kaṇva further condensed it for you, who are full of faith; thus,
this auspicious work, consisting of thirty-two chapters, is indeed the most essential of all.
"This scripture was heard from Padma, and thus it is considered to be named after Padma.
And this supreme secret should be given to one who is free from malice, faithful, devoted, pure, and initiated. (32.137)
One should not speak of this knowledge to a Brāhmaṇa who has sought refuge, nor to a learned and wise man,
nor to one's eldest son, nor to an enemy of knowledge.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, the friend of Brahmā, the bearer of Śrī, the imperishable Self,
who is the embodiment of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and who possesses a hundred forms.
Thus ends [the section] in the Kriyāpāda of the Pādmasaṃhitā within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
In the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Saṃvarta, the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Household Deity," which constitutes the Kriyāpāda, is completed.
The Pādmasaṃhitā; in the Śrī Pāñcarātra, the fourth section of the Pādmasaṃhitā, the Caryāpāda.
Chapter One.
Śrī Brahmā said:
The ritual acts, beginning with the plowing and ending with the consecration, are accomplished through him.
I now wish to hear the procedure for propitiating him.
O Blessed One, who are compassionate toward your devotees, tell me in its entirety: what is the method of propitiation, and what is the requisite qualification?
The Blessed Lord said: Listen, for I shall explain in its entirety that which you have asked—
the primordial Veda of the Single Path (Ekāyana), which establishes Brahman.
By that very [initiation], the Brahmins become consecrated and entitled to the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*).
For others—the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—entitlement is attained through initiation in due order; it belongs even to those born in the *anuloma* (natural) order, but to no one else.
In the ritual for the worship of the Lord, the Supreme Self,
the Sūta born in the inverse order (pratiloma) is praised as the foremost among the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriya who are born in the natural order (anuloma). || 1.5–1.6 ||
And especially for the Sūta, the initiation into the Self [should be performed] incessantly;
the Brahmins of both the primary and secondary classes should perform the sacrifice for the sake of others.
Those who are devoid of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) are not qualified, being merely secondary.
Just as Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are born from the initiatory rites (*dīkṣaṇīya*),
so too those who are born according to the prescribed rule of initiation are designated as qualified participants in the ritual worship of the Blessed One.
"O Blessed One, the birth and the deeds of the Brahmins and others are destined; even without that marriage, whatever it may be, however many there may be, and of whatever nature they are. (1.10)
"O Supreme Lord, you ought to instruct me, your devotee who desires to know, regarding all that in accordance with its true nature. (1.11) The Blessed Lord said:
"O Lotus-seated One, the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—exist.
Assuming a body composed of these, I created living beings in the past. When sattva was predominant, I emitted from my mouth the Brahmins, who exist in pairs."
When the quality of rajas was predominant, I created the Kṣatriyas from my two arms; likewise, through the equilibrium of the qualities, I created the pair of Vaiśyas from my thighs;
and when tamas was predominant, I created the Śūdras in the form of pairs from my feet.
And these castes are superior, each preceding one as previously described;
their superiority among them is established by two reasons: birth and action.
Among them, the first three are twice-born by virtue of the rite of binding the girdle of muñja grass.

And all four stages of life, O Brahmin, belong to the twice-born. Having been initiated by a preceptor and having first performed the observance of vows, the study of the Vedas is that which is the first stage of life, the most excellent. (1.16–1.17)
Having bathed, one should next take a wife for the sake of progeny;
likewise, the practice of dharma constitutes the second stage of life (āśrama). Then, having gone to the forest with his wife by the very path prescribed, [he should enter the third stage].

Subsisting on wild fruits in the forest and having achieved restraint over the senses—O Lotus-Seated One, this should be known as the third stage of life (*āśrama*) in the forest. Having entrusted his wife to his son, he becomes a *śikhin* (wearing a topknot), shaven-headed, and carries the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*). || 1.19–20 ||
Or else, devoted to the single staff, intent on meditation upon Brahman,
and with all desires ceased, the twice-born may dwell in the fourth stage of life (turyāśrama).
For a Kṣatriya, the previous stages of life exist, excluding the stage of renunciation (saṃnyāsa).
For one [Vaiśya], two wives are ordained, both facing forward (eastward) and not toward the west. And for the Śūdra, there is only one wife, consisting of the act of taking a spouse.
The Brāhmaṇa is to be known as one who possesses six duties through his actions, such as teaching and so forth.
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving gifts—these are the six duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa).
For the king, however, his livelihood consists of only three: giving gifts, studying, and sacrificing.
For the Vaiśyas, that same service is the sole way of life for the Śūdra.
Faith, straightforwardness, purity, austerity, self-control, tranquility, forbearance,
knowledge, and realized wisdom— these are the innate qualities of the Brāhmaṇa.
Valor, splendor, fortitude, audacity, and not fleeing in battle,
as well as generosity and lordliness— these are the duties of the kṣatriya, born of his own nature.
Agriculture, trade, and the protection of cattle likewise [are the duties of the vaiśya].
The natural duty of Vaiśyas is service to those born from the feet [of Brahmā]. The Śūdra’s wives are his female slave and his own; these are said to be the wives of the Vaiśya.
These [wives] and his own are the wives of the lord of the earth [the Kṣatriya]; and these and his own are the wives of the one born first [the Brāhmaṇa].
One's own offspring born of women of the same caste is known as the *cāturvarṇya*;
others, born of paramours, are designated as *kūṇḍa* and *golaka*.
These castes produced by paramours are born of women of their own respective castes who are timid.
The son of a woman who has another husband is a *kuṇḍa*, and the son of a widow is a *golaka*.
For these two, among those unfit for the Veda, the triad of activities beginning with teaching is forbidden.
A Kṣatriya woman of the same caste who is married by a Brāhmaṇa [produces] a physician.

Having been initiated with the sacred mantras, he should study Āyurveda; there, one born of theft becomes a practitioner of the Jyotiṣaveda. Having studied the science of astrology (jyotirvidyā) and having been initiated with the mantras...
From a Brāhmaṇa man and a Vaiśya woman who has been married to him, an Ambaṣṭha is born, also known as a Śalyakṛntaka (flesh-cutter).
His tonsure is prescribed to be above the navel, and his livelihood is ordained to be that of a potter, making pots and such items through the work of a thief. (1.34–1.35)
An image made of clay should also be fashioned according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
One born from a Śūdra woman married by a Brāhmaṇa is known as a Pāraśava. Worship of the seven mothers and the playing of musical instruments [are also permitted].

His livelihood shall be that of a Niṣāda; moreover, he becomes a slayer of wild animals through theft. Both the Kuṇḍa and the Golaka, born from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother who was previously married to another, are fit for the binding of a turban. He subsists by means of cattle-pens and trade.
One born through adultery from a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is a Māhiṣya and should be a horse-merchant.
One born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother is an Ugra; if born of a married woman (vinnā), he is a Karibandhaka.
One born through adultery [from such a union] is to be known as a Śūlika, whose livelihood consists of impaling criminals on stakes.
The jeweler and the shell-worker are two types of merchants; the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka* are born from a Śūdra woman by a Vaiśya father.
From a Vaiśya father on a *vinna*-Śūdra woman is born one who lives by gambling and other such means;
among them, the *kaṭakara* lives by theft, and his livelihood consists of making mats.
The Mālava and the Aśvapāla are always two types of horse-keepers born from a Śūdra woman.
An Ābhīra, who is a keeper of cattle and other animals, may be born from a Brāhmaṇa through an Ambaṣṭhī woman.
A Viloka, a chariot-maker, and a Kṣattṛ are born from a Brāhmaṇa through a Pāraśava woman.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karṇī mother is born a Rathakāra, a maker of chariots and such;
he is skilled in all crafts and is called a teacher of them.
Now, the livelihood of the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas who have become Vrātyas is described.
Slaying, decoration, security, and likewise crossing the ocean;
from a Kṣatriya by a Brāhmaṇī woman through marriage is born the Sūta, who is of the pratiloma class. Charioteering is his livelihood, as well as the instruction in the sacred laws (dharmas).
In the case of the investiture with the sacred thread (*upavīta-upanayana*), it indeed occurs accompanied by mantras.
From theft in that very rite, another [son] is born as a Sūta; he is the one who performs other sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*).
From a Vaiśya father on her [the Niṣāda woman], through marriage, a Vaidehaka is born, who is a washerman (*vastra-śuddhi-kṛt*).

From a Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇa woman, whether through marriage or even by stealth, is born the Māgadha, who subsists by the profession of a thief and acts as a messenger on foot. From the same union,
the Caṇḍāla is born— his eyes like those of a jhallarī drum— he is the one who performs tasks such as the removal of filth.

From a Vaiśya father and a woman wedded to a Kṣatriya, an Āyogava is born, who works as a weaver. From the same [Vaiśya] father and a Śūdra mother, an Āraṇya is born; from a Śūdra father and a Kṣatriya mother, a Pulinda is born, a hunter of wild animals. From a Śūdra father and a married Kṣatriya woman, a Pulkasa is born, who makes wooden liquor-vessels.

By a Vaiśya through illicit union with a Śūdra woman who has married a Vaiśya, there is born a Takṣan, who subsists by carving wood and similar crafts. He may also be a maker of bronze and gold, a Tvaṣṭṛ, living by manual labor.

He is to be known as a nail-maker, a dyer of blue cloth, and so forth. He alone may be a keeper of livestock; however, from a Śūdra by a Vaiśya woman is born a Cakrin, an oil-presser, a forger, and a cremator of corpses.
From a Brāhmaṇa and an Ambaṣṭhī is born an Āyogava, whose livelihood is that of a barber for the lower castes.
Through both the inverse (pratiloma) and the natural (anuloma) orders— from the inverse and the natural—
many mixed castes have arisen, such as the Ābhīra tribes and others.
"They are described not according to their essential nature, because that is of no use for the present context.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of Birth," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Chapter Two:
The Ritual of Initiation (Dīkṣā-vidhi) by Brahmā.
O Puruṣottama, those who are qualified for initiation and those who are excluded from it have been described by you in their entirety and according to the truth. Now,
I have a desire to know the true nature of initiation.
You ought to explain that essential nature which unfolds [within it].
2.2 O Blessed Lord,
[please describe] everything regarding the initiation pavilion from the beginning, according to the ritual procedure for installation (pratiṣṭhā).
Having caused it to be made in a pure place, O Four-faced One, in that very same manner;
and in the western part of the sacrificial altar, having caused a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) to be made at a distance of three tālas outside,
for the foremost of the twice-born and the other castes in their proper order.
Favorable, four-cornered, with an interval measuring two spans (tāla),
it is circular, and thereafter broadened by a pair of "cow-ears" (gokarṇa). Then,
shaped like a bow, it measures two spans in both width and length.
The other pit (kuṇḍa) is triangular and two spans (prādeśa) in width.
(2.6) Such are the dimensions for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth among the Brāhmaṇas and other castes.
On the tenth day, the sacrificial requisites (*yāgasambhāra*) and the items to be gathered, such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and others, [are prepared]. (2.7)
On the eleventh lunar day, in the evening, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) should take place;
having established [the deity] in the pavilion for sacrifice, preceded by the ritual of the door-vases and other rites,
the Guru— whose body has been purified through meditative concentration (dhāraṇā)— should fashion the lotus of the wheel (cakrābja).
A water-pot made of gold or other precious materials, and likewise a small vessel (karaka) of the same kind, both filled with water, containing gems and gold,
their entire surfaces wound with thread, and adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste.
The vessel, free from defects, shall be covered with two unwashed garments;
the preceptor should consecrate it one hundred times with the Astra-mantra and sprinkle water around the altar in an unbroken stream.
Having carried the *karaka* vessel clockwise and the *kumbha* pitcher behind him,
he should place them upon grain in the northeast sector of the lotus-diagram;
the *kalaśa* on the right and the *karaka* on the left, while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Having invoked Hari into the pitcher, one should worship him according to the path of the scriptures;
O Lotus-seated One, one should sacrifice to the God in the mandala of the lotus-wheel,
together with his limbs and retinue, according to the rule and in due order.
Having churned the fire with the eight-syllable mantra, one should place it within the sacrificial pit.

Having prepared the cooked oblation (*caru*) there, one should divide it into four parts and deposit them: one portion for Hari residing in the mandala, and another portion in the water-pot (*kumbha*). || 2.15–2.16 ||
The preceptor should consume one portion himself and offer one into the fire;
the best of preceptors should offer one hundred and eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*).
The knower of mantras should likewise perform the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya-homa*) with the root mantra.
He should perform the *caru* oblation with the *Nṛsūkta*, following it through to the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Then, he should [initiate] the disciple—who is peaceful, has conquered anger, is free from pride and other such vices, and is pure;
who wears unwashed linen garments along with an upper cloth, and is adorned.
Having summoned him and bound his eyes with a cloth by means of his own vidyā, the Guru,
having seated him on his right side facing eastward,
touched him with darbha grass while reciting the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā.
One should offer twelve oblations of clarified butter and likewise of sacrificial porridge (caru),
as well as with fuel-sticks, flowers, and sesame seeds; then, using the *prasṛti* mudrā, the preceptor should touch the disciple on the head three times while circumambulating him clockwise.
Then, having applied a white *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* mark made from ashes upon the head of the disciple with the eight-syllable mantra,
he should bind a protective thread (*pratisara*) on the hand with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

Having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with the Praṇava, the disciple should then eat the sacrificial porridge (caru) for the sake of purifying the body; he should clean his teeth with a tooth-stick. Having cast the tooth-stick upon the ground, he should observe its tip.
If the tip [of the branch] falls in the southwest, northwest, or south, it will be inauspicious;

however, if the tip of the branch falls in any other direction, it will be auspicious. (2.26) An inauspicious result may be pacified by a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śānti-homa*), and that [rite] brings about auspiciousness.

Then, one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds should be performed with the Nārasiṃha mantra. After that, having taken hold of the hand of the disciple who has sipped water for purification in the presence of the deity, the self-possessed Guru should bow to the Lord of Gods.
O Lotus-seated One, having recited this verse, one should make this request:
"O Lord, for these creatures bound by the snares of saṃsāra, you alone are the refuge; no other resort is found. (2.29)
"That which consists of the propitiation of you is the cause for release from the noose.
O Lord of Gods, by means of that, I shall free these beings born as animals who are bound by the noose of birth; it behooves you to grant me permission for this. || 2.30-2.31 ||
Having thus instructed that disciple, one should wrap him with a thread of illusion (*māyāsūtra*).
Having made the white, red, and black threads into three colors and tripled them,
one should again triple that same kind of thread.
Starting from the crest-lock and proceeding to the feet, he should encircle the body of the disciple on all sides twenty-five times with the root mantra. Then,
touching the disciple, the preceptor should perform oblations with that same mantra.
Then,

for the sake of the successful vision of dreams, the best of preceptors should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the mantra of the Lord of Dreams, followed by a full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) of clarified butter with that same mantra.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) of black-gram rice (*māṣaudana*) to the spirits (*bhūta*).
Having removed the blindfold from the disciple,
one should take the "thread of illusion" (*māyāsūtra*), which binds his body, and cast it into another shallow bowl (*śarāva*).
Having covered the side of the pitcher with a shallow bowl,
the preceptor should spread darbha grass upon that bed, and the disciple should then go to sleep.
At that time, one should not perform the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the deity residing in the mandala or residing in the pitcher.
Then, at dawn, if the disciple's dream-vision is auspicious, he should initiate him;
if it is inauspicious, he should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
Having bathed together with the disciple, he should enter the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa).
The worship of the banner, the archway, the water-pot, and so forth is prescribed as before.
Having offered the four kinds of food for presentation and having performed prostrations and circumambulations,
one should bind the eyes of the disciple with a new cloth as previously described.
Having established [the fire] on the side as before, the preceptor should offer oblations with sacrificial fuel and other materials one hundred and eight times for each, using the root mantra. Then,
having cut the thread of illusion (māyāsūtra), he should resort to the process of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
Having enumerated the principles (tattvas), the preceptor should offer oblations for each one,
either one hundred and eight times for each or eight times for each; the Guru,
having meditated upon the Supreme Person as the supreme light within the lotus of his own heart.
In that [liṅga], the one most skilled in mantras should withdraw the life-force of the disciple. Having likewise performed the withering and other rites upon the body belonging to the disciple,
he should then visualize the staff [of the deity] from the lotus of his own heart.
Having transferred the vital breath (jīva) again, one should emanate [the universe] through the sequence beginning with primordial nature (prakṛti).
At the time of creation, one should offer oblations to the principles (tattvas), established in their proper order.
Having brought forth [the world] up to the end of the gross body, one should contemplate the piercing of the spheres (maṇḍa-bheda).

Having meditated upon the Puruṣa in the midst of that [maṇḍala], and having perceived the Self as born from the Self by means of the Self, he should sprinkle [the disciple] with the root mantra and release the binding of his eyes.
Then the disciple, having put on another garment and having washed his feet, [should proceed]. (2.48–2.49)
Having sipped water and covered his eyes with another cloth, he should sit facing east before his own teacher; and the teacher should purify him by means of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
These are: the path of time (kālādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), and then the paths of words (padādhvan) and principles (tattvādhvan).
The path of mantra and the path of phonemes are proclaimed as the six paths.
Having first offered an oblation of clarified butter with the Mahāvyāhṛti-vidyā,
he should then touch the disciple's feet with the remainder of the offering and with sesame seeds.
Having offered oblations and touched the navel, then having offered oblations with lotuses (kuśeśaya),
and having touched the heart, one should offer oblations with the sacrificial porridge (caru) and touch the head.
There should be one hundred and eight oblations for each [limb] with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, having taken the disciple by the right hand and led him around the water-pot and the mandala as prescribed,
O Lotus-Seated One, he should stand at the entrance of the four doors.
At the end, the Guru should fill his joined palms with gems, pearls, corals, or even flowers alone; then,
directed by the Guru, he should scatter those blossoming flowers upon that maṇḍala.
On whichever portion of the ground the heap of flowers falls of its own accord,
one should assign the names of the presiding deities of those portions to that disciple— such as Keśava and so forth— and the word "Bhāgavata."

At the end of names, one should employ the term *bhaṭṭāraka*; or, if he is a Brāhmaṇa, he should designate the name of a Kṣatriya as ending in *deva*. For a Vaiśya, it should end in the word *pāla*, and for one born of the feet (a Śūdra), it should end in *dāsa*.
Then, having released the bond of [wrong] views, he should show the circle of the wheel (cakramaṇḍala).
Together with the disciple, the Guru should meditate upon Nārāyaṇa on the altar.
Having meditated, he should [place it] at the right ear of the disciple, accompanied by the Praṇava.
One should impart the mantra, along with its seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), deity (daivata), and limbs (aṅga);
first the twelve-syllable [mantra], then the eight-syllable essence,
and thereafter the form-mantra (mūrtimantra), having instructed [the disciple] according to the rule.
The Vaiṣṇava mantra alone—
consisting of the names of Keśava and the others, devoid of "namas" and the syllable "oṃ," and free from "hum," "phaṭ," "vaṣaṭ," and "svāhā"—
should be taught to women, Śūdras, and likewise to those born of the anuloma castes.
For those who perform the Sāvitrī [rite], that which is proclaimed by the wise is as follows:
the disciple should worship Hari residing in the water-pot and residing in the mandala.
Having propitiated Hari, he should always remain standing with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having meditated upon the maṇḍala, that guru should place his hand upon the head of the disciple;
thereafter, the preceptor should place his hand in the hand of Viṣṇu and instruct the disciple in all the rules of conduct in the presence of the fire.
The mantra of another must not be disclosed, nor should one display the rosary;
one should not reveal the mudrā, nor the siddhi, nor speak of the mantra oneself.
One should not utter the name of the preceptor, nor should one transgress his command.
One should not step over or leap across the teacher’s bed or other such items.

One should not revile the teacher with speech, nor should one do anything displeasing to him. Even in his absence, one should behave toward the teacher’s wife as one would toward the teacher himself. (2.69–2.70)

One should always honor the teacher, the imperishable, and the scripture—this triad. One should not touch atheists, those who have transgressed the boundaries of conduct, or those who revile the gods and Brahmins; nor should one converse with them even in times of great distress.
One should never stretch out one's feet in the presence of a guru, a deity, or the sacred fire.
One should always understand that the entire world is composed of Vāsudeva;
without having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should not engage in nourishing oneself.
One should perform hymns of victory, prostrations, and other rites at the time of the two twilights;
one should always delight in meditating upon the Lord and in performing those duties. Upon seeing a Vaiṣṇava ascetic, one should prostrate oneself on the ground like a staff.

One's wealth—consisting of sons, wife, house, fields, cattle, and so forth—should be designated in its entirety by the name of the Blessed One. Being equal toward all beings, one should abandon desire and anger. (2.75–2.76)
One should gradually withdraw the senses from their objects;
one should practice the study of the scriptures together with those who are averse to worldly existence (saṃsāra).
One should always perform the rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti, and nothing else.
The rites beginning with the *niṣeka* (conception) should be performed according to the procedure stated in one's own *sūtra*.
One should perform all ritual acts while being intent on meditation upon the Blessed One.
As for the secret name and the lineage (*gotra*), nothing other than those [prescribed] in the Prakrit [tradition] is desired.
Whether sitting, lying down, walking, or even eating,
one should proclaim and remember the eternal Vāsudeva. Having thus established these observances, one should perform the *śānti* oblation.

Having offered the entire sequence of oblations up to the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should dismiss the fire. Then, having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) of the deity residing in the mandala and the deity residing in the water-pot (kumbha), the preceptor (deśika) should cause the disciple to prosper with a benediction, and the disciple likewise [should do so] for the guru.
He should bestow cows, land, gold, ornaments, vehicles,
