and even female and male slaves, according to the extent of his own wealth. Having given wealth, he who is free from desire for riches should feed the Brahmins.

He should remain in that very place for the remainder of that day, eating only what remains from the sacrificial offerings. When the sun has set, permitted by his teacher, he should enter his home together with his kinsmen, adorned with all ornaments.
He who has been initiated into the wheel-mandala by this rite—
a learned Brāhmaṇa, a knower of the Vedas— is the best among those in all stages of life (āśramas). Even if he is addressed by those names, he should not be spoken of as an ordinary man.

He is the wise one, the friend, the devotee of the Lord, the follower of the Sāttvata path, and the knower of the five times; he is the solitary devotee, absorbed in Him, and is also called a Pāñcarātrika—
by such names as these, O Lotus-seated One, is He to be described.

The eightfold rule consists of: observance (*samaya*), right conduct (*sadācāra*), Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), accumulation of materials (*dravyasaṅgraha*), purification (*śuddhi*), renunciation (*tyāga*), praise (*stuti*), and meditation (*dhyāna*).
He who abides by this rule is called a *bhāgavata*.
He who does not act thus toward all beings as a doer of evil—
neither by deed, nor by mind, nor by speech— is not considered a Bhāgavata.
He in whom there is "bhaga," the aggregate of qualities such as knowledge and the rest, is so called.
"One who possesses devotion to the Blessed One is called a Bhāgavata.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the Śrī Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
The Third Chapter:
The Rite of the Eternal Sacrifice, [spoken by] the Blessed One.
Listen, O Brahmin, I shall describe the propitiation of Hari,
by which a mortal attains the station of Viṣṇu, which is difficult for others to reach.
All ritual acts have bathing as their root, and bathing is remembered as being of many kinds.

The Vāruṇa, Divya, Āgneya, Vāyavya, Pārthiva, as well as Māntra and Mānasa— thus the bath is of seven kinds. Having considered one's own capacity, as well as the occasion and the place, [one should perform it].
One intent on propitiation should perform one of these:
immersion within the waters is called the *vāruṇa* bath;
immediately following that is the *divya* bath, performed with rain accompanied by sunshine. (3.4)
And [the practice] of applying white ash from kindled fuel-sticks and burnt cow-dung to the limbs and the forehead and other parts in due order,
preceded by the recitation of mantras, which is the making of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*.
Then, that fire-related (āgneya) bath is remembered as the supreme purification;
when cows are passing by,
the touching of the body with the dust of the earth raised from their hooves is declared to be the wind-related (vāyavya) bath.
With white clay produced from a praiseworthy mountain peak or similar source,
having uttered the names beginning with Keśava, one should apply them to the limbs in due order;
this shall be the prescribed method for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* on the forehead and other parts.
An *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* made with clay should be worn with a gap between the lines and measuring three finger-breadths;
there, seated happily together with Lakṣmī, he rejoices in bliss.
This is the earthen bath performed with water-mantras uttered by the best of Brahmins.

O Brahmin, sprinkling with water is prescribed as that "mantra-bath. Having sipped water twice and put on unwashed garments, sitting comfortably and having restrained the breaths, one should meditate upon me residing in the lotus of the heart.
By this meditation, a person becomes cleansed of all impurity;
this shall be a mental bath, and having bathed thus, one should worship Hari.
Having washed the feet up to the ankles and the hands up to the wrists—
Having sipped water and gone to the side of the door, having first performed the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*),
and having made three claps with both hands while standing with knees slightly bent,
he then opened the door with the Vāyu-mantra, O Lotus-born One.
One should enter within with the right foot while reciting the *Sāman* known as the *Devavrata*;
one should bow the head to the Lord with the *Puṇḍarīkākṣa* mantra. When the lamps have been lit and the garlands have also been offered, [one should proceed].
When the altar, the vessels, and the images have been purified according to the rules,
and when the worship of the door, the face [of the deity], and the entire retinue has been performed by the disciple or by another attendant— (3.17–3.18)
The worshiper should be adorned, wearing a garland, dressed in clean white garments, and pure;
he should wear the sacred thread and an upper garment, be anointed with sandalwood paste and other unguents,
and bear the preeminent vertical *puṇḍra* mark fashioned from sandalwood, white clay, or water.
Having approached the side of the Lord on his own right side,
he sat upon a pure seat such as a grass mat (bṛsī) or the svastika posture,
having assumed either the lotus posture (padmāsana), while the sound of musical instruments was being played.
Then, having covered [the area] completely without gaps using a curtain (*tiraskariṇī*),
and having secured the quarters with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*),
the knower of mantras should meditate upon the sacrificial fire situated outside the enclosure wall with the fire-mantra (*tejomantreṇa*).
Having placed the *cakramudrā* in the sky with the mantra of the wheel, the practitioner,
thus concealing himself, should perform three successive breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*).
Then, joined in yoga and forming the *yogamudrā*, he should again [place it] situated in the root of the navel.

Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of air (yaṃ) in the form of a funnel, one should, by means of the smoke-colored wind produced from it, completely dry up the impurities of the body without remainder. Then,
[one should meditate] upon the triangular seed-syllable of fire (raṃ), red in color, within the heart-lotus.
Having meditated, one should burn away impurity with the seven-flamed crests arising therefrom.
Having placed the yellow-hued Māhendra-bīja in a square shape at the throat, one should,
by means of touch, arrest the fire that has arisen.

Having placed the seed-syllable of Varuṇa at the crown of the head, one should wash the entire body from the soles of the feet to the top of the head with the nectar-water produced therefrom, while the form resembling crystal is maintained by means of the *kumbhaka* breath-retention through the vital air.
Having withdrawn the principles beginning with earth into the Supreme Self by means of an intellect intent on meditative absorption, he abides in the sequence of dissolution:
[he dissolves] the earth, which possesses five qualities, has a yellow luster, and is four-cornered.
Then, having withdrawn the nose and the organ of generation along with their subtle elements into the subtle element of smell by means of profound yoga, the wise one [proceeds]; likewise,
together with the tongue and the anus, the western [quarter] possesses four qualities.
These [elements] have the form of a half-moon; such is their measure in the characteristic of taste (rasa).

Then, having concentrated his mind, he should visualize the fire, which consists of the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra), as triangular and pale-red, possessing three qualities and having its path directed toward the eyes. 3.32–3.33
With these characteristics of the subtle elements (tanmātra), together with the internal subtle element,
one should withdraw the twofold wind into the sense of touch, which has the characteristic of the subtle element [of sound].
Smoky and circular, [one should withdraw it] from the skin and hands along with the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra).

The yogi should again withdraw the quality of sound, which has the nature of the void, from its aggregate; then, from that, he should withdraw touch—which consists of the subtle element (tanmātra) and is accompanied by the faculty of hearing—along with sound, which is characterized as the subtle element and possesses the luster of the petal of a blue lotus. (3.35–36)
Having withdrawn the subtle element of sound into the internal organ, the internal organ into the ego,

the ego into the principle of intellect, and the intellect back into primordial nature (prakṛti); then, having withdrawn primordial nature into the individual soul (jīva), and the soul— which is overcome by latent impressions— into itself.
In one's own extremely subtle navel-cakra, [the practitioner] perceives that which abides with the brilliance of the sun.
By means of the *suṣumṇā* channel, as delicate as a lotus fiber,
one should cause it to ascend through the body by means of the breath held in *kumbhaka*.
Having pierced the aperture of Brahmā and emerged from the body,
it entered the orb of the sun and then emerged from it;
thus the bodiless *jīva* [became one] with the supreme, eternal Brahman.
One should meditate upon that which is situated; there, one should burn one's own body born of a womb.
Then, by means of the seed-syllable of Fire placed on the tips of the feet with the brilliance of a blazing flame, when one's own body has been burned from the feet up to the head, [it is purified].
One should meditate on the seed of cessation in the ether, resembling ten thousand full moons;
when a white lotus has arisen from that reservoir of nectar above,
one should then remember the individual soul born from the presence of Brahmā.

From the individual soul (jīva) [arises] primordial matter (pradhāna), from that the intellect (buddhi), and from the intellect the ego-sense (ahaṅkṛti). From that [arises] the mind (manas), from that the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), and from that the ether (kha) together with speech and hearing—[the latter] having sound as its quality; [then arises] the subtle element characterized by touch.
One should contemplate air, which has touch as its quality, together with the skin and the hands;
then the subtle element of form, and then fire together with the eyes;
then form as a quality with the feet, and from those two [the feet], the subtle element of taste.

O Lotus-born one, the wise man should likewise remember water, which has taste as its quality, together with the anus and the tongue; then earth, which has smell as its quality and consists of the subtle element of smell, as it has arisen from that [water], along with the sense of smell and the organ of generation. (3.47–3.48)
Having thus contemplated with the intellect that one's own body is born from the pure and impure elements, [one should imagine] it as a lotus awakened by those [streams] emerging from it—
[streams consisting of] full jars made of gold filled with nectar-water. (3.49)
Having contemplated his own body as bathed, pure, and sinless,
fit for the propitiation of Hari, the Supreme Soul,
he should meditate upon either the eight-syllabled or the twelve-syllabled mantra.
Having first performed the placement on the hands, one should perform the placement upon the limbs, from the head down to the feet, according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance,
and dissolution. Having purified the palms and backs of both hands with the Weapon-mantra (astravidyā), [one should proceed].
The placement of the *praṇava* is prescribed upon all the joints of the fingers, both those at the beginning and the end, as well as upon the middle joints.
One should place the syllables of the mantra [therein]; this is the eternal ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Starting from the joint of the right index finger and proceeding through the joints of the thumb up to the end of the joints of the left index finger,
the best of practitioners should perform this *sṛṣṭinyāsa*; however, the *saṃhṛti* (dissolution) is performed by reversing the order.
Having proceeded [from the heart], the rest of the placement for the eight-syllable mantra is said to be at the joint of the index finger and the joint of the little finger. Now,
the placement for the twelve-syllable mantra is being described.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) on the palm with the middle finger at the joint of the thumb and index finger,
one should then move clockwise around the joints with the thumb for the other fingers;
on the left palm, however, there is rest in the process of emanation (sṛṣṭi), while it is otherwise in dissolution (laya).

O Lotus-seated One, this is the placement of the twelve-syllable mantra: there is a progression on both the right and left soles of the feet, and a resting upon both joints of the two little fingers. (3.59–3.60)

Having meditated upon the heart and other limbs, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the five parts beginning with the thumb; [one should place] the two Gadādhara deities on the nails, the face, the eyes, and the palm of the right hand.
On the left hand, one should place the lotus and the discus; such is the ritual placement for both hands.
Having recited the mantra over the two palms and meditated upon it as blazing with splendors,
one should project it from those palms throughout the body, from the head down to the feet; or else, one should project the mantra syllable by syllable as a pervasive cloak.
Having touched the head, eyes, mouth, heart, navel, secret place, knees, and feet in succession, that is held to be the mantra-installation (*nyāsa*).
It should be known that the reverse order applies during withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), whereas the [standard] order applies during preservation (*pālana*).
The ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs is proclaimed to extend from the navel to the end of the heart.
These are the locations for the eight-syllable mantra:
the back of the head, the front, the right, and then the left.
And the knower of mantras should place the four positions of the Four-Faced One [on the body] with twelve syllables:
on the head with the middle finger together with the index finger;
on the two eyes with the ring finger together with the thumb; and on the mouth. (3.67)
The placement [of the mantra] at the heart should be performed with the thumb and index finger. Likewise, the placement at the navel is praised when done with the thumb and little finger.
Without the thumb, the remaining fingers should be used for the secret place and for both knees.
With all [the mantras], [one performs the placement] on the two feet; these are the stages of the eight-syllable [mantra].
On the front part of the head, the placement is with the finger [of the right hand]; on the right [side], with the thumb;
on the back part, with the index finger; and on the left, with the ring finger.
With the little finger, these [syllables] should be [placed]; they are the twelve stages of the syllables.
At the time of their deposition, one should also contemplate the forms of the syllables in sequence:
white, golden, black, red, and resembling saffron.
The eight [colors] are like the filaments of a lotus, possessing every hue:
white, black, smoke-colored, dark blue, and likewise resembling a star;
crystal-like, conch-like, red, pale, and crimson.

Having meditated upon that which is of the nature of darkness (tamas) and yellow in color, one should place the two-syllabled mantra in the prescribed location and perform the ritual assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa):
the heart, the head, the crest, and the armor.
The *astra*, *netra*, and these six [mantras] should be deposited in sequence upon the heart, the head, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), on both sides of the shoulders,
the two eyes, and in all directions across the various planes.

The forms of the six [deities] are the night-lotus, the bandhūka, and the black lotus; the lotus-stamen, the water-lily, and that which resembles the atasi flower. They bear divine weapons and wear divine garments, garlands, and ointments.

One should meditate upon oneself as the Supreme Lord manifest, bearing the Kaustubha gem, the forest garland (vanamālā), and the divine mark of Śrīvatsa. One should worship the seed-syllables of the ritual placement (nyāsa) in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should first worship the eternal Vāsudeva, who resides within the lotus of the heart, by means of mental offerings at the conclusion of the fire-oblation.
This is declared to be the purification of the self; now the purification of the mantra will be described.
One should dry the seed-syllables of the mantra with the twenty-sixth syllable, the seed of the waters;
one should burn them letter by letter with the twenty-seventh seed-syllable;
and with the twenty-eighth seed-syllable, one should perform the immobilization (*stambhana*) upon them.
One should wash those very [offerings] again with the twenty-nine seed-syllables.
The wise one should awaken them with the syllable *huṃ*, turn them toward [the deity] with the syllable *phaṭ*,
and purify them further with the syllable *oṃ*.
With a pure rosary of *akṣa* seeds, one who is concentrated in mind should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times,
or twenty-eight times,
or even eight times; the knower of mantras should enclose the mantra with the seed-syllable at the beginning and end.
One should wash all the articles of worship with water-filled [vessels].
Having placed the *galantika* (water-dripper) on the right or the left side,
and having taken the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings, one should [proceed] with the *gāyatrī* preceded by Viṣṇu.
Having washed his feet, O Lotus-born One, one should then offer them before the Deity:
the water for the feet (pādya) in the center, the water for honoring (arghya) on the right, and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) on the left.
Beside that vessel, however, on the left, should be the vessel for the bath-water (snānīya).
Having touched vessels filled with unbroken water using the *nigama* mantra and others,
he should place the ritual substances into the vessels for the *arghya* and so forth: namely,
the tips of *kuśa* grass, unbroken rice, flowers, fruit, and sandalwood paste.
One should place sesame seeds together with white mustard seeds in the vessel for the *arghya* offering.
One should set these six substances— sesame, *dūrvā* grass, *viṣṇuparṇī*, millet, lotus, and unbroken rice— in the vessel for the *pādya* offering.
One should place cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, black pepper, sandalwood,
flowers, fragrance, all medicinal herbs, gems, fruits, seeds, and *kuśa* grass into the vessel for the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). (3.92–93)
One should place sesamum seeds, unbroken rice, curd, milk, and likewise ghee;
these twelve items, along with turmeric, should be added to the bath-water.
Also, *koṣṭha*, *māṃsī*, the two types of *haridrā*, *murā*, *śaileya*, and *campaka* [should be included].
Vaca, kacoṛa, mustā, and all medicinal herbs are proclaimed [to be placed there]. One should also cast sesame seeds and tulasī into the water for pacification.
Within the center of the twelve-spoked, radiant wheel, however, is the Sun.
Having meditated upon [the syllable] blazing in the hand other than the left, and having again burned the substances without remainder by its rays so that they have become ashes,
[one should place them] upon the blooming white lotus held in the hand other than the right.

Having meditated on the moon, endowed with sixteen digits and gladdening [all] with its nectar-rays, one should contemplate that the [plants], having been sprinkled with the ambrosial waters arising from it,
have become fit once again for sacrifice. (3.98–99)
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa with both hands;
having touched the substances in the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings with those two hands,
one should gather them together once each with the *gāyatrī* mantra preceded by Viṣṇu.
Having consecrated [the vessel] with mantras, one should then display the *saurabheyī* mudrā.
One should visualize the vessels as being filled with that milk,
while reciting "Oṃ arghyaṃ" and so forth, preceded by "kalpayāmi."
One should touch the vessels with the hand, and immediately thereafter,
having taken a little water from the *arghya* vessel, one should place it into another vessel.
Having placed that vessel in the left hand, one should consecrate it with mantras.
Having sprinkled those substances and oneself seven times with that water using the root mantra,
and having sprinkled them with the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ* using the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], one should arrange the yoga-throne for the deity.
O Four-faced One, in this undivided, innate seat of the image,
first is the support Kūrma, and immediately after that, Kālāgni;
and above them is the Lord of Serpents with his hoods [supporting] the circle of the earth.
It is square, possessing a thousand [spokes], and is exceedingly powerful.
Above the earth, Dharma and the others are to be fashioned as the legs of the yogic seat;
O Lotus-born One, these four are located in the four directions starting from the southeast (āgneya).
And in the directions starting from the east, there are likewise as many [deities] beginning with Adharma, in due order;
in those same number of quarters, there are figures in human form:
four-armed, lion-faced, white in the east, and ruddy in the west.
With their two hands facing forward, they form a hollowed cupped añjali;
with the other two hands, they hold a yogic pedestal (yogapīṭhikā).
In the center, the god Sadāśiva is likewise established.
Below, in the directions starting from the east, the eight [deities] beginning with Puruhūta are, in sequence, the supporters of the eight legs of the pedestal.
There are four shafts starting from the east; upon them is the fourfold Veda.
The three types of egoism are the bonds; the qualities are the *guṇas*, beginning with *sattva*.
(3.113) The mattress consists of the five elements, and likewise, the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is the bedspread.
Above these, in successive order, are the orbs of fire, moon, and sun. (3.114)
One should visualize a white lotus above, with twelve petals,
filled with filaments and a broad pericarp in its center;
having prepared a fortunate seat (bhadrāsana) according to the very path previously described.
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings on the right side of the pedestal; likewise, having propitiated them,
one should honor Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sananda on the north.
Having meditated upon Durgā, Vighneśa, as well as Nārada and one’s own guru at the western side, one should begin the worship of Acyuta.
Then, having washed the vessel used for the invocation with water—
One should fill [the vessel] with the root mantra and lift it up with both hands.
Having invoked Keśava into this [vessel] at the level of the forehead,
it should be like a lamp derived from the original image, or like a lamp [lighted] from another lamp, without any alteration.
One should recite the mantra four times, joined with the words "āgaccha" (come).
With that water, one should sprinkle the ritual image (*karmārcā*) on its head using a *kūrca* [bundle of grass].
Therein, one should contemplate the deity as being present within the ritual image.
Having prostrated and risen slightly, immediately after saying "Welcome," he should display the image-mudrā and, having established its presence,
he should pray for the continued abiding of Hari there until the conclusion of the sacrifice.
One should perform the act of bringing [the deity] face-to-face by means of the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā;
and one should first offer the seat and other honors with the root mantra.
Just as [one performs it] in the body, so should one perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) in the deity.

Without performing the hand-placement (hastanyāsa), one should display the mudrās of the conch and the discus. One should not perform the invocation (āvāhana) for a single image when Hari has been brought down by gods or siddhas, or when he has been installed and consecrated by sages or men.
When [the deity] is well-established, his manifestation before one is itself the invocation (*āvāhana*) of Hari.
Just as one kindles fire in a hearth, or as one awakens a person himself at the proper time, so should one awaken the Lord during worship; one should awaken Dharima.
O Four-faced One, at the beginning of worship, when the image is stable, one should always perform the visualization of the yoga-pīṭha and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras;
[one should also perform] the offering of water for honor (arghya), garments, ornaments, flowers, perfumes, and ointments. || 3.128–3.129 ||

One should meditate on Him as standing when He is situated at the entrance; again, as standing for the water for the feet and the water for sipping; as seated at the time of bathing upon a comfortable lotus-seat;
and as seated upon a svastika-seat during the offering of food, incense, lamps, and so forth.
In other ritual services as well, according to the specific requirements of each rite,
the worshipper should meditate on the Lord as either standing or seated; then,
with a gentle voice, saying "I worship," he should cast a handful of flowers toward Hari.
"O All-pervading One, Lord of all worlds, Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Lord Hare!
Today I worship you with devotion through offerings such as the *arghya* and so forth, in due order.
Having thus addressed the Lord of gods, one should worship him with the *arghya* and other offerings in sequence.
With his head bowed in devotion, he should offer the *arghya* upon [the guest's] head;
he should offer the *pādya* at the reception of the *pādya* for the lotus-feet;
and at the time of giving the *ācamanīya*, he should meditate upon the Teacher of the World.
As if rinsing his mouth with waters during the formal reception of water, he was attended with ritual hospitality,
including the offering of *madhuparka* and other honors;
likewise, [he was honored] with both hands, with his head, with his feet, and with his mind and heart.
Having cast himself upon the surface of the earth with the thought "I am," and having prostrated before Janārdana with this act of obeisance,
he said: "O Lord of the World, I am your slave, together with my sons and all my dependents."
"Command me in what must be done; always appoint me to your service.
Having thus addressed the Lord of Gods, one should assign the attendants in due order upon the lotus petals of the yoga-seat, starting from the east.
In each of the twelve [discs], there are twelve powers, beginning with Śrīvatsa:
Śrīvatsa, Vanamālā, Māyā who is the essence of Yoga, Vaiṣṇavī, Vimalā, Sṛṣṭi, and also Utkarṣaṇī. || 3.140–3.141 ||
[He should worship] Prajñā, Satyā, and likewise Īśānā and Anukampā, the Grandmother (Pitāmahī),
in the first enclosure, in the directions starting from the east in sequence:
Vyāpti, Kānti, Tṛpti, Śraddhā, Vidyā, Jayā, and Kṣamā.
Having meditated upon these eight— Śānti and Śakti— as chowrie-bearers,
one should then, in the second enclosure, arrange eight male figures holding weapons such as the conch and others, in sequence starting from the east.
In the third enclosure, one should arrange Indra and the other deities in their respective directions;
likewise, in the outer enclosure, one should place Tārkṣya at the head of the Blessed One,
and Viṣvaksena in the northeast, outside the second enclosure.
All the attendants should gaze upon Hari with palms joined in reverence.
At the time of Hari’s rising for his bath, one should offer the sandals;
one should remember the mounting of the sandals while reciting the two verses beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
One should lift up Hari with the mantra "Arise, O Brahmaṇaspati," and bring the Lord of Gods to the bathing pedestal. Then,
with the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," one should place him upon the bathing seat.
One should offer the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) with the *Sāvitrī* verse, and the water for the feet (*pādya*) with the verse beginning "three steps" (*trīṇi padā*).
The act of sipping water (*ācamana*) is performed with the mantra "May the waters purify" (*āpaḥ punantu*).
And one should present the tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) with the mantra "That of Viṣṇu" (*tad viṣṇoḥ*).

There, one should perform the cleansing of the tongue with the mantra "tad viprāsaḥ," and then offer the washing of the Lord's mouth with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. One should perform the anointing with the Vāmadevya [Sāman] and then the rubbing with fragrant unguents.

The rite of sprinkling (abhiṣeka) should then be performed with *āmalaka* and other substances using the mantra "kāryaṃ viṣṇornukaṃ," with the two verses beginning "na te viṣṇo," and with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and "ato devā avantu."
One should comb the hair with a *kaṅkata* brush and likewise perform the ritual bathing with water-jars.
The anointing is done with turmeric while reciting the verse beginning, "The golden-hued, the greenish-yellow... (RV 10.186.1).
Then, one should bathe with the four verses beginning, "The golden-hued, pure, purifying ones... (RV 9.1.6–9).
The body should be washed with fragrant water;

then, having smeared it with saffron, one should wash it again with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and the Pāvamānī verses, as well as with the hymns beginning with *brahmajajñānam*, *kayā naścitra ābhuvat*, and so forth. (3.155–156)
Thus, with these offerings of water for honor (*arghya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), one should worship the primordial Maheśvara;
having sprinkled him with the *Sāvitrī* and the *Puruṣasūkta*,
there shall be a bath either by a thousand streams or by means of a water-pot.
With the mantra "Agnir mūrdhā," one should remove water from the limbs using a strainer.
With the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī, one should offer two washed and clean garments;
with the syllable Om (Praṇava), one should arrange the sacred thread and the upper garment.
Having supervised the sipping of water (ācamana), [he should place] the sandals on the seat of adornment;
then, for the God seated comfortably, he should offer the arghya and other honors as before.
With incense of agaru wood, he should moisten [the Lord’s] head with the verse beginning "divo mūrdhānam" (RV 8.44.16).

Having dried his hair with pure, fragrant sandalwood, he should apply it to his body while reciting the Vedic verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. He should also adorn himself with ornaments while reciting the mantra "jitaṃ te. (3.161–3.162)
One who knows the mantras should offer flowers with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ";
one should scatter unbroken rice grains at the feet with the mantra "irāvatī.
One should apply collyrium with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and gaze into a mirror with the Vyāhṛtis.
One should fumigate with incense arising from aloe-wood while reciting "Victory is yours! (jitaṃ te).
The offering of lamps is prescribed with the mantra "Be kindled! (uddīpyasva).
Likewise, one should offer sesame seeds, cloth, gold, betel-leaf, and even rice.
One should offer fruits, cow-products for food, cows, and grain according to one's wealth, as well as a morsel of grass for the cows, to the guide in the presence of the deity;
likewise, [one should offer] to the presiding lord, the king, and the entire kingdom.

Giving to the subjects, such as the Brāhmaṇas and others, brings about prosperity. (3.167) When the temporary cloth has been removed, out of compassion for the devotees, one should have it proclaimed with the sound of musical instruments and likewise perform dance and song. (3.168)
They should recite hymns, various narratives, the Vedas, and likewise the six auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas),
as well as all other auspicious texts, before the Lord.
Having offered his sandals from the throne, he should lead him to the dining seat.
Having offered the arghya, pādya, ācamana, and madhuparka, one should present them.
Then, with the syllable *praṇava*, one should give the betel leaf for cleansing the mouth.
Likewise, one should offer the prepared sacrificial food, consisting of various kinds of eatables and edibles.
It should be provided with sweet and other flavors as prescribed by the rules,
well-prepared and composed with well-refined foods, fruits, and the like;
one should arrange these according to what is appropriate, avoiding both undercooked and overcooked items.
When all the ritual services have been arranged like those for a king,
one should sprinkle with the Astra-mantra and surround [the area] with the Varma-mantra; then,
having offered worship with the Praṇava, [one performs] the burning, flooding, and other rites.
And when this has been done, the preceptor, having displayed the *surabhimudrā* while in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), touches with his right hand the *arghya* flowers placed in Viṣṇu’s hand,
while [the disciple] maintains contact with his left hand.
Holding flowers for the *arghya* offering and displaying the *grāsa-mudrā*,
the practitioner himself should offer the *naivedya* as previously described with the mantra "devasya tvā" into the right hand of the Deity.
When the beverage has been placed in his hand and the water has been well-prepared,
and the ritual rinsing (ācamana) has been performed, one should give betel leaf for the cleansing of the mouth.
Whatever collection of rites has been prescribed for worship and other such acts in the ritual of the image, [that should be performed].
One should perform all of that, as far as possible, in the case of the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) and so forth.
When the offerings (*upacāra*) such as the *arghya* and others are to be performed in their proper manner,
one should utter this speech at the beginning of all the mantras.

"During this auspicious occasion, I shall worship the Blessed Janārdana with divine offerings of water for the feet and other honors, according to my ability and in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Thus spoke the worshipper, being perfectly composed and free from falsehood.

The worship of the retinue is considered to be performed with exactly four [substances], beginning with fragrance (gandha). And when all the ritual services have been completed, ending with the hymn of praise, the worshipper should again recite the mantra according to the number previously specified.
Or else, at the conclusion of that, he should offer oblations outside with another twelve-syllable mantra;
he should also daily perform the offering of bali to the spirits and hold a great festival.
Having informed the Lord of the Gods of the gods, the worshipper himself should prostrate.
One should take all the remaining articles of worship in their entirety.
With them, one should perform self-worship; by that also Keśava is pleased.
He is to be propitiated with the mantras as prescribed, or with the Puruṣasūkta.
Alternatively, if the worshipper is free from desire, he attains the supreme good by taking refuge in Hari at the face of the image with mantras consisting of twelve syllables and so forth;
but if there is a desire for objects, he obtains the fruits corresponding to those desires. (3.187–188)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Rule for the Daily Sacrifice," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the fourth chapter.
Regarding the procedure for the fire-ritual:
O Blessed One, the daily festival and the fire-oblation have been previously described.
Tell me truly how he is to be worshipped by his devotees. The Blessed Lord replied:
One should worship Caṇḍa and the others in due order at the entrance and in the fire-sanctuary.
Having entered inside, [he should sit] in a pit smeared with cow dung and honored with unbroken rice grains.
Having sat down, he should place a vessel of flowers at his right side,
and deposit the other materials for the oblation on his left side.
The vessel for clarified butter, the pot for the sacrificial porridge, the sprinkling water, the fuel sticks, the *kuśa* grass,
the *praṇītā* water, the rice grains, water, the enclosing sticks, as well as the large and small ladles,
the spoon, the shifting of the fire, the fans, and the sprinkling [of the oblation].
Dry wood, perfumes, fragrant substances, and unbroken grains—
these pairs should be employed, provided they are available, with their tips pointing downward.
Then, three lines should be drawn separately, extending eastward, across the center of the sacrificial pit.
Having likewise drawn three lines extending northward with the root-mantra,
and having sprinkled them with water from two bunches of *darbha* grass, he should take the fire— either kindled by friction or that which is common— and having established it and spread it out; 4.7.
Having swept around the fire with water and having strewn it around with three sets of three [blades] each—
either five, seven, nine, or eleven [sets] of *darbha* grasses with their tips pointing eastward and northward. || 4.8–4.9 ||
With twenty-five [blades] whose tips are tied together in pairs,

having placed there in the center of the fire a vessel for the *praṇītā* water, filled with water, honored with unbroken rice grains, and containing a *kūrca* of two *darbha* blades measuring a span (*prādeśa*), ||| 4.10 ||
Having covered it with three purified *darbha* blades,

he who knows the mantras should pour the water from the *praṇītā* vessel into the *prokṣaṇī* using that *kūrca*. Then, having placed the *prokṣaṇī* before himself along with the *kūrca*, he should set it down.
Using the thumb and ring finger of both hands,
one should again purify that *kūrca* [strainer], then sprinkle the *prokṣaṇī* vessel three times,
and with that water, sprinkle all the materials for the oblation.
One should touch those substances, naming each according to its respective place.
Then, one should pour out the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel around it clockwise;
having filled the *praṇītā* vessel with water, one should honor the deity therein.
To the south of the fire, upon a seat made of darbha grass and a mat woven from the same,
one should mentally invoke Brahmā, worship him, and wash [the vessel] with water; then,
with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, one should place an āḍhaka measure of rice into the cooking pot there.
Having cast [the materials] and washed them with the heart-mantra and the other limb-mantras, one should place them on the fire.
Having poured clarified butter (*ājya*) into the *ājya*-pot, having melted and strained it,
the knower of mantras should throw two tips of *darbha* grass into it while reciting the mantra.
Having placed it on the coals in the fire, he should then circumambulate it with a blazing blade of grass;

having removed it, he should set it down in its proper place. Having purified it by sprinkling and floating it over water, he should indeed touch the sacrificial grass-bundle (*kūrca*) with water for the sake of the Fire (*uṣarbudha*).
Having offered [the oblation] and rendered it immortal with the *surabhi-mudrā*,
one should consecrate it with the *avaguṇṭhana* [mudrā] and worship the guardians of the directions, Indra and the others, in their proper order.
Then, having washed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and five blades of *kuśa* grass with warm water...
Taking the *kūrca* grass-bundle, they should wipe those two [the fire-drills] at the base, the middle, and the top;
having wiped them with the root, the middle, and the tip of the *kūrca* in sequence,
they should be heated over the fire and then placed to the north of oneself.
Having taken clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, one should sprinkle it over the items for the oblation.
Having sprinkled the *caru* with clarified butter, one should set it aside on the side.
Likewise, there should be pure rice, rice mixed with mung beans, milk-rice, and rice with molasses.
The sacrificial porridge (caru) is to be known as fourfold; its cooking on the hearth is also prescribed.
Whatever kind is offered to the image, that same kind is to be offered in the fire-sacrifice (homa).
The enclosing sticks (paridhi) are placed facing north and likewise begin from the west.
Likewise, two fuel-sticks (samidh) should be placed in the corners of Agni (SE) and Īśāna (NE).
Having placed them upright, while mentally meditating on Prajāpati as the fuel,
one should offer the ten prescribed [strokes] with a single motion, using the fist-gesture (muṣṭimudrā), with the tips [of the sticks] pointing in one direction.
One should take the vessel of clarified butter wrapped with a tuft of *kuśa* grass;
placing it in the left hand, one should perform the foundational oblation (*ādhāra-āhuti*) into the fire.
Then, one should likewise perform the oblations to Prajāpati and Indra, as well as the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*).

Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in the center, one should immediately thereafter meditate upon Agni: two-headed, seven-handed, three-footed, and seven-tongued; [placed] in the southern quarter as the Āgneya and likewise in the northern quarter as the Saumya.
He bears the gesture of granting boons (*varada*) and holds a spear (*śakti*) in his hand, as well as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
he bestows fearlessness (*abhītida*) and carries a shield (*carma*) in his left hand, while his right hand holds clarified butter (*ājya*).
Upon the tongue in the southern face, [the rites] such as killing (*māraṇa*) are performed when it is of a smoky color (*dhūmrā*).
In Lohinī, there is subjugation; in Kālī, the rite of pacification (śāntika).
In Sphuliṅginī, who is on the left face, there is the attainment of all siddhis.
In Viśvarūparasajñā, the great fruit consists of the powers beginning with aṇimā.
Karālikā bestows victory, Puṣṭidā bestows nourishment, and Manojava possesses the speed of thought. Their colors are blackness, redness, and a dark-greenish hue (śyāmatva).
Then there is the form of sparks, and thereafter a color resembling crystal.
It is said that [the tongue] on the tongue is like molten gold, in successive order.
For the pacification of one who has been born, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds mixed with honey and ghee one hundred and eight times, using the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra.
At the conclusion of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), having meditated, one should worship the blazing fire;
one should offer perfumes and other items to it, as well as unbroken grains (akṣata) to oneself, with the armor-mantra (varman).
Having sprinkled the fire with water, [one should visualize] the yoga-pedestal within its midst.
Having visualized [the deity], one should repeatedly offer oblations of clarified butter with those mantras.
Then, having brought down the Supreme Lord in the form of consciousness from the heart,
and having performed the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), one should perform the placement of the mantra (*nyāsa*) according to the rule.
Having first offered the food along with the *arghya*, he should perform a single oblation with clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*).
Then, for the purpose of the recitation (*japa*), he should likewise offer a single oblation with clarified butter using the mantras;
or else, he may offer with fuel-sticks (*samidh*), sesame seeds, flowers, seeds, or fruits.

O Four-faced One, for the sake of the retinue as well, one should likewise offer oblations once with clarified butter into the seven-flamed fire; this is the propitiation of Hari. If the propitiation is performed elsewhere, such as before an image and so forth, it follows immediately after.
One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and cooked food (*anna*) according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
The length of the fuel-sticks is, in order, one *tāla*, the span of the palm, and the width of the little finger.
If they lack bark, there will be destruction; if they are split, the lineage will become diminished.
Under Ārdrā, there will be the loss of kinsmen; under Purātana, the loss of sons.
Under Kṣatā, there is the death of the wife; Śākhinī leads to quarrels.
A thick [tree] brings about anxiety, while a short one causes drought.
One should avoid fuel-sticks that are too long, those that have been rained upon for too long, or those that are defective.
As prescribed, one should offer one hundred, fifty, or twenty-five fuel-sticks, or eight;
or half of that number, anointed with clarified butter, one should sacrifice with the root-mantra.
Sacrificial oblations (caru) sprinkled with clarified butter should be offered verse by verse using the "hand-gesture" (mudrā).
One should offer oblations of ghee with the *Nṛsūkta* and the root mantra (mūlamantra) in a number of one hundred or more, while meditating upon the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa).
One should offer clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, and fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the hand;
likewise, the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) may be offered with a *palāśa* leaf or otherwise with the hand and so forth.
Having first performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should then effect the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
Peace is attained through auspicious flowers produced from the sacrificial tree;
good fortune through incense substances; constant health and nourishment through curd; and purity through milk.
Through food one obtains various desires, and through clarified butter, long-lived progeny.
A man desiring the glory of Brahman should offer oblations with white lotuses;
one desiring prosperity should offer oblations with *lakṣmī* flowers or those of Varuṇa.
One desiring knowledge, however, should offer oblations with lotuses, *bilva* fuel-sticks, or clarified butter.

One desiring a daughter should worship with *kāla* flowers; one desiring cattle, again, with cow-dung. One desiring long life should worship with *dūrvā* grass, while one desiring land should worship with clay.
One desiring sensory power should worship with barley, and one who desires to be beloved by all people should worship with sesame seeds.

But one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) [should perform the rite] with materials produced from the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, as well as with bamboo, barley, wild rice (*nīvāra*), and likewise with *śāli* rice. All desires are accomplished by means of the seeds for the oblation as they have been described.
Through the oblation of parched grain (lāja-homa), all desires are accomplished; of this there is no doubt.
One who desires food should use grains; one who desires a son, milk-rice (pāyasa);
one seeking gold, nimba flowers; and everything is accomplished through clarified butter (sarpiḥ).
At home, a stream of ghee, honey, and milk should be four fingers wide;
the offering of sour gruel (śukti) and curd should be a mouthful, as should the offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) and the like.
The offering of solid foods (bhakṣya) should be half of that; [the same applies to] fruits and unbroken grains.
The oblation of incense substances should be the size of a *niṣpāva* seed.

Oblations of sesame, rice, barley, and so forth, should be half or a quarter of a handful respectively. The fuel sticks (*samidh*) and *dūrvā* grass should be eight finger-breadths long, or half that, or six finger-breadths long.
An oblation of cow dung is prescribed to be the size of a grape or an eye;
O Four-faced One, the final oblation of clarified butter should be the measure of a *kuḍupa*.
Any oblation of *havya* or *kavya* offered with a measurement smaller or larger than this [is deficient].

The Dānavas and Daityas consume it, yet it does not serve for the sake of fruit. Having placed a ball of sacrificial porridge (caru) the size of a hen’s egg, soaked in ghee, into the cavity of the *sruk* ladle, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter using the *sruva* spoon.

One should offer oblations with clarified butter using the root-vidyā together with kindled darbha grass and flowers; furthermore, for the sake of expiation, one should again offer with the five upaniṣads. Having filled the sacrificial ladle (sruk) with clarified butter, it should be provided with darbha grass and fuel-sticks.

Having lifted [the ladle] up to the tip of the nose and having sprinkled it with clarified butter using the *sruva* spoon, the practitioner should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra. Then,
having filled the *sruk* ladle with water, he should circumambulate the exterior of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) clockwise.
Having poured out the remainder of the water, he himself should pour it over his head;
having made a tilaka mark with ashes, he should release Hari from the fire.
Then the worshipper, taking the arghya offering, should present it to the deity in the sanctuary.

"O Supreme Lord, accept this as the very worship performed with devotion in the fire according to one's ability and according to the rules. Indeed, this procedure for the fire-rite has been described by me in brief. (4.68–4.69)
"The Brahmin who performs the fire-ritual day by day according to this rule goes to the abode of Brahmā after having enjoyed his desired pleasures.
Thus ends the "Rule for the Fire-Ritual" in the *Caryāpāda* of the *Pādma Tantra*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
The fourth chapter? The fifth chapter?
The division of time for the perpetual festival and ritual worship.
The Blessed One said:
Now, O Four-faced One, I shall describe the ritual for the daily festival, which removes all suffering for men and brings great joy to all living beings. 5.1

Bringing forth the Supreme Lord into pure rice placed within a vessel—[an act] that brings happiness to the king, the kingdom, the village, the sacrificer, and the home; it is auspicious, brings peace, and increases longevity. 5.2
Accompanied by ten and two Śaktis, he should circumambulate the sanctuary every morning and every day; at midday, however, when food has been prepared,
and in the evening during the gathering of flowers— he should perform these rites at the three junctions of the day in these three ways.
Either with the image or with the enclosing frame, every day at the three junctions of the day;
or else, with food at midday, while at the other two times there is worship alone. Or else, one should perform the daily festival of Hari with food at the three junctions of the day.
Or, at midday, having circumambulated for the sake of all purposes, one should offer the bali-oblation;
or else, one should lead [the image] behind or in front of the festival icon,
accompanied by whisks, umbrellas, canopies, and banners, during the three junctions of the day.
O Lotus-Seated One, having offered an oblation of either rice and other grains or food alone within the fivefold enclosure—
that is, in all five enclosures—
of the divine abode, one should perform a circumambulation preceded by song and instrumental music.
They say that a festival is "excellent" (utkṛṣṭa); they know one less than that to be "middling" (madhyama).
When deficient, it is "inferior" (adhama) or "lowest" (jaghanya); when even less than that, it is "trifling" (kṣudra), and otherwise [even worse].
Without the offering of oblations (balipradāna), a festival does not bring about prosperity.
[He saw him] wearing white garments, gentle, with a white sacred thread,
together with an upper robe and a turban, well-anointed and adorned;
having summoned an attendant who was purified by being identified with the nature of Garuḍa.
And upon its head or back, or on rice grains, food, or flowers,
the worshipper himself should invoke the deity from the primary image;
and having worshipped the deity there with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the prescribed rule.
Having again worshipped the Viśvādi deities and performed circumambulation,
[one should recite] the entire Sūkta for prosperity (svastyayana), as well as other auspicious hymns, over the twelve petals situated in the vessels beginning with the eastern direction.
Reciting [the mantra] and carrying the vessel, the attendant should proceed;
he should worship the gatekeepers headed by Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa,
and cause them to be proclaimed with drums, cymbals, and the like, preceded by the offering of oblations (bali).
There should be dancing and the Vaijayantī banner; the bull is desired as the object of song.
With canopies, white umbrellas, chowries, fans, and so forth, one should circumambulate all the enclosures in succession for the sake of the offering.
Having circumambulated the pedestal, one should enter the temple again;
having circumambulated that as well, one should enter the inner sanctum.
Having offered the arghya with the root mantra, one should present it to the principal image (mūlabera).
One should cast a small portion of the remainder of the *bali* offering upon the head of Viṣvaksena;
the rest, including the unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and so forth, should be placed on the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*).
If there is a daily festival with the image, that image [should be carried] in palanquins and the like.
Or else, it is desired that [the image] be placed upon the head and carried around.
(5.21) Accompanied by various musical instruments and dances being performed in many ways, there are many kinds of dance therein; I shall describe them briefly. (5.22)
Vilāsa, kartarī, viṣṇukrānta, ālīḍha, aṅgalepa,
bhadra, mālī, tārkṣyapakṣa, the karaṇa called svastika,
cārī, pracārī, sūcī, sāvarata, and pāribhadraka.
The gentle, the uneven-needle, the shield, and the contracted;
the waist-band, the ornament, the urinary stone, the grinding of flour; the leaping, that called the left knee, the demonic, and the encircled. 5.24–5.25
The movements of Vāsava and Īśvara are performed with the *nikuṭṭima* [footwork].
The *kuṭṭima* is a composed [pattern], while the *sthāyibhāva* is that which is expanded (*vijṛmbhita*).
The *maṇḍala*, the *kṛṣitārdha* and so forth, the *kuñcitārdhendu*, the *patākā*, and the *sarvamaṅgala* [are also included]. 5.26.
The *kāntārakuṭṭima* and the *āhvāna* were likewise performed preceded by the *prapūrva*.
The *vilāsa*, *sarvatobhadra*, *śuddha*, and *kuñcita* are desired;
immediately following is the *mārgacārī*, which depends on the hands and is radiant.
The *āveṣṭita*, the *parīvarta*, the *nirdhūta*, the *deśimaṇḍala*, the *samapūrva*, the *ghaṭita*, the *pada*, and the *viṣamapūrvaka*;
the *karkarī*, the *vikalāsa*, and likewise the *vigalita*. (5.29)
Here, the various distinctions consist of separate entities through the movements of the limbs of the body.
Due to the infinity of the varieties of musical instruments and songs, they are not elaborated upon here.
[The temple] is endowed with the splendor of flowers and provided with banners, umbrellas, and so forth.
It was beautiful with all kinds of musical instruments, endowed with every excellence,
accompanied by the Vedic chanting of those who know Brahman, and filled with lamps;
it featured the dance and the moderate song of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) as he strode like Viṣṇu.
Vilāsa, Sarvatobhadra, Kheṭaka, Cakramaṇḍala,
Kāntāra, Kuṭṭima, Pṛṣṭikuṭṭima, Kaṭibandhana,
and Vāmajānūrdhvanṛtta are prescribed for Puruhūta (Indra) and the other [deities].
Ṣaḍja, ṛṣabha, gāndhāra, madhyama, pañcama,
dhaivata, and niṣāda are the notes associated with Puruhūta (Indra) and the others;
these seven should be known, and dhaivata is held to be the note of Bhava.

The dance of Viṣvaksena is the Svastika, and his musical note is Ṛṣabha. The elephant-dance belongs to Gaṇeśa, and his note is held to be Pañcama. The note of Durgā is Dhaivata, and her dance is Sarvamaṅgala.
The dance of other gods as well may be entirely auspicious;
their song is said to be in the *dhaivata*, *gāndhāra*, and *pañcama* scales,
or according to the specific distinctions therein, by those skilled in what should and should not be sung.
In the western direction, the fire-god possesses the musical instrument called *samatāla*;
in the direction of Yama (the south), Bhṛṅgiṇī possesses that named *baddhāvatāla*;
in the southwest there is the *maṭṭatāla*, and in the western direction there is that called *maṅgala*.
In the northwest is the one called Jayatāla; in the north, the one named Bhadra;
in the northeast, the Ḍhakkarī-tāla; and for Tārkṣya, the one called Garuḍa.
For the Bhūtas, there is the one called Balitāla, and for the Lord of the Army (Senāpati) as well, it is the same.
For other gods as well, the auspicious tāla is praised.
In all directions and within all temple enclosures,
dance, song, and instrumental music are prescribed in their entirety.
Having displayed one's own banner and the eight auspicious signs (maṅgalāṣṭaka),
an offering (bali) is prescribed everywhere in the presence of the deity. Having offered there betel-leaf and food such as flattened rice (pṛthuka) and the like.
In this manner, one should perform the ritual regarding the location for all obstructions.
At the gate of the enclosure, there is an exit by means of the pure lotus-sound;
having exited, one stands upon the great pedestal facing the temple.
When the sound of musical instruments has resounded loudly throughout all directions of the pedestal,
and after the top of the pedestal has been washed, one should worship the attendants of Viṣṇu.
Having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) without remainder upon the top of the pedestal, [one should proceed].
Having circumambulated the throne and entered the interior of the temple,
[the priest] should place the sandals upon the throne and, having helped [the deity] descend from the vehicle,
seat the Lord facing east upon a cushion in the entrance pavilion (mukhamaṇṭapa) and honor Him.
Having offered the entire oblation at the appropriate time,
the worshipper himself should lead the deity into the inner sanctum.
[This should be done] while instrumental music, song, and dance are performed in the outer courtyards.
One should perform the Śuddhaṇḍava dance in order to restore what has diminished.
One should not perform the Nityotsava during disturbances such as great winds;
however, one should offer the bali-oblation if possible.

One should cast the bali offering either to Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa alone, or between those two in front [of them], while the practitioner, with the root mantra, scatters the bali together with water, saying: "Homage to the spirits (bhūta). (5.53)
For this procedure of propitiation is praised for these various divisions of time.
O Brahmin, I shall now tell you about them: at dawn and at night; one, three, six, or even twelve times [per day]. (5.54–55)
The five-fold time, the four-fold time, and the occasional time are considered manifold for the rite of worship according to one's means, as prescribed: namely,
the single midday session, or morning, midday, and night.
If the three [previous] were among the six, there would again be three distinctions of time:
midnight, afternoon, and likewise dawn are thus declared;
[alternatively,] dawn, midnight, morning, midday, and night. (5.57–58)
These five times have been proclaimed; thereafter, there are four times.
Among these, O Four-faced One, the period deficient [in merit] is to be known as the dawn. Twelve times are to be known, consisting of five and five *nāḍikās*.
The other variations of time are each measured by a watch (yāma).
Worship concluded with a festival is declared the best;
that ending with the fire-oblation (homa) is said to be middling; and that ending with the distribution of food (prāpaṇa) is the lowest.

The offering of inferior incense and lamps is a low form of worship to Hari. Two *ghaṭikās* should be spent on bathing [the deity], one *ghaṭikā* on ritual worship, one on dance and song, and half of that on the presentation of food offerings.
There is one *homa* during the festival, and two at the conclusion of the pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*).
Such is the procedure for bathing and other rites during the worship at the time of striking [the drum].
The time for bathing is one *ghaṭikā*, and likewise, the worship lasts for half a *ghaṭikā*.
Singing and dancing should last for one ghaṭikā, the offering for half of that;
half of the remainder should be for the fire-oblation, and the other half should be for the performance of the daily festival.
Among all the divisions of time, they know the three periods [of the day] to be the most excellent.
O Lotus-seated One, morning, midday, night, and the principal [time]— in these,
both the *balin* and the festival must necessarily take place.
In other divisions of time, it is recommended that they extend until the conclusion of the fire-oblation (*homa*).
One should worship the images that are the limbs of the festival, the Commander-in-Chief (Senānī), the Lord of Birds (Vihageśvara),
and Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa stationed at the door, at all times. At midday and at dusk, musical instruments should be played in front [of them].
One should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) during the evening watches; this is what is further described.
One should provide pairs of large golden vessels according to one's wealth, and in their midst, upon surfaces of rice, one should light wick-lamps.
Lifting up such vessels with their hands, women adorned with auspicious garments and ornaments emerged from the kitchen;
arranged in rows, they were accompanied by songs, dances, and musical instruments performed before them.
They should place [the vessels] on the ground in the presence of the God of Gods.
Then, the preceptor should worship the vessels upon their bases with the Viśvavidyā mantra,
and perform the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) upon the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) and other objects.

Having worshipped the deity with offerings such as the *arghya* and so forth, the worshipper should lift up the lamp-vessels and wave them before the deity from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. Then, reciting the three *guṇa-mantras*, he should place the vessels among the women.
In this manner, one should perform the waving of lights elsewhere, moving the vessels one by one in sequence for the *dhruvabera*, or alternatively, O Lotus-born One, all [the images] together.
In this way, one should offer the *nīrājana*; it is prescribed that the offering be performed separately for Śrī and Bhūmi.
While the *nīrājana* ceremony is being performed, one should raise the sound of musical instruments;
and the women of the royal court should perform various kinds of dance and song.
All the lamp-vessels should be placed upon the sacrificial altar (*balipīṭha*).
Having performed the daily festival, the ritual bath in the river, and worship elsewhere,
when midnight has arrived, one should perform the bathing and other rites for Hari,
offering in sequence pure milk-rice, mung-bean rice, cakes, and other sacrificial oblations.

One should offer cow’s milk, white sugar-candy, and other sweet substances. Before the rising of the sun, many bards and panegyrists should awaken the Lord of Gods while praising him with the playing of musical instruments.
At night, one should perform the *nīrājana* (lustration) of Hari before all the images.
One should display every ritual service (*upacāra*) just as in the royal protocol.
O Four-faced One, those distinctions of time that have been prescribed for day and night [should likewise be observed].
One should worship Hari among these [deities] in this manner, according to the distinction between the inferior and the principal.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Division of Times for the Daily Festival and Ritual Worship," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
The Sixth Chapter: The Ritual for the Nṛsūkta, Service, and Lustration (Nīrājana), by Brahmā.
"O Blessed One, how should the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs of the *puruṣasūkta* be performed? Or how, O Lord, may I worship you with it?
For me, who am asking out of doubt, what is the procedure for domestic worship?"
"If you have favor toward me, it should be told by me exactly as it is.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The meter is Anuṣṭubh, its seer is Vāsudeva, and its deity is Vāsudeva."
The placement [of the mantras] is performed in sequence upon the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the nose, and likewise the mouth;
the throat, the two arms, the heart, the navel, the limbs, the genitals,
the two thighs, and the two feet— using the verses beginning with the first in order.
With the first [verse] one should invoke the deity, and with the second, the seat;
with the third, the water for the feet (pādya), and with the fourth, one should offer the arghya oblation.
With the fifth, the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana), with the sixth, the bath (snāna), and with the seventh, the garment.
With the eighth *ṛc*, the sacred thread (*upavīta*); with the ninth, the application of fragrant unguents;
with the tenth and eleventh, flowers; with the twelfth, incense and lamps;
with the thirteenth, the food offering (*nivedana*); and with the fourteenth, prostration.
One should perform the circumambulation with the fifteenth [verse], and the dismissal (*udvāsana*) with the sixteenth.
The offerings of fuel-sticks, food, and clarified butter should be made to Jātavedas verse by verse.
One should worship Viṣṇu in one's own home in some pure place within the house.
Having meditated upon Hari on dry ground made of jewels, or likewise in a celestial chariot (vimāna) of that same nature;
or in water, fire, the heart, the sun, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in images—
taking a vessel of flowers and water, while standing, one should invoke the Lord.

Then, with each of the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ*, and with them both separately and collectively, as well as with the beginning of the Veda, one should offer a seat to Puruṣottama. Then, having consecrated the water contained in the vessel with the *Sāvitrī* mantra, [one should place] the purifier (*pavitraka*).
One should offer half of that with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī and with the mantra "trīṇi padā.
One should provide water for the feet and water for sipping with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Then, one should perform the ritual bathing with mantras containing the word "ap" (water) and wipe the limbs with those same mantras.

With the *vyāhṛtis*, with a cloth for wiping, and with the mantra "jitaṃ te," he should give clothing, knowledge, and so forth, as well as the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and an ointment. Having recited "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should perform the decoration with the *praṇava*.
With the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ," he offers flowers; with "jitaṃ te," incense;
with "uddīpyasva," the lamp; and with "devasya tvā," the oblation (havis).
He should also offer these with the mantras of Vāsudeva and others, as well as those of the Fish-incarnation and others, and Keśava and others.
Having offered flowers and meditated upon each respective form according to its place,
the worship of the four-faced Brahmā and other deities as part of the retinue should be performed;
they are not to be worshipped independently by a Vaiṣṇava in domestic ritual.
At the time of recitation, he should recite either the *Nṛsūkta*, or the twelve-syllable mantra,
or the eight-syllable mantra, or some other mantra, or even the *praṇava*; or, with a concentrated mind, he should recite those mantras that fall within the scope of the end of the three Vedas.

The householder who himself constantly worships Viṣṇu in his home shall lead twenty-one generations of men born in his family [to liberation]. Whether it be the abode of Viṣṇu, or residence in the same world (sālokya), or whatever else is desired—
Today, the ritual procedures for the worship of Hari have come within the scope of my practice.
One hundred and eight and twenty [verses] have been heard as they issued from my mouth;
following this are the invocation, the salutation, and the rising to greet him.
An offering of flowers, a welcome, a seat, a footstool,

water for honoring (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), a vessel for receiving the water, again water for the feet, the wiping of the feet with a cloth, and an anointing of the two feet with water mixed with powdered sandalwood.
The reception of water for sipping and for rinsing the mouth;
the sprinkling of water and the smearing with unguents such as sandalwood paste;
the offering of flower garlands, the presentation of incense, and the serving of the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Camphor,
betel leaves, items for bathing and seating, sandals, a bathing seat, and thereafter a bathing cloth; then a tooth-stick, a mirror, and a tongue-scraper.
A roll of betel-leaf, a garment spread out like a half-parārdha [in measure],
anointing, a garland for the head, and immediately thereafter a palm-leaf fan;
the body was then anointed with sandalwood and the waters of fragrant āmalaka.
A comb, bathing at night, clothing, fragrant unguents,
an upper garment, a sacred thread, and immediately thereafter dance and song;
water for the feet, and bathing with streams of water from a vessel with a thousand holes.
The lustration rite (*nīrājana*), the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), the head-wrap (*plota*), the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), the cloth for the wrap (*plotavāsas*),

the touching of the limbs (*aṅgābhimarśana*), the garment (*vastra*), the sacred thread (*upavīta*), and immediately after that the upper garment (*uttarīya*)— these thirty, O Lotus-Seated One, have been described. (6.30–6.31)
For Hari, who was seated upon his ornamental throne, there were at that time sandals, a helmet, the wearing of yellow silk garments,
and an anointing with camphor powder from head to foot.
Musk, deer-essence, and anointing with sandalwood;
a fan, a multitude of chowries, and anointing with saffron;
artificial perfumes, ornaments, and the fashioning of the sacred thread.
An upper garment, a crest-garland, and armlets hanging down;
one should apply a forehead mark with clay and collyrium with a stick.
O Brahmin, there is the scattering of flowers and the presentation of a great mirror.
Betel leaves, incense, lamps, and a vessel of śāli rice;

the study and recitation of the Vedas, giving gifts, dance, the sounding of flutes, the playing of lutes and other instruments, and the chanting of auspicious hymns followed immediately thereafter. (6.36–6.37)
There was the lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) and the casting of five rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) in each direction;
furthermore, the services for the journey-seat of Hari were appropriate for that time.
There were sandals, chowries, and a pearl parasol to ward off the sun.
A peacock-feather fan, a palm-leaf fan, a chariot, an elephant,
a horse, a palanquin, the raised banner of Vainateya,
a play-stick, betel vines, and an abundance of playthings.
Thus fifteen [deities] have been described as situated on the seat of departure;
when Hari has ascended the seat for the meal, they are present at that time. [They are:
the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the betel-roll (tāmbūlavīṭikā), and the mouth-cloth (mukhaśāṭikā).
Water for honoring, milk-rice, mung-bean rice, and rice with jaggery;
curd-rice, a refreshing drink, water for rinsing, and a hand-cloth;
and the purification of the two hands with water scented by the powder of cardamom and sandalwood.
And while the descendant of Daśārha sat at ease, he was provided with anointing unguents for his limbs,
garlands, and likewise cakes, flattened rice, parched grain, sesame balls, fruits, and boiled water, all prepared with sandalwood water.
The gift of coconut water, a roll of betel leaves,
circumambulation, prostration, praise, self-surrender, the offering of arghya,
and dismissal— these constitute twenty-one hundred [repetitions].
O Brahmin, the ritual services for Hari have been shown in detail:
the invocation and salutation, as well as the worship following the offering of a seat;
likewise the footstool, the water for honoring (arghya), and the reception of the water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, and the acceptance of gifts;
sipping water, mouth-perfume, sandals, a seat for bathing, a bathing cloth, a tooth-stick, and likewise a tongue-scraper. (6.48–6.49)
Betel, ointment, a fan, and the rubbing of the limbs;
bathing with fragrant *āmalaka* fruit,
cleansing with a comb, bathing with a paste of turmeric, and the adornment of an upper garment.
A bath with a thousand streams of water, as well as the lustration ceremony (nīrājana); the touching with a cloth, the garment, the arrangement of the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), the upper robe,
ornaments, the seat, and the drying of the hair.
A lower garment of fine linen, the anointing with fragrant substances,
a fan, ornaments, a garland of flowers, collyrium for the eyes,
betel, a mirror, incense and lamps— such was the expenditure for her mother.
The gift of the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), the parasol, sandals, chowries, and banners; vehicles, palanquins, musical instruments, as well as playthings and fruit;
the attainment of food and seats, and the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka). || 6.54–6.55 ||

O Brahmin, the sixty-four [services] consist of: honoring, bringing [the guest], water for the feet, a comfortable seat, offering cakes and other foods, betel-leaf, reciting hymns of praise, and dismissal. (6.56)
Next, I shall describe the thirty-two ritual services exactly as they are:

first the invitation and the seat, followed by the water for the guest-offering (arghya), the water for washing the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamana), mouth-perfume, sandals, and the tooth-cleansing stick. (6.57–58)
Oil for cleaning the tongue, bathing with *dhātrī* and *haridrā*,
an upper garment, fragrant ointments, and ornaments;
likewise, a garland, collyrium, the gift of a mirror, incense, and a lamp.
Then the taking of the mother [of the bride], the parasol, the fly-whisk, and the sounding of musical instruments;
the offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), the formal presentation, followed by food,
as well as betel-leaves, and finally the dismissal.
There should be sixteen services performed according to the capacity of the self:
first the invocation and the seat, followed by the water for honor (arghya) and the water for the feet (pādya);
then the sipping of water (upasparśa), as well as the bath, the garment, and the sacred thread (yajñopavītaka).
Likewise, there are fragrant unguents, ornaments, garlands, incense, and lamps;
the offering of honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), the presentation of food, and finally the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*).
And upon all the seats, there is the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the reception of that water for the feet.
O Four-faced One, the washing of the feet, the anointing of the feet with fragrant unguents,
and the sipping of water (ācāma) from that water are prescribed as forms of acceptance (pratigrahaṇa).
Having set aside one's food, procession, and seat, a footstool should be provided.
The offering of the honey-mixture (madhuparka) occurs at both the commencement and the conclusion [of the rite].
At the end of the meal, when putting on a garment, and likewise during a bath,
as well as after scraping the tongue, the act of sipping water (ācamana) is required in every instance.

In the offering of garments and likewise in the drying of hair, incense should not be offered without the ringing of a bell; nor elsewhere, except when accompanied by the bell. In the service of lamps and in the offering of food, there must otherwise be the sounding of the bell.
And at the place where wealth is destroyed, worship performed would be demonic (6.69).
One should discard the tooth-stick at the three junctions of the day into water suitable for ritual sipping,
using a vessel for receiving it (6.70).
From the time of eating until the end of consuming food and drink, one should wipe the hands with a cloth;
likewise, the wiping of the eyes with collyrium should be done with a cloth.
One should offer the respectful offering (arghya) at the time of the meal, never at the beginning of drinking or other such acts.
Immediately thereafter, there is the transition of thought toward another— whether subtle or gross— and likewise the welcoming of that [object] within the mental image (bimba),
as well as the greeting, the salutation, and the prayer for its presence. (6.72–6.73)
Thus is the eight-limbed invocation of the Supreme Self.
One should worship the God, having invoked Him according to the prescribed ritual, in gems, crystal, gold, silver, or even copper, or in a temporary image.
The mandala of the wheel and lotus, the water-pot filled with water and encircled by thread;
likewise, the seed, the flour, the food, the fruit, the flower, and the water;
the fragrance, the altar, the dung-broom, and so forth—these are considered to be momentary (kṣaṇika).
One should always perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) for Lord Hari installed in the inner sanctum,
using a pitcher made of gold or other precious materials, filled completely with water,
adorned with garlands, provided with a lid, and having its mouth decorated with leaves of the holy fig tree (aśvattha).
Honored with unbroken grains of rice and likewise sprinkled with scented water,
it was four finger-breadths in height and adorned with a lamp-wick;
lifting it high with both hands from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head.
Having circumambulated the Lord of Gods three times, one should place [the vessel] upon the *balipīṭha*.
This *nīrājana* rite is for the pacification of terrible [obstacles] and for the increase of prosperity.
Thus, in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Pādmatantra*, in the *Caryāpāda*.
The Sixth Chapter: The Ritual of the Nṛsūkta, Worship, and Nīrājana;
The Seventh Chapter:
The Ritual for the Adoration of the Maṇḍapa and the Consecration of the Preceptor (Ācāryābhiṣeka).
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, please tell me what kind of mandala is called Cakrābja, which,
when propitiated and fully worshipped, enables one to cross the ocean of worldly existence.
The Blessed One [described] the form as square, made from four auspicious wooden sacrificial posts, six finger-breadths thick and twelve finger-breadths wide.
One should determine the length and width according to the mandala;
[one should construct] pillars that are eight tālas in height, well-rounded and square,
and auspicious at the four corners of this closely situated [structure].
And one should place [the central post] above,
and set up four wooden beams according to the characteristics previously described;
and that group of four wooden beams [should be adorned] with a canopy, banners, and garlands.
One should decorate it all around and hang down garlands of pearls;
with pure clay, one should fill the space beneath the four squares and smear the interior of that [area] with cow-dung.
One should fashion images such as wheels, lotuses, and so forth upon that surface of the earth.
Their length and breadth are prescribed to be measured by a cubit,
or they may be twice, three times, or even four times that size.

Alternatively, O Brahman, one should lay down seventeen threads on the ground according to the available space, each possessing five qualities; likewise, O Lotus-seated One, one should lay down as many threads directed toward the north.
Furthermore, there are exactly two hundred and fifty-six squares; among them,
one should place a peg in the center of the thirty-sixth square and rotate [the cord] along the path of the thread.
There are five circles of equal size, with the middle one being a single unit;
from this, the area of the pericarp, and outside that, the circle is divided again threefold by means of the thread-path,
the first [division] being the ground of the filaments.
