The second [circle] is the ground of the navel, while the third is the circle of the navel itself. One should divide that single [area], or it may be divided into two or three parts according to the path of the lines; from the portion of the navel-ground outward, there shall be two circles.
The area outside the rim, not being a field, shall constitute a single circle;
then, with twenty-eight squares, there is a seat around the exterior.
With eighty squares, the outer walkway (vīthikā) shall be square.
O Soul of the Universe, outside the square [mandala], there should again be two rows [of squares].
There shall be one hundred and twelve squares, and there should be two rows for each direction;
within those squares, one should arrange four gates for each direction.
O Four-faced One,

for the sake of the accomplishment of the conch, one should erase two squares in each of the four corners of the two rows. (7.18) O Four-faced One, one should likewise erase two squares in each of the two rows.
Near each gate, on both sides as well,
two cells each should be placed in the outer row for the sake of establishing half-beauty in the outer and inner streets, and one cell in the row immediately following that.

O Lotus-born one, for the sake of beauty, one should sweep each of the outer sections in this manner; likewise, three by three cells should be swept for the sake of the secondary ornamentation (*upaśobhā*),
alternating in this way across the four [sides].
The sweeping of the chambers and their arrangement has been demonstrated.
Alternatively, O Four-faced One, having swept around the twenty chambers and two hundred [others], one may proceed without the construction of seats and the like. || 7.22–7.23 ||
One should construct the three enclosures according to the measure of the original lotus;
one should arrange four doors in the four directions according to the measure of the lotus. Or else, O Lotus-born One, one may construct a single enclosure in the desired direction.
Twelve lotuses are to be fashioned; this is the arrangement for each enclosure.
One is placed in each of the four corners, and two on each side of the circular rim.
It is endowed with twelve petals and provided with a pericarp and filaments.
One should fashion the cluster of lotuses according to the measurement of half the first lotus;
one should arrange the drops within the pericarp of the central lotus.
There are likewise one hundred and ninety lines for the twelve lotuses.
Having arranged the filaments in sequence, one should fashion them within the petal-field;
likewise, in the intermediate and cardinal directions, there should be four and twenty [petals],
with two lines each, and the petals should be like the tips of needles in the intervals.
One should display the spokes in the field of the circle toward the cardinal directions;
there should be two spokes each in the intermediate directions, and one each at the twelve points.
The spokes should be like the petals of a blue lotus, resembling the leaves of a lotus.
Or else, O Lotus-born One, their cavities may resemble the interior of a barley grain or be like those of a citron;
they may be shaped like the belly of an ant,
and these internal spaces should all be equal to one another.
Such a mandala is recommended for the worship of Vāsudeva.
In the case of Nārāyaṇa, however, those beginning with Bindu who were previously mentioned should be sacrificed to;
eight of each [of these] are to be arranged, making ninety-six filaments (kesara).
Having cleared the thirty-six previously indicated squares,
one should there fashion a lotus, excluding the central nave (*nābhi*).
Having taken up a peg (*śaṅku*) with a thread, one should divide that [space] equally into two parts.
One should first divide the field of the pericarp (karṇikā) and secondly divide it into three parts:
the first third is the field of the filaments (kesara), and immediately following that is the field of the petals (dala).
The third part shall be the intermediate space (antarāla) between the two—the petals and the pedestal (pīṭhikā).
O Lotus-seated One, one should make eight or twelve [sections] starting from the *bindu*;
this is the mandala named Bhadraka, which grants all desires.
Desiring to construct the Svastika image, one should prepare a field consisting of thirty-six [squares].
Having wiped clean that area, one should draw eleven squares; then,
having drawn threads extending eastward and threads extending northward,
one should wipe clean two paths each from the center, extending eastward as well.
In the same way, one should make a single [line] extending northward, and then again an exit [line].
From the two compartments extending eastward, outside the row, it is intended that there be an exit facing north, as well as exits facing east, west, and south. (7.40–7.41)
Likewise, when it is oriented toward the north, it is auspicious if it faces north and west;
if it has its tips pointing south in the eastern direction, it is called the *svastika*.
Having divided the previously mentioned mandala of thirty-six squares into two parts... [7.42]
In the center, the making of the lotus is performed; when the remainder is divided into three parts,
with two parts one rotates to form the circular mandala of the lotus,
while by the remaining part there shall be an outer interval.
This should be the solar mandala, and this very same one the lunar mandala;
for all the images, as before, they should be outside the pedestal (pīṭha).
One should not meditate on the pedestal and so forth, but only on the circle and the lotus.
Either the lotus may be without the wheel, depending on the power of the practitioner;
one should beautify the mandala with jewels of five colors, such as white and the rest,
or else with powdered gems, or those made of metal, or those derived from minerals.
Alternatively, with fragrant powders such as sandalwood, agallochum, and kuṣṭha;
or with white rice and other grains like śāli, ground and mixed together;
or even with black sacrificial leaves, crushed and burnt in a closed vessel (puṭa).
One should adorn the pericarp and other parts with dark-blue, white, crushed saffron-colored,
or pale-red substances; or with night-blooming powder, or with five-colored flowers that bloom at their respective times, O Four-faced One, according to the colors of those parts.
One should beautify the shape with materials such as jewels in those very colors;
all the intermediate spaces should be adorned everywhere with black or dark-blue [pigments].
One should beautify the pericarp with yellow [pigments] and adorn the dots with white.
One should form the line of filaments with *pāṭala* flowers, or the row of stamens with black ones;
having divided the eastern portion in two ways, one should use white flowers for the northern portion,
and yellow or red at the intervals, with white flowers for each individual stamen.
One should place drops with jewels and draw lines upon the tips of the petals;
one should further adorn the bases and tips of the feathers with white and red colors.
One should separately decorate the circular border at the edge of the feathers with either red or white.
The three lines at the navel should be dark, yellow, and red respectively.
When there are two navels, they should be dark and yellow; when there is only one navel, it should be dark.
However, the lines on the crest-lock (coṭīra) should be drawn as black alone.
One should distinguish the circle between the spokes with red [squares], the earth within the rim with black,
and the portion of the earth at the rim with white; having first divided one part in two,
one should further specify another part of the rim with black and the other with white.

One should color the pedestal with yellow, pale red, or white powders, and likewise the pathway with powders provided with creepers, canopies, leaves, and so forth. One should beautify the primary ornamentation with red and the secondary ornamentation with yellow.
One should beautify the door with white, red, yellow, and black [colors] in due order;
and one should decorate the corners starting from the north with black and then with white.
One should fashion a conch shell with that same [color], and a svastika of pale-red luster.
Alternatively, it may resemble yellow; the solar orb has a pale-red luster,
while the lunar orb is white, and the entire intervening space is of whatever color one desires— beautiful within the circle measured by the span of the hands.
On the lines, the height [of the powder] is equal to the little finger;
in a two-cubit [mandala], it is the measure of the ring finger; in a three-cubit [mandala], it is equal to the ring finger;
but in a four-cubit mandala, it is measured by the index finger.
The height is shown to be five cubits, measured by the thumbs [of the hands].
(7.64) Having thus painted the mandala, one should begin the worship;
immediately thereafter, one should propitiate the path of mantra within the pericarp. (7.65)
O Four-faced One, the path of principles (tattvādhvan) is in the filaments, the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) in the petals,
the path of words (padādhvan) in the region of the navel, and the path of kalās (kalādhvan) in the spokes;
while the sixth, the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), is in the portion of the rim.
One should worship the twelve syllables upon the twelve dots in the pericarp.
Having invoked the syllables into the pericarp with a concentrated mind,
the knower of ritual duties, having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, should worship the Supreme Self.

One should worship Śrī and the others on the filaments, and their ten and two attendant Śaktis on the surface of the petals, according to the prescribed rite. The Śaktis beginning with Śrīvatsā and those beginning with Vyāpti are situated all around.
Viṣṇu, located in the first pericarp, is to be worshipped on the circle at the edge of the petals;
Brahmā resides in the second pericarp, while the Three-eyed One (Śiva) is situated in the third.
On the twelve spokes, the twelve forms beginning with Viṣṇu are to be worshipped.
On the circle of the spokes, the ten forms beginning with Mīna are to be worshipped;
on the first circle of the rim, there is the worship of the weapons beginning with the conch (śaṅkha). In the four corners of the pedestal are Varāha and Narasiṃha.
Ananta and Hayagrīva [are to be worshipped] in the southeast and the other directions respectively;
on the pedestal, the world-protectors beginning with Puruhūta (Indra) are to be worshipped in order;
and at the doors, the two [deities] beginning with Caṇḍa are to be worshipped in each of the four [directions].
One should worship Viṣvaksena on the road in the northeast corner;
Garuḍa stands facing [the temple] on the ground outside the eastern door,
the Discus at the southern gate, and the Mace at the western gate.
Then, one should place the conch in the northern Valaja within the first enclosure.
O Lotus-born One, the forms beginning with Viṣṇu are to be worshipped in the twelve lotuses; likewise, in the subsequent enclosure,
there are twelve forms in the twelve lotuses as well, beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Kṛṣṇa.
At the end, in the lotuses and the enclosure, there is the worship of the twelve Ādityas.
In this maṇḍala, one should worship the god Vāsudeva;
however, in the image known as Nārāyaṇa, [one worships] those same [deities] in eight dots.
One should worship the placement of the eight syllables and the eight powers, such as Vyāpti and the rest, in the filaments;
the eight [deities] beginning with Śrī in the petals;
and in the eight spokes, one should worship the eight weapons beginning with the conch.
In the twenty-four lotuses are the twenty-four forms. Within these three enclosures, having invoked Hari Nārāyaṇa into that maṇḍala, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
On the new moon and the full moon, at the sun’s passage into a new sign, during the Śravaṇa constellations,
on the twelfth lunar day, at the equinoxes, during eclipses, and at the solstices—
and especially on one's own birth constellation— one should worship Hari in the maṇḍala.

This worship of the maṇḍala bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa. Initiations are prescribed for the wheel-lotus maṇḍala, and its maṇḍala should have a single entrance; it should be gentle for those of the first-born caste.
The eastern gate of kings shall be decorated with white color;
the western gate shall be decorated with red and yellow colors.
For the Vaiśyas, it shall be southern, and for those born of the feet [the Śūdras], it shall be black.
And the gates for those who follow the path in due order are held to be like those for the producer [of the lineage]:
the eastern gate for the Sūta, as for the women of the Śūdra caste;
[he should initiate] a disciple or a son who is all-knowing, free from malice, and has conquered his senses. (7.87–7.88)
Born into a lineage of teachers, capable of both restraint and favor, and likewise competent in rites for pacification and prosperity for those who seek them;
he was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and one who aspired to the status of an Ācārya. (7.89)
The preeminent teacher, a knower of reality, should, according to the procedure to be described,
make [the disciple] qualified for all the rites beginning with the plowing;
he should perform the worship of the mandala and so forth, ending with the sacrifice of the jar.
Having performed all that [preliminary rite] in the presence of the disciple, as in an initiation (*dīkṣā*),
one should offer oblations with clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), fuel-sticks, flowers, and sesame seeds,
reciting the two root-mantras one thousand and eight times.

Having tied the protective amulet (pratisara) on the right hand of the disciple, the Guru should pass the night with dances, songs, instrumental music, and the chanting of the Vedas. Then, at dawn, that disciple— having bathed and wearing new garments— [should be led forward].
Having summoned and propitiated the maṇḍala and the water-jar,
and having offered the four kinds of food, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rite at night.
[One should prepare] four jars filled with a *droṇa* measure, fashioned from gold or other precious materials.
Or, having fashioned [images] out of clay according to one's means and wrapped them in thread and cloth,
one should place gems and other items upon a heap of grain;
one should deposit all the gems into the pitcher of Agni.
In the southwest, all metals; in the northwest, fragrant substances;
in the northeast, waters from sacred fords (tīrtha); thereafter, one should worship the God.
In the southeast corner is Vāsudeva, and Saṃkarṣaṇa immediately adjacent to him.
One should place Pradyumna in the wind-corner (northwest) and Aniruddha in the fierce corner (southeast).
Then, having established the disciple upon the pedestal with the Bhadrā-vidyā and other mantras,
one should seat the disciple facing east and perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
Having performed the worship, one should proceed with the offering of clarified butter without delay;
one should cause it to be proclaimed with the sound of musical instruments, with song, and with the sound of Vedic recitation.
Then, in the four directions, one should offer perfumes, flowers, and rolls of betel.
He should satisfy the Brahmins present in the assembly with various kinds of abundant offerings that are pleasing;
he should especially gratify those who have taken refuge in devotion to the Blessed One.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, he should do so with the permission of the Brahmins.
Taking up with both hands the pitcher consecrated by an *ṛgveda* mantra, which was placed in the southeastern direction, he should enclose it with the *puruṣasūkta*,
using the twelve-syllable mantra as its form.
Immediately thereafter, the composed Guru, standing in the southwest (Nairṛta) direction, should consecrate the disciple with the water-pot,
reciting the Yajus-mantra consecrated [with it] and the Vaiṣṇava Sūkta at the beginning and the end, O Brahmin. (7.105–106)
Having encapsulated [the deity] with the Mūrti-mantra and the mantra known as Saṃkarṣaṇa,
O Brahmin, [one should perform the rite] with a water-pot (kumbha) containing air, its water resonating with the Sāmans; then, with the Pradyumna-encapsulation and the Vāruṇa Sāmans.
With water purified by the *Atharvaveda* and the *Kumbha*,
having enclosed it with the *mūrti* situated in the northeast corner,
[he performed the rite] with the mantra named *Aniruddha*, which is called *Nārāyaṇa*.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with all the jars while reciting the Vidyā, as prescribed.
Then the disciple, having been consecrated, pure, wearing new garments,
having sipped water (ācānta), his limbs smeared with powdered sandalwood, and well-adorned—
Wearing garlands and having tied a turban resembling a crown with his garments,
he wore an upper robe and a yogic belt;
his pair of eyes was smeared with collyrium, and he was adorned with many garlands.
His path was watched by Brahmins who had recited benedictions;

showers of parched grain were bestowed upon him, and he was fanned with white whisks. Sandals were offered to him, a white parasol was held over him, and mounts of horses and elephants were presented.

And having been consecrated, one becomes auspicious through the grace of the Guru. O Four-faced One, having personally attained the status of an Ācārya by means of this very consecration, one may desire to perform all the duties of an Ācārya.

One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, such as cows, land, gold, and so forth, according to the extent of one’s wealth; thereafter, having mounted a vehicle such as an elephant, fanned with white chowries and shaded by a white parasol—
Marked by all the insignia of his office and accompanied by Brahmins,
he should proceed by chariot along the main road, keeping the agrahāra to his right,
and enter either the temple of the deity or his own residence.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Maṇḍala and the Initiation of the Preceptor," in the Carya-pāda of the Pādma-tantra within the Śrīpāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the eighth chapter.
Regarding the Great Consecration,
Brahmā said:
That which is the means for the prosperity of the king, the kingdom, and mortals—
O Blessed One, for those who perform it, that worship of yours is unsurpassed, as it pacifies portents, dispels diseases, and accomplishes every desired object without delay. (8.1–8.2)
"O Supreme Person, if you have compassion for me, please tell it to me;
even that secret should be explained to me for the benefit of the world. (8.3) The Blessed One said:
The supreme consecration known as the Great Consecration (mahābhiṣeka) is approved by me for my [image].
It should be performed during the equinoxes, the solstices, during eclipses, at the two transitions of the sun's course,
on the twelfth lunar day, under the Śravaṇa asterism, and likewise on the three birthdays of the Creator.
On the three days of Vyatīpāta, on Rohiṇī, and on the three lunar days;
on the new moon and the full moon, especially on the two Punarvasus;
on the fifth day under an auspicious asterism, and on favorable lunar days and weekdays, O Lotus-born One.
O Brahmin, that which is being practiced—which accomplishes all aims and grants all peace—should be performed in three ways: superior, inferior, and middling.
Having considered either the excellence of caste or the excellence of wealth, the knower of reality [should act accordingly].

One should employ the supreme bathing rite; for others, the other [rites] may suffice. On the day before, there should be the placement of sprouts, the tying of the auspicious *kautuka* thread, and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the image; or all of this may be performed immediately.

The ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed upon the image, and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa), O Four-faced One, may be performed upon either the image or a representation of a sacred ford (tīrtha); if the former is not available, one should perform the adhivāsa [upon the latter].
Or else, it may be performed upon an image intended for a festival, or even upon a sacrificial effigy (balibimba).
Alternatively, for the sake of ritual action, one may use a *bimba* (image), or, in the absence of these, a tuft of *kuśa* grass.
For images made of plaster, clay, or those situated on a wall or a cloth, a mirror should be used;
and when no other physical form is available, a tuft of grass is employed. This is the eternal rule.
Then, one should construct a bathing pavilion in front of the temple;
it should be auspicious, ten cubits in width and twice that in length,
with four doors on the four sides and adorned with four archways.
This may take place in all directions within the entire enclosure,
or one may perform it in a prepared pavilion according to the available space.
Having divided that [space] into three parts, one should then [act] in the western third.
Taking as a guide the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) extending four cubits on all sides,
one should construct a bathing altar (snānavedi) four cubits in length, one cubit in height, made of stone or other materials;
it should be provided with sandals and the like, beautiful to behold, and endowed with auspicious characteristics.
And above that, there should be a circular or square rim, O Brahmin,
one span in width, or eight finger-breadths,
or six finger-breadths, and four finger-breadths in height.
Upon the altar, one should quickly prepare a moat-like trench for the flow of that [water] around the earth;
on images made of clay and other materials, the construction of the external altar is performed.
However, in the case of a single image (ekabera), there is no construction of an external bathing altar.
One should beautify the pavilion on all sides with garments of *dukūla* and *kṣauma* silk;
one should decorate the archways with full water-jars and other ornaments,
encircle them with garlands of *darbha* grass, and hang strings of pearls.
The ritual bath is to be performed in the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇṭapa), and likewise the half-pavilion (ardhamaṇṭapa).

In the case of domestic worship (gṛhārcā), as well as in daily rites and bathing ceremonies, one should not construct archways (toraṇa) and the like, nor perform the tying of the protective thread (kautuka) or the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Bathing with powders of *niśā* is not desired on the site of the pavilion.
Having smeared it with cow-dung water, one should decorate it with lime powder;
there, one should set up lamps and place the *aṅkurapālikā* (vessels for the germinating of seeds).
In the fierce (raudra) corner of the pavilion, one should prepare a water-vat or similar vessel filled with sweet-smelling water that has been strained;
it should be consecrated with the Pavamāna hymns and other such *sūktas*, and provided with a lid.
To the south of the Veda, one should prepare the water for the preliminary bath on the ground.
One should arrange the materials for worship, beginning with the *arghya* and ending with the lamp.
One should then lay down fourteen lines made of sandalwood paste.
O Four-faced One, there are just as many threads extending eastward;
likewise, those extending northward form sixty-nine squares.
Their length is one hundred [units], and their width is sixteen finger-breadths.
O Four-faced One, [the arrangement] should be in accordance with the *dhānyapīṭha*; likewise,
O Lotus-seated One, there should be nine compartments for the pitchers in each of the eight directions as well as in the center, across the nine levels.
Thus, one should prepare eighty-one squares as the site for the pitcher;
having cleared away another eighty-eight squares, one should arrange them as the pathways.
One should construct a pedestal with rice grains, individually upon each of the squares.
It may be one āḍhaka, half of that, or half of that again.
(8.32) The base [of the heap] shall consist of a fourth part of grain; the rice grains shall be on top of the base. Sesame seeds, being a fourth part of those, shall be placed upon them. (8.33)
O Four-faced One, one should place two tips of *kuśa* grass upon each pedestal;
the jars may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, according to one's wealth. They should be endowed with the proper characteristics and resemble ripe *bimba* fruits.
The earthen jars should be without cracks, resonant when struck, free from dark spots, unbroken, and devoid of stone fragments;
these "substance-jars" (dravyakumbha) should be filled with one *droṇa*, or half of that, or even a quarter of that. || 8.35–8.36 ||
The remaining jars should be filled with a quarter-measure, or else with half an āḍhaka;
having washed the vessels for the materials as well as the others with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
one should place them upon the left palm while holding them with the right hand.

One should wrap [the linga] with a thread while reciting the mantra "Indraṃ natvā. There should be a space between the wrapped threads equal to the width of a barley grain, or a space of half a finger-breadth, or else a space of one full finger-breadth.
On the western part of the earth that serves as the site for the water-jars (kalaśa),
one should prepare a pedestal of grain and consecrate the jars upon it.
Then, having spread *kuśa* grass all over that pedestal of grain, [one should proceed].

Having uttered "Om," one should place the pitchers— pointing eastward and northward— with their openings facing downward, upon those [nine] sites in ascending order. Furthermore, one should likewise place [the ritual items] above the already-positioned pitchers as before.
The preceptor should spread darbha grass with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra;
facing east, he should sprinkle it with the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) while identifying with the nature of Puruṣa.
He should scatter unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) upon the consecrated site with the *viśva* mantra.
When the jars have been turned face upwards, by means of the vidyā for the invocation of Nivṛtti:
"Bone is proclaimed as the gem; the vessel is the thread; flesh is the fine clay;
blood is the red clay; and water is likewise the fat. (8.44–8.45)
The broom is said to be white, wrapped in a garment of hide;
the twice-born should thus meditate upon the living soul as its reflection, in due order.
Having performed [the rite] one hundred and eight times with clarified butter using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, [he should proceed].
In the home, one should sprinkle the remains of the clarified butter (*ājya*) as the substance for the bathing ritual (verse 8.47).

One should fill those various jars with substances for bathing, such as ghee, which have been purified by the *astra* mantra and consecrated; once filled, one should lift them up with the appropriate mantras (verse 8.48).
With the *sarvamantreṇa*, O Soul of the Universe, one should place seventeen uplifted water-pots (*kumbha*)—
the material pots— upon a pedestal of grain, preceded by the mantra of Viṣṇu;
and with the *gāyatrī* and the twelve-syllable vidyā, one should place sixty-four [pots].
Facing either the east or the north, one should place other water-pots in sequence; however,
in the middle position of the group of nine, a pot of clarified butter should be placed in the central spot, and then, in the position of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.
One should place a pitcher of warm water, and immediately next to it, a jewel-pitcher;
a wooden fruit-pitcher in the direction of Yama, and an iron pitcher in the direction of Nairṛta;
a pitcher of cleansing water for Pracetas, and a pitcher of scented water in the direction of Vāyu.

In the northern quarter (Kaubera) one places water with unbroken grains, and in the northeast (Śārva), barley-water. In the eastern direction, among the nine jars, one places the jar for foot-washing (pādya) in its position;
the jar for the respectful offering (arghya) in the southern position; and again, in the position of Pracetas (the west).
In the western position, there is water for ritual sipping and the five products of the cow;
in the center of the nine jars belonging to Agni, there is a jar of curd in its position.
In the south-western direction, milk is in the center; in the north-western direction, there is a jar of honey.
One should place a jar of decoction in the northeast, and sixty-four jars of pure water— eight by eight— everywhere around it;
these jars should be made with seven, five, or even three blades of *darbha* grass.
One should place grass-bushes (kūrca) with their tips pointing downward into the jars, provided they possess the proper characteristics;
in the great jar, however, one should use a grass-bush made of twenty-four kuśa blades. With the Cakra-mantra, one should have all of them covered with shallow bowls (śarāva).
With the verse "The youth well-clothed" (RV 10.85.23), he should wrap the vessels containing the substances in cloths;
others he should encircle at the necks and cover with new garments,
together with learned Brāhmaṇas who have studied the threefold knowledge.
Accompanied by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), one who knows the mantras should go into the presence of the deity.
Having raised the deity, the preceptor (*guru*) should also rise with the sacred knowledge (*vidyā*).
With the *Sāman* chant called the *Rathantara*, the preceptor himself [proceeds] in the Brahma-vehicle.
He should place [the image] together with the officiating priests and Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas.
Having placed it upon a palanquin prepared with a soft mattress,
they should set the image down upon the pure surface of the bathing altar.
Thereafter, one should have the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) recited by those devoted to the five daily rites;
one should satisfy them with wealth in odd numbers, according to one's prosperity.
Having worshipped the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth, as before.
One should initiate the study [of the scriptures], dancing, instrumental music, and singing at the gates.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire according to the number of jars;
one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the root mantra according to the previously mentioned number.

Having worshipped the installed jars with the Nṛsūkta, the Guru should likewise perform the offering of ghee to the Deity with arghya and other oblations. He should then provide a tooth-stick, oil, and water scented with fragrant myrobalan.
Having offered a garment and an upper cloth, one should worship again with the arghya and other offerings.

(8.68) Having performed the worship ending with the lamp, the preceptor should bathe [the deity] in sequence using jars beginning with those for the foot-water and ending with those for the clarified butter. (8.69)

Having extracted the single thread from the consecrated water-pot (pādyakumbha) and having honored it with flowers, the image-keeper (mūrtipa) should place it in the palm of the hand of the preeminent teacher (deśikendra). Then,
taking the tuft of grass (kūrca) situated within the pot, the most excellent teacher should place it in his hand.

Then, with a *kūrca* of grass having its tips pointing downward, one should bathe [the deity] at the sacred sites (*tīrtha*) beginning with Brahmā using pure water for the feet (*pādya*) while reciting the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī;
one should bathe [the deity] with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) while reciting the mantra "Tad viṣṇoḥ."
With the Vedic verse "na te viṣṇo," he should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) with water from a jar;
with the mantra "viṣṇoḥ karma," the sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); and with the Yajus formula "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," the sprinkling with curd for the sake of the deity.
The bathing of the Enemy of Madhu was performed with ghee, milk, curd, and honey, accompanied by the *sāman* chant; then, with the mantra "madhuvātā," he was bathed with honey,
and with the mantra "oṣadhīḥ," he was consecrated with decoctions.
The bath with a stream of warm water is performed with the mantra *tad viṣṇoḥ*;
the bathing with fruit-water is performed with the *anuvāka* beginning *phalinī*;
and the bath with consecrated sprinkling water is performed with the mantra *śaṃ no devīḥ*.
He should perform the bathing with *akṣata* water and the *Sāvitrī*, with the *Sāman* chants beginning "trātāram," with precious gem-water and metallic water using the *Mahāvyāhṛti* formula,
and with fragrant water using the mantra "gandhadvārā. (8.77–8.78)
The bathing with barley water should be performed with the mantra *śatadhārā*;
the bathing of Hari with ghee should be performed with the mantra *ghṛtasnātā*.
Alternatively, one may perform the bathing with the waters for the feet (*pādya*) and so forth, in sequence, using the *Puruṣasūkta* hymns.

O Four-faced One, the bath may be performed with sixteen *ṛg* verses, or with the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," or with the eight-syllable mantra, or with the twelve-syllable vidyā, or even with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī. (8.80–81)
Alternatively, one may perform the bathing of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) with the *svamūrti-vidyā*;

and during the bath with clarified butter (*ghṛtasnāna*), there should be cleansing with ordinary warm water at intervals between the removal of the jars containing the substances for the *pādya* and other offerings.

O Lotus-born One, the bathing of the God should be performed with eight jars of pure water and eight other [substances], using the eight-syllable mantra. Likewise, there should be a secondary bath, as well as a cloth and an upper garment.
The water for honoring (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), as well as water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana), fragrance, flowers, incense,
and a lamp— these should be offered, each substance immersed in a jar.
One should lift up the jars of substances with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra.
And with the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra, one should fill jars of pure water;
nine, seven, or five jars— free from defects, provided with threads, and containing turmeric, rice, and gold dust.
Alternatively, three [pots] or a single pot may be placed for the distribution;
one should worship them in pots that have lids and sacred grass (*kūrca*) inside.
Having lifted the pots of Śrī, one should consecrate them with the *Śrīsūkta*.
Just as the *pūrṇāhuti* occurs in a fire sacrifice, so too should the bathing with the powders take place.
Those men who bear upon their heads these supremely purifying powders, fallen from the body of Vāsudeva, have shaken off all impurity.
Those who drink and carry the consecrated water of Viṣṇu go indeed to the station of Viṣṇu, from which there is no return;
they enjoy the great fruit of bathing in all sacred fords.

Having performed a circumambulation, bowed, and praised [the Lord] with hymns, the preceptor then bathed Janārdana with a thousand streams. Having thus worshipped Him up to the rite of waving lights (nīrājana), he then [placed Him] upon the ornamental throne.
One should perform the sacrifice up to the final gift of the measure; the number of measures is determined by the circumference [of the altar].
Those grains should be given to the preceptor as *khārī*, *droṇa*, or half of that.
Furthermore, one should feed him with the four kinds of food at the dining seat.

At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the preeminent teacher should worship the God according to the prescribed rite. Then, at the end of the ceremonial bathing, the patron should request Janārdana, who is seated comfortably upon his throne, for everything he desires.
One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) of one hundred gold *niṣkas* to the lord of teachers,
or half of that, or a quarter, according to one's wealth.
One should place all the materials gathered for the purpose of worship at the disposal of the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Likewise, one should provide garments and other gifts to the other officiating priests (ṛtvij) so as to bring them satisfaction.
One should bestow wealth upon the Brahmins who are devoted to dance and song as well as those distinguished by their Vedic study, in such a way that they are fully satisfied. (8.98–99)
Thus, the inferior and superior types of bathing have been proclaimed.
If there are thirty-two jars filled with pure water in the corners,
yet the bathing is devoid of those [other elements], it should be known as the inferior-middle type.
That which is deficient in any of the pure water-pitchers is the lowest of the low.

Likewise [it is so] regarding the pitcher for foot-washing, the pitcher for the *arghya* offering, the pitcher for the water for sipping, the pitcher for the astringent decoction and fruits, and the pitcher for the unbroken grains and perfumes. (8.101–102)

Into each one of these jars, one should place eight substances. The substances and their respective quantities for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the others are stated in order: *tulasī*, as well as lotus, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Śyāmāka grain, viṣṇuparṇa, bilva leaves, and sandalwood—
these remaining [substances] in the measure of a handful, along with one pala of sandalwood, white mustard seeds,
unbroken rice, tips of kuśa grass, and likewise fruit.
Barley, sesame seeds, sandalwood, and fragrant blossoms;
well-ripened fruit—of these, three *niṣkas* of sandalwood, and one handful each of the remaining [ingredients], as well as *takola* and *campaka*. (8.106)
Mukula, camphor, nutmeg, cardamom, and mace;
cloves, cinnamon, sandalwood, and fragrant flowers—each of these, O Lotus-Seated One, should be equal in measure to half a fruit. || 8.107–8.108 ||
Śamī, palāśa, khadira, bilva, aśvattha, vikaṅkata,
udumbara, and nyagrodha— likewise, the barks of these beginning with śamī should each measure one pala; as should the plantain and the citron.
One should place these broken fruits: the mango, the myrobalan, the wood-apple, the coconut fruit, as well as the jackfruit and the citron;
and also of wild rice, bamboo-seed rice, śāli rice, millet, and barley.
The grains of *kaṅku*, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, and wheat,
as well as saffron and *koṣṭha-candana*, should be known to measure one handful (*muṣṭi*).
[Likewise] the roots of *agaru*, *uśīra*, and *hrībera*, as well as those from the mountains.
O Lotus-born One, one *pala* each of *māṃsī* and *mura* should be taken;
likewise, one should cast in *māṇikya*, *padmarāga*, *nīla*, *vajra*, *puṣyaka*, coral, pearl, and emerald.
Lapis lazuli and the nine gems are placed in water from a gem-encrusted jar;
likewise, gold, silver, copper, lead,
tin, bell-metal, and the essence of iron are placed in water from jars made of the seven metals.
Each [ingredient] should be one *niṣka* in measure; *rajanī*, *sūryavartinī*,
*sahadevī*, *śirīṣa*, *sadābhadra*, and *kuśāgraka*—
these six cleansing substances should be added in the amount of a single handful.

Barley, bamboo-seeds, and rice— these three should be placed in barley-water, with one *kuḍapa* of each. Having collected the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in a new, auspicious earthen vessel, [one should proceed].
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter as the fifth—
this fivefold product of the cow (pañcagavya) from a tawny or an aged cow is highly commended;
however, in their absence, the products of other cows are prescribed.

The urine and dung of a cow should never be taken from one that is distressed, pregnant, old, or one whose calf is absent. Cow dung found on the ground should be collected while it is still warm and free from contamination by insects and the like.
Having squeezed it thoroughly, one should again take the juice of cow dung.
Freshly heated clarified butter is pure, as is curd that has stood for a day and night;
milk is to be taken even if not heated, provided it is more than ten days old since its production.

One should employ the cow products together: cow urine with the Viṣṇugāyatrī, cow dung with "gandhadvārā," milk with "āpyāyasva," and curd with "dadhikrāvṇo. Ghee should be used with "śukram asi. Thus one should combine the products of the cow.
Or else, [one may use] the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī or the five Upaniṣads;
the Parameṣṭhin-mantra for cow dung, the Puruṣa-mantra for cow urine, the Viśva-mantra for curd, and the Nivṛtti-mantra for clarified butter. || 8.125-8.126 ||
Milk should serve as the base for all mantras; for all of them, the eight ingredients are as follows:
curd is twice the quantity of the base, then nectar (pīyūṣa) is three times that, urine is six times that, and the water from cow dung is four times that.
The measure prescribed for the *snapana* rite is equal to that declared for the *prokṣaṇa* rite.
Cow urine should be equal in measure to cow dung; curd should be twice that amount;
clarified butter should be four times that; and milk should be eight times that.
This is declared to be the measure for the consumption of the five products of the cow:
the five products together amount to one *droṇa*, and the clarified butter is equal in measure to that;
likewise is the curd, likewise the milk, and likewise the honey.

It should be either half [a measure] or an *āḍhaka*; if it is less, it would be of the *āsura* type. For the bathing of the household deity’s image, one should provide at least one *prastha*. If other substances for the *pādya* (water for the feet) are unavailable, *dūrvā* grass and mustard seeds may serve as the *arghya*.
For the water for sipping (ācamanīya), *takkoḷa* is prescribed; for the water for sprinkling (*mārjanāmbhas*), *sahadevī* and fragrant water; for the powder of sandalwood, it is desired.
For the decoction water (*kaṣāyatoya*), the *aśvattha* [leaves] are used when hot water is not available. 8.133k–l.
O Lotus-Seated One, a single vajra is recommended in water containing jewels; a single plantain fruit in water with its own juice;
gold in iron-infused water; and unbroken rice grains in water with *śāli* rice; and *vrīhi* rice in a jar of barley-water. || 8.134–8.135 ||
If curd is unavailable, milk [should be used]; if milk is unavailable, there should be curd. If honey is unavailable, clarified butter; if that is unavailable, there should be honey.
If the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) are unavailable, clarified butter alone is prescribed.
If one should lack any of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), ghee is used in its place. I shall now describe the intermediate ablution; listen attentively to how it is performed.
Once the previously mentioned installation of the water-pots (*kalaśa*) has been carried out in the center... (8.137–138)
Then, O Lotus-Seated One, having swept two rows at a time from the outside, one should form the walkways all around; outside of those, one should provide a place for the jars.
Then, one should deposit forty-nine jars.
O Lotus-seated One, in each of the four directions beginning with the east,
there are four material jars; among them, others contain pure water,
as well as jaggery-water, sugarcane juice, and coconut water.
One should sequentially place the fourfold water of peace (śāntivāri) starting from the east;
in the absence of jaggery (guḍa), sugarcane juice is used, and in its absence, jaggery-water. The measure of the jaggery is eighty *palas*, or half of that, or even half of that again.
In the absence of coconut water, milk is desired in its place.
Tulasī, bamboo, wild rice, barley, white mustard, and sesame seeds—these six substances are for the peace-offering jar (śāntikumbha); among them, Tulasī must be present.
Any other substance measuring a mere handful, or separately a *kuḍuba* in measure,
or even a *tulasī* leaf, is accepted when others are unavailable.
When the ritual bathing has been performed with substances such as molasses-water and the like, [the following applies].

One should bathe Hari with jars containing substances beginning with water for the feet and ending with ghee. The bathing with molasses-water is performed with the mantra "madhu vātā," and the bathing with sugarcane juice is performed with the mantra "madhu naktam."
The bathing with coconut water is performed with the mantra "madhumānna";
then, with the mantra "vedāham," there is a bath with the waters from the jars of pacifying substances;
and the bathing of Hari with pure water is done with the mantra "jitaṃ te."
The middling-superior [rite] has been indicated; furthermore, in the middling [rite], there is the middling [subdivision].
Bathing the God of gods with four material jars, excluding pure water, constitutes the middling-inferior immersion when performed outside.
I shall describe the supreme ritual bathing, performed exactly as it was for [the Buddha] when he grew; it is done with all the material jars, but without the pure waters.
The jars should be placed in the intermediate directions as well as the cardinal directions, in the number previously mentioned.
And among those, O Four-faced One, you should place four other material jars filled with pure water in the intermediate directions from the fire;
[and also] the Indravallī sprouts, Aśvattha shoots, and Kuśa grass with Uśīra root.
A single-petaled lotus, kuṣṭha, saffron, the rohiṇa tree, the eight auspicious *sumanas* flowers, or else jasmine (*yūthikā*) and *mallikā*;
three types of blue lotuses, *jāti*, *campaka*, and likewise *ketakī*.
One should cast auspicious substances into the auspicious water:
two sprouts each, a single-petaled lotus, a handful of flowers, and one measure each of sandalwood and other [fragrant items]. (8.155–156)
In three separate jars, one in the southwest, [one should place] all the medicinal herbs:
māṃsī, kuṣṭha, the two types of haridrā, murā, śaileya, campaka, mustā, vacā, and karpūra; each [of these] should be equal in measure to a fruit.
Having ground [the herbs], O Lotus-Seated One, one should place them in a jar;
in the northwest corner, all fragrant substances should be cast into a jar:
camphor, saffron, costus, spikenard, sandalwood, and jasmine.
Priyaṅgu, kesara, mustā, tamāla, nāgakesara, the two types of mūla, kaccora, suraparṇikā, and kesara;
likewise uśīra, tagara, lodhra, and haricandana.
Two pieces of white agallochum, kuṣṭha, kāleya, granthiparṇa,
and a campaka bud— each measured as one fruit—
one should grind them all together into powder and place it in a jar of scented water.
In the northern jar for the root-medicines, there is the offering of root-medicines:
vyāghrī, śivā, balā, agni, śatapuṃkhā, śatāvarī,
bilva-root, vacā, cūrṇī, poraṇḍa, and śatamūlikā.
Each [ingredient] should be one *pala* in measure; having ground them, one should place them into a jar.
In the absence of the substances for the auspicious water (*maṅgalodaka*), sandalwood is best.
In the absence of all these medicinal herbs, *kuṣṭha* is prescribed.
In the absence of all perfumes, sandalwood is praised as the best;
in the absence of all root-herbs, *balā* is praised.
Having worshipped the presiding deity and extracted [the substances], one should bathe [the image] in due order.
First in the directions starting from the east, and thereafter in the southeast and so forth;
having recited "viṣṇor nu kam," one should bathe [the deity] with auspicious water and with water containing all medicinal herbs while reciting the mantra "oṣadhayaḥ."
One should bathe Hari with all-fragrant waters accompanied by the Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka;
then with the waters of root-herbs using the mantra "yā oṣadhī";
and here, one should bathe him with pure water using the eight-syllable vidyā.
One should bathe the deity as before, beginning with water for the feet and ending with clarified butter;
this is proclaimed as the most excellent of all bathing rites (uttamottama).
When it is deficient by half in pure water, it becomes the intermediate-excellent (uttamamadhyama).
Devoid of all pure water, it is called inferior; the best is said to be superior.
O Brahmin, in brief, twenty-five jars are prescribed;
in detail, four hundred and seventy-three.
Now I shall describe the presiding deities of all substances:
the Supreme Self and Vāsudeva are the presiding deities of clarified butter;
the Puruṣa is the deity for the pitcher of hot water, while Satya is the deity for the water with fruit.
Acyuta is for the cleansing with water; Ananta is for the unbroken grains of rice; Keśava should be used for water with jewels; Nārāyaṇa is prescribed for iron filings;
Mādhava is for scented water; and Govinda is for water with barley.
Viṣṇu resides in the water for washing the feet, and Madhusūdana in the arghya offering;
likewise, Trivikrama is in the ācamana water, and Vāmana is in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Śrīdhara is the deity in the curd, and Gopīkeśa is also in the milk.

Padmanābha is for honey; Dāmodara is for astringent decoctions (kaṣāya); Varāha is for molasses-water; and Nṛsiṃha is for sugarcane juice. Śrīdhara is for coconut water; Hayāsya is for the water used for pacification rites (śāntivāri).
Vāsudeva is the lotus-seated deity of the auspicious jar;
that god Saṅkarṣaṇa is remembered as being in the jar of water containing all medicinal herbs;
Pradyumna is in the jar of all fragrances, and Aniruddha is in the jar of root-herbs.
One should worship the image, along with its limbs and pedestal, within these jars; in all those jars containing pure water, there is the worship of Nārāyaṇa.
The deity of the jars filled with grains shall be Vasundharā.
The deity of the *kūrca* grass-bundles is the Astra-mantra; for the *cakrikā* vessels, it is Sudarśana;
the deity of the garments is Viṣṇu, or rather Janārdana for all of them.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, the ninefold ritual bathing has been described to you.
One should perform any one of these ablutions according to one's means;
by bathing Viṣṇu on the fifth lunar day, one enjoys the fruit as described.
On the birth-star of the three [ancestors], the merit is tenfold, and on the Śravaṇa asterism, it becomes twofold.
It is said that [the merit] of the moon is threefold; at the time of its waning, it becomes a hundredfold.
On the twelfth lunar day, however, it is fourfold; on the three asterisms [of Puṣya], it is threefold.
One should know it to be sixfold at the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), and it becomes threefold at the equinoxes (viṣuva).
During the southern transit (of the sun), a single bath becomes a hundredfold meritorious;
during the other transit prescribed [for bathing], the merit of immersion is a thousandfold.
During an eclipse of the moon by Rāhu, a bath offered to Hari is thirtyfold meritorious.
At the time of the sun, [the merit is] a hundred thousandfold; at the end of the age (yugānta), it is measured by ten million. When these times have passed, worship becomes infinite.
O Four-faced One, it is ordained that this yields the fruits mentioned immediately above.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I describe correctly the bathing of Viṣṇu with one hundred and eight jars, divided into three parts:
the Brāhma, the Divya, and the Mānuṣa. In two of these parts—
One should stretch eleven threads separately upon the ground for the first two [sections]:

extending eastward and transversely. Therein, in the center and in the intermediate directions, there are four [threads] each in the eight [directions], forming the locations for the pitchers and the walkways.
One should likewise construct the others so that there may be thirty-six squares;
therein, one should again place water-filled jars in the human portion,
nine in each of the directions, and eight jars should be set out.
In that case, one hundred and eight jars are prepared.
In the central Brahma position, among the four jars,
there is one containing the foundational substance (āghāra), and the remaining three contain pure water.
In the eastern divine portion, among the four jars, one should place hot water in the southeast;
in the south, fruit-water and iron; and in the southwest and west respectively.

Sprinkling with fragrant water is for the quarter of Vāyu, and in the northern direction [is sprinkling] with water containing unbroken grains; in the northeast is water with barley—these nine substances for the jars are thus described. Outside, in the human region, it should be as before.
The pitchers for the water for the feet (*pādya*) and other substances should be arranged as previously described in the east and other directions;
having lifted them up in the same order as before, one should bathe [the deity] sequentially.
With forty-nine pitchers, another method is taught.
O Lotus-seated One, ten threads moistened with sandalwood paste should be stretched out toward the east, and likewise toward the north; having expanded them,
one should place nine jars in the nine central squares.
One should place water-pots in each of the cardinal directions and six pots in the six compartments;
likewise, one should place four pots individually in the intermediate directions as well.
The pathways, the other compartments, and the materials shall remain as before.
Another bathing ritual with twenty-five jars is now described.
Having first extended ten lines upon the ground as before,
one should arrange nine jars in the middle nine squares.
One should arrange three jars each in the directions beginning with the east;
in the corners beginning with the southeast, one jar each is to be arranged.
Two jars each, containing pure water, are to be placed at the sides in the directions beginning with the east.
Excluding those eight, the other material jars are as previously described. In the central group of nine jars, one should fill them with the aforementioned substances;
or else, one may fill twenty-five jars with fragrant substances.
With sandalwood, agallochum, saffron, kuṣṭha, atagara, and vīraṇa;
with black agallochum and the water of yellow sandalwood;
and even with the mud of hrīvera—one should fashion nine new jars from nine [substances].
O Lotus-seated One, one should fill [the area] from the center up to the northeast with *tamāla*,
white *mustā*, particles of the pollen of *suraparṇī*,
camphor, *nāgakesara*, *mustā*, and the buds of *campaka*. (8.209–8.210)
With *priyaṅgu* flowers, *kāleyaka*, *granthi*, sprouts, and seeds;
with *māṃsī*, dates, *śaileya*, *hrīvera*, and the celestial tree (*suradruma*);
and with *mura*—these sixteen [substances], even those situated on the outside, should be used as appropriate.
Having set aside the corner-pitchers on the exterior, or else one should bathe Hari with others;
one should strike nine lines upon the ground as before,
and place four pitchers in the four squares at the Brahma-sthāna.
There should be two each in the cardinal directions starting from the east, and one each in the intermediate directions;
likewise, gems, metals, perfumes, and sacrificial substrates [are placed] in sequence.
These substances are to be placed in the jars situated in the southeast corner and the others, in due order.
Just as there are two jars for the water for the feet and the water for the guest-offering in the outer square dedicated to Indra, so too in the southeast corner there should be a jar of curd;
in the south, the water for sipping; and in the west, first the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
In the southwest corner, however, is milk; in the two jars in the west, unbroken rice;
elsewhere in the south, water for cleansing; and likewise in the northwest, water with *kuśa* grass. In the northeast corner, there is honey as well as astringent decoction and *kuśa* water.
In the northeast corner, one should offer water with barley and the ritual substances such as water for washing the feet in due order.
One should bathe Hari with the sixteen verses of the Puruṣasūkta,
using either twelve jars or four positioned in the center.
With eight jars filled with jewels, iron, all kinds of perfumes, and clarified butter, located in the outer compartments starting from Indra;
and beginning from the east with water for the feet, followed by those filled with curd, arghya-water, and milk.
In the same manner, with water for sipping, honey, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
water from fruits, or other substances numbering twelve,
[one should worship] in the center, in the southeast corner, in the south-western compartment, and in the northwest.
O Four-faced One, with the seeds of *granthiparṇa* and *pallava*, and with sandalwood water,
[one should worship] in the eight directions starting from the east in an outward sequence;
likewise with saffron, *māṃsī*, *tamāla*, and *mura*.
With water drawn from the mountain according to the root mantra, with particles of *suraparṇī* pollen,
with crushed *campaka* blossoms, and with dates,
one should bathe the deity with nine jars, or according to the rule of the ritual manual.

In the eight directions beginning with the east, one should [worship] in sequence with clarified butter as the substance, and likewise with water for the feet (pādya), water for the guest-offering (arghya), milk, water for sipping (ācamana),
honey, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and fruit, all filled [into the vessels].
Or, one may perform the ablution with nine jars filled with the nine jewels;
or with five jars placed in the center and in the directions starting from the east,
respectively filled with gems, coral, and pearls.

It may be made of vajras, fragments of vaidūrya, or the five auspicious metals; or it may be filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), honey, molasses, clarified butter, curd, milk, or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), respectively. || 8.229 ||
Or one may perform the bath for Hari with the aforementioned substances,
either individually or collectively, according to one's wealth, place, and time.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, consisting of gold coins equal in number to the jars.
Whether it be half, a quarter, or even half of that, according to one's means;
for one desiring results, an ablution performed without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is fruitless.
Therefore, even a small sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given by those seeking its fruit.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Great Consecration," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
The Ninth Chapter:
The Ritual for Consecration with a Thousand Vases; [spoken by] Brahmā.
"O slayer of Kaiṭabha, I have been appointed by you to the creation of progeny;
yet I am bewildered as to how I should create progeny and what must be done.
(9.1) The Blessed Lord said:
"Deprived of his sovereignty over the gods by the sin of killing a Brahmin,
the Lord of the Gods (Indra) attained his own station by propitiating me according to the prescribed rites.
In this same way, other kings as well have performed my supreme propitiation."
Having performed this and shaken off their sins, even those as great as mortal transgressions,
they attained worlds that are very difficult to reach— desirable realms free from all calamity.
They were consecrated with one thousand and one jars of water.
O Brahmin, my worship performed with sacred articles and filled with sanctified water is considered the supreme means of pleasing me;
it is the singular means for the removal of sins and the accomplishment of all prosperity.
It increases the lifespan of the subjects, the kingdom, and the king;
it has been practiced by those desiring sons as well as by those longing for victory, and it is the supreme pacifier of terrible calamities such as famine and ill omens. (9.6–9.7)
"By worshipping me according to the prescribed rite through that [mantra], which brings about all prosperity and is the sole means for achieving all human goals— you, O Brahmā... (9.8)
Free from delusion and devoid of sin, you are capable of creating living beings;
what is the procedure for the ritual bath with a thousand jars, and how should it be performed? What are the sacred objects required, and what indeed should be the sequence?
And regarding the installation of the jars, who is desired as the installer?
The illustrious Lord [describes] an auspicious [mandala] thirty-two cubits in width and twice that in length.
Having constructed a large pavilion on the ground where the water-pot (kalaśa) is to be placed, in accordance with its dimensions,
and having arranged the doors as before,
one should divide the area for the installation of the pot into twenty-five equal parts.
Having divided [the area] by the laying out of the lines for the Sūtra in the central Brahma-pada,
eighty-one jars (ghaṭas) should be placed; in the divine [area] immediately following that,
in each of the four directions beginning with the east.
Eighty-one jars should be placed at each of the four corners; furthermore,
forty-nine less [than that] for each of the human sections,
and in each of the sixteen directions, there should be twenty-five.
And pathways should be fashioned as appropriate at every step;
however, in the central ninth square of the Brahma-section,
[one should place] all metals, all jewels, and all fruits.
One should cast in all medicinal herbs and all powdered fragrances.
Having fashioned images of the Śrīvatsa and other [auspicious marks] weighing one niṣka each,
one should cast in gold, copper, and silver alone.
The Śrīvatsa, the forest garland, the conch, the discus, the mace,
as well as the lotus, the sword, and the Śārṅga bow— these are the eight insignia of the wielder of the Śārṅga.
One should worship Vāsudeva in a jar wrapped with two garments.
And on the Brahma plot, within a surrounding grid of nine squares,
one should place a sun-crystal (sūryakānta) and a ruby (padmarāga) in the central jar of the set of nine eastern jars; its presiding deity is Puruṣa.
O Brahmin, the materials and deities for the nine [vases] and likewise for the others shall be stated in order; the materials and deities for the central *kumbha* will be described separately.
The two materials are lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) and moonstone (*indukānta*), and their deities are as follows.

Vāsudeva is sapphire (*indranīla*) and Ayaskānta; these two have Satyamūrti as their presiding deity. Pravāla is the *gāruḍa* gem, and its presiding deity is Saṅkarṣaṇa; Puṣyaka consists of the two types of crystal (*sphaṭika*).

The substance is the god Acyuta, as well as ruby and gold; its presiding deity is Pradyumna, and its [associated] objects are the diamond and silver. Ananta is its deity, and its substances are copper and pearl.
The deity of Aniruddha should be present in all the jars;
in the divine portion in the eastern direction, at the site of the eighty-one jars,
there is a plantain fruit in the central jar within the middle group of nine.
The jackfruit, mango, citron, *havya*, rose-apple, *kesara*,
and jujubes— of these, the deity is said to be Tattvātmā.
In other cases, among the groups of nine, the deity and the substance are indicated by the eighth.
In due order, the substance for the central jar is citron together with pomegranate;
its presiding deity is Earth. Likewise, rose-apple and orange are used;
their presiding deity is Water, along with *takola* and the two types of cardamom fruit.
The radiant person is the deity; the two *kṣīrikā* and *āmalaka* fruits are the substance.
The deity is the breath of the world; the fruit born of grapes and dates is the substance.
The station of Viṣṇu is the deity; the mango tree accompanied by pigeons is the substance.

The deity is *manas*; the fruit is the small *panasa* fruit, which is the substance; [this is] the deity. (9.32) The deity is *ahaṅkāra*; the fruit is the *bilva* and *kadalī* fruits, which are the substance; [this is] the deity.
One should place *badara* fruits in all the jars together with the *buddhi*. (9.33)
Furthermore, the consecration of all the jars is prescribed with the eight-syllable mantra and again with the five Upaniṣads.
[The jars are placed] in the eighty-first jar in the southern direction, and the nine jars in the middle of the center.
Having ground uśīra, saffron, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, sandalwood, murā,
hrībera, and agaru, one should pour them into that jar;
then the best of those who know mantras should worship the god who deludes the three worlds.
Likewise, among the others in the east and so forth, in due order:
the aquatic-born (lotus) at Vairaṇī-mūla, where the brown-hued god (Brahmā) is worshipped;
and at Karpūra, both the substance is saffron and the deity is Śauri (Viṣṇu).
The *campaka* bud, *māṃsī*, and Dāśārha are the presiding deities.
(9.38) Sandalwood, red sandalwood, and Acyuta are the lords of food.
Sūraparṇī, *raja*, *mūra*, *kardama*, and *vastu*—these are the deities. (9.39)
The root of *vaikuṇṭhī*, the root of *girijā*, and the fine particles of the pollen of *priyaṅgu*—these substances, dedicated to the deity Puruṣottama, are said to be the two types of *kuṣṭha*.
*Mukunda* is blackish-white; it has a curved form and is known as *vṛṣākapi*.

One should place *tamāla* leaf upon all [the ingredients] with the essence of the Puruṣa mantra. One should consecrate each of those fragrant substances individually, eight parts each, as prescribed, with the *Pavamāna* and other mantras, reciting them once for each.
In the village of Ghaṭa, consisting of eighty-one [settlements], within the domain of Brahmā in the region of Vāruṇa, one should bring waters from jars,
wells, rivers, ponds, lakes, rainwater, snow, and flowing streams,
as well as the waters of the ocean, and pour them into the tanks.
Then, for the others—the nine [deities]—one should sequentially pour the aforementioned waters from the ponds and so forth into the middle jar.
One should fill all the intermediate material jars in this manner. (9.44–9.45)
One should place within the nine central jars two pairs of fish and tortoises fashioned from gold weighing two *niṣkas*, along with water from lotus ponds and mountain cascades.
9.46. One should deposit these into the nine central jars alone.
Excluding the deity in the form of the Fish and others, as well as Bhārgava,
one should worship them in sequence within the ninefold [arrangement] as described.
In the auspicious grid of eighty-one squares, one should worship in the center of the central ninefold group.
One should place therein and worship barley, wheat, *vrīhi*, *śāli* rice, mung beans, *priyaṅgu*, black gram, millet, and wild rice;
and one should worship the Lord of Gods, Padmanābha, mounted upon Garuḍa, according to the prescribed rite.

One should place each of these grains into the other eight jars; in the central jar, one should place *śāli* rice in every case. One should worship the forest garland (*vanamālā*), the conch, the discus, and the *kaustubha* gem.
The lotus, the Śārṅga bow, the mace, and the sword are said to be placed in sequence within eight jars;
likewise, in the direction of Agni among the eighty-five jars minus one,
one should fill the central group of nine jars with the Āghāra offering.
One should pour cow’s urine into six vessels belonging to Indra (the east), milk into those of Yama (the south), and curd into six of Varuṇa (the west).
Likewise, one should place cow dung into six vessels of Soma (the north).
It is taught that warm water should be placed in four vessels in the southeast corner.

In the southwest, the five products of the cow; in the northwest, the five nectars; and in the northeast, flour—within these, the vessel for Nārāyaṇa. In the southwest, within forty-nine jars at the station of Brahmā.
Having filled the nine [vessels] with oil, six [are] situated in front with scented water;
in the south with liquid camphor, in the western jar with parched grain;
in the north with consecrated waters, and in the corners with jujube-water.
One should worship Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, in those jars;
furthermore, in forty-nine jars dedicated to the Maruts,
one should fill nine of them with mustard-seed water, and six in the eastern direction with barley-water.
O Lotus-seated One, one should fill six jars in the south with half-measures of [consecrated] water, six in the west with water for rinsing the mouth,
and six in the north with auspicious waters;
there, in the corners, Aniruddha is to be worshipped with sugarcane juice.
In the forty-nine jars belonging to Īśāna, nine should be filled with honey in the station of Brahmā; six in the east with all kinds of perfumes;
six elsewhere with waters of pacification; and six in the southwest corner.
And in the southeast, jars filled with coconut water should be placed;
in the northeast and the northwest,
one should worship Hari, the consumer of lotuses, in these jars with coconut nectar.
In the human portion, in the eastern direction, one should fill the middle of twenty-five jars with the eight kinds of earth that are about to be described:
[earth] from a field, a sacred bathing place, the ocean, and mountains, as well as from an elephant and a boar.
The earth from an anthill and from a bull’s footprint is placed in the central jar;
one portion of each should be deposited into each of the other eight jars.
Keśava is to be worshipped within them in sequence, as is described elsewhere.
Sahadevī, vacā, śatamūlā, śatāvarī,
kumārī, gulūcī, siṃhī, and vyāghrī as the eighth—
these roots one should place in the middle of the central jar.
In each of those other eight [vessels], there is a worship of Nārāyaṇa.
[The ingredients are] the juices of the barks of the nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, jambu, and bilva trees,
as well as the barks of the palāśa, madhuka, and śirīṣa.
They should be placed individually in each of the other eight jars in the center;
Mādhava is to be worshipped in them, and these are the sprouts of the trees:
the leaf of the *palāśa*, the *bilva* leaf, and those born from the *kadamba*, *āmra*, and *śirīṣa*.
Furthermore, those made from *nyagrodha* and *aśvattha* wood should be placed in the positions prescribed by the ritual rule.
Govinda is to be worshipped individually among the others;
[the trees to be used are] the *jāti*, *mallikā*, *priyaṅgu*, *padma*, *bakula*, *nandyāvarta*, and *cūta*.
And jasmine flowers should be placed in the center among these;
in the other eight [positions], one flower each is to be placed. Among them, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity.
Siddhārtha, rājasiddhārtha, bamboo, and gorocanā as well—
Indra, veṇu, yava, ṣaṣṭi, śamī, and likewise caṇaka—these [should be placed] in the central jar; one of each of those [other items] in the others.
In them, let there be worship of the Enemy of Madhu with lotuses.
Sesame from the forest and that which is cultivated, the two kinds of cumin, the seed derived from linseed, *śatapuṣpa*, and *kumāraka*,
as well as *ṛṣibīja*— these should be placed in the central jar, while the others are to be treated as before.
For them, the god Trivikrama, together with his limbs and pedestal, is to be worshipped.
O Four-armed One, there should be śyāmāka, ṣaṣṭika rice, śāli rice, and nīvāra;
as well as sprouts of dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, indravallī, and the pippala tree.
The deities Vāmana and the three divine herbs— kuśa, kāṃsyamūla, and the root of uśīra and śarapuṃkha— are deposited in the central jar as before, along with the other jars. (9.79)
Likewise, the root of *astagaru* and the root of *apāmārga*.
These [are placed] in the middle jar; in the other jars, as before, the deity is Śrīdhara, and there are two *tulasī* plants, one white and one black.
On each leaf of the *veṇu* and *kesarin*, as well as on each leaf of the *ketaka* and *bilva*, one should likewise place a *śamī* leaf; in the middle of the *jāti*, and elsewhere as before.
The deity is Hṛṣīkeśa, and the two [substances] are *mustā* and *acoraka*.
One should place the bulbs of the white and blue lotuses, the *kahlāra*, and the *śītalīyaka*—and the water-lily (*kuvalaya*) in the center—in the eight jars as before.
Their presiding deity is Padmanābha; [one should also offer] sprouts of mung beans, black gram, and barley.
Then, the sprouts of *niṣpāva*, *varī*, *vrīhi*,
and *kulattha* [should be offered] in the middle of the jars of *āḍhaka* and *kumbha*, as before in the other cases.
Therein, one should perform the worship of Dāmodara with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* and likewise with *balā*.
Viṣṇukrāntā, Sadābhadra, the single-petaled lotus,
Mura, Sahā, and the two Sahadevīs are to be placed in the station of Vidhi;
elsewhere, as before, the deity shall be Yajñanārāyaṇa.
The white arka, likewise fire, bhadrā, brahmasuvarcalā,
sarasā, viraktā, pṛśniparṇī, and sthirā;
the castor plant should be placed in the middle of the jar, while the others remain as before.
There, Hari is to be worshipped with a fragrant lotus filament;
cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, and nāgakeśara,
as well as the jasmine creeper and nutmeg, should be placed in the center upon the seat of Brahmā.
Each of these should be placed among the others, and Kṛṣṇa is their presiding deity;
having fashioned each of them— gold, silver, and copper— in the shape of a lotus, weighing five *niṣkas*, along with a bell-metal mirror and cups.
Tin, lead, and brass, having the forms of an iron strainer and so forth—
these three are placed in the central jar in their natural form;
each of the others has Hayagrīva as its presiding deity.
In all the other jars, there is filling with fragrant waters.
For the bath of a thousand jars, many preceptors are prescribed;
four, or even double that number, as well as sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, there should be worship of the presiding deities (*adhideva*).
With the five Upaniṣadic mantras, one thousand oblations of clarified butter should be offered;
for the sake of pacification, one should sacrifice with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) using sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) and other materials.
From the bathing of the Enemy of Madhu with turmeric-colored powders in the human realm,
proceeding to his ablution at the station of Brahmā with a thousand jars of water containing jewels, until— 9.97.
The bathing with clay was performed with the mantra *Viṣṇor nu kam*, and with the root-liquids;
the bathing of the God [Viṣṇu] was performed with the water from the jar of decoctions with the mantra *Tad viṣṇoḥ*;
and that of Īśa [Śiva] was performed with the water from sprouts using the *vidyā* mantra *Pratad viṣṇuḥ*.
The bathing with flowers is performed with the mantra "devasya tvā," and that with mustard seeds with "tavāmī";
the bathing with sesame-water is performed with the mantra "dhruvaḥ pātu.
The immersion with ṣāṣṭika-grain water is performed with the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ."
O Four-faced One, the bathing of Hari is performed with water from the roots of *kuśa* grass while reciting "Na te viṣṇuḥ";
with water and *tulasī* leaves while reciting the mantra "Irāvatī";
and with water from *mustā* grass while reciting "Ato devā avantu."

One should perform the bath with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and "trīṇi padā," using white and red *śaṅkhapuṣpī* flowers and water; one perceives the ritual acts through these. Then, one proceeds with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ paramam" using fragrant waters and the like.
With the mantra "tad viprāsaḥ," the bathing of men is performed with metals in the eastern sector;
however, in the divine eastern sector, which is the site of eighty-one jars,
the bathing is prescribed in sequence from the east up to the ground of Brahmā.
The bath with water from the Indra-vessel is performed with the *yajñāyajñīya* mantra.
The mantras for the eight vessels containing the substances are stated in their proper order as follows:
the mantra beginning with "indrāviṣṇū" is for the *pade*, and that marked by the word "manīṣā" is for the *pade*.

"Vaṣaṭ te viṣṇo," "tisro vācaḥ"—these are declared; likewise "iṣe tvā ūrje tvā" with the mantra, and "stariḥ tvam asi," as well as that which is characterized by "yasmin viśvāni" and "parjanyāya. (9.107–108)
In the eighty-one squares of the southern [mandala], one should perform a bath with jars of scented water,
using the first eight verses of the Nārāyaṇānuvāka, both individually and collectively; however, the middle [bath] is performed with all [the verses].
O Brahmin, in the western quarter, which is the site of eighty-one jars,
the bathing with waters from the ponds and other sources— beginning from the east and ending at the ground of Brahmā—
will be described in sequence, along with the mantras for the immersion of each substance and jar.

The bath [is performed] with the mantra "yā āpaḥ," with the *vidyā* "sindhudvīpa," with the *ṛc* "eṣa te," and with "imaṃ me varuṇa"; also with "śaṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye" and the mantra "eṣa yāsāṃ rājā. (9.112)

With the mantra beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ," with the vidyā beginning with "yāsāṃ deva," and indeed with the Vāruṇa Sūkta, one should perform the bath using vessels of ritual substances; specifically,
in the northern direction, one should use eighty-one vessels, starting from the east and ending at the lotus-pads.
The mantra for nine new jars containing grain and other substances is now stated:
with the *Indra-sāman* "trātāram indram" and the mantra "ā tvā vahantu.
This mantra, "jitaṃ te," is characterized as carrying the waters.
The mantra is "eṣa sa tvaṃ no agne" (9.116),
and with the verse "tvaṃ no agne," as well as the Mahāvyāhṛtis,
ending with "aṇor aṇīyān," these are the mantras for the ritual of bathing in their proper order. (9.117)
In the forty-nine jars [placed] in the corners of the fire [altar],
the sequence of mantras for the ritual bathing with the jars of cow’s urine and so forth is now declared:
Gāyatrī is the first among them, followed by Payas (milk) and Vṛta (clarified butter).
He should perform the bath with the mantra "Dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," with "Gandhadvārām," and so forth;
with the verse "Viṣṇor arāṭam," with the ṛc "Mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ," with the Hiraṇyagarbha mantra, and with the knowledge-mantra "Āpyāyasva."
The mantra "ghṛtasnātā" and the sequence for the rite of bathing with ghee [are prescribed];
in the forty-ninth jar, in the position within the domain of Nirṛti,
the mantras will be stated in order for the immersion with the jars of medicinal substances.
"Rakṣoghnam," beginning with "Sāma," and "Pavitraṃ naḥ"—
these are the names of the Vāsudeva-vow of the Sāmaveda;
likewise, the Vairāja-sāman is mentioned, as well as the Aparājitas.
Likewise, in the rite of the mantra-bath, they are said to be in the northwest corner;
the twelve-syllable mantra is "drupadādiva," and the mantra known as the eight-syllable one is remembered as "śaṃ no devīḥ."
"Hiraṇyapāṇiḥ" and "Vedāham" are recited in sequence;
in the northeast corner, the mantra is remembered as "Ā no vīrya," followed by the Śrīsūkta,
"Madhumānna," and "Madhuvātā."
The ritual application of the mantra "madhu vātā" is prescribed for the corners;
however, in the central Brahma-square, the Puruṣasūkta is applied from the beginning in successive order.
For the eight vessels containing the substances, the mantra is likewise intended for the eight [squares].
In the middle group of nine, one should first bathe [the deity] with eight jars of pure water using the root mantra a thousand times;
after the Lord of the God of Gods has been bathed, [one should bathe him] subsequently with the waters of jewel-jars.
The preceptor himself should perform the bathing with the *puruṣasūkta* and with other jars filled with pure water, using the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
[He should also perform the bathing] with twenty-five jars completely filled with turmeric powder.
The ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed with seventeen [verses], or with sixteen, or with twelve, or with nine according to one's means;
