having propitiated the deity and offered the appropriate great oblation (mahāhavis). || 9.131–9.132 ||

He performed oblations with a thousand offerings of clarified butter, fuel sticks, and the four kinds of food, using the root-vidyā verse for each line of the hymn while identifying himself as the Supreme Person.
Immediately thereafter, he satisfied the preceptors with garments and other gifts, accompanied by the Puruṣa-sūkta.
At the bath with a thousand jars, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of gold equal to that number;
or else half of that, or a quarter, according to one's faith and according to one's wealth.
Whatever the fee for those [priests] may be, half of it is for the officiating priests (ṛtvij).

One should feed a thousand Brahmins with food and give them a gratifying sacrificial fee; one should also satisfy others who have arrived. Those mortals who perform service, endowed with faith and devotion, [attain the highest state].
At the time of the god’s bath with the waters of a thousand pitchers,
they obtain the great fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā and other rivers;
whatever fruit there is in the thousand-pitcher bath of the Rājasūya sacrifice, [they obtain that].
At the conclusion of the worship, it is not stated here in its entirety because it has been previously explained;
know that this is remembered as having a fruit equal to the fruit of a great festival.
Thus ends the [ninth chapter] in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Pādma Tantra*, in the *Caryāpāda*.
The ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Thousand-Pot Consecration.
The tenth chapter:
"The Ritual of Hoisting the Banner."
Brahmā said:
When does some great festival occur, what is its nature, and what is its fruit?
One who desires the fruit cannot perform it without knowing these things.
Be gracious to me, who am desirous of knowledge; O Blessed One, you ought to explain this unsurpassed great festival. (10.2) The Blessed One said:

O Brahmin, this propitiation, when performed by those desiring liberation, is wonderful; yet for those desiring fruits such as cattle and the like, it is difficult to perform. This auspicious, superhuman act has been performed to my satisfaction.

In ancient times, for the sake of removing the sin arising from the slaying of Vṛtra, even Indra, while dwelling in heaven, performed an auspicious rite dedicated to me. I shall describe its form; listen attentively as I explain it exactly as it is.
The wise call this festival by the name "Utsava," for it is the eight-syllabled mantra that enables all to cross the ocean of worldly suffering.
That great festival is threefold: the permanent (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya).
There, he dwelt constantly and equitably according to the arrangement of months and fortnights;
on auspicious lunar days and constellations, at the equinoxes and the two solstices, having performed the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha-snāna), he was attended by all the deities.
The prognosticator’s prediction should be understood as being formulated when the specific omen is present—
such as during a drought, a famine, or the falling of a meteor at night;
likewise upon the sighting of a rainbow or the appearance of a crab.
When there is trembling or breaking of the images of deities,
as well as their laughing, moving, weeping, or falling;
and when there is the breaking of gate-towers, dwellings, halls, and pavilions.
Likewise, upon the breaking or the falling of mountains,
or upon the toppling of a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), or when a fire is seen;
when another kind of fruit is seen on a tree, or when stars are seen during the day.
During the terrifying appearance of spirits and the like, as well as during an earthquake;
likewise during a conflagration of the quarters, a great wind, or heavy rain;
and when a planetary conflict has arisen, or when a mock sun is seen. || 10.13–10.14 ||
When a king is overcome by disease, or likewise when a village or a district is afflicted;
when terrible diseases such as smallpox enter,
or when an enemy army invades, or when there is the sound of chariot-rims in the sky.
When the sky was stainless and resounded with the blast of celestial drums; when there was rain accompanied by the falling of thunderbolts and the collapsing of Indra’s banner;
and likewise when water produced fire and other such wondrous sights occurred—10.16–10.17.
Thus, at the beginning of a great portent, during a grand festival of omens,
a desired festival was performed for the sake of one of the four aims of human life, bestowing the fruit intended by its resolution.
The time for the avabhṛtha bath at the conclusion of the threefold festival is said to be during the month of the asterism,
at the equinoxes, during eclipses, at the two solstices,
on the new moon, on the full moon, and on the Śravaṇa day at the end of every month.
On the day of the installation, as well as under Rohiṇī and Punarvasu,
on the king’s birthday, and likewise on his consecration day—
O Brahmin, the ceremonial bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*) performed on these aforementioned occasions accomplishes all goals.
O Four-faced One, a festival should not be held for a month, or half a month, or again for twelve days;
nor for nine days, seven days, five days, three days, or even for a single day. || 10.22–10.23 ||
On a single day or a three-day period, the wise man should not have the rite of raising the banner performed;
rather, having first made a formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), he should do so after considering the month, the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*), and the lunar day (*tithi*).
Or else, there may be an immersion in a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) at the conjunction of a specific lunar day and asterism.
During the equinoxes and solstices, as well as when the moon is situated in the *nāda* asterisms,
even if there is a conjunction with an inauspicious day or other such factors, the result is indeed auspicious, just as it has been declared.
This applies even in a city, town, or village that is presided over by those who act contrary to the natural order.
One should perform the offering of oblations (*balidāna*) and other rites outside [the temple] on streets that are not empty;
otherwise, one should conduct the great festival (*mahotsava*) within the enclosures themselves.
In a sanctuary devoid of villages and the like, one should not perform the festival outside.
One must never, under any circumstances, abandon [the ritual] even when there are internal obstacles;

for if a defect occurs simultaneously in both the site-component (*vāstuaṅga*) and the independent abode (*svatantra dhāman*), or in both the site-component and the site-structure (*vāstu*), it results in a total failure. (10.28–29)
The independent (*svatantra*) and the dependent (*paratantra*) are declared to be the substratum (*āśraya*).
Through the distinction of "supreme" and so forth, the *ālaya* becomes threefold.
Having first conceived the abode of Viṣṇu, one subsequently conceives the village and other such structures.
The *ālaya* known as "independent" (*svatantra*) is the supreme; it should be understood thus.
Having first conceived of a village as an *ālaya*, and subsequently conceiving of the [main] *ālaya*, that *ālaya* known as "non-independent" (*asvatantra*) is the middling one. (10.31–32)
O Lotus-born One, in the independent streets and alleys that have been laid out,
that which is situated within them is the abode of the lowly;
this applies whether it be in an independent or a dependent [district], when a festival or similar occasion has taken place.
First, that which is to be performed independently [in the main temple] should be performed with double the worship in the subsidiary structures (vāstuaṅga).
When [the installation] has been performed in images such as those in shrines (āśraya) and so forth during festivals and the like,
one should perform it in their respective enclosures (āvaraṇa), but one should not do so in the outer circumambulatory path (bāhyavīthī).
Whether through delusion or greed, when something contrary has been done,
there is humiliation by enemies and affliction by great diseases and the like;
[this occurs] in all courtyards, in palaces and other buildings, and in sacred images.
If, out of delusion, he should perform a mere consecration with joy, even without the festival of bathing and other rites, and likewise cause oppression of the subjects, then he should,
with every effort, never act in such a contrary manner. (10.37–10.38)

If a king should cause things to be done otherwise out of delusion, the kingdom perishes; likewise, if he performs a festival consisting of nothing but merriment, devoid of the village-site offerings and the like, for those who rely on villages and their dwellings. (10.39)

Even when a festival for another deity is taking place, one should certainly perform a Vaiṣṇava festival; but never, under any circumstances, should one perform another [festival] during a Vaiṣṇava one,
since Vāsudeva is indeed proclaimed as the deity of all deities.
When a festival of the God of gods, preceded by the hoisting of the banner,
has commenced, and a divine sacrifice (devayāga) has been set in motion, no sacramental rites such as the tonsure (caula) and others should be performed.
Furthermore, even when a festival is underway in a temple that is not a primary branch (anaṅga) of the village or other such places, [the same applies].
One should perform a sacrifice for another deity, but not any sacrament such as the tonsure ceremony (*caula*).
When there is a festival for other virtuous deities, one should remove their arches and so forth from the streets; otherwise, the festival of Hari shall not take place. (10.43–10.44)
During the festival of Viṣṇu’s *kltpā* [chariot], other festivals should take place on the streets and such;
there should be no uprooting of permanent structures such as archways (*toraṇa*).
When there is an intercalary month, or when Venus or Jupiter has set, [the same applies].

A festival should not be planned for the first time by a king or his kingdom; for the subjects there would be suffering, or perhaps disease, or even death. However, in the case of a second or subsequent festival, none of the aforementioned faults will occur in any way whatsoever.
O Brahmin, the time for hoisting the banner during the festival days beginning with the month— extending up to five days— is now being shown;
it occurs on the nineteenth day from the offering of the "tīrtha-sprout."
Or it may take place on the eighteenth day, or even earlier at an auspicious time;
or it may occur on the twelfth day from the hoisting of the Garuda banner,
or on whatever day is auspicious, after multiplying that number by three.
O Lotus-born One, at the beginning of the days, the hoisting of the banner should be performed;
having first offered the sprouts on a Puṣya day as previously described,
one should subsequently raise the banner— an auspicious act— on an auspicious day.
If, for some reason— whether from a god or even from a human—
the flag has been prepared according to the prescribed rite prior to the commencement of the festival,
one should hoist the flag at night on the very day the festival begins.
One should beat the drum and subsequently scatter sprouts into the offering bowls;
having first sounded the drum, the hoisting of the banner follows. Then there is the offering of sprouts, or alternatively, the offering of sprouts may take place at night.
At dusk, the flag should be hoisted while the sound of drums follows behind.
O Four-faced One, even when the flag is hoisted at that time, there are three types [of cloth]:
that produced from threads, linen garment, and fine, flawless, imported silk.
Or, O Four-faced One, a wise man should prepare a banner out of cotton according to his means—
ten cubits long, five cubits wide, and firm—
or even nine, eight, or seven cubits.
The length of the base-bera, or alternatively the width of the door, [is the unit];
it is expanded by half that length and has its crest (śekhara) made by one-quarter [of the base].
The tail (puccha) is equal to the crest, and the ear-tail (karṇapucchaka) is half of that.
Having brought forth Garuḍa, who is well-washed, free from defects, dried, endowed with auspicious marks, possessing the luster of gold,
measuring nine tālas in height, two-armed, and wearing a tunic, in the middle of the cloth— (10.60)
The all-pervading Lord held his hands joined in a hollowed cup of flowers, wore white garments,
had a face made formidable by fangs, eyes curved with a frown,
a blue tip to his nose, and his left foot drawn up.
With his left foot placed upon his back, beautified by the flapping of his wings,
beginning his flight through the sky, well-rounded yet terrible to behold,
wearing a basket-shaped crown and with locks of hair arranged upon his forehead.
Resplendent with ornaments of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and anklets;
with Ananta as his left bracelet and Vāsuki as his sacred thread;
with Kārkoṭaka placed upon his chest and Takṣaka serving as his girdle.
He bears upon his right ear a serpent named Padma, and likewise a Mahāpadma on the other; a conch-serpent upon his head, and a Gulika serpent upon his armlet. Their colors are now described.
Resembling crystal, resembling blood, resembling gold, and smoke-colored;
resembling a red lotus, tawny, and with the luster of snow;
resembling a black bee—these were the umbrellas, adorned with pearls and gold, in successive order. (10.67–10.68)
Above [the central figure], two chowries should be depicted on the two sides;
below, a lotus, a full water-jar, and small vessels filled with water and sprouts should be drawn. Two lamps should be placed on the two sides.
One should thus draw [the design] with five colors, with the interior being dark blue. The most skilled painter should fill the intermediate space with black;
he should likewise paint a banner and a pennant equal in size to half the standard.

When the day of consecration arrived, the preceptor himself entered the artisan’s workshop during the darkness; then, having had the opening of the eyes performed by an artisan, he released the image once it was completed according to the artisan’s wishes.
After satisfying [the officiant] with wealth, he should place the banner upon his head; then,

accompanied by the sounding of musical instruments, he should lead it around the temple and other sacred sites, having first offered it to the presiding deity (mūrtipati) in a vessel made of gold or other metal.
Then the supreme preceptor should cause [the image] to enter the sacrificial pavilion;
other than the opening of the eyes, he should perform [the rites] as in the case of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
He should immediately perform the ritual of the shadow-dwelling (chāyādhivāsana) in water according to the rules.
One should bathe [the deity] with sixteen jars; the ritual bathing may take place before a mirror.
One should worship [the deity] with the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Gāyatrī*.
One should cause [the deity] to lie down upon a layer of rice and the like, spread over a new cloth.
Beneath the spread cloth, on the right side, together with the eight [vessels],
one should pour water from the jars placed all around and from the *vardhanī* into the main jar.
Having invoked Garuḍa into the large jar (*kumbha*) and Sudarśana into the small vessel (*karaka*).
One should worship Indra and the other deities well within the eight jars located in the directions starting from the east.
Then, having purified Garuḍa depicted on the cloth by means of the rites of drying and so forth,
one should dissolve the constituent principles (tattvas) and subsequently generate the bird in due order.
In the four side-pits and on the sacrificial altars,
or likewise in the pit or the kitchen, one should perform the rites with fuel-sticks and clarified butter as before;
the sprinkling for the peace-offering and the ritual touching should also be done as before.
Having spread out the cloth, showing the Garuḍa facing the temple, he should invoke him there with the *vyāhṛti* mantra and then effect his presence. Thereafter,
the preceptor should entreat him with the verse that is about to be recited.
O one of great strength, O mighty-armed Vainateya, lord of birds, be present upon this cloth; salutations to you, whose form is the *praṇava*.
O Lord of Birds, being invoked, bring about the accomplishment of our actions.
The three worlds are summoned for the success of the festival of the God. One should worship Him with the *gāyatrī* of one's own deity using offerings such as the *arghya*;
then, one should present to Him the fourfold food offering (*naivedya*).
Having offered food to Kumbha, one should satisfy Garuḍa with hymns of praise for the sake of the vehicle of Mahāviṣṇu, Tārkṣya of immeasurable splendor:
"Obeisance to you, Garuḍa, the death of all the lords of serpents."
Homage, homage to you, O Lord of Birds, whose body is sacred study; homage!
(10.88) O Lord of Birds, let there be homage to you, who uprooted the Kalpa tree, who are a jar of nectar for those who have taken refuge in you, and who liberated your mother from servitude. (10.89)
Salutations to you, the conqueror of the lords of gods and asuras, who are adorned by the lord of serpents;
salutations to you, whose support is that upon which all this world rests.
You, whose two wings are the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* Sāmans.
The two eyes are the Gāyatrī, and the Trivṛt-sāman is remembered as the head.
Homage to Him whose limbs are the perfection of the Vāmadevya-stotra;
homage to the Lord of the vital breaths and other winds, who has Garuḍa as His self.
"Remove all defects, bring forth unbroken virtues from every side;
destroy all obstacles and make even me your own.
Having thus offered praise, one should recite the Gāruḍa mantra with a one-pointed mind.
One should pass the night with the sounds of musical instruments, the chanting of the Vedas, and keeping watch.
Having offered the oblation and formed it into morsels,
the knower of mantras should consecrate them with mantras dedicated to Puruṣa and Garuḍa, even for women who have borne no children.
Having meditated upon Garuḍa, Acyuta, and Hari, they should cast [the offerings] into their cupped hands;
by consuming three morsels, they shall produce many sons.
Having worshipped Him at dawn and offered the oblation in due order, [they should proceed].

One should adorn the bird depicted on the cloth with garments, ornaments, and flowers. Having mounted it upon the back of an elephant, a chariot, or some other auspicious vehicle such as a palanquin, one should lead it around the village or the temple in a clockwise direction.
One should cause it to be proclaimed before him with kettledrums, clay drums, and tabors, as well as with conchs, trumpets, and banners, accompanied everywhere by dances and songs.
Between the two musical instruments of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa), there should be earthen bowls containing sprouts.
All the Brāhmaṇas, with their senses restrained, should carry it on their heads;
or else, according to the wish of the patron, they should follow the festive image near Garuḍa, accompanied by every auspicious rite.

In front of the sacrificial altar (balipīṭha), or outside the temple gateway (gopura), one should dig a flagstaff (dhvajastambha) into the ground; it should be made of wood, free from defects, and stable. Trees are of three kinds: those with pith inside, those with pith outside, and those without pith.
They know that *kāmuka* and similar woods, which have their strength outside, are excellent and supreme for pillars;
whereas *candana* and similar woods, which have their strength inside, are excellent for the construction of pillars.
One should avoid a pillar that is pithless, even if it is auspicious and one hundred *tāla*-lengths in height. (10.103–10.104)
According to the measurement of the *mānāṅgula*, [the height] may be twenty units less,
or else it may be equal to the height of the temple or the size of the gate-tower (*gopura*). One should divide the pillar into four parts and make the capital (*mastaka*) one part.
And for those three pedestals, which serve as the foundation and are perforated from the base, their placement is upon the top of the pillars; furthermore,
O Four-faced One, the pedestals are elongated by two tālas.
One should plant trees that are wide at the base, half as thick at the middle, and half as thick again at the top; they should be stout at the root and tapering toward the tip.
At the top, in the two cavities of the pedestals, one should fix the consecrated flagstaff.
O Four-faced One, having pierced it, one should fix the flagstaff;
or one should fix a bamboo pole of nine, seven, or five [cubits]—
such a flagstaff, on the northern side of the pedestal.
Having summoned Brahmins learned in the Vedas, the preceptor should cause the pillar to be laid down with its top pointing eastward,
or else northward; having washed it with mantras containing the word *ap* (water),
he should cover the pillar with auspicious *kuśa* grass, complete with their tips, arranged with the points facing upward.
Having wrapped it with garlands of *darbha* grass while reciting the *Viṣṇu-sūkta*, O Preceptor,
and having placed purified iron filings and other materials into the pit for the flagstaff,
he should firmly establish the flagstaff in that pit so that it is stable.
Facing the temple, he should fix a banner in the opening at the top of the bamboo pole,
having tripled it with a cord the thickness of a thumb;
or else, having climbed the pillar, he should fasten the banner there.
Or one should erect a pillar with the tip of the banner fixed upon it, according to one's capacity.
Having thus prepared the top of the staff during an auspicious *muhūrta*,
the Guru should likewise hoist the banner in the forenoon or at midday.
Having bound it with the *puruṣamantra* along with a banner and a bell,
the hoisting of the flagstaff should take place with the mantra "Suparṇo 'si.
Having placed the Lord of Birds, depicted on a cloth, facing the temple, [one should proceed].
Likewise, one should cause the sound of musical instruments and the sound of the sacred scriptures to be proclaimed in all directions.
At that time, the preceptor should recite the *mālā-mantra* of the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and other mantras.
On the ground at the base of the pillar, he should prepare an altar seven cubits in length.
One should fashion it as wide as those same [dimensions] and one cubit high,
either five or three cubits square.
In the middle of the third part of the altar, one should fashion a pedestal.
It should have a height of four finger-breadths and be joined with three girdles (mekhalā).
On its third part, there should also be a lotus endowed with eight petals; the wise one should construct it so that the pillar stands upon the pericarp (karṇikā).
Then, a water-shed (prapā) provided with sixteen pillars should be constructed all around;
it should be equipped with four doors and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and other ornaments.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should then sprinkle [the area] with water from a ritual pitcher (*kumbha*).
With the Gāruḍa mantra itself and likewise with eight water-pots,
one should sprinkle the pillar with Indra and the other deities using their respective mantras in due order.
One should then pray for its stability within the interior of Garuḍa’s banner.
O destroyer of enemies, until the concluding bath of the festival, by means of the verse to be spoken,
and by the abundance of wind from the waves of the flapping of your wings, O Lord of Birds,
you shall cast away the armor of the asuras in battle.
"Keep [the image] on the cloth until the conclusion of the festival's purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
Having placed the festival image upon a vehicle such as a palanquin,
one should bring it to the ground near the flagstaff and show it to the bird."
Having appointed the Lord of Birds to summon all the worlds without exception,
the deity should thereafter proceed to the site of the pavilion.
He should worship Garuḍa at the three times of day and offer oblations to him.
Just as one would always protect a lamp from being extinguished day and night, so too,

having worshipped the festival image there in the pavilion according to the prescribed rite and having presented the offerings, one should worship it until the conclusion of the oblation of clarified butter.
And having thus performed worship at night for the sake of attaining success in the sounding of the drum,
one should smear the ground in front of the pedestal of the banner with cow-dung water and decorate it in a square shape with lime powder.
Having prepared a square grain-platform with five *droṇas* of rice,
one should place the *Kālacakra* in its center;
one should also establish the offering and worship right there, facing the banner.
Having performed worship and offered various oblations,
one should then place a great drum wrapped in new cloth upon a pedestal of grain on the ground smeared [with cow dung] before him. 10.135
On the right and left sides of that small drum (bherikā),
one should worship Viṣṇu and Śrī respectively according to the prescribed rite;
and in the middle portion, one should honor Prakṛti, who consists of the three guṇas.

At an auspicious moment, the Guru himself should strike the drum with the *koṇa* stick, employing the knowledge of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*), while meditating upon the three forms (*mūrtitraya*).
Then, a man of mixed caste (*pāraśava*)— having bathed, adorned himself, and holding *darbha* grass in his hand— [should proceed].
Wearing the sacred thread as an upper garment and carrying a decorated drum,
accompanied by conchs and other musical instruments, and knowing the rules for the various rhythmic beats (*tāla*),
he should cause it to be sounded while the Guru offers oblations to Indra and the host of Maruts.
The invocation of the divine weapons, as well as that of the inhabitants of Vaikuṇṭha,
and likewise all the attendants protected by Viṣvaksena—
Kumuda and the others, together with their leaders— were to be summoned to that sacrifice.
And by the sages beginning with Marīci who dwell in the world of Brahmā;
and there was an invitation to Viriñca together with those dwelling in the world of Indra,
as well as Rudra, whose vehicle is the bull, along with the hosts of Pramathas.
Likewise, others who were to be invited, dwelling in their respective worlds,
arrived at that great festival together with their vehicles and retinues;
as did the sciences personified and the triple Veda embodied along with its auxiliary limbs.
There was a formal invocation of all those to be summoned by their own names.
Around the perimeter of the processional paths were constant festivals and worship, featuring the beautiful image of the Lord of Good Fortune (Sudarśana),
fashioned from food and surrounded by many lamps.
Having sent [the proclamation] out in every direction preceded by the beating of drums,
and having reached the center of the village, the Guru, having invoked the Four-faced One there,
worshipped him in that sacrifice and requested his presence.
Having likewise worshipped Indra and the other deities stationed in their respective directions for the sake of the offering,
and having caused the sound of musical instruments to be proclaimed while keeping time himself,
he should cause the *Garuḍa* hymn to be recited elsewhere in the intervals between them.
Having entered the temple there, he should install [the deity] as before,
either taking the festival image or the Sudarśana alone,
or performing the rite of the food-idol (annamūrti), or taking the drum alone.

In the streets, the invocation of the deities was performed here and there according to the prescribed rule. Those men who heard the kettledrum at the time of the invocation of the deities did not have to cross a river, nor travel more than a yojana by vehicle.
If, out of delusion, a person should disregard the festival and go far away,
he goes to a place of hell after death, or experiences suffering even in this world.
Therefore, one should stay right there until the concluding bath (avabhṛtha) and not depart.
If that supreme guide for whom the sprouts were sown for the sake of the banner should, for some reason,
become incapable or die,
another person— such as his son— with his permission, shall complete the remainder. (10.154–10.155)
Whether it be a disciple, or a brother, or a priest who is more virtuous—
thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Hoisting the Banner," in the *Caryāpāda* of the *Pādma-tantra*, within the illustrious *Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad*.
Chapter Eleven:
The Procedure for the Great Festival.
The Blessed Lord said:
On the seventh day prior to the commencement day of the festival,
the best of preceptors should offer the ritual germinating of seeds (aṅkura) at an auspicious moment under a favorable planetary conjunction,
using one hundred and eight earthen vessels according to the prescribed rite.
Alternatively, one should subsequently perform the decoration with thirty-six ornaments.

(11.2) The entrance to the pathway should be adorned with arches made of either areca-nut wood or timber; likewise, the courtyards at the fronts of the gate-towers (gopura) should be decorated. (11.3)
Plantain trees, areca palms, and others, bent low under the weight of their fruit,
should be placed at the sides of the archways as pathways for the arrival [of the bridegroom].
These paths should be made with level ground and adorned with sand.
One should beautify [the area] on all sides with banners, with garments of *dukūla* and *kṣauma*, with hundreds of *darbha* garlands, and with water-stalls and the like;
and one should purify the entire ground by sprinkling it with water mixed with cow dung.
The walls of the palace should be decorated with the five colors,
[adorned] with plantain trees, full water-jars, rows of lamps,
pearl necklaces, and hundreds of flower-pots together with sprouts.
During that festival, the patron should bring satisfaction to the various classes of people who have gathered from every region by means of food and other offerings to serve the Lord of the Gods,
day and night, through water-stalls, drinking halls, and similar facilities.
Then one should treat those afflicted by disease with medicines and heaps of wealth; O Brahmin, having constructed a pavilion in the first enclosure,
it may be situated in the second enclosure according to the available space.
In all the intermediate directions and in the desired quarters, that [mandala] should be made;
it should be seven cubits long or auspiciously five cubits long, with its width and length being equal, and provided with four doors. || 11.11–11.12 ||
One should have a pavilion constructed, and around it one should have a water-shed built.
In the middle of that, at the third part, one should construct an altar (vedi) one cubit high;
one should arrange it to be two or three cubits wide toward the east of the altar.
The sacrificial pit for the Āhavanīya fire was square, as prescribed;
that for the Dakṣiṇāgni fire was in the southern direction and shaped like a bow;
and the pit for the Gārhapatya fire was in the western direction, circular and wonderful.
Immediately thereafter, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the assembly master should be triangular in the north;
and in the northeast or the southeast, there should be a square pit for the fire of the household (āvasathya),
for the supreme festival of the five fires.
Alternatively, one may arrange four fires facing the four directions without the *āvasathya*;
or, omitting the *sabhya* and *āvasathya*, one may provide three fires;
or, according to the wish of the performer, one may establish only the single *āhavanīya* fire. || 11.17–11.18 ||
One should have door-arches made from trees such as the *aśvattha* on the four sides;
one should have the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles fashioned, and the eight auspicious symbols (*aṣṭamaṅgalāni*) as before.
One should also provide seats for the officiating priests and various vessels for the fire-oblation (*homa*).
In front of the pavilions, there should be a water-shed, as well as on both sides.
(11.20) One should cover the pavilion and the water-shed with various fine fabrics such as *dukūla*, *kṣauma*, and *kauśeya*, and one should wrap the pillars situated both inside and outside. (11.21)
One should hang strings of pearls everywhere and garlands of lamps; one should also fasten rows of banners upon the pillars.
One should tie up a canopy of pearls and place flower garlands on all sides.
One should decorate the pavilion and other structures with such articles of equipment as these. One should hang large,
variegated curtains in front of the four preceptors and officiating priests.
Likewise, there was the acceptance of sixteen other female attendants;
and they were adorned with ornaments such as bracelets according to their wealth, as well as with various new garments, in accordance with their respective ranks.
The consecrated image should be diligently adorned in every way by the patron with turbans, upper garments, and ointments of fragrant substances. Furthermore,
the ceremonial bath should be performed as prescribed at the commencement of the festival and at its conclusion.
On the day before [the consecration], the Guru should perform the ritual for the deity and bind the *kautuka* (protective thread).
In a vessel made of gold or silver, filled with *kalama* rice to a measure of two *khārīs*, half a *khārī*, or one-quarter of a *khārī*— || 11.28 ||
One should place a thread made of gold, or of linen, or even of cotton;
or a thread consisting of seven or five strands of linen and other fibers,
along with one hundred and sixty betel-nut seeds.
Together with betel leaves, the number of fruits should be fourfold,
or half of that, or even half of that again, using fruits such as plantain;
then, having placed that vessel together with its stand upon his head.
The image-maker [should place the image] covered with cloth, accompanied by an umbrella, chowries, and fans,
provided with a thousand lamps, and furnished with a canopy, while Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas recite the Śākuna Sūkta.
Having led [the image] around it clockwise, accompanied by the auspicious songs of musical instruments, he should likewise circumambulate the abode of Viṣṇu as well as its outer enclosures;
or, having performed the circumambulation, he should enter the village and approach the presence of other deities.
On the ground before the deity, having smeared the surface with cow-dung water and made it square,
and having filled it with a measure of śāli rice,
one should place the vessel there and, according to the prescribed rite, cause the proclamation of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Having consecrated that thread with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), the preceptor,
taking it between his thumb and ring finger of both hands,
[should empower] the thread with the *aparājita* [mantra] and sandalwood powder mixed with water.
Having smeared [the thread] on the right hand and tied the festive *kautuka* [knot],
one should touch the thread with the right hand and recite the number of times [prescribed for] it.
Then, having worshipped the deity with the *astramantra* and offerings such as *arghya*, one should present it.
One should offer large cakes, as well as small cakes, parched grain, and even fruits;
one should perform song, dance, and instrumental music in the presence of the deity.
With three devotees of the Lord, one should install the deity in another location.
Having bathed, wearing linen garments, anointed with ointments and the like,
adorned with all ornaments, and garlanded like a deity among gods—
having worshipped him according to the scriptures, one should offer him the finest rice-milk (paramānna).
Just as it was prescribed for the consecration, so too should the preparation of the bed be arranged;
having placed the image upon it, one should set it on a comfortable bed. One should place lamps in the corners, as well as oil-lamps containing sprouts.
Having praised the Enemy of Madhu with the sounds of musical instruments, the Vedas, and hymns of praise,
the preceptor should spend the night in vigil with a concentrated mind.
When the auspicious dawn has arrived and the sun has risen, at that favorable moment...
With the mantra beginning "Arise," together with three devotees of the Lord,
and while the Brahmins were reciting the Śākunika hymn in all directions,
he raised the God from his bed with the verse "Idam Viṣṇuḥ."
They should place him upon a palanquin together with the golden radiance;
the Brahmins should carry the vehicle while meditating upon the Lord of Birds,
and they should scatter fragrant flowers in all directions.

One should cause parched grain together with pearls to be scattered while sounding the music of musical instruments; having passed through all the stages of the enclosure with such and other auspicious rites,
one should descend from the radiant vehicle after performing a circumambulation.
Having seated [the deity] upon a splendid throne adorned with variegated spreads of fine silk and other materials,
within a pavilion cooled by the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree and fashioned of gold, one should perform every ritual service.
The preceptor should display all the materials brought forth and gathered for the festival to the Deity in the assembly of the people;
having performed the entire ritual service, he should present that image in the bathing pavilion.
One should bathe the Lord of the gods according to the procedures previously described.
Having observed the extent of their wealth, both the preceptor and the patron,
at the conclusion of the offering of the great oblation, should perform the fire-sacrifice with the sacrificial offerings according to the rules.
One should lead the sanctified earth for the foundation of the sprouts to the inner sanctum of the temple, accompanied by auspicious rites; then, at the time of afternoon,
[one should go] outside from the garden grounds or from the riverbank to fetch it.
Having mounted him upon a Garuda-vehicle or a well-adorned chariot,
and placing the command of the gods at the forefront, accompanied by every auspicious rite,
they first carried forth the *pālikās* and the decorated spade.
Having been led around the village in a clockwise direction by many Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas, the preceptor then departed from there and,
taking up earth from either the eastern or the northern direction, [proceeded].
Having entered the abode as previously described at the onset of night,
at the hour of dusk in the sacrificial hall, there were twelve *pālikā* vessels,
and likewise sixteen groups of them, each accompanied by a ladle (*śarāva*) and a water-pot (*kumbha*).
Having established [the vessels] in the northeast direction, provided with jars of Soma,
the Guru should sow the seeds into them during an auspicious moment.
Then, both the sacrificer and the Guru shall enter the hall.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground before the Lord, the source of all festive abundance,
the preceptor followed by tying the auspicious marriage-thread and requested [the deity] for the sake of the festival-bath and offerings for the images, in due order.
And on a couch prepared in the Sudarśana hall, as previously described elsewhere,
having tied the protective cord (pratisara) and consecrated everything in due order,
he should immediately rise and, having worshipped, circumambulate the temple clockwise.
Having led [the deity] and caused him to enter the pavilion for the sake of sacrifice,
and having seated the Cakra— the object of worship for the daily festival—
there upon a throne, he should thereafter prepare a pedestal of grain upon the altar according to the sequence previously described.
There, nine water-jars that had been washed and wrapped with thread,
filled with scented water and containing the nine jewels, mixed with the pollen of all fragrant flowers, and provided with small pitchers (karaka), [were placed].
Each [of these] was adorned with a placed golden coin and a *nyagrodha* sprout,
together with a bundle of *kuśa* grass, and jasmine flowers at the openings;
the central one was wrapped in a pair of garments, while the remaining ones were wrapped in a single cloth.
One should place them wrapped upon heaps of grain on the ground of the altar;
the cloth should be seven, six, or five cubits in length,
and its width should be fixed at half that measurement.
One should have the Brahmins devoted to the Lord recite the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) formula;
and one should worship the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth, as in the ritual of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
One should place the primary image (*mūlabera*) in the central pot and Sudarśana in the small vessel (*karaka*).
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others when the pitcher has reached the eastern and other directions;
in the corners beginning with the southeast, Puruṣa and the others are to be worshipped in sequence— namely Puruṣa, Satya, and likewise the deity Acyuta.
And with the mantra "anantaś ca," there is the offering of oblations for the four [deities].
Likewise, at the door-jar, at the weapon, and at the image of the offering, one should place the eight auspicious symbols.
These are wrapped in cloth and placed upon heaps of grain beneath the sacrificial altar.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and worship, while the sounding of drums and other instruments upon the altar proceeds in the four directions, one should offer oblations into the fire,
meditating upon Vāsudeva in the Āhavanīya fire and Saṅkarṣaṇa in the adjacent southern fire.
One should worship Pradyumna in the west and Aniruddha in the north;
having worshipped the primary form (Mūlamūrti) in the Āvasathya fire at the conclusion of the ritual bath,
and having prayed for the presence [of the deity], one should offer oblations of clarified butter and other substances into the sacrificial pits.
O Lotus-born One, with clarified butter, flowers, incense materials,
sacrificial fuel, milk, curd, sesame seeds, rice, and barley,
one should offer [oblations] separately one hundred and eight times for each respective deity, accompanied by their specific mantras.
Or, beginning from the east, the oblation should be performed twenty-eight times in the sacrificial pits.
With milk-rice, rice-and-pulse mixtures, sweet rice, turmeric rice, and mung-bean rice,
one should offer into the five separate fires while reciting the Puruṣa-sūktas.
In the fifth [offering], one should offer the supreme food (paramānna) to the deities beginning with Brahmā;

having uttered the mantra ending in "svāhā," which includes their respective names in the dative case followed by their attendant titles, and having meditated upon the deities such as Brahmā and the others.
Brahmā, Prajāpati, Rudra, and all the gods in their proper order;
the meters, the Vedas, the seers, the Gandharvas, and the reptiles;
the Yakṣas and the Apsarases, along with the months and the years.
The rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and likewise the streams;
the elements, the animals, the trees, and likewise the medicinal herbs are recorded [as his offspring].
So too are the lords of the forest, the plants that sprout, those born from sweat, and those born from eggs.
The womb-born beings, as well as the seven worlds beginning with Bhūr;
likewise the seven worlds beginning with Atala, and the deities beginning with Caṇḍa—
one should offer oblation-material to these with the root-vidyā.
Having recited "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
He should not burn the enclosing sticks (paridhis) nor the darbha grass; he should not dismiss the deities while they remain present.
He should maintain the sacred fire every day until the day of his departure for the pilgrimage site.

One should offer oblations every day, throughout the day and night, according to the prescribed method. O Four-faced One, even when there is but a single fire, the sacrificial materials must be offered in their entirety; the same applies when there are three or four fires.
First, one should perform the offering of oblations (balipradāna) in the pavilion of the sacrifice.
Taking the Cakra and the image of the oblation together with the Annamūrti,
one should depart from the house and [place] the Kumuda and other [deities] at its door.
Having performed worship, one should offer the *bali* oblation on the pure surface of the ground.
One should also place the materials for the *bali*, scented water in a vessel, a flower container,
a water-pot filled with water, a lamp-vessel, and a lantern before [the deity].
Let the attendants go ahead, carrying incense burners;
let the image of the deity go in front, followed immediately by the wheel.
Thereafter, the daily festival procession shall proceed, complete with canopies and other ornaments.
Then, having worshipped Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and the others at the gates and in the enclosures according to the procedure for the perpetual festival, he should offer the bali-oblation;
and in the village, beginning from the center, he should likewise worship Brahmā and the other deities according to the rule.
Having offered [the oblation] throughout the regions as far as Īśāna, and having likewise worshipped [them],
one should offer the remaining sacrificial materials in their entirety upon the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha), O Lotus-seated One, with reference to all the attendants (pāriṣada).
When an auspicious moment had arrived, the preceptor,
having brought the one lying on the bed forward for the festive rite of awakening, recited the mantra beginning with "Arise," together with Brahmins chanting the Svasti-sūkta.
Having departed from that palace and having caused the *Rathantara* chant to be sung,
he mounted a chariot yoked with four excellent,
swift-moving elephants, or with horses, or with bulls.
Having placed upon the chariot a decorated golden pedestal joined with a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma), one should lead it while a charioteer is seated therein;
or else, by means of a mechanical device operated by eminent Brahmins who are learned and powerful.
Whether on an elephant, or if a chariot is unavailable, or if no vehicle is at hand,
the preceptor should cause him to mount a vehicle with the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ.
It should be adorned with flowers and endowed with the golden luster of blossoms.
It was provided with a golden canopy, adorned with flowers and other ornaments;
or it was furnished with a peaked roof, beautified by peacock feathers,
endowed with every kind of decoration, and surrounded by blossoming flowers.
Having worshipped the Lord seated there in the vehicle according to the ritual of *nyāsa*, one should offer Him food such as parched grain (*pṛthuka*) and other delicacies.
One should not place food at His feet, nor should one apply powdered substances of the night (*niśācūrṇa*) anywhere.
With many lofty lamps fed with ghee and other substances,
he should illuminate every place with more than a thousand lamps, each less than a hundred in height,
while many eminent leaders of the twice-born, adorned and dressed in white garments, [look on].
[He was attended] by those wearing robes and turbans, with whisks made of yak-tail hair in their hands,
and likewise by those holding palm-leaf fans or peacock feathers;
[he was shaded] by white pearl parasols that bore the grandeur of clouds.
Carrying incense burners emitting fragrance on all sides,
O Lotus-born One, [the gods] were preceded by Tārkṣya, who was mounted upon his vehicle with palms joined in reverence and bearing a tall banner aloft.

And behind him, attended by the god Viṣvaksena, who held a staff in his hand, he was served as the latter bowed from behind his gold-glittering palanquin while clearing Viriñca and the other gods out of the way.
Having placed the two sandals and the pair of shoes, as well as the bowl fashioned of gold,
before [the chariot] while adorned brahmins carry them,
one should proceed without delay with the other royal insignia.
It was attended by Brahmins learned in the three Vedas who were devoted to silent recitation and praise,
as well as by courtesans dancing and singing,
and by other bards intent on playing the lute and other instruments.
By those skilled in songs beginning with the note ṣaḍja and experts in playing musical instruments,
by those reciting brilliant hymns in prose, verse, and mixed form,
and by those speaking various wonderful languages here and there; (11.116–117)
By sophists skilled in debate and trained in argumentation,
by those devoted to the discourse on reality and by logicians who know the categories;
by Mīmāṃsakas, ritualists, Vedic scholars, and experts in Sāṃkhya.
By those who know yoga, those who know the Purāṇas, grammarians, and knowers of reality;
and by groups of astrologers desiring to overcome one another—
the object of knowledge has been established in many ways according to the methods taught in their respective scriptures.
By learned Sāttvatas devoted to the Pañcarātra, who were speaking aloud, proclaiming the majesty of Vāsudeva, and uttering Sanskrit,
Prākṛt, and mixed languages here and there; (11.121)
By people standing in front of, behind, and at the sides of the Lord, all intent on displaying their complete proficiency in the scriptures;
and by an army rich with the fourfold forces in every direction.
On both sides of the god, there were variegated wooden mechanical devices in the shape of birds, moving here and there with poles dyed in lac;
likewise, there were mechanical figures of deities and machines in the form of elephants and other creatures.
They displayed a wonderful dance upon various paths by means of women mounted on mechanical figures of Niṣādas and others as described by Bharata,
as well as by women mounted on line-engraved machines and other similar contrivances.
He was followed by those who were agitated, coming and going;
thus, having circumambulated the entire enclosure outside,
he likewise circumambulated the streets of the village and other areas, keeping them to his right.
At the time of entry, having likewise circumambulated the circular rampart in a clockwise direction, one should enter the interior of the pavilion; there,
one should install the deity’s *balibera* (processional image) within the temple.
And one should always cast the food-offering (annamūrti) upon the sacrificial wheel (cakra) situated outside on the pedestal of offerings (balipīṭha) in the sacrificial hall;
with double the usual materials prepared for worship, one should constantly venerate the permanent image (dhruvabera).
When the remainder of the night has passed, having placed the festive image upon the lion-throne in the pavilion, one should worship it according to the path of the scriptures; there,
one should perform the ritual bathing either upon that image or upon the bathing-curtain.
In the case of the ritual for a single image, however, there should be consecration upon the primary image;
one should perform the daily bathing according to one's capacity and according to one's wealth. Then, having offered the great oblation to the image fashioned for the auspicious occasion.

Having reached the abode of Maṇḍana, one should adorn it with ornaments and the like. Once the image is situated there, the preceptor should proceed to the sacrificial pavilion, worship the ritual jar and other items, and present the offerings as prescribed.
Having offered the oblation (bali) upon the pedestal according to the previous ritual procedure,

and having likewise performed all other rites for the worship of the bali, one should lead the procession through the streets of the village and so forth during the night, and conduct the festive worship outside.
Having arranged the ornaments as before, as well as the various attendants,
and having raised on all sides other items appropriate for the day such as banners and the like,
he distributed rolls of betel-leaf gathered from various places.
Having offered pṛthuka grains and other such foods, coconut fruits,
as well as water for drinking and rinsing the mouth, according to the prescribed rule,
and having presented all the offerings and sprinkled them with water while reciting the Astra-vidyā;
One should announce the cakes and other such items; however, cooked food should be presented silently.

Likewise, one should offer sweet water and the like, as well as milk and other drinks that have been brought, along with flower garlands and whatever else, including vessels containing powdered sandalwood. || 11.140–11.141 ||
The preceptor, having consecrated with the Astra-mantra all the ornaments such as rings and whatever else is offered with devotion, should then join them to the limbs of the deity.
Having led [the image] around the village in a clockwise direction, he should likewise do so for the surrounding enclosures.
Having brought him into the palace and placed him upon another auspicious palanquin,
they set him down from the vehicle onto a supreme golden throne within the bathing pavilion, provided with a comfortable cushion.
Having established the marriage pavilion facing the desired direction,
the devotee of the Lord, adorned with all ornaments, should perform the worship with a new,
very fine garment of smooth thread.
With his turban bound and upper robe draped over one shoulder, he was adorned with earrings and other ornaments.
Resplendent in white golden trousers,
his body clad in armor, his hands purified, and himself pure,
he was accompanied by attendants carrying the articles required for worship.
One must be equipped on all sides with a tunic, a turban, and garments.
On the right side of the Lord, the chief worshipper Indra shall sit;
thereafter, one should sit at the sides and behind the Blessed One.
All the ascetics— whether bearers of the triple staff or the single staff— should remain with one-pointed minds as exclusive devotees,
intent on meditation upon Brahman, following the sequence of the rules for worship.
Those who seek spiritual realization should constantly remain in his presence;
and outside [the temple], they should be surrounded by auspicious Vaiṣṇavas whose senses are restrained and whose limbs are bathed in tears born of joy, as well as by Brahmins.
The other members of the assembly, however, should wait outside the pavilion;
they are to sit in the drinking hall (prapā) below, in all directions.
Below and in front [of them] are those skilled in dance, song, and instrumental music.
There was manifold dramatic performance and excellent instrumental music existing in many forms;
there were dances and songs accompanied by the notes beginning with *ṣaḍja*, following the proper timing, while they displayed various musical instruments, both those fixed in place and others.
They made manifest other things as well— both that which is audible and that which is visible—
and they displayed the three Vedas (*trayī*) as established through their private recitation (*svādhyāya*),
while narrating the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas* in every possible way.

It should be placed surrounded on all sides by women of other castes. Having thus worshipped the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) in that pavilion, he should then lead him back to his former place upon the bathing throne.
One should bathe Puruṣottama with as many as a thousand streams;
having led him to the ornamentation throne, one should perform all the rites there.
Then, having placed the Lord, together with his retinue, upon the procession throne—
Having led him into the pavilion, he should seat him there upon a dining chair. Then, having offered the great sacrificial oblation ending with the beverages as prescribed,
and having seated him on a comfortable seat, one should perform everything just as for a king.
Having brought him to the seat of adornment and placed him upon the auspicious vehicle,
he set him down there upon his seat and decorated him as before;
then, having performed everything without exception, from the fire-oblation to the offering of the bali.
Taking the festival image, one should thus perform the great festival.
And every day, according to the sequence prescribed by me,
it should be performed with unprecedented ornaments, garlands, and likewise with unprecedented garments.
Just as curiosity arises from unprecedented gardens, vehicles, and such,
so too should one perform [the rites] with special distinction until the day of the pilgrimage site (tīrtha).
On whichever portion of the assembly ground those enjoyments were previously arranged—
In that very place, they should be established for the God, provided it is possible;
[this applies] always during festivals in villages and other locations, together with Śrī and Vasudhā,
or there may be a circumambulation of the Lord alone.
On the first day and subsequent days, the offering of the *bali* should be made in due order:
minced meat, powdered turmeric, and *karambha* mixed with parched grain flour (*lāja*). Having combined these with the *caru* oblation, one should present the *bali* according to the prescribed rite.
On the second day,

having combined sesame and rice with the sacrificial porridge (caru); on the third and fourth days, likewise parched grain (lāja), various grains, and cakes mixed with the porridge along with coconut water.
Having mixed roasted barley flour and rice flour with the sacrificial porridge (caru),

one should offer it on the fifth day. On the sixth day, having combined lotus seeds, milk-rice (pāyasa), and rice grains with the sacrificial porridge, one should cast the oblation (bali) along with cakes (apūpa).
In all seven [directions] and the others, together with the four kinds of food,
one should daily deposit the bali offering of cakes and likewise of parched grain in the eight locations, from Brahmā to Īśāna, as before.
Having prepared offering-stands upon floors smeared with cow dung,
and having performed instrumental music, dance, song, and constant festivities upon them,
one should present the sacrificial oblation (bali) preceded by water and likewise followed by water.

Having displayed the *balimudrā*, one should display the eight auspicious signs (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*). Having circumambulated the offering (*bali*), the offerers of the *bali* should depart on the night of the commencement day and on the day of the completion.
One should offer a single oblation at midday; two oblations during the middle parts of the day;
and the offering of oblations everywhere, both by day and by night, according to the prescribed rule.
On the final day, at night, during an eclipse, and on the day of the equinox—
When that [time] has arrived, he should perform the concluding bath (avabhṛtha); if there are two offerings (bali),
then in a place devoid of villages and the like, the best of teachers should present the offering in the middle or in front of the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) for the sake of Brahmā.
On the day preceding the day of the sacred ford (tīrtha), there shall be a hunt for the deity;
on the day preceding the hunt, there shall be immersion in a wooden water-vat (jaladroṇī).
On the day prior to the day of immersion, one should worship the deity.
One should show [the deity] seated upon a single, vast throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi;
furthermore, one should display the Lord’s departure from the garden and other such places along with his two goddesses,
as well as his various sports there, and again present offerings.

Having personally presented the gifts brought from various regions to the God of Gods within the pavilion in the assembly of people, the Guru said, "Go away from here, all of you; go away from here! and so forth.
Then, at the proper time, he should inform the gods and others who are to receive the offerings.
Because of his identification with that [deity], the lord of teachers should contemplate, "I am the God.
Having gazed upon the face of the God, he should perform all acts of grace.
Having understood the king’s intention,
those standing near him spoke to the kings regarding that particular favor,
whether accompanied by Sudarśana and Annamūrti or even without them. 11.186
One should perform that great festival either together with the offering of oblations or without it,
using only the festival image for the days up until the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
On the day of the water-bath, one should prepare a wooden vat for the immersion as was done previously.
The auspicious festival of the God of gods is to begin in the morning;
immersion in a wooden trough filled with water is prescribed for the afternoon.
One should place the wooden trough in a pond at a spot provided with steps.
Or one should fill a golden basin with fragrant waters;
on the ground surrounding it, one should scatter unbroken grains of rice in the shape of pearls.
Having invoked the Gaṅgā and other rivers into the waters, one should honor them while recollecting them.
When the water has been consecrated with mantras containing water-related terms (*abliṅga*), one should cause the worshipped deity to immerse itself in it,
along with the ritual services (*upacāra*) as before, ending with the bath.
At that time, they should recite the *Vāruṇa-sūkta* aloud.
Therefore, I shall cause this proclamation to be heard loudly in all directions:
"Having bathed the deity and placed him upon the litter, one should bring another [image] there and honor it just as before. (11.193–194)
This sacred ford has been frequented even by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
By those who have drunk its waters, who have carried them upon their heads,
and who have performed ablutions here, their sins are shaken off and they go to the eternal Brahman.

Or on a day for hunting, beginning in the morning as before, one should celebrate a festival in its entirety; at its conclusion, the hunt shall take place. Then, he should be adorned with all ornaments suitable for the hunt.
Having equipped artificial elephants and the like with appropriate weapons and armor, and having mounted him upon a fabricated horse, one should lead him to the village and other places as before.
Accompanied by the two goddesses, he should be led on a lion or similar mount, joined by an army consisting of elephants and other units.
Furthermore, in the pavilion of the garden, upon a golden seat in its center,
one should worship him as he sits there, preceded by a ritual bath;
and in another pavilion, having offered the great oblation according to the prescribed rite.
Having mounted the vehicle, he should lead it into the interior of the temple that night;
thereafter, he should perform the auspicious constant festival as before.
In the latter part of the night, however, there is the consecration (adhivāsana) of the sacred bathing image.
O Four-faced One, having tied the *pratisara* [protective cord] in the absence of a shrine image;

or, in the absence of a representation for the daily festival, there should be the consecration (*adhivāsana*), whether for the bathing and worship or for the image that performs the festival. (11.202–203)
One should conduct the festival, beginning in the morning, according to the sequence previously described.
Having raised the image that was laid down and having placed it in the pavilion of the face (mukhamaṇḍapa),
one should take the jars that were established in the grounds of the sacrificial pavilion (āgamaṇḍapa).

Having led [the image] clockwise around the temple and placed it near the bathing image (tīrthabimba), the Guru, having worshipped the edge of the cloth according to the rite, should place the bathing image upon a heap of grain at an auspicious moment. || 11.205–11.206 ||

The primary consecration is performed once; otherwise, it is a mere ritual for outsiders. The knower of mantras, having drawn water from the jars, should consecrate the deity with the root mantra according to the rule, starting from the eastern jar and ending with the central one.

The preceptor should perform the worship for each jar, beginning with the ritual bath and ending with the lamps, while the excellent Brahmins recite the Vedic study loudly in all directions and the musical instruments resound with mantras dedicated to the deities of the waters.
When Hari has been worshipped with new garments, upper cloths, and so forth, ending with lamps,
one should smear the ground in front of the flag-pedestal with cow-dung water,
making it square, and scatter it with heaps of rice.
The mortar was adorned with garments, ornaments, and other decorations.
O Four-faced One, having washed it and placed it upon a seat on the sacrificial ground,
one should meditate upon Lakṣmī while reciting the Śrīsūkta-vidyā; then, having consecrated and worshipped it,
one should likewise wash the pestle and consecrate it with the root-vidyā.
Taking it together with the image-makers, the preeminent teacher, composed in mind,
should pound the powder of the night [substance] placed in that mortar,
while the courtesans and temple-servants sing auspicious songs.
One should pound the night-plant powder until it becomes extremely fine.
Then, having placed that powder inside a jar wrapped in cloth,
one should set upon a seat a bowl provided with a fringe, prepared with rice grains.
Having established [the deity] with the root mantra and worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings,
one should take those powders from the jars and perform the consecration with the Śrīsūkta.
Then the officiating priests and the chief preceptor, having gone around the deity clockwise, [should proceed].
Having prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation and scattered flowers with joined palms, he praised the God many times with various hymns;
[he was accompanied] by adorned devotees of the Lord who carried parasols and yak-tail whisks.
All of them together should proceed in great numbers into the presence of the deity.
Having mounted the Lord— whether on an elephant or another vehicle— along with the consecrated image of the sacred site (*tīrthabimba*) adorned with ornaments,
they should then proceed as before with the festival image (*utsavabimba*) being carried ahead.
Having led [the deceased] together to a sacred ford on a river or to the bank of a river,
on the new moon day or the full moon day— or even within the distance of one *yojana*—
or else to the shore of the ocean, or there in a pavilion prepared for that purpose.
When he has ascended his vehicle and is seated upon the throne,
having placed twenty-five, ten, or seven water-pots before him— or whatever number as nine— according to the rule and as was done previously.
One should consecrate the wheel with water-pots and the remaining waters;
having invoked the sacred fords (tīrthas) by name at rivers and other holy sites,
one should immerse the image there according to the rule with the Cakra-mantras.
When the image has been brought for the sake of the pilgrimage site or during a festival, having sprinkled it with water falling from the tips of the *kūrca* grass,
one should immerse the image in the wheel [of the mandala].
In the absence of the wheel, however, that *kūrca* alone should be immersed in the presence of the deity.
And those people who at that time immerse themselves together with the god,
having shaken off all their inauspiciousness, even great sins,
go certainly to that place which is very difficult to attain, as long as the moon and stars endure.
Having brought the deity into the pavilion and worshipped him as before,
one should then offer the great sacrificial oblation and feed the Brahmins.
Every day, one should feed either a thousand or a hundred Brahmins.
Having placed [the deity] upon a vehicle within the inner sanctum, one should then lead it there.
That night, having brought the Lord into the pavilion and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
and having offered [oblations] in due order, one should do so again at dawn within the pavilion.
Somewhere on a portion of the earth frequented by devotees and followers of the Bhagavata,
having drawn a lotus with a discus according to the prescribed method, accompanied by Varuṇa,
[he should worship] with seasonal blossoms and dark, black tulasī leaves.
One should decorate it with the five colors, such as white and so forth, using pigments that are free from deficiency or excess; and there, in the center of that decorated area,
one should place an auspicious and festive auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) as is appropriate.
Having established [the deities], one should worship them in sequence with the *arghya*, *pādya*, and other offerings.
11.234 One should worship, in due order, the syllables of the twelve-syllable mantra as they correspond, using the nine items beginning with *arghya* and ending with ornaments. 11.235
One should worship Hari with flowers for every single syllable of the mantra.
Then, one should offer worship with hands joined in *añjali* while addressing the limbs, beginning with the heart (*hṛdaya*).
At the conclusion, one should say: "May there be fruit for me through these flowers; obeisance. (11.236)
Having uttered each respective mantra, the preceptor, the best of teachers and knower of mantras,
should consecrate the ornaments, such as the Śrīvatsa and others, in their proper order,
as well as the divine weapons, such as the discus and others, in due sequence.
In the same manner, one should perform the worship of the deities residing in the enclosures;
offering flowers directed toward the ten forms beginning with Matsya, as well as others beginning with Keśava, numbering twenty-four in total.
O Lotus-seated One, the preceptor should offer flowers at the two lotus-feet of the God, verse by verse, with the *Pauruṣa-sūkta*, the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, and the *Viṣṇu-sūkta*.
Likewise, those most proficient in mantras should recite the four Vedas in the cardinal directions with the five Upaniṣadic mantras that purify all;
and in the intermediate directions, those of pleasant countenance, being absorbed in that, should likewise recite the Ekāyana branch.
Likewise, they should study with hymns and dances performed with constant diligence;
they should gratify the Lord of the God of Gods with songs in various modes and with flower-offerings consisting of white and other blossoms.
Having prepared four kinds of food, such as milk-rice (pāyasa), for the deity,
and having offered that food to the god, one should perform oblations in the fire located in the northeast corner of the pavilion,
using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and cooked rice (caru), each separately for the four [deities].
The knower of mantras should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, having performed a circumambulation and offered praise to the deity upon the ground,
he should prostrate himself like a staff and mount the vehicle, such as a palanquin or similar conveyance.
Standing there, he would cause the first veil to enter,
and [he would admit] the devotees and the followers of the Lord (bhāgavatas) who were overcome by the experience of service,
as well as even Brahmā and the others who had come to contemplate his auspiciousness.
Having dismissed those who had bowed down so that they might each return to their own abodes, Hari, the Lord of All,
performed a circumambulation from left to right around the one stationed at the entrance,
and departed together with his eternal inner attendants and followers.
Accompanied by auspicious rites, he should enter the interior of the temple;
that day, at night, he should place [the deity] in the previous bathing pavilion (snapanamaṇḍapa).
He should perform the ritual bath appropriate for the conclusion of the festival with water-jars in the proper sequence.

Then, having brought that great sacrificial offering (mahāhavis) into the interior of the pavilion and having reached the sacrificial hall, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules. Thereafter,
one should perform the propitiatory oblation (śāntihoma) according to the sequence previously described.
For atonement, one should offer clarified butter with the five Upaniṣadic mantras;
having offered either a thousand or a hundred oblations, one should perform the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should then dismiss the fires and the deities stationed there upon the archways and other structures.
Having approached the flagstaff and worshipped the Lord of Birds (Khagādhipa),
and having offered oblations to Garuḍa and circumambulated him clockwise,
one should dissolve that Tārkṣya from the cloth, resorting to the sequence of withdrawal.
Having planted the flagstaff and uprooted it during the deep of night,
the preeminent teacher himself should then take hold of the staff and the flag.
This seizing by the preeminent teacher shall bring satisfaction to Tārkṣya.
Having offered oblations at each respective place to the deities who had been invoked and were stationed there, and having made proclamations with the sounds of musical instruments at every spot,
O Four-faced One, he dismissed them by uttering their own names.
The preceptor, together with his silent attendants, should mutter the eight-syllable mantra.
Having entered the temple of the deity and announced the cart and other items,
he should place the sacrificial image upon a vehicle and bring it into the interior of the temple.
At dawn, or when the sacrificial rite has been performed during that night,

the patron of the sacrifice, having adorned and honored the preceptor with garments, ornaments such as bracelets and the like made of gold, and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, [should proceed].
Having given the highest sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)— consisting of one hundred gold pieces or even more—
according to his wealth, he should give other fees every day,
such as ten niṣkas, half of that, or half of that again, according to his means.
One should give a formless [image] to the preceptor according to one's faith,

or half of that; having given half of that to the officiating priests and half of that to the attendants, one should satisfy them with gold, garments, food, and other offerings through respectful service.
He [honored] all the people, such as the singers and others, according to their respective offices—
both those who were auxiliary to the ritual performance and others who had come to witness the auspicious event—
as well as the devotees, the followers of the Lord (bhāgavatas), and common folk, with desired wealth.
Or one might give even a very small sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in the performance of a sacrifice.
O Lotus-born One, for those who perform rituals, a sacrifice devoid of a sacrificial fee is fruitless for the performer;
on the contrary, it leads to the performers' transgression.
Therefore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given in accordance with one's means;
with faith, [one should offer] that of Vāsudeva along with its limbs and sub-limbs and the sacrificial fee.
Whoever should personally perform the entire festival of the God of gods, [attains the supreme goal].
Rescuing others, he himself certainly attains union with Viṣṇu.
He who performs a thousand horse-sacrifices with a concentrated mind,
and he who worships with a festival— these two possess an equal succession of fruits.
Through the ritual of the festival, the sacrificers obtain the entire fruit of all sacrifices from the God; there is no doubt in this matter.
Those mortals who assist in the festival rites of the God [attain the same].
Through action, mind, or speech, they too go wherever they desire.
Whether in a village, a city, a town, or even a kingdom, wherever there may be a great festival of Viṣṇu, [there they go]. || 11.273–274 ||

There is no fear of death, nor of disease, nor of the occurrence of famine and the like; thieves perish there, and unrighteousness does not prevail. The king shall be endowed with righteousness, and the people shall be devoted to righteousness.
All become happy and are freed from all suffering. Whatever water, food, or clothing is given to those who seek it while a great festival is taking place, that becomes a thousandfold in merit.
Worship of the God performed with flower garlands, fruits, ornaments,
and other offerings according to one's ability leads to infinite results.
Those who serve the God there day and night without weariness [attain the same].
It is impossible to state that "this" or "that much" shall be their fruit. [Namely:
anointing, sweeping, as well as the settling of dust; lighting lamps with water, and acts such as spitting and slapping [the limbs]. (11.279–280)
Those who construct a world of Brahmā go to that state which is difficult even for the immortals to attain;
those Brahmins who carry the vehicle go to the abode of Brahmā,
and others who carry the chariot likewise go to the residence of the gods.
Moreover, those men who carry the parasol and other [emblems] rejoice in heaven. Likewise, the guides, the image-keepers,
and the attendants who are appointed for the festival of Viṣṇu obtain whatever they desire.
Those people who study the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas there dwell in the highest ether, by the side of the God, free from desire.
This [state] is the supreme means for bringing about all peace and for eradicating all suffering.
It bestows happiness upon the king and his kingdom, increases longevity and health,
and is a great means for securing the welfare of the subjects of Vāsudeva.
All the gods and others [should celebrate] this supreme festival of Viṣṇu.
Having established a permanent abode that is exceedingly difficult to attain,
they reached it when a festival— requiring only one day or three days to complete— was initiated with faith.
Therein were the offering of oblations, the worship with flowers, and the consecration ceremony.
O Lotus-born One, the immersion in sacred waters using nine jars, as well as hunting and the use of wooden water-tubs, are to be avoided on festival days,
whether at the edge of a sacred ford or within the streets of a village.

Having immediately invoked the deities beginning with Brahmā, one should offer the bali-oblation; at night, there is the consecration consisting of an oblation of plain rice in the fire. On the equinoxes and other such occasions, there is bathing and immersion in rivers and similar bodies of water.
Flower sacrifices, water-vessels, and hunting are not appropriate.
All else should be performed as before by those desiring results;
O Brahmin, this is the most secret and supreme means of propitiation.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Great Festival," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[The twelfth chapter begins.]
Regarding the ritual procedure for flower offerings, Brahmā said: "By which flowers, leaves, or sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) is Hari to be propitiated?"
"Tell me, what other fruits and roots are suitable? The Blessed One replied:
"Flowers from the Nandana grove, or from one's own garden, or even from oneself."
Or having taken them from the forest, or purchased from the marketplace;
or obtained unasked, O Lotus-born One—
whichever of these is acquired later should be accepted in preference to each preceding one.
Furthermore, flowers acquired by unjust means, or those dedicated to other deities,
as well as those that are broken, unopened buds, or fallen, are not to be accepted. Likewise, those that are withered, stale, infested by insects, or stepped upon by feet [are forbidden].
