[Flowers] that are withered, touched by those who are untouchable, or brought by those born of inverse unions [are unfit].
Having bathed, wearing clean garments, and observing silence, one should wash one's feet with water and take flowers in a vessel made of bamboo or grass.
Flowers brought from the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpadruma*), produced from the *pārijāta*,
originating from the lineage of *haricandana*, born from the *mandāra* tree,
and produced from the *saugandhika*— these six are born of the celestial trees (*suradāru*).
The palāśa flower is the seventh used in worship;
these, after being washed with water, should be offered again as unworn remains (anirmālya).
Each subsequent one is held to be a thousand times more meritorious than the preceding.
In worship, two lotuses are recommended in the morning, as are three blue lilies;
their fruit should be understood to be as previously described, and the same applies to the *śatapatrikā*.
Likewise, the *campaka*, *ketaka*, the glorious *mālatī*, and the *mādhavī* [are also recommended].
The *nandyāvarta*, the *punnāga*, the *suraparṇī*, and the *ekaparṇikā*; the pair of *priyaṅgu* and *pāṭala*, as well as the two kinds of *mandāra*;
and likewise the *lakṣmī*, the *karṇikāra*, the *yūthikā*, and the *kuraba*.

Garlands made from these are recommended; their fruit is held to be as previously described. A white karavīra flower is recommended for worship at midday, as are flowers from the kiṅkarāta, the sauvarṇa, and likewise the sahacarī.

One should know that the fruit is as previously described, and it is also praised when offered at twilight. The pair of *jātī* flowers, the *vicakila*, the two kinds of *mallikā*, the *vakula*, the wild species, and likewise the *navamallikā*— 12.14–12.15. One should know that the fruit is as previously described, and it is also praised when offered at twilight. The pair of *jātī* flowers, the *vicakila*, the two kinds of *mallikā*, the *vakula*, the wild species, and likewise the *navamallikā*.
The *kumuda* and the *vanamallī* are remembered as having fruit as previously described;
flowers that have blossomed at dawn are suitable even for midday,
while flowers said to bloom at evening are commended for midnight.
One should worship with flowers that bloom by day during the daytime, and likewise with flowers that bloom at night during the night.
In times of distress, one should worship Puruṣottama according to what is appropriate.
One should worship with *mālatī* in the morning and with those born from the *karavīra* at midday.

In the evening one should worship with jasmine flowers, at twilight with *vakula* flowers, at midnight with *mallikā* flowers, and always with water-born flowers. At dawn, one should worship with *nandikāvarta* flowers; this is declared to be the proper time.

One should not make [garlands] from water-lotuses and the like that are less than three days old. Furthermore, there is no fault in using night-lotuses even if they have stood overnight. A garland made of bound flowers is more highly praised than one made of loose flowers.
Among garlands (*mālā*), the *sragvara* is a wreath made of flowers of a single species;
whereas a *srak* is fashioned from various kinds of flowers and the bark of the plantain tree.
Likewise, there are *hrībera*, *tamāla*, and the three types of *damanaka*.
One should never worship Hari with stale offerings.

Furthermore, there are two types of *tulasī*—the white and the black—as well as the *kevala*, the *akṣapaka*, and the four varieties of *tulasī*; likewise, *dūrvā* grass and *bilva* leaves [are acceptable]. (12.23–24)

One should worship with karavīra flowers those who are worthy of being propitiated by all gifts; however, in the absence of flowers, leaves, and other such offerings, one should perform the worship of Hari in the home with unbroken white grains of rice grown from barley.
Nīvāra, veṇu, śāli-kalama, and others,

as well as barley (yava), are fit for the sacrificial oblation; likewise, rice (vrīhi) and, in its absence, millet (priyaṅgu), and other varieties of grain suitable for sacrifice, with the exception of kodrava.

Rice-grains such as *kalamas* that have been given by low-caste persons, touched by those who have fallen from their status or by those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), or handled by others who are in a state of ritual impurity, are not recommended for use in sacrificial oblations (*caru*).
However, they are recommended when cooked in the absence of such persons.
Rice grains free from defects, offered by members of the four castes—
whether unbroken, broken, or, in their absence,
husked— the vessel for the *caru* should be made of copper or, alternatively, of clay.
When the vessel has been washed with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and filled with filtered water touched by the Praṇava, one should place rice grains therein while reciting the Mūla-vidyā;
or alternatively, one should wash it again with waters [consecrated] by the five Upaniṣads.
One should fill [the vessel] with the *praṇava* alone and cover it with the *cakramudrā*.
Having placed [the vessel] over the fire with the root mantra,
one should kindle the fire with wood untainted by insects and the like, using the five *upaniṣad* mantras.
Once it is cooked, having drained even the water and sprinkled it again with clarified butter,
he should set the *caru* aside on a plank made of sacrificial wood with *darbha* grass pointing northward.
The initiated one should prepare that cooked offering according to the prescribed rule, while his wife [performs the remaining tasks].
Or they might accomplish it silently, having prepared cleaned side-dishes;
among these, first were fruits—plantains, the finest jackfruit, cucumbers, bṛhatī, and karkārī. (12.35–36)
One should avoid the kāravallī, the malābu, the kūṣmāṇḍa, and the tintriṇī;
likewise the karavarta, the niṣpāva, the gavākṣa, and the trapusa.
One should also avoid varieties of mung beans that are defective, though those that are faultless may be consumed.
Food that is leavings, bitten by worms, stepped over by dogs and the like,
smelled, touched by saliva, produced from impure substances,
touched by feet, fallen, or remaining in an impure place at an improper time; || 12.38-12.39 ||

O Four-faced One, one should avoid the remnants of what has been eaten, that which has been touched by those who are untouchable, and the leftovers of what was offered; likewise, the three types of creepers, the bulbous roots, the two kinds of *sūraṇa*, the *utpala*, and the two types of *piṇḍāraka*— these are unfit for use as sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
Jīvantī, vāstuka greens, and likewise the leaves of kāravallī;
tumbī leaves, bhāñjalī, śimbī, and the leaves of mudga;
śākinī, śataparvan, and likewise aśvāsamardana.
One should cook the *āgastya* vegetable, which is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
one may also take other plants that have a single root, provided there is no prohibition.
O Lotus-seated One, one may even take the sprouts of bamboo and similar substances.
Having cut them with a sickle, they were then seasoned with salt and black pepper,
along with mustard seeds, cumin, and a mixture of asafoetida and śrīparṇī leaves,
together with coconut fruits and clarified butter, prepared as appropriate.
The prepared condiment, either combined with broth or even without it,
should be rubbed with ghee in an iron vessel or indeed in an earthen one. [These include] peas,
mung beans, flat beans, chickpeas, black gram, and horse gram.
Whether they are cooked together or separately, the grains to be boiled should possess the proper qualities;
or else, having removed the husks, the *kulmāṣa* grains should be prepared as previously described.
And for dried fruits such as mangoes, one should use *tintriṇī* in accordance with the specific properties of the fruit.
Mixed preparations are to be cooked, as well as those seasoned with salt;
likewise, mango and ginger are desired when used alone.
The breadfruit, plantain, mango, wood-apple, and jujube fruit—
Grapes, rājādana, jambu fruit, and also toṭaka; dates, cane-apple, mātuluṅga, and pomegranate—
one should employ these fruits when they are ripe, ripened by time.
Milk is its one constituent; water is half of that, and rice is half of that again.
There should be an equal amount of rice, and split mung beans half of that.
Having combined all these with ghee, one should offer the *paramānna* (milk-rice).
When an equal portion of the previously mentioned ingredients is combined with an amount of rice equal to itself, and molasses is added in proportion to the fruit, the wise know that as *gulānna*.
When split green gram (*mudga*) is well-cooked, freed of its skins, and made equal in measure to the rice... [12.54]
One should offer rice mixed with mung beans and fruits that have ripened naturally, drenched in clarified butter;
one may prepare this simple food using only rice.
Fruits, tubers, vegetables, various kinds of mung beans, as well as sprouts— [these are the offerings].
Milk, curd, and ghee, as well as fruit ripened in its own time;
mangoes and other fruits prepared with salts and ginger and the like; varieties of sugar-candy and molasses, and whatever else serves as a side dish (upadaṃśaka). || 12.56–12.57 ||
Their quantity should be according to one's faith and wealth;
substances such as *marīci* and the like should be used as appropriate for the preparation of the ingredients.
Furthermore, there should be at least eighty betel leaves.
Twenty betel nuts are also required as the minimum number.
The ingredients include oil, *takola*, cloves,
nutmeg, citron peel, and other powders mixed with camphor.
A coconut fruit produced from stone that is ripe yet waterless,
or camphor— whether alone, raw, or even dried—
with these and other such items, provided they are free from deficiency.
Having offered betel— consisting of rolled leaves, oil, and soft areca nuts—
to the patron according to his faith and wealth,
as well as prepared cakes made from the flour of wheat and rice; || 12.62-12.63 ||
Various kinds of preparations, soaked in jaggery syrup and combined with ingredients such as sugar, ghee, black pepper, and cumin according to their respective requirements;
and sesame seeds roasted in a closed vessel and drenched in the boiled juice of sugarcane.
One should offer cakes of minced meat mixed with black pepper and cumin;
or flattened rice, either roasted in a closed vessel or soaked in molasses,
likewise combined with black pepper and cumin, along with coconut fruits.
He brought roasted barley flour mixed with molasses-liquids, black pepper, and cumin;
also *karambha* preparations refined with the aforementioned condiments;
and vessels from the kitchen, washed externally with water.
Having made vertical marks (puṇḍraka) with ashes in the four directions using the Astra-mantra, [the images] should be covered with cloths within a cane enclosure; or else,
they should be established upon the ground preceded by a stream of water.
Brahmins, intent on service, wearing turbans and clad in white tunics, should carry [the image] in the pavilion or the temple;
having led it to the wooden platforms on the right side of the deity.

Then, having washed the vessels made of gold and other materials with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and wiped them thoroughly, one should sprinkle them with a stream of clarified butter while reciting the Praṇava;
likewise, one should consecrate the vessels and the sacrificial oblations with the perfected mantra using the ladle.

Taking up and setting down the food offered with mantras, one should eat a *khārī*, half of that, a quarter, or half of that again; this is considered the supreme [measure]. O Four-faced One, for each cooking pot, there is a measure of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other foods.
The various side dishes should be set down accordingly along with clarified butter (ghṛta).
Having prepared all the foods together with curds and side dishes,
the worshippers should offer whatever riches they possess.
One should offer things to be sucked, licked, and eaten according to the extent of one's means;
then, one should set aside a fourth part of what has been offered for Viṣvaksena. Having cast that into deep water, or else one should feed those who are devoted to Him.
By that alone, the attendants shall be satisfied for the sake of satisfying the spirits.
Or rather, female slaves, courtesans, and the attendants of the God should be fed;
however, what has been offered as an oblation is never to be eaten by Brahmā, Īśāna, and the other gods.
Likewise, nothing belonging to Caṇḍa and the others,
nor to the goddesses such as Śrī, nor to the son of Vinatā (Garuḍa),
nor to the weapons such as the discus— whatever object has been offered [to them]— should be touched or stepped over.
It must certainly be eaten by all, including the Brahmins and others, without hesitation.
That which has been offered to Viṣṇu is pure, the purifier of purifiers;
this food, difficult to obtain, should never be rejected.
Prosperity increases for those who enjoy [moderation], while it diminishes for those who renounce [all].
Fasting and religious observances are weighed against his meal, for that meal is his purification;
like a sacrificial cake to dogs, it is not intended for the base.
One should worship other deities with food offered to Viṣṇu;
that same food should also be given to the ancestors, for it then conduces to infinity.
The sandalwood paste and other unguents from Viṣṇu’s remains (nirmālya) should be worn.
For one who wears it day and night, there shall be no further rebirth;
for indeed, the water of the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā), which touches the feet of Viṣṇu,
purifies the hosts of Siddhas and celestial rishis, destroying their sins.
The water from the feet of the Lord is considered the supreme purifier.
Having offered water for the feet to Viṣṇu with the root mantra,
the preceptor should take it and hold it over his head with the hundred-streamed vessel for the sake of purification.
It is the purification of all sins, the destroyer of all evil dreams,
the constant increaser of fortune, and the supreme promoter of longevity.
Dying while the water that has touched the feet of Viṣṇu himself [is upon one's lips], [one attains liberation].
Having drunk it, one attains a happy rebirth and is not born again upon this earth.
When the ancestors are gratified by that excellent water, they are satisfied; freed from their debts, they dwell in heaven like gods.
The water from the feet should be given to a devotee who is peaceful, performs auspicious deeds, knows the ritual of the five times, and is habituated to its performance.
It should not be given to an atheist; it should not be given to one who is envious.
"It should not be given to a heretic; one should protect [the offering] from them with great effort.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Prescribed Method for Flowers and Oblations," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Chapter Thirteen:
The Rule for the Five Times.
Brahmā said:
"O Blessed One, the knowledge of the ritual of the five times is praised here;
the rites prescribed for the five times and those five times themselves—tell them to me exactly as they are, for I am desirous of knowing. (13.1)
"If this which I have asked is not an absolute secret: [tell me] the first action, which is approaching [the teacher], and after that, the receiving [of instruction]. Śrī Bhagavān said:
Sacrifice comes after that, then self-study, and after that, yoga.
These are the five injunctions; their times are likewise five in sequence, O Four-faced One, beginning with the collection of rites ending in auspicious conduct.
This procedure for the ritual approach has been declared in its sequence beginning with rising:
one should awaken during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, meditating upon the supreme Nārāyaṇa;
having risen, one should remain on the bed reciting the name of Viṣṇu.
Having sequentially touched the principles (tattvas) and produced the body, the knower of reality (tattvavid),
having assigned the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) to the body and uttered the mental mantra,
[should contemplate] the ten incarnations (avatāra) and the manifestations (vyūha) of the four, as well as the guardians of the months.
Having meditated and recited those [mantras] individually by their respective names,
and having covered his body with a cloth, he stepped upon the earth with his right foot,
first recollecting Trivikrama.
Having uttered the mantra "Obeisance to Kṣitidhara," remaining silent,
he should go outside the village toward the southwest; having placed [the deity] to the south,
he should position his sacred thread over his ear, separated by grass or similar material.
Immediately thereafter, one should void urine and excrement on the ground.
During the day, as well as during both twilights, one should do so facing north;
at night, one should face south, or follow the direction of the wind if it is blowing.
Then, with his left hand, he should grasp the penis.
Having risen with the clay in his right hand and gone to a body of water toward the east,
north, or west, he should perform purification.
One should wash the anus with twelve applications of clay and the penis with six; having washed the intervening spaces and the left hand with water,
one should finally wash both hands with twelve measures of clay.
Having washed the feet, the shanks, the hips, and the thighs with water,
one should cleanse each part with four portions of earth.
Having sipped water and facing the east, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth.
Nyagrodha, udumbara, aśvattha, plakṣa, āmra, arjuna, dhātakī,
pālāśa, veṇu, khadira, śamī, and dāru—
these eleven, O Lotus-Seated One, are prescribed for the cleansing of the teeth. (13.17)
The tooth-cleansing stick should be twelve finger-breadths in length;
likewise, ten finger-breadths or eight finger-breadths in length are prescribed respectively for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
One should scrape the tongue, perform gargling and sipping water again,
and having washed the mouth with water, one who has sipped water should perform the bath.
One may immerse oneself in a step-well or bathe in lakes.
In the absence of ponds and the like, one should certainly not perform immersion in wells.
Or, when an imbalance of the humors occurs, one may bathe with warm water;
having washed the body below the navel,
the best of those who know the mantras should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) and sprinkle his own person with water.
Having sprinkled oneself with water consecrated by the Gāyatrī mantra preceded by *oṃ*,
one should throw up a handful of water;
this is for the sake of warding off the Rākṣasas who desire to fight during both twilights.
The waters, struck by the vajra and propelled by the hands, become pacified;
for the atonement for violence is the wandering of the self. Then, having sat down, one should cross over while reciting the respective mantra.
Standing in the water, facing the east, he should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra for the sake of the gods and others until sunrise;
then, seeing the sun, he should worship that dispeller of darkness with palms joined,
using the mantras prescribed in his own Vedic branch, while meditating on the one who dwells within the heart.
Having saluted his gurus, elders, and devotees of the Lord in due order,

and having entered his own hermitage, he should approach the deity according to the prescribed rite. He should worship until the conclusion of the recitation and fire-offerings, and he should offer a morsel of food according to the rule.
Adorned with ointments, garlands, garments, and ornaments, as well as with lac-dye and other such items for cleansing the mouth such as betel,
and accompanied by other auspicious rites, he should perform the act of approaching [the preceptor]. (13.29–13.30)
Then, one should collect the materials for worship according to the ritual rules:
flowers, fruits, roots, various medicinal herbs, as well as curd and other substances suitable for oblation, rice, and molasses. (13.31)
Having brought bathing garments, sweet waters,
*darbha* grass, leaves, and sacrificial fuel— as far as his ability and wealth permit—
or with materials required for sacrifice, he should place them in the place of worship.
Having thus brought about the time for the ritual materials (*upādāna*), one should thereafter perform worship.
When midday has arrived, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rule.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) before [the deity], one should take earth in the hand.
Having placed [the water] in his left hand and divided it into three parts— at the root, the tip, and the middle—
he should first consecrate the earth situated at the root with the Astra-mantra and then scatter it in the intermediate directions,
the cardinal directions, above, and below.
Then, having cast the clay situated in the center into the water with the root-mantra,
and having divided the portion standing at the front between his two hands,
he showed the mud to the sun along with the waters.
Having anointed his entire body from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head with the mantras of the Astra and Hīnāṅga, and having immersed himself in the waters,
he should then invoke the Lord, the Master of Lakṣmī, and offer the arghya and other ritual gifts.
Having sprinkled oneself with the purifying water used for washing his feet, poured from the hands using the *kumbha-mudrā* upon the head,
and meditating upon Vāsudeva, one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
Having completed all the rites appropriate for the midday hour,
O Lotus-seated One, one should worship the Lord of Gods until the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa),
and then praise the God with a hymn while prostrating on the ground like a staff.
"Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
Salutations be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Great Being, O Primordial One!
Salutations to Vāsudeva, whose nature is peace, bliss, and pure consciousness!"
Salutations to you, O Unconquered One; salutations to you, the treasury of the six divine attributes.
Salutations to you, O Supreme Person, who abides in great majesty;
salutations to you, who possess a thousand heads and a thousand feet.
Salutations to you who have a thousand arms, salutations to you who have a thousand eyes;
salutations to you who are formless, salutations to you who possess a single form.
Salutations to you who possess manifold forms, and salutations to you who are imperishable.

Salutations to you, the all-pervading Supreme Self, who is to be known through the Vedas. Salutations to you, whose nature is pure consciousness, the ground of the Upanishads; salutations to you, the most minute, the most massive, and the greatest.
Salutations to you who are nearest and farthest, and to you who are most swift;
salutations to you who are oldest, youngest, and most junior. Salutations to you, the fivefold self, salutations to the inner controller of all.

Salutations to you whose nature is free from conceptual construction, the cause of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; salutations to you who consist of the qualities (*guṇa*) and yet transcend the form of the qualities;
to you who are both differentiated and undifferentiated, and whose form is both the whole and the parts.

Salutations again and again to You who are empty of beginning, middle, and end, and who possess those very qualities; salutations to You who are expressed by the *praṇava* and whose form is the *praṇava*;
salutations to You who assume the forms of Brahmā and the other gods for the sake of establishing the course of worldly affairs.
Salutations to you, Viṣṇu, who manifests in various forms such as Nṛsiṃha;
salutations to him whose body is untouched by the afflictions of sinful actions.
Salutations to the God who is the friend of Brahman, salutations to the treasury of splendors.
Salutations again and again to the one who is eternal, unique, and the protector of many worlds, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is most excellent;
salutations again and again to the sacrificer, to the sacrifice, and to the object of sacrifice.
Salutations to you, whose very self is the fruit of sacrifice, who are endowed with the merit of Vedic study;
salutations to you, the supreme swan, salutations to you, the embodiment of the quality of purity (sattva).
Salutations again and again to you who abide in the highest ether.

O Hari, with supreme compassion, [rescue] one who has fallen through his own karmas into the terrible ocean of saṃsāra— crowded with whirlpools of sense-objects, shoreless, difficult to cross, and bottomless; one who is helpless, without refuge, and fearful.
"O Ocean of Compassion, lift me up from this ocean so difficult to cross.
O God of gods, forgive any loss of mantra, loss of ritual action, or any other lapse in your worship; for you are indeed the one who endures all offenses."
"From birth I have been your servant, your disciple, and your son;
you, O Mādhava, are my master, my teacher, and my mother and father.
I do not understand what is beneficial for myself; I simply worship you alone. (13.61)
"Having understood this, O Govinda, lead me by means of the path of skillful methods.
You alone know what is truly beneficial for me— what is this and what is not—
and grant me the yoga of discernment by which I may attain you."

Having thus informed the Lord of the Gods, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice and the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) in his own abode according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras. At that time, he should also honor guests according to his ability.
Having fed those who are to be supported, he himself should eat with self-restraint.
O Lotus-Seated One, the time for that sacrifice has been declared:
it may be performed in the temple of Hari, on the bank of a river, or in the grounds of a monastery.
Whether in a secluded forest, on a mountain, or even in a house,
the *ṛg*, *yajus*, and *sāman* verses— though divided in many ways by the various branches of the schools—
have their single point of convergence in the root branch.
Seated comfortably and composed in mind, he should study the Veda consisting of the three collections (trayī).
Or, while studying together with others who are experts in the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga),
he may teach students or various treatises (śāstra).

Furthermore, those Brahmins who are fearful of saṃsāra and skilled in discerning the essential truth should, according to their respective capacities, thoroughly study the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras, as well as those works devoted to the practice of ārādhanā.

The time for private recitation (*svādhyāya*) has been declared, and private recitation itself has also been described by those who are skilled in the methods of instruction and so forth, including the use of laughter.
Then, when the evening twilight (*paścimasandhyā*) had arrived, that which was prescribed therein was performed.
Having performed all [rites] such as recitation and fire-offerings, and having worshipped the Supreme Person according to rule and in full detail as before,
he should eat, lie down upon his bed, and rise during the dead of night.
Having sipped water and become pure, and having meditated upon the Supreme Person,
O Four-faced One, sitting comfortably in the yoga posture, one should unite the self within the self according to the prescribed method and according to one's capacity.
Relying on the sequence of withdrawal, one should dissolve the principles (tattvas) into the self;
or, while established in the supreme self, one should dissolve the self into the lotus of the heart.
Having arisen from yoga, one should perform the withdrawal and proceed to that sleep which removes all afflictions.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this yoga been described, as well as time as the fifth.
Indeed, these five methods have been shown by me within those [categories].
In this way, through actions performed during these times, a man [attains his goal].
Performing the propitiation of the Blessed One, he does not falter;
practicing thus for twelve years with a concentrated mind,
he attains the perfection of union through the entirety of the ritual complex.
In six years, the states of sārūpya, sāmīpya, and so forth are well-ascertained;
in a single year, the fruit of sālokya is attained—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the rule for the five periods (pañcakālavidhi) in the Carya-pāda of the Padma-tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Chapter Thirteen:
[The Name]. Chapter Fourteen:
The Ritual for the Pavitraka and Other Festivals.
Brahmā said:
O Janārdana, which are the auspicious lunar mansions (nakṣatras) month by month?
O Blessed One, in which of these is worship considered supreme?
"And what are the birth constellations (*janmarkṣa*) of the partial incarnations (*aṃśāvatāra*) in each age?
O Lord of Gods, let them be told; I wish to hear them according to the truth. The Blessed One said:

O Lotus-Seated One, on the ninth lunar day, under the asterism Punarvasu, in the month of Caitra, at the rising of Cancer, there occurred the auspicious birth of Rāma, the immeasurable descendant of Raghu. At that very asterism, the son of Raghu was born.
Together with Queen Sītā, having performed the worship according to the prescribed rites,
a festival filled with every auspiciousness took place there.
And under the asterism Puṣya and the sign of Pisces, Bharata was born.
There, the worship of the Goddess should be performed together with Māṇḍavya as before;
likewise, the festivals [should occur] under the asterism Āśleṣā, and Lakṣmaṇa was born under the sign of Cancer, and Śatrughna also— therefore, his worship [is performed] at that [time].
On that day, a great festival was held for both of them: for Lakṣmaṇa together with the lady Ūrmilā, and for the other [Bharata] with Śrutakīrti;
or rather, all the descendants of Bharata celebrated on the birth-star of Rāma.

The great festival [of the chariot] is to be honored by Hanumān along with all these [others]; and at that very time, on the day of Śravaṇā, in the evening, the Man-Lion (Narasiṃha) is to be worshipped. For it was he who then slew the mountain-demon Hiraṇya.
On that very same bright fortnight, one should worship Viṣṇu on the thirteenth day,
or alternatively on the full moon of the two months of Vasu (Vaiśākha),
for the sake of satisfying the spring season with the riches gathered therefor.
One should worship the God, who is seated facing south in a beautiful pavilion constructed in the middle of the altar, with various kinds of flowers;
or [one may worship Him] in a garden or a temple adorned with artificial groves.
And at a river or similar location as appropriate, provided with fruits, flowers, and water,
on the full-moon day of that month,
having prepared a water-shed in a pavilion with *damanaka* leaves and flowers, one should worship Hari.
One should perform every kind of adornment with flowers and *damanaka* blossoms;
there should be a festival on that occasion, and an oblation (*homa*) should be performed with *damanaka* leaves.
Or, O Lotus-born One, one may perform the Spring Festival in the month of Vaiśākha.
Or else, one may perform the auspicious *damanī* rite as previously described.
Or, in the month of Vaiśākha, or during the bright fortnight of Caitra on an auspicious day,
one should celebrate the festival of *kalhāra* flowers just like the *damanī* leaf festival.
One should worship the God in the various locations, including the four jars and other vessels;
then, having offered the great sacrificial oblation and performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should conclude the rite.
Having also gathered fruits, both those growing wild and those produced by cultivation—
In either the month of Jyeṣṭha or Śrāvaṇa, one should present [the image] to the God;
one should also perform a great festival endowed with all ornaments.
Thus, whoever should cause this worship to be performed with a mind purified by faith— || 14.19–14.20 ||
Having obtained all desires here, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, at the time of the forenoon, is the birth of Vāmana;
at midday, during that same period, is the worship of the enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu).
The worship of Hari is prescribed on the full moon day of Vaiśākha. On the Anurādha constellation, which is the birthday of Hanumān,
one should celebrate that [festival] together with Rāghava, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa.

O Lotus-seated One, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, during the full moon of Anūrādha, one should perform the ceremonial bathing of Hari with water-pots; this brings extreme delight to Rāghava, who is identical with the Self.

Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rite within a maṇḍala of a wheel and lotus, one should then place the bridegroom upon a couch prepared therein— either in a bedchamber or a temple, according to one's means. || 14.25–14.26 ||
One should perform the daily worship there for four months, accompanied by auspicious rites, together with the two goddesses and the *kūrca* grass, or that triad in their absence.
One should lead [the deity] by means of the couch itself, and one should cause any other *kautuka* (sacred thread) to rest upon it.
Having prescribed vows, fasts, and observances beginning with those,
those who practice them there, having resorted to the four stages of life and remaining self-controlled, shall cross that river.
As long as the Lord remains reclining upon his serpent-couch,
on the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
under the asterism Rohiṇī, occurs the birth of Kṛṣṇa, which brings auspiciousness to the worlds.
She is renowned by the name Jayantī, for she conquers all that is inauspicious (14.31). Therefore, at midnight on that occasion, one should perform every auspicious rite;
even when the lunar mansion alone is in conjunction with the truth [of the yoga], worship is prescribed (14.32).
On the following day, there was a great festival for the God, the son of Devakī; meanwhile,
those residing in the hermitages performed, in due order, the daily, occasional, and optional rites prescribed by the Vedas.
For the sake of pacifying omissions and other defects in the mantras of the castes,
the daily propitiation of the Blessed One by men is considered equal to the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Through any deficiency or excess in that [propitiation], all evil karma comes to be.
Then, having performed the full collection of rites, the desired worship was completed;
every year, in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
the sacred thread (*pavitra*) made of fibers, adorned with many garlands, was offered to Viṣṇu.
Having performed [the rite] according to the rules in either the month of Bhādrapada or Āśvayuja,
the ritual act that has fallen due to the omission of mantras or other defects is restored;
through this expiation, the rite protects the performer once again.

"Because of the etymological definition that 'that sacred thread (pavitra) grows again with fruits when it is properly concentrated,' those who know [the tradition] consider this to be the *pavitrārohaṇa* (the ritual ascent of the sacred thread).
This is performed on the twelfth or even the first lunar day (*pratipad*) during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa."
On the tenth or the full moon day, or on the fifth lunar day;
or on the eleventh, the thirteenth, or even the second; during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious weekday, or at a most favorable moment (lagna). || 14.40–14.41 ||

The consecration of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for Hari should be performed under any one of these lunar mansions: Śravaṇa, Puṣya, Rohiṇī, Revatī, Bharaṇī, Svātī, Hasta, Punarvasu, Aśvinī, or Anurādhā (the deity Mitra). 14.42.
One should purify threads made by Brahmin maidens and free from defects—
whether made of cotton, silk, or purchased— with pure water;
having been washed and mixed with mung-bean powder, they should be cleansed outside.
Then, having purified them in the sun and dried them, fold them three times;
having folded them again three times, make them four times that size—
or, O Four-faced One, having brought them to a triple fold, achieve a fourfold state.
Having tripled the three [lines], or else one should bring them to a single unity. Then, on a surface of ground smeared with cow-dung according to the prescribed measurement,
two stakes made from sacrificial wood should be fixed.

Having installed [the image], the devotees of the Blessed One—whether facing east or north—should sit down; so too the preceptor or another person appointed by him, being composed, bathed, skilled in the ritual procedures, and absorbed in the Blessed One. (14.48)

They should fashion a purifying thread that is auspicious and serves as the finest of ornaments. This primary purifying thread, intended for the rite of consecration (adhivāsa), is prescribed to extend from the navel downwards; it should consist of one hundred and eight strands and be provided with thirty-two knots.
This is prescribed as the purificatory thread (*pavitra*) for the primary and secondary images;
it is equal in measure to the lotus in the mandala, and likewise in the jar (*ghaṭa*).
Its measure is also that of the girdle (*mekhalā*) in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); its measurement was declared for the preceding day.
On the following day, the measurement of the *pavitra* [sacred grass rings] is now described.
Within the circle of the lotus-like wheels of the noble ones, which have Padmanābha as their hub and Arana as their rim, those *pavitra*s are measured; the outer measurement is equal to the exterior.
Their knots and threads are described here in due order:
there are four hundred sutras and twenty-seven knots;
the number of threads is three hundred, while the knots are considered to be double that [number].
Two hundred multiplied by three is six hundred; immediately thereafter, one hundred knots.
The number of knots multiplied by four is for the outer thread, which consists of four hundred [units];
the knots multiplied by five are for the *kumbha*, which consists of one hundred and eight.
The number of threads and knots is held to be twenty-seven;
eighty-one threads are considered appropriate for a water-pot (karaka),
and twenty-seven knots are likewise proclaimed.
I shall tell you those ten numbers of the *pavitra* for the images;
they are known as the *prāmāṇya*, the *granthi*, and likewise the one called *alaṅkāra*.
Immediately following [the crown] are those known as the kirīṭa, divided into superior, inferior, and middling;
likewise, those called the śrīvatsa, the kaustubha, and the vanamālā. Their respective measurements, threads, and knots follow in due order.
The lines (sūtras) extending from the navel as their limit are said to be one hundred and eight;
its knots (granthis), immediately thereafter, extend to the heart and number thirty-two.
It is taught that its lines are eighty and its knots are twenty-five.
The length situated in the middle of the shank is fashioned with one hundred threads;
it is joined with eight additional knots multiplied by thirty-two.
The total number of threads for that which is called "excellent" shall be four hundred.
The number of knots up to the limit of the knees is one hundred and eight;
three hundred threads are prescribed with eighty knots.
Furthermore, extending to the middle of the thighs, there are two hundred threads.
Up to the navel, there were sixty knots and four hundred threads;
thereafter, at the measure of the crown, there were thirty-two knots,
fashioned in the form of a necklace with three hundred threads.
Furthermore, with twenty-seven knots, there are two hundred knots;
reaching as far as the breasts, there are one thousand and eight threads,
along with many knots extending to the length of the feet.

The sacred thread (*pavitra*) spread over the seat (*viṣṭara*) together with its upper part is equal to that [in measure]. (14.68) There are one hundred and eight threads and twenty-five knots; the radiance is equal to that sacred thread, while many knots are traditionally taught. (14.69)
This has been declared for all independent (*svatantra*) images;
however, regarding dependent (*paratantra*) images, there are three types, beginning with the "excellent" (*uttama*).
Likewise, the purificatory rite (*pavitra*) is prescribed for goddesses such as Śrī and others.
A sacred thread (*pavitra*) consisting of one hundred and eight threads and provided with seven knots [is used] for the fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*). For the girdles (*mekhalā*),
there is a sacred thread provided with twenty-seven threads and an equal number of knots for each girdle.
The length of the fire-purifier (pavitra) held in the hand is proclaimed to be equal to the span [of the hands].
The medium size is twenty-five [finger-breadths], and the inferior is considered to be twenty-two.
A purifier for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements consists of twenty-five threads.
O Four-faced One, its length and width should be equal, and it should be provided with many knots; likewise, for the arghya vessel, the incense vessel, the lamp vessel,
the bell, and the rosary, in every case [the measurements] should be one hundred and eight [units].
With threads, a knot should be made according to one's desire, twelve finger-breadths in length,
for Viṣvaksena, Tārkṣya, and likewise for Duścyavana and others,
for the deities of the directions, for Druhiṇa, Durgā, and the Lord of Obstacles.
For Rudra and his attendants, the purifier (pavitra) should be made with threads;
it should consist of one hundred and eight strands and be provided with thirty-two knots.
It should be made one cubit in length for Caṇḍa and all others.
Constructed with twenty-seven threads and divided into knots,
the measurement for the pitcher, the archway, and so forth, should be one cubit; likewise,
the sacrificial pedestal and the sacred thread should be measured equal to the pericarp.
For the teachers and the ascetics, it is a purifier made of threads;
for the officiating priests, the worshippers, and likewise for the Brahmins, it is provided with one hundred and eight strands, knots, and joints.

The king’s purificatory cord was fashioned from eighty-one threads, suspended within the navel; it was further constructed with a hundred and eight threads and fashioned with clusters of knots as desired, filled with cotton.
This [measure] should not extend to the navel for those who live under him; likewise for his dependents.
For the Vaiśyas and others, the purifier (pavitra) is made with eighty-one threads, like the sacred thread (upavīta), and for them it consists of twenty-four strands.
When all the purifiers (pavitra) are available and one possesses the means, they should be extensive;
however, when resources are lacking, their number may be reduced by a quarter, a half, or even a third.
Then, one should tie a knot in the purifiers using substances such as musk and the like.

Having filled [the vessels] with gems such as jewels, pearls, and corals according to one's wealth, or with metals such as silver in its absence, or even with cotton wool, and having bound them firmly with knots made of thread-ropes; 14.86–87.
The knots are shaped like conch shells, or they have the form of *dhātrī* fruits, or they resemble pearls and the like;
[they are marked] with saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and likewise with sandalwood. (14.88)
One should smear the spaces between the knots with red frost-like powders ground together and mixed with mud so that they may be beautiful;
or else, one should fill the knots with fragrant flowers such as jasmine and the like.

One should color the spaces between them with flowers or indeed with night-pastes; the threads and the knots may also be colored according to one's desire. O Four-faced One, these should be fashioned with as much elaboration as one’s means allow.
When wealth exists, one should neither practice stinginess nor lack for it;
nor indeed should one practice extravagance, for that alone is what pleases Hari.
Having either immediately consecrated him [with the image] or having fasted there, one should worship Hari.

Whether in domestic worship, in a small shrine, in a mandala, or even in a water-jar, worship should be performed with faith; for this world is purified by faith. [This should be done] within the prescribed purificatory rites, following exactly the path as it has been described.
One should begin the worship of Viṣṇu on the tenth day, and the offering [of food] on the eleventh;
at the onset of night, the preceptor, being well-composed, should enter the temple of Viṣṇu together with the image-keepers and accompanied by the patron.
Having entered and worshipped him, the Guru himself, together with them, should make this request while standing with palms joined and reciting this verse:
"For the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess, the supreme *pavitrāropaṇa* [is performed]. || 14.97 ||
O Blessed One, worship is capable of dispelling all misfortunes and is the unsurpassed means for producing all forms of prosperity;
may that prescribed rite be performed without any obstacle.
"Thus I request permission from you; grant me leave for that rite.
Having made this announcement and departed from the palace, the preceptor again went to the pavilion, spread out the darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, and sat upon it facing the east.

Having sat down and undertaken the fast, being fully composed, he should spend that very night constantly devoted to recitation and meditation. On the following day, at night, there should be the rite of consecration (adhivāsana).
One should begin by tying the *kautuka* (sacred thread) upon a single-liṅga image;
in the case of multi-liṅga images, the *kautuka-maṅgala* should be tied upon the auspicious central image (*kalyāṇabimba*).
Then, having gone out to a spacious pavilion, one should arrange the arches (*toraṇa*) and other decorations.
Having worshipped as before in the cardinal and intermediate directions,
he likewise stationed Brahmins who were learned in the four Vedas and the Ekāyana Veda while the sounds of musical instruments resounded. || 14.104–14.105 ||
And even when other auspicious rites have been performed according to their true nature,

having taken up vessels containing sacred materials in a pavilion on ground sloping toward the northeast and having placed them upon heaps of grain, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.
One should purify those [vessels] placed upon the offering-stand through meditations on burning and nourishing;
one should fumigate them with fragrant substances, smear them with musk and the like,
and scatter many fragrant flowers upon them.
One should wrap those vessels containing the ornaments with a new cloth;
one should display the wheel-mudrā and worship them with the weapon-mantra (astra-vidyā).
Having encircled the pavilion with threads starting from the northeastern direction, [one should proceed].
Having meditated upon the wheel above the pavilion, he should likewise place a lotus and a mace on the surface of the ground, and conchs at the gates and in the eight directions,
for those who create obstacles and run about searching for a vulnerability in him.
One should offer an oblation of black gram (māṣa) food to the spirits, such as the Rākṣasas and others.
Having placed the auspicious image outside on the bathing seat among the many icons,
one should perform the ritual service according to the rules, ending with the sacred thread (upavīta).
O Four-faced One, having again brought forth the mandala of the wheel and lotus at the conclusion of the offering of the oblation,
when the rite of propitiation is completed,
one should invoke the deity into the *karaka* and the *kumbha* pitcher and worship him.
Having presented the oblation and offered into the fire as before,

in the case of a single image (*ekabera*), one should perform all other rites according to the sequence previously described, with the exception of the propitiation of the auspicious *kautuka* thread. (14.115)
During that festive occasion, one should again place the sacred ornament into the water-pot;
immediately thereafter, while reciting the mantra "Idam Viṣṇuḥ," one should cast it into the fire within the mandala of the lotus-wheel.
Having entered the temple accompanied by all auspicious rites, the preceptor approaches the primary image (mūlabera) and then performs the placement of the purificatory thread (pavitranyāsana). Then,
all the images should be worshipped in due order with the mantra previously mentioned.
Having performed the placement of the purifying ornaments with threads of five colors,
one should encircle the temple at night with the chanting of all the sacred scriptures,
accompanied by musical instruments, songs, dances, and hymns, while the people remain awake.
And on the following day, they should lead the Lord of Gods, who has been placed upon the mandala for the sake of the rite of curiosity, to the bathing altar;
having brought him there, they should bathe him according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having adorned the Lord of Gods in the mandala with cleansing and other rites, [they should proceed].
Having purified [the site] and drawn a lotus-wheel with five colors,

one should perform the worship of the doors and so forth as before; having established [the deity] in the mandala and propitiated the Lord up to the offering of lamps, one should also worship the jars and other implements.
Having offered the four kinds of food to the deity in the water-pot,
he should offer the four kinds of food, such as milk-rice and others,
into the fire with the *Puruṣasūkta* alone, using barley, rice, and bamboo-seeds.
With sesame seeds, parched grain, flowers, as well as agallochum and clarified butter,
and with sacrificial fuel sticks, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations separately using the root mantra when an auspicious moment has arrived, as determined by an astrologer.
Having taken up the purifiers (pavitra), one should again adorn the discus and the lotus;
likewise, the lotus and other [emblems] that are its limbs, with the verse beginning "yathāsvamidam.
Then, [one should place them] upon the water-pot (kumbha), the small vessel (karaka), and the deity immediately thereafter.
That same mantra [is used] for the sacrificial pit, the fire, and the archway;
likewise for the pitchers at the doors and the purificatory threads placed therein.
Then, having circumambulated the Teacher of the World situated within the mandala, || 14.128–14.129 ||
Having entered the temple with all auspicious articles, the preceptor first performs the rites beginning with the ceremonial bath; thereafter,
the worship is described as being carried out until the offering of the sacrificial oblation to the deities residing therein.
Starting from the primary image, one should adorn [the deities] with their respective purificatory ornaments (pavitra).

Having worshipped all those who are independent and those who are dependent with the previously mentioned mantra and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should [present] the purificatory ornaments individually for each.
At the time of giving, those skilled in playing musical instruments,
as well as dancers, singers, and those proficient in sacred recitation,
should all perform their respective dances and other arts in his presence.
Purifying offerings (pavitra) should be presented to Caṇḍa and the others of his retinue who are present in the courtyard, continuing until the end at the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha);
and likewise for the deities beginning with Brahmā, as well as for Tārkṣya and Senāpati.
For others as well who have not been mentioned, there are purificatory rites according to their respective status;
and the mantras are this *Viṣṇugāyatrī*,
"That which [is pervaded] by Viṣṇu," or else the twelve-syllabled mantra itself.
The preceptor, together with the images and joined by the patron,
having entered the temple of Viṣṇu himself with his hands full of jewels,
or else with handfuls of golden flowers, or even with hands bearing ordinary flowers; || 14.137–14.138 ||
Praising him with many hymns, he should scatter at his feet jewels, golden flowers, and fragrant blossoms— those things which,
as is appropriate, are considered pure for human beings.
Having placed [the offerings] at the feet of the Lord of Gods with great concentration, as if offering flowers,
the preceptor, having informed the God, takes for himself the linen and other sacred threads that he has prepared.
One should give [the offerings] to the chief worshippers, the officiating priests, the assistants,
those devoted to the Ekāyana path, and other learned men as well,
according to their respective qualifications and in due order, after having beheld the face of the deity.
Then, having touched the lotus feet of the Lord in the presence of the people, the preceptor should recite this verse for the sake of pacifying any deficiency or excess:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace! (14.143–144)
"This worship was performed by me for the sake of completing the services offered throughout the year;
please accept it out of a desire for the welfare of your devotees.
I am not independent; I perform only that which is ordained and beneficial."
"But impelled by you, I perform everything for you and not of my own accord.
Therefore, whatever has been performed through the omission of rites must be forgiven entirely.
At the proper time, however, the sacrificer [should give] a cow, land, and likewise gold."
Having fed the Brahmins with garments and the like, as well as grain,

and having given the preceptor a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his desire— consisting of at least one hundred niṣkas, or even cows, land, clothing, grain, and so forth— and having bowed down to him; 14.148.

Likewise, to the image-bearers and others, gifts should be given according to their respective deeds; indeed, that which brings satisfaction should be given to those who assist in the sacrifice. In the afternoon, one should thus perform a great festival outside the village.
O Four-faced One, after sprinkling these daily at the times of worship, they should be deposited by the worshippers for fourteen days,
or perhaps twenty-one, or even seven days.
For three nights or one night thereafter,
he should descend from those [elevations] while reciting the Pauruṣa Sūkta, or the Rathantara Sāman,
or the Trisuparṇa mantra, or even the Mūlamantra. (14.152–14.153)
Having performed the planting [of the sacred grass], the purificatory offerings (*pavitra*) should then be given to the preceptor;
those [offerings] given to the preceptor are for the gratification of the Slayer of Madhu.
Otherwise, there would be fruitlessness of the ritual act, and there would be ruin for the king and the kingdom.
One should dismiss [the deity] residing in the mandala, that residing in the water-pot (kumbha), and that residing in the fire.
On the day of the Pavitrāropaṇa, a postponement of the time is not appropriate;
having performed their removal (avaropaṇa), the ritual bathing (snapana) follows immediately thereafter.
Then one should enter the temple according to the prescribed rite.
Thus, O Brahmin, has this procedure for the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) been described.
By this rite, one should perform the offering of the sacred thread for Viṣṇu.
Performing [this], one shall obtain infinite fruits; of this there is no doubt.
One lives happily, free from disease, prosperous for as long as life lasts;
and having attained a full lifespan, the seeker of dharma shall acquire dharma.
One who desires pleasures shall obtain them; one who seeks wealth shall obtain wealth;
one who seeks liberation attains liberation; and one who seeks offspring obtains offspring. Moreover, he shall obtain reunion with kinsmen living abroad.
One who desires fame attains supreme fame; of this there is no doubt.
One who seeks knowledge attains knowledge, and one who seeks peace shall attain peace.
Furthermore, enemies perish, as do the afflictions caused by planets, spirits, and other such calamities.
One who desires health shall obtain health; one who desires prosperity shall obtain prosperity.
What need is there for much speaking here? Whatever fruit one desires, all that shall be within one's grasp; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures and meditated upon the Enemy of Madhu at the end,
those devotees endowed with faith who maintain the purificatory rites attain that world and are not born here again. (14.164–165)
Having shaken off their sins, they too rejoice in heaven like gods—
namely the preceptor, all the image-keepers, and whatever other attendants there may be,
as well as those who hear, see, or proclaim that deed.
All of them, having their goals fulfilled, obtain every prosperity.
O Brahmin, the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice may take place in the month of Śrāvaṇa, or in Prauṣṭhapada, or in the month of Āśvayuja,
or in the month of Kārttika.
Thus during the rainy season;
at other times, it may be performed in the months of Taiṣya, Māgha, Phālguna, Caitra, or Vaiśākha.
It should likewise be done under the asterisms of Hasta, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Āśleṣā, or Rohiṇī.
Under the asterisms of Vāruṇa, Puṣya, Vāyavya, or Aditidaivata;
under Maghā, Maitra, Citrā, or Śraviṣṭhā; or under Saumya and the three known as the Uttarās—it should take place according to what is favorable for conception.

All odd lunar days (tithis), with the exception of the ninth, are auspicious; however, even lunar days are not desired, except for the second and the tenth. The planets Soma, Bṛhaspati, Saumya, and Bhṛgu are auspicious.

In the signs of Aries, Scorpio, and Pisces, as well as Virgo, Capricorn, and Cancer, this sequence of ritual action should be performed during the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). First, one should offer curd-rice to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla) upon the sacrificial ground.
When the hour for harvesting has been declared, one should then perform the harvesting;
the grain should be taken by the cultivators in bundles of stalks (*kaṇiśa*).
Likewise, [the fruits of] plantains, jackfruit, and so forth, as well as curd, clarified butter, and the like [should be collected].
Likewise, they should carry loads of grain and leaves of plantains and other such plants,
accompanied by dance, instrumental music, song, and ornaments;
with the commander of the army and the lord of birds at the front and at the rear.
Adorned and mounted upon vehicles such as elephants according to their wealth,
and accompanied by the full regalia of parasols, yak-tail whisks, silken garments, banners, and so forth,
they led the garland of the Slayer of Madhu around the village in a clockwise circumambulation.
Having entered the granary,
they should worship the grain that has reached the state of ears with the Śrīsūkta; then, having placed it in new vessels, they should carry out its collection in those storehouses.

For those performing the ritual, one should offer grains and other items according to their respective qualifications at an auspicious time, as is prescribed for the worship of the God of gods. (14.181) One should take fresh rice grains, wash them, and husk them three times.
The Guru, during an auspicious moment, [should offer] those [foods] prepared with pepper and cumin, well-seasoned in the cooking of molasses,
accompanied by coconut fruits and stalks of sugarcane,
for the deities beginning with Mūlabera and Berā. || 14.182–14.183 ||
Then, one should offer [oblations] with the root-mantra one hundred and eight times;
one should sacrifice rice-grains into the fire for Brahmā and the others as before.
On that day or on the following day, one should present fresh grains of food.
"Many offerings, well-prepared and finished, upon plantain leaves.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Pavitra and Other Festivals," in the Caryāpāda of the *Pañcarātra*, the *Mahopaniṣad*, within the *Pādma Tantra*.
Fifteenth Chapter:
The Procedure for the Performance of Vows; The Blessed Lord.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the God, the Primordial Person,
the auspicious Lord Varāha, the enemy of the Asura Hiraṇyākṣa,
together with the Goddess Dharā, for the sake of accomplishing all goals.
In that [month], there is also the worship of other various forms [of the deity].
Having bathed in the month of Āśvayuja, one should perform sacrifice with ritual ablutions and other rites;
and when the month of Kārttika has arrived, on the twelfth day of either the dark or the bright fortnight.
On the [lunar] fortnight, having worshipped the God according to one's means, one should awaken Him;
this mantra beginning with "ud ity am" is for the awakening, as is the word "uttiṣṭha.
Having awakened Him, one should worship the risen Lord according to the prescribed method.
Having worshipped the festival image situated within the mandala in the pavilion,
and having performed the worship of the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth as before,
a great festival accompanied by every auspicious rite should be conducted in the village.
And all those in the stages of life (āśramins) should perform the formal dismissal of their vows,
giving ten niṣkas or half of that as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor at that time,
on the full moon day of Kārttika under the constellation Kṛttikā, for the sake of the Enemy of Madhu.
Or it may occur during the conjunction with the Kṛttikās, or on the lunar day alone. Then, one should illuminate the entire temple of the God;
having hoisted lamps everywhere upon the high pillars of the Slayer of Madhu.
In all directions everywhere, as well as upon the enclosures,
pyramidal shapes should be fashioned, and within them there should be rows of lamps.
Likewise, on the walls of the ramparts, in the pavilions, and at the gate-towers.

There should be many rows of lamps in all directions. On the eve of the festival of lights, at night, one should fasten auspicious and festive ornaments upon the festival image, which is endowed with every mark of good fortune.
And on the following day, there should be the worship of the primary image (mūlabera) and the others.
At twilight, one should perform the occasional rite (naimittika) of the consecration of the lamps (dīpādhivāsana).
Having placed a new vessel before the primary image, [one should proceed].
Then, having poured purified ghee measuring one āḍhaka— or alternatively, oil from a Kapila cow— into that heap of grain,
[one should place] a straight wick made of threads or a new cloth.
Having fashioned [the wick] and extracted it, one should kindle the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with that;
one should show the fire-gesture (*agnimudrā*) with the wick while reciting the Āgneya mantra.
Then, having worshipped the fire with the mantras during an auspicious moment, the Guru—
Taking lamps placed in vessels,
one should illuminate all the lanterns in the watchtowers and other locations, while musical instruments resound in every direction and there is the exertion of dancing, singing, and the like.
While the Brahmins were reciting the mantras dedicated to the fire-god,
he took up the festive image, adorned with every ornament.
Having placed [the deity] upon a vehicle, one should lead him through the streets and into the enclosures;
one should show him dramas and other such performances, both artificial and otherwise,
and display to the God of gods the various linguistic distinctions as they have been described.
Having approached that pavilion and offered the great oblation—
prepared puffed rice, parched grain flour, and straw for the satisfaction of the fire—
and having at that time presented cakes to the Enemy of Madhu; || 15.21–15.22 ||
One should cause [the image] to enter the interior of the temple accompanied by auspicious rites;
the method of worship through the Kṛttikā-lamp is thus declared.
This brings about unsurpassed prosperity for the Vaiśyas, the king, and the kingdom.
O Brahmin, it pacifies calamities and is pleasing to Jātavedas (the Fire-god). In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there is this unsurpassed vow;
because it is preceded by the Dvādaśī vow, it is the propitiation-vow of Hari.
Performing such supreme service to the Blessed One on the tenth day, having worshipped Hari and fed the brahmins, he,
being composed in mind, gave them sacrificial fees according to his ability.
Having made known to them, in the presence of the Blessed One, the vow of the twelfth day (dvādaśīvratam),
he— having performed worship preceded by formal permission and preceded by the vow, which yields great fruit—
sat upon darbha grass, facing eastward, with a concentrated mind.
Having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observed the vow, and having likewise performed all the daily rites (āhnika),

he should at night engage in yoga with the Blessed Lord according to the prescribed rule. On the following day, the eleventh (ekādaśī), he should perform the entire collection of rituals according to the rule.
Previously, bathing at the three sessions of the day and firmly established in his observances,
he worshipped the God while fasting; maintaining silence until the conclusion of the fire-oblation, he remained devoted to meditation on the Blessed One and withdrew from worldly affairs.

Remaining silent, he should stay there without touching his mind to physical actions such as gestures and the like; likewise at night, having bound the "curiosity-bond" (kautuka-bandhana) and worshipped the Lord of Gods, he should spend the night lying upon *darbha* grass.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed the twilight devotions (*sandhyā*) according to the rules, he should go before the gods and perform worship as before. He should [invite] Brahmins learned in the four Vedas to the directions, starting with the east, in due order.
Having seated them upon seats of darbha grass facing the deity,
as well as the brahmins in the corners who are conversant with the Ekāyana,
he should cause them to recite their study, just as a teacher causes his own pupils to recite.
In the absence of those who sing the *sāman* chants, he should feed those who are solely established in austerity,
or even those who know the *ekāyana*, for they are supremely pleasing to Hari.
Observing the vow, he should partake of this together with Brahmins for the purification of his body.
Kuśa-grass water, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the provision of food in due order;
sleeping during the day, food from others, and the act of eating again;
service to women, the use of oil, and eating from a bell-metal vessel.

On that day, one should abandon the eating of meat and avoid censurable actions. One should feed [the Brahmins] according to one's ability and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the conclusion. If one is unable to fast, one should observe the night-vow on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
And breaking the fast on the thirteenth day out of ignorance would result in becoming a Rākṣasa; one should avoid the days of Saturn, Venus, and Mars,
O Four-faced One, as well as the lunar mansion presided over by Yama at the commencement of the vow.
Breaking the fast and fasting are both not considered a fault during the three days [of the lunar change].
One should not converse with those who follow heretical ways and are censured by men,
nor even through negligence with other atheists or those born of inverse unions.
One established in the vow should not look upon those who are impure on the twelfth day,
nor during the *ārdrā* asterism in this month, nor under the birth-asterism of Garuḍa.
For his propitiation, Hari should be worshipped according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
At dawn, one should offer milk-rice and jaggery-rice; then,
having prepared the image for the festival procession, one should have it proceed through the streets and enclosures,
accompanied by Garuḍa and attended with auspicious rites.
During the northern course of the sun, one should worship the deity with ritual ablutions and other rites;
one should anoint the deity with ghee or immerse him in ghee and similar substances—
either in ghee, curd, fresh milk, or prepared honey.
Or upon fruits with the juices of those fruits, or in the liquids of the five products of the cow;
or in foods such as milk-rice, or in heaps of seasonal flowers;
or on the leaves of *tulasī* and the like, or in collections of the nine gems.

Having fashioned golden spheres, radiant with well-formed limbs, within beautiful flower-shaped vessels of refined gold— spheres that were equal in appearance to auspicious images adorned with fashioned ornaments— 50.150.
Having covered [the structure] with those [bricks] shaped like pedestals, one should decorate it.

Having fashioned five globes (golaka) resembling the five weapons, with forms similar to hands and so forth, individually according to their beauty, in the shape of bodices (kañcuka). || 15.51–15.52 ||
One should adorn all the limbs and weapons with those [grains] in every way;
or else, one should cover Adhokṣaja from head to foot with other grains such as rice (vrīhi) and so forth.
One should cover him with all the materials while reciting the root mantra.
Or likewise, one should fill [the time] with three [verses], or even three times four along with the *tripāda*, or double that amount.
One should provide auspicious music, instrumental accompaniment, dance, song, and so forth;
all of this should be performed according to the extent of one's wealth.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter using the root-mantra until the vessel is full;
and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of gold should be given to the preceptor according to one's wealth. This filling of the vessel with ghee and other substances bestows the fulfillment of all desires.
In the month of Puṣya, under an auspicious asterism, or even on the full moon day;
or in the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, on the fifth lunar day, one should perform the worship of the Blessed One, the enemy of Madhu, which destroys all sins. || 15.57–15.58 ||
Having propitiated [the deity] according to the scriptures before the Lord upon the surface of the earth,
[on a site] smeared with cow dung and measuring two cubits by both hands,
or again, four cubits in length and breadth, and covered over; 15.59.
Likewise, having covered [the image] from above with a new, unworn garment,
and then with a pure black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) free from tears or cuts,
one should place a cloth over that.
Having prepared a sacrificial altar (vedikā) with one or two loads of sesame seeds,
[one should fashion] upon that sesame a three-tiered structure in the shape of a lotus;
or else, a golden lotus-line weighing three niṣkas should be placed upon the sesame seeds.
Having placed the nine jewels, one should deposit them in the eight directions.
In each direction, one should place two vessels filled with grain in succession;
likewise, one prastha of oil, ghee, and curd, each increasing fourfold [in the subsequent directions].
Having placed the vessel on the ground at his sides and in front of him, the Guru,
with his senses restrained, shall subsist for three days on sesame seeds and clarified butter while facing eastward;
or, O Four-faced One, he may first fast for one night.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and immediately thereafter with sesame and rice,
while the Brahmins were reciting and the sound of musical instruments resounded,
and while other auspicious rites proceeded accordingly.
One should offer sesame seeds into the fire a thousand times with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
[One should honor] the preceptor (ācārya), who knows the five periods (pañcakāla), is learned in the scriptures of the Lord (bhagavat),
is devoted to auspicious conduct, and is endowed with all virtues.
Having honored that devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata) with unbroken rice grains and other offerings, one should present a sesame-lotus in his presence preceded by water;
the preceptor, knowing the mantras, should say: "May the Blessed Viṣṇu be pleased. || 15.69–70 ||
At the conclusion of that, having worshipped the deity and fed the Brahmins,
one should give them and to the preceptor a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed.
Thus, whoever should give a "sesame-lotus" together with grain and other offerings—
He purifies all his ancestors as well as himself, both those who have gone before and those who follow.
By performing worship with ritual bathing and other rites on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, under the constellation Phālgunī, one who desires prosperity should worship Hari. (15.72–73)
Having fasted previously, self-restrained and meditating thus with a concentrated mind,
he stayed in the midst of a vast grove of bilva trees, adorned by lotus ponds,
within a great lake crowded with flocks of warbling birds.
There, within that Maheśvara mandala, surrounded by a perimeter wall,
adorned with wish-fulfilling trees at its four gates in the four directions,
it was made of gold and endowed with many auspicious jeweled pillars.
Seated comfortably with Śrī upon an excellent lion-throne, which is joined with an eight-petaled jewel-lotus and endowed with a pericarp and filaments;
Vāsudeva and the others are to be meditated upon on the petals in the directions beginning with the east.
In the corners beginning with the southeast, there are four elephants in sequence:
Guggulu, Kuraṇḍa, Damaka, and Śalala.
Furthermore, the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma, are on either side of the lion-throne.
Facing one another and constantly pouring forth abundant wealth,
the eight [deities] beginning with Earth stand in the directions starting from the east, holding chowries in their hands.
And Indra and the others, eight in number, are stationed in the eight directions beginning with the east.
At the four gates stood women with charming appearances, disguised as hunchbacks, holding canes and keys, keeping watch;
likewise Balākinī, Bhīṣikā, and Vanamālinī.
And Śāṅkarī— O Four-faced One, these [goddesses] are to be placed in order starting from the east;
likewise, the gates are adorned with *pālikās*, full jars, twice-born men,
arches, pearl garlands, lamps, and other auspicious items.
Having thus meditated upon them as adorned, one should worship the Goddess and the God;
or one may worship Śrī alone, seated upon the pericarp of a lotus in the pavilion previously described, accompanied by her retinue.
The oblation should be performed with *lakṣmī* flowers, lotuses, and the tender leaves of the *bilva* tree and others,
using fuel-sticks and clarified butter while reciting the eight-syllable mantra of Śrī. Furthermore,
the *Śrīsūktas* should be recited by the Brahmins in the four directions.
Having propitiated her, he should finally praise Śrī with various kinds of hymns:
"I bow to you, O Goddess, mother of the worlds, born from the lotus, beloved of the Lord of all the lords of the worlds, who is difficult for the base to attain. (15.87–88)
O Goddess, bestower of auspiciousness, sovereign deity of the gods, salutations to you, the vessel for the singular flavor of the bliss arising from the touch of Vāsudeva’s limbs;
even those upon whom your side-glances fall but once by mere chance— || 15.89 ||
Those lords of the three worlds become arrogant even toward the lowly;
yet those glances of yours do not touch even the lords of the three worlds.
In an instant, the lowly are brought to ruin, even if they have fallen from the very summit of heaven.
O Goddess, who is capable of praising those limbs of yours, wherein qualities such as loveliness reach their supreme perfection?
You are Māyā, you are Avidyā, and you are the power (śakti) even of karmas.
You are the power of consciousness, the primordial nature (prakṛti) consisting of the three qualities.

You alone are knowledge, the three Vedas, and the triple Veda; you are both the supreme and the inferior, within a ten-thousandth part of a fraction of whom the goddesses of speech and the other senses abide.
You are the indivisible embodiment of bliss and the other attributes of the Supreme Self, whose nature is truth, consciousness,
and bliss; you shine eternally as the radiance of that luminous Supreme Self.
You are the twilight of the Brahmins, to be saluted day after day.
You are the triad of Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ; you are Bhūḥ, you are Bhuvaḥ, and you are Svaḥ.
You are the sacred utterance (vyāhṛti) and the source of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
You are the oblation, you are the sacrifice, and you alone are the sacrificial fee;
success in all actions comes from you, O Abode of Lakṣmī, for there is nothing else besides you.
You are the science of polity, the science of inquiry, the science of commerce, and other worldly sciences as well.
O Goddess, seeing the three worlds deprived of you and as if dead,
you manifested yourself through efforts resembling the churning of the ocean;
and as a secondary result, even the attainment of the Apsarases was secured.
Even so, O Indirā, in the abode of Hari, anything other than nectar—
even the poison hālāhala— arises for the welfare of your birth,
having manifested in the form of an obstacle within the ocean of milk. 15.101
Thus, the birth of you, the enemy of Madhu, is indeed most venerable. Since even the Supreme Self attained the state of animal births such as a tortoise,
you are the mother of all worlds, and Hari is the father of the worlds.
By you and by Viṣṇu, this world of the moving and the unmoving is pervaded.
Do not abandon our treasury, nor our cow-pen, nor our home, nor our belongings; do not abandon our bodies, our wives, and our progeny.
Learned, virtuous, skillful, intelligent, wealthy, and upright;
endowed with good conduct, kinsmen, prosperity, cattle, and grain;
possessed of merit, fame, and noble lineage—such a lord is one in this world. (15.105–15.106)
"O Goddess, the man who has become the object of your sidelong glance is long-lived, victorious on earth, likewise healthy, and possesses praiseworthy speech.
One who is devoid of the aforementioned qualities and deprived of the sight of you [is as described] in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra. (15.107)
Fifteenth Chapter: The Sequence for the Performance of Vows;
Sixteenth Chapter:
The Proclamation of the Fruits of Sweeping and Other Rites, and the Faults of Stealing the Property of the Gods.
Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, when inauspicious signs and omens have arisen that indicate the future results of actions which are themselves of an inauspicious nature— (16.1)

"O Acyuta, please explain what kind of supreme rite there is for the pacification of those afflictions— such as the malefic influences of planets— that arise suddenly for men, for their lords, and for kings;
and tell us how it is performed."
Out of supreme compassion for me, even that secret must be told.
16.3 The Blessed One [spoke] while Mars and other planets were situated in inauspicious positions relative to his birth star and so forth.
During cruel and ill-omened events, at times of bad dreams,
and likewise when anthills arise upon houses, fields, and the like, when rains of blood have occurred, and when there is the burning of dwellings by fire— (16.4–16.5).
When clothing and such are bitten by mice, when beds and other items are burnt,
in other distresses as well— such as quarrels with sons and others,
