in royal wrath, mental anguish, or imprisonment in fetters— [one should practice].
In times of affliction by enemies or their factions, by piśācas and other such beings, or by crocodiles;
upon the violation of vows, the prior absence [of sons], the loss of wealth,
or when portending undesirable events, at the birth of a son, or when calamities occur— 16.7–16.8.

O Brahmin, propitiation of me in the presence of such and other faults leads to peace; the method for that is now being told. Having performed the ritual acts preceded by bathing according to the rules and with reverence—
On a clean patch of ground, one should place a water-pot made of gold, silver,
or copper, according to one's means; it should be filled with water, provided with a brush,
wrapped with threads, containing seeds and water, and accompanied by a small vessel.
Thereafter, one should choose a preceptor who is intent on propitiating me,
endowed with qualities such as tranquility, and devoted to the five-fold ritual cycle (pañcakāla).
Having placed [the image] upon heaps of grain, with gems and gold deposited therein—
And [he should place] the auspicious leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, accompanied by the substances for pacification;
it should be wrapped in a new red cloth and joined with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Having invoked the Lord of Gods in the eastern direction upon a pedestal of clay (*ghaṭikā*), [he should perform the rite].

Facing the western direction with bundles of *kuśa* grass, one should worship with the eight-syllable mantra using the water-offering (*arghya*) and other rites; or else, his worship may be performed even with empty vessels. Having invoked [the deity] into the pitcher, one should perform the sacrifice and offer oblations of clarified butter from a cow.
Then, with the eight-syllable mantra alone,

the Guru— having meditated upon Hari, the bringer of all peace and the bestower of all prosperity— should perform one hundred thousand, ten thousand, a thousand, or even one hundred and eight oblations in the sacrificial pit.
Having duly considered both gravity and lightness,
one should exert effort in all respects regarding the worship and other rites of the defects.
At the end, the preceptor himself [should address] the sacrificer with the syllable *praṇava* and the water-mantras (*abliṅga*).
One should sprinkle [the image] with water from the jar while reciting the root-mantra;
one should bathe it a thousand times with the remaining water using a *kūrca* [bundle of grass].
One should give gold and other gifts as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor according to one's wealth.
One should feed Brahmins and give them even a small sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the pacification of all calamities of all masters,
as well as for the attainment of all desired objects; this is the special worship of Hari.
On that day, after the daily worship has been performed, one should first carry out the ritual bathing;
at its conclusion, the rite for pacification (*śāntika*), and in the afternoon, the rite for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*).
The daily rites prescribed for the forenoon are here [performed] with double the materials.

The worship with ritual substances is performed upon the primary image (mūlabera) when there is only one image; however, O Lotus-seated One, it should be performed upon the festive image (utsavabimba) when there are many images. In the case of special worship, the preceptor himself should perform the worship.
The fire-offering pit (homakuṇḍa) should be very beautiful, shaped like a lotus.
For rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika) and pacification (śāntika), it should be circular, and one should perform oblations daily with fuel-sticks and other materials.
There should be ten thousand (ayuta) oblations of sesame seeds for each, or at least one hundred.
Every day he should feed Brahmins according to his capacity and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
He should perform dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the daily recitation of the Vedas. This should continue until the day the ritual concludes, as well as the maintenance of the sacred fire.
It may last for seven days, or twice that, or thrice, or four times as long.
A ritual bath should be performed every day, as well as offerings, fire-sacrifices, and so forth.
In rites for pacification (śāntika), Hari should be meditated upon as resembling crystal in appearance.

In the rite for nourishment (pauṣṭika), however, [the deity] has a golden luster and is seated upon a throne together with Śrī, within a mandala of a wheel and lotus; where the first worship is performed in the ritual jar (kumbha), there alone on the following day he is to be propitiated. Yet, there is no state of being "worn-out" (nirmālya) for those two.
And also the teacher’s fee (dakṣiṇā), according to the extent of one’s wealth; and,
having considered the gravity or lightness of the rite for those authorized to perform it,
one should satisfy with riches the officiating priests who are rendering assistance.
O Lotus-born One, when the days are favorable, one should commence rites for prosperity; when they are unfavorable, one should perform rites for pacification for the patron. Brahmā said:
O Blessed One, for those men who perform cleansing and other rites in the temple,
who bestow lands and other gifts upon Viṣṇu, and who provide articles of worship,
ornaments, and garments, the fruit is that of worldly prosperity.
Of what nature were those very gifts given, and for whom who was taking them back?
Tell this to me, who am full of doubt, for it seems to me to be purposeless.
While performing the cleansing in the temple of Viṣṇu, he cleanses away that which is born of the body.
The Blessed One,
performing the daily cleansing of all accumulated impurity and sin— both that pertaining to this world and the next— destroys evil every single day. (15.37)
By smearing the ground of the temple with cow-dung to the extent of a cow’s hide,
a man immediately obtains the fruit of giving a cow.
By performing the sweeping and smearing in the abode of Viṣṇu, a man [attains great merit].
Having dwelt for a long time in heaven, by the remainder of his merit,
he is born once again on earth as a king in a great and honored family—
he who, having fashioned a garland of beautiful flowers, offers it to Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he shines resplendent upon the vault of heaven;
by offering lamps within and without the temple of Viṣṇu,
he dwells like a god in the celestial realm and is born as a knower of the supreme truth.
A man who offers lamps, whether regular, occasional,
or special, does not behold the hell filled with manifold sufferings.
A man should offer a lamp that remains unextinguished day and night.

With his soul purified of all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. He who performs the sprinkling of water upon the abode of Viṣṇu reaches the world of Varuṇa and rejoices there for many years.
Having swept and anointed the abode of Hari, if a person scatters flowers upon the ground,
he obtains all abundant desires;
he makes the earth belong to Viṣṇu, yielding many crops and fruits.
He who, by the gift of a flower garden, undoubtedly attains all the worlds, is glorified in the world of austerity (tapoloka). [Likewise,
one who gives] land provided with fruit-bearing trees and endowed with water...

He who gives [gifts] in Maharloka dwells there for a long time, certainly. He who plants fruit-bearing trees, such as coconut palms and others, in a field sacred to Viṣṇu goes to heaven, which is difficult to attain after death.
He who diligently plants *tulasī* for the sake of propitiation,
as well as fragrant flowers, is honored by the gods in heaven.
He who constructs ponds, wells, and tanks on the grounds of Viṣṇu’s temples...
All prosperities come into his hand; he generates them.
Sins accumulated even over many lifetimes do not bind him who constructs a Vaiṣṇava temple endowed with both devotion and faith. (16.51–52)
If a temple is broken, cracked, or defiled by substances such as lime-wash,
one who restores that temple goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu.
By providing water for Viṣṇu’s bathing and drinking, one becomes a partaker of his same world.
By the gift of substances for bathing, one becomes free from disease and rejoices after death. By the gift of linen and other such materials, one obtains great happiness in the next world;
by the gift of ointments, one obtains eternal desires.
By the gift of camphor, betel, oil, and so forth, one becomes happy in both this world and the next for a long time; of this there is no doubt.
By the gift of chowries, fans, and umbrellas, one enjoys the sovereignty of heaven.
Through the gift of ornaments and such, one becomes radiant and rejoices in heaven.
By the gift of the nine jewels, one attains residence in the same world as the gods;
by the gift of a mirror, one shall become visible to all.
By the offering of incense materials, one’s own place shall become that of the denizens of heaven.
Whoever, having adorned them, gives sandals, wooden shoes, a vehicle, or even a carriage decorated with jewels and gold, [attains such a state].
He attains a celestial mansion that is very difficult to reach; of this there is no doubt.
Bestowing an adorned auspicious throne, he partakes of all desires;
raising a banner and displaying it, he reaches the abode of the Joy of Vinatā.
O Four-faced One, he who suddenly raises a banner and musical instruments and dedicates them to Viṣṇu attains immediate proximity to Viṣṇu;
having reached a place abounding in divine drums, he shines resplendently.
Then he offers his own male and female servants, as well as himself, into servitude to Vāsudeva. For one who serves Vāsudeva, liberation rests in the palm of the hand.
[This is achieved] through various kinds of dances, various kinds of songs, and likewise manifold instrumental music.
Those who likewise propitiate the Lord in his presence with divine sounds worthy of hearing and with services such as the offering of seats,
will undoubtedly be honored by them in celestial realms for all time after they have passed away.
Those who worship the God, the supreme deity of the gods, with circumambulations, prostrations, and service consisting primarily of hymns of praise,
are described by the gods in the hereafter just as the Blessed One is.
Even those who, by mere chance, behold the God, the Lord of the lords of gods, whether he is standing, reclining, or seated, attain the supreme state;
how much more so those who gaze upon him for even a moment with devotion?

Having shaken off all evil deeds, they go to whatever worlds they desire. Those men who pay homage by prostrating with the eight limbs quickly obtain the fruit of those whose nature is austerity and sacred study.

Who is capable of remembering or describing the fruit obtained by those who bow even once to the Lord, the enemy of Madhu? [This fruit is so vast that] it cannot be measured as "only this much"—whether by the head, the ears, the mind, or the hands. (16.71)
Whether with both arms, or with both feet, or with both knees, or even with the chest—
bowing to the enemy of Madhu with each individual limb—
one attains vast and infinite desires that are difficult for others to obtain.
Furthermore, those who prostrate with all eight limbs day after day, recounting the stories centered on Vāsudeva,
undoubtedly attain the eloquence of Vācaspati when they go to the temple of Vāsudeva.
By the gift of cows, such as Kapila and others,
a person attains eternal residence in worlds beginning with the world of Brahmā,
through the offering of oblations such as milk-rice (pāyasa) to Hari.
His self filled with the singular flavor of bliss, he shines in the presence of Viṣṇu;
by the gift of food to be chewed, drunk, and eaten, as well as other things, they dwell happily forever in Śvetadvīpa near him. (16.77)

What need is there for much speaking here? He who, out of reverence, gives all kinds of objects for the sake of Vāsudeva, attains his desired abode after the enjoyment of the fruits of his actions, such as the purification of his deeds.

Through the remnants of their karma, those who experience rebirth in wombs corresponding to their actions always obtain happiness, even in the most excellent ones. These are the enjoyers of the palaces, pavilions, and other structures belonging to the enemy of Kaiṭabha (Viṣṇu).
Those of deluded minds who, after death, dwell in the hells without end,
are certain to be born again in low wombs.
That man of evil intellect who steals ornaments, umbrellas, garments, and the like— || 16.81–16.82 ||
Those who, out of delusion, seize the mounts and vehicles belonging to Vaiṣṇavas are dragged into the hells with nooses fastened around their necks;
they dwell for a long time within the belly of the Aṅgāra hell.

After death, they are born yet again in the wombs of donkeys, camels, and other such creatures. Even those who steal substances such as sandalwood or fragrant flowers belonging to Viṣṇu go to the torments of Yama.
Having experienced [the fruits of their deeds], O Brahmin, they are born again as musk-rats.
Those who steal sandals, wooden shoes, seats, or fans,
after dwelling in the hells, are born into the lineage of serpents.
Those who, having seized wealth such as cattle, land, gold, and clothing belonging to Viṣṇu’s property,
enjoy it, dwell in the hells without respite; after passing away, they are born again in the wombs of horses and other such creatures.
Thus, in all the hells, those of deluded mind who steal the property of gods or Brahmins dwell, experiencing the abundant sufferings of Yama.
[They lack] exercise, massage, ointment, bathing, drinking, eating, and so forth.
Those who perform [acts of desecration] in the temple of Viṣṇu go to hell;
they are cooked there once again and are born into low wombs for the acts of breaking,
cutting, and so forth, committed against the image of Vāsudeva.
Those of evil mind strive toward deformities and other such things against others;
these go in succession through all the most dreadful hells. Even in other transgressions, whether gross or subtle, human beings [suffer].
"Even the skillful, having passed away, are cooked in hell as partakers of suffering.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Fault of Stealing the Deity’s Property and the Fruit of Sweeping," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Chapter Seventeen:
The Procedure for the Ritual Sprinkling (Saṃprokṣaṇa) of Renovated [Temples], by Brahmā.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the restoration of dilapidated images and sanctuaries; please tell me that according to the facts. (17.1) The Blessed Lord said:

In all four types of images— those made of self-existent stone, those of divine stone, those of human stone, and those born of jewels— even if a limb is missing, it must be restored with refined gold; it must not be discarded, even in the case of those made of mountain stone.

In exactly the same way, one should perform the restoration for the five types of images made of wood and so forth. However, having set aside those images that have missing limbs, one should create them anew; this applies both when restoring a single limb and when restoring the entire body.
Having invoked Śakti into the pitcher and having fashioned it as before,
one should perform all the rites such as the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) and so forth, just as in the case of a formal installation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
If meditative absorption (*samādhi*) can be maintained while the [deities] reside within their respective images, [then that is sufficient].
"O Lotus-born One, the abandonment of all of them is not appropriate.
Once the metal image has been discarded, one should have it melted down and create it again;
when the god is remade after he has decayed, the goddesses remain as they were before."
The deity should be joined with those very [mudrās] alone; one should not create others again.
Furthermore, no further marriage ceremony should be performed for their progeny during worship.
Even if there is a deficiency or movement in the radiance, the lotus seat, and so forth—
Furthermore, one who is not composed should not worship the weapon, such as the discus and so forth.

(17.9) Having dismissed the power of the image into the primary icon or into a vessel, the concentration of the discus and other [implements] should be performed once that [primary icon] has been concentrated. (17.10)
Having sprinkled [the image] with water, one should worship the Śakti after invoking her into the icons;
if the old image has become worn out and a new image has been made,
one should install that deity upon the pedestal— there is no fault in this, O Lotus-born One.
Even if the pedestal is new or worn out, having made it new again as before,
one should always install that image upon the pedestal through the rites of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
O Four-faced One, no fault should be recognized in that regard concerning the radiance and other qualities.

Having constructed a temporary abode for the child [the deity] there, among stones and other materials, one should invoke the power (śakti) into the image; this is the worship of Hari in dilapidated [shrines].
Once the image has been abandoned, one should bury it in the earth or cast it into water.

One should worship [the deity] even in a dilapidated palace or in a small dwelling, provided the Lord is accompanied by his own retinue, just as he is at the root [of the tree]. However, when the *dhruvabimba* has decayed and the temple itself is in ruins, one should worship those [deities] who remain there.
One should install the gods and their retinues in the primary image (mūlabera).
For those whose abodes are not yet decayed, they remain there; however, when they have decayed, they are placed in the permanent image (dhruvakautuka).
O Four-faced One, the removal (udvāsa) of the gods and others should not be performed elsewhere.
One should never perform [the rite] when there is indigestion, when one is deficient in limbs, or at the beginning of the sacrificial hall and such places.
Even if a mortal should perform it out of delusion despite these being more numerous [faults],
the destruction of that sacrificer along with his lineage is certain.
If, due to negligence, a temple or similar structure was previously constructed without conforming to the authoritative rules,
then one should subsequently reconstruct it in accordance with those characteristics.
In the case of temples with many faces or a single face, the construction should be carried out as before.

There are many images, not just one; likewise, there may be others besides the single image. If, previously, a multi-image [shrine] was made without the Goddesses, then upon its re-consecration, it may be performed either together with the two Goddesses or without them.
Furthermore, even in the case of restoring a dilapidated image or the like that was previously devoid of the [thirty-two] marks,
it must be executed in exactly that same manner and not otherwise.
Whether it be a bed, a seat, a standing posture, or a vehicle, it should be made just as it was before.

Furthermore, O Four-faced One, the restoration of an image in a non-human realm would occur in that very same way. In the case of humans, the re-creation of images that have become stationary and so forth may happen by will; if that is so, there is no fault. (17.24–25)

Whatever celestial mansion there was, whatever its substance, its measure, and its appearance previously, it should be fashioned exactly like that again upon creation; one should not conceive of it otherwise.
To conceive of it otherwise would certainly result in misfortune for both the king and the kingdom.
Whether it be a human dwelling, one belonging to the Ṛṣis, made of bricks, or even of clay—
if it is dilapidated, one should restore it using stone or brick. Furthermore,
for the sake of protection, one should construct everything outside, such as the pedestal-base (upapīṭha) and other structures.

And when the retinue deities situated there, as well as the pedestal (*upapīṭha*), have been enlarged, one may install them for the sake of protecting the primary image (*mūlabera*); there is no fault in this.
[This applies] even when the temple, its gate-tower (*gopura*), the pedestal, and so forth, have collapsed or become dilapidated.

One should construct [the temple] firmly with stone and other materials, whether it be extensive or otherwise. If a temple or similar structure is shaken or destroyed by the force of river water and the like, one should re-establish it in another location free from such obstacles.
Whatever form [is prescribed] by whichever tantra for whatever kind of qualified practitioner in the first ritual procedure,
that same form, that same tantra, and that same installer shall likewise apply in the second ritual procedure. (17.32)

When the original [deity] has become worn out and both [the old and new forms] are restored, there is no doubt that the fruit of the conceptualizations regarding the abode and so forth is equal for both. However, when the forms of the deities who preside over the Tantras are again conceptualized in a different arrangement, [the result differs]. 17.33–17.34.
There would be destruction for men, for the lord of men, and for the kingdom,
as in the case of the restoration of what was ruined when many pillars have collapsed.
One should install the ritual image upon the altar and cause it to rest within the pavilion.

One should not perform the immersion in water, nor likewise the opening of the eyes; there is no dissolution or generation of the principles (tattvas). One should perform all other rites, and having approached the primary image, one should perform everything as before.
Having worshipped the Bālakautuka [image] and its corresponding procession elsewhere,
the Guru himself, having invoked the Śakti into the water-pot (kumbha) which is again placed upon grain, should worship it when the proper time has arrived at the Mūlabera [the primary image].
One should install the Śakti in Hari according to the procedure seen in the scriptures.
The arrangement of the retinue is performed with the water remaining in the pitcher;
at the end, one should cause a festival to be held, for that indeed brings about all peace.
"Brahmā, for the purpose of consecration, what is his form and of what nature is he?
Tell me, O Blessed One; my desire to know persists. (17.41)
The Blessed One [is to be worshipped] when a temple has been newly constructed or its broken parts repaired; likewise when a statue, a pedestal, a halo, or even a weapon has been newly made.
O Lotus-seated One, when the worship has been interrupted for a month or more,
or when it is defiled by touch from those of inverse birth and the like, who are censured for their perpetual impurity, or by menstruating women and other such craftsmen— 17.43.
When the temple is defiled by the impurity of feces, urine, blood, or the touch of the undrinkable;
when there is birth or death [within it]; when the image is touched by dogs, jackals, corpses, and the like; and when a confusion of the tantras has occurred—17.44–17.45.
In these and other such cases, the procedure for sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) should be performed. Furthermore, if the temple and so forth, as well as the image and so forth, have not been sprinkled,
then during worship, the kingdom, the sovereign, the subjects, and the abode of Hari [are affected].
The land would become empty, like a barren wasteland, and overwhelmed by calamities.
Famines, diseases, strife, and death would prevail as the primary forms of distress.
Therefore, the ritual sprinkling of dwellings and other sites must be performed according to the prescribed rules.
The sprinkling with clear water using the mantra "viṣṇornukam" is prescribed;
likewise, the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, should perform it with other mantras containing the word "ap" (water).
This is done when the purification and washing of the permanent image and other icons have been completed.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing according to one's ability, preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), using the most purifying mantras beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the door-arches, the water-pots, and the other ritual objects.
Having placed the great jar, wrapped with thread, cloth, and other materials, in the beautifully adorned central part of the pavilion upon a mound of grain,
one should worship the Supreme Self within it according to the previously described method.
One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and other materials either in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
For each [deity], one hundred and eight oblations should be performed as before for the rite of pacification (*śānti-homa*).
One should tie the protective thread (*kautuka*) upon the image and sprinkle it on the following day.
When the auspicious time of dawn had arrived, the most excellent preceptor,
taking the installed pitcher, led it around the temple by way of circumambulation;
having brought it before the deity, he placed it upon a pedestal of grain.
Taking water from the jar with a *kūrca* [purifier] while reciting the root-vidyā,
the best of Brahmins should, at the proper time, recite the five Upaniṣadic mantras, as well as other mantras containing the word "water" (*ab-liṅga*) and the peace-mantras (*śānti-mantra*).
One should also feed Brahmins according to one's capacity and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
the fee for the preceptor (ācārya) should likewise be at least ten niṣkas.
One may perform this either immediately, or at night, or even during the day.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Re-consecration of a Decayed [Temple]," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[Now begins] the eighteenth chapter.
The Procedure for Expiation for Omissions in Daily Worship:
O Lord Hari, Brahmā [is the authority] regarding occasional and daily rites.
The deficiency or loss of the means of accomplishment is generally designated as "obstruction" (*prāya*).
Its etymological derivation is "the settling of the mind" (*samādhāna*). What is its settling, or what is its nature? Let this be explained. (18.1–18.2)
A man who worships the Lord of the Gods without having bathed, without wearing the sacred thread, or likewise without applying the sectarian mark (tilaka), becomes liable to perform penance. 18.3
Concentration and the recitation of the root mantra a hundred times constitute that worship.
If one performs worship without having purified the feet or even without sipping water,
the recitation of the five Upaniṣads constitutes the expiation for that worship.
Whether with disheveled hair, or with perspiring limbs, or laughing, or panting,

or angry, or even while speaking incoherently— one should nevertheless recite the mantra a hundred times during worship; thus, following the ritual for propitiation, one should recite the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) one hundred times.
There is no ritual impurity at all from touching hair, bones, body hair, clods of earth, and the like.
Even if one is wearing blue, soiled, or worn-out garments and lacks purificatory grass,
the remedy for that is the recitation of the root mantra.
Having gone [to a woman], one should worship and bathe Hari without having bathed oneself.

Then, there is the recitation of the five great Upaniṣads with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) when there has been contact with feces, urine, semen, blood, hair, or similar substances. (18.8–18.9)
If one performs worship without bathing, one should bathe the deity with water containing *kuśa* grass;
the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) is prescribed as the expiation for that act.
Likewise, if one has touched the garment of a woman in her menses while performing the worship of the deity, [the same expiation applies].
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the recitation of the five Upaniṣads.

(18.11) Having touched a dog, a woman in her menses, a sacrificial post (yūpa), a Caṇḍāla, a seller of the Vedas, a funeral pyre, or a tree standing upon a low altar (caitya), one must perform that same worship. (18.12)

One should bathe [the image] with water containing *kuśa* grass using the five *Vāruṇa* mantras. Having touched crows, heretics, outcasts, those born of inverse unions, donkeys, and so forth— or indeed any other untouchable— one should perform the same remedial rite as previously described.
If worship is performed with flowers defiled by defects such as hair,
one should perform a bath with milk and a pacificatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) as the remedy.
If one should worship without having bathed while treading upon excrement and the like, [the same remedy applies].
The bathing [of the image] with water containing *kuśa* grass, the recitation of mantras as before, and the remedial rite;
or a woman or one who has not been initiated may touch the image, and then the remedial rite [must be performed].
The sprinkling [of the image] with *kuśa* water is done with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra.
When the practice of propitiation has begun, if there is an interruption such as spitting,
one should perform *ācamana* (ritual sipping) at the beginning and the end, or touch the right ear;
likewise, if the body has not been purified through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) according to the sequence starting with dissolution (*pralaya*).
If one has not performed the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa), the recitation (japa) during worship is as before;
having again performed the entire worship (arcana) of the deity, there is expiation (niṣkṛti).
If the sacrificial offering (havis) has been touched by untouchables such as Caṇḍālas and others, one should offer it.
If [this occurs] through negligence, the remedy is bathing with cow's ghee;
O Lotus-Seated One, a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa) must also be performed at its conclusion.
And likewise, that which has been seen by, touched by, or defiled by jackals and the like [requires the same].
If the offering is presented with other things lacking proper conduct, or likewise with impure substances,
or with unfit sacrificial oblations such as *kodrava* and the like,
the restoration is as before: one should recite the root mantra ten thousand times.

[The ritual is performed] with vegetables, roots, and fruits, while avoiding foods such as linctuses and drinks. There is bathing, a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), and likewise the recitation of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā). Furthermore, there is the offering of food that is excessively hot, excessively cold, or even putrid.
The recitation of the *nivṛtti-mantra* and the sequential recitation of the *viśva-mantra*,
as well as the offering of cooked sacrificial oblations (*havis*) in a house defiled by a corpse or other such things,
require bathing, as well as rites for pacification (*śānti*) and fire-oblations (*homa*).
If an offering is defiled by worms, hair, or the like,

one should perform a purificatory consecration using the *Puruṣasūkta* alone. This applies also to that which has been struck by breath from the mouth, smelled, or contaminated by dust, husks, or grains.

If one offers that which is defiled by earth, stone, or dung, or likewise if it has become stale, one should perform the recitation of the root mantra. If that which has already been offered as an oblation is offered again, [one should likewise perform the recitation].
First, there is bathing, followed by worship, as well as the recitation (*japa*) of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
One should offer the remains of the flowers (*nirmālya*) or the remnants of the food (*ucchiṣṭa*) as a counter-measure (*pratikriyā*).
Furthermore, there is bathing with twelve jars, a fire-oblation for peace (*śāntihoma*), and likewise recitation.
O Four-faced One, teachers and others who are mentally, verbally, or physically approved [for the rite], as well as sacrificial offerings such as clarified butter and flowers placed in the hand,
are unfit materials for the act of propitiation.

With those five jars used for worship, the bathing should be performed as before, along with the recitation of mantras (japa). O General, one who bows to Vāsudeva must discard from his hands any objects of worship that remain there, as they are no longer fit for worship.
If there is worship by them, there should be a ceremonial bath with seven jars;
likewise, a peace-offering (śāntihoma) must be performed, as well as the recitation of the root mantra.
[This applies when] creatures such as frogs, mice, snakes, cats, and so forth [have been encountered].
If the sacrificial offering (havis) has been touched or bitten by worms, insects, moths, or birds such as crows, it must not be offered if it was intended for presentation. In that case,
one should perform an ablution with three ritual jars (kalaśas) and conduct the worship up to the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa).
If [the food] has been touched by flies or other such insects, one should sprinkle it with water and offer it to the deity.
If, out of negligence or greed, one should worship the deity with the remnants of what has already been eaten,
ten thousand recitations of the root mantra serve as an expiation for that.
Likewise, atonement is achieved by giving away the remnants of what has been eaten.

For bathing with water that has stood overnight, atonement is likewise declared to consist of bathing again with pure waters while reciting purificatory mantras containing the word "water" (ab-liṅga). || 18.38–18.39 ||
In the waters of a sacred ford or a river, there is no defect due to standing overnight;
however, sea water becomes defiled after ten days.
[This applies unless it has been] stepped over by animals, untouchables, or humans.
Water that has been touched [by such beings] is not fit for bathing, nor for ritual ablutions performed with Vāruṇa mantras. For the sake of pacifying that act, one must perform the bath again.
However, contact with the mouths of goats and horses never leads to any fault.
That which has been touched by the mouth of a cow must be avoided during worship.
The expiation consists of bathing again, as well as the recitation of the root mantra.
[This applies when using] substances such as water that are mixed with feces, urine, blood, or undrinkable liquids.

One should not perform worship with jars that are the lowest of the low during a ritual bath. When worship is performed with substances such as water that have been defiled by the remains of Shiva’s offerings (*nirmālya*), the bath with jars shall be considered inferior; it would be middling [only] if [the substances were less so]. (18.44–45)
In a well defiled by a corpse or similar impurity, one should draw out the water as before;
at the conclusion of that process, for the sake of purifying the water, one should have the *puṇyāha* (declaration of auspiciousness) recited.
In the case of the death of an animal or the like in a well, or if a *caṇḍāla* bathes or drinks there, [the same procedure applies].
Likewise, O Lotus-Seated One, one should draw out all that water situated in a well when it has been defiled by menstruating women and others who are of inverse caste or censured;
in the event of the death of a muskrat or similar creature, one should remove half of the water.
One should draw out water during the day, or at night if fire is present; otherwise,
one should do so with water,
and when using it for consumption, one should offer oblations five times into the fire and also feed Brāhmaṇas.
If the lamp goes out at the time of worship, one should perform double the worship.
Having relit the lamp, the Viśvamantra should be recited at least one hundred times.
If it should go out unexpectedly, there is peace; however, this is not the case for a causeless extinction.
One should perform the bathing of Hari with milk for the sake of the non-extinguished lamp,
and the recitation of the root mantra one hundred and eight times;
one should also offer lamps with clarified butter and sesame oil.

One should not perform the application [of medicine] with other oils such as castor oil, nor with those derived from goats, sheep, buffaloes, and the like; nor with fats originating from the limbs of living beings.
If, through negligence, one uses oils produced from fruits for bathing or clarified butter (*havis*) for kindling the fire, [the following applies]. 18.53–54.
In the case of an offering and a fire-sacrifice performed with fats or other censured substances,
once the rite has been carried out, one should bathe [the image] with medium or superior jars.
Likewise, there should be a propitiatory fire-sacrifice, as well as gifts to the twice-born and a meal for them.

O Lotus-seated One, when the offerings beginning with the oblation (havis) and substances such as curd have been prescribed for the bath and other rites, one should perform the expiation (prāyaścitta) as previously described. However, if there is a deficiency in the arrangement of the preliminary services (upacāra), one should compensate with the materials already prepared.
Having further propitiated the Enemy of Madhu with double the usual offerings,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the root-mantra.
In the event of a deficiency in mantra, a deficiency in ritual action, or likewise a deficiency in mudrā—

In the event of the omission of recitation (*japa*), the omission of meditation (*dhyāna*), or any other minor deficiencies, the remedy for him is the recitation of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) according to his capacity. This applies also when there are omissions regarding the singing, instrumental music, and dancing previously ordained for the worship.
Hari is to be propitiated by means of bathing in any inferior case;

however, in the event of the omission of instrumental music, one should offer water, and in the event of the omission of dance, clarified butter. But in the event of the omission of song, one should perform oblations with honey according to the previously mentioned number.

If the previously prepared side-dishes and other offerings are lacking, one should present double the amount of substances after first performing a ritual bath; likewise, even when there is a lapse in the proper time,
the deity is to be propitiated with double the usual articles of enjoyment, saying, "May you forgive me."
Likewise, one should recite [the mantra] even when the twilight prayers have been passed, or during any of the twelve appointed times, even if some portion of the time has been lost. At these times,
one should worship with double the usual materials, increasing them progressively for each subsequent occasion.

Beginning from the first time, one should worship with substances that are doubled, tripled, quadrupled, quintupled, and so forth; likewise, one should perform recitations, fire-offerings, and other rites according to the circumstances.
This procedure has been proclaimed for when the course of the day has passed; however,
if the worship is omitted at the beginning of the two-day period or at the end of the fortnight,
one should bathe [the deity] with water-jars according to the lower or higher path for the sake of his pacification.

If the monthly worship is deficient, one should perform oblations with sesame, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge using the root-vidyā, following either the middling or the superior method. This should be done for up to three years, but if no worship has been performed for more than a month, [the following applies].

The sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) shall take place thereafter; the procedure for re-consecration (pratiṣṭhāvidhi) is now described. Having lifted up the image—even one that was buried underground—for a single day, one should sprinkle it again in the case of a domestic shrine when its worship has been interrupted.
One should perform the ceremonial bathing with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.

For the sake of pacification, one should offer oblations into the fire and also gratify the Brāhmaṇas. O Four-faced One, if worship has been omitted for more than a month up to six months, [one must perform these rites]. 18.71–72.
One should perform a bath with sixteen jars using the Puruṣasūkta;
one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and again offer oblations into the fire for the sake of pacification.
Thereafter, a sprinkling [of water] should be performed until the end of the year.
The rite of consecration (pratiṣṭhā) after one year [is performed] according to the path previously described.
In the consecration of deities such as the Tridaśas, the omission of worship is not a fault;
however, an expiation (prāyaścitta) has been declared for the consecration of those of middling status.
The omission of worship for the Śālagrāma stone and other such objects is not a fault;
likewise, if they are touched by impurity, one should wash them and worship them again. In the event of a total omission, expiation (śānti) should be performed at the time prescribed.
Whether out of ignorance or knowledge, if the offering to the fire is omitted,

one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the five Upaniṣadic mantras. If the lapse of time exceeds one [day], the penance shall be doubled and so forth, according to the duration.
One should bathe the deity with many jars for more than a day;
for up to a month, or beyond that, for up to a year. One should perform the bathing with one hundred and eight jars and then offer oblations once again.
With one thousand and eight oblations of sesame, clarified butter,

and sacrificial porridge, performed in sequence with the twelve-syllable mantra, there shall likewise be a propitiatory fire-offering (śānti-homa). After a year has passed, however, the bathing ceremony shall be either middling or supreme.
Having established the fire in the sacrificial pit, one should offer oblations with sesame, rice, barley, parched grain,
black flowers, sacrificial fuel, cooked rice, and clarified butter,
reciting the root-mantra one thousand and eight times.

Then there is the *śānti*-oblation, as well as gifts and the feeding of Brahmins. (18.83) It is declared that even when the fire exists but no oblation is performed, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be undertaken.
Having kindled the fire by friction once the [existing] fire is extinguished, one should perform the *śānti*-oblation. (18.84)

Having strewn the ground well with kuśa grass using the five upaniṣadic mantras as well as those headed by the vyāhṛtis, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the knowledge of the syllable Om (praṇava).
Likewise, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter while reciting the root mantra.
In the event of a deviation from the prescribed order, an expiation is likewise ordained.
(18.86) In rites performed for specific desires, enclosing-sticks are not required; in obligatory rites, they may or may not be used.
In the absence of sacrificial fuel, the oblation may be made with clarified butter or with cooked rice-offerings. (18.87)
In the absence of those two, or when the fire is defiled by hair and the like, or likewise by contact with the untouchable, an oblation should be performed with seeds or fuel-sticks as prescribed,
using the *vyāhṛtis* one hundred and eight times.
Ten thousand [repetitions] are required upon touching a woman in her menses or similar [impure persons], as well as when touching fire produced by friction;
likewise, when touching a cooking place or a hearth, men should smear the kitchen with cow dung, just as previously described for dogs and other [unclean animals].
Having brought in another fire onto the hearth, one should have the Brahmins recite the *puṇyāha* formula.

In the event of contact with feces, urine, or similar impurities, purification is prescribed as before. When the hearth has been defiled by cooked food, or when the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) has been offered [to an impure source], [purification is required].
One should bathe the deity with nine jars or else with three;
when the worship of the retinue has been interrupted, one should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire, reciting their respective names, eight times for each.

If the sacrificial oblation intended for the offering is spoiled by hair, insects, or other such things, or likewise by untouchable persons, crows, and the like— at the beginning of the two-fold time-periods and so forth— one should abandon that [oblation] and perform that rite with another oblation, provided it is doubled and so on.
If one should offer the oblation with a defiled sacrificial substance through negligence,

then a rite of pacification (śānti-homa) must be performed according to the path prescribed in the scriptures. This applies when rice, boiled rice, or flowers have been collected in the vessel intended for the offering.
If, when that deity has been invoked, there occurs a defect as previously described—
whether the offering substance has fallen, or [the defect occurs] in the primary image (*mūlabera*) or in the self (*ātman*)— then,
having dismissed the deity and brought back another unblemished substance, [one should proceed]. 18.97–98ab.
Having invoked the Lord of Gods into that [liṅga] as before, one should lead it back again.
Thereafter, for the pacification of that fault, one should bathe Hari with curd or milk,
perform a fire-oblation, and likewise recite the root mantra for peace.
When the *bali* image has been cast down during the festival of the vehicle and so forth,
one should place it outside and then carry away the remains of the offering as before.
If it falls to the ground, one should bathe it with nine jars for the sake of pacification.
Through the most base and lowest path, there shall be propitiatory fire-offerings and recitations; likewise,
women devoted to dance and song— whether they be courtesans or others,
or even temple-servants— shall defile the surface of the earth with their menstrual discharges.
Having dug a knee-deep hole in the ground that has been defiled by the dust of a menstruating woman,
and having filled the earth with other soil,
one should smear it with cow-dung and water, and then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.
Sprinkling with the five products of the cow and the application of the *kautuka* [protective cord] should be performed.
One should bathe Hari with water-pots according to the lower or higher path.
An oblation (*homa*) should be offered with sesame, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), each accompanied by the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Thereafter, the fire-oblation for peace (*śāntihoma*) and the recitation (*japa*) should be performed one thousand times;
furthermore, any other part, such as the door-panels and so forth, that has been touched must be washed with water. Their paths should also be purified by sprinkling them with cow-dung and water.
Even when an image has been touched by those such as Brahmins who have become thieves— though they were not authorized [to do so]—
there must be a bath of Hari with water-pitchers on account of that contact with thieves;
this follows the sequence of the castes, beginning from the lowest of the low.
Beginning with these calculations, one should perform the ritual refinements (*saṃskāras*); through these as well, that [result] shall come to pass.
A ceremonial bath (*snapana*) performed with jars consecrated by seed-syllables (*bīja*) shall lead to peace (*śānti*).
There should be a fire-offering for peace (*śāntihoma*), as well as the feeding of Brahmins and the giving of gifts.
If one has unknowingly touched a Jāti [image], one should bathe it with the most excellent of substances.
(18.110) If a three-substance image, an earthen image, a plaster image, a mural painting, or a painted image is touched by Caṇḍālas or others of low status, [it must be purified]. (18.111)
One should perform a renovation, as well as the ritual of sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa),
or an installation (pratiṣṭhā) according to one's wealth, or else because of the abundance of defects.
Upon touching the cloth, having washed it, one should create it again just as before.
If one who has been initiated is touched by those following other scriptures, one should perform a ritual bathing (*snapana*).
Whether by other initiated persons or even by Śūdras, one should act in the same manner.
Upon contact with a perpetrator of a great sin (*mahāpātakin*), the most excellent bathing is required.
In the case of contact with those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin), bathing is required, whether the offender be inferior or superior;
likewise for those addicted to approaching the wives of others and those of irregular conduct.
Upon contact with these nine types of persons, bathing with nine jars of water should take place during the rite of purification (kautuka).

If one touches those who are untouchable, others, or persons such as those born of adultery (kuṇḍa), a bath must be performed as previously prescribed; the same applies when touched by wicked women. Women of the anuloma classes and Śūdra women may enter the lying-in chamber.
One should sprinkle the ground with the five products of the cow or with cow-dung water.
However, if Caṇḍālas, Pulkasas, outcasts, liquor-drinkers,
or dog-cookers enter within the interior of the house, one should discard earthen vessels.
There, having washed the ground inside the door-frame and other areas of the site,
and having smeared it with cow-dung and water, one should cause the twice-born to proclaim an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).
Then the preceptor should bathe the images situated there with ritual jars (*kalaśa*).
The fire-sacrifice for peace, the recitation of mantras, the giving of gifts, and the feeding of the twice-born—
when one enters [the house] while in a state of ritual impurity, the rule is held to be as previously stated.
Even if a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapaca, or those such as the Pulkasa and others [should enter], [the same applies].
If, out of ignorance, those authorized for ritual duties should dwell within the inner sanctum (garbhageha) together with them, or if food or such-like substances are touched,
or if the object of worship (ārādhana) is touched, or if the auspicious thread (kautuka) is touched; 18.122–18.123.
The expiation here is declared with reference to the repetition of the act.
First, one should purify the temple by smearing it with cow dung and other such means;
then, having caused the Brahmins to pronounce an auspicious day, one should feed them there.
Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas should perform their private recitations;
or they should read the Itihāsas and Purāṇas day and night.
And one should cause tawny cows to graze in various places there.
Thus, having considered the gravity or lightness of the defects over periods such as months,
one should satisfy the Brāhmaṇas with wealth once the sanctuary has been purified;
or, the images should be raised up or renovated as appropriate.

Then, one should perform [the rite] as before, or when the signs have been renewed. Having installed it according to the scriptures, one should also establish it with a thousand jars for the removal of faults committed in the past.
Another great festival should be performed, provided there is no destruction of the kingdom or the king;
likewise, one should not move a stone image, nor perform a renovation, in the case of a divine, Ṛṣi-made, or self-manifested image. (18.130) Likewise for a festive image.
Likewise, with others such as those from Māgadha and so forth, who are of inverse birth and despised,
one should bathe the deity with a thousand jars for his pacification;
even when there are beasts of prey such as jackals and the like, or those who are despised such as Caṇḍālas and the like.
If the ground of the enclosure of the sacred abode has been entered by the first [initiate] and others,
one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Likewise, in the case of contact with another person or with the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) and so forth, [the same procedure applies].
Having performed the ritual touching as before, one should carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
If the entire dwelling has been touched by adventitious creatures such as cocks and the like,
one should sprinkle it with water purified by mantras and perform the propitiatory rite.
In this manner, one should bathe the deities in the first enclosure and the others;
the oblation of clarified butter and rice-gruel should be performed with the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
Upon the touch of a firefly, O Lord, one should bathe the deity with nine jars.
If the door is locked during the time of worship when there is no crowd,
the recitation of the root mantra one hundred and eight times is prescribed; however, when there is a crowd, locking the door does not constitute a fault in any case.
Through contact with the light, the pedestal, or the weapon, it is held to be like touching the actual image;
this applies likewise to the teachers, the worshippers, and other attendants.
(18.139) By devotion, they may sit upon the seats and likewise lie down as is appropriate.
If those authorized for the task perform it, no fault shall arise at all.
(18.140) If others should perform it, one should sprinkle the ground with cow-dung and water, as well as the enclosure wall, the pavilion, the temple, the gate-tower, and the kitchen. (18.141)

Once the fire has been extinguished, one should arrange the pavilion and other structures as before; having installed [the deity] according to what was prescribed, one should perform the rite of pacification (śāntikarma).
The ceremonial bathing (snapana), performed according to either the inferior or superior method, shall bring about peace.
A pacificatory fire-offering (śānti-homa) must be performed for the twice-born, along with gifts and a feast; and even when an image has been burnt, having restored it as before,
one should perform a bath with a thousand jars and re-consecrate it according to the rules.
In the case of the burning of garments and so forth, as well as the burning of its [the Sudarśana’s] radiance and so forth,
there shall be a bath with nine jars, followed by fire-oblations and other rites.
When the Sudarśana has been consumed by fire, there must be a bath with nine pitchers.

If the banner, the canopy, the parasol, or the coverings and so forth are burnt, all of these must be produced again, and rites such as the *śānti-homa* (propitiatory oblation) should be performed. If there is an expansion of the space for the temple and other structures on all sides, [the following should be done].
Alternatively, growth in the east or the north is auspicious, but not elsewhere;
if there is growth in the south or the west, the ritual bathing is most excellent of all.
There should be a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) by the best of the twice-born, as well as libations and feeding with meals and other offerings.
An auspicious increase in size on all sides is desired for the *upapīṭha*.
This applies as far as the first enclosure; otherwise, there would be a defect in the divine construction.
If the previously mentioned [dimensions] are increased, the consecration (*snapana*) shall be a bestower of peace.
One should not diminish what was ordained from of old, nor should one alter the sanctum and so forth; the ancient head-pedestal, the sanctum, and the Vaiṣṇava emblem must not be removed,
nor should they be filled in, nor should there be an enlargement of the gate-towers and other structures.

The Guru should first increase the small collection of divine items, such as the celestial palaces and so forth, with wealth; then, with faith, he should bring about the worship using the most excellent materials.
Thus, in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Pādmatantra*, in the *Caryāpāda*.
The eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Expiation in Case of Failure in Daily Worship";
the nineteenth chapter;
and the "Nārāyaṇa-bali" as an expiation for festivals.
If the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya) rites should fall simultaneously,
the teacher, having performed the occasional rite, should perform the obligatory one immediately thereafter. (19.1)

When the ritual bathing of the household deity is to be performed and there is ample space within the house, the bathing should take place right there; however, in the event of a shortage of space, it should be done outside. On a pure location such as a mountain, one should first construct a water-shed (prapā) and then perform the rite.
That bathing of the God of gods must be performed by a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
O Four-faced One, the image installed in the temple should never be taken outside; it must always be bathed while remaining within.
At the time of the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), it should take place on the bank of a river or similar body of water;
otherwise, one should perform a propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*), which bestows all prosperity.
This applies even when the ceremonial bath is performed without the ritual sowing of seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and accompanied by the marriage-thread (*kautuka*).
If the bathing is performed with water-pots when the rite of *adhivāsa* has been omitted,
a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) must be performed to remove all defects. If the intended bathing is abandoned, the bathing ceremony must be performed twice over.
If it is not performed for the king and his kingdom, there will be a depletion of prosperity;
there will be a loss of wealth for the patron, the temple, and the subjects.
However, if the bath is performed at an improper time, such as during the equinoxes and so forth as previously mentioned, [the same result follows].
Peace should be performed at Kāryāyaṇa, and likewise at the commencement in the south;
also in the north and in the west—these are the most excellent and are not subject to fault.
It is the same for the equinox in Caitra, or likewise in Āśvayuja in due order.
And when the jars that have been set out are broken or fall,
or when they are corrupted by defects such as time, or defiled by worms, hair, and the like;
or when they are stepped over, touched by impure things, or defiled by crows and other such creatures.
If [the water] has been touched by censured beings such as beasts of prey, or likewise by impure things,
by heretics, by those of inverse birth, or defiled by a woman in her courses and the like,
one should draw up that specific jar and set down others in its place once more.
One should mutter mantras dedicated to those deities at least one hundred and eight times;

if one performs a ritual bath with them, one should also perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma). If the bath is performed by extracting [the mantras] out of their proper sequence, [the rite remains defective].
The recitation of the five Upaniṣads should be performed as before.

(19.15) If there is an interchange of the deity, the mantra, the location, or the ritual substance, the recitation of the mantra should be performed as previously, even if each substance has not been individually worshipped. (19.16)

Likewise, one should perform the recitation with the *arghya* and other offerings, and then bathe [the deity] again with substances such as milk, using [the fat] derived from buffalo, goat, and camel. O Lotus-seated One, one should offer oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks while reciting the root mantra.

If the bathing has been performed with water that has stood overnight, one should bathe [the deity] again. When there is a deficiency in the components of the ritual service (*ārādhanā*), such as the peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), the recitation of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) one hundred and eight times, and the accompaniment of dance, music, and so forth, [these must be performed].

O Four-faced One, there should be a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*) upon the altar during the ritual bathing (*snapana*) as well as when there is movement; likewise, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) when an image moves. Indeed, while the bathing is taking place, whether there is movement or even falling [of the image], [an expiation must be performed].
Having established [the deity] as before and bathed it according to the ritual rules,
O Four-faced One, a *śānti-homa* sacrifice must be performed in the event of the breaking of the pedestal and so forth, as well as of the innate hands, feet, and other limbs. 19.21–19.22
But in the event of breakage, having invoked Toṣā and Hari residing within her into the *kūrca* grass and other materials, one should complete the ritual.
When [the image] is broken, one should again install the radiance (*prabhā*), the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and so forth,
and perform the sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*) rite as before.
If there should be either an excess or even a deficiency in the substances used for the bathing ritual,
one seeking liberation should always perform the recitation of the root mantra one hundred and eight times, whether at night or by day. 19.24–25.
One seeking the destruction of enemies [should practice] during the day; one seeking the Dharma at midday;
one seeking all enjoyments at the end of the day; and for the sake of expiation, always.
When the image has a protective thread tied around it, the mantra-practitioner should perform the ritual bathing.
Nor is there another *pratisarā* when the interval between ablutions has been reached;
likewise, [the rite is not repeated] when the jar has been touched, stepped over, lost, or replaced by creatures such as frogs, mice, snakes, or shrews. (19.27–19.28)

Having abandoned the other [rite] and performed it in that manner, the Guru should mutter the root mantra. However, if the consecrated jar has been touched by heretics, those born of inverse unions, or others who are in a state of ritual impurity, [the rite must be repeated].
Having removed the jar containing the ritual substances, one should likewise place another there.
Then, having had the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) recited, one should perform the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma).
When the rites such as the ceremonial bathing have commenced, the most excellent preceptor [should proceed].
If one hears of a birth-impurity or death-impurity while engaged in a rite, one does not become pure;
likewise during a festival as prescribed by the scriptures, even if there is a lapse,
O Brahmin, it is then called *śānti* (pacification)— let this be understood.
One should not perform a festival for Hari in a place devoid of a vimāna;
or one may perform it after raising a banner, or the festival in due order.
One should perform the rite of pacification according to the rules in the northwest or the southeast corner.

The flagstaff should remain in that very place until the end of the year, following the hoisting of the flag in a temple where the daily festivals have been neglected. One should not perform optional (kāmya) festivals; if one has performed them, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti).
If the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) on the banner is deficient in the prescribed measurements, or if the bannerpole and so forth are likewise deficient,

or if it has been defiled by mice and other pests, or if it has come into contact with impure substances, one should perform a rite of pacification (śānti). Having removed it, one should install another banner.
A pacifying oblation (śāntihoma) must be performed, as well as a feeding of Brahmins.
As part of the rite for hoisting the banner, one should either the banner or the staff itself;
once it has been employed, it must be discarded, and the banner-pole should be abandoned.

If a pillar or similar object that has already been consecrated once is employed again, there shall be no penance in that case; however, an excellent and most superior ritual bathing must be performed, as well as a peace-offering (śānti-homa) and the feeding of Brahmins. || 19.39-19.40 ||

When the banner of Vihageśāna has been erected, there shall be no fault if its color fades due to wind, heat, and so forth; rather, it is held that worship should continue. Even if it should fall by the force of the wind or by any other cause, [the same applies].

Having lifted [the image] and bound it again, there is once more the ritual bathing; this is the middling or inferior procedure. Likewise, in the event of a loss of color, or when the banner is deficient, or even if the banner is broken somewhere, one should produce another banner after discarding the fallen banner.
Or one should arrange another suitable staff, but one must not wait for the [proper] time.
If, through negligence, one should fasten the banner-cloth in a contrary manner,
then having released it or having fastened another, one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana).
If the flagstaff has fallen, or is broken, or even if it is hollow,
one should install another pillar and perform a propitiatory rite preceded by a ritual bath.
This applies also in the event of its falling, or swaying, or if it falls accidentally.
The pacification oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed as before, and likewise the recitation of the root mantra.
If the jar presided over by the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is broken or lost,
or if it has been touched by the hands of those who are unfit to touch it, another jar must be established once again.
Having invoked the bird there, one should complete the remainder of the ritual.
If the flagstaff is touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) or other despised persons,
another staff should be installed and one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).
If the flagstaff is touched by those born of birth-impurity (sūtaka), by those born of death-impurity (pretaka), or by such persons of inverse caste (pratiloma),
one should sprinkle it while preceded by the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha).
Having discarded the earthen vessels and other items once they have been employed, [one should proceed].
If [the sprouts] do not appear, one should perform the pacifying homa and other rites.
Even if the sprouts are reddish or dark-colored, or if they all fail to grow, or if they grow horizontally, [one should likewise perform the rites]. (19.51–19.52)
Furthermore, if they touch something untouchable, or if their vessels and such are broken or cut,
or if they are lost or fallen in any manner;
or if anthills grow upon them, or if they are eaten by mice and other such creatures.
A peace-offering (śānti-homa) must be performed, as well as the feeding of Brahmins.
If, in the midst of the commenced rite, another occasional rite (naimittika-karma) should occur,
the preceptor should perform it again and offer half of those [same] sprouts.
If, by chance, through divine or human agency, there should be a failure of the ritual when the seedlings have been offered,
then one should abandon even those prepared seedlings and offer oblations into the fire for the sake of pacification, as well as perform the recitation of the root mantra.
If another rite for the sake of ritual action should fall between while the image has its protective thread bound,
one should bind the *kautuka* again.
If it falls during the interval, once the bath is completed, the consecration (*snapana*) is performed once more.
O Four-faced One, that which was previously commenced should be performed according to the scriptures;
however, in empty villages and such places, there shall be no bali offering nor a street festival (vīthikotsava).
If there were to be a street festival, it should take place only within the temple precincts as desired.
A bath with a thousand jars is prescribed as the expiation for that.

(19.60) If, while the festival is underway, there should be a great wind or similar disturbance, and the village or other site becomes disordered, one should perform the expiation and hold the festival again. (19.61)

The work must not be abandoned; however, if it is abandoned, one should perform a ceremonial bath with one hundred and eight jars, as well as fire oblations, recitation, offerings, and the honoring of the twice-born.
Even for all ritual acts performed during the sequence beginning with a muhūrta, there is a rite of pacification (śānti).

Afterwards, the commencement of the ritual acts should be performed with burnt offerings (homa) and other rites, as previously described. When the officiant or the image-makers have first been authorized for the rite— for a specific purpose, whether for a deity or a human— among those who are duly qualified for the prescribed duties.
The rite that has been commenced must be performed by other such twice-born men when a festival is obstructed by fate or by human agency, as previously described.
One should simply cast the sacrificial offering (bali) upon a wall, at the entrance of the village, or even along the pathways.
When the offering of bali has been commenced on a certain day,
if one should perform the bali after it has been passed over, one should perform the bali in this manner;
even if the constituent parts of the festival have been omitted, they should be arranged as before.
In the case of activities such as visiting gardens, going on excursions, hunting, or entering water reservoirs,

a propitiatory rite (śānti) should be performed, as well as feeding Brahmins and the recitation of prayers (japa). If a pilgrimage to a sacred site is unsuccessful, one should perform the festival again.
Having first performed the ritual bathing by means of the most excellent path,
when the prescribed month has passed and the asterism and other factors have arisen as stated, or even if it should occur before the end of the year following the festival; || 19.69–19.70 ||
If one performs [the rite] after a year has passed, one should proceed by performing a propitiatory rite (śānti).

There should be a bath with a thousand jars, a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), recitation (japa), and so forth. When a festival or sacred occasion (parva) is omitted, there is a propitiatory rite and a ceremonial bath according to one's capacity.
When other festivals of Viṣṇu, such as Śravaṇa and others, have been omitted,
the expiation for that is a ritual bath (snapana) performed according to the most excellent method.
If there is a transposition of the sacrificial offerings (balivastūni), one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter.
When an image has been affected by wind, heat, and so forth, one should perform the supreme ritual bathing;

this should be carried out in the sacrificial hall, at water-stations, or during a great festival. In the case of images damaged by fire, having restored everything to its former state, [one should proceed as before].
For the foremost of the twice-born, one should perform a peace-offering (*śānti-homa*), as well as a meal and a gift.
When there is a burning of the Sudarśana [disc], an immersion with nine jars should be performed;
likewise, when the image (*bimba*) or other parts are consumed by fire, one should carry out the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
If dogs, jackals, or similar creatures enter the sacrificial pavilion or other areas,
or if they touch anything there, one should discard the previously prepared items and place others in their stead;
then, a propitiatory oblation (*śānti-homa*) should be performed by the foremost of the twice-born, and the feeding of them and other rites should proceed as before.
If a Caṇḍāla or the like should enter, one should abandon that defiled object.
(19.78) One should perform a propitiatory fire-offering for objects intended for a festival;
when the festival fire itself has been extinguished, one should perform the propitiation in the proper sequence. (19.79)
During the equinoxes and the solstices, a pilgrimage to a sacred site (tīrthayātrā) does not incur any fault;

even at night, it may be undertaken on occasions other than those. If, however, the pilgrimage should take place due to negligence, the ritual bathing (snapana) must be performed as the most excellent of the excellent.
During a festival, if the fire-oblation (homa) is interrupted, one should perform double the number of oblations.
If the image is lost to thieves or other causes while a great festival is underway,
one should produce a new image as before for the rites of worship and so forth.
When the image has fallen during the great festival of the procession, one should propitiate it;
then, having placed the image back upon the vehicle as before, one should lead it around the streets.
Furthermore, for the sake of pacification, one should bathe it again with eighty-one jars.
In the event of the loss of a limb of the image, one should likewise replace it with another.
If the image is missing a limb, one should perform a sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa) immediately after restoring it;
for the sake of pacification, one should perform a ceremonial bath (snapana) and satisfy the Brāhmaṇas.

In the event of a vehicle breakdown, O Lord, one should lead the deity to the main road by means of another vehicle; furthermore, rites for pacification must be performed for the charioteer in the event of a fall, a stumble, or similar mishaps.
O Lotus-seated One, ceremonies such as the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) should also be performed.
If those who are untouchable should carry the vehicles or even the image itself,
one must wash the vehicles and bathe the image with jars of water.
A flower sacrifice should be performed at night for the sake of pacification or for the attainment of enjoyment.
In the absence of a flower sacrifice, the ceremonial bathing (snapana) is the most excellent rite;
it should be performed for up to five days starting from the day of the Tīrtha festival.
If the descent of the banner (dhvajāvarohaṇa) is to take place later, it should be done afterwards.
There may be a defect; the bathing that pacifies defects is middling or superior.
(19.90) Having lowered the banner-cloth after the bathing, and having dismissed all the deities from the cart by means of the bali-offering, (19.91)
A rite designated as *vaiśeṣika*, which has fallen within the midst of a great festival, must certainly be performed and not omitted; if it is omitted, one should perform the ritual bath (*snāpana*).
Regarding the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*), another expiation is observed.
In a vessel that is either inferior or pure, or in a *kuṇḍa*, a mandala, or similar site,

one should recite the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) a hundred times and worship the weapon-increaser (*astravardhana*). Having discarded the sacred thread (*pavitra*) if it is defiled by hair or other impurities, one should perform it once again.
Having performed [the rites] as before and having placed [the deity], one should then perform the rite of pacification (*śānti*).
If the water-pot (*kumbha*) has been touched by an untouchable, or if it is broken or lost,
one should again invoke [the deity] into another pot and recite the root mantra.
If a trident has been placed in the wrong location, or an image and so forth have been installed elsewhere,
one should install them in their proper place and then perform the ritual bathing and other rites.
Even if the measurements of the altar and other features have been conceived as either too small or too large, [one should correct them].
A hundred oblations for peace should be performed with the five Upaniṣads;
in their absence, one should likewise perform the rite of peace and the opening of the eyes.
If one performs the opening of the eyes without first performing the rite of peace during the installation, [it is improper].
If the consecration of the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) is performed without the preliminary water-soaking (*toyādhivāsa*), the bathing,

the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*), and likewise the [other] ancillary rites must be repeated in case of such omissions. Furthermore, if the consecration was not performed by a preceptor (*ācārya*), one should perform the re-consecration.
One who has ascended to the rank of an Ācārya, even if possessing some slight defect due to deficiency,

remains indeed qualified provided he himself has reached the further shore of knowledge. When the Lord of Gods, whose form is consciousness, is installed by one superior in knowledge, [the rite is perfected].

Indeed, the fire of knowledge burns away all defects; there is no fault in this. (19.102) For as long as the stay in the house of the child was previously requested, once that period has passed, there is the ceremonial bath of the enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu). (19.103)
Furthermore, one should determine the duration of its stay in that very place;
or else it may be in the house of a child, or in the root-abode (mūlālaya).
Having placed it upon the pedestal for ritual purposes (karmārthapīṭhikā), one should perform the rites.
Whether at a city gate, a stable, a rampart, or a pavilion,

[one should act] where loose earth, honeybees, bottle-gourds, anthills, or similar things have arisen; having removed those [defects] and purified that spot, one should restore it to its former state.
One should perform the bathing (*snapana*) of the God of gods in the highest or middling manner;
likewise, there is the fire-oblation for peace (*śānti-homa*), the feeding of the best of the twice-born, and indeed the giving of gifts.
When a confusion of the *siddhāntas* has arisen through negligence, and when such a confusion exists therein—
"There would be fault in plowing and such activities, bringing about the destruction of the king and the kingdom.
Brahmā said: "O Janārdana, what is that which is called the Siddhānta, and what is its distinction?"
"I wish to hear all of that, provided this is not a secret. The Blessed One [replied]:
"It is the Great Upaniṣad, designated by the term 'the state of the perfected doctrine' (siddhānta-pada)."
Those wise ones who have attained mastery in the Mīmāṃsā and other such treatises possess the qualification for this [work] at its conclusion; thus it is designated as the Siddhānta.
That scripture exists in four parts, and like the Ṛgveda and others, it is manifold.
Each individual tantra is further divided extensively by way of various branches:
the first is the Mantrasiddhānta, the second is called Āgama,
the third is Tantrasiddhānta, and the fourth is Tantrāntara.
Only one form is to be worshipped as the primary object; furthermore,
the other goddesses, such as Śrī and the rest, are also to be fully honored as part of the retinue,
along with the weapons such as the conch and discus, and the ornaments such as the Śrīvatsa mark.
Where the Lotus-Seated One is described as being either surrounded by [deities] in embodied form or alone,
that is declared the foremost system of Mantra-siddhānta. Furthermore,
the fourfold manifestations (vyūhas), such as Vāsudeva and the others, are [described] there for practitioners as well.

Those who belong to the same rank as those descended through lineage are to be honored when their origins are undecaying. Furthermore, O Lotus-Seated One, in that scripture where even the renunciation of actions is taught, the established doctrine of that scripture is what has been declared therein.
