Wherein the preeminence of even the nine forms is declared;
the twelve limbs are those very forms, and others likewise;
there are also other groups of manifestations, which are qualities of the various forms.
Accompanied by various manifestations, along with the deities of the directions and their weapons,
and clearly with the goddesses in embodied form such as Lakṣmī and others—
this is the fourth supreme invocation according to the established tenets of that system.
O Four-faced One, a single form—abounding in gentle lions and other [emblems], or distinguished by various types of faces such as two or three—is worshipped;
whether surrounded by a retinue or alone, it grants all desires. (19.121)
O Four-faced One, that which is known as another tantra is the fourth;
by whichever path of the Siddhānta the rites of ploughing and so forth were performed at the outset, by that very same path everything [should be done], and not by the way of any other Siddhānta.
Even according to a tantra, whatever [rite] such as plowing and so forth was performed by one person,
that same person alone should perform the entire task, not by way of another tantra.
Indeed, even in another tantra, what has been stated or what has not been stated must certainly be adopted.
There would be no confusion of established tenets, nor indeed any confusion of the Tantras.
When a confusion of established doctrines arises through negligence, it leads to harm for the king, the kingdom, and the imperishable abode; therefore, for its pacification,
one should first perform a ritual sprinkling followed by an immersion in a thousand jars.
It should be performed; one should carry out the ritual bathing when there is a possibility of a confusion of tantras.

One should perform a great festival preceded by the hoisting of the flag; when the deity has been installed, [the rite] takes five nights, or otherwise six paths. If hostility is committed toward the beginning of the installation, the fault consists in the destruction of everything.
Furthermore, his peace shall be secured by the path prescribed in the *Pañcarātra*:
the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of Hari with a thousand jars,
followed by a great festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner.
O Four-faced One, an excellent twice-born who has been initiated into one Tantra or Siddhānta should not perform rituals elsewhere, such as agricultural labor and the like;
nor should he assume the office of an Ācārya, officiate as a priest, or engage in the worship of the Enemy of Madhu [Viṣṇu] in another tradition.

Furthermore, it is not tenable [to claim that] atonement for sins such as the killing of a Brahmin— as enjoined by the Smṛtis— is possible through the various Tantras or even through the various Siddhāntas,
[especially] for those who have died by means of violent acts such as poison, weapons, or fire. || 19.132–19.133 ||
The supreme propitiation known as the Nārāyaṇabali is the cause for [attaining] the goal;
without it, no other means to that goal exists.
Furthermore, beginning with cremation, one should perform the Smārta rites in their entirety.
Having performed the rites up to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, immediately thereafter,
one should worship the God of gods according to the method to be described,
either in a temple of Viṣṇu, on a riverbank, on a mountain, or even in a forest.
Or else, in another meritorious place or in the auspicious abode of the performer,
one should sacrifice on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight during the two solstices.
Having fasted on the preceding day, the performer should remain with a restrained mind.
Having invited Brahmins who are devotees of the Blessed One and distinguished by their vows and Vedic study, and having understood [the ritual] through the mantras just as Keśava himself would,
one should purify the ground upon a mat of *kuśa* grass with water mixed with cow dung.
Having seated those who have been chosen facing east, O Lotus-seated One,

and having honored them with the arghya and other offerings while reciting the names beginning with Keśava and ending with "namas," one should give betel leaves and the like and anoint the twice-born.
Having performed the oblation in the domestic fire (aupāsana) in the presence of those who have bathed,

and having performed the "mouth of the fire" rite for Agni, one should, if one wishes, invoke the Deity upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), upon a lotus-diagram of the discus (cakrapaṅkaja), or upon a bundle of kuśa grass (kuśakūrca) in the eastern part of the fire-altar.
Having risen with a handful of flowers and reciting the *Nṛsūkta* and other verses,
he should worship Puruṣottama with the *Vyāhṛtis* preceded by *Oṃ*,
followed immediately by the various forms beginning with Keśava, using their respective names.
Having invoked [the deities] and performed worship individually with the six services beginning with the *arghya* offering,
and having gratified Keśava and the others with water and sesame seeds while reciting their respective names, one should worship Puruṣa by means of the Puruṣa-verse, ending with the lamp offering.

Having meditated upon the Supreme Person seated on a lotus throne in the fire, one should, O Lotus-born One, begin with the *pāyasa* offering by reciting the hymn (*sūkta*) according to the sequence of the names beginning with Keśava,
starting with the verse "viṣṇor nukam. (19.146)
Thereafter, one should offer the oblation with the *yājyā* verse beginning "paro mātrayā" (19.147).
Then, remaining absorbed in meditation, one should offer clarified butter (*sarpiṣā*) while reciting the twelve names beginning with Keśava, in the dative case and ending with "namaḥ" (19.148).
One should offer food mixed with milk, clarified butter, and molasses to those very [deities].
The offering to Mahāviṣṇu is performed with the mantra "devasya tvā savituḥ.
Furthermore, one should perform oblations in the fire with clarified butter while reciting the seven vyāhṛtis.
Having seated those Brahmins upon seats of *darbha* grass that had been brought for them,
he honored them according to his ability with garments, finger-rings, umbrellas, earrings, sandals, and other gifts, while reciting the eight-syllable mantra.
Having first obtained their permission, one should offer oblations into the fire with an offering mixed with sesame seeds and clarified butter, using the *vidyā* that will be described hereafter:
"To the fathers, to their fathers, and again to their fathers. (19.152)
To the mothers, to the paternal grandmothers, and likewise to their fathers;
to the maternal grandfathers, and to those who are their fathers;
to the maternal grandmothers, and to the paternal grandmothers of one's mother.
To his father, and to his paternal grandmothers, and likewise to his teachers;
to their wives, to his gurus, and to the wives of his gurus;
to his friends, to their wives, to his kinsmen, and to those women who are theirs.
Having uttered "and to them," he should say "svadhā namaḥ" (svadhā, obeisance) to those [deceased] ministers, all their wives, and whatever women [belonged to them];
and for each one separately, he should offer an individual oblation with the formula "svāhā to Nārāyaṇa."
The word *agni* ending in the dative case, followed by *kavyavāhana*,
and at its end the word *sviṣṭakṛt* with the same suffix as before;
having thus offered oblations of clarified butter, one should afterwards [offer] with the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Likewise, with the eight-syllable vidyā, one hundred and eight [offerings] for each;
similarly, one should feed Brahmins with food containing the six flavors,
give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and, having bowed to them, perform a circumambulation.

Having obtained permission from those remaining, saying, "Let the food be prepared as desired," he should spread *darbha* grass with the tips pointing eastward upon a purified spot to the south of the fire. Then,
being composed, he should offer the *bali* offering upon those *darbha* blades.
And immediately thereafter, [he offers] to all the gods and the Sādhyas;
likewise to all the gods, to Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa,
and to the thousand-headed one, as well as to the station of the Self of Sacrifice (Yajñātman).

Having pronounced "Puruṣa," "Yajñapūrva," and likewise "Sarveśvarapada" in the dative case, followed immediately by "namaḥ" and "svāhā," one should apply this suffix everywhere, as well as the sacrifice to Sviṣṭakṛt and other rites.
Having performed the rites up to the gift of a cow and a boon, he should announce the deceased:
"I announce this one, named Yajñaśarman, to the god Keśava," [offering him] in turn into the twelve images. (19.165–166)
Having thus offered [the oblation] to the twelve, one should then present the supreme food (paramānna).
This is indeed declared to be the Nārāyaṇa-bali for the twice-born.
Thus, for whomsoever this Bali, consisting of the worship of the gods, has been performed and given.

Having shaken off all evil, he goes to the eternal Brahman. Whether they be other sinners or even those who perform meritorious deeds, this sacrifice leads to the attainment of the state of the Supreme Self; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Nārāyaṇa Bali for Expiation during Festivals," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[The twentieth chapter begins.]
The ritual for Hiraṇyagarbha and others [is performed by] Brahmā, the king, or his minister, whoever is established in the burden of sovereignty.
O Blessed One, they are constantly vigilant and ever-exerting themselves in the protection of their subjects.

Yet they are overwhelmed by despicable sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, and are engaged in terrible deeds prescribed by the scriptures that consist essentially of bodily affliction. || 20.1-20.2 ||
Being unable to apply themselves to the means for the removal of evil,
how could they— having shaken off all those evils—
become once again qualified for ritual action and esteemed in the assembly of the virtuous? (20.3)

They are capable of meditating upon the Blessed One and also in the ritual of his worship. O Lord, tell me truly that method which is the supreme means for removing sins such as the killing of a Brahmin.
"O Four-faced One, for those kings who are unable to perform actions consisting of bodily mortification, an easy penance has been ordained. (20.6)
One rite is proclaimed by the name Hiraṇyagarbha, and another is known as Tulābhāra; by these two, their impurities are shaken off,
and they become further qualified for the performance of the meditation on and worship of the Blessed Lord.
Then the two types of ritual action are described in their entirety.
Having resolved to perform the rite, one should first choose a preceptor who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures and has reached the further shore of the mantras. || 20.8–20.9 ||
Having diligently examined a twice-born Bhāgavata who is compassionate toward all beings, free from anger, devoid of greed, knowledgeable in the performance of the two types of rites, and upright,
the king approached him.
Having requested the best of the twice-born according to the rule and having honored him, he should,
being self-restrained, begin meritorious rites at the proper place and time during the six months beginning with Taiṣya, or under the asterisms Śravaṇa or Citrā.
O Brahmin, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Āśvayuja, under the asterism Rohiṇī or even Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā),
or under Puṣya, or under the auspicious asterisms of the three Uttaras;
in a region, on the banks of rivers, or on the shores of the ocean— 20.14.
Alternatively, in a place endowed with all auspicious qualities, such as a temple of the Blessed One,
if this rite is occasional (naimittika), there is no need to examine the time and other factors. First, one should construct a pavilion if the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is to take place in a temple.
Or else, in another place as specified, according to the path taught in the scriptures,
one should first offer sprouts on any one of the days previously mentioned, in a location adorned with all ornaments and containing an inner altar constructed within.

O Four-faced One, having gathered the necessary materials there according to one's wealth and according to the prescribed rule, two golden skull-cups (kapāla) should be fashioned— one for the lower part and one for the upper— each being equal in thickness to a single finger-breadth.

Having entered together, they remain within the womb like two eggs joined together. The Creator, having fashioned that blissful state in the form of a dual egg known as Hiraṇyagarbha, it is there that this [being] is born again.

The king should have all the sacrificial vessels made of gold alone. When all the necessary materials have been gathered, on the day before [the ceremony], the monarch, being pure and having restrained himself, should have his hair, beard, and nails clipped.
Pure-toothed and wearing clean garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents;
having fasted and consumed clarified butter, he should spend the night devoted to his observances. Having passed the night, on the following day at dawn, he should bathe with a restrained mind.
Instructed by his preceptor, he himself should have the ritual performed by the officiating priests.
Having placed a golden image upon a seat made of nine loads of rice in the center of the altar,
and having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, he should install it there.
When the skull-bowl is placed below and the archway and other ornaments are worshipped above,
and once the auspicious dances, songs, and instrumental music have been performed as before,
one should place vessels filled with water in the four directions around Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having placed four jars upon grain-seats,
and having set gems within those jars which were wrapped in new cloths,
[he should worship] the four deities in sequence by their respective names.
The True Person (Puruṣa) is to be invoked in the east and likewise in the south;
Acyuta and Ananta are to be invoked in the west and in the north.
Having thus proclaimed them, one should offer the guest-water (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, ending with incense and lamps.
One should also offer four kinds of food into each of the jars,
in the directions starting from the east, following the same sequence as in the ritual of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Having prepared the fires in the sacrificial pits, one should offer oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks and clarified butter in due order.

The Guru should offer one hundred and eight oblations for each [deity] with the root mantra. Then, having meditated upon the deity to be worshipped, he should perform sixteen oblations for each of the four kinds of food while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
When the auspicious moment arrived, the Guru himself, having obtained the permission of the Brahmins,
took the king by the hand with his own hand according to the sequence of dissolution; he then withdrew the body of the protector of the earth until only the physical frame remained.
Having meditated thus, O Lotus-seated One, one should cause [the image] to enter the womb;
and the Lord of the Earth, seated comfortably upon the lower golden portion,
should be covered by the upper portion— this is the method of entry.

The Guru should perform the oblation of the withdrawal of the principles (*tattvasaṃhāra*) with sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter; then, having again contemplated [the process] by way of the generation of the principles,
he should touch the body of the king and perform the oblation of emanation (*sṛṣṭihoma*) as before.

O Four-faced One, one should perform [the rites] in all four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). Having brought forth from that pit the king of the earth who has been born according to the mantra, and having placed him upon a tiger skin, one should consecrate him with the water-pots (kalaśas).

By means of the supreme or inferior path, the best of mantra-knowers [performs] that very same mantra-bath and such a collection of substances as for a deity. By this rite, his impurities are shaken off, and he becomes the most excellent of merit-makers.

Having been born through the grace of his guru, he should honor the guru in his presence. O King, the sacrificial fee for all the officiating priests is considered to be one thousand niṣkas of refined gold; such is the prescribed dakṣiṇā.
The king should provide all the necessary materials for the ritual;
he should cause a golden mandala to be given to learned Brāhmaṇas.
For one who has acted thus in the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites—
Thus, for one who performs the rite twice, eligibility is attained.
And the fruit of Viṣṇu—consisting of sālokya, sārūpya, and sāyujya—is threefold.
Now, the second rite, called Tulābhāra, is described.
Having constructed a pavilion as before, one should erect in its center two firm pillars made of sacrificial wood, six cubits in height,
two cubits in circumference, well-rounded, and fashioned by a skilled craftsman.

Two [posts] were firmly established on the ground with an interval of two cubits between them. Upon those two, a single superior beam of solid wood was placed, one cubit in width, of the same measurement in length, and firm in its thickness.
The beam of the balance should be three cubits long and made of iron;
one should attach it to the north with an iron hook.
Having thus prepared the balance, the other materials and requisites should be arranged as before.
Having performed the ritual as before, including the subsequent rites for the teacher,
he should carry out the entire procedure up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa) without omission, as appropriate.
Then the king, having bathed and being adorned with silken garments and ornaments, [should proceed].
Pure, meditating upon Vāsudeva who likewise holds a shield and a sword,
and having circumambulated and paid homage to those deities beginning with Puruṣa,
he should likewise place the balance on its western side.
Having stood and turned his face toward the east, he should ascend to the western jar.
Reciting the auspicious hymn beginning with the verse "Svastidā," he should deposit the finest gold, equal in weight to the king, into the eastern jar.
While dances, instrumental music, and songs proceeded in the four directions,
and while the Brahmins were likewise reciting the four Vedas,
the king himself attended to the fire-pits where the rites for peace were being performed.
Having sat for some time meditating upon Hari made of gold upon the surface of the pitcher,
and having been previously authorized by his preceptor,
the king should then descend from the pitcher and [take off] his gold and ornaments.
Then, having divided [the wealth] appropriately, one should distribute it among the Brahmins;
one hundred *niṣkas* to the preceptor (*ācārya*), and the same amount to the image-makers (*mūrtipa*).
To all those who were employed as assistants in that ritual, [one should give] accordingly.
Having observed their respective deeds, he should bestow [the rewards] upon them accordingly.
By performing such work as the *tulā* and *bhāra*, the lord of the earth—
or any other wealthy person— shall be liberated from all sins.
Having passed away, he enjoys desired pleasures in heaven like a god;
performing such actions repeatedly, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
This action dispels evil and brings happiness in the next world.
It increases longevity, pacifies all diseases, and is supreme;
it brings about prosperity, causes the increase of fame, and grants all desires.
O Four-faced One, this other rite is endowed with a golden womb.
Listen to the eternal secret called the Puṣyābhiṣecana,
ordained for the lords of the earth and practiced even by Indra and the other gods;
it is to be performed in the month of Taiṣya, in the month of Proṣṭhapada, or in the auspicious month of Āśvayuja.
Then the preceptor should commence the rite of the great consecration (mahābhiṣecana) under the asterism of Śravaṇa, or the asterism of birth, or that of the patron himself;
in one of the previously mentioned locations, whichever is most honored.
Having made the ground five cubits long and circular in shape,
having properly prepared its interior space to a height of one cubit, O Four-faced One, and having installed the archways and other features in the four directions; 20.66.
Having decorated it as before with a canopy, banners, and garlands,
one should fashion Mount Meru in its center, shaped like a mṛdaṅga drum;
it should be made of smooth clay and the like, and its height should be three cubits.
At both the base and the top, the width shall likewise be one cubit;
and in the four directions, its four sections should be arranged in due order as white,
reddish-brown, yellow, and black on all sides.

Likewise, the six mountain ranges of the world-system (kulaparvatas) are to be adorned with jewels and gold; they extend from east to west. Immediately following [the central range] are Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Nīla, and the mountain Śveta.
And their supporting pillar, Śataśṛṅga, should be sixteen finger-breadths [in height].
One should decorate them in sequence with colors made from metallic powders and dusts: white, tawny, red, blue, and with a luster like that of the moon; and golden-colored. 20.72
Having thus drawn Jambūdvīpa surrounded by the salt ocean,
one should draw Plakṣadvīpa in the cardinal directions, encircled by the sea;
then the island marked by Śālmalī, surrounded by waters of sweet flavor.
Having drawn in sequence for all [the continents] Kuśa surrounded by libations, Krauñca rich in curd,
Śāka cast into an ocean of milk, and Puṣkara an ocean of clear water,
as well as the great mountain Lokāloka.
One should conceive of Arāvatī, the city of Indra belonging to the east, like a rampart;
likewise, one should conceive of Saṃyamanī, the city of Yama,
in the south, and similarly Varuṇa’s city in the west.
One should fashion the city of Soma in the northern direction, facing the night;
one should likewise arrange the stations for Indra and the other world-protectors in their respective places.
Having invoked them there upon a sandy altar, one should worship them.

And upon the summit of that Mahāmeru, one should worship the form of Vārāhī. On the northern side of Meru, having dug a pit according to the prescribed measure, one should place a golden skull-bowl at the bottom and worship there.
Furthermore, having placed the upper skull-cup upon it in due order,
the officiating priest himself, remaining composed, [should place] sixteen golden jars filled with sixteen *prastha*s according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having placed them all around the eggshell, wrapped in thread, cloth, and so forth,
and having set them upon a heap of grain with their lids closed and adorned, he,
being pure and composed, performed the binding of the *kautuka* amulet.
Having entered there, he himself should face the east within that golden pavilion;
having entered, he should sit meditating upon the Lord of Gods,
who is like the moon, the embodiment of sacrifice, and who supports the Goddess Earth with his own tusk.
While the king is thus seated in meditation, the officiant himself,
with the permission of the preceptor, should perform the consecration using the prepared jars,
while the knower of mantras recites the mantras over the substances such as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is performed with the *vasoḥ pavitra* mantra;
the bath with milk is performed with the *śaṃ no devīḥ* mantra, and the sprinkling with curd follows.
Then, the bath with ghee is performed with the *iṣe tvā* mantra, and likewise again with the *agna āyāhi* mantra.
Reciting "Agnim īle," he [should sprinkle] with honey; reciting "Mā nas toke," with water infused with yellow sandalwood; likewise, with water containing unbroken grains (akṣata);
and reciting "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," with water mixed with powdered saffron.
With the mantra "ahārṣam" and likewise with camphor water,
he should then bathe the lord of the earth with gem-infused water while reciting the Gāyatrī;
and having uttered the hymn "catvāri śṛṅgā," he should bathe him with water containing all kinds of fruits.

Having recited the mantra beginning with "sarvaṃ rājānam," the knower of mantras should perform a bath with water containing all kinds of grain using the *vidyā* "śatam anviti," and a bath with the waters of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) using the *vidyā* "āpo hi ṣṭhā."

Having recited the *taratsamandī* hymn, the king underwent the consecration with all kinds of perfumes. Having emerged from the womb, he was sprinkled with auspicious water; wearing pure garments, purified, having sipped water for ritual purification, and having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, O Four-faced One, having divided the golden egg, one should bestow it upon the preceptor according to one's wealth in an elaborate manner, and likewise give it to the Brahmins;
or else, one may give all of it to Viṣṇu, or half, or even a quarter.
"Through the repeated performance of the consecration, liberation is held in the palm of one's hand.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Hiraṇyagarbha and Others," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Chapter Twenty-One: The Rule for the Classification of Authorities Regarding the Different Siddhāntas and Pañcarātras. Brahmā.
The distinction between the four Siddhāntas has been heard from the mouth of the Blessed One.
Now I wish to hear the established rule regarding those who are qualified [for them]. (21.1) Śrī Bhagavān:

O Lotus-seated One, once all the brahmins have been born from my mouth— belonging to various lineages and clans, and devoted to various duties— I shall declare their rules to you according to the scriptures.
Among them were eight thousand highly fortunate sages,
headed by Aupagāyana; belonging to various lineages, they were seekers of liberation and were studying the Kaṇva recension as well as that called Mādhyandina.
The realization that yields liberation as its sole fruit arose within them.
Having all come together, they spoke to the imperishable Brahmā:
"O Brahmā, we are seeking liberation; we desire to know the means to liberation."
"O Four-faced One, we have come here to you for refuge, desiring to conquer birth and death— those foremost among the Aupagāyanas who have approached you. To them,
as they were speaking thus, he called out, desiring to bestow his grace upon them.
Having initiated them according to the rules along the paths taught in the *Pañcarātra* and by way of the *Mantrasiddhānta*, within the mandala of the lotus-circle,
Brahmā commanded those who had been summoned and initiated as follows: "This must be done."
"Study both the Kāṇvī and Mādhyandinī recensions of the Veda, which are contained within the branches; study those two root-branches and the purificatory rites beginning with the *niṣeka*;
and perform the rituals such as the Soma sacrifice according to those two alone."
Accompanied by meditation on the Blessed One and consisting of His propitiation,
that which is declared in the Vedas as something to be performed is thus devoid of [worldly] fruit.
For those who perform action with the thought "it must be done," the supreme goal is ultimate liberation (niḥśreyasa).
"By means of this path of the mantra-siddhānta, that which is to be attained shall be reached by you.
From this day forward, the worship of the Lord must be performed according to the scriptures at the five appointed times, whether in the home or in the temple, and not otherwise."
"O Four-faced One, you have become Bhāgavatas through the worship of the Blessed One and by practicing devotion to the Blessed One; being thus born into the lineage,
you are Bhāgavatas by name, having been initiated according to the prescribed rite."
"Performing the actions as they have been described, they attain the supreme state.
Study also those purifying mantras found in other branches which were revealed by the supreme seers; with those mantras, worship Adhokṣaja."
The worship of Viṣṇu for one's own sake brings about prosperity;
likewise, the worship for the sake of others— whether in a village, a town, a city,
in one's own home, or in an independent sanctuary— should be performed by men devoted to the Lord.
It brings about the supreme good for both oneself and others.

(21.18) However, among men who do not belong to a lineage of Vaiṣṇavas, even if they are initiated, their performance of sacrifice is solely for their own sake and never for the sake of others. (21.19)
O best of Brahmins, performing sacrifices for the sake of others is censured for them;
even one who is not born of a lineage of devotees may perform sacrifice for others if he has been initiated according to the path of the scriptures and acts by the command of a devotee.
Govinda himself is remembered as the manifest Bhāgavata.
Upon seeing him— even if he is devoid of learning, a doer of evil deeds,
or lacking in virtues— one should rise to greet him with palms joined in reverence.
The Soul of the Universe entreated those great seers of immeasurable power:
"In this world of mortals, the worship of the Blessed One must be performed by you;
whether for your own sake or for the sake of others, it must be done at my command."
Having spoken thus to them, Brahmā vanished right there.
(21.24) I shall now describe that which is to be meditated upon by men who have attained perfection in mantra: Vāsudeva with two arms, [marked] on the palms of his hands with lines. (21.25)

One should meditate on Him as marked with the conch, discus, and other symbols, and again with twice that number; furthermore, one should visualize Him holding the conch and discus, as well as the mace and lotus, with His two hands.
Or else, with his two principal arms, he grants protection and supports [the devotee] at the waist;
when the multitude of serpents exceeds this number, Hari holds many weapons.
He is beautiful and dark-complexioned, or else possesses a white luster.
An image fashioned from materials such as stone, situated in the primary position—
whether seated, reclining, or mounted upon Garuḍa—
the knowers of the three Vedas should meditate upon and worship with the mantras of the three Vedas.
One should meditate upon [the Lord] established in the conclusion of the Agamas, with two long arms;
Vāsudeva and all the others are free from ornaments and devoid of weapons.
The four [forms] wear white and dark garments and face the four cardinal directions.
They were content with a single mat, devoid of beds and seats; deprived of their two queens and their retinues, they remained in yogic postures.
They possessed the six political expedients with equal importance, along with the secret counsels of force and the other means. || 21.31-21.32 ||
Having consecrated them, O Lotus-born One, they should be worshipped in due order perpetually;
yet they are devoid of the offering of oblations, free from regular festivals,
and lacking the rites of the investiture of the sacred thread, the ritual sleep, and the ritual awakening.
O Four-faced One, in this world or in a temple,
at the time of midday, those who are devoted to the five times without interruption,
who are free from desire, and who have renounced ritual action, should perform the worship of the God.
By means of the *balādi* mantras, through the unbroken observance of the five daily rites (*pañcakāla*),
by the single path (*ekādhvan*), and by the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as *niṣeka* and the *balādi* offerings,
the ritual of guidance (*nayakarma*) is prescribed for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
For them, the twelve-syllable mantra alone is knowledge, and not the triple Veda;
there is neither the Sāvitrī nor any other mantra for the rites of personal study and silent recitation— [a mantra] devoid of seed-syllables, powers, and limbs, and stripped of seers and meters.

The very nature of the mantra is the act of recitation and study for all four castes; their designations have been declared in due order. For "bhaga" is the designation of the foremost of the twice-born, or it is used for a king, as in the case of a Brahmin.
The name of the Vaiśya is Vardhanī, and that of the Śūdra is Maudgalī.
All four are equal, being devoid of lineage (gotra) and ancestral sages (pravara); among them, superiority or inferiority is not recognized by birth.
All were free from desire for fruits, contemplating the twelve-syllable mantra; they were intent on liberation as their certain goal and were exempt from the impurity of birth and death.
They had no authority over any activities such as agriculture and the like.

Employing these through delusion, those of unrefined intellect fall. Because of them, there is the destruction of the king, the kingdom, the people, and the sacrificial hall; therefore, they should not perform agriculture and such tasks.

In the tradition of Mantra-siddhānta, one should request a most excellent brahmin who has received initiation for the purpose of worshiping oneself or for performing the consecration of an image and other rites.
He, in turn, [should perform it] with the twelve-syllable vidyā, devoid of seed-syllables and the like.
The preceptor, the most excellent knower of mantras, should perform the consecration for the sake of worship.
Having received the fourfold form of Ekāyana, he should worship it;
and the worship is performed in four locations: in water, in garlands, in images, and in fire.
The four learned ones, beginning with Maudgalya, have no authority over mantras consisting of seed-syllables, clusters, or words;
nor, even at the departure of their vital breaths, should they touch or cremate a corpse.
One should cast out like a log from the exterior anyone who is destitute of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
For them, the worship of another image leads to sin;
likewise for an image installed in a temple according to the path of another philosophical system.
Whether out of ignorance, delusion, or because it is prescribed as a singular path,
one who worships [the Buddha] attains freedom from all calamities both in this world and the next.
Circumambulation, prostration, and so forth exist elsewhere only in the final philosophical systems (rāddhānta).
No ritual worship should be performed as prescribed, for it brings about the destruction of the king and the kingdom.
Neither initiation, nor the purification of the body through cremation and the like,
nor the entire practice of nyāsa on the limbs is desired on the path of Ekāyana.

This is the sequence for those who have entered the single path and possess the threefold knowledge; now, the current practice is described according to the way of the Tantric Siddhānta, for all four castes and others born therein. (21.54)

The initiation for all was exactly the same, as was their conduct according to the path of the Tantra (21.55). Their purificatory rites, beginning with the *niṣeka*, were performed according to the method taught in the Tantra;
having abandoned the Triple Veda (*trayī*), they remained taking refuge in the Tantra alone (21.56).
O Lotus-born One, the practice taught in the *Pañcakāla* is likewise performed with intervals, just as it is in other tantras for men;
so too are the ritual placements (*nyāsa*) upon the hands and the body for the dissolution and generation of the principles (*tattva*).
There is the arrangement of the yoga-seat and the fashioning of the nine lotuses.
(21.58) The two forms [of the deities] are placed upon those nine lotuses, with the presiding presence in the central one.
Those eight forms likewise gaze toward the directions as is appropriate. (21.59)
Whatever middle form is perceived as belonging to the Lord (Īśvara),
and observing which a person remains engaged in the act of propitiation— that is to be known as the Pauruṣī, the Prājāpatyā, and the Vāsavī.
O Four-faced One, [this concerns] the arrangement of the Dharma and others who have the yoga-seat as their feet;
the retinues ending with Ālaya; the son of Suparṇī;
the pedestal for the offering of oblations; and the gateway.
Moreover, for these external [deities], the eastern direction should belong to Īśvara;
but when imagining other external retinues,
the eastern direction belongs to Prajāpati, while in cases of confusion regarding the directions, it belongs to Puruṣa.
Having gathered [the deities] starting from the East and so forth, one should perform the arrangement of the retinue.
For the mantras preceded by twelve syllables, which are joined with the seed-syllable (bīja), the power (śakti), and the limbs (aṅga),
the recitation (japa) is prescribed even without the sage (ṛṣi) and the meter (chandas).
The method of propitiation is the same for the other castes,
as well as for the nine forms (mūrtis), the group of subsidiary forms,
and even the group of manifestations; these are considered to be castes and female individuals.
There shall be no hoisting of banners, nor the occurrence of festivals such as those at the beginning of a month; rather,
there shall be only the ceremony of rising from the couch, devoid of offerings, oblations, and the like,
and the festive procession around villages and other places performed by circumambulation.
The occasional worship of Hari in four locations is performed independently:
in the circle of the lotus of the discus, in the water-pot, in the image, and in the fire.
Furthermore, the current practice according to other Tantras and the Siddhānta is now being described.
One should visualize the Lord— whether with three faces, four faces,
or even more— seated upon the yoga-pīṭha and attended by his retinue,
[worshipping him] with piṇḍa-mantras, kalā-mantras, and those joined with seed-syllables (bīja), powers (śakti), and limbs (aṅga).
Even those devoid of the knowledge of seers and meters— the four classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas—
all should perform the entire series of rites, beginning with the *niṣeka*, for everyone;
these should be performed according to the path taught in other Tantras as well as by means of the three Vedas.
Confusion among the four established doctrines brings about calamity.
(21.73) Among the four doctrines, if a man abandons that which was practiced by previous men and resorts to another, he becomes a sinner. (21.74)
Therefore, from birth onwards, one should remain fixed in a single established doctrine;
otherwise, one will certainly destroy one's entire lineage and oneself.
[One should do so] by means of mantras, mandalas, sacrificial pits, and the like, as well as ritual actions, mudrās, and offerings.

That lowest of men who, out of delusion, leads [others] to yoga by means of the path taught in his own established doctrine— he too leads the men born of his own family, as well as the Supreme Self itself, straightway to a most terrible hell. (21.76–77)
His ritual action would be fruitless and, on the contrary, a cause of misfortune;
moreover, the deity would become angry, and that anger brings about the destruction of both the king and his kingdom.
Both the performer and the one who causes it to be performed, along with their lineages, shall perish.
There shall be no lack of proximity to the abode of Hari, nor any loss of prosperity.
Therefore, one who performs the rites prescribed by the established conclusions must not engage in the confusion of castes,
even regarding the four principal systems of Mantra-siddhānta as they were before.
Those best of men who perform the unwavering rite of propitiation without confusion are indeed worthy of such a relationship.
But those who are ignorant of the Lord of Gods, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace—
One should avoid association with those base persons who do not understand the meaning proclaimed in the Mahopaniṣad according to its true essence;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the rites prescribed in the Pañcarātra.
The association with those who practice [this] alone brings about prosperity.

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Rule for the Determination of Eligibility for the Siddhāntabheda-Pañcarātra," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma-tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Chapter Twenty-Two:
The Ritual for the Characteristics of Mudrās; Brahmā.
"O Blessed One, what is the nature of the mudrā, and what are its various divisions? What is its purpose? Please explain all of this in its entirety. The Blessed One said:
Because the various arrangements of the fingers are shown as *mudrās*,
they instantly cause the joy (*muda*) of all those who would do harm to dissolve (*drāvayati*).
Therefore, the purpose of that [practice] is the repelling of them by means of the *mudrā*.
The propitiation of the gods through ritual action has also been demonstrated.
These [practices] must be performed in secret and not in public assemblies;
this is the eternal secret of the mantra-circles and mudrās.

Having smeared the two hands with perfume, one should perform the display of the mudrās. Having inserted the extended thumb between the ring finger and the middle finger and formed a fist, one should place it at the heart; this is the Heart Mudrā.
This very [mudrā] consists of binding the fist downward and placing it upon the head;
striking with the tip of the thumb and the index finger is the *śīrṣamudrikā*.
Having firmly bound the fist with the thumb pointing upward, one should place it at the location of the topknot (*śikhā*).
This is declared to be the *śikhā-mudrā*; now the *varma-mudrā* is described:
having inserted the thumbs within and formed fists, one should slightly raise the tips of those fists and extend them outward.

One should visualize the armor bound; this is the "armor-finger-seal" (kavacamudrikā). O Four-faced One, while recollecting the Discus, one should snap the tips of the index finger and thumb like a wheel, and having formed a fist with the remaining fingers, [one should ward off] in all directions.
This very same [mudrā], when turned face downwards, is to be known as the *śikhā-mudrā*;
one should place it between the eyebrows—this is declared to be the *netra-mudrā*. Among these six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) mudrās, the right hand is used in every instance.
Having formed a fist with the three fingers beginning with the little finger, with the thumb raised, one should quickly rotate the index finger with it like a wheel.
This is the mudrā of the fire-rampart; by means of it, one should protect oneself at all times.
Having placed the left palm below the navel, one should then place the other [right hand] above it with the palm facing upward; such is the *yogamudrā*. The left palm is positioned below the navel.
With the face turned downward,
one should again form the *yogasaṃpuṭa-mudrā* by placing the palm of the left hand over that [right hand], with the thumbs aligned.
This is used for the dissolution and emergence of the *tattvas* through the practice of yoga.
O Brahmin, these two mudrās have been taught for the benefit of yogins. This is the Yoga-sampuṭa-mudrā; it is sealed like a jar.
This is the Kumbha-mudrā which should be held upwards; with it, one should perform the ritual bath.
Having wrapped the tips of the ring finger and the index finger in sequence,
and likewise the thumb and the little finger, this is known as the *saṃhāramudrā*.
It is used for the withdrawal of the principles (*tattvas*) as well as for the dismissal of the deities.
This mudrā should be employed at all times in all rites.
When the three fingers are brought together, it is the *saṃhṛti* (withdrawal) mudrā;
when the index fingers are again released, it is proclaimed as the *sṛṣṭi* (emission) mudrā.
This mudrā is proclaimed for invocation and for the emanation of the principles (tattva). The joining of the thumb and the index finger is the *tattvamudrikā*;
this mudrā is also proclaimed for the time of depositing the principles.
This very same [mudrā] is also the *jñānamudrā*, which dispels the darkness of ignorance.
One should touch the middle of both hands with the two middle fingers.
Having turned the hands palms-upward, it is proclaimed as the *nyāsamudrā*.
This mudrā is declared for the placement of mantras upon the deity and one's own body. One should touch both thumbs, both index fingers,
and both middle fingers, while the others are likewise extended.

It should be known as the *japamudrā*; one should display it at the time of recitation with all the fingers of both the right and left hands joined together. This joining of the palms is designated by the wise as the *brahmamudrā*.
The two thumbs and the two little fingers should likewise be joined together; when the tips of the two index fingers are pressed together, it is proclaimed as the Viṣṇu-mudrā.
That same [mudrā], with all the fingers joined to one another and the thumbs likewise pressed together, [is the next].
That mudrā with both thumbs joined is said by you to belong to Rudra. Covering the ears with both hands, one should extend the right hand like a staff in the act of saluting one's gurus.
Placing the fingers of the left hand at the ear and likewise the other [hand], one should extend them;
this is the mudrā of Vighnarāja, which destroys obstacles.
Internally, however, the two index fingers are joined together with the two thumbs pressed together.
That is the venerable *mudrā*; when the two hands are joined in a hollowed cup (*sampuṭa*), that is the auspicious *varāha-mudrā*, which bestows all accomplishments.
O Brahmin, in the sequence of the lineage of gurus, all these *mudrās* have been demonstrated.
On the palm of the left hand, one should visualize a red lotus;
in its center, one should contemplate the fire, a triangle and treasury of splendors.
Having turned the palm downward, one should place it over the substance.
This is to be known as the Dahanamudrā, which always bestows the purification of substances.
O you who sit upon the lotus, on the palm of the right hand is a white sixteen-petaled lotus,
joined with the sixteen digits of the moon.
Having visualized that [syllable] in their midst, one should contemplate the nectar being poured forth.
One should then contemplate that the ashes, washed by that nectar, have arisen once more.
O Lotus-Seated One, this is declared to be the mudrā of nourishment.

O Brahmin, one should place two thumbs and two little fingers together, as well as the two index fingers; the remaining fingers of both hands should be extended. Likewise, the middle finger should be on the right hand and the ring finger on the other.
Having withdrawn [the fingers], one should extend the remainder on both hands;
this is to be known as the *surabhimudrā*, which purifies the sacrificial substances.
Having formed the *añjali* with both hands, it should be clearly and slightly opened.

This is the mudrā for invocation; by its display, [the deity] attains presence. When both hands are joined in a hollowed añjali gesture directed upward at the heart and the head, it should be known as the *praṇāma-mudrā* (gesture of salutation), which quickly propitiates the deity.
O Lotus-Seated One, this should be known as the mudrā for the forms beginning with Vāsudeva,
as well as for the twenty-four forms beginning with Mīna; O Lotus-Seated One, this mudrā has been described for other forms as well.
Extending all the fingers and bringing the two wrists together,
one should insert the two thumbs inside and touch their backs;
this is the Padma-mudrā, which one should display while seated.

O Four-faced One, for all the goddesses beginning with Śrī, the lotus mudrā has been prescribed; it bestows the fruit of all desires. Having placed the right thumb within the fist of the left hand, [one forms this mudrā].
Having joined the thumb and forefinger together and extended them evenly,
one should bind the other three fingers of the right hand into a fist pointing upwards;
this is declared to be the Śaṅkha-mudrā, which bestows knowledge and liberation in no long time.
Having rotated the hands, which are level with the wrists, sideways in succession,
the Cakra-mudrā, which brings great prosperity, should be performed alternately.
Then, having formed fists with both hands, both thumbs should be extended.
One should extend the pair of middle fingers straight upward;
with the remaining fingers, they should bind them to one another. When the two elbows are pressed together, this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā*.

One should touch the tip of the index finger with the middle finger; this is the bow mudrā (cāpamudrikā). Having formed a fist with the left hand, with the thumb held straight upward, one should bind that thumb with the right hand (the apasavya hand).
Extending the right thumb is known as the *musala-mudrā*. Then,
having withdrawn the little finger first with the thumb,
one should again bind the index finger, keeping its tip bent.
That should be known as the sword mudrā (*khaḍgamudrā*), which strikes fear into all the wicked.
O Brahmin, one should let the two hands hang down with the fingertips interlaced;
that is the forest-garland mudrā (*vanamālā*), in which the two thumbs are drawn together.
The gesture known as añjali is the mudrā of the gods beginning with Ākhaṇḍala;
one should join the backs of both palms together with the little fingers interlaced,
bind the pair of index fingers, and extend them gradually like a beak.
One should gradually hang down the two big toes of both feet;
with the middle and ring fingers of both hands, one should perform a movement like the flapping of wings— this is to be known as the Garuḍa-mudrā.

O Brahman, having contracted the three fingers beginning with the little finger and binding the index finger with the thumb, this is again the mudrā of Viṣvaksena. Then, having extended all the fingers, keeping them slightly apart and pointing upwards—
Having extended the length of the hand, one should gradually curl its fingers;
this is known as the *mudrā* of Ananta, resembling the tip of a serpent’s hood.
This same fist-mudrā is the *bali-mudrā* for Caṇḍa and the others.
The cloth-seal (vastramudrā) is formed with the thumb and the ring finger;
the fist-seal (muṣṭimudrā) is a clenched fist encircled by the thumb. That same seal, when the little fingers are released, is to be known as the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā).
It should be known as the *gandhamudrā*, and it is released by the ring finger.
It should be known as the *puṣpamudrā*, and likewise released by the middle finger;
for it is the joining of the tip of the middle finger with the first joint of the thumb.
The *yajñopavīta* mudrā consists of the little finger being held by the thumb;
this auspicious *ākalpa* mudrā should be known as that which brings pleasure to Viṣṇu.
Having brought the fingers together, one should then interlace them.
The incense mudrā is formed by both hands with the thumbs raised together.
Having raised the middle fingers and drawn back the thumbs,
one should likewise draw back the little fingers with the index and ring fingers.

That which is formed with the right hand while the left is held [in its place] is called the Lamp Mudrā; it is exceedingly dear to the God of Gods. For the other services, the mudrā is that of the joined palms (añjali).

That which is formed with the thumbs raised upward while the remaining fingers are held in fists should be known as the Pratimā-mudrā; it brings about what is dear to the God of gods. Having turned the hand palm-upward, one should gradually bend the tips of the fingers.
Having separated the thumb [from the other fingers], it should be known as the *svāgata-mudrā* (gesture of welcome);
that same [gesture] is the *prārthanā-mudrā* (gesture of supplication), and it is also this *dāna-mudrā* (gesture of giving).
O Lotus-seated One, having joined the tips of the five fingers together—
With the left hand held in support and the right hand [offering],
having presented the supreme food and so forth, that mudrā is designated as "the morsel.
It consists of the joining of the tips of the middle and ring fingers with the tip of the thumb.
Having made the pair of the little finger and the index finger long in whatever manner is appropriate,
it is recommended for the rite of *homa* with sesame, rice, barley, and so forth.
Thus, in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, in the *Mahopaniṣad*, in the *Pādmatantra*, in the *Caryāpāda*.
The twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Characteristics of Mudrās";
the twenty-third chapter,
"Description of the Meaning of Mātṛkā and Other [Terms]."
But what is the distinction of names for the castes, and of what nature is the extraction of mantras?
What is its purpose? Let that be told in its entirety. (23.1)
The Blessed One said: "I shall tell you; listen to everything exactly as it is.
O Lotus-born one, they are distinguished from my mouth according to the division of short and long [vowels]."
The vowels beginning with *a* arise in sequence, as do the other half-mātṛkās beginning with *ka*;
having placed them upon the consecrated wheel, they are to be worshipped in a praiseworthy, secluded, protected, beautiful, and level spot of ground. (23.3)
A square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), two cubits in width,
elevated by four finger-breadths and resembling the surface of a mirror,
should be prepared; having filled any cavities with earth and smeared it with cow dung.

Having sprinkled [the site], one should fashion a wheel adorned with sixteen spokes, complete with a hub and a rim, marked with lines of sandalwood powder. In its center is the first of the Vedic meters (gāyatrī), and likewise, the vowels are placed upon the spokes.
The consonants from *ya* onwards are located in the center of the navel and in the middle of the rim.

(23.7) When the phonemes have been thus deposited by means of the twelve-syllable vidyā, one should worship the self as the essence of the phonemes with all enjoyments, beginning with the arghya offering. (23.8)
The distinction of the names of the syllables situated in the wheels is now shown:
Udgītha is the beginning of the meters, as well as Praṇava and Tāraka;
and likewise Brahmā, Brahmakośa, Vyāpin, and Oṃkāra.
The eight renowned names are as follows: Viṣṇu is said to be the syllable *oṃ*;
the immeasurable Madhusūdana is the syllable *ā*;
Ādideva and Gopana are the syllable *i*; and Trivikrama is the syllable *ī*. (23.10–23.11)
Māyā, Bandhu, and Rāma are mentioned immediately after that;
likewise, Pañcabindu, Mahāmāyā, and Vāmana are remembered. Ukāra is called Bhuvana, and Śrīdhara is likewise Udaya.
The letter Ū is the Lord of the Upper World, Hṛṣīkeśa, whose abode is the cave of the heart.
The letter Ṛ is Ṛtadhāman, and he is likewise called Padmanābha.
The letter Ṝ is named Pīṭha; he is the Yogin and likewise Dāmodara.
The syllable *l* is Keśava, the Protector, the support of wisdom, and Maheśvara;
the syllable *l* is also Dīrghaghoṇa, known by the name Nārāyaṇa.
The syllable *e*, which has the name Samprasāraṇa, is called Mādhava.
Devadatta is Mṛgeśa; the vowel Ai is known as Godhana. Govinda and Vīrasena are Okāra, who is the Four-faced One (Caturmukha).
Otadeha is Vāsudeva, also known as Brahmasādhana. || 23.16–23.17 ||
The syllable *au* is the invocation of the medicinal herbs, its deity being Aurva Saṅkarṣaṇa Manu.
The syllable *aṃ* is Kapilākṣa Pradyumna; he is remembered as the deity.
The syllable *aḥ* is named Aniruddha, the end of the digits (*kalā*), designated as the source of creation (*sargisaṃjñita*).
The letter *ka* is Kamala, Brahmā; Karāla is remembered as the bearer of the conch (*śaṅkhin*).
The letter *kha* is Kharvadeha, the wielder of the discus (*cakrī*) whose vehicle is Garuḍa.
The letter *ga* is Gadadhvaṃsī, the wielder of the mace (*gadī*), and is remembered as being fivefold in nature.
The syllable *gha* is Padmapāṇi, who has five forms and rides upon an elephant;
the syllable *ṅa* is Śārṅgapāṇi, who has a single tusk and the monkey as his banner.
The syllable *ca* is Vakratuṇḍa, the wielder of a sword, and the leader of the spirits (*pretanāyaka*).
The letter *cha* is known as the destroyer of deceit, independent, and possessing earrings (*kuṇḍalin*).
The letter *ja* is known as the mace-bearer (*musalin*), the destroyer of rebirth, and the one who possesses the quarters (*kakubha*).
The letter *jha* is the soul of the Sāmaveda, a devourer of fish (*jhaṣāśin*), and golden-hued.
The letter *ña* is known as Bhṛgu, white as the moon, holding a noose in his hand;
the letter *ṭa* is known as Parvata, who gladdens the heart and holds a shield.
The letter *ṭha* is known as Kaustubha, the cloud-like Tomara, who is difficult to withstand.
The letter *ḍa* is Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Jhaṣa, Bhūmi, and Vanālaya.
The letter *ḍha* is Puṣpabhadra, Dṛḍhakarmā, and Pratardana.
The letter *ṇa* shall be Vanamālī; he is remembered as Pracaṇḍa and Sumukha.
The letter *e* is Ekanetra; *tha* is known as Vairāja and Vijaya.
*Tha* is Sarvarodha, Rasātman, and Supratiṣṭhita.
The letter *da* is Vaidhara and Dṛṣṭi; it is threefold and the destroyer of Tripura.
The letter *dha* is the giver of wealth, meritorious, fortunate, and the destroyer of delusion.
The letter *na* is Bhadrapāṇi, the Lord of Obstacles, and the Sovereign of Men. The letter *pa* is the slayer of sin, pure, and facing the west.
The syllable *pha* is Phullanayana; Śikhaṇḍin is the result of *vi-karman*.
The syllable *ba* is Jṛmbhala; the short vowel is Matimān, the conqueror of Kālanemi. The syllable *bha* is Bhallāyudha; Subhadra has subtle eyes.
The letter *ma* is Mandara, the skillful one, who is fond of the *mādhavī* and the *pāṭala* flower.
The letter *ya* is the self of the Puruṣa, Vāyu, the conch, and the fourfold state.
The letter *ra* is Anala, the great flame, the self of the universe, and the eternal burner.
The letter *la* is known as Mahendra and Pulaha, with a yellowish-white luster;
the letter *va* is Varuṇa, Kumbha, the essence of nectar, and the moon;
the letter *śa* is the bestower of auspiciousness, Lakṣmī, Śrīvatsa, and the increaser of wealth.
The letter *ṣa* is the form of Krodha, fierce in nature and the slayer of enemies.
The letter *sa* is the full moon, consisting of its digits, and is designated as Śukla.
The letter *ha* is the twelvefold self; it is remembered as the radiant Bhāskara (the Sun).
The letter *la* is the Dundubha snake, Bharga, Viṣkambha, and the uneven path;
the letter *kṣa* is Garuḍa, Ananta, the Peak-syllable (Kūṭa), and is remembered as Narahari.
The Anusvāra is Dhruva, the Bindu, the Staff (Yaṣṭi), and is called the Half-moon (Candrārtha).
*svāhākāra*, *hutānna*, and *ṭeṭha* are proclaimed [as mantras];
*namaskāra*, *nati*, and the phonemes (*varṇasaṃjñā*) are recorded as such, and so forth.
The deities of the phonemes situated upon the wheel are described in sequence.
Since the letter *a* is the cause of all phonemes, Viṣṇu is its presiding deity because he is the form of all causes. The letter *ā* has Madhusūdana as its deity; the letter *i* is Trivikrama.
The letter *ī* is the god Vāmana, and likewise the letter *u* is the Lord of Śrī.
Immediately after the syllable *ū*, there is Hṛṣīkeśa;
for the syllable *ṛ*, the god Padmanābha, who is Dāmodara, should be [the deity]. 23.40–23.41
The letter *rk* is the god Keśava,
and the presiding deity (*adhideva*) of the letter *lk* is Nārāyaṇa; O Four-faced One, the letter *lk* has Mādhava as its deity, while Govinda shall be the deity of this subsequent syllable.
Vāsudeva is the deity of the vowel *ai*;
likewise, Saṅkarṣaṇa is the deity of the vowel *au*,
while Pradyumna is the presiding deity of the syllable *aṃ*.
Aniruddha resides in the syllable *aḥ*; thus, O Brahmin, the deities of the vowels have been described in sequence. Now the deities of the consonants are being told:
the deity of the letter *ka* is Vidhi, and that of the letter *kha* is Sudarśana.
The deity of the letter *ga* or the letter *gha* is Vāṇī and Śārṅga.
The deity of the letter *ṅa* and the letter *ca* is held to be Nandaka;
the deity of the letter *cha* is Yama, and the deity of the letter *ja* is likewise [Yama]. (23.46–23.47)
The letter *jha* should be Musalī, and its presiding deity is Aṅkuśa;
for the letter *ña*, the deity is Bhṛgu, and for the letter *ṭa*, it is Mahīdhara.
Meru is the presiding deity of *kaustubha*; the letter *ṭha* is Pārthiva.
The letter *ḍha* has the Mothers as its deity; the letter *ṇa* is the Vanamālika.
Likewise, the letter *tha* is the Dṛṣṭi; the letter *stha* has the Rasas as its deity. Atri is the deity of the letter *da*, and Dhaneśvara is the deity of the letter *dha*.
Lambodara is the deity of the syllable *na*, and Pavitraka is that of *pa*.
Śikhaṇḍin is the deity of *pha*, while Bakāra is the deity of *ba*.
Jṛmbhala belongs to the syllable *bha*, and likewise Subhadra is its deity.
The letter *ya* is the deity of Vāyu and corresponds to the letter *ma*.
The letter *ra* is Dhūmadhvaja (Agni), and the letter *la* is Divaspati (Indra).
The letter *va* has Varuṇa as its lord, and the letter *śa* has Māhī as its presiding deity.
The letter *ṣa* has the form of Krodha; the letter *sa* has Candra as its deity.
The letter *ha* is Sahasrāṃśu, and the letter *lkāra* has Bharga as its deity.
Narasiṃha is said to be the deity of the letter *kṣa*; thus the deities of the letters beginning with *ka* have been described.
O Four-faced One, for the practitioner who knows the names of the castes ending with the [six] wheels and their respective deities, these [deities] bestow the fruit. Furthermore, O Wise One,
whatever constellation is known by scholars to belong to each particular caste—
And now the colors corresponding to those [months] are described here in sequence:
the letters, excluding the first vowel, are traditionally held to correspond to the months of Vaisakha and Ashvayuja.
For the letter *i*, the constellations are Bharani and the three Uttaras beginning with Krittika.

The four [nakṣatras] beginning with Ṛkāra, Rohiṇī as one, and then Eḍakā; Raudra should also consist of a single syllable, while Punarvasu is measured by two. Likewise, Pauṣṇa consists of two syllables, or according to another opinion, it is at the beginning and end.
Among the [nakṣatras] beginning with Kṛttikā, the first is Puṣya; two are Sārpa (Āśleṣā); two are Maghā;
one is Arthamaṇa (Phalgunī); and a pair is said to have Bharga as its deity (Hasta).
A pair indeed is Sāvitra (Citrā), and two have Indra as their presiding deity (Viśākhā).
One [nakṣatra] is Niṣṭyā; Viśākhā has two; immediately following is Maitra with three;
Indra has one; Mūla has three; Pūrvāṣāḍhā has one;
Uttarāṣāḍhā has one; and Abhijit is considered to have only one.
Two belong to Viṣṇu, while Śraviṣṭhā and Śatabhiṣaj are each one;
Aja Ekapād would have three parts as his color,
and Ahirbudhnya has three colors— such are the stars among the colors.
In the beginning, the four vowels [a, i, u, e] are Aries; the three consonants [ka, kha, ga] are Taurus.
Likewise, the pair [gha, ṅa] is Gemini; the pair [ca, cha] is Cancer; and likewise the pair [ja, jha] is Leo.
The remaining two parts and so forth are Virgo; the letter *ku* is the first of Libra. (23.64–65)

The cavarga is said by the wise to be Scorpio and Sagittarius; the ṭavarga is Capricorn and Aquarius; the tavarga is Pisces; the pavarga belongs to the final sign, as do the letters beginning with ya.
Whichever asterism corresponds to the first syllable of the practitioner’s mantra—
One should examine their compatibility or incompatibility as if between a man and a woman.
Having drawn a four-square grid on the ground, one should place the letters beginning with 'A' therein;
[one should observe] in which square the first letter of the practitioner's name is located.

If the first syllable of the mantra should be situated in that very [place], it is "accomplished" (siddha); but one should know that in the second it is "to be accomplished" (sādhya), and in the next, "well-accomplished" (susiddha);
while in the fourth, it leads to the opposite result.
If [the mantra] is *siddha*, it is successful through recitation and other means; if it is *sādhya*, it is successful when well-mastered;
and if it is *susiddha*, it certainly leads to great fruit as soon as it is merely studied.
However, if it belongs to an enemy, there will be misfortune, and the script may even lead to the destruction of the student.
One should examine the compatibility after having examined the signs;
the practitioner should then accomplish the mantra of the deity, for the course of the gods is crooked.
One should not examine for incompatibility regarding the four root-mantras.
The Tāra, the eight-syllabled mantra, and likewise the twelve-syllabled one, as well as the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī—these four are considered primary.
When there is an excess of thirty-two syllables, it is the root mantra; when there is an excess of ten, [it is another].
Seed-mantras are beautiful when old in all [mantra families], or else when young; likewise, others are beautiful even in childhood.
The classes of mantras are divided into three genders: female, male, and neuter.
Mantras ending in *svāhā* are feminine; those ending in *namaḥ* are neuter;
and the remaining ones are masculine mantras—thus they are said to be of three kinds.
[These are used] for the rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*), subjugation (*vaśya*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), and minor magical acts (*kṣudrakarma*).
Feminine mantras lacking masculine gender markers are praised for rites other than those involving worship;
however, regarding mantras with masculine gender markers, only a brief indication will be stated here.
Mantras ending in *phaṭ* are for purposes such as causing death, while the Teacher [prescribes them] for afflictions caused by spirits and the like.

Those ending in *huṃ* are praised, while those ending in *vauṣaṭ* are likewise used for nourishing, as well as for virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation. Those ending in the dative case are praised, and those ending in *oṃ* bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
All mantras and all their fruits are heard directly from the mouth of the Guru; however,
a mantra heard by chance, or through concealment or deception,
whether on paper or on the ground, is considered useless and even harmful.

A single mantra, when properly accomplished through recitation, fire-offerings, and libations, brings about every goal for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt. For one who has perfectly mastered even a single mantra, nothing in this world remains unattainable.
How much more so for many? What need is there to mention him? He is Hari himself.
For the performance of rites for Kṛṣṇa, one should sit upon blades of *kuśa* grass, on a mat of *bṛsī*, or in solitary places, facing the east or other directions, but never facing the south.
Seated, pure, with the *pavitra* in his hand,
having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* marks and not uttering any other speech,
he should first bow to his guru and then recite the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*.
In a temple of the gods, by a river, on a mountain, on the shore of the ocean,
in a forest, at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), or beneath a banyan or a pipal tree—
or elsewhere in a pure location— he should build a hut and begin his practice.
Either fasting entirely, or subsisting on air, or subsisting on water while immersed in it;
or eating withered leaves, or consuming vegetables, or fruits,
or even cooked roots, provided they are without salt.
One who has conquered the senses, subsisting on barley, warm water, mung beans, milk, or alms-food—
each preceding item being more highly recommended as a purifying diet—
should [practice] the mantra of the deity during the lunar days and weekdays appropriate for the practitioner.
On the twelfth lunar day, on the full moon, or during an eclipse, the ritual is praised.
Performing a special sacrifice, one should practice the recitation (*japa*) at the lotus of the disc;
one may wear a topknot or matted hair, and be clothed in bark, deerskin, or rags.
Constantly performing ablutions at the three junctions of the day and avoiding anointing with oil,
the practice of mantra-repetition is prescribed for as long as the Kṛta Yuga lasts. In the three ages beginning with Tretā, it is said to be doubled and tripled respectively.
Or even four times that amount, according to one's desire for the fruit of the mantra. (23.94) The mantra bestows all accomplishments; accomplishment is achieved through the power of ritual action.
Ritual action is understood from the scripture, and the scripture comes from the person who is the teacher. (23.95)
It is the reflection of all sentient beings and a protection from the ocean of saṃsāra;
because it combines reflection and protection, it is called "mantra" by the wise.
Alternatively, it is called "mantra" because one deliberates with others due to its nature as something to be kept secret.
This word *pratyānta* is masculine in gender in both common usage and the Veda.
(97) The deity is established by means of mantra, and by mantra alone is he dismissed; the wise know that among all forms of knowledge, the knowledge of mantra is the supreme knowledge. (98)
Everything pertaining to this world and the next is accomplished through mantra alone.
Because he perceived that which exists within the meters, mantras, and syllables, he is called a seer (*ṛṣi*).
And they say that his "vision" refers to the vision of the fruit [of the mantra], not merely the vision of the mantra itself.
The deities, when propitiated by means of mantra, bestow the fruits of the mantra.
Those who know reality recognize the abode, the field, and the reality itself.
The classification of mantras, such as the "white" (śukla) and others, is proclaimed according to the syllables of the mantra.

Now listen to the method for accomplishing the root mantra and the other mantras. Having prepared flowers, roots, and fruits suitable for sacrifice, one should avoid leafy vegetables and other such greens.
O Lotus-born One, I shall describe those flowers which should be avoided.

One should discard flowers that have a pungent scent, no scent at all, or a foul odor; likewise, flowers touched by clothing or the leaves of the *arka* plant should not be used in the worship of Hari.
Unmatta, śālmalī, bījapūra, dhattūraka, japā, bandhūka, asitakoraṇḍa, droṇa, kanyā, aparājitā,
bṛhatī, agastya, kūṣmāṇḍa, paṭolī, and āragvadha are equal [in their medicinal properties]. || 23.105 ||
Nirguṇḍī, damayantī, kiṃśuka, and pāribhadraka;
kośātakī, priyāla, tapasvī, and girimallikā; nimba, vyāghrī, karañja, śvīṣaṇḍa, and pāṇḍurapaṭṭikā. (23.106–107)

The flowers of the *vibhītaka*, *kiṅkiṇī*, *kola*, *lāṅgalī*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *nāraṅga*, *nandikāvarta*, *vallikā*, *akṣīrikā*, and so forth, are to be avoided; hear now likewise regarding the vegetables.
Śṛṅgāṭa, gṛñjana, śigru, nālikā, and suniṣaṇṇaka;
saubhāñjana, raktabāṣpa, grāmabāṣpa, and trikaṇṭaka; droṇapatra, liliṅgā, taṇḍulīya, and tapasvinī. || 23.109–23.110 ||

And the *kośātakī* is to be avoided; among roots, that which is to be rejected is said to be the mushroom, garlic, the palm fruit, the eggplant, and the bottle gourd. One should completely avoid the *bimba*, the *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the orange, and their roots.
The practitioner should carefully avoid eating from the leaves of the *bilva*, *udumbara*, *bodhi*, *arka*, and *vaṭa* trees. He should also abandon laziness and long-winded reflection;
he should renounce quarreling, sleep, despondency, and both restraint and favor.
The pure practitioner should hang a rosary of lotus seeds around his neck;
he should wear a golden wheel for the pacification of all obstacles.
Alternatively, at the time of recitation, it may be of the form of a wheel or a conch shell, in whatever manner is appropriate.
The wise man should mark the body with the emblems in the form of the Śārṅga bow, the sword, and the mace;
O Four-faced One, on the limbs of the body— the two arms and the region of the chest—
he should adorn them with the five [emblems] beginning with the discus, thus refining his limbs with the marks of knowledge.
Seeing a man from afar, beings such as Bhūtas and others, overwhelmed by fear, flee;
likewise, through the mere sight of him, terrible sinners perish, and heaps of merit enter [him]. 23.117. They are destroyed, and thus masses of merit enter [him].
Likewise, the gods and the most eminent celestial sages bow down to him.
Even while performing what should not be done, or eating from here and there,
the embodied soul marked with the signs of the discus and other weapons is not defiled by sins.
The *havya* and *kavya* offerings should be given to him; that gift is inexhaustible.
Without tying the topknot (*śikhābandha*) and without applying the forehead mark (*tilaka*) with clay, they then held *darbha* grass, not binding it with threads as a sacred thread (*anupavīta*).
The lowest of men, performing [other] actions, shall not obtain the fruit.
One who has loosened his topknot, whose head is covered with a cloth,
or who is walking, lying down, or talking, does not enjoy the fruit of the *japa*.
Establishing himself in silence while reciting, the best of mantra-knowers should not engage in conversation or similar acts, nor should he speak in a low voice using reversed syllables or the like.
Even when speaking for the sake of a specific purpose, he should always do so with his mind fixed entirely upon that [mantra].
One should recite another twelve-syllable mantra, or one consisting of other syllables, a hundred thousand times.
One should offer half that number as oblations into the fire and prepare a sacrificial hall that is square,
pleasing to the mind, and provided with an exit for the smoke.
In the center of that, one should fashion an auspicious sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) suitable for the oblations,
either circular or square, provided with three girdles (*mekhalā*) and a womb-shape (*yoni*), O Brahmin; now the measurement of the pit is being declared.
At the conclusion of ten thousand oblations (ayuta-āhuti), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure;
for one hundred thousand (niyuta), it should be two cubits; likewise, for one million (prayuta), three cubits;
for a conch-oblation (śaṅkha-homa), four cubits; but for a great conch-oblation (mahā-śaṅkha), six cubits.
In the Bṛndā fire-offering, it should be seven cubits; in the Mahābṛnda, eight cubits;
in the Arbuda, nine cubits; and in the Nyarbuda, ten cubits.
In the Kharva, it should be eleven cubits, and in the Parārdha, twelve cubits in length.
Thirteen cubits in the middle, but fourteen at the edge;
fifteen cubits on a lotus, and sixteen on a great lotus;
twenty cubits in the ocean, and twenty-two are recorded for the great flood.
In this procedure for the offerings exceeding this [number], the measurement is twenty-four cubits;
the count is stated here incidentally, so understand it in due order:
one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and likewise ten thousand.
A niyuta, a prayuta, a śaṅkha, and beyond that a mahāśaṅkha;
then a bṛnda, a mahābṛnda, an arbuda, and likewise a nyarbuda;
a kharva, a parārdha, and at the middle and end, a padma, and then a mahāpadma and so forth.

Padmottara would be the ocean, and that would be the great flood (mahaugha), the highest; beginning from one, one should count up to a prayuta in due order. From place to place, one should increase tenfold until reaching a prayuta.
A hundred thousand is called a *lakṣa*, and ten million is called a *koṭi* or a *prayuta*.
One should count starting from a *śaṅkha* up to the end of the *mahaugha* in successive order;
a hundred thousand *koṭis* is declared to be the designation of a *śaṅkha*.
In the same way, *mahāśaṅkha* is proclaimed as *vṛnda*;
likewise, *mahāvṛnda* is [the next], and *arbuda* is remembered in this very manner. Thus is *nyarbudha* declared, and in this way *kharva* is illustrated.
In this very way, O Four-faced One, there would be a *parārdha* as the middle;
likewise, there is the *anta*, the *padma*, and similarly the *mahāpadma*.
There are also the *sāgara* and the *pralaya*; beyond that, there is no further number.
Where there was wood, that was his ear; where there was smoke, that was his nose;
where there was a small flame, that was his eye; and where there was ash, that was his head.
Where the darbha grasses were properly situated, those are proclaimed to be his hair.
Wherever the fire blazes, that very place is declared to be the tongue.
An oblation offered in the ear of the fire causes disease; in the nose, it causes mental anguish;
in the eyes, it brings about death; and in the hair, it results in poverty.

Sin would reside in the head when offered; therefore, one should offer oblations upon the tongues [of the fire] with sacrificial fuel-sticks, seeds, cow's ghee, and likewise with leaves. When the fire is kindled, one should offer flowers and summon Agni.
Having prepared a seat for Yoga made of forest wood, gemstone,
or iron within the consecrated sacrificial pit, one should again invoke Lord Hari there; the deity remains present until the conclusion of the fire-oblation.
Having propitiated [the deity], he should pray and perform the fire-oblation day after day;
until the time for the final oblation, he should guard the sacred fire without weariness.
He should not remove the enclosing sticks or the darbha grass spread out at the commencement [of the rite].
For the practitioner who recites the supreme mantra according to the path thus described,
dreams will arise without deliberation,
indicating the success or failure of the mantra, as well as what is auspicious or inauspicious.
The preceptor, the image of the Goddess, the articles for worship,
the Brahmin, the devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata), the king, the parasol, the fly-whisk,
the elephant, the lion-throne, the water-pot filled [with water], the maiden, and the womenfolk— [these should be honored].
A lamp, a conch, as well as a vehicle, the śrīvatsa mark, and sandals; white cloth and garlands, sandalwood and ornaments;
jewels, trumpets and the like, milk-rice, curd, and small bowls. || 23.151–23.152 ||
Betel, a book, a bell, rice, and immersion in water;
crossing the ocean, climbing a mountain, and climbing a tree; the acquisition of land, the acquisition of earth, and the sight of riverbanks, wells, and the like.
If one undertakes a journey while facing either the east or the north,
and beholds a celestial chariot of Viṣṇu, the radiant moon and sun,
a blazing fire, the chanting of the Vedas, or beings such as Siddhas and Vidyādharas; || 23.154–23.155 ||
Beholding the assembly of deities and roots and fruits,
as well as cakes and other edible foods, a bundle of *kuśa* grass, a water-pot,
a sacred thread, and sacrificial vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; (23.156) observing these things, he [proceeded].
One should predict [success] through such auspicious dreams as one involving a rosary (akṣamālā).
One should also describe the attainment of mantras in many ways, as well as inauspicious bad dreams,
conversation with those who have shaven heads, and associating with them.
O Lotus-born One, he himself was shaven-headed, wearing a worn-out blue garment,
and bearing upon his head a red and a blue maiden as well as a garland of flowers;
he mounted a donkey and took his seat upon a broken vehicle.
Or carrying a severed umbrella, likewise mounting a buffalo;
going toward the south, or mounting a camel-drawn vehicle;
and being bitten on the body by monkeys, jackals, or wolves.
