The cutting off of ears, feet, and head, as well as the falling out of teeth; wearing new clothes, suffering pain, being bound with a noose by soldiers;
embracing a widow, and [association] with low-born heretics born of inverse unions.
The construction of gate-towers and the like, the falling of trees,

mounting a horse, eating [with them], and visiting the temples of Buddhists and others, as well as associating with those who drink liquor, those afflicted by sinful diseases, and gamblers; 23.163–164.
The spinning [of thread], extinguishing a lamp, a festival for the gods, the burning of villages and the like, the eating of forbidden fruits and such,
beeswax, a reflection, a procession, battle, and sacrifice with soldiers.
Seeing in a dream anointing with oil, the acquisition of oil, black pepper, or likewise salt— one should perform rites for pacification regarding such things through recitation,
fire-offerings, and the like, based on the conviction arising from one-pointedness of mind.
I shall describe before the practitioner those signs that arise bringing prosperity:
the sight of hosts of gods in the sky, the sound of chariot rims, the resonance of kettledrums, conversation with the Siddhas, and the vision of celestial chariots.
Likewise, on the surface of the earth, there is the vision of spirits, ghosts, and piśācas;
and at the time of the fire-oblation, the seven-flamed fire is seen with three peaks,
resembling pure crystal and adorned with a clockwise whorl.

One should observe these signs of success during the performance of the *pūrṇāhuti*: the perception of divine fragrances, as well as umbrellas, images, banners, and the like; and furthermore, the hearing of the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, lutes, and the chanting of the Vedas. (23.171)
The practitioner should not speak of those signs without his guru.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the wise one should feed twelve other Vaiṣṇavas.
He should worship Hari until the perfection of the mantra is attained.
Having fashioned an image according to one's desire from wood or other materials,
one should daily recite the mantra while offering oblations into the fire as before.
O Brahmin, hear now the supreme preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) for the Praṇava.
Understand correctly the seed-syllable (bīja) along with its limbs and its extraction (samuddhāra).

Having gathered the three syllables—which constitute the three parts and represent Hari—beginning with *aprameya*, arising [from the vowels], and ending with *mandara* in the middle; [this is] the designator (*vācaka*) of Hari.

O Brahman, one should extract the first seed-syllable of this [mantra], which possesses the *pluta* and *udātta* accents and is established in the center of the disc; it has the staff as its crest and is the representative form (*pratīka*).
This is proclaimed everywhere as the Vaishnava power that should be wielded.
Those mantras that are devoid of seed-syllables (bīja), power (śakti), and limbs (aṅga) are useless.
Therefore, [a mantra] endowed with limbs, joined with a seed-syllable, and joined with power bestows the fruit.
The seed-syllable and the power have been explained; now hear the classes of the limbs.
The seer is Brahmā, its metre is said to be the goddess Gāyatrī;
the deity to be propitiated is the supreme god, the Supreme Self.
Its reality is the intellect, the supreme ether, the field, and its color is white.
Knowledge, power, as well as vigor, sovereignty, along with splendor, and strength— these,
ending in the dative case, followed by *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*,
*huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *vauṣaṭ* respectively at their conclusion, bring about auspiciousness.

The limbs [of the mantra] should be applied by the practitioner to the six locations beginning with the heart; when these are employed, the mantra becomes complete with its limbs. Furthermore, they should be applied to the body, the palm of the hand, and all twelve locations.
The placement of the twelve syllables is the *praṇava*, which has the luster of crystal.
(23.184) In ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it ends with *namaḥ*; likewise, it ends with *svāhā* during recitation (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), and oblations (*huti*).
For the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), it should end with *huṃ*; for eradication (*uccāṭa*), it should be the sound *huṅ*. (23.185)

In rites of killing, the syllable *phaṭ* is to be known; in paralyzing, inciting hatred, and deluding, there should be no other limb [of mantra] except for the prostration (*nati*). In rites such as the attainment of Dharma and so forth, that prostration alone is used. Eating vegetables, barley-gruel, or alms-food, one who is pure should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.
Half of that is the number for the libation (tarpaṇa), and half of that again is for the rite of fire-offering (homa).
At the conclusion of the homa, his successes arise as much as he desires;
all fruits pertaining to this world and the next are obtained through the Praṇava.
O Four-faced One, there is no mantra superior to the Praṇava;
what is the use of describing other mantras for rites of pacification, nourishment, and subjugation?
And at the time of death, having meditated upon me while uttering the syllable of the Praṇava...

One should cause the individual soul (jīva) to ascend into the heart according to the prescribed method for the practice of yoga. Then, from the middle of the eyebrows, one should lead the soul to the aperture of Brahma (brahmabila);
uttering the Praṇava while piercing that aperture, it dissolves into Brahman.
One should practice the syllable *praṇava* until the release of the vital breath;
liberated from all sins, one goes to the eternal Brahman.
Thus, O Four-faced One, the ritual of the *praṇava* has been declared to you in brief.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Meaning of Mātṛkā and Other Subjects," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the Śrī Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
[The Twenty-fourth Chapter begins.]
O Four-faced One, hear the ritual procedure for the twelve-syllable mantra of the Blessed Lord, which is itself the twelve-syllable ritual procedure.
Having worshipped the wheel of the *mātṛkās*, one should extract the twelve-syllable mantra:
the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by Paramātman, Bhadrapāṇi, Viṣṇu, Dakṣa, Utadeha, Subhadra, Gadī, and Sudhā. (24.1–24.2)
Then Viṣṇuśīrṣa, the triad, Vijaya, Samprasāraṇa, Varuṇa ending with Ādideva, Śukla, Bhuvanaśīrṣaka,
Atri ending with the name Mādhava, Pīyūṣa, and Madhusūdana.
Vāyu, and likewise up to Aprameyānta— such is the sequence of extraction.
Its seed-syllable is said to be the twelve-fold staff-head (daṇḍaśīrṣa),
which is wrathful, great, heroic, and possesses a thousandfold celestial splendor.

These six words ending in *svadhā*, preceded by the word *ulkānta* and in the dative case, should be placed upon the limbs beginning with the heart; likewise, the seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) are to be placed in their respective locations.
The limb-mantra consisting of the seed-syllable of the Supreme Vāsudeva has thus been declared.
The radiant one [ending] at the upper worlds, the seed-syllable, the staff, and then the head;
24.7 the radiant one joined with the jar, the head of Madhusūdana;
that same one with the head of Vāmana, and likewise Hṛṣīkeśa as the head. 24.8
Vīrasenaśiras, Kalkya, and immediately after that Toya;
the sixth is said to be Aurvaśiras. Furthermore, the limbs [of the ritual] follow in sequence: all [the mantras] beginning with Daṇḍaśiras are preceded by the word *vibhava*.

Vāsudeva should be employed in all six [limbs], beginning with the heart. However, in the case of the Vyūha-mantras, Viṣṇu is the seed-syllable (bīja), while the altar and other elements are as before;
or else, the twelve-syllabled mantra serves as the limb, while the heart and others belong to the preceding [mantras].
The six vowels [are assigned] to the six locations— the navel, the private parts, the arms, the thighs, the knees, and the feet— by the wise in their respective order.
Both the seer and the deity for these three are remembered as Vāsudeva.
The deity is Chanda, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the color is white with four faces.
(24.13) The reality is the intellect, the supreme ether; this is declared to be the field (*kṣetra*) of the mantra.
For each syllable, there is a seer (*ṛṣi*), a metre, a deity, and an expansion of colors. (24.14)
The reality (tattva) and the field (kṣetra) are said to be all [present] sequentially even within the twelve [spheres]:
Parameṣṭhin, Sananda, Sanaka, Prajāpati,
Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Marīci, Atri, and Aṅgiras— these are declared to be the sages in order.
The meters are Daivī Gāyatrī, Prajāpati as the head,
Triṣṭubh, Paṅkti, Bṛhatī, Virāṭ, and the sixfold Ṣaṣṭhivṛt.
O Brahmin, among all twelve castes, Uṣṇik and Śrī are [the presiding deities];
Viṣṇu and the others are the month-protecting gods; now I shall declare the principles (tattvas) to you:
consciousness, the individual soul, primordial nature, intellect, mind, and the qualities such as sattva.
Space, fire, and wind are also declared to be the essence (tattva) of the letters.
The fields (kṣetra) are the supreme space, wind, fire, and likewise water;
as well as Satya, Tapa, Jana, Maha, Svarga, and Bhuvaḥ.

The earth and the netherworld (Pātāla)—these have been described to you in sequence. [The sequence begins] with Āmna as the abode, ending with Śreyāṃsa, followed by Gopana, then Sadaṇḍaka, Natyanta, Pāpahanana, and Viṣṇu; the supreme one is Vahni.
Śaṅkha, Mādyakṣara, Para, Kamala, Madhusūdana,
Pulaha, the other Vighnanāyaka, Pītasūdana, Ekanetra, Mandara, and Bhadrahastaka ending with Viṣṇu. || 24.22–24.23 ||
The best of mantra-knowers should extract the *samprasāraṇa* as the head;
this is declared to be the "Agni-prākāra" mantra, O Lotus-seated One. Furthermore, there are the words for Durgā, Gaṇapati, Tārkṣya, and Kṣetrapāla.
The mantras ending in the dative case and beginning with *namaḥ* and *praṇava* (oṃ) should be employed by the practitioner in the intermediate directions,
starting from the direction of Agni (the southeast) in due order. I shall now explain the commentary on the twelve-syllable mantra exactly as it is.
The syllable *om* is declared to be the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is bliss, eternal, and stable.
Because it is all-pervasive, it is remembered as the signifier (*vācaka*) of that which is signified (*vācya*), being itself omnipresent.
It is sought by all the gods, demons, and great seers who are intent upon the goals of human existence.
The God alone is bowed to; he alone is the supreme refuge.
In the beginning, he creates all beings out of a desire to show favor to them;
he also effects their protection through his many forms.
For the sake of the rest of all beings, he withdraws the entire universe;
there is no other goal for those who possess a goal than Vāsudeva.
He withdraws the beings who have become his own self and creates them again through his illusory power (māyā).

When the God is awake, he awakens; when he sleeps, all this world sleeps. This entire collection of beings, consisting of the fourfold classes of moving and non-moving things, is addressed by the twelve syllables, resting upon his majesty.
Having attained the state of Brahman, Brahmā; having attained the state of the gods, the deities;
and the sages such as Marīci and others, as well as the munis such as Sanaka and others—by relying on the majesty of the mantra, they went to the unsurpassed station.
The planets, such as the sun and the moon, go forth again and again and return;
but those who contemplate the twelve-syllable mantra never return.
What need has he for sacrifices, what need for sacred fords, and what need for acts of charity?
What is the use of vows for one who possesses this mantra characterized by twelve syllables?
A person should, with every effort, be devoted to that mantra.
For those terrified by the fear of saṃsāra and desiring liberation as their sole fruit—
This twelve-syllable mantra is the supreme means for liberation.
Devas, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, vidyādharas,
and others bow down to that great soul who contemplates the twelve-syllable mantra.
In the kingdom of that monarch where ministers are fearless,
wealth, grain, and other riches flourish and increase greatly.
Living beings flee [from calamities], and the planets do not become terrifying.

O Lotus-Seated One, it is impossible to describe the fruit in its entirety— even by all the divine mouths of the Four-Faced One over hundreds of years— for those who are oppressed by the kingdom, the royal city, and the presence of the king. (24.40–24.41)
First, one should perform the *puraścaraṇa* for the purification of the body;
the *puraścaraṇa* is intended as the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the body through the mantra.
Having first invited at least twelve Brahmins who are absorbed in that [mantra], [one should proceed].
Having fed [the guests], he should then worship the deity within the maṇḍala. Having first informed the preceptor and being permitted by him, the practitioner, accompanied by his assistants,
[should proceed] to the hermitage where asceticism was formerly practiced by sages.
When the fruit of the perfected mantra has been attained there in the abode of Vāsudeva— at the western gate or elsewhere in the previously mentioned places and grounds—
in a location that is pleasing, [one should prepare] with flowers, sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, fruits, and water.
Endowed with these as described, having obtained desired food that is wholesome, he should eat alms-food or [food] in the houses of devoted people who are absorbed in that [deity].
Whether a celibate student or a householder, he should accomplish the twelve-syllable mantra. (24.46–24.47)
Or he may be a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), self-restrained, devoted to austerity, pure,
eating food obtained as alms, observing celibacy, and subsisting on vegetables, roots, and fruits.
Or, if he is a householder, he may eat what is cooked by himself, or by his sons, or even by his wife.
Or, having offered food cooked by a disciple before Hari,
and having fed the guests at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva and other rites, one should satisfy the disciple, the wife, and likewise the son according to their needs.
He himself should eat the food according to the rules afterwards, without disparaging it;
then, pure and following the Vaikhānasa way of life, he should recite prayers either accompanied by his son and wife,
or else remaining alone and self-restrained.
One who eats in moderation should eat only food that has been cooked by oneself, following the straight path.
For the purification of the body of all, one should first perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
as well as the consumption of water from the foot-washing of the deity (pādodaka), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and the Brahmakūrca water.
Having drunk [the water] for the sake of purifying the body, one should perform the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*).
The commencement of ritual acts should take place in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa;
or else, O Brahmin, on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra.
Having first observed a fast, one should worship Janārdana on the twelfth day— either before a discus-marked lotus, or before an image,
or upon a grass mat (kūrca), or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or in whatever place is suitable—
concluding with a fire-oblation (homa).
Devoted to celibacy and knowing the proper place and time,
he should resolve upon the restriction of time as well as the rules for the vow and so forth;
[he should observe] daily bathing at the three periods of the day and sleeping on the ground.
O Lotus-born One, having made a formal resolve, one should sleep on a bed of kuśa grass, leaves, or deer-skin;
likewise, one should avoid black gram, oil, alkaline substances, and salt, as well as eating food with sesame seeds from a bronze vessel, sleeping during the day, and other such acts. (24.58–24.59)
Having first performed the purification of the body, one should perform the recitation of the mantra with a rosary,
joined at the beginning and end with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and likewise accompanied by the *praṇava*.
At the time of recitation, one should recite the mantra neither too quickly nor too slowly.
Taking Acyuta as the object, one should meditate with the movement of the mind dependent upon Him.
O Lotus-seated One, I shall describe meditation, which destroys all sins:
[meditate on Him] who has four arms, noble limbs, and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
Resembling pure crystal, with a radiance equal to ten thousand moons;
possessing a beautiful smile and lovely red lips, his eyes extended as far as his ears;
shining like a lotus gem cleansed of impurities, he was exquisitely adorned by the luster of his teeth.
Broad-chested and long-armed, with a face like the bright moon,
with beautiful brows and forehead, a lovely countenance, and hair that was thick and curled;
possessing the luster of a hundred thousand flashes of lightning, he was clad in pure yellow garments.
With the lotuses of his palms and soles, with eyes as long as white lotuses,
marked with the Śrīvatsa, adorned with all ornaments such as a crown,
bearing the lotus, discus, mace, and conch, and having the Kaustubha gem upon his chest.
With his limbs anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial garlands,
the four-faced Lord sat comfortably upon the vast coils of the serpent Śeṣa,
accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi, with white clay applied to his forehead.
Adorned with the *tilaka* of the upright sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*),
he was as if gathered together in one place by millions and tens of thousands of suns, moons, lightning bolts, and millions of fires of cosmic destruction— all spreading forth as masses of radiance.
Having purified all defilements, one should meditate upon Him who is radiant and difficult to behold, illuminating the entire world with rays issuing from the orb of His body;
having worshipped the God during the evening twilight according to the prescribed rule.
Having discharged [the excrement], rising again, and being pure with washed hands and feet,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and, remaining silent and fully concentrated,
recite the mantra correctly until the appearance of the Brāhma-muhūrta.
Having bathed and performed the ritual for the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in due order as prescribed, and having worshipped the Lord with offerings such as the arghya-water as described,
one should recite the mantra while maintaining the stability of the body through fruits and other such items.
Thus, with a purified inner self, one should recite the twelve-syllable mantra one hundred and twenty thousand times;
half of that is prescribed for libations with water,
and half of that, the practitioner should offer into the fire with sacrificial wood and other materials.
By reciting the mantra twenty-four hundred thousand times, all the *kiṅkaras*,
*siddhas*, and *vidyādharas*— whether in the netherworld (*pātāla*), in heaven, or on earth—
will come to the twice-born practitioner in whatever place he desires, even if it is difficult to reach.
Attendants lead him there and serve him constantly;
by thirty-six hundred thousand recitations (*japa*), one attains divinity. By eighty hundred thousand recitations and an equal number of fire-oblations (*homa*), one shall dwell [there].
In Maharloka he shall enjoy eternal happiness, honored by those residing there.
By a million times a hundred thousand recitations (*jāpa*), one may attain the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and others;
one shall dwell in the world called Janaloka, highly honored by its inhabitants.
By means of a hundred great arbudas of recitations and burnt offerings, one dwells in the world of Tapas; by that same number of recitations and burnt offerings of the Mahāpadma,
one dwells in Satya, O Lord of Gods, with Hari, who is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
Having seen [the deity] there, one free from affliction shall dwell with the inhabitants of that world.
By reciting [the mantra] a hundred times over great floods, according to the number of oblations,
one who directly perceives Vāsudeva certainly becomes absorbed in him.
What is the use of these many things being spoken? Whatever goal a person desires, he attains it through the rites of propitiation.
Subjugation, attraction, and other such primary effects are achieved through the performance of recitation, fire-offerings, and other rituals.
The practitioner himself should display fruits of various forms.
Whatever enjoyments exist in the netherworld, in heaven, or on earth— those that are difficult to obtain on this world—
a person attains them through the worship of Puruṣottama.
The turning away from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is said to be the duty of the minister;
it is the abode that grants the sole fruit of liberation, the supreme southern gate.
Having reached the Siddhāyatana, one finds there the fourfold divine [assembly].
Having propitiated the self-manifested form of the Enemy of Madhu— which consists of human, rishi, and divine forms— one who desires liberation, being composed in mind,
attains without doubt the fourfold liberation beginning with *sālokya*.

From a human [liṅga] one attains sālokya; from one fashioned by a ṛṣi, sāmīpya; from one fashioned by a god, sārūpya; and from one that is self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta), one attains the same [state of sāmānya] in due order.
And when the conch is blown at the gate of the temple, there arises for him a great sound.
It is heard that in a Vaiṣṇava region within the human abode, [the merit] is twofold; in a region created by the Ṛṣis it is threefold;
and in a self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) region, prosperity increases progressively fourfold.
Devoted to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), sleeping on *kuśa* grass, with senses conquered,
one who desires liberation attains perfection through a hundred thousand recitations of that mantra.
One should practice according to the method of yoga upon the seat of the heart-lotus.
Having meditated upon the Person, who is seated comfortably on the pericarp, possessing the luster of pure crystal,
four-armed, with noble limbs, situated in the midst of a circle of light,
and measuring only the size of a thumb, one should [worship] with offerings in due order.
One should worship with a stainless mind, being well-composed;
by the power of yoga practice alone, the excellence of the qualities arises.
The seed consisting of the moon, sun, and fire is like the orb of the sun.

Then, the wise practitioner should know that an even subtler image, with a radiance like a royal mung bean (*rājamudga*), stands pervading all mantras. Thereafter, one should gradually contemplate it as being the size of a *rājikā* seed.
Then, that which generates [it] by means of others, at the end of which the *nāda* is supported—
having dissolved that [which has arisen], one perceives what has arisen as being the size of a horse’s tail-hair.
That [hair-like form] moves into the ether, and the ether comes into the heart.
Then one should contemplate the subtle [channel] the size of a horse's hair;
by practicing meditation with this, one quickly perceives the *brahmanāḍī*.
Then, [one perceives] a network of seeds the size of a body hair all around.
One should meditate, established in the observance that illuminates the *brahmanāḍī*;
meditating thus, one should abandon this body once it is fully matured.
Having previously recognized the body and its supreme signs of ripeness.
Having brought the breath of the body to a mere cessation of its connection,
and having released it through the aperture of Brahmā by means of the method of departure (*utkrānti*),
one who is devoted to constant practice should meditate and abandon the body. (24.103–104)
He attains the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, the imperishable;
just as oil is in sesame seeds, clarified butter in ghee, milk in milk, and water in water,
so too no difference is perceived between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).
Just as water that has merged into heated iron does not emerge again,
and just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout once more,
even so, O Lotus-seated One, the individual soul (jīvātman) is not born again.
Sārūpya is declared by the wise to be the attainment of the Lord’s own form;
sāmīpya is service in the presence of the God through attendance;
and sālokya is said to be residence in the world known as Vaikuṇṭha.
"This is his eternal residence, free from rebirth.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the signs of the falling away of the body."
In brief, O Blessed One, it is the cessation of the movement of the vital air (vāyu).
O Lotus-born one, for one who is engaged in activity and moderate in food and recreation, the Blessed One [has taught this].
For one who is always disciplined in sleep and waking and constantly engaged in yoga,
the sound within the heart, like the roar of a drum, ceases forever;
and the sense of touch perceives neither cold nor excessive heat.
When the light situated between the eyebrows is established at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths],
it indeed quickly sets and does not rise again;
one established in samādhi no longer perceives the lotus within the heart.
The blood located in the body, characterized by phlegm, dries up.
One no longer perceives the scent of the earth, nor likewise that which is external or internal.
Then, after a long time, the physical mass is to be awakened [by dissolution].

Established upon the earth and concentrated in dhāraṇā, he does not perceive the previously mentioned sound at the fifth moment after the fifth [moment]. Remaining thus with steady intelligence, he no longer experiences external cold or heat.
If, having performed that meditation on form according to the previously mentioned method for four consecutive days, he observes it with focused vision,
yet the Lord of Light does not shine within the space of his heart or externally; || 24.117–24.118 ||
Indeed, alms-food must certainly be obtained when one recognizes the previously mentioned signs of death on the third day at that very moment, O Four-faced One;
provided that the yogi is correctly engaged in the Vāyavya-samādhi.

He experiences supreme bliss, yet when thirsty, he trembles. If, according to the previously mentioned method, he remains in the portion of the sky for two days, his fall occurs at the second moment of the *piṇḍa*. || 24.120-24.121 ||

By this method, the yogi whose mind is solely intent on meditation, having meditated correctly according to the rule, does not perceive smell by means of the ritual procedure, nor does he perceive anything auspicious or inauspicious externally— whether on that very day or at the first moment of the [meditative] sign. (24.122)
With his mind fixed upon me while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra,
he himself ascends from the *piṇḍa* and other stages to the abode of Yoga;
there, seated comfortably on the Śeṣa-throne in the jeweled pavilion of Vaikuṇṭha.
One should meditate upon Hari, the Lord, who has eight arms and large eyes, who wields eight weapons,
and who is adorned with all ornaments; he is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
and may have four arms, embracing the lotus-born goddess with his left hand.
Eight women stand around him, holding chowries in their hands; behind them stand those bearing weapons such as conchs and other arms.
Therefore, men serve him from within, while his physical forms remain outside.
Then there are twenty-four forms beginning with Mīna; likewise, along with the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and Viṣvaksena, and the group beginning with Kumuda,
there are the great Bhāgavatas there who meditate upon the twelve-syllable mantra.
They constantly serve in the pavilion, freed from rebirth.
Performing here such action as consists of the worship of Viṣṇu,
men, by resorting to yoga, are liberated and attain the supreme state.
Even after attaining [those states], they perform various [deeds] and serve the Supreme Person;
or else, having recognized the falling of the body through the previously mentioned signs and through worldly enjoyments, those rulers of the earth create [merit].
O Lotus-Seated One, they enter another body by means of a skillful method;
I shall now explain that, so listen with respect to these words.
[One should take] a fresh, pure, whole corpse from a person in the middle stage of life.

One should lay out the corpse in a secluded place with its face turned upward and its feet extended— whether it be the body of a Brahmin endowed with all auspicious marks and free from diseases caused by sin, or the body of a Kṣatriya. 24.134
Then, having assumed a yogic posture, one should lie down at his feet.
O Four-faced One, with one-pointed concentration, one should practice yoga as before,
[visualizing] the living soul situated in the navel-center, revolving and possessing the radiance of the sun.
Having assumed the form of a swan, white as a jasmine flower, emerging from the nostril through either the iḍā or the piṅgalā,
it travels through the sky like a bird together with the vital breaths.
O Four-faced One, having gone again and again for the distance of a *tāla*, a *hasta*, a *daṇḍa*, a *krośa*, and even a *yojana*, they turn back;
one should cause [the breath] to enter the navel-wheel through the cavity of the nostril.
Having practiced yoga constantly and without ceasing, the vigilant yogi,
having drawn his own self out from his body through the path of the nostril-passage,
[should enter] by means of the other's nostril-passage.
Upon the dissolution of his own body, he should cause the food of others to enter;
then, having entered the navel-cakra, he should move at ease through the channels.
Remaining there, the yogi should always practice as before, pervading all places.
"For the sake of strengthening the body there, having remained for a long time in happiness,
one should observe its fall and then place [the consciousness] into another physical body.
Thus, O Brahmin, this entry into another's body has been described.
For the sake of accomplishment, the root mantra has been briefly explained to you.
It is called the "root mantra" because it is the direct designator of the deity;
it gives birth to the creeper of mantras and produces the [eight] supernatural powers, such as the power of becoming minute (aṇimā) and the rest.
How much more so, O Lotus-born One, for one who desires the goals of Dharma?
There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by means of this mantra consisting of twelve syllables.
I tell you this as the truth regarding all worlds everywhere.
There exists no mantra superior to this, which grants all desires.
This imperishable majesty of the mantra has been declared as a secret;
it is indeed the most excellent among the eight forms [of Śiva] by virtue of its four syllables.
By means of this sixteen-syllable [mantra], the twenty-four forms are to be propitiated; if so, great and rare enjoyment is obtained.
Having extracted the twelve-syllable mantra from the tantra according to the previous method, [one should proceed].
One should extract four syllables from the wheel of colors. O Four-faced One,
the Sun-god, who resides in the cave and has a staff for a crest,
possesses a limb consisting of twelve syllables.
The seer of the mantra is determined to be the one who meditates upon the eight forms;
the meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and Vāsudeva is the presiding deity.
The phoneme resulting from the combination of the syllables [of the mantra] is like crystal in appearance.
The field is the supreme ether (paramavyoman), and the cognition of reality (tattvadhī) has been described previously.
For the remaining syllables, the sun, Vāsudeva, the Man-lion (nṛkesarī), and the mind-born one (manobhava) constitute the arrangement of the presiding deities for the four [syllables]. 24.153–24.154
In worship, one should recite [the mantra] ending with *namaḥ*; in both cases during the rite of fire-offering (*homakarma*), it should end with *svāhā*.
Likewise, in the rite of nourishment (*āpyāyana*), it should end with *vauṣaṭ*.
But in the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), it should end with *phaṭ*; in other cases, one should apply it accordingly.
The ritual placement (nyāsa) is performed on the head, the forehead, the two eyes, and the ears in sequence;
likewise on the two nostrils, the mouth, the hollow of the throat, the heart,
the region of the navel, the secret place, as well as on the two thighs and the two shanks.
The placement of the creation and other rites in accordance with the task at hand is for all rituals;
that worship, which is the cause of all accomplishments, is now described.
[One should meditate upon] the Sudarśana, the unsurpassed eight-spoked [discus], a treasury of splendors.
Having meditated upon the four-faced Brahmā in the eastern direction,
Saṅkarṣaṇa in the southern, Pradyumna in the direction of the lord of waters (the west),
and Aniruddha in the north, [he should place] Śrī and the others in the intermediate directions.

Having worshipped the four goddesses and Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, in the center with offerings such as the *arghya* and so forth, and having recited the mantra one hundred and sixty thousand times,
he should offer oblations into the fire and perform the libation with water according to the prescribed rule.

Thus, when the mantra has been perfected, it shall accomplish the fourfold goals of human endeavor. O Brahmin, whatever among those goals one desires to attain, all that is obtained; what is the use of other excessively elaborate methods?
O Brahmin, if a desire for the state of Brahmā arises,
one should worship the form of Brahmā, meditating with a mind focused on nothing else.
O Lotus-born One, standing on the ground on one big toe during the month of Grīṣma, [one should perform this].
Raising one leg and stretching out his arms, remaining motionless, he should dwell in a leaf-hut during the rains; outside during the autumn and the cool season;
and during these three—the winter, the spring, and the summer—in the five fires.

The recitation of mantras should be performed with a neutral mind; thus it should be done year after year. Whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is superior, and mental recitation (*mānasa*) is superior even to that.
The deities obstruct his ascetic practice, which is exceedingly difficult to perform.
Fearing a loss of his footing, the Gandharvas and others, led by the Gandharva king,
sought to entice him with celestial nymphs through dance, instrumental music, and song.
Therefore, having become firm in mind, one should attain perfection through recitation.
The Blessed Lord himself, the Lord of the Three Heavens, comes in person;
he bestows the state of Brahmā or some other great fruit. If one desires the station of his other forms as well, [he grants that too].
Meditating upon each respective form, one should recite the mantra as before.
By their grace, the practitioner shall attain his own respective supreme station;
by means of this primary mantra, the adept shall accomplish the fruit.
Whatever [fruits] belong to this world or the next, there is no need for deliberation here;
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or even a Vaiśya, he may perform the recitation (japa). No one else has the qualification for this recitation, for this king of mantras is itself supreme.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Twelve Syllables," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the Mahopanisad of the glorious Pancaratra.
[The twenty-fifth chapter begins.]
The majesty of the glorious eight-syllable mantra:
Brahmā [proclaimed] the unsurpassed greatness of this eight-syllable mantra.
Now, out of a desire to favor me, [tell me] what kind of specific meter is to be recited, along with its seer and deity;
what is considered the fruit of the muttering of that mantra, or what is its form;
and also the means for accomplishing the deity. || 25.1–25.2 ||
O Acyuta, speak to me, who am eager to hear, everything in its entirety;
for it is not possible [to describe] all the fruits of the eight-syllable mantra. (25.3)
Even in a hundred years, only a mere indication of them can be told—
[this teaching] which is auspicious and bestows the exclusive fruit of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
(25.4) For one who recites the mantra according to the prescribed number, there are manifold accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The greatness [of this] is inconceivable, like that of the Lord who is the enemy of Madhu.
(25.5) Having drawn the circle of colors upon the ground in a pure, secluded, and solitary place, free from all defects, by means of the materials for worship such as offerings and so forth. (25.6)
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should then extract the phonemes.
First, the *udgītha* [Oṃ] is to be employed, followed by Vighneśa (Gaṇeśa).
Thereafter, Mandara, conjoined with the means of Brahman (*brahmasādhana*), should be used.
Ādideva and Vrata, followed by Bhadrabāhu; then Vahni clothed in Gopana, Śvasana with Viṣṇuśīrṣaka;
thereafter Vanamālī should be employed together with Madhusūdana.
The syllables are said to be the Praṇava, the head, and Vāyu, as they arise in sequence;
Viṣṇu is the seed-syllable, and the Anusvāra is further declared to be its power.
The wise know that there are six limbs for this mantra of twelve parts.
The goddess is Gāyatrī, and the sage is remembered as Antaryāmin.
The deity is Nārāyaṇa himself; the divinity is declared to be the sense of hearing.
The supreme ether is the intellect, and the truth is likewise the white color.
O Brahmin, for every syllable, Gautama is remembered as the first seer;
followed by Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and Jamadagni;
then Vasiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, and Atri, who was born from a jar.
The Vedic meters, beginning with the Gāyatrī, and those ending with the Virāj;
Dharas, Dhruvas, Somas, Āpas, Agnis, and Jalādhipas; Pratyūṣas and Prabhātas—these are the deities for each syllable. || 25.14–25.15 ||
Space is the supreme field because it is the ultimate limit of the imperishable (akṣara).
The seven worlds beginning with Satya constitute the levels (bhūmis) in reverse order.
O Lotus-born One, for the seven [elements] ending with earth, these are the seven [levels] of the imperishables.

Fire, earth, wind, space, the sun, heaven, and then the moon, as well as the constellations and the zodiac signs—these are the principles (tattvas) in their proper order. I shall now explain the etymological interpretation (nirukta) of this mantra exactly as it is. || 25.17–25.18 ||
The word *āpaḥ* is recorded as having a feminine ending with the sense of pervasion (*vyāpti*), functioning as the agent (*kartṛ-sādhana*).
There is a transposition of the vowel *o*;
however, O Lotus-born One, there is a transposition of the letter *m* for the letter *v*, and this [form] ends in *u*.
It pervades all that is both internal and external; thus it is proclaimed.
Alternatively, it may arise from the continuous succession of threads;
thereafter, there is the elision of the letter *ṭ* and the vocalization (*prasāraṇa*) of the letter *v*.
The prefix *upa* establishes the sense of "prior," and the internal vowel modification (*guṇa*) has been applied.
That in which all this is woven is thus designated [by the word *upaniṣad*].
Because the root *ava* signifies "protection," and because the suffix *aṭil* has been elided, it functions [in this way].

It is taught that the augment *ūṭh* occurs after the vowel *v* and after the penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) when both are present. That supreme state which protects all forms through the process of *guṇa* substitution is declared to be the etymological meaning (*abhidheya*) of the *praṇava*; such is its derivation (*nirukti*).
Only the God is bowed to; He alone is their supreme refuge.
Nara is the God, the Supreme Creator, who at the beginning of creation [is present] in the waters.
Therefore, the waters are called *nārāḥ*, and He is said to have them as His *ayana* (abode).
And for the sake of that god, he is called Nārāyaṇa.
Water (nārāḥ) is the support and dwelling-place of the Person (puruṣa), the enemy of Madhu;
the suffix -aṇ is used in the sense of the base itself, and thus he is called Vāsudeva.
Having thus received this mantra correctly from the mouth of the Guru,
one who is devoted to serving the Guru shall accomplish all mantras;
remaining in celibacy, observing silence, eating pure food, and being observant of vows.
I shall now describe those foods that are fit for consumption and conducive to purity; listen to them as well.
(25.29) Milk, barley-gruel, vegetables, water, fruits, roots, parched grain flour, water infused with *kuśa* grass, curd, and food obtained by alms—these are pure and fit for eating. (25.30)
Listen to the time prescribed for the recitation of mantras during the practice:
on the twelfth day of the waxing moon in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should worship Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion, with a mind focused on no other.
Thus, with a concentrated mind, one should meditate upon the deity within the mandala of the wheel and lotus:
four-armed, with magnificent limbs, attended by weapons such as the discus, resembling a dark cloud, and possessing eyes as broad as lotus petals. (25.32–33)
Clad in yellow garments, gentle, with a face like the bright moon,
possessing a beautiful smile and lovely reddish lips, his earrings radiant with jewels;
with beautiful eyebrows and forehead and a handsome countenance, he was adorned with every ornament.
On his forehead was a gentle tilaka made of white clay, shining like a lamp;
he was adorned with shimmering bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and the Kaustubha gem,
possessing a radiant luster like the sun and graced by a forest garland.
Adorned with ornaments possessing the brilliance of a thousand suns,
his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and decorated with celestial garlands,
he sat comfortably upon a beautiful golden lion-throne together with Śrī and Bhūmi.
Having thus meditated upon the Lord of the Gods of gods, one should become intent on the recitation of the mantra.
Seated comfortably at the appropriate time, having become pure and composed,
one should worship the Lord of the World day by day and recite the mantra.

It is taught that one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred thousand times, half of that for water libations (tarpaṇa), and half of that one should offer as oblations into the fire; then the king of mantras becomes perfected.
Now, when the mantra has been thus accomplished, whether in sleep or likewise in the waking state, [it grants its fruits].
The practitioner constantly perceives the signs of success regarding the mantra.
Then, by means of that perfected mantra, he should accomplish the supreme Dharma.
Now, for one who desires the accomplishment of Dharma through the power of the mantra: || 25.41–25.42 ||
The best among those who know the mantras,
who desires liberation from all three debts and from everything else,
should fast and become pure, and [perform the rite] upon a jar or within a mandala of a lotus with a disc.
Having invoked the deity and worshipped him properly with the means of offering such as the *arghya*,
and having offered substances such as cows, gold, sesame seeds, and *kuśa*-grass water accompanied by the recitation of mantras, he shall cause [the deceased] to attain the imperishable world.
By the power of the mantra, one may [liberate] the ancestors even if they reside in hell in an instant;
Having first observed the fast on the previous day with a well-concentrated mind, the knower of mantras,
on the fifth day of the month of Māgha, should worship the mandala consisting of a wheel and a lotus, and then the Lord, the Teacher of the World, in its center.
One should sacrifice with *kṛsarā* rice and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with that very same substance;
likewise, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sesame seeds with the mantra,
pronouncing the names of the ancestors and others, joined with the word "tāraya" (save).
Having arranged his sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), at the conclusion of the fire-oblation,
facing south and having spread kuśa grass with its tips pointing southward upon the ground, he should remain absorbed in meditation;
and having meditated upon the divine Nārāyaṇa, he should offer libations of water mixed with sesame seeds.
That inexhaustible water, when offered, shall bring satisfaction to the ancestors.
Having gratified the Brahmins of virtuous conduct who are absorbed in the Blessed One,
one should feed at least twelve of them a meal endowed with the six flavors.
Then he should give them sesame seeds, garments, cows, gold, and so forth.
Then, with a concentrated mind, having placed the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) on his left arm,
he should place darbha grass with its tips pointing south upon the ground in front of the Blessed One.
Having spread out the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing forward and being well-seated facing south,
he should take mouthfuls of the food placed in the vessel— curd, sesame seeds, and jujube fruit— and while pronouncing the mantra, he should offer those equal-sized balls of food.
With the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," he should scatter [the offerings] upon the sacrificial grass (barhis).
Having pronounced the lineage name, he should perform the sprinkling with water for the fathers;
likewise, he should offer cakes (piṇḍas) to the fathers, to the maternal uncles, to the brothers, and to the teacher.

Established in meditation, the knower of mantras should offer rice balls (piṇḍas) preceded by the pouring of water to the teacher, as well as to others and his kinsmen, while reciting this mantra and meditating upon the god Nārāyaṇa Hari.
The wise man should perform the ritual rinsing once again.
Having performed this according to the rule, he is instantly liberated from the [three] qualities (guṇas) and,
ascending a divine celestial chariot (vimāna), goes to the eternal Brahman.
One who is unable to easily perform various kinds of fasts should worship the Lord situated in the center of the disc and lotus with offerings such as the *arghya* and other requisites,
using this perfected mantra and the fourfold food offerings.

Having offered one hundred and eight pieces of fuel-wood with clarified butter into the fire, he should feed Brahmins made of that same substance and give gifts according to his means. Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Gods, remaining firm in his vow and with senses subdued— (25.62–63).
The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Parāka, the Kṛcchra, as well as the Sāntapana,
the year-long fast, and likewise fasting on the Ekādaśī;
[these are performed] on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and also during vows such as the Jayantī.

Whatever supreme fruit has been declared for each individual fast, one should know that the fruit of the rite of worship is a hundredfold greater than that. One who desires the fruit of sacrificial acts shall obtain that very fruit.

The fruit of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) is obtained through worship for seven days; likewise, by the investiture of the *pavitra* thread, by the fulfillment of vows and other rites, by ritual bathing, during festivals, and by attending to the five daily observances (*pañcakāla*).
Whatever fruit is obtained from the construction of gate-towers, temples, halls, and the like, as well as from images,
and from the gift of sacred fields, groves, ponds, and so forth to the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu),
and from the offering of lamps with ghee— that fruit is multiplied a thousandfold.
The fruit of propitiating the Lord of Wealth is swiftly realized; no deliberation is required here.
Having invoked the God—the enemy of Madhu—into the transit [of the sun], into the mandala, into the water-pot, and into the fire, one should worship Him with the four kinds of supreme foods.

One should offer oblations into the fire one hundred and eight times with this mantra. One should then affectionately feed those who are devoted to that [deity] and give gifts according to one's wealth.
Whatever fruit has been declared for each respective dharma, [that shall be attained].

The fruit of each respective [rite] shall be a hundred times greater through that particular mantra. During the northern solstice, in the month of Kumbha, before the fire in a mandala of a lotus-wheel, having become pure and fasting, one should invoke the Teacher of the World.
One should sacrifice as before, and afterwards perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before.
(25.74) Now, if a person desires a mantra that accomplishes worldly aims, the knower of mantras, having prepared an auspicious mandala, should worship therein. (25.75)
With sesame seeds, bilva fruits, fuel-sticks, nimba flowers, and rice,
with campaka, mallikā, mālatī, and karavīra flowers,
and with nandyāvarta and yūthikā flowers— one hundred of each— [he should offer].
O Four-faced One, the wise one should offer oblations with this knowledge for seven days;
by the power of this mantra, he obtains inexhaustible wealth.
[He should offer] sandalwood, saffron, costus, yellow pigment, and lac.
Having ground camphor (ghanasāra) and musk (mṛgamada) with their own powder-water,
one should draw the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) upon the ground for seven nights with undistracted mind.
One should worship him with offerings beginning with perfumes and present him with rice cooked in molasses (gulaudana).
Then, having stepped upon the heart of the Giver of Wealth with his foot,

one who has conquered the senses and is the best among those who know mantras should recite the King of Mantras ten thousand or even a million times, while meditating on the god Nārāyaṇa at its conclusion.

O Four-faced One, by means of the mantras of Māṇibhadra and others, and through their power, one directly perceives the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), who instantly bestows inexhaustible wealth brought from his own abode by the lords of riches.
Having performed meditation for seven days within the auspicious maṇḍala,
and having offered oblations at its conclusion, the best of practitioners, having meditated upon himself as the god Nārāyaṇa, should perform the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas.
Standing outside the agrahāra, seeing the pure surface of the earth,
many treasures likewise become visible to him.
Or, one who knows the mantra, having anointed his eyes with collyrium, [perceives them] by means of this mantra.
He beholds treasures that are difficult to attain and desired, at that very moment.
Having first worshipped the god Janārdana in the auspicious Maṇḍala,
he then fastens the sacrificial wood to the shoulder of the bull and [places] the plow upon it.
One may extract pure gold and jewels from white earth;
thus one attains a great desired object, O Lotus-Seated One.
Likewise, having prepared an auspicious mandala near an anthill, [one achieves success].

One should worship the deity as before; finally, upon anthills, one should cast an offering to the Nāgas consisting of ground flour mixed with coconut water. Having dug down to the site of the anthill, one will see great wealth there.
Having washed the spade, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at night;
having worshipped the deity upon a mandala or a svastika and likewise offered oblations,
one should further offer one hundred and eight oblations, and then, at dawn, cast [the spade] into the ground.

One should dig in pure ground with a spade and obtain very great wealth. Having prepared processed mercury and held it in the hand, one who is composed should recite the mantra a million or ten million times, according to one’s ability.

By the mere touch of its liquid, everything— whether stone or a clod of earth heated by fire— would undoubtedly turn into gold. And all medicinal herbs, O Lotus-born One, would become endowed with its essence.
Just as iron, when brought into contact with [mercury], produces great gold,
so too, for those possessed of wealth, what limit can there be to the ocean of their desires?
To attain that [state], one should form a lotus-mandala and meditate upon it therein.
Having first worshipped Mantreśa with one-pointed mind as before,
the wise practitioner should perform oblations for seven days according to the prescribed method. Recalling the Lord who possesses the luster of a ruby, he should mutter the mantra.
If one desires the rare enjoyment of women according to the number previously mentioned,
then, having reflected upon the fruit, once the fire-oblation rite is completed,
all those excellent women pray for the accomplishment of eightfold childhood.

Those afflicted by desire do not abandon the best of mantra-knowers as long as they live. One who desires a maiden should worship the god whose banner is Garuḍa and offer a thousand oblations day after day with ripe fruits, flowers, and parched grain.
At its conclusion, one obtains a desired maiden; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now describe the yantra that brings about subjugation; listen to it exactly as it is.
One should draw an eight-spoked wheel on birch bark using yellow pigment (rocanā) and other substances.

With these fragrant substances— sandalwood of two kinds, saffron, camphor, and musk— as well as others, one should draw with a golden needle a wheel possessing eight spokes, complete with a hub and rim, and endowed with flames. (25.103)
O Lotus-born One, one should clearly write eight syllables in the eight directions, proceeding clockwise; the syllable *hrīṃ* is in the central square,
and the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) along with the syllable *oṃ* follows immediately after it.
One should project the syllable *huṃ* into the navel-circle and into the eight directions;

the syllable *hrīṃ*, the letter for subjugation, [is placed] upon the rim of the wheel. Likewise, in all directions, one should perform the act of subjugation accompanied by the word "subdue" (*vaśam kuru*).
Having invoked the Lord of Gods into that [liṅga] and worshipped him, one should then mutter the mantra.
One should offer one thousand and eight oblations;
for him who wears the pill, everything immediately comes under his control.
Alternatively, having taken dust from the feet mixed with red sandalwood and fashioned a representation in either male or female form as desired,
one should meditate upon Hari as being present within that image.
One should strike [the target] with red flowers from the *hayamāraka* plant while reciting the root mantra.
There should be a daily recitation of the mantra one thousand and eight times;
at the end of seven days, through this recitation, a woman or even a man will become submissive.
For as long as one lives, by means of wealth given or according to one's own desire,
through ten thousand oblations of sesame, rice, and dūrvā grass respectively,
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are brought under control by the power of the mantra.
Or, by means of an oblation with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, one shall bring Vaiśyas under control.
Or, by an oblation with *audumbara* fuel-sticks or even with *palāśa* fuel-sticks,
Brāhmaṇas become submissive according to the previously mentioned number of oblations.
If one offers oblations into the fire ten times with fuel-sticks of *apāmārga* sprinkled with three sweet substances, the king will become submissive in an instant.
It is taught that subjugation may also be achieved with fuel-sticks of *aśvattha* or *khadira*.

By means of a collection of fuel-sticks from the *vaṭa* tree, all Vaiśyas are brought under control. But a Śūdra is brought under one's power in an instant by an oblation of *plakṣa* wood fuel-sticks,
while applying a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) made of clay mixed with fragrant substances.
Merely by being seen, the knower of mantras brings people under his control;
having meditated upon the moon in the palm of his hand, with Hari situated in its center—seated comfortably upon the pericarp of a lotus, radiant white in hue. (25.118)

By meditating and touching with the palms of one's hands, everything becomes subject to one's will in an instant. Having touched food to be chewed, food to be eaten, as well as drinks, fruits, or even flowers, and reciting the mantra a thousand times, one brings everything that is given under control.
I shall describe the procedure for attraction; O Brahmin, attend to it.
One should draw an eight-spoked wheel on birch bark according to the previous method.
A wise person should write the mantra with fragrant substances using a golden needle.
One should wrap that consecrated yantra with a golden thread;
having placed it within a sheath of peacock feathers and meditated upon it, one should then recite the mantra joined with the person's name, saying, "Being enraged, draw [them] forth! (25.122–123).
The wise one, having conquered his senses, should recite [the mantra] one thousand times daily for seven days,
meditating upon himself as Hari mounted on Garuḍa, possessing eight arms and holding weapons,
resembling a Bandhūka flower in color.
Immediately thereafter, having meditated upon Goddess Lakṣmī seated on the left lap of Hari, overwhelmed with passion, and holding a noose and a goad,
one should bind the king by the neck with nooses and strike him with the goad and other weapons.
With weapons at his back, having recited the mantra accompanied by the *ākarṣaṇa* (attracting) words ten thousand times for seven days,
the practitioner swiftly brings even a king from a distance of a hundred *yojanas* by the power of the mantra.

Kings endowed with great wealth come of their own accord; by performing this rite, they become submissive. One who knows the mantra may likewise bring even Brahmins and others, and by performing this ritual, he may also attract women.
One should visualize a woman pierced in all her limbs by the five arrows of the God of Love,
bound with nooses, and likewise severely struck by other weapons; in this way,
like the speed of an arrow, one shall lead that solitary woman within seven days.
Even if she is situated at a distance, such as the king's queen herself, she,
afflicted by desire and with eyes unsteady from intoxication, presents herself; or else, she does so through one who has attained great wealth, or by means of riches according to her wish.
She satisfies the practitioner through the recitation of mantras as previously described,
or by means of substances such as *rocanā* (yellow pigment) applied to the skull of a dead woman;
having drawn the wheel as before, one should place the beloved woman in its center.
Having written her name upon that skull and heated it again in the fire, one should recite the mantra for seven days according to the previously mentioned count;
then that woman will be accomplished as desired, even if she is situated at a distance.
Now listen as the accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the yakṣas and yakṣīs is being told:
having constructed a hut at a banyan tree (*vaṭavṛkṣa*), one should worship the deity there within a maṇḍala of a wheel and lotus, and offer oblations with fuel-sticks of the banyan tree.
Having recited the mantra ten times every day for seven days,
the practitioner should first draw a yakṣa or a yakṣī upon a banyan tree with saffron and other substances; then, facing it himself, he should personally perform all those rites.

On the seventh day, at night, when the banyan tree trembles, the one most skilled in mantras should remain there undaunted and burn guggulu mixed with clarified butter as incense. Rising up facing the banyan tree, he should [invoke] either a yakṣī or a yakṣa.
One directly perceives her or him, or may request whatever supreme desire one wishes for;
whether motherhood, sisterhood, or brotherhood as it truly is,
or fatherhood, or even wifehood— one shall obtain everything desired.
The Yakṣī and the Yakṣa bestow [their power] upon the practitioner as is appropriate;
if she is his mother, she protects him like a mother, and if he is his father, he protects him like a father.
In the same way, other relatives such as brothers and so forth likewise devote themselves to protecting him according to their respective roles.
Listen to another procedure for the subjugation of a Vidyādhara:
one should perform worship and other rites at the foot of an Aśoka tree on the ground, as before;
whatever can be accomplished by a Vidyādhara shall also be possible for this [practice]. (25.143–144)
One should perform this rite according to the rules for the other classes of divine beings as well;
being pleased by the mantra, they will all grant everything exactly as requested. Now listen also to the secret means of accomplishing the netherworld (pātāla) exactly as it is.
Having performed the rites such as worship at the conclusion of the fire-oblation as prescribed, one should,
with single-minded focus, recite the eight-syllable mantra one hundred thousand times near the entrance of the cave,
using wood from milk-exuding trees, *śamī*, *dūrvā* grass, sesame seeds, and so forth.
The most excellent practitioner should perform ten thousand oblations for each [deity]; then,
from that subterranean opening, a long-eyed maiden, afflicted by desire, emerges of her own accord along with a retinue of a thousand.
Having taken the minister to her own palaces, she enjoys herself at her pleasure with various divine and superhuman delights. Furthermore,
she should cause a sacrificial pavilion to be constructed beside the entrance to Pātāla.
One should fashion a lotus-wheel there, adorned with banners and archways and beautified by water-pots at the gates, having meditated upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
then, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with the previously mentioned number of offerings, one should sacrifice as before.

Restraining his senses and focused on no other thought, he limited his food to eight hundred thousand [mouthfuls]. At that very moment, the daughters of the lord of nāgas, overcome by the god of love and surrounded by thousands of attendants, stood before the minister.
Having been won over by other maidens equal to herself,
those [nāga women] take the minister and, having entered the excellent city of the nāga abode,
they subjugate the minister with various enjoyments.

Having drunk the elixir (*rasāyana*), he shall sport with those who are timid until the dissolution of all beings, like the Lord of the Gods in heaven; now the wondrous accomplishment of the sword (*khaḍgasādhana*) will be described exactly as it is.
The practitioner, having ground together blood from the body and charcoal from a cremation ground,
should smear a beautiful sword four tālas in length. Then,
in a cremation ground, the wise one, touching its base, should recite the mantra.
At midnight, in a secluded place, he emits flames until such time as they blaze forth.
O Four-faced One, by these flames the ten directions are made beautiful;
various kinds of beings become causes of fear.

Fearless and unmoving, thus concentrated, one should recite the mantra while firmly grasping the sword with the hand as it flashes. Reciting the mantra, one goes through the sky to where the Vidyādharas and others dwell.
By the power of this knowledge, that king becomes a knower of mantras;
he is a conqueror of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Daityas—how much more so among mortals?
Always with sword in hand and chanting the mantra, he goes to the third heaven.
There too, he obtains a multitude of celestial nymphs as his retinue;
or else, having taken up a sword and quickly rendered himself invisible with leaves derived from the *pippala* tree, he should perform one million recitations (*japa*).
One should offer oblations with sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, and seeds, at least ten thousand times.
Having smeared a sword with human blood, elephant ichor, and bear bile, mixed with rājāvarta, one should worship Hari with them.
In that regard, it is taught that one should touch the sword while reciting the mantra according to the previously mentioned method;
after eight hundred and eight recitations, heat and other signs will arise.
When heat occurs, the accomplishment is inferior; when smoke arises, it is middling.
When a supreme fire is seen, one who himself carries a sword may thereafter wander through the desired worlds and obtain abundant enjoyments.
One should write the mantra within the interior of a conch-shell or a pearl-oyster using water mixed with *gorocanā*.
Having touched [the object], one should recite the supreme mantra until the appearance of flames. Then, a maiden who grants all boons shall arise from within it.
She provides a forehead mark (tilaka), a rosary (akṣamālā), a pill (gulikā), collyrium (añjana), and magical sandals (pādukā).
By the power of the mantra, that maiden gives everything to the minister: divine medicine, mercury, and *rasāñjana* placed in a skull-cup.
For him who bears the *tilaka*, men, women, deer, and other creatures [become submissive].

Merely by recollecting it, that [deity] certainly appears before one's eyes. A mantra recited with that rosary, even without the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), swiftly grants him all desired objects.
Having placed the pill in his mouth, he wanders fearlessly throughout the entire world as he pleases and attains a long life;
with eyes anointed by this ointment, he becomes invisible even to gods and asuras.
Merely by touching his sandals, he moves through fire and water;
or he may quickly go to whatever distant place he desires.
By consuming a divine medicinal herb, even a malignant disease perishes in an instant.
Even leprosy and other such diseases are incurable; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
O Brahmin, even stones and the like, when touched by the lord of mercury (rasendra) and heated in fire, become gold; and likewise, having drunk the elixir (rasāyana), one becomes so. 25.176–25.177
Though he be powerful, radiant, and free from wrinkles and grey hair,
one should cast him into the fire of a skull and place him upon the head of an enemy.
Or else, his kinsmen and friends shall die, gasping for breath, along with their entire lineage.
Displaying an illusion like a magical net, one should draw the goddess Māyā upon the ground—
black, four-armed, gentle, adorned with all ornaments,
and beautiful in every limb; then, having worshipped her, the practitioner of mantra should perform recitation.
Whether ten thousand or a hundred thousand times, the mantra known as the eight-syllabled one brings success into the palm of one's hand— that goddess is a great fourfold army;
on earth and in the sky, it is a wondrous force with weapons raised.
Having quickly shown herself to the mantra-practitioner by means of the mantra, she grants the accomplishment of the mantra;
when pleased, she reveals even the entire three worlds. This is called the pill (*gulikā*), O Brahmin; its manufacture is now described.
Having ground together realgar, kuṣṭha, yellow orpiment, saffron, gorocana, and cakrāṅga with the three sweets (honey, sugar,
and ghee), one should form a pill and place it in the center of a wheel and lotus.
Or one should worship the imperishable Hari on the night of the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
Having performed worship on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), one should recite the mantra as before;
thereafter, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) in the fire with ghee a thousand times.
This perfected pill shall indeed accomplish everything for the practitioner.
O Brahmin, I shall now describe the rite for accomplishing a *vetāla* exactly as it is:
[one should take] a young man, whether a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, who has died without any wounds.
At that very moment, having seized him, one should place him in an empty house.
Having washed away all impurity and placed him within the wheel-lotus,
one should stand in meditation, pressing his heart with the foot.
One should recite the mantra day and night; at midnight, the corpse trembles.
Fearlessly, one should strike its body with consecrated white mustard seeds.
As the body trembles, it rises up and stands before [the practitioner].
Then, with palms joined in reverence, saying "What shall I do? to that minister, he gives him whatever is desired:
a chosen sword, as well as a divine medicinal herb and an elixir (*rasāyana*).
The pill, the sandals, the perfected elixir contained within a bamboo tube,
the foot-ointment, the rosary, or whatever else is difficult for men to obtain—
by means of the foot-ointment, the wise man travels through the skies.
The slaughter of enemy armies and even of lions by means of a sword [is described];
the fruit of all divine medicinal herbs has been previously declared; and now follows the ritual procedure for the pacification of diseases, beginning with epilepsy.
Having first constructed a pavilion on a piece of ground free from thorns,
one should place twenty-five jars that are unblemished and endowed with auspicious marks,
filled with substances such as ghee measuring one *droṇa* each.
One should arrange water-pots at the four doors along with sacred threads, kusa grass, lids, and cloths; and one should consecrate each and every jar individually with the mantra. (25.197–198)

With each [syllable] of the eight-syllabled mantra, at least one hundred and eight times, [one should worship] with water from the night, sandalwood, and white *dūrvā* sprouts. On the surface of the *bhūrja* leaf, there is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
Outside the lotus, one should draw an eight-spoked wheel provided with a hub and rim.
One should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the region of the pericarp, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the center,
the eight syllables on the eight petals, and the consonant (*sparśākṣara*) in the hub.
O Four-faced One, in the field of the rim, one should again place the vowels upon the eight spokes beginning with *ya*;
then, conjoined with the fire of Mahāmāyā, [one places] Bhāskara and Daṇḍaśekhara in the cardinal and intermediate directions of the rim in due order.
Having done this, and having wrapped it continuously with a white thread,
one should place the pill inside a jar situated in the midst of a drona-measure of rice.
Then, having invoked the Lord of Mantras from the heart into that lotus of the wheel, [one should worship him].
With white garments such as sandalwood paste and other similar flowers,
and with śāli rice, one should worship Hari with a well-composed mind—
[Hari] who stands within the orb of the full moon and pours forth the essence of nectar.
Having meditated upon Hari Nārāyaṇa, who resembles a hundred moons, one should utter at the end: "Grant great peace.
Then, when the moon has risen in the direction [of the north], one should [perform the rite] in a circular pit using rice grains mixed with *śrīrājya*.
One should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) for seven days with *guggulu*, honey, and seeds,

using the previously mentioned number of oblations. One should bathe the afflicted person with water from jars placed there while reciting the root mantra, and one should likewise meditate upon Janārdana.

With one-pointed mind, he visualizes [the nectar] resembling a hundred full moons, flowing with the essence of ambrosia from his lotus feet; entering through the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), it floods [the body], which is everywhere afflicted by disease.
Having meditated, the knower of mantras should recite the root-vidyā for one afflicted by disease;
by placing that pill beneath [the patient] while fixing it upon his head,
all [ailments] such as epilepsy and the like are pacified by the power of the mantra.
Then, taking an earthen vessel, or one made of bronze, or even one made of wood,
and having placed within it nectar (pīyūṣa) combined with curd and clarified butter,
as well as cooked rice, he should offer this *bhūtabali* at the root of a sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*) or the like.
At the end, one should feed the Brahmins and give them gifts according to one's wealth.
I shall now describe to you the rite for prosperity (*pauṣṭika*); the pavilion and other preparations should be as before.
One should draw the *yantra* on birch bark as previously described, joined with the lotus and other elements.
One should write the Śrībhūmi mantra upon the filaments and the petals;
having wrapped the pill with red threads, one should place it in a jar of honey. Then, one should invoke the omnipresent Lord of Mantras, who has the luster of coral.
In the northern direction, there should be a lotus-pool and pitchers with red cloths;
all the materials as prescribed should be present if possible. And at the conclusion of the rite, O Lotus-seated One, the offering of oblations (bali) must be performed.
When a rite for pacification (śāntika) has been performed, there shall indeed be a great rain.

One desiring long life, however, should offer oblations with dūrvā grass smeared with ghee as prescribed; the arrangement of the pavilion and other elements should follow the previously mentioned procedure.
O Lotus-seated One, at the conclusion of the ritual, the person to be treated should bathe with water-pots;
when this is performed according to the scriptures, he attains abundant longevity.
One who desires health should worship Hari within the solar mandala.
One should worship [the deity] of golden luster through knowledge, using offerings such as arghya according to the prescribed method, as previously described.
There should be recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and so forth; the homa is performed with guggulu resin.
At the conclusion of the recitation, the self-possessed practitioner should always bow down with the eight limbs [of prostration].
Through the power of the mantra, one obtains longevity and health;
for one afflicted by fever, there shall be peace through *amṛtā* and mango sprouts.
All else is as previously stated according to the prescribed ritual.
At the end, there shall be a pacification of fever through the power and majesty of the vidyā.
(25.224) Whether an image is fashioned from sandalwood and other trees or from metals, when worshipped as before, it swiftly grants all desires. (25.225)
O Lotus-Seated One, the fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with substances appropriate to the ritual;
by touching an aśvattha tree with the right hand on Saturdays while reciting [the mantra] the previously mentioned number of times, one shall not suffer untimely death.

Having touched either powdered *vacā* mixed with ghee, or *brāhmī* soaked in ghee, or even the juice of *jyotiṣmatī*, one should drink it while reciting [the mantra] a hundred thousand times when an auspicious moment has arrived; for him, the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) is certain. (25.227–25.228)
Or, in a vessel made of udumbara wood, one should place four *pala* of cow's clarified butter mixed with the powder of white *vacā*,
when the moon is conjoined with the asterism Maghā;
or during the auspicious *Sārasvata-yoga*, [one should worship] the white-colored, four-armed [deity].
Having worshipped the God seated comfortably upon a white lotus in the center of a lunar disc, one should offer oblations of cow’s ghee according to the prescribed rite;
thereafter, while touching the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one obtains supreme speech.
Having visualized oneself as having eight arms, resembling the moon, seated comfortably upon the serpent Śeṣa as a throne, one should cover the opponent with a loincloth; then,
strike the tongue with a mace, the heart with a mace, and the head with goads.
Having bound his body with nooses, one should strike his back with a mace;
then, having placed the Māhendra [mantra] at the tip of the staff within the very middle of his tongue, the wise practitioner should paralyze his speech while meditating in this manner.
Between oneself and the opponent debater, there should be a curtain.
Having recited the mantra a hundred times, the debater should utter his speech.
Immediately, the defeat of the other will occur and victory for oneself.
In the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), there shall be no fault whatsoever, even if it is directed externally against an opponent.

(25.236) If one desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) should be made from the *brahma* tree; or, for a minister desiring sovereignty, there should be an oblation (*homa*) of white lotuses. (25.237)
The fuel sticks should be red in color; O Lotus-born One, [one should offer] bilva flowers, or else *sumanasa* flowers, or those produced from the Bodhi tree,
[to the deity] seated upon a white lotus throne in the center of the lunar disc.
Standing two cubits tall, he was handsome and adorned with the ornaments of childhood;
in his state of youth, he possessed the luster of the bright moon and dark blue locks of hair.
A silver vessel was filled with food consisting of milk-rice (pāyasa).
Having meditated upon the God with a concentrated mind— holding a morsel of curd-rice in his left hand and bestowing [it] with the other—
he should offer oblations of food into the fire; thus he shall obtain abundant food.
One who desires cattle should perform a fire-oblation with cow-dung and their milk;
through the power of the mantra, the knower of mantras immediately obtains a cow.
One who desires land should perform a fire-oblation with earth; he obtains land that is otherwise difficult to attain.

O Four-faced One, through oblations of fruits produced from the *bilva* tree, there arises prosperity for the kingdom; and for one desiring garments, [there is success] through oblations of seasonal flowers, white,
black, and other colors, performed ten million times.
He obtains various kinds of garments; there is no doubt in this. Whatever variety of grain the practitioner desires, all that he obtains through the fire-oblation by the power of the mantra.
A seed sown when consecrated with the syllables of the mantra will yield abundant fruit.
One desiring a son, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), should worship the Teacher of the World;
having performed the rites such as the installation of the water-pot within the mandala of the lotus-circle, [he shall succeed].
Having sprinkled her with the waters from the jars placed there at the conclusion of the oblation— just as before with the milk-rice— he should have the woman who has come there drink that water;
she shall obtain many desired sons, skilled in learning.
Having worshipped the Lord Nārāyaṇa according to the prescribed method on the Discus-Lotus,
one shall become empowered to both favor and restrain all beings; likewise,
one shall possess the power to cause the earth and other elements to tremble and to split even the mountains.
Just as Hari is the agent of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the oceans, or even the paralyzing of serpents,
so too [one becomes such] in an instant through meditation on the God of gods and the recitation of his mantra.

O Four-faced One, by the power of this mantra, malevolent beings headed by bhūtas and vetālas perish; of this there is no doubt. Having steadied one bitten by poison and meditated upon the one whose banner is Garuḍa, [the poison departs].
Having recited the mantra of the deity and the vidyā, one should strike with the sharp-beaked [tool] upon the head of the one bitten by poison,
while meditating on Garuḍa with his two wings;
thus, having dispelled all the poison, one should raise up the dead.
Food, seed, or fruit that has been mixed with poison, when consumed,
