is digested immediately by means of this knowledge, and it destroys every defect.
Furthermore, for one who desires it, there shall be inexhaustible increase of wealth.
Having touched everything with the mantra recited many times, one should cast it [into the fire].
Meditating upon oneself as identical with the Blessed One, resembling a *bandhūka* flower in hue,
the angry king will be pacified once he has entered that assembly hall.

All unmentioned accomplishments, even those that are extremely extensive, are achieved through the power of the mantra in this scripture; one attains divinity. One who desires rain should go outside to a hall prepared according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed the rites such as the mandalas of the wheel and lotus as before,

the wise practitioner should offer oblations for seven days with fuel-sticks sprinkled with clarified butter— specifically those made of cane— at the count of one hundred thousand or ten thousand each day.
Rain falls in that kingdom or that region within three days [by performing the rite] with mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*) mixed with *marīca* and *kṣuṇṇa*,
using the previously mentioned number of oblations; furthermore, excessive rain is pacified by this same *homa*.

One who desires to attain the state of a deity or other such status, through knowledge, obtains that very wondrous fruit corresponding to the greatness of the desired world, such as heaven; of this there is no doubt. (25.263–25.264)
In the same way, one who desires to obtain another jewel such as the *cintāmaṇi* or other qualities of status,
the knower of mantras attains it through ten million recitations of the mantra.
One who desires to behold the deity who is the presiding divinity of the mantra must have conquered the senses.
For six months, one should recite the mantra incessantly, remaining established in its meditation.
O Four-faced One, by the majesty of the mantra, the Lord of the gods appears before the minister in an instant and bestows upon him boons that are difficult to obtain and according to his desire.

Whatever accomplishment for other mantras is proclaimed in the ritual manual (kalpa), all of that shall be successfully attained through the power of this very [mantra] alone. So too are the six limbs, the Vedas, and hundreds of other mantras.
Furthermore, the entirety of all that consists of speech is perfectly contained within this mantra.
For those desiring freedom from rebirth, the eight-syllabled mantra is considered the ultimate refuge. Whatever great sin has been accumulated in this life or in past lives—
By the mere recitation of that mantra, [the obstacle] certainly goes to destruction.
Dying while remaining pure and uttering this mantra,
one attains the Vaiṣṇava abode, which is difficult to reach and imperishable.

What need has he for many mantras, what need has he for extensive learning, for him who has brought this vidyā, which accomplishes all aims, under his control? Those who hear and recite this greatness of the mantra—

The wise have also declared the fruits for those [other observances] as previously described. Even the four-faced Brahmā, while demonstrating its fruits with his four mouths, did not reach the end of its vastness; therefore, this brief summary has been uttered.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Majesty of the Auspicious Eight-Syllable Mantra," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the Mahopanisad of the glorious Pancaratra.
[The Twenty-sixth Chapter begins.]
The extraction of the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī and other mantras:
O Brahman, the Blessed Lord [taught] the Vaiṣṇava Gāyatrī consisting of twenty-four syllables.
Listen, I shall speak; the supreme secret is now being told.
Having worshipped the wheel of the Mātṛkās, one should extract the beginning of the meters:
the Primordial God (Ādideva) is the head here, and immediately after that, Vighneśa.
Ending with fire (va), it is the protection (go); the five branches (pa) are known as Viṣṇu’s head (śiras).
Sumukha is joined with protection (go), and another is possessed of the wind (ma) and so forth.
It rests upon Māyā (mā), the abode of nectar (su), and following Vaidhara is Mandara.
Viṣṇuśīrṣa, Bhāskara, and then that presided over by Mādhava; Ādidevasamākrānta, Kumbha, and Śuklodayāvaha; Vaidhara, Devatānta, and Pīyūṣarucirāśirā—these follow in sequence. (26.4–26.5)
Anila begins and ends with the *praṇava* (om), has Mahāmāyā as its head in sequence;
then Dhanada, followed by Dakṣa, then Viṣṇumūrdhā, and then Bhāskara.
Vairāja has Māyā as its head and ends with Viṣṇu, joined with Bhadrapāṇi.
Otadeha is the supreme Kumbha; Trivikrama is remembered as the next.
Krodhana and Vanamālya—these two extend to the end of the worlds.
Visarga and Pāpahantā are joined with the first syllable, Vahni. || 26.7–26.8 ||
The letter *ca*, the *u* vowel, the letter *ta*, the letter *de*, the letter *ha*, the two [dots] (*dvau*), the *dṛṣṭi* (the *bindu*), and the one situated on the head of Viṣṇu (*mūrdhaga*);
the letter *da*, the letter *ra*, both *go* and *pana*, and the *ūrṇa* of Vijaya extracted.
26.9 The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, the seer is Brahmā, and the presiding deity is Brahman.
O Lotus-born One, the six limbs of Viṣṇu, as well as Kruddholkā and the others,
are considered to be the placement of syllables from the head down to the feet;
[specifically] upon the head, the forehead, the two eyes, and likewise the two nostrils.
The placement [of mantras] is upon the two ears, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the two armpits,
as well as the two elbows and likewise the two wrists;
[and it is performed] on the two hands, the middle of the belly, the private parts, the two thighs, and the two shanks.
O Four-faced One, the placement [of mantras] upon the feet is likewise declared in this sequence:
yellow, red, smoke-colored, white, black, and crimson;
likewise, the colors of the Valarṣa [mantra] are yellow, red, dark-blue, and resembling a conch shell.
It is pale-red, resembling crystal, yellow, like silver,
similar to the rays of the moon, and like the filaments of a lotus; it has the luster of stars, the hue of the bandhujīva flower, and the brilliance of the constellations.
Resembling a hibiscus flower, with the luster of molten gold.
And the distinction of the colors among the classes was shown as having the radiance of the sun;
[he saw] Acyuta, gentle, resembling a dark cloud, four-armed, wearing a crown,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and mounted upon Garuḍa.

Having meditated thus, one should worship the God at the time of dawn with a concentrated mind. Having worshipped Him— who resembles a crystal stone and whose form is mounted upon Garuḍa— at midday, the self-possessed practitioner should perform his recitation (japa).
At the twilights, meditating upon the dark-complexioned, lotus-eyed one who stands upon Garuda with four arms, one should recite the mantra while observing the vow,
performing the three daily ablutions, and keeping the senses restrained. (26.20)
Through twenty-four hundred thousand recitations of the mantra, one attains success.
The practitioner who knows the mantra, performing libations with water and the rite of fire-oblation (homa),
obtains every desired accomplishment that is otherwise very difficult to attain.
Subsisting on cow’s urine and barley gruel, one should recite the mantra a hundred thousand times without sloth;
one is liberated even from great sins—of this there is no doubt.
Drinking the *brahmakūrca* and reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times, the wise man [attains his goal].
The best of mantra-knowers, liberated from sins equal to those [great crimes],
desiring to bring all the gods beginning with Brahmā under his own control,
seeking the fruits such as *aṇimā* and the like, likewise exerts himself in the practice of attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).

O Four-faced One, one who desires to bring all beings under control, to go to the netherworld (pātāla), and to always place the foremost among the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others at his own command, should practice according to the eight-syllable mantra.
By reciting once the mantra known as the Viṣṇugāyatrī,

one partakes of the merit of repeatedly studying all the branches of the Vedas; likewise, by remaining absorbed in meditation, one purifies sacrificial offerings defiled by hair, insects, and the like.
"O Lotus-born One, by touching [the object] and reciting this mantra, it becomes instantly purified;
by this, the fruit of the four root-mantras is accomplished.
I shall now declare another mantra that brings prosperity and accomplishes all aims."
O Four-faced One, listen to this supreme secret of eight syllables.
Having first drawn the wheel of letters (varṇacakra) and having worshipped it properly,
one who knows the power of mantras should extract the eight-syllabled mantra that bestows prosperity.
First, one should extract the *tāra* (the syllable Om), and immediately after that, the rising [syllable].
Then follows the one with two eyes (the letter *i*), the *māyā* (the letter *ī*), the wrathful one (*krodhana*, the letter *huṃ*), and the syllable of the Kaustubha gem (*phaṭ*).
After that, the head of Viṣṇu (*namaḥ*), then Lakṣmī (*svāhā*), and thereafter Anala (*vauṣaṭ*).
The lotus joined with Mahāmāyā is immeasurable and immediate.
O Four-faced One, beginning with Agni, the seed-syllable called Śrīkara is "Ṭhaṭha"; I shall declare its essence as it is truly uttered.
The seed-syllable is the radiant fire (Ra), with five dots and resting upon a half-moon; the six limbs, beginning with Kruddholkā, are as before. The metre is Gāyatrī, and Prajāpati is its seer.
The deity is the Lord of the gods of gods, as previously remembered for every syllable.
Now the seer, the meter, the deity, and the meditation are being described: having taken recourse to the shade of a Kalpa-tree, which is pleasant and cool. (26.36–26.37)
[He saw] the eight-armed [Viṣṇu], wearing a crown, seated comfortably upon the shoulders of the four-armed Garuḍa, who bears all ornaments;
he was as white as a kunda flower or the moon, gentle, and adorned with every kind of decoration.
His limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial garlands;
he wore yellow garments and was graced by dark blue locks of hair.
With his arms, he bore the discus, the mace, the arrow, and the goad.
With his other four auspicious right hands, he holds the conch, the Kaumodakī mace, the Śārṅga bow, and the noose; his face resembles the bright moon.
And Garuḍa, with both his hands, [holds] the two lotus feet.
Holding a jar full of nectar-water for the god with two hands,
he sat touching with his other two arms Śrī, who was seated there upon his beautiful thigh, radiant as gold and clad in silken garments.
Her limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and she was adorned with every ornament;
her beautiful brows, forehead, and crown were exquisite, and her eyes rested gracefully upon her ears.
She seemed to be raining down the nectar-water of loveliness on all sides.

Having thus meditated upon Lakṣmī, who holds a noose and a goad, and who is tormented by the arrows of Kandarpa, and having worshipped her while remaining established in the vow with senses restrained,
one should recite the mantra for twelve days while visualizing two treasures at her side.
Standing in water up to his chest with arms raised and composed in mind,
the practitioner facing the sun should offer one hundred oblations of sacrificial wood.
Likewise, he should offer [oblations] of *bilva* flowers, *lakṣmī* flowers, and milk-rice to obtain prosperity.
With eight hundred and eight grains of *śuddhodana* smeared with ghee,
when this ritual procedure is performed in this manner, unshakable nourishment (*puṣṭi*) arises;
and the previously mentioned results, such as those of the *pauṣṭika* rite, are obtained according to the previously stated number.
One should accomplish the rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika) with this mantra.
This mantra for the invocation of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is extremely difficult to obtain.
I shall proclaim its extraction; listen to it according to the sequence of its syllables.
He [saw] Udgītha, the lord of men, Viṣṇu, who was like the bearer of Mount Mandara; the foremost one of subtle vision, the other one bearing a mace, Kumbha placed [there],
Vijaya given as the beginning and the end, and the immeasurable Māhendra.
Garuḍa, Dakṣa, the other [form], Mahāmāyā, Vināyaka, the Primordial God (Ādideva), then Vahni, Gopana, and the four states;
the first, Pracaṇḍa, Ākāra, Śaṅkha, the beginning, and the syllables *ṭha-ṭha iti*.
Having extracted that sixteen-syllable seed-mantra, it is thus described.
One should extract the "jewel of the sky" (the letter *ra*) with a bindu, and the "dwarf" (*va*) with a bindu.
The limbs have been stated previously, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
Know that Śukra is the divine sage (muni) and is remembered as Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
sixteen hundred thousand recitations (japa), half of that for water libations (tarpaṇa),
and half of that again for the fire oblation (homa) of this mantra— thus they declare the fruits in their proper order.
The *mantra* for the three forms beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa is now being declared.
O Brahmin, the extraction of the first seven syllables is as previously described; the extraction of the remaining syllables is now being told in their proper sequence. (26.57–58)
Dīptimān, Vahni, Aurnava, Dhruva, Śukla, as well as Ādimān;
Bindu, Prajāpati, and the first Vahni; Ugra, then Mukha; Sumukha, Gopa, Yuta, Vāyu, Ādya, ending with Ṭhaṭha.

The mantra consists of twelve syllables; the seed-syllable and the limbs are as before. The meter is the Gāyatrī goddess, the seer is Nīlalohita, and the deity is Saṅkarṣaṇa; this is the determination of the color and the reality of the deity.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) is declared to be known as being like that of the twelve-syllable mantra.
The fruits have been stated previously; there shall be great perfection of speech (vāksiddhi).
One attains great knowledge and whatever else is further desired.
All that shall be accomplished without delay through the power of the mantra.
[He is] white as a conch shell or cow’s milk, four-armed, wearing a diadem,
clad in linen garments, and with a face resembling the full moon.
Wearing a very beautiful golden [ornament] set mostly with pearls until the end of the kalpa,
holding in his principal hand the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā),
and bearing a book in his left hand— [thus] with both arms.
In his two upper hands, he holds a crystal conch and a rosary exactly as they are;
adorned with a forest garland beautified by white flowers blooming in all seasons,
and seated comfortably upon a white lotus— thus should the knower of mantras meditate [upon him].
For one who meditates, the intellect becomes stainless and abundant knowledge arises.
By this, O Lotus-born One, one should perform rites for pacification and nourishment.
What is the use of much talk? The fruit is like that of the twelve-syllable mantra.

O Lotus-seated One, by means of this mantra, the practitioner attains everything. Now I shall speak of the Pradyumna-mantra, which bestows the fruit of all desires; its extraction is being described syllable by syllable in due order.
The extraction of the first seven syllables has been previously described; now, the extraction of its uncommon syllables is stated:
[the syllable] *pāpmānaṃ*, *analaṃ*, the Viṣṇu-mantra, and *vāyu* like the letter *u*.
Mandara, Bhadrapāṇi, Madhusūdana, and Māruta;
Āgneyī, Daśa, Eka, Arṇasa, and Saṃhanana are considered [the names].
Viṣṇu followed by the anusvāra is the seed-syllable (bīja); the limbs (aṅgas) are as before.

The seer is Sanatkumāra; the meter is said to be Gāyatrī; Pradyumna is the deity; and the mantra, the means of accomplishment, and the fruit are as previously described. Beyond this is another mantra, that of Aniruddha.

Listen, O Brahmin, to the extraction of the seven vowels in their proper sequence as it was in the past; now the extraction of the remaining vowels is being told. [The first] begins with the *praṇava*, then *bhadrahasta*, *māyā*, and *saptārcis*.
The two *udaya*s are auspicious; the first *gopana* is *vāyu*.
Its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *aprameya*, and its *visarga* is at the end.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Sanaka, and the meter (*chandas*) and deity (*devatā*) are as before.
Aniruddha, consisting of twelve syllables, has been proclaimed in sequence.
As before, there are the six limbs, the means of accomplishment, and the fruit;
and the enumeration of the twenty-four forms is by means of the twelve and so forth.
These are well-known as ending in the dative case and preceded by seven syllables;
the seed-syllables (bījas) of these [mantras] are their initial letters, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ).
With a nasal bindu at their head, they are declared to be extracted under the name of the Fourfold Array (caturvyūha).
The invocations for the eight other forms are as follows:
the first mantras are said to consist of seven syllables ending in the dative case.
[These are] Nṛsiṃha, Adhokṣaja, Acyuta, and Puruṣottama.
Janārdana, Upendra, Hari, and Kṛṣṇa are thus proclaimed;
their seed-syllables (bījas) are the initial letters [of these names], and their limbs (aṅgas) are as before.
The meter is the Gāyatrī goddess, and the deity is the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
Those various forms are the sages, and the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) is as before.
The fruit of these, consisting of both this-worldly and other-worldly results, has already been stated.
Thus [ends] the *Caryāpāda* in the *Pādmatantra*, the Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpañcarātra*.
The twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras such as the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī";
the twenty-seventh chapter:
"The Narration of the Mantras for the Matsya and Other Incarnations."
The Lord Śrī Bhagavān, following the sequence of the ten incarnations beginning with the Fish, is called Manu;
as before, one should draw the wheel of syllables. (27.1)
O Four-faced One, having taken the common phonemes as before,
that uncommon form is now being extracted in sequence:
the first [consonant] ending with the touch-sounds (sparśa), then Vijaya, then Candra, followed by Anvak, and then Caturgati.
Ādimagni, Hṛṣīkeśa, Pavitra, Madhusūdana,
Śvasana, and Aprameya— these are declared as the twelve-syllable [mantras].
Mādhava, Puruṣātmā, and Hṛṣīkeśa with the nasal bindu.
The form of the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the limbs is said to be unique:
everywhere it begins with [the letter] ending in *sparśa* (the labial *m*), and in the six [limbs] it is the first [letter] endowed with the nasal drop (*bindu*).
[These are] Ādideva, Mahāmāyā, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Gopana.

Having thus extracted the Viṣṇumauryī—the middle syllable as proclaimed in sequence within the six limbs—it should be employed. Its seer is remembered as Manu; its meter is the Gāyatrī goddess; and its deity is the Supreme Person in the form of the Fish.
The deity is formless, and the mantra is remembered as having five syllables;
its seed-syllable, its limbs, and its method of accomplishment are as before.
Now hear the extraction of the syllables of the mantra for the immediate [form] of the deity.
The uncommon form has touch and so forth as its abode in the cave (guhālaya). Fire, Mandara, and Viṣṇu—[these constitute] the twelve-syllable [mantra] as before.
The extraction of the seed-syllables is the one in the form of the Boar (Kroḍarūpī), who is the upholder of the earth and whose abode is the cave.
O Four-faced One, this seed-syllable with its anusvāra constitutes the six limbs.
Its seer is Dūrvāsas, and its meter is held to be as before.
The deity is the Lord in the form of a tortoise, who is present right now.
One should extract the mantra of the Boar-form from the wheel of syllables (varṇacakra).
Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Anala, Ādideva, Bhāskara, Gopana, Puruṣātman, and Viṣṇu—these are extracted [from it]. (27.12–27.13)
Its uncommon phonemes have been declared, and the common ones were mentioned previously;
now this seed-syllable (*bīja*), consisting of eleven syllables, is being described.
It extends up to the subtle point (*bindu*), and its sequence of limbs consists of six *ācamana*s.
The Sage Śaṅkha is the seed-syllable, and the Gāyatrī is said to be the meter. Nārāyaṇa is its deity, and the six-syllabled mantra ending in *namaḥ* is used.
Alternatively, O Lotus-seated One, the limb and the seed-syllable are exactly as before.

Having extracted the thirteen syllables previously mentioned, one should then extract the three *vyāhṛtis*. Immediately thereafter, one should extract the word "pati" (lord) in the dative case. Following that, one should say: "Grant to me the lordship over the earth. (27.17)

The sequence of thirty-two syllables ending in "dāpaya" and "ṭhaṭha" constitutes [the mantra]. The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the seer is the former one (Prajāpati), and the deity is the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
The seed-syllable has been stated; having analyzed the limbs of the mantra, one should fashion the ritual application.
One should assign the syllables, resembling gold in color, to the limbs as before;
having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra sixteen hundred thousand times without sloth.
By the power of the mantra, one shall immediately become the lord of the earth.
O Lotus-born One, its fruits include even the descent into the netherworld (pātāla) and other such powers.
A garland-mantra (mālāmantra) consisting of sixty-four syllables is observed;
first there are thirteen syllables, followed by the word *ekadaṃṣṭra*.
Likewise, having pronounced the word *megha* twice in the dative case (*caturthyanta*) in succession,
one should thereafter utter the pair of words for the color of a meteor (*ulkāvarṇa*) in the dative case,
ending with the suffix *-maya* and in the vocative case (*sambuddhyanta*).
The two forms of *loḍanta* (the imperative) should be uttered externally, as well as *hanti* and *mathi*.
Then *paci*, followed by the sequence beginning with *mahat* and ending with *ādi*, and the pair of words *bhauma iti*.
Having uttered *huṃ* twice, one should likewise utter *ariśiraḥ-svam* and again *khaniṃ*.

The placement of the mantra words is "loḍantamāyamāgnīyīm. Having stated the seed-syllable, one should apply the mantra by breaking it down into its constituent limbs. Jāmadagnya is declared to be the sage, and Aticchandas is said to be the meter.
The deity is known as Devadeveśa, whose body has a large nose.
O Four-faced One, one who desires land should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should offer oblations of clay until he obtains the earth.
This mantra is declared to yield a fruit equal to that of the eight-syllable mantra.
At the end of each syllable, one should append the color of the meteor (ulkāvarṇa) followed by the dative case-ending. This is the sixty-four-fold mantra of Nṛhari as taught by me.
It is not possible to describe it in detail, nor even to comprehend it.
Therefore, O Lotus-Seated One, three or four varieties are now being told:
the extraction of the wheel of phonemes and so forth from each individual syllable.
O Brahmin, the mantra is said to be preceded by the treasury of Brahman (*brahmakośa*);
"Nṛsiṃhakārṣaṇa-bindu" is declared to be its single syllable.
This very [syllable] shall be the meter, and the goddess is called Gāyatrī.

The deity is considered to be the sage Durvāsas and the god Nṛsiṃha; the complexion is pale-red (pāṭala). A wise person desiring to conquer [the world] or seeking the fruit of the four aims of life and other desired objects should perform three hundred thousand recitations.
The three-syllable mantra is *natyantam*;
from this very [mantra], the extraction (*uddhāraṇa*) of its eight-syllable self follows in sequence:
*praṇava*, *nati*, *anvak*, *vighneśa*, and *madhusūdana*.
Anala, Ādi, Indu, Rāma, and Anusvāra;
Gopati, Gopana, Śaṅkha, and Viṣṇu—this is remembered as the eight-syllable [mantra]. Its seed-syllable has been stated; the sages Vyāsa and others have described its limbs.
O Lotus-Seated One, the fruits of its recitation count are likewise;
the seven-syllable mantra ends with *namaḥ* and is otherwise devoid of the *praṇava*.
All else, beginning with the seed-syllable, is as before, and the recitation consists of five limbs.
The seven syllables are common, and likewise five are uncommon.
The one consisting of the previously mentioned twelve syllables is named Śaṅkhodara;
its six limbs and its seed-syllable are exactly as before.
When recited one hundred thousand times for every single syllable, along with the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa),
this mantra— consisting of thirty-two syllables— is the supreme means for accomplishing all human goals when properly practiced. It belongs to the one who possesses the form of Nṛsiṃha.
Its extraction from the phonemes will be explained; it is now demonstrated: the beginning of the meters, the rising [vowel], the letter *ga*, fire (*ra*), the mouth of speech (*a*);
the staff (*ya*), the jar (*u*), the great illusion (*māyā*), fire (*ra*), and likewise the Vaiṣṇava (*ha*). (27.42–43)
Ending with *sparśa*, beginning with the two vowels, the twelvefold *gopana* consists of Parjanya,
Bindu, Ugrātman, Pracaṇḍa,
Coda, Mandara, Janmahantṛ, and Pīyūṣātman; that indeed is the Vaiṣṇava.
Mahendra is the opening of speech; Padmapāṇi is known as Vijaya.
Vibhāvasu is white, shaped like a half-moon, and begins with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Varuṇa, Aprameya, Vairāja, and Brahmasādhana [are likewise].
Ending with *sparśa*, its arising is with *sparśa* as the second; its deity is Viṣṇu.
It is Mādhava, Bhadrapāṇi, and Padmanābha, whose nature is the *kalās*.
Trivikrama, Dhruva, Pūṣan, and Svarādi are remembered as Mandara.
Bhallāyudha, Mahāmāya, Krodharūpin, Vaiṣṇava,
Vanamālin, Svarādin, Mādhava, Sūkṣmalocana, Aprameya, Dhara, and Jvalana joined with Oṃkāra. || 27.48–27.49 ||
Dvirmandara, Padmanābha, Vijaya, Caturbhuja,
Udaya, and Mandaraśiras—
having equated these syllables, one should utter "I bow" immediately after this sequence.

Virāj is the seer, Anuṣṭubh is the meter, and Narahari is remembered as the deity. O Lotus-seated One, having analyzed the mantra, the seed-syllable is declared for it, and the assignment of the limbs (aṅgakalpanā) and the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the limbs are to be performed according to the previously stated sequence.
One should meditate upon [the deity] with the luster of the color of crystal; the count for the recitation is as before.
This mantra of Nārasiṃha wards off all calamities, generates all prosperity, and must not be disclosed to anyone.
O Four-faced One, the garland-mantra (mālāmantra) of Narasiṃha is said to consist of three hundred syllables increased by seventeen;
first is the beginning of the meters, and immediately after that, the salutation.
The word ending in the dative case, "nārasiṃhāya," should be uttered by the practitioner;
that same word preceded by "mahat" (great), followed by "devadānavapūrvakam" (the foremost of gods and demons),
then the word "śoṇite" (in blood), preceded by "digdha" (smeared) and followed by "nakha" (nails).
One should utter a single word ending in the dative case and terminating with "namaḥ.
Furthermore, the word *graha* is extracted as ending in the suffix *śuṣiṇya*;
likewise, *grathni* ends in the causative suffix *ṇic*, and *hanti* is that which arises from the extraction of *santila*.
Having uttered *huṃ phaṭ* immediately thereafter, and likewise the word *kali*, then saying *cara* and *lupa*, and after that *kṣara*;
[and] *hāṃ hoṃ khara ciraṃ*, as well as *drūṃ nhyoṃ jvalana*.
*Jvali*, *śuci*, *dravi*, and *spheti* ending in *ṇic*, with the imperative middle voice;
*bhidi* and *chidi* with *taṃ* as the vikaraṇa, followed by the imperative middle voice; and from *hiṃsi* and *mṛj* ending in *ṇic*, one should utter the imperative middle voice. (27.60–27.61)
The root *nī* (to lead) preceded by *āṃ*, ending with *huṃ phaṭ* in the imperative mood (*loṭ*), is proclaimed;
then *drava drava* (melt, melt), followed again by that same pair preceded by *vi*;
then the word *sarva* ending with *pātāla*, and finally *vāsinām*.

One should recite the *hṛdaya* and other [limbs], ending with *kṛṣi*, in the middle. Preceded by *āṅ*, the root *vidviṣ* ending in *ṇi* is used in the imperative (*loṭ*), followed by the vocative case as a heading. Having uttered the word "Bhagavat," one should then utter the word "Nārāyaṇa."

One should utter the two words "Vāsudeva" and "Hṛṣīkeśa," followed by "Dānavādi-laḍanta" (the devourer of the beginning of the Dānavas), and then "Jahi rākṣasapūrvakam" (slay the one preceded by the Rākṣasa).
After that, having spoken the word "Antaka," one should say "Kaumodakī" and "Dhanuḥ."
One should hold [the mantra] beginning with "Garuda" and ending with "dhvaja," O Lotus-born One (Padmaja).
The phrase "to him whose abode is preceded by the three" and the word "obeisance be to you"—
having uttered "I have taken refuge in you," this mantra is thus recited.
The seed-syllable has been stated; now the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are proclaimed word by word:
beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ), ending with *namaḥ*, and having the name in the dative case;
likewise, [the limbs] beginning with *puruṣa* and *mukha*, and the term *narasiṃha*.

Having uttered the word "vajra" twice, one should then sequentially utter the forms "nakhavigraha" (27.69), "vajra," "nakhadaṃṣṭra," and then the term for the weapon; the sixth [mantra] is said to consist of the terms from "mahānara" up to "siṃha. (27.70)
Reciting "The Sage is Aniruddha; the meter is the Gāyatrī,
and the deity is the Blessed One in the form of Nṛsiṃha," the practitioner of mantra,
remaining restrained, should mutter [the mantra] sixteen times at the entrance of the cave.
It brings hundreds of thousands of those dwelling in the netherworld (pātāla) under one's control instantly;
it also becomes capable of subjugating those who have gone to other worlds.
It is impossible to describe how many other such fruits there are.

Therefore, another mantra of Nārasiṃha, which accomplishes all aims, consisting of four hundred syllables, is now set forth; its extraction is demonstrated. First, having extracted the Udgītha, ending with "namas," it is the means for attaining Brahman.
Bhallāyudha, Gadadhvaṃsa, Vāruṇa, Vijaya, as well as Mādhava, Bhadrahasta, Pāvaka, Śvetadīdhiti,
Vikrama, Sadhruva, O Brahmin, Bhāskara, and Madhuvidviṣ.
O Brahman, [he is] Māruta, Mādhava, Dhanada, Madhusūdana,
Śvasana, Vāruṇa, Janmahantṛ, and Ṛtadhāraka;
he is Dvirada, Sarvadeha, and thereafter Vyaidhara.
He saw Acyuta in the form of Krodha, together with Aca, Ādi, and Dhruva; he saw the Enemy of Madhu as the mountain and the fire,
as well as Śaṅkara with Candra, and Mādhava as the blossoming spring and the water of the mountain.
Savikrama, Kamala, Parvata, Pāśapāṇi,
Sabandhu, Kamala adorned with five dots and eight [marks],
Sumukha, Agniśiras, Karāla, and Mṛgavallabha.
O Lotus-born One, [one should meditate on] the Moon, the lord of the night, approaching thus;
he who is the delight of the heart, whose form is the fourfold states of existence,
who is Nṛhari, the world, the subtle-eyed one, and the head of Rāma.
Vijaya, Pāṭala, Bhānu, Sudana, and likewise Sumukha;
then Yānta, Tacchiras, Vāruṇa mounted on an elephant,
Vāsudeva, as well as Krodharūpa, Ākāra, and Māruta.
Vaidhara, Sūdana, Bhadrahasta, Vāruṇa, Aindava,
the one named Pūrṇendu, then the one called Madhusūdana,
Vatsotadeha, Sumukha, Vikrama, and the one designated Vijaya.
The King of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), beautiful and having cast aside the noose of the assault of [wrong] views;
then the second pair, Acāma and Ādi, as well as Śvasana;
Mādhava with Dhruva, Bhānumant, and the two, Mādhava and Bhāskara.
Rāma, Bhallāyudha, Pañcāntaka, Sudhārasa,
Bhadrahasta, Acāmādi, Bhānta, Māntara, Sūdana, Bhadra, Vasu, Śvetaruci, Vikrama, and Saddhruva. (27.87–27.88)
Mārtāṇḍa, Mādhava, Bhānu, Gopananna, Anta, Ādhara,
Yānta, Śrīdhara, Ugra, Vasu, Vāruṇa, Godhana,
Kuśeśaya, [another] Mādhava, Sumukha, and Kaustubha.
Vighneśa, Gopana, O Brahmin, Rohitāśva with Gopana;
Śvasana, Sumukha, and afterwards Varuṇa, Madhuvidviṣ; Dākṣāyaṇīśa, Udaya, Vaidhara, and then Mādhava.
Amṛta, Vaidhara, and Acā; the second is Mānta, O Lotus-born One.
Then Otadeha, Dṛṣṭi, Yānta, and the syllable Ākāra.
Vakratuṇḍa, Gandhavaha, Viṣṭara, and likewise Vijaya.
Amṛta, Vikramapara, Śrīvatsa, Varuṇārpita;
Yānta, Guhālaya, Nānta, Ṣānta, and Madhusūdana; Sudhruva, Druhiṇa, Krodha, Pāvaka, and again Sumukha.
[One should worship] Padmanābha with Sapaścima, Vaidhara, Caturmukha, Pavamāna with Sabhuvana, Bhānta, Kuñjara, Gopana,
Bhadrahasta with Sarāma, Yānta, and likewise Śrīdhara.
Bhadra, Dhanada, Pāpahanana, Jaya, Mandara,
Vighneśa, Sūdana, Bhalla, Bhāskara, Caturgati,
Śubhada, Vāmana, Para, Ugra, and Vasuśiras— these likewise [are the names]. (27.96–27.97)
Pradyotana, likewise Yānta, Ṛtadhāman, Ugravāmana, Kamala, Mādhavapara, Sarasīruhasambhava,
Vānta, Śubhada, Daṇḍa, and again Kharva and Khaḍgadhara.
One should utter the lotus-born, the abode of nectar, the third [letter], and the one belonging to Vidhara (27.99).
Having pronounced the second of the vowels, the giver of wealth, the "bahula," the one between Saura and Māntara,
and the nasal (nāsikya), one should join them with the heads "huṃ phaṭ" (27.100).
One should employ the thirteen seed-syllables ending in *huṃ phaṭ*;
for each of the seed-syllables, one should utter the syllable *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having proclaimed [the mantra] of the knower of the twelve limbs, one should address Bhāskara together with his secret abode.
Nāsikya, Nṛhari, Aurva, Ardhacandra, Yānta, Auṣadha;
Saddhruva, Māruta, Aurvī, Sadaṇḍa, Kṣapākara; Samara, Saddhruva, Bhānu, Aurva, Nāsikya, O Lotus-born One. (27.102–103)
Pradyotana, Sabhuva, Ardhendu, and Sānta;
likewise Sāgni, Savāmana, Sārdha, Candra, and Saroruha;
Vāsava, Vāmanapara, and Sadhruva, with Kattṛtīyaka as the third.
Māhendra, Aurva, Nāsikya, Mādhava, and Dviradānana;
Subhadra, Śrīdhara, Bhadrahasta, and Gāruḍa; Citrabhānu, Śaśidhara, Pīyūṣa, and Vasuśīrṣaka. || 27.105–27.106 ||
Māruta, Bhadrahasta, Vijaya, Vasusūdana,
Pracaṇḍa with Bandhu, Vakratuṇḍa, Guhālaya,
Sumukha, Arṇa, Saptārcis, Dara, and Candramasāmukha.
One should contemplate Agni, the lord of waters, Jṛmbhala with the face of an elephant, Dhanada, Varuṇa, Māyā, Bhānta, and the means for attaining Brahman;
then the serpent Sumukha, the destroyer of sin, as he goes forth, O Lotus-born One. || 27.108–27.109 ||
Amṛta, Vikramayuta, Vaidhara, Dhūliketana,
Gopana, Saddhruva, Candra, Sārdhendu, Bhāskara, Vasu,
Sapaścima, Hutavaha, and Matimadvāsava.
Pāṭala, Sarvarodha, Kuñjara, Mandaradvaya,
Lakṣmī, Savijaya, Agni, Hṛṣīkeśa, Caturmukha, Bhadrahasta, Mānuṣeśa, Sūdana, and Harimandira. (27.111–27.112)
Śaṅkha, Kalānidhi, Apāṃnātha, Vasu, Madhudviṣ, Paścima, Vijaya, Agni, Subhadra, and Puruṣātmaka;
and the pair Kalānidhi and [the other], Vāruṇa, and Vasuśīrṣaka.
One should utter twice the syllable *vaidhara*, *madhuvidveṣī*, *mādhavī*, and *madhuvidviṣam*;
then the *ardhacandra*, *hutavaha*, *ananta*,
ending with the nasal (*sānta*), followed by *savikrama*, *sendra*, adorned with the bindu on its head.
The ten and five seed-syllables (*bīja*) ending in *hūṃ phaṭ* are as before:
Mandara, Vikramavaśa, Aindra, and likewise Traivikrama;
Khaḍgahasta, Sarāma, Vāsava, and Sahavikrama.
Vaidhara, the Lord of the Upper World, the seed-syllable of Śrī with the nasal,
Otadeha with the staff, the first of the short vowels with the staff,
the second of the short vowels, the half-moon, Kapila, and likewise Saṅgin. || 27.117–27.118 ||
Māṭhara, Gopana, Daṇḍa, Māṭhara with five dots,
Nāsikya, Bhāskara, Vīrasena, Yaṣṭi, and Bhāskara; Otadeha with a staff, Patana, Caura, and Uvanāsika.
And Rohitāśva, Kalaśa, Vikrama, O Lotus-seated One;
Vāsudeva, who gladdens the heart, Bandhumastaka;
Śukla, Sahasrakiraṇa, Aindava, and Agnimastaka.
Vairiñca, Bandhusāhita, Pavaka, and likewise Sumukha;
the fifth was Ṛtadhāmān, followed immediately by the one named Kakubha;
then Savāruṇa, Surapati, Sabandhu, and likewise Vijaya.
Lakṣmī, Madhudviṣ, and then Ekadaṃṣṭragati; Agniśīrṣa as the second, and Jhaṣa is considered the ender of the five (Pañcāntaka);
Druhiṇa, Udaya, O Brahman, Vāsava, and then Vāmana.
The western face bestows auspiciousness; O Lotus-seated One, the second is Kamalāsana.
The second is Saddhruva, and in the lotus of Śrīdhara are Abjayoni, Śrīvatsa, Aja, Vijaya, Rāmamastaka, and Mandara.
Udaya, Śukaśatru, Vijaya, Brahmasādhana;
Mandara, Yāntadhanada, Yāntacandraghaṭa, Vasu;
Bhallāyudha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Ekanetra, and again Ghana. || 27.126–27.127 ||
[He saw] Sabandhu, Mandara, Dṛṣṭiyugala, Agniśīrṣaka,
Bhadra, Caturgati, and then Phaṇīndra and Yāntasūdana; [he saw] Nṛhari, Kalānidhi, Acyuta, and Ādi, as well as Yānta and Madhudviṣ.
One should meditate on the destroyer of the serpent's poison, the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), who has a man as his vehicle;
on Amṛta, named Vasu; on Madhusūdana, the supporter of the earth;
on Kamala, intent on valor; and on him who goes with a dwarf-like hand.
The one whose end is *na*, the abode of virtues; the one whose end is *ṇa*, the enemy of Madhu whose end is *ḍa*;
the western one, the lunar one, and then the one whose end is *bha*, endowed with secret protection;
the giver of wealth, the one of excellent form, the auspicious one, the skillful one, and the destroyer.
O Kamalasana, the second among the Indira-mātṛkā-mantras is Vaidhara;
then Trivikrama, Bhadrakara, Mahāmāyāṅkita, Vasu,
Mṛgeśa, Varuṇa, and Vairāja with five dots (pañcabinduka).
Then there should be Kṣapākara, Kañjabhava, Vighnanāyaka with his gaze, Vaidhara, Devadatta, Kumbha, Caturmukha,
Gata, the one named Ṛtadhāman, Mārtāṇḍa, and Pāśahastaka.
There would be tranquility, victory, concealment, and a difficult path;
a lotus, the upper world, and that which arises from the lotus;
Padmā, and two forms like Mount Mandara, resembling fierce fish.
Vaidhara, Varuṇa, Rāma, Bhūdhara, Vahnimastaka,
Jṛmbhala, and Ṛtadhāmā; Bhāskara and Mandara shall be the beginning and end, the letter *ya*, the letter *ta*, the letter *ā*, Gāruḍa, and Himadīdhiti.
Oṃkāra, Śaśidhara, Saviṣṇu, Varuṇa, Vasu,
Sudhārasa, Pracaṇḍāgni, Ṛtamanantara,
Krodharūpa, Sarāma, Gada, and Ṛtadhāmaka. (27.138–139)
The Lord of Cows, the Lord of Varuṇa, Valor, the Lord of Aquatic Creatures, the Foe of Madhu, the Fire, the Fierce One, the Lord of the Night,
the Essence of Nectar, the One Endowed with Wealth, the Destroyer of Birth, and the Lord of Waters.
O Lotus-born One, [I salute] Madhusūdana, who is going toward his kinsman who is the essence of nectar, who has a twofold form,
who possesses Lakṣmī, who is an elephant, who destroys sin,
who is the source of victory, whose womb is the form [of the world], and whose lower lip is like the moon.
The Fire-god (Pāvaka), yellow in hue, the means for attaining Brahman, and the Lotus-born (Abjaja);
Bhadra, Vikrama, Toyeśa, Ākāra, Indu, and Savikrama;
then Ibha, Ākāra, Dyumna, Bhāskara, Abhūta, and Vaidhara.
Mārutākārabhadra and Māntākāramahotpala; Ugrātman, Vasu, Vāyavya, Sūdana, and Vidhi, O Lotus-born One;
Ugraśīrṣaka and Mārutya, and Paścimadyuti, the son of Indu.
Vāmana, Vaidhara, Sūkṣmalocana, Kattṛtīyaka, Kumbha, Bhadrakara, Mādhavī, Bhāskara, Madhu,
Sūdana, Tridaśāhāra, Vikrama, and Ugrarūpaka.
Pracaṇḍa, Motadeha, Śubhada, Vittavardhana,
Pāvaka, Sumukha, Bhadrahasta, Vairāja, Akṣara, Kumbha, Sudarśana, Kapilākṣa, and Caturmukha. (27.147–148)
Having uttered the words "I have taken refuge twice," O Grandfather,
one should place the Brahma-treasury (brahmakośa) in front, as well as Nṛhari and Anala;
thereafter, the seed-syllables of the Brahma-attainment and the nose-tip are proclaimed.
One should extract the power of the mantra from *nigama*, *ādi*, *subhadra*, *pāṭala*, and likewise *sadhruva*. One should then extract the beginning of the meters:
*gāruḍa*, *madhuhantṛ*, *nāsikya*, *vijaya*, and *vasu*.
Sapadmanābha, Māyā, Sūkṣmadṛk, Mādhava, Ghaṭa,
Bhadrahasta, Vaidhara, Śrīdhara, Agni, Vikrama,
Vairāja, Bhāskara, Yānta, Madhuśatru, and Samīraṇa.
Mandara, Māṭhara, and Acā—the second being Vighnapāvaka;
Kalānidhi with Bandhu, Sārdhacandra, Tviṣāmpati, Sūdana, and another Śaṅkha—the third being Kattṛtīya and Caturmukha. (27.153–154)
O Four-faced One, having uttered twice the word "sānta" (sa) joined with "vasu" (va),

ending with "huṃ phaṭ" and concluding with "namaḥ," this is proclaimed as the Heart-mantra. It begins with the Veda (oṃ), followed by the serpent (śrīṃ), and its head is adorned with five dots (bindus).
Nāsikya, Bhadrahasta, Madhudveṣin, and Vasu; Aindava, Vikramapara, Nāsikya, Bhāskara, Ghaṭa;
Sabandhu, Kamala, Padmanābha, and Vāmanahastaka.
Puṇḍarīka, Sabandhu, Vairāja, Vaidhara, then Godhana, Vijaya, Mānta, Vaidhara, Madhusūdana,
Mānuṣa, Amṛta, Bhadrakara, Gopana, and Padmaja.
Sagopana, Dara, Mādhara, and Kattṛtīyaka; Ṛta, Saindhava, Bandhu, Saddhruva, and Māṭharatvacā;
the second Puruṣa, O Brahmin, and again Mādhavī and Mādhara. (27.159–160)
Then, having uttered "Bhṛguṃ" and "Khaḍgakaram" twice, follow with the Śiromantra ending in "Hūṃ Phaṭ" and concluding with "Ṭhaṭha.
This consists of the first Veda (the letter *a*), the serpent (the letter *r*), the sixth vowel (*u*), the half-moon (*m*), and the lunar digit (*anusvāra*). 27.161.
The Phullanetra, Sabhuvana, Garhita, Bhūdharātmaka,
Kumbha, Savikrama, Padma, Kheṭakī, Kalaśa, Tvacā,
the third Kamala, Pañcabindu, and Sumukha, O Lotus-born One. (27.162–163)
And [he saw] the Lotus-born,
the Lord of the Moon, the bearer of the *svāhā* mantra, the wearer of the moon, the face, the slayer of the mountain-demon, the four-fold state, Śatānanda, Vāsudeva, and the Western one.
"Kalānidhiṃ sarāmaṃ ca yaṣṭiṃ bhāskaragopanau,
caturgatiṃ kharvadehaṃ sūdanaṃ bhānuvikramau, dvirasenduṃ humphaḍantaṃ"— this is declared to be the Śikhā-mantra. (27.165–166)
The knower of mantras, having joined the word *devānām* with *dāsa* at the end,
[recites] Oṃkāra, Nṛhari, Vīrasena, Nāsikya, Aindava,
Māṭhara, Yāminīnātha, and Ṛtadhāmasadabhita. (27.167)
The form of the Lord of Ākhaṇḍala, the form of the Lord of All, the third form as the agent;
the elephant, the one intent on valor, the abundant, the two strides of the jar;
the lotus, the body of water, and the strides that gladden the heart.
Kalānidhi, Subhadrānta, Sumukhānta, Samādhava, Cānta, Śaśadhara, Devadatta, Cānta, Sakumbhaka,
Aindra, Kuñjaramukha, Pīyūṣadyuti, and Vikrama.
One should twice extract the mantra of the Primordial God (Ādideva) as he departs for the Himalayas, which includes the staff (*yaṣṭi*) and two jewels (*maṇi*).
One should also twice extract the mantra of Garuḍa, the kinsman, together with the staff (*daṇḍa*).
The armor (*kavaca*) is proclaimed to end with *hum phaṭ*, and the head (*śīrṣa*) to end with *huṃ phaṭ*.
Āgamādi, Nṛhari, Caurva, Nāsikya, Abjaja,
Vaidhara, Gopana, Ṇānta, Mārutya, Mādhava, Madhu,
Sūdana, Bhadrahasta, Pīyūṣa, and Sarasīruha.
Gopana, Pulaha, Sūdana, Māruta, Vasu,
Kūṭa, Phullāyudha, Aca, the sixth being Vairāja, Kattṛtīya, Padmanābha, Bhāskara, and Madhvidviṣ.
The knower of mantras should raise up Dṛṣṭi along with Savāmana and Bhadrahasta, together with Agni; having twice uttered Bhāskara and Bhadrahasta,
[he should then invoke] the western Vakratuṇḍa, Mandara, and Supratiṣṭhita.
Then the knower of mantras, having recited those [mantras], again [recited] Subhadra and Aindava;
O Lotus-dweller, [he recited] Sadakṣa, Vāmanaśiras,
Ambhoruha, Sabhuvana, Pāvaka, and likewise Bhuvana.
Nṛhari, the destroyer of sin, Vikrama, and again Vijaya; Vairiñca, Vāmana, Dakṣa, Aumra, and Caturmukha;
Guhālaya, Savijaya, Agniśīrṣa, and Māruta.
Eṇeśa, Mandara, Bhānu, Sūdana, Vighnanāyaka,
Yānta, Tārādhipa, Māyā, Saddhruva, Māṭhara, Madhudviṣ, and Māruta— these are proclaimed as the *humphaṭ* weapon-mantras. (27.180–27.181)
One should extract the word for the weapon (*astra*) ending in the dative case and followed by *phaṭ*.
[Then follow] Udgītha, Nṛhari, Sarga, Andhara, Māṭhara, and Tvacām;
the second, the western [syllable], Padmanābha, and the first [syllable].
With sword in hand, fair-faced, lotus-eyed, and lotus-like;
accompanied by Gopana, the lord of the gods, with Gopana as his second;
with auspicious hands, together with Rāma, Vāsava, the means for achieving Brahman.
O Lotus-born One, [he is] sword-in-hand, elephant-faced, the destroyer, and the one who transcends the four states of existence;
he is the beginning of the non-eating [fast], the elephant-faced one, the medicine, and that which has no end;
likewise, he is Mādhavī, the wind, the one who goes, and the lower lip of the West.
O Four-faced One, Sabandhu, Sapracaṇḍa, Eṇeśa, Pāṭalāpriya,
Mārtāṇḍa, Madhuvidveṣin, Bhadra, Ṛtadhāmaka, Dākṣāyaṇīśa, and Rāma constitute the Anusvāra. (27.186–187)

And having applied [the mantra] ending in "hum phaṭ" to the two eyes, one should employ the syllable "vauṣaṭ" for Divākara, Ādideva, the god Vaidharagopana, Pāvaka, and Puruṣātman, O Kamalāsana, [repeating each name] twice.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the rules, up to the Viṣkambha [deities] along with the staffs,
the knower of the procedure should extract the six syllables of the Heart-mantra, which possesses the splendor of a thousand suns;
[and he should visualize] the blue lotus, the white water-lily, the red Japā flower, the Bandhūka, and the Kiṃśuka.
The colors of the six [limbs], beginning with the heart, shall be pale-red (pāṭala) in sequence.
I shall now proclaim the protective mantra; one should extract the beginning of the meters:
Vighneśa, Padmanābha, Dvijarāja, and Savikrama.
Sadaṇḍa, Samārtāṇḍa, Bahula, and Saguhālaya; Paścima, Vāmanapara, Pracaṇḍa, and Hariṇa;
Bhallāyudha, Gadadhvaṃsa, Lānta, and likewise Bhadrakara.
Ācāmādi, Dinamaṇi, Mādhava, Sauramakṣara,
Eṇeśa, Dhanada, Dakṣa, Vasuśīrṣa, Sūdana,
Dhanādyakṣa, as well as Dakṣa and Pāvaka situated at the head.
The letter *dh* is dark with valor; the letters *kh* and *h* are tawny. Furthermore, the letter *k* is tawny.
One should extract twice the syllables: "dviradāsyaṃ," "bandhuparaṃ," "mādhavīṃ yāntaśīrṣakam," "vāsudevaṃ khaḍgadharaṃ," "caturgatim anantaram," and "mukhaṃ savaidharaṃ brahman māṭharaṃ. (27.196)
The purifier (pavitra) is immeasurable; the beak (tuṇḍa) is the primordial Mandara.
Having twice uttered "the obstruction of all" (sarvarodha), one should utter "lotus with eyes" (kamalaṃ savilocanaṃ).
Then, as before, [one utters] "with staff" (sadaṇḍaṃ), "destroyer" (sūdanaṃ), and "going wind" (yāntamārutau).
It should be stated twice: Subhadra, Vikrama, Vighna, and Vaidhara;
likewise, Tadviruddha, Chala, Dhvaṃsī, Bandhu, Vighna, and Savaidhara;
as well as Aindira, Utadeha, Ugra, Mānta, and Caturmukha.
O Lotus-born one, having twice uttered the names Atri, Agni, Madhudveṣin, Amṛta, Dhūliketana, Tārkṣya, Saṅkarṣaṇa,
and Daṇḍa, one should thereafter recite Mārtāṇḍa and Ūrdhvanāsikya.
Having uttered Pāvaka, Aurvaśiras, Sadaṇḍa, Gopana,
Gadadhvaṃsa, Chaladhvaṃsa, and likewise Jaya; Vairāja,
Yāntaśiras, Śukla, Vairāja, and Pāvaka.
Jṛmbhala, Samata, O Brahmin, Māṭhara known as Dakṣa, Pracaṇḍa, Mādhava, Kalaśa, Bandhuśīrṣaka,
Kamalā, Vāruṇa, Yānta, and Hṛṣīkeśa in the west. || 27.203–27.204 ||
Māyājita, Pracaṇḍa, Mādhava, and the one ending with *ṭha-ṭha*—these are declared as the seed-syllables and the limbs; Durvāsas is said to be the seer (*ṛṣi*).
The meter is *anuṣṭubh*, and the deity is the great Narahari, Hari.
In the *mālāmantra*, there should be three colors: white, yellow, and black.

Furthermore, there should be the reality (*tattva*), the supreme ether (*paramavyoman*), as well as the process of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the process of disintegration (*vikalīkaraṇa*), and the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the mantra.
And liberation as well— these, O Lotus-Seated One,
have been declared within this great sixty-fourfold Nārasiṃha mantra by the wise;
namely, the Nṛsiṃha known as Vyomacakra and that known as Pātāla.
One should meditate [on this] in the fear of death, when a malevolent spell (*kṛtyā*) has entered, in battle with enemies, for the purpose of eradication,
for the destruction of beings, and for their expulsion;
this meditation on him is declared to be remembered as being within the solar disc.
Seated upon the inner surface of a seat in the center of a blossoming, radiant white lotus,
he has sixteen faces and is endowed with twice that many arms,
bearing weapons such as the conch and the discus, which are difficult to behold and garlanded with rays of light.
Regarding the repelling of enemy armies and other difficult tasks,
Brahmā said:
"He who knows the twelve limbs [of the scriptures] is worthy to know the mantra."
"Thus it has been said, O Blessed One; yet further inquiry persists regarding them. The illustrious Blessed One replied:
"The seed-syllable, the power (śakti), and likewise the limbs such as the heart and so forth—these constitute the sixfold [division]."
The seer, the meter, and the deity, as well as the illumination of the phonemes;
nourishment, liberation, and likewise the process of integration (sakalīkaraṇa);
and the process of disintegration (vikalīkaraṇa)—these twelve, O Lotus-born One, [are the rites]. || 27.214–215 ||
I shall describe their essential nature in due order; let that be attended to.
The seed-syllable extracted from a mantra is its *prakṛti* (source-form);
it is the soul of the mantra, which, like a power (*śakti*), bestows the fruit of the mantra.

O Grandfather, the six limbs of the mantra, beginning with the heart, are like the face and other features of a deity; the mantra is established within them. The seer (ṛṣi) is the beholder of the fruit, and that which is recited is called the meter (chandas).
O Lotus-born One, the finite number of syllables, the deity who is expressed, that which is spoken, the differentiation of forms such as white and so forth— these are the *varṇas*. Furthermore,
there is the encasing (*sampuṭīkaraṇa*) by means of the letters *ra* and *la*, and the illumination (*dīpana*).
Through all the syllables as previously described, and by means of the refinements such as drying and so forth,
that which is called the "nourishment" (*āpyāyana*) of the mantra like a deity has been declared by the wise;
the application known as the "liberation" (*mocana*) of the mantra is used for paralyzing (*stambhana*) and other such purposes.

O Four-faced One, know that the encapsulation (*sampuṭīkaraṇa*) of each individual syllable of the mantra by means of the *praṇava* is called *sakalīkaraṇa*. This is performed with the *vauṣaṭ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *huṃ* utterances pronounced separately.
The presence of the desired deities within the *puṭas* and other vessels,
which is invoked, is called "the mutilation of the four-faced one" (*vikalīkaraṇa*).
One should employ these very [mantras] for the two primary *vidyās* as well.
The eleven-syllable mantra of Vāmana is now revealed.
The seven syllables previously mentioned remain, and the specific distinction is now declared:
one should extract the Nectar (Amṛta), the Primordial God (Ādideva), and Mandara as the first [syllables].
O Four-faced One, [the syllables] Vighneśa, Gopana, Vāyu, and Ādya constitute the seed-syllable (bīja) for the head; Yaṣṭi and Caturgati constitute the upper world (ūrdhvaloka).
The six limbs, beginning with Phala and ending with the vowels, are to be applied in their proper sequence.

The syllables should be joined with their respective anusvāras; the sage is held to be Kāśyapa, the meter is the divine Gāyatrī, and the deity is Vāmana. One should recite eleven hundred thousand [times] during the fire-oblation and the water-libation.
Then this mantra accomplishes the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha),
as well as whatever other desired fruit has been proclaimed regarding the eight-syllable [mantra].
It begins with *oṃ* and the others, with the first four preceded by salutation (*nati*), as before.

The practitioner of mantra who performs the practice of this seven-syllable mantra as prescribed obtains the stated fruit from seven hundred thousand recitations. Having taken the seven preceding syllables, [they are] Vairāja, Agni, and Trivikrama.
The Lord of Sea Creatures, Māyā, and that which is oriented toward fire beginning with touch—
O Lotus-Seated One, the mantra consisting of twelve syllables is said to be the Primordial God, Śaṅkha, and Viṣṇu, ending with touch. 27.232–233.

The seed-syllable of Trivikrama, Bhāskara, Viṣṇu, and that which has the form of a half-moon—these are the sixfold ancillaries (aṅga). The seer, deity, and meter are exactly as previously stated; these constitute the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
As before, the fruit of this [mantra] is also held to be the attainment of kingship and so forth.
However, O Four-faced One, it is not possible to state [the fruits] for Rāma Jāmadagnya alone, because the abundance of fruits is infinite. 27.235–27.236
Having first taken the seven common syllables as before,
now hear the sequential extraction of the uncommon syllables:
Janmahantā, Gopana, Mādhavī, and Viṣṇu thereafter.
Dṛṣṭi, Ādigati, Bhadrapāṇi, and Vāyu Gopana;
Caturgati, Svarādi, Vahni, and Ākāra; Mandara, Ādideva, Śvasana, Viṣṇu, and Abjaja. || 27.238–239 ||
The seventeen-syllable mantra is said to end with "hum phaṭ";
it begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ), and together with the *yaṣṭi*, it is declared to be the seed (*bīja*).
According to the system of Gārgya, this very limb (*aṅga*) is repeated six times.
The *chandas* is the *gāyatrī*, and its deity is Jāmadagnya.
One should recite it twenty lakhs of times; then it becomes the accomplisher of all goals.
Alternatively, there is a ten-syllable mantra, omitting the word "Jāmadagnya."
All that was previously mentioned, beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), is the mantra that brings about the destruction of enemies.
O Brahmin, the excellent mantra of Rāma, the incarnation of Viṣṇu and son of Daśaratha,
is now being told in sequence, along with those of Bharata and the others, as well as their goddesses.

Then, O Lotus-born One, the knower of mantras, beginning with the twelve-syllable mantra and uttering the word "to the one consisting of four forms," should pronounce the term "of beautiful body" in the dative case.
"Rāma," ending with its case-termination, followed by "ṭhaṭha"—
O Four-faced One, this mantra consisting of thirty-two syllables has been declared.
Its seed-syllables are known to be Anala and Viṣṇu, respectively, together with their vowel sounds.
Its six limbs and its seed-syllable should arise from the sequence beginning with the letter *a*.
O Four-faced One, I shall tell you another Rāma-mantra:
having first uttered the *praṇava*, followed by the five dots (*pañcabindu*) together with the staff (*yaṣṭika*).
Having first uttered the word "caturmūrti" ending in the dative case,
thereafter [one says] "caturgatimayāya"; following that, [one says] "śaraśārṅgabhṛt" ending in the dative case, and likewise the word "indīvara" preceded by "śarat" ending in the dative case.
The word *tviṣā* should be employed afterwards, followed by the word *bhagavat*. Then, the word *abhirāma* should be uttered in the dative case;
having said *śarīrāya*, one should likewise utter the word *rāmāya*.
The extraction of the words of the mantra "na atyantam" has been demonstrated;
its seed-syllable, its six limbs, and its seer are remembered as Śarabha.
Its meter is as before, and its deity is the Lord Hari, whose essence is Rāma.

One should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; then the king of mantras is perfected. One swiftly obtains the great, desired fruit that is otherwise difficult to attain, having well-mantrified the clusters of syllables arranged upon the wheel of the Mātṛkās.
Having worshipped with flowers, one should generally extract the Lord from that [heart];
thereafter, O Brahman, I shall now duly explain the collection of other mantras and the *mālā-mantra* exactly as they are— let this be understood correctly.
First, Nāda, Saptavarṇa, Vasu, Madhuniṣūdana;
then Sparśānta, Gopana, Śaṅkha, Mukha, Viṣṇu, and Jaya;
then the fifth of the vowels (Ū), Āhendra, and those beginning with Nāda, namely Ghaṭa and Vikrama.
Śaṅkhin, Śikhin, Dakṣa, Karāla, Vasuniṣṭhita,
Hānta, Madhudviṣ, O Brahman, Dhūliketana, Ādima,
Nānta, Yānta, Sadakṣāhva, Paścimodaya, and Akṣara.
Atri, Ramadhara, Krodharūpin, and the one named Anala;
Acām’s second [son] Pavana, Kalasa, and Bindumastaka;
Ugrātman and Sumukha; and Yādonātha and Mṛgādhipa.
Dineśa, Ādi, Nāsikya, Śaśāṅka, Madhuvidviṣ,
Vairāja, Mādhavī, Bhadrakara, Mādhava, O Lotus-born One;
Vakratuṇḍa, Acāma, and the one named Vijayodaya.
Likewise, one should place Pañcāntaka, Jayanta,
Rāma, Mandara, Śaṅkha, Gopana, Pavana, and Mukha upon the head.
Then, Ādi, Bhalla, Ayudha, Rāma, Vasu, Gopana, and Pāṭala [should be placed].
Śrīvatsa, Ādimānala, Vāmanāgni, Madhudviṣ,
Caturgati, Khaḍgadhara, Ekadṛk, Vaidhara,
Dakṣa, Agni, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Vijaya— the pair that follows.
He went after that wind, the beloved of the deer, which was carrying away his head;
and the one-eyed lord of the bears, the slight protector, and the king of obstacles,
followed as kinsmen, while the two sons of Vidhara, the suns of merit, departed for the world.
Śvasana, Dakṣa, Bhuvana, Cakra, Vighneśa as the seventh, Aca, the cause [of all], Eṇeśa, Kalātmā, Vasu, Vikrama;
Karāla, Gopana, Pāpahanana, and likewise Vikrama.
Māhendrakumbha, Anala, Madhusūdana, Bhāskara,
Yānta, Gopana, Saptārcis, Madhusūdana, Māruta,
Pracaṇḍa, Gopana, Khaḍgadhara, Śrīdhara, and Vaijaya. || 27.268–269 ||
The two protectors of nectar, the two who bear the splendor of the lotus, and the two who wear forest garlands;
the five forms of the cloud, the elephant, the lotus, Lakṣmī, and the enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu).
The yellow ones are the lord of beasts (Śiva), the wind (Vāyu), and the protector (Viṣṇu); the white ones are Śrīdhara (Viṣṇu) and others.
Pāvaka, Sthāna, Govinda, Vairāja, Daravaidhara,
Madhusūdana, Vighneśa, Sudhārasa,
Brahmasādhana, Saptārcis, Gati, and Bhāskara as the seventh. || 27.271–272 ||
The bearer of the *acāma* and other [weapons], the Creator, the wielder of the *brahmasādhana* shield;
and Agni, O Brahmin, with his tawny hue, possessing the prowess of the *bhallā* weapon;
Vighneśa, Vaidhara, the leader of the *preta*s, and Rāmaśīrṣaka.
Bhadrapāṇi, likewise Tathādṛk, and Sarasīruhasambhava;
Dakṣa and the other gods, the consumer of oblations (Agni), and the four states of existence (caturgati) immediately following;
Śrīvatsa and Vāsudeva, the two, Krodharūpa and Samīraṇa.
Karāla, Ṛta, Bhadrapāṇi, Vairāja, Māruta, Vasukarman in the west, Vikrama, Dṛṣṭigopa,
Naya, Vighneśa, Chhalavidhvaṃsa, Ādhava, and Vaidharātman.
The lotus-born destroyer of sins, the fire-eating stainless jar,
Vakratuṇḍa, as well as Dyumna, whose prowess is like that of the elephant-faced one;
the radiant Agni, the body of water, Vakratuṇḍa, and the four-fold path.
And at the two ends of the western face, they are endowed with bodies that have descended;
[there are] the two Vairājas, Dakṣa, Gopana born from Vāsika,
Gadadhvaṃsa, Kapila, Atri, and Madhuniṣūdana.
He who traverses the four states of existence, who is white, who is Varuṇa, Agni, and Vāyu; who has a single tusk and a single eye, who is manifold, the enemy of Madhu;
whose prowess is fierce, who has a curved trunk, and whose abode is the cave—[to him I bow].
Sumukha, Hutabhuk, Śaṅkha, Anala, Madhuvidviṣ, Yaṣṭi, Dakṣa, Tathākāra, Nāsikya, Dhūliketana,
Dhruva, Māhendra, Ākāra, Ardhāṃśu, Kumbha, and Gopana.
Saddhruva, Janmahantṛ, Vāruṇa, and Pulaha;
Musalī, Kumbha, and Ākāra—these grant the yellow weapon and wealth;
as well as Śrīdhara, Bhadrahasta, Hari, and Svāhāmayāvaha.
"O Lotus-born One, these nine seed-syllables ending in *hum phaṭ* are for Padmapāṇi,
Padmanābha, Vanamālā, Trivikrama,
Śrīvatsa, Śaṅkhībhuvana, Bhadrahasta, and Savikrama. (27.285)
Agni, Mṛgeśa, Varuṇa, Vairāja, Bandhumastaka, Dara, Tārkṣya, as well as Ādideva, Śukla, and Śrīpati;
Vasu, Gopana, Śītāṃśu, Bhuvana, Anala, and Vāruṇa.
Mṛgeśa, Vijaya, Ākāra, Viṣkambha, Śukla, Vikrama,
Dṛkpuṇya, Ādideva, Bhāskara, Ṛtadhāmaka,
Sūkṣmadṛk, Śaṅkha, Dakṣa, Vaidhara, Agni, and Caturgati.
In the west are Trita, Dakṣa, and the others; Agni, Vāyu, and Saroruha;
Ṛtadhāman, Jaya, Gopa, and Paścima; Śukla, Abjaja, Bhānu, Gopana, Saptārcis, Bhallāyudha, Guha, and Ālaya.
Vairājaka, Kakubha, Kumbha, Havyavāṭ, and the one named Kapila;
Vaidhara, Bhāskara, Pāpahanana, and Vakratuṇḍaka; Gadin, Ṛtadhāman, Bhāskara, and likewise Sumukha.
Kumbhavikrama, Janmāhva, Padmanābha, Sadevarāj;
Subhadra, Śaṅkha, Dakṣāhva, Motadeha, and then Bhāskara;
Pavana, Pāpahanana, Gopanau, Vijaya, and Dara.
Udaya, Pītakamala, Madhusūdana, Vighnarāja;
Māhendra, Śubhada, Vahni, Godhana, Kumbha, Vikrama;
Agni, Atri, Kumbhadhara, Lakṣmī, Kharva, Caturmukha.

Likewise, Śuklodaya, Dṛṣṭi, Śrīvatsa, and Vasuśīrṣaka—these two, O Lotus-born one, are bestowers of auspiciousness upon Vighneśa. Furthermore, know Madhusūdana, Śārṅgapāṇi, and Pañcāntaka. || 27.295–27.296 ||
Aurva, Dakṣa, and those embodied beings, as well as Dṛṣṭi, Sarasija,
Vāmana, Dhanada, Yānta, Subhaga, Agni, Vanasraj,
Rāma, Puṇya, Agni, Garuḍa, Vikrama, Jaya, and Vikrama.
The fortunate Agni, the primordial god, whose syllable is "Kuñjara";
Karāla, Kapila, the destroyer of sin, the son of the Wind; Śrīdhara, the bestower of wealth through his glance, Pañcabindu, together with Vighnarāja. || 27.298–27.299 ||
Śubhota, Dehāvu, Ugrātman, the mouth of those in the four states of existence,
Śailadvaya, Dvādaśātman, Gopana, Śukla, Paścima,
Śrīdhara, Sumukha, Bhūmi, Anala, and Pañcabinduka.
Karālāgni, Mahāmāyā, Subhaga, Bandhu, Anvata;
Vairāja, Vikrama, Pāpahanana, Bandhumastaka; Pracaṇḍa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Vāsudeva, Jaya, and Vasu.
Sūkṣmadṛk, Kumbha, Varuṇa, Paścimānana, Ādharā,
Ugrātman, Mṛgada, Dakṣāhvā, Gopanā, Dhanada, Kuṭa,
Dakṣa, Puṇyodaya, Śukla, Śubhadṛṣṭi, and Vināyaka.
Vaidhara, Madhuhantṛ, Mandara, and Brahmasādhana;
Atri, Agni, Pavitrāhvaya, Vaidhara, and Sparśapaścima;
Bhadrādi, Devabhallāhvaya, Ugrabhūmi, and Madhudviṣ.
Ekadṛk, Dakṣa, Vighneśa, Mādhava, Amṛgavallabha, Bhāskara, Devadatta, Bhānu, Bandhu, Subhadraka,
Gadadhvaṃsa, Kumbha, Dvirada, and Paścimānana.
Aurva-agni, Bhuvana-vugra-yaṣṭi, Vedhas, Śriyaḥ-pati (27.307);
Agni, Ramādharadvī, Agnikūṭavigarhita,
Bhadramadhudveṣin, and Dṛṣṭigopanama-staka (27.308).
Vairāja, Dakṣa, Kamala, Gopana, Bindu, Pakṣirāj;
the Manu, Dhruva, Agni, Ākāra, Bindu, Candra, Madhu, and Dviṣ;
Nāsikya, Ādi, Atri, Bandhu, Mandara, and Viṣṭapa.
Vairāja, Repha, Śaṅkha, Āhna, Mādhava, Vādi, Vighnarāṭ;
Mṛgeśa, Kamala, Dakṣa, Guha, Ambhoruhāsana;
Jaya, Agni, Vāyu, Eṇeśamukha, Garuḍavāhana.
Bandhupīta, Pavitrāhva, Madhusūdana, Vaijaya, Gopana, Bhārgavākāra, Śuklodaya, Hutāśana,
Pītotada, Dehakamala, Vighnavikrama, and Mādhava.
Gopana, Somabandhu, and Karigopanayaṣṭi;
Dineśa, Mṛtadhāman, Dṛṣṭi, Śaṅkha, Madhudviṣ, Vighna, Vāyu, Gopa, Kamala, and Śatrudāhaka. || 27.313–27.314 ||
Dhānta, Śākha, Madhoḥhantā, Padma, Krodha, Agni, Māruta, Ādicakrī, Subandhu, Pīta, and Sarvapurāntaka;
between Udaya and Antara, these indeed shine as Pavana and Agni.
The first is the dwarf-bodied one; the enemy of the one who drank the lotus-honey of his kinsmen; the pale-red western one; Padmanābha; Vaidhara and Mādhava;
the one with the mace-weapon; the wielder of the mace; the enemy of Kumbha; the king of elephants; and the beloved of the deer.
Śrīvatsa, Agni, the syllable *īm*, the water-pot (*kumbha*), two yellow [syllables], as well as Subhadra, Gopana, Śaṅkha, Mandara, and Dinakṛt;
the fourteenth birth of the vowels, and Śaśin, Śaṅkha, Mṛga, and Vallabhā.
Hutāśa, Gopada, Kṣāhvā, Mādhavya, Guhālaya,
Vairāja, Yugasaptārcis, Daradeva, Hutāntima, Anala, and Yaṣṭisahita— this is declared to be its seed-mantra (bīja). || 27.319–27.320 ||
The Ṛṣi of this [mantra] is Śarabhaṅga, and its metre is said to be Varivaśchanda.
For the recitation (japa) of that three-lakṣa [mantra] consisting of one hundred and eight syllables,
it belongs to the Supreme Soul who manifested as Rāma, the Supreme Person.

This garland-mantra, consisting of four hundred syllables, has been extracted. As before, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) and the attainment (siddhi) are exactly as before; [it applies] to others such as Bharata and the rest, by means of the names of their respective arrays (vyūha).
O Lotus-born One, the names should be recited in the form of mantras, accompanied by their own heads (ātmaśīrṣa) in the dative case, or likewise in the dative case;
one should employ the seed-syllables as the initial letters, together with the *anusvāra*.
The invocations for the goddesses Sītā and the others consist of their names in the dative case;
the mantras end with "ṣaṣṭhi" (the sixth), and the seed-syllables are their initial letters.
Their preliminary ritual (*puraścaryā*) is like that of the Śrī-mantra, and the attainment of results is likewise.
The mantra of Rāma and Balabhadra is now being told:
having first uttered the seven-syllable word, one should thereafter pronounce "rāmāya" in the dative case, and likewise the word "balabhadra. (27.327)
O Brahmin, its seed-syllable is said to be *jṛmbhalampula-ha*. Hṛṣīkeśa with the anusvāra is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi), Paiṅgala;
the meter should be as before, and the deity is the wielder of the mace (Musalāyudha).

Rāma, whose eyes are like lotus petals, is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the sequence of limbs (*aṅga-paddhati*). For the accomplishment of the mantra, there should be hundreds of thousands (*lakṣa*) of syllables. One attains the desired fruit, such as traveling to the netherworld (*pātāla*) and so forth.
The fruit of attaining the fourfold aims of human life rests in his hand.
Now, the mantra of Kṛṣṇa, the descendant of Yadu, is being declared:
having first uttered the *udgītha* in the mouth, followed by the *sparśa* and the rest. (27.331–332)
Then follows Ṛtadhāmā, immediately after that Krodharūpa,
then Vanamālinākāra, Śvasana, and Viṣṇumastaka.
These six syllables of the mantra have been declared by me as "natyantam."

The seed-syllable (bīja) shall be the primordial lotus, followed by the seven-rayed one (Saptārcis). After that comes Aurva with the staff (Yaṣṭi); by this very [formula], the arrangement of the limbs (aṅga-kalpanā) is established. Sanaka shall be its seer (draṣṭṛ), and the Gāyatrī metre is said to belong to it.
The deity is the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, and the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is as before.
The fruits have been stated previously; they are not mentioned again here for fear of prolixity.
Now, the extraction of the phonemes (varṇoddhāra) of the mantra named Govardhana is demonstrated.

Having first uttered the beginning of the Vedas, O Four-faced One, [place it] in the first group of five consonants (the *sparśas*). Likewise, [place] the third [vowel] among the *ya*-group and among the vowels.
This is the "Good and Firm," the "Speaker," the "Means for Brahmā," and the "Essence of Nectar."
Ādi, Saptārcis, Puṇya, and Makara immediately after that; then Bhadrabāhu as the second, and Śvasana at the end of the mouth.
Thus, the extraction of the nine syllables has been fully described.
The mantra is that very thing; it is declared to be the means of accomplishment beginning with the seed-syllable, as well as the fruit.
O Lotus-Seated One, the extraction of the Gopāla mantra is now told:
having uttered the first of the vowels, one takes the third, which is known as a sparśa consonant.
Oṭa, Deha, Pavitra, Vāmana, Kakubha, then Aniruddha, Vighnarāja, Akāra, Yādasāmpati,
Ādya, Pulaha, Āvṛtta, Sparśopānta, and Gopana.
The first among the vowels is *prabhañjana* (the wind), and the one ending in *ṭha* and *ṭha* is declared to be *manu*.

The third seed-syllable of the consonants (*sparśa*) is yellow; from the vowels (*ac*), the fourth is the nasal (*nāsikya*). The limbs (*aṅga*) are again the protection (*gopana*) known as the sword (*khaḍga*).

The primary [mantra] consists of *sparśādimanala*, as well as *gopana* and *sparśana*. The first [group], ending with *ṭha-ṭha*, is the first limb; immediately thereafter is the limb preceded by *vi-* and followed by *adhika*. Then follows the limb preceded by *trailokya*.

The word "rakṣaṇa" (protection) ending in the dative case, followed by the same case-ending [suffix], comes after "asura-ādyantaka" (the end of the beginning of the Asuras). The word "graham" (seizure), followed by "nivāraṇāya" (for the sake of warding off), is said to end with "huṃ phaṭ. || 27.346–27.347 ||

Nārada is the seer of the mantra; its meter is Virāj and its deity is the Lord in his incarnation as Kṛṣṇa. The place for recitation has been previously described. O Four-faced One, it is taught that the recitation should be performed a thousand times at each location.
Through recitation, this mantra is perfected; it accomplishes every fruit.
27.349 O Lotus-seated One, I shall declare another wondrous mantra:
having first uttered the *praṇava*, immediately thereafter [the syllable] *mādhara*. 27.350
Then, having uttered the word ending in the fourth case, one should likewise utter the wonderful word *bhogeśvara* ending in that same case-ending, followed by the word *taduccakrī*,
and then the word beginning with *suvarṇa* and ending with *dhvaja*, likewise ending in that same case-ending.

Then the word *vāsudeva*, ending with the suffixes for yellow garments (*pītādivāsaśśabdānta*), should be joined; its head should be provided with the appropriate case-ending and the mantra is recited ending in *namaḥ*. First, the limbs (*aṅga*) should be applied as before; it does not exceed that.
The seer, the meter, the deity, and the fruit are as before;
dharma, artha, kāma, mokṣa, and so forth are not further elaborated here.
First, the *mālā-mantra* consists of [one hundred and eight] syllables of the Lord, the enemy of Madhu.
I shall extract, according to the truth, that which bestows the fruit of the four aims of human life upon the form of the Kṛṣṇa incarnation; let it be understood exactly as it is:
the six-syllable mantra beginning with "Nigama," which is the lotus-abode of nectar. (27.355–356)
Krodha, Pracaṇḍa, Madhu, Śaṅkha, Kumbha,
and Tān; Krodha, Caṇḍakrama, Kumbha, Śaṅkha, Khāgni, and Madhusūdana.
Dara, Śrīvatsa, Eṇeśa, Krodha, Sūkṣma, and beyond that;
Vāsudeva with the mace, the destroyer of sins, and the fourfold course (caturgati);
Agnibindu, Viriñca and the other gods, the conch, and the face of the earth.
Furthermore, [he is] the purifier Agni, Madhubhit, and Bhadrapāṇidvaya;
Vaidhara, the western Vasu, and Dakṣendubhuvanātman;
Sūkṣmacakṣus, Gati, Soma, Kumbhāgni, and Saguhālaya.
Pavitragopanau, Vāyu, Paścimāgni, Madhudviṣ,
Vairāja, Mādhavī, Vighna, Sāraṅga,
Asidhara, Para, Bandhu, Vairāja, Hutabhuk, Pañcātman, and Dviradānana.
Gopana, Śaṅkhadinakṛt, Ṛtavaidhara, and Māruta; Abjota, Dehāva, Adri, Yāntabhadra, Trivikrama,
Māhendra, Śaṅkha, Madhubhit, Māruta, and Kakubha— these are the names [of the wind-gods].
Bhṛgu, Gopana, Vighneśa, Janmahantṛ, Eṇa, Saṃhitā,
Māruta, Gopana, Vāyu, Indu, Bhāskara,
Maindava, Ṛta, Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Krodha, Agni, and Varuṇa.
Atri, Vighnadvaya, Śaṅkha, Dvirada, Sūkṣmalocana,
Śriyaḥpati, Janmahantṛ, Vakratuṇḍaka,
Hutāśa, Caṇḍa, Madhubhid, Dhara, Śukla, and Dineśvara. (27.365–27.366)
Kālātman, Pratimākāra, Jayapāvaka, Bhadraka, Udaika, Cakṣus, Amṛta, Vikrama, Vidhi, Pāvaka,
Dakṣa, Vidhi, Cintadhāman, Dakṣagopana, and Abjaja.
The conch, the beginning, the destroyer of the mace, the Māhendra, the five dots (pañcabindu),
the excellent *dhruva*, the seed-syllable of Indirā, and thereafter the seed-syllable of Puṣṭi;
then the seed-syllable of Kāma, the seed-syllable of the noose, and the Śrīvatsa with a dot at its head.
Brahmā holds the discus and sword; then Padmanābha is in the west. Vaidhara, Dakṣakamala, Śrīdhara, Pīta, and Vāmana [are there].
Indirā destroys sin, protects, and increases wealth.
Madhusūdana, Nāsikya-kuśeśaya, Ramādhara;
Śrīvatsa, Dvaṃdvabahula, Vitteśa, Madhuvindviṣ;
Kapidhvaja, Gadī, Yāntadakṣa, Śrīdhara, Candramas.
The deity beginning with Pīta, Śītāṃśu, Māyākamala, Abjaja,
Manu, Dakṣa, Utadeha, Dṛṣṭi, and the one named Śaṅkhaghaṭa;
[and] Māyā, Karāla, the syllable Mī, Caṇḍārṇava, and Sumastaka.
Nāda, Ādi, Paścima, Padmanābha, Vairāja, Vikrama, Pāvaka, the Lord of the Upper World (Urdhvalokeśa), the western Aprameyaka,
Kharva-vikrama, Mahendra, Bhallāyudha, and Sudhārasa.
Vighna, Mandara, Vighneśa, Mādhavī, Supratiṣṭhita,
Kumbhodara, Amaśubhada, Pīyūṣa, Agniguhālaya,
Paścimānanavighneśa, Māyā, and Mandarāśmaka.
Vasumūrdhan, Mahendra, and the other gods, together with Kapila;
Jṛmbhala, Yānta, Subhaga, Hutāśa, Dhanada, Para, Govinda, Vighna, Bhuvana, Vidhi, and those designated as Paścima. || 27.377–27.378 ||
Saptārcis, Pītavarṇābha, Devara, Matimān, as well as Śaṅkha, Gopana, Vairāja, Śrīdhara, and the one named Dhanada;
Madhudviṭ, Kuñjaramukha, and those belonging to the four states of existence along with the serpents.
Bhadrahasta, Madhudveṣin, Gadadhvaṃsin, Dvayānvita, Bhadrapāṇi, as well as Puṇya, Sarasīruhasambhava, Sudhārasa, Vasu, and Bhūmi; after these comes the one named Gopana. || 27.380–27.381 ||
Karāla, Bandhu, Vighneśa, those named Pañcabindu and Śubha, Madhuhantā, as well as Brahmā, Māyāvighna, and Vāmana;
Yānta, Mādhava, Pīyūṣa, Vairāja, and Pañcabinduka.
Śaśāṅka, Kamala, Bhadra, Pāṇi, Dṛg, Vaidhara,
Eṇeśa, Kumbha, Dṛk, Saśrī, Śrīdhara, Anta, Ādi, Gadī, Ṛtadhāman, Dinakṛt, Varuṇa, and Mṛga. || 27.383–27.384 ||
Vairāja, Madhuhantṛ, Viṣṇvābha, Bhadrasādhana, Mānuṣeśa, Dakṣa, Madhusūdana,
Vaidhara, Ṛkṣeśa, Bhuvana, Yānta, Madhuśatru, and Himālaya.
Udaya, Agnipavitra, Bandhu, Śrī, Madhuvidviṣ;
Vakratuṇḍa and Viriñca; Hṛṣīkeśa and Śubhābhidha; Bhānta and Ādideva; Sumukha and Puṇḍarīka—these are the Vidarbhas. (27.386–387)
Pūrṇacandra, Sarāma, Vaidhara, Mohanāśana,
Pīyūṣarāma, Dṛk, Śaṅkha, Madhuśatru, Dhanādhipa,
Svāhādhara, Vaidhara, Govinda, and the one named Vijaya.
Śvasana, Dṛṣṭimat, Bhid, Hiraṇyambu, and Makarālaya;
Kuśeśaya, Madhudveṣin, Pīta, Mādhava, and Māruta;
Acān, Dvitīyanṛhari, Vasu, and Mastaka, O Lotus-born One. (27.389–390)
Sūkṣmadṛk, sa, ūrdhvalokeśa, vairāja, madhuvidviṣaḥ,
pāpahantā, tathā, somadakṣa, ākara, vidarbhitau;
acāṃ dvitīya, anala, kamalā, amṛta, vaijayāḥ.
Likewise, Dvayabandhu, Dakṣa, Sandhava, Agni, Trivikrama,
Svayambhū, Janmahantā, Pīyūṣāgni, Madhudviṣ,
Dṛṣṭivikramayānta, Kumbhabandhu, and Caturmukha. (27.392–393)
Atri, Māruta, Ākāra, Bhadra, Hasta, Savikrama,
Vakratuṇḍa, Anila, Vighna, Dṛk, and likewise two Dineśas;
Kuñjarāsya, Paścimāsya, Vakratuṇḍa, and Akṣara.
Mandara, Sparśarodha, Gadī, Ṛtadhā, Ravi,
Pracaṇḍa, Piṇḍa, Mākāra, Madhubhit, and the one named Varuṇa—
O Lotus-seated One, having extracted the eleventh vowel *a* along with Lakṣmī from these. || 27.395–27.396 ||
The two jars of wind, auspicious for their kin, [go] to the abode of the sea-monsters;
along with the poet, the one of white luster, and those whose prowess is borne by the winds;
on the eleventh day, the enemy of Madhu [is reached], as well as the white conch and the moon.
Phullalocana, Ākārakheṭakī, and the one named Māruta; Subhadra, Vasu, Vighneśa, and Vaidhara—these are the leaders of the pretas. Following them are Sarāma, Vighnadṛk, Dakṣa, and Madhusūdana.
Yānta, Vāyu, Dhanādhyakṣa, Rāma, Adhara, Gaṇādhipa,
Bhujaṅga, Hutabhuk, Puṇya, Dakṣa, Dvipa, Sugopa,
Nātha, Subhaga, Mandara, Dvandva, Māgnibhadra, and Karāhvaya. (27.400)
Bandhu, Mastaka, Pañca, Anta, Viṣkambha, Dyumna, Bhadraka,
Vikrama, Dakṣa, Hutabhuj, Brahmasādhana, Abjaja,
Vakratuṇḍadhara, Śukla, Kumbha, Agni, and Dviradānana. || 27.401–27.402 ||
Madhusūdana, Pañcānta, Paścimānta, Mandara,
Vaidhara, Agniśiras, Śaṅkha, Śukla, Kumbhavapu, Śiras,
Sūkṣmadṛk, Ūrdhvavijaya, Varuṇa, and Vittavardhana.
The western fire, along with the oceans, followed the staff and the lotus as they went;
likewise, the sun, together with Dhruva, followed the white belly of Varuṇa,
as well as Otadeha, Dakṣa, Vakratuṇḍa, and Karālaka.
Agni, Reṇeśa, Śrīvatsa, Kumbha, Agni, Sahapaścima, Ṛta, Bhallāyudha, Gopa, Pāśapāṇi, and Janārdana;
Atri, Śrīvatsa, Anala, Vāyu, Śukla, and Jalāśaya.
Vasu, Madhudviṣ, Candra, Śrīdhara, Agni, Caturmukha;
Samprasāraṇa, Vairāja, Vasu, Śukla, Madhudviṣ; Vaidhara, Bhadra, Caṇḍāṃśu, Śvasana, Dakṣa, and Śrīdhara. (27.407–408)
The Discus-bearer, Mandara, the Unmoving, the Lotus-born as the fifth,
Udaya, Vighnanayana, Āvādi, Khaḍgadhara, and Āramā;
Vairāja, Padma, Hutabhuj, Pañcabindu, and Dhanādhipa.
Agni, Ugrātman, Madhubhit, Hṛdayāhlāda, Akṣara, Gadadhvaṃsa, Śriyaḥkānta, Vanasrak, and its wind (Tatsamīraṇa);
Kumbha, Vikrama, Pañcānta, Ṛtabhāskara, and Vaijaya. (27.410–411)
Bhuvana, Amṛta, Vairāja, Vasu, Bhallaka, Karāla, Kāla,
Vairāja, Janma, Hantāra, Dvirada, Kumbha, Vaijaya,
Svaśiras, Agni, as well as Śukla and Pītakumbha are in the abode.
Nātha, Ramādhara, Vighna, Māyā, and Saroruha;
Hutāśa and Kapila—the two who uphold the western vow; Chaladhvaṃsī, Pavitra, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Hutāśana.
*Kāntādi*, *pītaphaṇabhṛt*, the heads of the right and left [sides], *hairamba*, *agni*, *madhudveṣī*, *śubhadaudaramaindava*,
*pāṭaladvandva*, *oṃkāra*, *caṇḍāṃśu*, and *kapilākṣara*.
Kamala, Agni, Sabhuva (or Sabhuvana), Dakṣa, Gopana, Yaṣṭika;
Hutāśa, Tārkṣya, Madhubhinna, Āsikya, Caturānana;
Śrībīja, Gadadhvaṃsa, Pīta, Aurva, Dhruva, and Ādimat. || 27.416–27.417 ||
Pāṭala, Bandhujīva, Vairāja, Mṛgavallabhā,
Kakubha, and Mādhavavara— this mantra is said to end with *ṭha-ṭha*. Nārada is its seer (ṛṣi), and Varivas is said to be its meter (chandas).
The deity is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the gods of gods, O Lotus-born One.
His limbs [and mantras] are as before, and the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is also as before;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with jasmine flowers, bilva fruits, and sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh).
In the shade of a bilva tree, the recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and other rites should be performed;
this mantra, when properly mastered by those who know the mantras, bestows the supernatural powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the four aims of human life.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Discourse on the Mantras of the Fish and Other Forms," in the Caryāpāda of the Padma-tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Chapter Twenty-Eight:
The Extraction of Mantras Beginning with Yajñamūrti; the Blessed One.
O Brahmin, this mantra whose body is the sacrifice is now being declared;
attend closely to this which is being proclaimed as yielding great fruit.
One should extract it up to the word "ātmane," consisting of eight syllables.

Then follows the word ending with the body (*vigraha*), situated between *kāla* and *analā*, in the dative case (*caturthyanta*). After that comes the head of the form (*mūrtiśīrṣa*), followed by *yajña* and so forth, ending with *parama*.
Another [word] follows, ending in the same case-ending, concluding with *ṭha-ṭha*; this is declared to be the mantra. (28.2–28.3)
One should extract its primary seed-syllable ending in the anusvāra;
then the six limbs, beginning with Fire and ending with Bhāra, should be joined in sequence along with the anusvāra. Furthermore, Kratudraṣṭā and Virāṭ [are to be added].
Chanda is the soul in the form of the sacrifice, and the deity is the Blessed Lord Hari.
For the accomplishment of this mantra, a recitation of three hundred thousand times should be performed;
it yields the fruit of the four aims of human life, beginning with dharma.
