O Brahmin, the power and the very form of the mantra presiding over food are now being told; it must not be spoken of to just anyone. Every mantra begins with the *praṇava* (Om), but its specific details are stated now.
First is Mukhyamarṇa, then Bhadrapāṇi repeated;
then Ādideva, Dhanapati, and Māyā extracted last;
then Viṣṇu named Vijaya, and after that, the first Vāyu.
And then they praised Devadatta, Dakṣa, and the others, as well as Dakṣa again— the primordial god and lord of men— repeatedly, as the foremost one;
and Mandara, the destroyer of evil, the immortal, the syllable of Viṣṇu.

O Four-faced One, the mantra for the Lord of the Dead (Pretanāyaka) begins with the conch (Śaṅkha), followed by the syllable *cā*, and is recited twice; it begins with the *praṇava* (Om) and ends with *ṭhaṭha*. I shall declare its seed-syllable (*bīja*); one should extract the twelve-fold self.

Jvalana, Vāmana, and Bindu—this alone is said to be the limb (aṅga). Through the sequence beginning with the letter Ā, the division of the long vowels produces the distinction. Viṣṇu and the Visarga are declared to be the distinction of the Astra-mantra.
Vyāsa is the seer of this mantra, and its meter is Bṛhatī.
O Four-faced One, the deity of this mantra is said to be the Lord of Food.
Listen now as I shall describe another auspicious [mantra] that bestows the fruit of abundant food.
One should not excessively recite the Praṇava first, nor Varuṇa, nor Trivikrama;
nor Krodharūpa, nor Pracaṇḍa, nor Viṣṇu, nor Varuṇa thereafter;
[nor] Mādhava, nor Pūrṇacandra, nor indeed Pīyūṣātmā.
Ādi, Vaiśvānara, Mukhya, Pavitra, and Praṇava;
Ekanetra, Akāra, Śvasana, and Mādhava; then Mandara, preceded by Praṇava, and Dīptimant, O Four-faced One. (28.17–28.18)
Gopāna, Jṛmbhala, Viṣṇu, Māhendra, Gopana, Vāyu, Ādya, and Ṭhaṭhāta—this is declared to be the extraction of the syllables (varṇoddhāra).
The seed-syllable and the limbs are as previously stated; its seer (ṛṣi) is Parāśara.
Chanda is the goddess, the Gāyatrī meter, and the deity is the Lord of Food (Annapati).
[He is] seated upon a white lotus situated in the center of the full moon's orb, at the Vikara-svara;
he has a white form and dark, curly hair.
Wearing a *dukūla* silk garment and ornaments suitable for a child, he held in his right hand a vessel made of gold filled with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and in the other hand, curd-rice (*dadhyodana*).

The wise one should meditate three hundred thousand times, reciting with a mind focused on that [deity]. The best among those who know mantras should regularly offer oblations of food into the fire; he shall attain an abundance of food and obtain everything he desires.
O Four-faced One, I shall now declare the mantra of Śaktīśa;
first, the extraction of the seven syllables from the beginning has already been described.
[These are] Krodhana, Hṛdayāhlāda, Bhuvana, and then Bhāskara.
The anusvāra residing in the cave, the sun, fire, and wind;
the yellow first syllable with its staff, the lotus, the one in the form of wrath,
Mādhavī, the five dots, and the immeasurable slayer.
Vairāja, Aprameya, Puruṣātman, and Mādhava; Nārāyaṇa ending with the dative case, followed by *ṭhaṭha*—this is declared to be the mantra. Aṃśumān, Vītihotra, Vāmana, and Bindumastaka.
The limb and the seed-syllable are as previously stated; the seer is Parāśara, the metre is the Gāyatrī goddess, and the deity is Śaktīśa.
One should recite this twelve hundred thousand times and shall obtain everything desired.
O Brahmin, Kālanemi is said to be the mantra that accomplishes all things.
The first seven syllables are as before; [the remaining names are] Trivikrama, whose essence is nectar;
Ugradeha, Pracaṇḍa, Viṣṇu, Kalaśa, and Mādhava.
Kamala, Gopanayuta, Māhendra, Viṣṇumastaka,
Vighneśa, Devadatta, Dakṣa adorned with Māyā, Pataṅga, Amṛtadhāman, Vaidhara, and Caturgati. (28.32–28.33)
ĀDYAṂ, SUDHĀRASAṂ, MĀYĀ, ATRI, GOPANA, HAVYAVĀṬ,
ĀDYAṂ, SUMUKHA, ĀDYAṂ, ŚVASANA, and APRAMEYAKA—
ending with HUMPHAṬ and followed by ṬHAṬHA— thus is the mantra extracted.
I shall declare the seed-syllable as Dinakara, the world as Yaṣṭimastaka;
the limbs begin with "Kruddha" as before; Nārada is the seer of the mantra, Virāṭ is the metre, and the deity is the four-faced Kālanemi.
The number of recitations and the fruit shall also be like those of the six-syllable mantra.
I shall now describe the Trailokyamohana mantra exactly as it is:
[the syllable] Ud-gītha, the yellow lotus, Vāmana, and the bindu upon the head.
This single-syllable mantra is the deity; its limbs [of nyāsa] follow in sequence.

One should employ it together with the six [limbs], beginning with *acām* (the vowels) and including the *anusvāra*. The seer is Vṛddhamanu, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the divinity is [the same]. (28.38–39)
The deity is Trailokyamohana; the deities are the recitation and the libation.
The fire-oblation and its fruit are the discovery of the location of a treasure.
By reciting further, one likewise enjoys every fruit that is difficult to obtain.
O Brahmin, this sixteen-syllable mantra is said to be the very essence of the enchantment of the three worlds.
As before, one should extract the first seven syllables;
after that, the word "Trailokyamohana" ending in the dative case. (28.41–28.42)
One should extract that word with its case-ending, ending in "svāhā," which is the station of Viṣṇu.
This mantra is indeed his limb; the seed-syllable is declared as before.
Pulastya is the sage, and the meter and deity are likewise as stated previously.
The number of recitations and the fruit thereof are prescribed for one who knows the root mantra.
There is another nine-syllable mantra whose nature is the enchantment of the three worlds;
it consists of the word "trailokyamohana" in the dative case, followed by "namaḥ."
The seed-syllable consisting of the limbs, which bestows the fruits of all desires;
the word beginning with the Veda (the syllable *praṇava*) ending in the dative case, which deludes the three worlds;
the fire garlanded with rays (*aṃśumālin*), together with the five dots (*pañcabindu*) and the staff (*yaṣṭika*).
[One should worship] Śaṅkhin and Pulaha, endowed with five dots and a staff;
having repeated that seed-syllable twice,
followed by an obeisance, this twelve-syllabled mantra is the very essence of the enchantment of the three worlds.
A hundred thousand recitations for each syllable yields a result equal to that of the twelve-syllable mantra;
this mantra named Kāmakāmeśvarī bestows all fruits.
Having first uttered the *udgītha*, one should then utter Bhāskara and Jvalana.
"Mahāmāyāṃ yaṣṭiyutām"—thus one should extract the single-syllable [mantra].
This very limb is declared; the sage is said to be Śaunaka.
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is Puruṣottama.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and shall obtain all desires.
[One should meditate on the Lord] white as a conch, a kunda flower, or the moon, four-armed, wearing a crown,
mounted upon Garuḍa, with the Goddess seated upon his left thigh.

One should meditate with a one-pointed mind upon Lakṣmī, who resembles the flower of the pomegranate tree, adorned with all ornaments, holding a noose and a goad, her eyes overwhelmed by passion— the mistress of desire and the object of desire. (28.53–28.54)

Now the mantra named Trailokyamohana is being described. First, one should utter the Brahmakośa, and immediately thereafter, ending with the word "namas. A wise person should extract the words ending in the vocative case in their proper sequence.

"Puruṣa" and so forth up to "Uttamapada," "Rūpa" and so forth as "Apratima," [the sequence] from "Lakṣya" up to "Nivāsa," the entire series beginning with "Sakala" up to "Jagatpada," and [the sequence] beginning with "Sarva" up to "Kṣobhaṇa," ending with "Strīhṛdaya. (28.56–28.57)

Then [he recited] "Vidāraṇa-śiras," beginning with the third [world] up to the end of the universe, ending with "Unmādakara," followed by the words "surāsura-padam. Then, having uttered "manuja," he [recited] the names of beautiful women thereafter.
Having uttered "manāṃsi" (minds), O Four-faced One, [utter] "tāpaya" (heat);
then the word "dīpaya" (illuminate), and then "śoṣaya" (dry up) and "māraya" (kill);
and the series of action-words ending with "stambhaya" (paralyze), "drāvaya" (liquefy), and "ākarṣa" (attract).

Then, O Brahmin, it should be recited twice, up to the word *paramaṃ subhagā*. Then one should utter the word *saubhāgya* ending in the vocative case (*sambuddhyanta*), followed by the phrase *sarvakāmapradaṃ*, and then the word *amuka*. (28.61)
Having uttered "haneti" twice, and then "cakreṇa" and "gadaya," one should then recite "khaḍgena," "sarvabāṇaiḥ," and "dvirbhindeti.
Then follows "pāśena," and the two words "bandha" and "bandha. (28.62–63)
Having uttered "With the goad," one should repeat "Strike" twice;
having pronounced "Do it" twice, [one says] "Why do you stand? followed by the word "pada.
Then, having uttered "pada," one should subsequently state the desired destination.
"May success be mine," having uttered this, "me hūṃ phaṭ" is the head [of the mantra].
Thus, this extraction of the garland-mantra has been demonstrated.
It begins with *nigama*, is endless, and has *aurva* as its crest-ornament with the half-moon.
Having thus extracted the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the mantra is again divided into six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
It should be divided in six ways; its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Nalakūbara.
Its meter (*chandas*) is named Aticchanda, and its deity (*devatā*) is Puruṣottama.
The best of mantra-knowers should meditate upon that very Puruṣa and accomplish [the rite]:
Acyuta, who has eight arms, large eyes, and is mounted upon Garuḍa;
who resembles the stainless moon and has a face like the full moon.
With his forehead and eyebrows adorned by a crown, an ocean of the nectar of loveliness,
wearing yellow silken garments, and with earrings brushed against his cheeks;
holding a discus, a mace, an arrow, and a goad in his right arms.
Holding a conch, the Kaumodakī mace, the Śārṅga bow, and a noose in his left hands;
endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,
his limbs anointed with divine sandalwood paste and decorated with divine garlands.
Eight goddesses stand around him, fans of hair in their hands;
with eyes overwhelmed by passion, they constantly fan the god.
Outside of these, in the eight directions, are those who bear the discus and other emblems.

The men, having prostrated before the Lord of the Gods, stood outside. (28.74) Thus, with a concentrated mind, having meditated upon that God together with his retinue, women among men become submissive through the recitation of the mantra for seven days. (28.75)
And during those same days, all the women of the yakṣas and other classes stand before him with their minds possessed by the god of love;
they attend upon the practitioner and, through the power of his mantra, cause him to be infatuated.
Furthermore, the reciter undoubtedly attains all desires in this way.
What more need be said? The Lord shall become manifest; there is peace, prosperity, righteousness, as well as pleasure, wealth, and even liberation itself.
Traveling to the underworld and through the sky, invisibility and the state of being unseen;
the discovery of treasure, the power of Bali, as well as digging for [treasure] and medicinal herbs; sandals, pills, and the unsurpassed elixir of immortality (rasāyana).
The rosary, the conch, the sword, as well as the accomplishment of the vetāla—
such fruits, though difficult to attain, are accomplished through the power of the mantras;
they are not displayed individually here by those fearing excessive prolixity in the text.

O Four-faced One, this direction of fruits has been declared for those that are difficult to obtain— namely, for the mantra known as Trailokyamohana and for Kāmakāmeśvara. O Lotus-born One, the fruit of the Ekākṣara-mantra has also been described.
O Lotus-seated One, I shall declare the mantra of Yajñavarāha.

Having taken all the letters in their proper sequence as before, beginning with the first [consonants], ending with the final letter of the *sparśa* class, followed by the Sun (the letter *ra*), the first [vowel] (*a*), the water-pot (*ka*), and the *praṇava* (*oṃ*). 28.83–84.
Anala, Ādideva, Anta, Bhāskara, Madhusūdana, Śvasana, the first letter (A), Oṣadhīśa, the mouth of the vowels (I),
Vahni, Pracetas, Mukhya, Māruta, and that which begins with Praṇava (Oṃ).
Immediately after, [he saw] Musalin, who is as white as the moon; then Acāma; then Śrīvatsa, who is fire-like and the protector against the fire of Mahāmāyā;
likewise Dara, Viṣṇu, Vijaya, who wields a sword, and Śrīdhara.
The nectar-like, stainless Mādhava, likewise Vaidhara,
the primordial one of pure vision, adorned with the Praṇava and other [mantras],
the breath, the immeasurable, the essence of the digits (kalā), and Viṣṇumastaka.
Varuṇa occupied by Dahana, Vaidhara, and the syllable of Mādhava;
Varuṇa and the first letter, likewise conjoined with Ugra-ātman; Anala joined with Mādhava, Mandara, and the first Marut.
Madhusūdanavikrānta, Pavana, Śvetarocis,
Varuṇa, Vītihotra, Subhadra, Guhālaya,
Vairāja, Ādideva, Vijaya, and Mandara.
Bhadrapāṇi, Mṛgeśa, Vaidhara, Yaṣṭimastaka,
Ugrātman, Parvata, Ādi adorned with the abode of Truth (Ṛtadhāma),
Vighneśa, Māruta, Ekanetra, and likewise Śuklaśiras.
And Subhadra, the Lord of the Upper World, born from the navel-lotus;
Mādhavī and the Immeasurable; likewise Vanamālī and Jhaṣa;
Māhendra accompanied by Gopa; and Māruta, the first tone.
Bhallāyudha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Subhadra, Bhuvana, Vasu,
Pracetasa, Kalātmā, Amṛta, Savisargaka,
Pavitra, Ādi, Vairāja, Mukhya, Pavana, and Ādhava.
One should utter *subhadra*, *maurva*, *dakṣa*, and the two-footed *mukha*; one should recite the two-footed *śaśāṅka*, *vahni*, and *bhuvana*.
One should indicate the second of the vowels (*ā*), the *dṛṣṭi*, the *māyā*, and the *kalaśa*.
Havyavāṭ, Gopana-yuta, Bhāskara, Madhusūdana,
Prabhañjana, Akāra, Sūkṣmadṛgbhuvana,
Mādhavī, Rāmasahita, Paścimānana, and Ādimat.
One should utter twice the syllable *eka-netra*, as well as *ikāra*, *vijaya*, *kalaśa*,
*mandara*, *devadatta*, *vaidhara*, and *viṣṇumastaka*;
[this] is the beginning of that which faces west and ends with *gopanā*.
The letter *a* is the breaker (*prabhañjana*), and the seed-mantra ending in *ṭha-ṭha* is proclaimed as the *manu*.
This seed, which is the world of subtle vision and the creation itself, has been extracted.
Having divided the mantra into six parts, the sage Kāśyapa performed the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*). || 28.101–28.102 ||

The meter is Virāj, the nose is the Stoma chant, the deity is the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā), and the recitation should consist of twelve hundred thousand [japas]; the fruit shall be as before in its entirety.
Now, the mantra of Darodarasiṃha is being told.
Having first extracted the syllable Oṃ, [one should utter] the lotus that burns the enemy,
the abode of the cave, together with the staff, the lord of rays, the world, the fixed,
the primordial one with blossoming eyes, and likewise the delighter of the heart.
"Bhadrapāṇi, Svarādi, Jvalana, Ādima, Oṣadhīśa, Ikāra, Yaṣṭi, Bhāskara, Gopana,
Śvasana, and Nati— this is declared to be the Nārasiṃha mantra. (28.106)
This very Manu is the seed-syllable; the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed [for it].
Nṛhari is the deity, Kapila is said to be the seer, and meditation is described as follows:
[he is] seated comfortably upon a blossoming hundred-petaled lotus in a cave.
Resembling molten gold, with four arms and uplifted weapons,
beautiful in his cross-legged posture with two arms extended, and adorned above the knees with every kind of ornament.
With mouth wide open, three eyes, and terrifying with claws like thunderbolts;
half-lion and half-man, with a roar as deep as a cloud—
having thus meditated, the practitioner, composed in mind, should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times.
One should meditate upon the God seated within the solar orb, the granter of all desires;
by so doing, one shall obtain the four aims of human existence, beginning with Dharma.
What need is there for much speaking on this matter? One shall attain all desires.
The mantra for the four beings, beginning with Puruṣa, is now being described.
Having extracted the seven syllables beginning with the *praṇava* as before,
one should formulate their mantras by appending each individual name in the dative case.
I shall now describe their seed-syllables (bījas) in sequence through the extraction of phonemes:
the "Scorching Ray" (tigmāṃśu) joined with "Gopana" (the letter *u*) and with the "Staff" (daṇḍa, the visarga) belongs to the Self in the form of Puruṣa.
Mārtāṇḍa, with five dots (pañcabindu, the nasal *m*) and with the Moon (sendu, the vowel *i*), is said to be Satya.
Vairāja, Pāvaka, Pañcabindu, and Nāsikya; Trayītanu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Yaṣṭi, and Anantanāman—
likewise, for the eight-syllabled [mantra], there are the seer, the meter, the deity, and the fruit.
The extraction of the syllables of the Hayagrīva mantra is now demonstrated:
having extracted seven syllables, then the "Victory" (vijaya), the "Abundant" (bahula),
the "Soul of Time" (kālātman), the "Single Eye" (ekadṛk), "Fire" (vahni), "Lord of Cows" (gopati), and the "Head of Viṣṇu" (viṣṇumastaka).
The breath (ŚVA), preceded by the *praṇava* (OM), followed immediately by Lakṣmī (LĀM) and the Bindu (M);
then Fire (RA), joined with the cow (GO) and the nose (V), as well as the Moon (SA) and Mādhava (DHAVA);
ending with Svāhā—this is declared to be the sixteen-syllable mantra of Aśvaśiras.
That very [mantra] is the seed-syllable; its limbs are as before, beginning with *kruddholkā*.
Bṛhaspati is indeed its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (*chanda*).
The deity named Hayaśiras is the presiding divinity (*devatā*), whose seat is the lotus.
One should recite the mantra one million times and shall attain great gnosis.
Preceded by the syllable Oṃ and ending with a salutation (namaḥ), [the name of] the deity in the dative case in sequence,
this king of mantras ends with Ṭhaṭha and is interspersed with the ten-syllable [mantra].
O Lotus-seated One, everything regarding the seed-syllables should be performed as before;
thereafter, I shall tell you another *mālā-mantra* of Vājiśiras. Having extracted seven syllables, the word "Hayaśiras" [is likewise added].

After the word *sarvavidyālaya* ending in the dative case (*caturthyanta*), one should extract the word *guruve* preceded by the word *sakalāmara*. Immediately after that, [one should extract] *hantānantya* preceded by the word *samastaprati*. (28.125–126)
Then follows the station of vigor and splendor, and after that the station of knowledge and sovereignty;
then indeed power and strength, and thereafter the abode of all that is primordial. Then follows its division, and after that the station of the Supreme Self.
The word *Vāsudeva* ending in the dative case, followed by a word with the same case-ending,
[is used]; likewise for the words *jñāna-jñeya*, *vyakta-avyakta-parāya*,
and having uttered *sarva-duṣṭāsura*, as well as *durita* and *vrajina*.

Having uttered the word "Pramāthin" ending in its case-suffix, preceded by "tat-sat-ruci-apūrva," and having pronounced the mantra "jñānam uccārya mūrtaye turagāya," and then having recited after that [the name] a thousand times or ten million times; || 28.130 ||
Abandon the collection of words beginning with *vidyā* and proceed to the word *pada*.
Then, the word *sphoṭi*, followed by *vijṛmbhiloḍantaṃ*, and the verbal form (*tiṅpada*) should be stated twice.
Furthermore, there are three words: that which begins with *sarva*, that which is in the middle of *tejas*, and that which ends with *nidhi*.
Having uttered the word ending in the fourth case, followed by the word *nirdhūta*;
having uttered the word *vikīrṇa*, then the word *pradīpta*;
and then the filament (*kesara*), the word *kaṭa*, and the word *kalāpa*—each followed by the word *pada*.
He was like the blazing rays of the sun, with a station resembling that [light];
his form was like the sun, and he emitted heat rising from his head.
His feet were white as a conch shell, and he possessed the brilliance of a spreading mass of light.
Having uttered the molten gold [syllable], with a face as long as Piṅgalā,
possessing the form of the Great Sound (Mahāsvara), and then having teeth that are perfectly pure;
having likewise spoken the path that has emerged, which is a resplendent state.

Having uttered the words "lokatrayadravaddīptapadaṃ cāmīkarādimat" (the blazing state that causes the three worlds to flee, possessing gold and so forth), one should recite the expanded phrase "piṅgalāyata" (tawny and long). Then one should recite the great sound beginning with "locana" (the eye) accompanied by the word "vibhiṣaṇa" (the terrifying).

Having uttered the beautiful word "nāsikāpuṭam" (the nostril-cavity), which is joined with the form of the peak of the king of mountains, and likewise the word "vikuñcita-padam" (the contracted foot),
one should recite the word "śreyaḥ" (prosperity) joined with "mahā-śravaṇa" (great hearing).

And immediately after that word ending in the dative case, [one should utter] "duṣṭasattvān," followed by the verbal roots *bhindhi*, *chinddhi*, *māri-mardi*, and *trāsi*. Having pronounced these twice in the imperative mood (*loṭ*), one should then utter the two words *svauṃ* and *vaum*. (28.140–141)

*Dhvasi* destroys, and likewise *dhmāpi* destroys; *grāhi* seizes and *tāḍaya* strikes. *Paci* and *mandi*—these are formed twice from the root *loḍ*. Having uttered the word of the supreme vidyā, let it be employed ending in *chindhi*.
Having spoken thus, "Amī," the woman is likewise known as the middle head of salt (loṇmadhyamaśiras).
Immediately after the word "Come, come, O Blessed One" (ehy ehi bhagavan), one should utter the sound of the vajra,
followed by "With the hook" (aṅkuśena) and then "Draw it forth" (cākarṣaya).
One should place [the seed-syllable] preceded by *bhakti* at the heart and other locations;

having declared the abode of the tongue and so forth, one follows it with the submarine fire (*baḍavānala*) addressed in the vocative case as "O Viśvamūrti," and immediately thereafter with "O Saumanasya."

Then one should utter "Bhagavan," followed by the heart-mantra Oṃ. Then, from the abode of Brahmā, the word "Ātman" should be uttered; thereafter, one should pronounce the word "Bhagavat," beginning with "Cidghana" and ending in the dative case.
One should thus extract Hayagrīva ending with *ṭha-ṭha*, O four-faced one;
his seed-syllable is exactly as previously stated, and the procedure for the limbs (*aṅga*) is as before.
Vyāsa is the sage, Hayagrīva is the deity, and the meter is *utkṛti*.
Meditating on the formidable foam vomited from the mouth of Hayagrīva,
the wise knower of mantras should recite the king of mantras as if drinking it;
he should perform ten thousand or even a million recitations for the sake of attaining mastery over the mantra.
O Lotus-born One, one attains the perfection of knowledge, mastery of speech,
the status of an expounder, and authorship of scriptures on many paths; indeed,
by a single instance of grasping it, all sciences become firmly established.
And there shall be no forgetting of those [teachings] regarding the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha). For him, nothing is unattainable, and he attains a long life.
Now, Manu is being described in relation to the six [sages], headed by Mukunda. 28.152–153.
Having first uttered seven syllables, one should likewise join the six names ending in the dative case;
in this manner, one should extract the remaining syllables.
Jīmūta is the beginning, [placed] in the nose, and Varuṇa preceded by the *praṇava*.

The sun with a bindu, the letter *ra* with five bindus and a staff, and the letter *ṭha* ending in *ṭha*—thus is the mantra of Mukunda extracted. The sun, fire, five bindus, and accompanied by a staff [are likewise]. (28.155–156)
One should repeat twice the syllable *akṣara* and *mārtāṇḍa*, which is associated with Guha;
one should then repeat twice the word *viṣṇu* together with the *anusvāra*.
Ending in the dative case and terminating in *ṭha*, this is declared to be the mantra of Babhru.
One should extract Parvata, Bhuvana, Bhānu, Ūrdhva, Lokeśa, and Nāsikā; then Bhāskara, Pāvaka, Pañcabindu, and the nasal [Nāsikya];
and finally the syllable *phaṭ* and the end of the oblation (*hutānta*)—such is the mantra of Vṛṣākapi.
"Śubhadaṃ pāvakaṃ caiva pañcabinduṃ sadarthakam | Akṣaraṃ tad dvir uccāryaṃ ṭhaṭhānto mantra īritaḥ ||" "O Lotus-born One, I shall likewise declare another mantra for Śauri, the Dāśārha mantra."
Savitṛ, Bṛhadbhānu, Sayaṣṭi, and Pañcabinduka;
the mantra ending with *huta* is proclaimed, and it is called the Vaikuṇṭha-mantra.
The Supreme Self (*paramātman*) followed by the dative case-ending, and Varuṇa as the first vowel.
Then the nasal (nāsikya), the pitcher (kumbha), the form (ākāra), the half-moon (ardhendu), the sun (bhāskara),
Hṛṣīkeśa, and the anusvāra; then the word Nārāyaṇa in the dative case ending in the letter ṭha— this is declared to be the Vaikuṇṭha-mantra.
The seer, the meter, and the deity, as well as the seed-syllable and the six limbs— O Four-faced One, the fruits of these are like those of the eight-syllable [mantra].
Now, O Lotus-seated One, I shall declare the Aparājita mantra.
Having first taken the seven classes beginning with *nigama* as before,
one should extract the word *antaḥ* preceded by *ananta* ending in the dative case;
then again, the word for the case-ending beginning with *sahasra* and ending with *śīrṣa*.

Having uttered the word *tatsugandham*, followed by *tathākṣīram* and *udārṇavapadānvitam*; then having spoken the word *śāyinā*, as well as the word *śeṣabhogapadam*; then *paryaṅke* in the dative case (caturthyanta), and likewise its case-ending for the vehicle (*vāhanam*).
After that, the word *garuḍa* and so forth, then the word *vāsudeva*; its case-ending, ending in *namaḥ*, and likewise [the words] *pītavāsas* and so on;
followed by the word *karṣaṇa* preceded by *sam*, ending in the vocative case.
From Pradyumna to Aniruddha, that is remembered as the section of divisions (vibhaktipada).
In the case of the Perfectly Awakened One (Sambuddha), Varāha is likewise desired as the head;
following that, Nṛsiṃha and Vāmana constitute the Trivikrama section.

Having uttered the word "Rāma" three times, one should raise the word "Kṛṣṇa"; then the word "Varaprada," followed by "Nata" (in the vocative), and the verb "asti" (is). Then those [words] in the dative case, and the word "Asura. || 28.172 ||

Having uttered the words "daitya" and "yakṣa," and then the word "rākṣasa," [he should utter] "bhūta," "piśāca," "siddha," and "yoginī" and "ḍākinī. Then, omitting the word "brahmā," he should utter the word "rākṣasa" and then the word "vināyaka."

One should recite the words "the uprooting of Pūtanā, Revatī, Skanda, and those who go before them," followed by "the planets and so forth, and the lunar mansions and planetary deities in due order," and then "and others," preceded by the word "great" (mahat), and finally the word "houses" (gṛhān).

Having recited the names twice, he should likewise say, "Take [it]," while [the victim] is being killed, burned, cooked, and churned together with the sacrificial substances; and while [the victim] is being struck by the blades and falling upon the paths, he should likewise recite the names twice.
"Enter!"—this is the form ending in the *si* suffix; "harm!"—these end in the *loṭ* suffix. O Four-faced One, these four verbal roots should be uttered twice in the mantra.
One should pronounce the discus, the mace, and the thunderbolt with the third case-ending.

Having recited "reduce to ashes," followed by "the arm," "the perfectly awakened one," "the head," (28.179) "the thousand-spoked word," "all," "foremost," and "weapon," O Lotus-born One, he spoke twice the two words "Victory! and "O Victor! (28.180).
Ananta, apara, pūrva, jita, and likewise pratihata;
preceded by the negative particle (nañ) up to the word netṛ, followed by words beginning with "sahasra";
then prajvali and jvali—these two, ending in the imperative mood, one should utter twice.
Having extracted the Viśvarūpa [mantra], one should then recite the names Madhusūdana,
Mahāpuruṣa, Vaikuṇṭha, and Nārāyaṇa; then the name Padmanābha up to the end of the word "nābhi," and thereafter the name Hṛṣīkeśa.
Having uttered "sarva" and likewise "tathābhūta," one should extract the word for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
After uttering "śaṅkha-cakra-gadā," one should then say "dhara.
Having extracted "sarvabhūta" and likewise the word for salutation (*namaskṛta*), [one should proceed].
Having recited in due order the entire *manvaṅga-nāgapada* accompanied by the *pramardana-pada*, one should then proceed with the subduing of the asuras;
having followed all the gods in sequence, one should then invoke Maheśvara.
Having recited the entire *graha* [mantra] as well as the words for warding off,
and then another *yantra* beginning with "sarva," followed by the words for the wind (*prabhañjana*),
it pacifies all suffering and destroys all fevers.
Having followed all the bonds, one should likewise extract the word for liberation;
it removes all mental anxieties and bad dreams from their midst.
This consists of three words: that which has "namas" at its end, "sarva" at its beginning, and "bhūta" in the middle. (28.188–189)
The two words should be as before; one should perform the extraction.
"O Janārdana" is the vocative, and the word following it is "namaścāstu.
The seed-syllable "aprameya," accompanied by the anusvāra, has been declared.
Having divided the mantra into six parts, the seer of the limbs is said to be Pradyumna.
Its meter is Aticchandas and its deity is Viśvarūpa.
The knower of mantras should accomplish the mantra through the eight-syllable samādhi.
By means of the Aparājita mantra, there is no fruit that cannot be accomplished:
subjugation, eradication, as well as the rite of killing; and immediately thereafter, the warding off of the defects caused by malevolent spirits and the like.
"One who desires all fruits should take recourse in this mantra.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Extraction of Mantras beginning with Yajñamūrti," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Chapter Twenty-nine:
Description of the Mantras of the Retinue. The Blessed One said:
I shall describe in due order the arrangement of the seats for the goddesses, Śrī and the others,
as well as the mantras of their retinues in the first enclosure and so forth; listen attentively to how it is done.
The first letter of the *chandas* [is the first], the fourth [letter] immediately following *agni*, *agni* itself, the great *māyā*, and finally the *anusvāra*:
this single-syllable mantra, O Brahman, bestows all fruits of prosperity. || 29.2–29.3 ||
The seer is said to be Maṅkaṇaka, the meter is called Gāyatrī, and Śrī is its deity; one should fashion its limbs according to their own forms.
One should accomplish the goal at the root of a Bilva tree by reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should offer oblations with his fuel-sticks (*samidh*) ten thousand times.
One should offer oblations with *śrī* flowers and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in the stated number;
one who desires prosperity attains great fortune—of this there is no doubt.
The name preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), ending in the dative case and followed by "namas," is declared [to be the mantra].
This four-syllable mantra is another [form] of Śrī.
The seer of this is the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), the meter is *śrī*, and the deity is likewise Śrī.
The practitioner should recite each syllable one hundred thousand times for the sake of attaining success in the mantra.
As before, the seed-syllable, the limbs, and the fruit are also as previously described.
[One should worship] Nigamādi, Bhadrahasta, Hairamba, and Mandarādhipa.
Śubhada, Dahana, Māyā, Māruta, and likewise Mādhava—
this seven-syllable Śrī-mantra is as before, with all other [elements] remaining the same.
Having first taken the single syllable Bhānu, Agni, and Vāmana...
Bhalvāyudha, Māhendra, Hṛṣīkeśa with his staff; Śaśāṅka, Aurva, Nāsikya, Subhadra with his mace, the supreme;
Jalādhidaiva, Ādyarṇa, Vairāja, Godhana, and Dhara.
One should then conclude with Pulaha, Kamala, Śakra, Dāhaka, Pāṭalapriya,
Godhana, Kamala, Citrabhānu adorned with illusion,
Prabhañjana, and Mṛgeśa within Svāhā.
O Lotus-born One, this sixteen-syllable mantra of Śrī consists of the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end, followed by Kamala, Mandara,
Māhendra, Varuṇa, Ādideva, Candra, and Trivikrama. (29.14–29.15)

"O Four-faced One, this has been declared as ending with *hutānta*, beginning with *vighneśa* and *pañcabindu*; all [the preceding] elements, such as the seed-syllables and so forth, are to be taken up as before.
Thus, O Lotus-born One, another mantra of Śrī has been extracted."
Having first extracted the Udgītha, the Śrīvatsa, and likewise the Anala;
then the Vāmana, the Yaṣṭiśiras, the Dineśa, and the Yānta, O Lotus-born One;
as well as the Pañcabindu, the Sayaṣṭi, the Śubhada, and the Vasumastaka.

The staff [mantra] marked with Mahāmāyā, ending with "ṭhaṭha," has Maṅkaṇaka as its seer, Gāyatrī as its meter, and Śrī as its deity. One should recite this mantra three hundred thousand times and then accomplish the practice in a grove of Bilva trees.
The accomplishments of subjugation, attraction, obtaining land, mines, jewels, and so forth—[these belong to this deity].
I shall now describe the meditation upon Śrī within the Maheśvara-maṇḍala;
one should worship her as she sits, along with her attendants, Indra and the others, in due order.
O Lotus-born One, having uttered one's own name in the dative case and followed by the word "namas" as the mantra,
[one should place] the four Vyūhas, beginning with Vāsudeva, in the petals of the lotus within the maṇḍala, starting from the east and proceeding through the directions. (29.22)
Their names, ending in the dative case, ending in *namaḥ*, and accompanied by the *praṇava* (oṃ),
should be placed along with guggulu, karaṇḍa, damaka, and śalala within the corner sections, preceded by those respective names.
Rati, Sarasvatī, Bhūmi, Prīti, Kīrti, O Four-faced One, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi are the Śaktis situated below Śrī;
their names have been declared as those of the Manus in successive order.
And on her right side stands the lotus-treasure (Padmanidhi), and on her left the treasure named Śaṅkha; their mantras are as before. [Also there are] Dhanada, Māṇibhadra, Jṛmbhala, and Nalakūbara.
Pūrṇabhadra, Calendra, Kalisṛk, and Śibikuṇḍala—
these are said to be the mantras for beings in the directions starting from the east:
Subhadra at the beginning of the Vedas, Ekadanta, and Sayaṣṭika.
The mantra of Dhanada is declared to be "Nama" followed by "Nantya.
O Lotus-born One, the mantra of Nalakūbara is said to consist of the five-dot [seed-syllable] with the lotus-navelled one (Padmanābha) and the staff (daṇḍaka), preceded by "Bhallāyudham. 29.29–30.
Kakubha, Padmanābha, Nāsikya, Jṛmbhala, Manu,
Sparśānta, Pulaha, and thereafter Urdhvalokeśa— this mantra,
which is like that of Māṇibhadra, accomplishes all aims. (29.31)
The western world-sphere has the appearance of yellow and is topped by a staff;
O Four-faced One, this is declared to be the mantra of Pūrṇabhadra.
Furthermore, there is the syllable *ma* for Vakratuṇḍa, and the world-sphere of Pulaha. (29.32–29.33)
In this age named Śibikuṇḍala, Manu will be Nāsikya;
Brahmā, Ādipulaha, Guhālaya, and Yaṣṭika [will be the sages].
Thus has been described the extraction (uddhāra) of the Kali-yuga, which is full of impurity.
Vakratuṇḍa, who is yellow in color, and Hṛṣīkeśa—these are certainly fixed there.
The mantra of Carendra is declared in due order starting from the east:
Mandara, Pulaha, Guṇālaya, and Yaṣṭika.
O Lotus-Seated One, this mantra of Mahendra is declared as "Manu," and that of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) is said to be "Subhaga," arising from Pulaha. Furthermore,
on the right side, the attendants of Śrī should be worshipped as they stand there.
Khaḍga, Dāmodara, and Mahāmāyā with the bindu—
this is declared to be the mantra of Cintāmaṇi, residing on the eastern petal.
[Then follow] Srīvatsa, Agni, Bhuvana, Daṇḍa, and Caturmukha.
And the mantra of Balā has been taught, with worship performed in the place of Tārkṣya;
Indra and the other world-protectors are stationed all around in their respective directions.
Furthermore, in the third enclosure are Balākī and Vanamālinī.
Vibhīṣī and Śāṅkarī are likewise stationed in the directions starting from the east;
they wear bodices, hold canes in their hands, and their names are identical to those of the mantras.
Then, one should worship Puṣpadhāriṇī in the station of Viṣvaksena.
One should place the *kalpaka*, the *pārijāta*, and the tree of *haricandana*, as well as the *santāna* and *mandara* trees, at the door-decorations;
likewise, the *bilva* and the lake filled with lotuses (*śatapatra*).
Having thus assigned attendants to Śrī— who is surrounded by her splendor and filled with the warbling sounds of flocks of birds— one should worship them using their respective names,
preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the dative case and the word "namas" (salutation). || 29.44-29.45 ||
O Lotus-born One, I shall proclaim the garland-mantra of Śrī:
having first uttered the Udgītha, and immediately thereafter a salutation;
having spoken the word "Bhagavatī," one should then follow it with the name of Śrī in the dative case.

The vocative *dhīra* and *sambuddho*, preceded by *śrī*; likewise *nilayaḥ* preceded by the letter *ā*; then *bharaṇam* adorned with a hundred [syllables]; and the vocative *śarīra*—one should extract the words in this manner. (29.47–48)

One should utter twice this seed-syllable: Bhāskara, Anala, Pañcabindu, adorned with the crescent moon as its crest, consisting of the Kalās and ending with the Visarga. Having uttered it twice, the word "Bhara" follows immediately after the word "Pāpa."

One should say "Alakṣmīm" (O Misfortune), and then utter "Nāśaya" (Destroy) twice. Following that, one should practice the mantra of Bhāskara, Pāvaka, Pañcavindu, and Yaṣṭi three times; likewise, [one removes] what was previously acquired over seven births.
Having uttered "akhilaṃ" (the whole), then "dāridryaṃ" (poverty), and likewise "padaṃ dūrāt" (the state far away),
having twice uttered "utsāraya" (drive away) as emitted by Candramas and others,
one should immediately thereafter utter three times the word "tvadbhaktajana" (your devotee).
Having joined the word *vasum*, one should again utter the word *dhāraya*.
O Lotus-Seated One, having twice uttered the word *pūraya*,
and having thrice uttered the syllable *hrīṃ* for the world that has sought refuge, [one should place] the horse and the elephant.
Having pronounced "vividhaṃ paśu," immediately thereafter "nicayam";
then, at the end of that, look twice upon "dāsīdāsaṃ parijanam.
Then, having said "māṃ ca saumya," accompanied by a glance.

"O Lotus-born One, having uttered three times 'Sacrifice! (yajeti) and twice 'Become! (bhavati), [one should call] Lakṣmī, Agni, and Vikrama, as well as Śrīdhara and Yaṣṭimastaka; and immediately after the words 'O Gods and Asuras' (surāsura), [one should call] the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas. (29.56–29.57)

Desiring the entire state of Yakṣas and Vidyādharas, along with the title "Lord of Beings," and immediately thereafter union with those who are "pleasing to the mind," [he addressed] the Sun, the abode of the caves, with the vocative address "O Beloved."
Having uttered this seed-syllable of the half-moon three times at the beginning,
and having likewise uttered the various boons, the white garland,
and the garment; and having fully uttered "Dhāriṇī," [one obtains] all splendor and wealth.
"May the lotus-like accumulations become [united] with the Perfectly Awakened One; therein these three are the words. 'The state of Śrī' is also [included], and 'may there be' is the verb.
The word *yuṣmad* ending in the dative case, and the mantra ending in *ṭha-ṭha* has been declared. (29.61)
As before, having analyzed the seed-syllable and the mantra of this [deity] as well, one should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*).
Its meter is *Aticchandas*, and its deity is the illustrious Lord of Wealth (*Śrīdhanādhipa*).
The fruit of beholding [the deity] and the fruit of reciting its mantra are like those of the twelve-syllable [mantra].
Now, O Four-faced One, I shall proclaim the mantra of Vasudhā:
the Brahmakośa, its mouth, as well as the Śrīvatsa and the Jvalana;
and the Vāmana, Mādhava, Devadatta, and the Śrībīja.
Kamala, Bahula, Pañcabindu, Subhaga, Anvata,
Bhadrahasta, Vidhātṛ, Anala, Vāmana, as well as Subhaga, Gopanayuta, Vighneśa, and Samīraṇa.
One should employ the sixteen-syllable mantra beginning with *karālam agnim ī* and ending with *ṭhaṭhā*,
as well as that which begins with *tārā* (Oṃ), has *vasu* (the letter *va*) in the middle, and ends with *ṭhaṭhā*, for the heart and other limbs.
One should also append the word of salutation (*namaskāra*) and the word "Śrī" following each [mantra].

Likewise, the two words *saumyau* and *sambuddhau*, followed by the two words *samaya* and *iti*; having uttered *abhayaṅkari* immediately thereafter with a great sound; ending in *ṭa*, possessing *samaya*, and ending in *ḍha* and *ḍha* in the vocative case (*sambuddhau*). (29.68–29.69)
One should go to the end of *hy*, and likewise go to the word *pūrva* from behind.
The pair of words should be spoken twice, as well as *bhaga-pūrvāvadhi*. One should give the word *vasu* as the head, ending with *ṭha-ṭha*, and with that one should invoke [the mantra].
And one should meditate upon the Goddess Earth, possessing the luster of molten gold,
seated upon a lion-throne, always adorned with many ornaments,
holding the stem of a pomegranate tree in her left hand and likewise in her other [right] hand.
O Four-faced One, she holds in her hand an auspicious *cintāmaṇi* jewel,
and an upward-facing jar filled with various kinds of gems;
at the big toe of her right foot is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) of the western quarter.
On both sides, she was attended by women with fly-whisks in their hands,
and by others bearing white betel;
[she was also flanked by] the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures, vomiting forth vast wealth.
The two attendants stand again looking at each other’s faces;
those whose attendants have not been mentioned should be understood according to the path of Śrīmanu.
Standing facing the east in the current of a river flowing toward the ocean, [one should perform the rite].
One who is concentrated in mind should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while standing at the height of the breasts for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi.
In the month of Vaiśākha, during the bright fortnight, at the end of the lunar mansion of the month,
one should conclude the vow and perform worship of the Cakra at the dead of night.
With jasmine, *vakula*, and other auspicious, fragrant flowers that bloom in season,
along with cow’s ghee, sesame seeds, and whatever else is desired—
one should constantly perform this ritual of libation and the recitation of mantras. (29.79)
For one who practices thus correctly as a counselor for as long as life lasts,
prosperity dwells in his house, remaining steadfast for seven lifetimes.
I shall now declare the mantra of the Earth and its ritual application exactly as it is.
Having extracted the beginning of the *chandas* syllables, as well as *pulaha*,
and *hṛṣīkeśa* ending with the *visarga*, this is remembered as the one-syllabled *mantra*.
Then follows *gopana* with five dots (*bindu*), and thereafter the *mantra* of the Lord of the Upper World.
Vīrasena, Kalānta, and the one named Saṅkarṣaṇa.
One should visualize the continuity of movement together with the bindu in the heart and other centers.
Its seer is Paiṭhaka Mauni; its metre is said to be Gāyatrī;
and its deity is the goddess Dharaṇī. One should recite this mantra a hundred thousand times without weariness.
O Lotus-Seated One, the seven-syllable mantra of Dharaṇī is said to be:
*dhandaṃ pāvakaṃ cādiṃ sumukhaṃ godhanāhvayam*, ending with *namaḥ*; thus the seven-syllable mantra of Dharaṇī has been fully revealed.
O Lotus-born One, the mantra of Manu is said to consist of thirty-four syllables;
having first taken seven syllables, the mantra begins with the word *kumbha*.
It begins with *śaśāṅka*, followed by *bhuvana* and *subhaga*, and ends with the name *datta*.
Subhadra, Mūrdhvalokeśa, Vijaya, Viṣṇuśīrṣaka,
Mohanāśa, Tathākāra, Vairāja, Agnivikrama,
Bhallāyudha, Māhendra, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Vidarbhitam. || 29.88–29.89 ||
The lotus with the anusvāra, the fire together with the cave-dweller,
the nasal sound, the food of the thirty gods, that which is called Trivikrama,
the form of wrath, the fair-faced one, and then the water-pot with the water.
One should extract the Praṇava as the beginning, followed by Māhendra, Pulaha,
Pāvaka, Pāṭala, Brahma, Māhendra residing in the cave (guhālaya), Prabhañjana, Pūrṇacandra, Auṣadha, and Yaṣṭi. (29.91–29.92)
Subhadra, Devadatta, Bhāskara, Yaṣṭimastaka,
and Virati in Svāhā— this is the mantra declared, O Lotus-seated One.
The previously mentioned seed-syllable, the limbs, the seer, the meter, and the deity [are as follows].
I shall proclaim the Sārasvata Manu-vara exactly as it is:
the Nigamādi Śvetaraśmi, the Manu who has the crescent moon as his crest-jewel;
thus the son of Kaśyapa himself shall uplift the Earth and behold her.
Chanda is the goddess, Gāyatrī the deity, and Bhāratī herself;
one who observes the rules, being unwearied, should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times.
He shall possess incomparable power of speech and attain supreme knowledge.
By merely grasping it once, one attains firm mastery.
For him there is no loss of memory and no defeat in the assembly.
Now I shall tell you another mantra of Sarasvatī.
Its face is the Brahma-casket, its wealth is the bull, and its crest is the moon;
it is the lotus, Pulaha, and Māyā adorned with the anusvāra (99).
Following this, one should take the staff ending in the visarga, and then the previously mentioned mantra.
O Lotus-Seated One, the extraction of the three-syllable mantra has been told:
Vasiṣṭha is the seer, Virāṭ is the meter, Sarasvatī is the deity,
and the number of recitations for the japa is declared to be three hundred thousand.
One who knows the higher and the lower and is eloquent should drink water over which the mantra has been recited seven times; his speech will certainly become auspicious.
O Lotus-Seated One, the six-syllable group of mantras is now being told.

*Tāraka*, *Varuṇa*, *Ādi*, *Nāsikya*, and the one called *Jvalana* (Fire), followed by *Madhusūdana*, ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*, and the salutation (*namaskṛti*). Maheśvara is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chanda*), and he alone is the deity (*devatā*). || 29.103–104 ||
The ten-syllable king of mantras is declared through the extraction of its phonemes:
Vyāpin, Sudhārasa, Vaidhara, and Viṣṇumastaka.
These four [phonemes] at the end of the syllables have been explained immediately thereafter.
Having likewise dispatched Kumbha after Madhusūdana,
Pañcāntaka followed with Pāśapāṇi; then Madhusūdana followed behind, and Vaidhara accompanied by Rāma followed Vighneśa, who was at the head of the host.
Having extracted the syllables ending with *hūṃ*, this mantra is proclaimed;
thus the limbs (*aṅga*), the form, and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra have been distinguished.
[She is] situated in the center of the lunar disc, possessing the luster of a mass of snow.
One should visualize her tongue situated in the center of the mouth, emitting nectar.
For that practitioner who meditates thus, incomparable perfection of speech shall arise.
[He should likewise meditate on] the beginning of the Veda, ending with obeisance, as well as Subhadra and Gadin.
One should extract the mantra beginning with *kumbha*, followed by *ādi*, *vijaya*, *govinda*, and *madhuketana*; then *vijaya* joined with *mādhava*, ending with *ṭha-ṭha*.
One should likewise extract the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of *jvalana* (the letter *ra*) preceded by *ādi* (the letter *a*) and the half-moon (*ardhendu*).

Devala shall be its seer, the Virāj metre, and the goddess Rati its deity. One should recite the mantra one million times; thereafter, the practitioner attains success, along with a continuous stream of fruits such as subjugation, attraction, and inciting enmity.
There will also be a journey from afar, and for one who has been away, his return shall occur before long; immediately after reciting the previously mentioned seven syllables,
one should then utter the *pavitra*, the *pīṭha-mantra*, and the five dots (*pañcabindu*).
One should extract the mantra beginning with Vairāja, Godhana, and Vāyu, ending with *ṭha-ṭha*.
The seed-syllable of this mantra is said to be Ekacakṣuḥ and Pīṭha, together with Hṛṣīkeśa and the bindu; the sage (ṛṣi) of this mantra is remembered as Aṅgiras.
The deity is said to be Chanda, the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is called Prīti.
Having accomplished [the rite] as before, one shall partake in the fruits beginning with Dharma.
One should take the seven syllables as previously described, followed by Karāla and Vāmana.
*Edṛg* (or *ekadṛg*), *godhana*, *citrabhānu*, and *madhusūdana*;
*yaṣṭi*, *karāla*, *agni*, *dhruva*, and the wife of Agni;
that very same *bīja*, the seer *Manu*, and the deity *Kīrti*. (29.118–119)
And the *chandas* is the Gāyatrī of the Goddess, as before, for the accomplishment of success;
having taken the seven letters at the beginning, one should extract the remaining ones:
Śrīvatsa, Gopana, Bhadrapāṇi, and likewise Vijaya. (29.120)
Sparśana, Vīrasena, Śubhada, Dahana, Manu, Yaṣṭi accompanied by Bhāskara, Pāvaka with the five dots (bindus),
and [the mantra] together with Yaṣṭi and the seed-syllable, ending with the word "Śriye Svāhā."
The meter is Virāḍ, Gautama is the seer, and Śānti is said to be the deity.
O Brahmin, by means of this mantra, one may accomplish great results such as the attainment of sandals and other boons.
One should [place] the seven syllables in their proper order, as well as Nṛhari and Pāvaka.
Having extracted Mahāmāyā, Anusvāra, Vijaya, that which begins with Praṇava, Udaya, Krodharūpa, Bhūdhara, Gopana,
and likewise the end of *ṭha-ṭha*, the mantra should be known by the wise. (29.124–29.125)
Vyāsa is the seer, Virāṭ is the meter, and Tuṣṭi is declared to be the deity.
By the recitation of three hundred thousand [times], great satisfaction shall indeed arise.
The seven syllables are to be taken as before; the extraction of the remaining syllables follows in sequence.
Bhāskara, Pāvaka, Pañcabindu, and Yaṣṭisamanvita;
Pavitra, Bhuvana, Krodharūpa, and Bhūdhara;
following these, Govinda and Āgneyī—having extracted [these], the mantra is declared.
From the Seer [Viśvāmitra] came the deity Īśāna, and the Virāj meter became Puṣṭi.
One desiring prosperity, being composed in mind, should recite the mantra eight hundred thousand times;
having done so, one enjoys abundant pleasures, foremost among which are elixirs of immortality.
The practitioner moves like a god through the worlds beginning with Atala.
O Four-faced One, regarding the limbs of the yoga-posture, such as the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and the rest,
their visualization should be preceded by the extraction of the phonemes.
I shall declare the mantras in their proper sequence; listen attentively as they are correctly explained.
One should know the "Treasury of Brahman" (brahmakośa) as the mouth, the pure abode of nectar (amṛtadhāma), Hṛṣīkeśa, the supreme Bindu, and thereafter Pratardana.
One should likewise utter the salutation to Padmanābha, Nāsikya, Gopana, Subhaga,
Ādideva, Hutavaha, Śrīvatsa, Kamalāhvaya, Vairāja, and Vīrasena. (29.133–134)
O Lotus-seated One, this is declared to be the mantra of the Support-Power (Ādhāraśakti).
[He is] four-faced and four-armed, with the luster of pure crystal,
adorned with ornaments such as crowns, necklaces, and armlets.

One should meditate upon the one who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, who is endowed with the weapons of the conch, discus, mace, and lotus; who stands in the midst of a circle of splendor, who is the form of the foundation,
the treasury of Brahman, the sun, and the world called Pāvaka.
The cave-dwelling, the eternal, again the lotus with its cave-dwelling, the purifier, the mantra, the lotus-shaped, the vast,
likewise the protection, the destroyer of disease, and immediately after, Vināyaka.
One should utter the mantra, bowing deeply to Prabhañjana and Mādhava:
[He who has] one face and four arms, with a luster like the Japā flower,
holding a conch and a discus, wrathful, and bearing a lotus and the Kaumodakī mace.
Immediately thereafter, one should meditate upon the Tortoise (Kūrma), situated in the center of a circle of fire, with a body blazing yellow in color, endowed with all ornaments;
[and likewise] Udgītha, Bhānumākāra, Yaṣṭi, and the first Vināyaka.
Having extracted the elephant (dvirada), the form of victory (vijaya), the breath (śvasana), the first vowel (prathamaṃ svaram),
and the prostration (nati), this mantra of Ananta has been revealed.
[One should meditate on him] resembling a mountain of crystal, four-armed, and wearing a crown.
He has a face like the full moon, is gentle, and is resplendent with white flowers; he is auspicious,
holding a plow and a pestle in his two principal hands,
and the pair of conch and discus in his two secondary hands, each in its proper place.
Wearing blue garments, he was endowed with a face made terrifying by its fangs;
yet he possessed a tranquil form, with a thousand uplifted hoods,
resplendent with the lustration of the rays from the thousands of jewels upon those hoods.
One should meditate on Ananta, whose body is encircled by the coiled hoods of the lord of serpents, emitting upward-flaming fire from the cavities of his infinite mouths;
and on both sides of the serpent-lady, one should meditate on [the two] Nāgas.
The goddesses sit comfortably upon him, who is adorned with a circle of hoods.
After meditating thus, the Manu of the earth will later speak by means of the extraction of the phonemes (varṇoddhāra):
"The Tāra [syllable], the one named Subhaga, Arciṣmat, and Caturmukha."
One should visualize the wind-god Vāyu as having a pleasant countenance and possessing the wealth of cattle;
above him, one should fashion for the enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu) a beautiful, auspicious, and square great pedestal that resembles refined gold.

O Lotus-seated One, the mantras for the conceptualization of the four [groups] beginning with Dharma, and likewise for the corresponding number of quarters beginning with Dharma, shall now be declared;
as well as the initial syllables, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and accompanied by the *anusvāra*, each according to its proper order.
One should utter the names ending in the dative case and offer salutation;
one should arrange the word "Sadāśiva" in the middle as the feet [of the mantra].
That [name] ending in the dative case should be placed at the beginning, followed by Bhāskara together with Guhālaya.
One should not at all fashion *mantras* from nine syllables.
O Lotus-Seated One, the four Vedas begin with the *Ṛgveda*, and their *mantras* consist of the initial syllables of those [Vedas] preceded by the *anusvāra*. 29.154–155.
The names of the *Ṛg* and the others ending in the dative case are again for their salutation;
one should thus fashion the *mantras* for the elements and so forth, beginning with the ego-principle (*ahaṅkṛti*).
Afterwards, one should fashion three [others]; I shall tell you their *mantras*.
[One should utter] the Praṇava and so forth, with blossoming eyes, beginning with *acāma* and including the staff;
then the *bhautika* and so forth, the *ahaṅkāra* ending in the dative case, likewise the salutation (*nati*),
the western wind, the Lord of the Upper World, and the Bindu at the head.
The remaining fiery foot was declared by Manu as before;
after that came the Kumbha, Aurva, Sanāsikya, and Vaikāri feet.
The rest of everything was declared by another Manu, just as previously.
One should subsequently assign the qualities (guṇas) as sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Then, one should likewise assign the mantras consisting of the initial syllables of those [qualities] together with their anusvāras, ending in the dative case and bearing those same names; such is the assignment of Mahī and the others.
One should again employ the mantra with the word "ātman" in the dative case, preceded by words such as "mahan," ending in "huṃ phaṭ" and "namaḥ.
[Then follow] the Praṇava, Mandara, Yaṣṭi, Musala, and Pañcabindu.
The knower of mantras, having performed prostrations, should place Amṛta, Gopanayuta, Vijaya, Mādhavī, Bhadrahasta, and Mṛgeśa; then,
by means of the mantra, he should perform the laying out of the spread and the superimposition of the three maṇḍalas beginning with Vahni.
Above that, one should sequentially place all the mantras:
the triad of Fire, Moon, and Sun, together with the vowel *ā* and the bindu.
Having thus extracted the mantra, one should then arrange the lotus above it.
Praṇava, Paścima, Yaṣṭi, Pavitra, and likewise Vijaya;
Dakṣa, Gopanapara, Śvasana, and Vināyaka; Viṣṇu, Mandara, and Svarga—having extracted these, it is remembered as the Aja-mantra. (29.166–167)

The mantra for the auspicious seat (Bhadrāsana) is said to consist of the twelve Śaktis beginning with Śrīvatsā, whose names are identical [to those Śaktis], ending in the dative case, accompanied by the nasal (Anusvāra), and preceded by their initial syllables; such is the sequence of its conceptualization.
Afterwards, the triad beginning with Brahmā, then again the triad beginning with Sanaka;
Vināyaka and Durgā, followed by the ministers and the Guru.
Their names are to be preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ), ending in the dative case, and concluding with the word "namas" (salutation).
One should worship Brahmā and the others through the modes of service to Hari;
one should worship the eight Śaktis, beginning with Vyāpti, in the first enclosure.
As before, one should also worship the five weapons with mantras bearing their respective names.

Then, O Brahmin, one should worship all the divine guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, as well as the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) and the Lord of the Army (Kārttikeya), in the second enclosure, using their own names in the dative case ending in -e and followed by the word "namas," as previously described.
One should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa as the two door-keepers stationed within, along with Manu;
[and one should worship] Nigamādi, Khaḍgadhara, Ṛtamota, and Sayaṣṭika,
as well as Vakratuṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, and Gopana.
The immeasurable Prabhañjana is called Manu by those who bow;
he is the first beginning of the meters, the final abode of Truth (Ṛtadhāman),
the one with the staff, the destroyer of evil, the burner, and the one with the curved trunk.

The mantra for Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa is proclaimed by extracting the syllables: "Pracaṇḍa" followed by "Puṇḍarīkākṣa" in the dative case, and likewise the word "Nati" (salutation). For Udumbara, it consists of the word "Śānti" with the first case ending, followed by "Nati."
The presiding deity of that [wood] should be invoked, and its deity is Śānti;
Sarasvatī is in the southern beam, Rati in the northern, and Śrī in the western;
below it, the deity is Śānti. || 29.178–179 ||
O Four-faced One, that name ending in the dative case is said to be the mantra.
Thus, Viśvanetra is the deity on the southern door-panels,
and Viśvavaktra is the deity on the cane and wooden [panels] to the north.
The Vedic scriptures and the gods likewise dwell within the iron shafts (nārāca);

the sages reside in the joints (kīla), while the Lord of Beings (Bhūteśa) dwells upon the surface of the band (paṭṭikā). The abode of the Creator of the Universe (Viśvabhāvana) should be in the two cloth-bands (kandapaṭṭa).
O Brahmin, the mantra of those [deities] consists of their names in the dative case, as does that of Vāstupati; one should likewise extract the beginning of the meters for the mantra of Kṣetreśa:
"Nṛsiṃha, Udaya, Dakṣa, Ṛtadhāman, together with Daṇḍaka."
Ending in the dative case and ending with "namaḥ," [the name] of Tārkṣya stands at the head of Hari;

one should worship the pair of conch and discus on the side of the door by means of their respective names. In the worship of the Abode of Speech (Vacmi-dhāma), one should extract the first of the meters as the mantra.
Varuṇa, Bandhuśiras, Krodharūpa, Vanasrajas,
Varuṇa, Devadatta, and Vahnigopana in the west; then Śaśāṅka, Ādideva, Vaidhara, and Dahana.
Hṛṣīkeśa is the western [deity], and Rāma is next with Sumukha;
Mādhava ends with "hum phaṭ," while the mantra for Adhika ends with "svāhā.
O Lotus-seated One, the forms of the directions are now described in their proper sequence.
Indra and Īśāna, Nṛsiṃha and Viriñca, should be placed in order;
or else the directional deities (diṅmūrtayaḥ) [should be placed], namely Śaktidhara, Paśupati, Śrīdhara, and Dhanada; or alternatively, Hari in the form of a boar.
Nṛsiṃha and Śrīdhara, as well as the one with the form of Hayaśīrṣa; or there may be Caturvaktra, both Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
Hari and Kṛṣṇa are mentioned, or else Satya and the others in sequence.
The Vyūhas, beginning with Vāsudeva, or else the deities representing the directions in sequence,

are placed in order at the ends of the archways (toraṇa) of the eastern and western sanctuaries; likewise, in the square and oblong sanctuaries, they are placed at the front and rear nostrils (nāsā) of the structure.
Furthermore, Pūrṇa and Puṣkara are both located in the Adhiṣṭhāna in due order.
In the southeast is Hastivadana; likewise, Paśupati is in the south;
Dakṣiṇāmūrti is in the west; and Viśvarūpadhṛk is in the north.
And in that [shrine] of Śaṅkara with four faces, the Blessed Lady likewise [is present];
on both sides of the gate of the inner maṇḍala, there are the Moon and the Sun; and likewise upon the earth, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate points, [the other deities are located].
Manmatha, Vidhātṛ, Vighneśa, and likewise Ṣaṇmukha;
Durga, Dhana, Daru, and Rudra; and immediately thereafter Kṣetreśa; and between Someśa and Īśāna, Viṣvaksena is established.
On the surface of the right thigh are the Seven Mothers and Vīrabhadra;
on their sides are Vighneśa and Jyeṣṭhā on the surface of the earth in the south-west (Nirṛti).
Furthermore, in the second enclosure, Indra and the other gods are in their respective directions.
Then, in the second enclosure, Tārkṣya is situated at the head of the Blessed One;
on the two sides of the gateway of that [enclosure] are Puruṣa and Acyuta;
and on the grounds of the training-grounds (khalūrikā), they are placed in order according to the directions starting with the southeast (vahni).
Hayaśīrṣa, Karṣaṇa, and immediately after him Kroḍākṛti;
then Pradyumna, Ananta by name, Aniruddha, and Nṛkesarī.
[He holds] the discus, the mace, the conch, the sword, the Kaumodakī mace, and the bow.
The Vajra and the Padma are proclaimed [to be located] in the third [directions], starting from the east.
The Gopura [is situated] at the side of Bhaya; the twelve Śītaraśmis [are located there].
Between Yama and Agni are the Vasus; between Yama and Rākṣasa are the Pitṛs.
The Viśvedevas are situated between Nirṛti and Varuṇa;
the Maruts are intermediate between the noose-handed [Varuṇa] and Śvasana;
and the seven sages are stationed between Pāśī and the Maruts.
Between Kubera and Īśāna, the eleven Rudras are stationed.
Kṣetrapāla is also right there, as are Kumuda and the others in the eastern direction and so forth; and at the gate of the Sāla tree called Maryādā, there are Pūrṇa and Puṣkara.
On the surface of the ground, on a seat prepared in the courtyard,
the supreme Gaṇas are to be propitiated and installed in the eight directions starting from the east in due order;
likewise, Upendra and the others are to be installed in the great enclosure.
On the surface of the earth, the Viśveśa and other deities belonging to the central group are situated in their respective directions;
Jayā and the others are established on the ground outside the gate-towers (gopuras),
and [the remaining deities] are located upon the sacrificial pedestals (balipīṭhas) throughout all the first enclosures and so forth.
May those beings who are primordial and those born of karma, who dwell in the eastern direction— serene and well-pleased, desiring the offering— accept it;
as do those stationed upon the earth, in the sky, and likewise upon trees, mountains, and so forth.
May Vināyaka, the Kṣetrapālas, and the heroes Kumuda and others,
together with all their other attendants, accept your bali offering.
Then [offer] to Caṇḍa and the others stationed at the gates by reciting their names in the dative case.

O Four-faced One, they should be worshipped in their respective places, accompanied by the attendants of the Goddess, together with their vehicles, using mantras beginning with the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*.
This applies to all those who desire the acceptance of the sacrificial offering (*bali*) upon the *balipīṭhas*.
Having uttered each respective name, the offering (bali) should be given by the wise.
If one should worship Dhāmeśāna without that offering of bali,
[the spirits] will seize the kingdom, the king, the temple, and even his own self.
Without having worshipped the retinue, as well as the fuel for the fire,
and without offering enjoyments to the deity, the worship would be useless.
Therefore, worship performed according to the prescribed path bestows prosperity upon the site.
It is the increase of kings and kingdoms, and the honor of those who desire prosperity.
To the beings who subsist in both visible and invisible forms and who long for offerings,
this oblation must always be given by one who desires their own well-being.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Mantras of the Retinue beginning with Śrī," in the Caryāpāda of the Pādma Tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
[Or] the thirtieth chapter?
O Four-faced One, I shall explain the extraction of the mantras for the deities of the lunar days (tithi) and the Tithi-yāga, which is a means to attain happiness, as taught by the Blessed Lord.
The time for rites performed for specific desires is the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) as well as the appropriate lunar day (tithi).
At the proper times, the wise person should properly propitiate [the deities] through recitation, fire-oblations, and worship:
Agni, Brahmā, Dhaneśa, Īśāna, Vighneśa, Śrī, and Ṣaḍānana.
The Sun, Śiva (the bull-bannered), Durgā, Yama, Indra (the slayer of Bala),
Viṣṇu, Kāma, the two Aśvins, and the Moon— these are said to be the deities of the lunar days (tithis).
Then [one should worship] the Praṇava, the nine dots (Navabindu), Varuṇa, and Śrīdhara.
Then, having extracted the mantra of Jātavedas ending with *ṭha-ṭha*— namely *gadadhvaṃsaṃ bhadrahastaṃ pāvanaṃ mādhavam*—
the seed-syllable of Agni is the first letter [ga] followed by the anusvāra; by that, the sequence of the limbs (*aṅga*) is established.
Chanda, Virāj, and Devala are the seers; Agni is the presiding deity.
One's own name, ending in the dative case and followed by "namaḥ," is another mantra.
For this mantra as well, the seer, meter, and deity are as previously stated.
The recitation syllable by syllable is the means for the installation of the two mantras.
(30.7) The attainment of all that is desired is the fruit, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
[This is] the Nigamādi, composed by Kālanemi Ṛtadhāman. (30.8)
"Salutation to the fierce Mādhava, joined with Mārtāṇḍa and Mandara"—thus one should extract the Brahma-mantra; now the extraction of another is being told.
The word "Brahman" ending in the dative case, followed by the word "niṣṭhita" [in the locative], is the mantra.
Vairāja, Akṣaprathama, Vijaya, and Rohiṇīpati;
the letter A, Ekanetra, and the seed-syllable conjoined with the Praṇava—
this indeed is the lineage of limbs, the vowel, the meter, and Lohita.
The sage is Brahmā and the deity is the Lotus-Bellied One (Viṣṇu), who is to be worshipped within the interior of the lotus;
having extracted the Praṇava, the subtle vision, Bhadrapāṇi, together with the bindu,
this one-syllable mantra of Kubera is proclaimed.
The metre is Uṣṇik, the sage is Vahni, and the deities are Dhaneśa and Īśāna. [One should worship] Ārambha, Nati, Anvaka, Subhaga, Vighnanāyaka,
Pavitra, Vijaya, and then Dhvaṃsana and Mādhava.
Having uttered *kamalam*, *codayam*, *jṛmbhalam*, *mṛgavallabham*,
*pāvakam* joined with *gopa*, and immediately after that *sadāgatim*;
[then] *kumbham*, *śaśāṅkam*, *bhuvanam*, and *herambam* joined with *rāma*.
Having extracted Vakratuṇḍa, Jagatprāṇa, Mandara with face to the west,
Agni as the first, Māruta, Prathama, Pretanāyaka,
Acāma as the first, and [the syllable] belonging to Agni, the mantra is thus declared.
The sky is said to be the seer of Dhanada; the meter is declared to be Gāyatrī;
the deity is the Lord of Wealth (Dhanādhipa); and the seed-syllable is declared as before.
[30.18] On the thumb is the one named Māṇibhadra, and on the forefinger is Pūrṇabhadra.
One should assign Kali-mālin to the middle finger and Vikuṇḍala to the ring finger;
Makhendra to the base and the middle of the little fingers and the two wrists;
and Dhanādhipa to the palms of the hands during the ritual assignment of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Having bathed, one should offer a handful of water with the *jṛmbhala* mantra,
[visualizing] within the center of the lotus pericarp a being of great body and great belly,
two-armed, wearing yellow garments, with a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāratna*) held in his hand.
One should worship him who holds his beloved mind and wealth that is feared by ministers,
while meditating upon the male and female Yakṣas and their retinue with offerings such as the *arghya*.
One should also worship Ṛddhi and Gupti at his side, using their own names in the dative case (with the fourth case-ending).
Having worshipped them with the arghya and other offerings, O Lotus-born One, [he then honored] Jṛmbhaṇa,
Kalimālin, Maṇibhadra, Carendra, Pūrṇabhadra,
Mukhendra, Śikhipūrṇa, Kuṇḍala, Nala, and Kūbara.
In the center of the lotus pericarp and on the petals, beginning with Indra and the others in sequence, one should worship.
One should likewise worship the Śaṅkha-nidhi and the Padma-nidhi in front;
one should place Śabalā in front and the Kalpa-tree behind.
Just as the fruit of recitation, fire-offerings, libations, and so forth depends upon the root mantra,
I shall now describe the fruit of the *jṛmbhala* mantra through its division.
[It begins with] "Oṃ," followed by the auspicious syllable, the "Bhadrahasta" syllable, and the "Vaidhara" syllable.
Ādideva, Māruta, Dhanada, Bhadrabāhuka;
Pavitra, Vijaya, Māruta, and likewise Mādhava; Jamnahantṛ, Āmnāya, Madhava, and Sūkṣmadarśana.
Viṣkambha is the primordial deity, and Sparśana is joined with Svāhā;
the seed-syllable is the first letter, Bharga is the seer, and Virāj is the metre for the mind.
Jṛmbhala is to be made the deity; he bestows every fruit.
Having extracted the mantra of Vighneśa, I shall state its syllables in their proper sequence:
the Udgītha, the third [sibilant], among the consonants the Pulaha-mantra, and "daṇḍa"—thus the mantra is extracted; likewise, there are six Gaṇikās and the Virāṭ.
The recitation of the mantra of the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja) for three hundred thousand times is prescribed;
the knower of mantras sees the past, present, and future in a dream.
The undertaking of an action, free from obstacles, yields its fruit exactly as desired.
The third [syllable] and so forth, the "fair-faced" (sumukha) which is designated as the first and the last; the "mouth of vowels" (acām mukha), Vijaya, Prāṇa, and thereafter Mādhava.
With "namas" at the beginning and the previously mentioned mantra, it is declared to be the Manu-mantra.
The sage is Aja, the meter is Uṣṇih, and the deity is Vighnanāyaka.
One should recite the mantra seven hundred thousand times; the accomplishments (siddhis) have been described previously. This single-syllable mantra is said to have "salutation" (namas) at its head.
Nigamādi, Dinakarajvalana, Pañcabindu (with the anusvāra), Gadadhvaṃsa, Padmanābha, Vāmana,
Yaṣṭi, Sahasrakiraṇa, Pāvaka, and Daṇḍaśekhara.
O Brahmin, the three-syllable mantra has been described as the means for accomplishing all things.
Its limbs and so forth have been declared, beginning with the consonants and ending with the vowels starting from 'A'.
O Lotus-seated One, another mantra shall now be spoken.
The *udgītha* as the beginning, the lotus, the fire, and the five dots;
together with the half-moon, the auspicious fire, the dot, and the dwarf (*vāmana*);
the lotus, joined with the great Indra, and the Great Māyā along with the staff.
One should utter the seed-syllable consisting of that vowel and the following consonant, which destroys speech and is most fierce;
then the western face, Vairāja, Māyā, and the essence of the earth;
and finally, the letter 'A' preceded by fire—the two six-footed mantras.
Śaśin, Varuṇa, Vahni, Kakubha, Bhadrabāhuka; Mandara, Dvaya, Ekāra, Varuṇa, Kamalāmukha;
Acāṃ, Dakṣa, Gopana, Vighneśa, and likewise Śvasana.
Thus has been described the extraction [of the mantra] ending with *ṭha* and *ṭha*, beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), as previously stated.
By means of this, one should accomplish all fruits pertaining to this world and the next.
One should worship the Goddess Śrī with offerings such as the *arghya* according to the path previously mentioned.
By the falling of her sidelong glance, one obtains supreme prosperity.
[One worships] Tāra, Nati, Krodharūpa, Pracaṇḍa, Dakṣamanvata, Udaya, Kharvadeha, Gopana, and Prabhañjana.
Śaśāṅka, Śrīdhara, Hrasva, Ṛtadhāmasamāhvaya, Dineśa, Mādhavīmanu, Pracaṇḍa, Madhusūdana,
and Svāsana together with Svāhā— this is declared to be the mantra.

Jṛmbhala, Urdhvalokeśa, Pulaha, and Yaṣṭimastaka—this is the extraction of the seed-syllables (bīja). Furthermore, the sage of that very limb is said to consist of the phonemes; the meter is Gāyatrī and the deity is Guha.
One should consecrate [the image] resembling a pomegranate flower with that mantra.
For one who has done this, the planets such as Subrahmaṇya and others do not afflict the members of that lineage; those born in that lineage become long-lived.
One should extract the nasalized vowel (anunāsikya) following the Lord of Herbs (the letter *u*) at the beginning of the *nigama* (the letter *o*).
This one-syllable mantra is said to accomplish all aims;
Hārīta is its seer (*mantradṛk*), the *virāṭ* is its meter, and the Sun is its deity.
One should extract Brahmakośa, Padmapāṇi, Mṛta, and the one known as Sumukha;
Rāma, Indu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Agni, Vāyu, and the mouth of Acā;
Vaidhara, Bindu, Vairāja, Vāyu, and Tāra.

Thus, the eight-syllable mantra is known as the single-syllable seed (bīja). Having extracted the supreme seven-syllable mantra from among all mantras, it is described [as follows]: Atri is the seer (ṛṣi), and Pūṣan is the presiding deity (adhidevatā). || 30.55–56 ||

The seven syllables are to be taken as before: Subhadra, Madhusūdana, Bhadrahasta, and Kalaśa; Mādhava was mentioned previously. Having placed the seed-syllable within, one likewise repeats Kakubha twice.
Immediately after this, one should invoke the immeasurable Gandhavaha Ādya;
then the two feet, Ādideva, Pāvaka, Vikramayuta, Vaidhara, and Ṛtadhāman. (30.58–30.59)
One should utter the syllable of Māruta, which is nasal (nāsikya), and the syllable called Gopana, which is Vighneśa;
then one should pronounce the first syllable of Kamalā, which is the primordial wind (ādipavana) consisting of two letters.
One should recite the syllable of Mādhavī together with its initial [vowel], which is the syllable Dvirada.
One should recite the *pavitra* together with the *gopana*, joined with its own vowel-sounds.
One should extract twice the syllable *loḍanta* for Vighneśa, Dahati, and Dhātu.
For the cessation of disease and the attainment of happiness, the middle [syllable] should be preceded by *loḍanta*.
Having uttered "Yama Caṇḍa" twice, followed by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) three times after each word,
and [ending] with his own name preceded by *praṇava*, the mantra is thus extracted.
The seed-syllables and the limbs [of the ritual] have been declared, as did Sindhudvīpa behold them.
By this, Attic-chanda and Svayam-chanda, as well as Sūrya, are described.
One should then worship the Sun within the pericarp in the center of the lotus, and the other planets in the directions beginning with the east upon the petals of the disc. 30.64–65.
In succession, all six seasons as well as the planets, together with their favorable influences,
bring about longevity, health, beauty, prosperity, and the wealth of happiness;
these remain unrestrained throughout seven births within his lineage.

Having extracted the Praṇava, the skin (tvak), that which bestows auspiciousness (śubhada), Trivikrama, Varuṇa, Gopana, and Vāyu as the first [syllable], the knower of mantras should form the five-syllabled mantra; now the seed-syllable (bīja) is being described. || 30.67–68 ||
One should extract Gopati together with Viṣṇu and the anusvāra;
O four-faced one, this is the seed-syllable (bīja) which they declare to be the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Upamanyu is the seer (ṛṣi), and the meter (chandas) is said to be the divine Gāyatrī.
The one to be propitiated is Maheśāna; the recitation should consist of five hundred thousand [mantras].
Its fruit and its means of accomplishment are exactly like those of the eight-syllable mantra.
One should worship him seated upon a red lotus throne, and [the deities] upon its petals.
Having sequentially assigned the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) to the east and the other directions, as well as Pārvatī and Nandikeśvara, one should properly worship the vehicle in front.
In the eight directions, one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Surendra with offerings such as the *arghya*.
Having first performed the placement (nyāsa) of the creation and so forth,
O Lotus-born One, one should thereafter perform the placement of the syllables in these locations:
on the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and likewise on the soles of the feet.
Now the sequence of colors for the five elements is described:
one should contemplate them as crystal, pale red, yellow, white, and blue.
The best of mantra-knowers should meditate upon himself, thinking, "I am Śiva."
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods, the one whose banner is the bull, as he meditates,
he abandons the suffering of worldly existence and attains the imperishable state,
even after enjoying the pleasures of this world that are difficult even for the immortals to obtain.
The extraction of the seven syllables beginning with *om* has been previously described:
Vaidhara, Nṛhari, Māyā, Pracaṇḍa, Madhusūdana, Mandara, and Urdhvalokeśa; and Vairāja twice, O Four-faced One.
Pāvaka, Pavana, Devadatta, and Pāṭala; Gopati, Māruta, and Mandara;
