likewise Mādhavī, O Brahman, and he who is known as Madhusūdana and Dhanada. || 30.79–30.80 ||
One should utter twice the mantra "nāsikyaṃ paścimaṃ padmanābhaṃ ca pavanāhvayaṃ khaḍgaṃ svāhā" and extract it.
I shall now proclaim another mantra; I extract that by means of its syllables.
Tāra, Matri, Garutmant, Rāma, Sumukha,
Anvata, Gopana, Mandara, Urdhvalokeśa, Vijaya,
Tamarṇa, Abhiśaṅkha, Mādhava, and the one named Varuṇa.
Gopana, Karāla, Kamala, and then Jṛmbhala;
Śrīdhara, Subhaga, Māyā, and immediately after that Janmadhvaṃsa; Pāśapāṇi, Ādideva, and finally Bhadrahasta.
Then, having extracted the *natim* (the bowing syllable) from the *ṛtāhvaya*, the *vaidhara*, the *madhubhit*, and the *māruta*,
sixteen syllables are declared;
O Brahmin, in these two mantras, the *jīva* is said to be the observer.
Dharmavartī, Maheśāna, Devatā, Dakṣiṇā, Tanu;
[and] Dineśa together with Rāma, Śvasana, and Matibindu—this is the seed-syllable (bīja). Therefore, I shall describe to you the meditation (dhyāna) upon Īśāna.
Resembling jasmine, the moon, pearls, and a conch shell, he was adorned with all ornaments;
clothed in a tiger skin, he was graced by a mass of matted locks;
his eyes were fixed on the tip of his nose, and he was radiant with a crescent moon.
The god with a serene countenance, four-armed and the granter of desires,
has his right lotus-foot placed upon his left knee;
he holds a crystal rosary in his right hand.
Holding a book of wisdom in his own lotus-like left hand,
displaying the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), and served by hosts of great sages—
by meditating thus upon him, the practitioner indeed accomplishes all arts and powers.
The flow of his speech proceeds like the current of the Gaṅgā;
the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life is certainly held in his hand.
Reciting further, he easily enjoys even those desires that are difficult to obtain.

On the ninth lunar day, one should properly worship the divine goddess Durgā. Having correctly extracted them in their proper order, the single-syllable mantra is declared to consist of *nigamādi*, *vaidhara*, *bhuvana*, and *visarjana*.
Having first accepted the single syllable *pūrvam*, which is the fire (*hutāśana*) whose destruction has passed;
[the syllables] *sparśana*, *gopa*, *nāhvāna*, and *tati*—this is declared to be the *manu*.
I shall extract its seed-syllable (*bīja*): *gopati*, followed by *pāvaka*.
The sage Kātyāyana [prescribes] the Vāmana [meter] with the *yaṣṭi* as its head;
the meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and the deity is Vanadurgā.
I shall now proclaim another mantra based on Durgā, which is unsurpassed.
[Namely] Nigama and others known as Viṣṇu, Kapila called Jṛmbhala, Mādhava and Surendra, Pradyumna born of Kālanemi,
and the one named Madhusūdana who was Pulaha enveloped by Māyā.
Having extracted Karāla, the one named Devadatta, Śaśāṅka, Kamalānuga,
the pure Ādideva, that Nṛhari, Sparśana,
Brahmā, Agni, and immediately after, Pañcabindu; || 30.100–30.101 ||
Ādi, Śrīvatsa, Udaya, Subhadra, the one called Nāsika, Bhāskara, the two Bhadrabāhus, Vaidhara, the two Gopatis,
the two named Pavitra and Khaḍga, and then Dakṣa.

Having uttered "supratiṣṭham" twice, one should extract the syllables "dinakṛt," "mādhavī," and "dhruvau," followed by the syllable "phaṭ" and the sequence beginning with fire (agni). Having thus extracted [the mantra], one should recite it. O Four-faced One, I shall now speak another mantra according to this method of extraction.
One should extract the Praṇava, then Vaidhara, Śrīdhara, and likewise Gadin;
then Vaiśvānara, Mṛgapati, and immediately after that, the same syllable (Arṇa);
then Yānta, Nṛsiṃha, Sumukha, Rāma, and Svāhā.
This other Manu has been extracted; the seed and the limbs are as before.
The seer is Jayamati, the metre is Chanda, and the deity is Giridurgā.
[The mantras are] Udgītha, Srīdhara, Dṛṣṭidvandra, and Trivikrama.
And Krodharūpī, Jīmūta, the western one called Bhuvana,
Bahula, Śrīdhara, Krodha, Vikrama, Sarasīruha,
Vikrama, Dharmaśītāṃśu, Śaśāṅka, and Sudhāmaya.
The western [face] is Rāmaśiras, having the form of wrath and being purifying;
likewise Bhallāyudha, Śaṅkha, the two Mādhavas, Mādhava,
Śukla, Ādi, Mṛgapati, and Śrīdhara, with faces turned toward the west.
Nīhāradīdhiti, Sarvarodha, Vikramaśīrṣaka,
Vairāja, Kapila, Śaṅkha, Vaidhara, Bandhumastaka,
Śubhada, Kamala, Vāyu, Mandara, and Vittavardhana.
Ādi, Karāla, Anila, Nāsikya,
Yādasāmpati, Gopana, Vijaya, Vighnanāyaka, Dakṣa, Mādhava, Subhadra, Gadi, Kumbha, Vairāja, and Bandhuśīrṣaka.
The mantra is declared as *śubhadaṃ mandaraṃ śaṅkhaṃ ṭhaṭhāntam*.
Having divided that mantra into six parts, one performs the ritual assignment (*kalpanā*) of the limbs, beginning with the heart.
The seer is named Vareṇyaka, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh.
The deity of Vanadurgā shall yield results equal to those of the eight-syllable mantra.
I shall now extract for you the mantra of Sarvadāhvayadurgā,
which consists of the Udgītha, the salutation (namas), and the head-mantra (śīrṣaka) containing the vision of the subtle seer.
O Four-faced One, [worship] Gadadhvaṃsaka, Kumbha, Ādya,
Vairāja, Rājamāna, Vaidhara, Śrīdhara,
Gadin, Bandhu, Svāhāśīrṣa, and the Lord of Śrī.
Gadīna, Pāvaka, Dṛṣṭimīkārapāvaka,
Deha, Vikrama, Caṇḍa, Rāma,
Mandara, Madhusūdana, Gandhavaha, Mādhava, and Mandarāhvaya.
Āditya, Gopana, Dakṣa, Ādideva, Māruta, Mṛgeśa, Mandara, Bhānu, the one named Madhusūdana,
Pulaha, Devadatta, and Dakṣa Yadubhāskara.
They perceived Rāma as the fierce-souled Self, and Madhusūdana thereafter;
Śaśāṅka, Śrīdhara, Saptajihva, Kumbha, Trivikrama,
Gajānana, Gopati, Lakṣmī, Bhadra, and Trivikrama.
Vaidhara, Bhuvanāhvāna, Ugrarūpa, Kheṭaka,
and then, O Brahmin, Bhallāyudha, Śvasana born from the nose,
Vidhātṛ, Hutavaha, Vikrama, and Sudhārasa.
And Rāma, Bhadra, Subhagama, Anila, Vighnanāyaka;
Rāma, Mahendra, Subhaga, Maheśa, Gaganāhvaya; Mārtāṇḍa, Ādideva, Śaśāṅka, and likewise Śrīdhara.
Citrabhānu, Dakṣa, Vaidhara, Havyavāhana, Vighneśa, Vikrama, Dṛṣṭi, Devadatta, Apāmpati,
and thereafter the one named Madhusūdana, who is the soul of all arts (Kalātmā).
Bhuvana, Pāvaka, Dṛṣṭi, Gopana, and likewise Vijaya;
Vāyu, Pavitra, Ākāra, Musala, and again Vikrama; Ekanetra, Mādhava, Kalaśa, and the one called Pāvaka.
Vaidhara, Devadatta, Vighneśa, Madhusūdana,
Dahana, Gopana, Māruta, Vanamālin,
Māyā, Vaidharāhvāna, Madhusūdana, and Mandara.
They beheld the body of water, the fire facing west, behind them;
having uttered three times "Ṛtadhāman," "Vikrama," "Śvasana," "Mṛganāyaka," and "Puṣṭibīja"— the one called Sahasrakiraṇa— 30.130–131.
One should extract this seed-syllable, the anusvāra residing in the cave, three times:
Bhadra, the one residing in the cave, Vijaya, and likewise the wielder of the mace;
Padmanābha, Gopati, Kalaśa, and likewise the king of beasts.
Vairāja, Ādideva, Ḍuṇḍubha, Locana, Udaya,
Ugrātman, Kheṭaka, Vahni, Gopati, Vihagādhipa,
Śvetāṃśu, Paścima, Lakṣmī, and immediately after, Ādideva. (30.133–30.134)
One should practice twice Vakratuṇḍa, Gopana, Bhadrapāṇi, and immediately after that Vijayākāramādi, Śaśāṅka, and Sadāgati. One should recite Kālanemi and Bhadra Puṇya twice.
O Brahmin, one of subtle vision should utter twice the words *mandaram*, *ādidevam*, *dahanam*, and *śvasanam*; then again *karālam* and *vijayam*,
followed by *pīyūṣamādi*, *vijayam*, and *vasumastakaniṣṭhitam*.
O Four-faced One, [worship] Nīhāradīdhitimat, Ādi, Pīta, Samādhava, Subhadra, Kamala, Ekadṛṣṭi,
Pavitra, Ṛtadhāman, and after that, Trivikrama.
The Puruṣa, the Ātman, the Lord of the Deer (the Moon), the Western one, and likewise the Eastern one;
Dhruva, Dhruva, as well as Hrasva, Māhendra, and then Mandara; Sarvarodha, Gajāsya, Māyā, Kamala, and Mandara.
Ekanetra, Amṛta, Śūla, Bahukukṣi, Trivikrama,
Karāla, the one named Padmanābha, Vighneśa, Vijaya,
Bhadrahasta, Rāma, and Śaśāṅka— [these are] from Manu onwards.
Subhadra, Gopana, then Pañcāntika and Anila;
the western one named Padmanābha, endowed with Ṛtadhāman;
Jṛmbhala, Pulaha, Pāpahanana, and Padmanābhaka. || 30.142–30.143 ||
Dṛṣṭi, Mṛgeśa, Amṛta, and Māyā; twice Guhālaya; Pavitra, Ṛtadhāman, Vaidhara, and then Mādhava;
Māruta, Kamalā, Padma, and Pavitra-Ṛtadhāman.
Atri, Mṛgapati, Lakṣmī, Bahula, Pañcabinduka; Pavitra, Ṛtadhāman, Vairāja, Vikrama;
the western one named Padmanābha, Vaidhara, and Mṛgavallabha.
Dakṣa, Ravi, Gopana, Subhadra, Bhuvana,
Kukubha, Mādhava, and then Mādhavī, the one named Bhāskara,
Gopana, Matimant, Pulaha, and Mādhava-Ravi.
And one should utter *yaṣṭim* and *brahman*, likewise *madhusūdana*;
*dhruvam*, *nabhomani*, *gopam*, and *bindum*, O Four-faced One.
Thus one should utter three times: *arṇam*, *sugata*, and *sāgarottama*.

"Mandaram, Bhāskaram, Paścāt, Gopanama, Mādhavīm, as well as Ādidevam, Jagatprāṇam, and Mādhavan— these one should extract. Thus, O Brahmin, the mantra has been extracted, which bestows the accomplishment of all goals."

That [seed-syllable] is measured by a hundred [units] through the [mantras] beginning with *varṇa* and *raśmi*. Having extracted the seed-syllable from *bhāskara*, *mandara*, *pañcabindu*, and immediately after *yaṣṭi*, one should fashion the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of this.

The seer is Kakutstha, the metre is Aticchandas, and the deity here is [the one addressed by] the mantra for the universal invocation. It is taught that four hundred thousand recitations of this mantra should be performed.
Through knowledge, meditation, and recitation, the mantra bestows all accomplishments.
For one who is constantly disciplined and daily devoted to self-restraint,
[this practice] bestows all fruits, both of this world and the next. O Brahmin, on the tenth day, one should worship Kṛtānta, the bestower of results.
Having offered salutations to Nigamādi, Gandhavaha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Anantara,
Daṇḍa, Prabhañjana, Dakṣa, Ādideva, and Sadāgati,
the Manu named Vaivasvata was described.

Having extracted the seed-syllable from the vowels, [one takes] the wind (ya) and the head of the staff (ha). With that arisen seed-syllable, one performs the ritual assignment of the limbs, beginning with the heart.
Satyatapas is said to be the seer, Gāyatrī the metre, and the deity is proclaimed [as follows].
The mantra dedicated to the ancestors as deities should be recited five hundred thousand times;
by propitiating the Lord of Śrāddha with that, one attains all desired things.
First, [one should worship] the beginning of the Vedas, Vikrama, and Mānuṣeśvara.
O lotus-born one, having extracted the *natim* (the nasal *ṃ*) of Maghavan (Indra), the mantra has been declared.
The *vaidhara* [syllable], the lord of the upper world (*ūrdhvalokeśa*), and the *nāsikya* seed-syllable have been extracted. (30.160–161)
The seer is the god Virāj, the meter is [Virāj], and the deity is the slayer of Bala.
By worshipping the conqueror of the gods (Indra) with this [mantra], one enjoys the fruit of universal sovereignty.
On the twelfth lunar day, one should worship according to the stated method with the root mantra.
Desiring the fruit that is difficult to obtain, one should worship the Blessed One, the beloved of Śrī;
likewise, the beginning of the Vedas (Nigamādi), the end of prostration (Natyanta), the Western Udayana, as well as Krodharūpa, Pavitra, Śrīvatsa, and Pāvaka.
Then Adideva, Pavana, Gopana, Yaṣṭiman,
Gopati, Bahula, Pañcabindu, Narahari,
Aurva, Yaṣṭi, Kamala, Gopana, and the one named Mandara.
Having extracted Vaidhara, Devadatta, Kamala, Gopana,
Śaṅkha, and that which ends with Ṭhaṭha, this mantra has been proclaimed.
One should extract Svargādi, Pulaha, Bandhu, and the nasal seed-syllable.
The seer of this [mantra] is declared to be Śrīnidhi, its metre is Virāṭ, and its deity is Manmatha;
it should be worshipped by those who desire all fruits.
O Lotus-born One, I shall now extract another mantra consisting of a single syllable.
The mantra is said to be *tāra*, *garuḍa*, and *aurva*, together with the *bindu*.
A practitioner of mantra should recite this one hundred thousand times for rites such as attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
I shall now tell you another mantra dedicated to Kāma, which is capable of granting all desires.
Udgīta, Kamala, Pīta, Māyā, Ardhenduśekhara,
Karāla, Gopana, Dakṣa, Vaidhara, and immediately after that,
Mṛgendra, Varuṇa, Ādideva, and the one known as Śvasana.
Śukla, Sudhāmaya, Vahni, Kakubha with Vināyaka;
Śaśāṅka, Mādhava, Brahmasādhaka, and the one named Bhāskara; Hairamva, Gopana, Vāyu, Kakubha, and the Lord of Aquatic Creatures (Yādasāmpati).
One should utter Pulaha and Nigamādi twice;
then one should utter the western [deity] Ṛtadhāman, complete with its joints.
Śaśāṅka is the beginning, Jalaja is yellow, and Varuṇa is born from the lotus.
First [he saw] Kakubha, Viṣṇu, and Vighneśa; then the one of fierce rays (the Sun), Padmanābha, Vaidhara, Vāyu, and the primordial Mandara.
Furthermore, he saw the pair beginning with Mandara, and immediately after that, those very same ones again.
Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, and the lotus-born ones, as well as Yaṣṭi, Abda, and Udaya;
Dahana, Śrīdhara, Varṇa, Pulaha, and Brahmasādhana;
Karāla, Ādya, Kalaśa, Mukha, and thereafter Śrīvatsa.
Having extracted *prabhañjana*, *gopana*, *sparśa*, the first of the waters (*apām pati*),
and the one ending in *ṭha-ṭha*— this is declared as the mantra, O Lotus-Seated One;
Kaliṅga is the seer, Aticchandas is the meter, and Kāma is the deity.
One should recite it one hundred and six lakṣas; for that practitioner, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Both Rati (pleasure) and Virati (renunciation) will always stand by his side.
The mantra for these two consists merely of their names in the dative case, with three heads.
Madana is the first arrow, and likewise Unmadana is the other;
Mohana and Dveṣaṇa are two, and Dīpana is remembered as the fifth.
Mallikā, Ketakī, Jāti, Paṅkaja, and likewise Yūthikā— 30.181–30.182
They say that the flowers are the arrows (*bāṇa*);
furthermore, their mantra consists of the phonemes of consciousness (*saṃvit-varṇa*) joined together, followed by the name in the dative case (*caturthyanta*).
They know that their worship is performed with those [mantras] accompanied by the word "namas" at the end.
The bow, the goad, and the noose are the weapons of that Mind-born One (Kāma).
O Four-faced One, their mantras are as before, and their names are likewise.
[He dwelt] in a place mostly adorned with flowering trees, resembling the wish-fulfilling tree of the Kalpa.

In a garden frequented by flocks of birds warbling melodiously, in the midst of a great lake filled with blossoming lotuses, upon a golden seat placed there, beautiful and provided with a coverlet— 30.186.
He was seated together with his two goddesses, adorned with all ornaments;
his limbs were anointed with red sandalwood paste and he was graced with red garlands;
handsome and youthful, he wore beautiful earrings and silken garments.
One should worship him— who dwells surrounded on all sides by hosts of women who are the foremost of the *apsarases*—
by means of the *arghya* and other offerings while meditating with this mantra;
and one should also worship the fish-bannered god (*makaradhvaja*) with the *kāma-gāyatrī*.

All [practices] such as recitation (*japa*) are as before, and the three worlds are brought under control. For the practitioner who is constantly disciplined, what need is there for other excessively elaborate methods?
O Lotus-Seated One, I shall now speak the mantra of the Aśvins.
Having first extracted the Udgītha, Vighneśa who is fond of the *pāṭala* flower,
the one named Brahmasādhana, Śrīvatsa, and that which consists of nectar (*sudhāmaya*),
[one should utter] Māyā, Subhadra, Ākāra, and the mantra of the Aśvins as it has been taught.
The seed-syllable is accompanied by the initial *mardhendu* (the crescent moon); by that, the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*) is performed.
Bhṛgu is the seer, the *bṛhat* meter is the metre, and the two Aśvins are the deities to be propitiated.
By reciting it five hundred thousand times, one achieves success (*siddhi*) and becomes a master of all syllables.
Diseases such as consumption (rājayakṣmā) do not remain in his lineage,
and medicines become expert in the removal of diseases.
By the mere touch of his hand, every object becomes medicine.
On the full moon day, the best of men should likewise worship Soma, the source of the Vedas,
whose body is the full moon, who is with Mandara,
the Lord of Obstacles accompanied by the honeyed winds, and Mādhavī at the time of dismissal.

The mantra of Soma has been declared; I shall extract its seed-syllable for you: one should make it white, beginning with the syllable *manu* (the letter *m*) and ending with the nasal *anusvāra*. With that, one should perform the succession of limbs (*aṅga*).
Its seer is named Kaumodaka, its meter is *paṅkti*, and its deity is [Soma].

The recitation (japa) for this is exactly as before, or one may worship with the Gāyatrī; furthermore, the entire fruit previously mentioned, including even residence in the same world as the Moon (candrasālokya), [is attained]. Thus, O gods, the lunar days (tithis) have been described, along with their mantras and modes of worship.
And all those fruits have been declared by you in their proper sequence;
there is no fruit pertaining to this world or the next that cannot be accomplished through those lunar-day conjunctions (*tithi-yoga*),
by the grace of the mantra, and through the greatness of those deities.

"O Four-faced One, even well-performed deeds do not bear fruit when obstructed by an obstacle; they are destroyed by such an impediment. Therefore, those who wish to perform their work must first propitiate the Lord of Obstacles."
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Mantras of the Deities of the Lunar Days," in the Carya-pada of the Padma-tantra within the Mahopanisad of the glorious Pancaratra.
[The thirty-first chapter begins.]
The manifestation of Viṣvaksena, the extraction of mantras such as the Kirīṭa-mantra,
the birth of the Lord Brahmā, and the nature and origin of Vighnarāja.
The ornaments, beginning with the crown, were presented exactly as they were;
likewise, the discus and other weapons, as well as Tārkṣya and Sena—the Manavas who worshipped these [deities] thereby worshipped the causes of the fruits [of their merit]. (31.1–31.2)
"Tell me all this, if you have favor toward me:
the gods are being oppressed by the Asuras, who are powerful and difficult to defeat in battle. (31.3)
The gods went for refuge to Pradyumna, the protector who grants fearlessness, saying:
"In battles, even though we are powerful, we are being oppressed by the Daityas. (31.4)
"Act in such a way that they, struck by obstacles, flee," thus was Pradyumna addressed by them. Enraged, with eyes bloodshot,
he whose face was like that of a rutting elephant produced [an army] from his anger.
Seeing him standing before him with palms joined in reverence,
he whose face was like that of an elephant then spoke these words at the time when the battle between the gods and the asuras had commenced.
"Having stationed yourself there, create an obstacle for the Daityas.
Having spoken thus while he looked on, the blessed Lord Pradyumna vanished,
and the gods also returned as they had come.
From that time forward, by the grace of Vighneśa, the hosts of deities slew the asuras and did not suffer defeat.
Until the end of the kalpa, I shall now describe the lineage of Kirīṭin.
Having extracted the pervasive *nati* (namas), followed by the lotus (*kamalam*),
then *mahāmāyā*, the seven-tongued one (*saptajihvā*), that which is called the five dots (*pañcabindu*),
the form that gladdens the heart, the wind (*pavana*), the white (*śukla*), and the two Mandaras.
Dākṣāyaṇīśa, Vijaya, Mandara, and Saroruha; Śrīdhara, Hṛdayāhlāda, Mādhava, and Vittavardhana;
Kumbha, Hutāśana, Devadatta, and Kṣīra, which consists of nectar.
Dahana, Gopana, Vāyu, Karāla, Kamalodbhava,
Otadeha, Kṣitidhara, Vikrama, Dhūmaketana,
Amṛta, Bandhusahita, Bhadrahasta, and Trivikrama.
Caturgati, Śrīdhara, Vijaya, and likewise Mādhava; Hastivaktra, Vaidhara, Bhuvana, and Kāmaga;
having uttered Vairāja and the one called Vaidhara thereafter, [he recited] what follows.
Rāma, the Purifier, Victory, Gopana, the Elephant-faced One;
Mahendra, the Elephant-headed One, Vikrama, the Subtle-eyed One; Gopana, the one whose name is Touch, the Primordial God, the one with symmetrical lotus-feet.
Māhendra, the western Adideva, and the one called Dhanada;
Vikrama, the western Vijaya, O Four-faced One,
as well as Prabhañjana, Mṛgeśa, and the one named Madhusūdana.
Mārtāṇḍa, Pāvaka, and then Pañcabindu with its bindu; Karāla, Mṛtadhāman, Mahāmāyā with its staff (yaṣṭi);
Gopati joined with Śrīdhara, Nāsikya, and likewise Phaṭkṛti.
The mantra for Svāhā is now declared; its seed-syllable is [the letter] *ma*.
The lotus, the abode of Truth (*ṛtadhāman*), adorned with Mahāmāyā, is extracted;
likewise, the six limbs are seen by Cākhaṇḍala. (31.21–31.22)
It is said that Chanda is the *paṅkti* [meter] and Kirīṭin is the deity;
one should visualize him as two-armed, with a large body and a protruding belly, standing firm, adorned with ornaments, and bowing with palms joined in reverence. (31.23)
Having meditated thus, the knower of mantras, unwearied, should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times.
[He should include] *natyanta*, *chandogāmādi*, the word *śrī*, as well as *kalaśa*,
*ekanetra*, *hutavaha*, *śaśāṅka*, and *madhusūdana*.
Sadāgati, Ādideva, Nāsikya known as Yaṣṭi,
Lakṣmī, Karāla, Pulaha, Mahāmāyā with the bindu (31.26),
Tārkṣya, Aurva and the rest, Yaṣṭi, the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*, and the end of the oblation (*hutāntima*).
The seed-syllable of Śrī is that very seed; the seer is Prajāpati.
The metre is Virāṭ-Gāyatrī, and Śrīvatsa is considered the deity.
O Four-faced One, I shall now describe another mantra of Śrīvatsa.
Oṃkāra, Soma first, Svarādi, Jaya, Māruta, Mādhava, Tārakādhīśa, Ekanetra with Māruta,
Kalaśa, and after that Vijaya, adorned by Mahāmāyā.
Śukla, Tāra, Śvasana, Kumbha, and Vairāja; Anala, Pūrṇacandra, Pulaha, and Mādhava;
as well as Natyanta, Śuklavijaya, Śvasana, and Śvetarociṣ.
Dakṣa, Dara, Devadatta, Oṣadhīśa, and likewise Abjaja; Vairāja, Prathama, Kumbha, Mṛtadhāman, and Vidarbhitau; Jaya, Sadāgati, Devadatta, and finally Ṭhaṭha.
The seed-syllable of Śrī has already been mentioned; Devala is said to be the seer (ṛṣi).
The meter is Akṣarapaṅkti, and Śivatsa is considered the deity.
Then, by merely performing one hundred thousand recitations (japa), one shall attain all desires.
One should likewise [worship] the Creator (Brahmā) preceded by the Praṇava and ending with a salutation, as well as the Manu,
Sakara, Vijaya, Loka, Subhadra, Madhuidviṣ,
Prabhañjana, Pāvaka, Vairāja, and Vighnanāyaka.
Gopana, Dhanada, Māyā, and the western [seed-syllable] which is the first vowel;
Vairāja, Māruta, and thereafter the letter *e*, which is the first vowel;
Mādhavī, Padmanābha, Vijaya, and Brahmasādhana.
Agni, Bhallāyudha, Kumbhākāra, and likewise Māruta;
the second of the Apsarases, Kamala, Pulaha, and Pavitraka;
Ādideva, Dhanada, and immediately after, Trivikrama.
The western [deity] Vijaya, the first Sparśana, and likewise Mādhava;
Oṣadhīśa, Ikāra, Dṛṣṭi, and again Dhanada;
Rāma together with Pradyumna, and the western Padmanābha.
Prabhañjana, followed by Chaladhvaṃsa, with "svāhā" at the end—
this is the seed-syllable (bīja) Kaustubha, accompanied by a bindu; furthermore,
Jamadagni is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), and the deity is the one named Kaustubha.
Having uttered the word "Kaustubha" in the dative case, one should perform a prostration.
Through five hundred thousand recitations of that mantra, one's desire is fulfilled.
[One should worship] a pitcher preceded by the seven-syllable [mantra], with a favorable hand, and dear to the enemy.
Bhadrahasta, Mandara, Madhusūdana, Abjaja, Pulaha, Devadatta, Mādhavī, Madhusūdana,
Māhendra, the one named Rāma, Vighneśa, and Pañcabinduka.
To the west is Śrīdhara, and after that the world Vahni;
then Krodhāgni, Vāsudeva, and the two Vairājas, as well as Mandara;
to the west is Padmanābha, and Māyāśirasa is situated around it.
The mantra is said to end with *ṭha-ṭha*, beginning with *māruta* (the letter *ya*) joined with *mādhava* (the letter *sa*).
Then follows the *kalaśa* (the letter *va*), followed by *māruta* (*ya*), then *udaya* (*u*), and *aniruddhaka* (*na*).
The seed-syllable is the sage, the deity is the giver of wealth (Kubera), and the meter is the *paṅkti*.
I shall now declare the supreme *vanamālā* mantra, which yields great fruit:
Brahmakośa, Nati, Kumbha, Mukha, Vighneśa, Mandara, Gopana, Pulaha, Ādideva, Śaṅkha, and Godhana. (31.48–31.49)
Mādhava, Sūdana, Vāyu, Mṛgeśa, Dakṣa, and Gopana; Caturgati, Ādideva, Anala, and Guhālaya;
Paścima, Vikramapara, Pracaṇḍa, and Pañcabinduka.
The right eye is Dinakara, and the second is Śvetadīdhiti.
Vāsudeva is Dakṣadvaya, Tigmāṃśu is Bandhuśīrṣaka,
Dviradāsya is Pañcabindu, and the first is Śvetaroci.
Amṛta, Vahniśiras, Kamala, the one called Gopana, Mandara, Vaidhara, Māyā, the fifth, Gajavāhana,
Mādhava, Śvetadīdhiti, Kumbha, and Bahulaśīrṣaka.
Vijaya, Ekadṛṣṭi, Varuṇa, and Pāṭalapriya; Caturgati, Sūdana, Māruta, and likewise Ādimat;
the fourth, Ṛtadhāmā, and again Agni and Śvasana.
And Brahmakośapara, Bhadrapāṇi, and Padmajā; Vijaya, Praṇavādi, and Śvetadīdhiti, O Lotus-born One;
Śaśāṅka, Padmanābha, Vaidhara, Māyā, and Mahādhanu.
One should utter the western [face] Vijaya, Māyāśīrṣa, and Vighneśa. O Four-faced One, one should twice utter Vikrama, Sūkṣmadṛṣṭi, Gopana, Janmadhvaṃsa, Kalaśa, and Pulaha.
Having repeated [the preceding] twice as before, one should then extract the seed-syllable of nourishment (*puṣṭibīja*):
Gopati, Gopana, Yaṣṭi, Varuṇa, and the initial Bindu;
Bhāskara, Bhuvana, Yaṣṭi, Phaṭkāra, and finally Ṭhaṭha.
Pīyūṣa, Pavana, Brahmasādhana, and Yaṣṭiśīrṣaka—
this is the seed-mantra (bīja) of the four-faced one, the arrangement of limbs for the principal syllables.
Bhava is its sage, Uṣṇih its metre, and [Brahmā] its deity.
She is a two-armed young girl, adorned with full breasts,
wearing a crown with a casket and bearing a forest garland;
she holds a mirror in her left hand and [the other object] in her right.
Having visualized Puṣpamañjarikā with two [hands], one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Regarding other ornaments as well, one should know that the name in the dative case followed by "namaḥ" constitutes the mantra; one should arrange the seed-syllable at the beginning.
I shall proclaim the lineage of Prabhā; listen attentively as it truly is:
beginning with Udgītha and ending with Nati, and finally Ṛtadhāmaka;
then Bhallāyudha, Ādideva, Śvasana, and Sūkṣmalocana.
Of these [names], the second is Śvetāṃśu, and the first is Kamala;
then Pāvaka, Oṣadhi, Padmapāṇi, Vairāja,
Mṛgeśa, Janmavidhvaṃsa, and the one joined with Brahmasādhana.
[Kṛṣṇa] saw Kakubha, Kalaśa, Ādideva, Pulaha, and the Lotus-born (Brahmā);
Oṃkāra, Mādhavī, and Agni adorned with the head of Māyā;
Pāṭalapriya, Mākāra, and the yellow-hued Madhuvidviṣ (the enemy of Madhu).
Śrīvatsādi, Vijaya, Śaśāṅka, Viṣṇumastaka, Mārtāṇḍa, Indu, Anala, Madhusūdana, Māruta,
Śriyaḥpati, Ekākṣa, Gopana, and Kamalodbhava.
Amṛta, Ṛtadhāmāna, Vijaya, Kamalālaya,
Otadeha, Subhadra, and Bandhumastakabhūṣita;
Vijaya, Gopana, Prāṇa, Huṃphaṭkāra, and Ṭhaṭhāntaka.
The first syllable, joined with the letter *ya*, is proclaimed as its seed-syllable (*bīja*).

Bhāskara is its seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter is its metre (*chandas*), and Prabhā is its deity (*devatā*). The recitation (*japa*) of this mantra is proclaimed to consist of one hundred thousand counts.

Having enjoyed abundant pleasures through the power of the mantra, the knower of the mantra attains the supreme state upon the casting off of the body; of this there is no doubt. [One should meditate on] the beginning of the Veda, the Kaustubha gem, the Gopana, the Bindu, and the lunar [Aindava].

The wise man should thus extract the mantra from the rosary of syllables: *vikramaṃ*, *vaidharaṃ*, *puṇyaṃ*, *rāmaṃ*, *śuklasamāhvayaṃ* (31.75); *vairājaṃ*, *agnimākāraṃ*, *sparśanaṃ*, and *viṣṇumastakaṃ*, ending with *namaḥ*. (31.76)
One should meditate upon [the deity] holding a rosary, two-armed, with the luster of crystal,
adorned, wearing yellow garments, and seated upon a lotus pedestal;
his hands are in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and likewise, there is the recitation of the mantra.
And the minister obtains a great fruit that is exceedingly difficult to attain:
the auspicious Udgītha, the Conch, the Urdhvayaṣṭi,
the Dhanada, Hṛṣīkeśa, Mandara, and the Brahmasādhana.
"Bahula," "Ekanetra," "Pañcānta," "Bandhumastaka," "Anala," "Gopana," "Śaṅkha," and "Acāmādi," followed by "Nati"—
this is declared to be the mantra for the incense vessel (dhūpapātra). Now the bell mantra (ghaṇṭāmantra) will be proclaimed.
One should offer salutations to Āmnāyādi, Kṣitidhara, Hṛṣīkeśa, and likewise Ravi;
to Guhālaya, Nāsikya, Padmapāṇi, and Pracaṇḍaka,
who is joined with the form of a fish— this is the salutation to the four states.
And Manu has declared, O Brahmin, that the vessel for the lamp is said to be the *udgītha*,
the *kakubha*, the beginning, the face of the *gadadhvaṃsa* meters,
the *pāvaka*, the *vijaya*, the destroyer of rebirth, and the means to attain Brahman. (31.83)
Vairāja, Vikramaparama, Anala, Guhālaya,
Paścima, Ādideva, Śvasana, and Natiśīrṣaka—
these are declared to be the mantras of the lamp-vessel; now they are being described.
O Brahman, the mouth of the Brahmakośa is followed by Saptārṇa,
Śaśāṅka, Śrīdhara, Dṛṣṭi, Ādilakṣmī, Hutāśana,
Lambodhara, Ādideva, Dara, Viṣṇu, and Mādhava.
Then [they saw] Nabhomaṇi, Rāma, and likewise Pulaha as the first;
Vakratuṇḍa, Vidhātṛ, and the face of Vakratuṇḍa;
Kamala, Ṛtadhāman, and Madhusūdana as they were departing.
One should thus extract the seed-syllable: the pestle (mu), joined with the cowherd (sa), then the wind (ya) and the quarter (ka);
followed by nectar (a), having the luster of yellow (pī), the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*, and ending with *ṭhaṭha*; white, with a face (mukha) and a bindu. Thus one should extract the seed-syllable.
*Tāram*, *karālamākāram*, *pulaha*, and likewise *ādimat*;
*vakratuṇḍa*, *vidhātāram*, *bahulam*, and *madhuvidviṣam*;
*ādi*, *caturgatim*, and *hum phaṭ* and so forth—[these are to be placed] in the heart and other [limbs]. (31.90–91)
Then the venerable Kālarudra is the seer;
the meter is proclaimed to be Gāyatrī; and its deity is Sudarśana, the king of weapons.
For the sake of accomplishment, one should recite it twelve hundred thousand times, as with the root mantra.
O Four-faced One, [one should worship] the seven syllables from the beginning as previously mentioned, as well as Śaśin,
Śrīdhara, Vaidhara, Viṣṇu, Śrīvatsa, Anala,
Bhadrahastādideva, and Śaṅkhādin.
The twelve-syllable mantra of Sudarśana has been declared;
its seed-syllable and limbs are as before, and Kapila is remembered as the seer. Virāj is the meter, and the weapon-king Sudarśana is the deity.
The recitation (*japa*) of twelve hundred thousand [times] yields a fruit equal to that of the twelve-syllable mantra.

Then, one should employ the word *sudarśana* preceded by the beginning of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*) and ending with an obeisance (*nati*), in the dative case; the fruit is likewise as in the eight-syllable mantra.
The seer is Bhava, the meter is Gāyatrī known as Heti;
one should extract the first [syllable] of Mādhavī, which was previously mentioned as consisting of twelve syllables,
as well as Nabhomaṇi, Ādideva, and Vakratuṇḍa, the face of the meters.
Karālamṛta, Agni, Gopana, and likewise Kakubha;
