The seed-syllables and limbs are as before; the seer (ṛṣi) is Nīlalohita.
Chanda, known as Varivas, and the deity Sudarśana—
O Brahmin, one should recite [their mantra] eight hundred thousand times, whether in the netherworld, in heaven, or on earth;
by the power of the mantra, the movement of the practitioner shall not be obstructed.
O Four-faced One, I shall utter the mantra known as Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha:
Udgītha, Nṛhari, Padmanābha, and the one named Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Nāsikya, Śukla, Ādi, Gopati, Praṇavādi,
Nīhāradīdhiti, Padmanābha, Madhuvidviṣ, Anala, Kakubha, Kumbha, Gopana, and Pulahātmaka.
The second of these vowels, ending with the consonant *s*, is called Sudana and Pulaha;
[one should worship] Vikrama, Kuñjaramukha, and Mādhava upon his head,
having twice uttered Mārtāṇḍa, Bhadrahasta, and Prabhākara.

Śrīdhara, Kapilākṣa, Phaṭkāra, and Kheṭakī; ending with Ṭhaṭha—thus it is said to consist of twenty-two syllables. The seed-syllables and the limbs have been declared, and the meter is stated to be Gāyatrī.
Jamadagni shall be the seer, and Sudarśana the deity.
Within the heart of Sudarśana resides Hari, the Man-lion,
resembling a mountain of crystal and bristling with more than a hundred manes.
With a deep and cavernous roar like the thundering of the clouds at the end of an aeon,
he held the conch and the discus with two hands,
while with the other two he stretched out his formidable knees, which were terrifying with claws like thunderbolts.
Seated upon a lotus throne with his two feet crossed,
his brow knit in a frown, his yogic belt firmly bound,
he has opened wide the cavity of his mouth, possessing fangs and quivering lips.

The practitioner of mantra should meditate thus upon the three-eyed one, who is fashioned by all the kalpas and whose roar is like that of Brahmā; by doing so, he crosses over misfortune. Merely by remembering him once, one obtains the fruit according to one's desire.
One obtains whatever has been stated in other mantra-kalpas.
I shall now declare the mantra of Pāñcajanya, which accomplishes all aims:
having first extracted the Udgītha, one should then extract seven syllables immediately thereafter.
The western world is Caṇḍa, Puṇḍarīka, and Hutāśana; Mahāmāyā, Karāla, Gopana, and Pannagādhipa;
likewise Sūdana, Śaṅkha, Kalaśa, and Madhusūdana.
Māruta, Bhuvanāhvāna, Mandara, Bhuvana, then Kharvadeha, and likewise Ādideva, Śvasana, Ādimat,
Vaidhara, Pañcabindu, and then Vijaya as the last.
One should worship Yānta, Guhālaya, Pāpahanana, Madhuvidviṣ,
Śaṅkha, Lakṣmī, and likewise Ayaṣṭi; then Kharvadeha in the west,
Ādideva, Mahendra, and Madhusūdanaśīrṣaka.
The great mantra is declared to be "vāyuṃ ṭhaṭhāntamuditam" (the wind, ending with *ṭha*, and *udita*).
This is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) known as Śrīvatsa, the staff (*yaṣṭi*), and the Udgītha. Sanaka is the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) of this mantra, and its meter (*chandas*) is Bṛhatī.
The deity is Pāñcajanya, and four hundred thousand recitations are prescribed.
O Four-faced One, hear now another mantra of Pāñcajanya:
one should first extract the seven-syllable [mantra], and the final [part] is Madhusūdana.
Bhṛgu, Candradhara, Khaḍgadhavala, Kakubhāhvaya, Gajavaktra, Vāyu, Ādideva, Samīraṇa,
and the seventh, Paścima, who is Sumukha and the source of the Vedas.
Pīyūṣamatri, Subhaga, Varuṇa, Madhuvidviṣ,
Gajāsyā, Ādideva, Śvasana, Śvetarocis,
Vaidhara, Gopana, and Gadadhvaṃsa, O Four-faced One! (31.273)
Vairāja, Vikrama, Dakṣa, Śrīdhara, and he whose vehicle is Tārkṣya; Gopana, Sparśana, the slayer of Jamna, and the lord of the waters;
Māhendra, Ādi, Jvalana, and likewise Aṃśu—the sixth and fifth [of the group].
Gopana is the western guardian (gopa), yellow in color, the enemy of Madhu;
together with Śvasana and ending in Ṭhaṭha, the mantra is thus declared.
Its seed-syllables, its limbs, and its deity are indeed as before.
Viṣvaksena is the seer, the metre is Supratiṣṭhā, and Pitāmaha is the deity.
By reciting this mantra five hundred thousand times, the practitioner, through the power of the mantra,
moves unimpeded through the worlds beginning with Atala.
Furthermore, O Lotus-born One, what of Dharma, Kāma, Artha, and Mokṣa?

[They behold] Govinda, who holds the mace, at the forefront of the seven oceans; the two destroyers of the gaze; the one who transcends the four states of existence; the heroic one; and the one whose weapon is the crescent-headed arrow, the mouth of the waters.
The Lord of Waters, the Fire-bearer, Ākāra with his face turned westward;
Rāma, Pracaṇḍa, Govinda, as well as Brahmā and Saṅkarṣaṇa;
Mandara, Vāyu-devāhva, Vaidhara, and Viṣṇumastaka.

"Kuśeśayadhare vīrasenaṃ hum phaṭ ṭhaṭha at the end"—thus one should extract the mantra of Kaumodakī; its seed-syllable, however, is "sparśa" (the letter *sa*) followed by a second "ardhendu" (the letter *u*). By this very [seed-syllable], the arrangement of the limbs (*aṅga*) is performed.
The seer is Kṛṣṇa, and likewise the metre is Paṅkti; furthermore, the deity is Kaumodakī. For one who recites this Lakṣa-mantra, it shall become a bestower of success.
Having first extracted the syllable Oṃ, [the mantra consists of] Gopana, Dṛṣṭi, and Vikrama.
The Vairāja, the Māruta, the destroyer of evil, and the Vasumastaka;
the Vairāja, the Bandhuśiras, the Mādhavī, the Sūdana, and the Dara;
the Pāṭalapriya, the Ākāra, the Samīraṇa, and the mouth of the waters.
O Brahmin, [he goes] to the western Bandhumastaka, which is a cave-dwelling;
then to Sumukha, Devadatta, Humphaṭkāra, and finally Ṭhaṭhāntima;
furthermore, to Nāda, Pakāra, Mūkāra, and that which has the half-moon as its crest.
O Brahmin, one should fashion the seed-syllable (bīja) by this very means; the assignment of the limbs (aṅga-kalpanā) is likewise performed thereby.
Viriñca is the seer (draṣṭṛ), Virāṭ is the metre (chandas), and Padmā is the presiding deity (adhidevatā).
By reciting [the mantra] one million times, a person shall attain all supernatural powers (ṛddhi).
Thus the mantra of Padma has been declared; the assignment of its limbs is performed by means of its seed-syllable (bīja).
Furthermore, [the syllables] Śukla, Viṣṇu, Vahni, Pīyūṣa, and Gopana, followed by the extraction of the seven letters, [yield] Mandara and Kamalāsana.
Śaśāṅka as the beginning, Pulaha, Gopana, Pavana again,
Jvalana, Gopana, Dakṣa, Gopana, Kamalodbhava,
Caturgati, Bhuvana, Sumukha, Madhu, Dviviṣa.
The knower of mantras should extract the mantra ending with *ṭha* and *ṭha*, preceded by *da-ra-mu-kha*. "Mandara," "Bhuvana," and "Yaṣṭi"—this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra.
Mudgala is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāj is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Manu is the deity (*devatā*) of this mantra.
They declare the mantra of Musala to consist of five hundred thousand [recitations].
Having extracted the seven syllables— Hairambha, Madhusūdana,
Gaja-hva, Atri, Kamala, Madhu-śatru, and Caturgati— [one attains success].
Viṣṇu, Śukla, again Viṣṇu, Vahni, Pīyūṣa, Gopana,
Śaśāṅka, Bhuvana, Vahni, Śrīvatsa, Brahmasādhana, Sumukha, Vikrama, Vijaya, and likewise Vaidhara.
The mantra of the sword is said to consist of Rāma, Pañcāntaka, Puṇya, Gopana, Yaṣṭiśīrṣaka,
Pañcāntaka, Gopana, Śvasana, Huṅkṛti,
Phaṭkāra, and Svāhā.
The seed-syllable of the Cakra-mantra is said to be the sage Śrīnidhi. Virāḍ is its meter, and Khaḍgarāva is the sovereign weapon.
By reciting the mantra three hundred thousand times, the practitioner attains the desired accomplishment.
Having first fashioned the seven oceans, [he fashioned] Śrīvatsa, Madhusūdana,
the one with the Śārṅga bow in hand, the destroyer of the mace (Gada), the head of Madhusūdana,
Jvalana, Pavana, Ādi, Vahni, Śukla, and Apāmpati.
Madhusūdana, Pūrṇendu, Bhuvana, Havyavāhana, Pavitra— the seventh of the waters— Śrī, Mandara, Ādimat,
Vighneśa, Gopana, Śaṅkha, Mukha, and Paścimaśrīdhara.
Bahula, Bhuvana, Krodha, and likewise Trayodaśa; Acas, Hutāśa, Ekadṛṣṭi, and two Mandaras; Padmasambhava, Pavitra, Mṛtadhāmā, Vāyu, Yaṣṭi, and Madhudviṣ.
Having formed the mantra ending with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, and having *ṭhaṭha* at the end, one should extract the seed-syllable as the first letter.
The seer of the mantra is *Hutānta*; the meter is *Chandaḥ*, and the presiding deity is *Devadā*.
Chanting eight hundred thousand times while holding [the rosary] in the hand, one shall be victorious in battle. [The mantras are:
Brahmakośa, Nati, Sarga, Kalātmā, Kamalāhvaya, Māhendra, Gopanapara, and Śubhada Madhuvidviṣ.
Śaśāṅka, Śrīdhara, Vahni, Varuṇa, Bandhumastaka,
Vighneśa, Ādideva, Śubhada, Gopana,
Pavana, Kūṭa, Aurva, and Nāsikya— these are the mantras of Bhāskara. (31.307–31.308)
One should extract the mantra ending with *huṃ* and *phaṭ*, preceded by the syllable *yaṣṭi*.

One should conceive of the nectar (*pīyūṣa*), the crescent moon (*ardhendu*), and the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of that [mantra]. Having seen the mantra a hundred times, its meter is *māccha* and its deity is also [that same one].
One should recite the mantra five hundred thousand times to swiftly conquer enemies.
The mantra consists of the *udgītha*, the destroyer of sins (*pāpahanana*), the protection (*gopana*), and the eternal (*sadhruva*).
The final part is the protection (*gopana*), followed by Lakṣmī, the Primordial God (*ādideva*), and Vāyu (*samīraṇa*).

The sage is remembered as Prācetasa; one should not excessively conceptualize the mantra. The meter is Virāj, the presiding deity is Pāśa, and the recitation consists of three hundred thousand repetitions.
[It is] the treasury of Brahmā, beginning with the letter 'a', located in the nose, the lotus of the heart.

One should then recite the mantra "Bhuvanaṃ śubhadaṃ paścād ādidevaṃ sadāgatiṃ" until one becomes a seer of truth and a Virāṭ. The meter is Aṅkuśa, the deity is [the same], and one should mutter this three hundred thousand times.
The name preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ), ending in the dative case, and followed by *ṭhaṭha*,
as well as the seed-mantra (*bīja*) at the beginning of the other weapons—
by reciting these, all the *siddhis* arise exactly as before.
Therefore, O Brahman, I shall speak the mantra; listen as it is now being told.
It is used for subduing, attracting, creating enmity, killing, and expulsion, as well as for withering, paralyzing, possession, and all rites of summoning.
In cases such as the loss of wealth, the administration of poison, crossing the ocean, and so forth;
in leaping into the sky, entering the wind, fire, water, or earth;
in the sciences of sorcery (*indrajāla*) and the like, as well as in the victory over sages; [these are the spheres of the *khecarīs*].
In the knowledge of the past and future, in the enchantment of beings,
as well as in the presence of deities and the like, in acts such as the *sphoṭa* and *muṣya*,
and in such things to be accomplished, as well as in other rites.
Thus one should employ the mantra and meditate upon Garuḍa;
having first extracted the seven syllables, [one should worship] the wielder of the mace, the bearer of oblations,
the world, the lotus-eyed one, the protector, and again the purifier.
[He worshipped] Paścima, Bhuvana, Vahni, Śrīdhara, Krodhavigraha,
Brahmasādhana, Vairāja, Jaya, Mandara, Ādimat,
Amṛta, Gopana, and also Gopati and Dviradānana.
Ādideva, Nabhasvant, Anala, and Ramādhara; Pracaṇḍa, Kamala, Bhadrahasta, and Vāmanamastaka; Śvasana, Rohiṇīśa, Mṛgeśa, and Mānuṣeśvara.
Then Gopana, Gadina, Kamala, and likewise Bhuvana;
Vāsudeva, Pracaṇḍa, Vikrama, and likewise Vijaya;
and Vairāja together with Rāma, the wielder of the mace who destroys delusion.

One should extract the third vowel [I], the half-moon [bindu], the five-faced one [M], the enemy of Madhu [K], the wind [Y], and the comet [R] seven times. Then [extract] the sound *huṃ*, the sound *phaṭ*, *svāhā*, *mota*, *deha*, and likewise the *dhruva* [oṃ].
Pulaha seven times, and the syllable *hum phaṭ* ending with *ṭhaṭha*; Tāra, Varuṇa, Govinda, Vighneśa, and then Mādhava;
the letter *a* at the end of the consonants (*sparśāntaka*), and Sadāgati five times.
Six times [recite] Varuṇa, ending with *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*;
then the western Nigama, Kūṭa, Vikrama, Vahni, and Gopanau (31.330);
then Kakubha and Gopana; and again six times Māruta.
Desiring that all consonants and vowels be easily articulated,
one should extract the vowels according to the method taught in the *Manu-śāstra*.
Then, one should extract the Gāruḍa mantra, ending with *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
One should conceive of its seed-syllable as the anusvāra at the end of the fifth [vowel].
First, there is the word for Suparṇa, then the speech of Vakratuṇḍa,
then "Mahāsuparṇa," and likewise the head of Khageśvara.

O Four-faced One, having fashioned the mantras of the limbs by prefixing them with the *praṇava* (oṃ), ending them with the dative case, and concluding with the word "namas," using these six [names] in their proper order: Ananta, Vīravanta, Āravya, and finally the King of Birds (Garuḍa).
The one skilled in mantras should touch the limbs, beginning with the heart;
Kāśyapa is its seer, and the *paṅkti* is declared to be its meter.
Garuḍa is its deity, and three hundred thousand recitations of it are prescribed.
Beneath the banyan tree, the practitioner should accomplish the mantra:
"Āmnāyādi," "Narahari," "Vāmana," "Paścimānana," "Vairāja," "Pāvaka," and "Tāra"— this is the five-syllabled mantra.
The seer of this [mantra] is Marīci, and its deity is Garuḍa;
the meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, and its six limbs are themselves:
Udgītha, Kamala, Vāyu, Vāsudeva, and Dhruva.
The western [section] consists mostly of the Brahma-sādhana, Yaṣṭimastaka,
Vighneśa, Vikrama, Vahni, Mahāmāyā, and Dhruva; furthermore, Puṣpabhadrā, Pīṭha, Vāmana, Yaṣṭi, and Kaustubha.
One should extract the mantra beginning with the *bindu*, the water-pot (*kalaśa*), the half-moon, and the nature of the sun, the half-moon, and the digit (*kalā*);
[then] the lord of serpents, the kinsman, Varuṇa, the mouth of aquatic creatures, and ending with the oblation-eater (*hutānta*). This is the supreme Gāruḍa mantra.
Perhaps this preeminent bird is directly perceptible to the world;
he is the sheath of Brahman, the lotus, the nasal one called Bhūdhara,
the staff that destroys evil, the drop, and the Mandara of the lotus.
One should utter the other Gāruḍa mantra as follows: Ardhendu, Kalaśa, Bindu, Paścima, Pannagāśana, Vikramāgni, Śatru, Kakubha, Madhusūdana, Vāyu, and Svāhā. Thus it is said.
"Through the recitation of that [mantra], the accomplishment of ascending into the sky will come to pass.
Having thus performed this, one should utter twice the primordial *oṃkāra*, the first god, who is at the end of oneself, as well as Svacchanda, the wielder of the mace, and the bearer of oblations."
One should utter twice *bhuvanam* and *medinīm*, then *mandaram* and *madhusūdanam*;
thereafter, one should utter twice *vairājam*, *vipulam*, and *vāmanam*;
and [finally] *pavitram*, *padmakam*, *jambum*, *nāgendram*, and the primordial *vāyum*.
Having thus fashioned this [mantra], one should then arrange the final *yaṣṭi* as the protection;
forming the mantra with the half-moon of the seed-syllable of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) ending in *ṭha-ṭha*,
and having placed the seven syllables at the beginning— namely, *bhāskara* and *havyavāhana*.
Gopana, Yaṣṭi, Mārtāṇḍa, Havyavāhana, Vāmana, Candrārdha, Dvādaśātmā, Hṛṣīkeśa, and Dhruva;
Varuṇa, Hṛdayāhlāda, and the pair Kamala and Mādhava.
Vairāja, Śrīdhara, and again the seat (pīṭha) consisting of two worlds; one should then utter Vijaya, Śrīdhara, Vahni, and the world. [These are] Lokanetra, Ūrdhvanāsikya, Karāla, and Brahmasādhana.
One should know that the Gāruḍa mantra, which serves all purposes, consists of the sequence: *analaṃ*, *yaṣṭim*, *anilaṃ*, *yaṣṭim*, *kumbhodbhavaṃ*, and *hutāntam*.
Having extracted these seven syllables, one should then add *kalaśaṃ* and *bandhumastakam*.
Krodharūpa, Pracaṇḍa, Tridaśāhāra, and Mādhava; Candra, Svāhāpati, Śaśin, and likewise Bahula;
Mṛgāṅka, Śrīdhara, Vahni, and Bhuvana—the four pairs.
The one skilled in mantras should thus mentally construct another Gāruḍa mantra: "Bhānumat," followed by the pair "Pulaha," ending with "Hum Phaṭ" and concluding with "Huta.
[This is done] by means of Pavana, Hutāśa, Māhendra, and Pracetas.

One should remove poison by means of these four [mantras] individually, applied either in forward order or in reverse order. By employing them all together in reverse order, one should perform rites such as paralyzing (stambhana).
[The mantras are: Vyāpin, Vighnarāja, Dāmodara, and Dhruva.
"O Brahmin, one should extract this three-syllabled mantra beginning with 'evamādi'.
By means of this very mantra, when accomplished, which is characterized by the King of Birds (Garuḍa), the three worlds shall come under his command. (31.360)
The first and second worlds, the five-fold end, and likewise the nectar;
Gadin, Śrīdhara, Vahni, Udaya, Bhadra, Ambuja,
Vairāja, Vikrama, Svāhā, Aurva, and the one called Kamala.
Bhuvana, Parvata, Bandhu, Māhendrādīśrī,
as well as Vikrama, Tārkṣyavāha, Mṛgeśa, and Mandara;
Ādisūrya, Gopana, Mandara, Bhuvana, and Diśa.
"Agni and also the Lord of Beasts, ending with the utterance of Svāhā"—
O Brahmin, having thus prepared the mantra and the mudrā, one should then fashion the maṇḍala.
As for those who observe its details, their number is not known.
The practitioner of mantra, with undistracted mind, should contemplate himself as Garuḍa.
O Lotus-born One, I shall now describe the meditation upon the King of Birds:
his form is like the peak of Mount Meru, and his circle of wings is made of gold.
With a nose-tip like lapis lazuli and blue, with a curved snout that was terrifying,
with claws shaped like diamonds, and seated in the utkaṭika posture;
emitting a deep roar, with shoulders as broad as a mountain of stone.
He has infinite earrings as ornaments and Vāsuki as a decoration upon his head;
he possesses the interior of a great lotus, with ornaments entwined by garlands of lotuses;
Kārkoṭaka is bound upon his crown, and he is encircled at the waist by the splendors of the digits [of the moon].
It was adorned by Śaṅkhapāla, who acted as his sacred thread (upavīta);
it was further graced by Jaya and Gulika,
and by the serpent named Dhanañjaya and Vijaya.
Holding two bracelets with his left and right hands,
he is adorned with a breastplate as red as a young sprout;
likewise, he has a frown formed upon his brow and wears a crown shaped like a casket.
With wings outspread, creating a deep illusion of upward movement,
his face formidable with fangs, and his eyes copper-red and round—
having thus meditated upon Garuḍa with a one-pointed mind.
One shall accomplish those things that are to be accomplished, even those difficult for the gods to attain,
by reciting the mantra as prescribed while fixing one's gaze upon the sun;
with arms raised upward, the lords of serpents will become like servants.
O Brahmin, the mantra of Viṣvaksena is said to bestow all perfections (siddhis).
It consists of the syllable *tāra* (Om), the nectar-like Rāma, the wrathful form who is nectar-like,
Karāla, Śaśin, followed by Mādhava and Kuñjarānana.
One should extract the mantra ending with *ṭha-ṭha*, including the *gopana* and the *māruta*.
One should fashion its seed-syllable (*bīja*) by means of the *tāra* and the *bindu*.
O Lotus-Seated One, the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*) are to be fashioned by this very same [method].
They declare Viśvanātha to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is said to be the meter (chandas).
And the deity of that [mantra] of Manu is the mighty Viṣvaksena.
Now, O Lotus-born One, another mantra of Viṣvaksena is fashioned: [31.379–31.380]
Udgītha, Bhadrapāṇi, Mandara, Brahmasādhana, Subhadra, Gadin, Kumbha, ending with Sumukha, together with Ādhava— these,
O Kamalāsana, are preceded by the sparśa [consonant], accompanied by the bindu, and joined with Dhruva.
Darānta, Gopana, O Brahmin, Dhanada, Rājaśīrṣaka; Paścima, Nigamādi, and the one called Vairāja;
Khaḍgahasta, Sarāma, Jaya, and likewise Vasuvara.
Śubhada, Saroruha, Vairāja, Vikramamastaka,
Padmapāṇi, Bhadrapāṇi, and Pāśapāṇi in the west;
Sodaya, Śatruhanana, Mṛgeśa, and Vakratuṇḍaka.
Pracaṇḍa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Madhuśatru, Caturgati;
Khaḍgahasta, Acāmādi, Pracaṇḍa, Jhaṣamarṣita;
Subhadrānta, Madhudveṣin, Vairāja, Dvirvasu, and Para. (31.385–386)
The second of these is Subhaga, adorned with lotuses;
Vaidhara accompanied by Viṣṇu; Pracaṇḍa, whose abode is the sacrifice;
Śrīvatsa together with Dhruva; and likewise Khaḍgahastadhara.
Kamala, Ṛtadhāman, Subhaga, Vasugopa, and Nava;
Caturgati, Acāmādi, Vaidhara, Gopana, as well as Vijaya, Śvasana, Datta, Sūdana, and Mṛgalāñchana.
Then Mādhava ending with ṭha-ṭha, followed by Kayala and Mādhava;
then the yellow Dhanada, the Kumbha, and again Sadhruva;
then Kalānidhi, Puradhni, Ādideva, and Caturgati.
One should extract Vaidhara, Varuṇa, Māyā, and Kheṭaka;
then Paścima, Padmanābha, Māvṛta, and Śubhamālinī; followed by Samandara, Darānta, Madhudveṣin, and Sumantrajit.
The Aindava, the Katṛtīya, and the one known as Māṭhara are esteemed; likewise the Sundara, the Vaidhara, the Pañcabinduka, and the Bhadraka.
O Four-faced One, among the touches, there is also the sixteenth, the Padmanābha.
One should twice extract the syllables *gopanaṃ*, *aindavam*, then *caturgatim*, followed by *bhāntaṃ*, *madhudviṣaṃ*, *yāntaṃ*, and *daraṃ*;
then *kadvitīyaṃ*, *sūdanaṃ*, *vaidharaṃ*, and again *caturgatim*. (31.394–395)
The Dinakara should be recited twice, followed immediately by the Bhadrapāṇi;
likewise Vaidhara and Bhāskara, and finally Vakratuṇḍaka.
Mandara and Sarvarodha should each be recited twice; thus the "Gatis" are reckoned as twelve.
Gopati, Sumukha, and also Śubhada, the means to Brahman;
Krodha, Caturgati, and also Ādibīja, O Four-faced One; likewise Ādideva, Kumbha, Saṃprasāraṇa, and Akṣara.
Śrīvatsa, Puruṣātman established in the power of mantras,
Varuṇa, the other Śaṅkha, and the western Padmanābha; Subhadra, Madhudveṣin, Kumbha, and likewise Bhadrakara.
O Lotus-seated One, one should utter the Vaidhara, the auspicious Agni, and immediately thereafter the fourfold Gati; one should also utter the Huṃkāra and the Vaṣaṭkāra,
as well as the auspicious Vāmana, the supreme Krodha, and the Fire who is the enemy of Madhu.
Caturgati, Sūdana, Vakratuṇḍa, Samīraṇa, Mādhava, Vijaya, Bhadrahasta, and again Samata;
Vidhātṛ, Mṛgeśa, Bhāga, Yānta, and Savikrama.
Saroruha, Madhudveṣin, Paścima, Rāmaśīrṣaka;
Māhendra, Amṛta, Bandhu, Katṛtīya, and likewise Mṛga; Bhāskara, Sūdana, and then Śaṅkha, and again Khaḍgadhara.
Vairāja together with Sodaya, the third supreme Vasu,
the second Vāsudeva, the third Bandhusaṃhita,
Mādhava, Varuṇa, Pārśvamedhara, Dara, and Gopana.
The rhinoceros-horned one (Khaḍgadhara) with the four states of existence, together with the *sa* and the means of attaining Brahman;
likewise the western [syllable] with the bindu, for the seventh accomplishment of speech;
the seed-syllable of Indirā together with Dhruva, and the seed-syllable of Puṣṭi together with the sound *huṃ*.
O Four-faced One, [the mantra consists of] *sudhārasa*, *cauḥ* followed by *para*, *mādhava*,
*vauṣaṭkāra*, as well as *lakṣmī*, ending with *darānta* and the five dots (*pañcabindu*).
It ends with *yānta*, *sūdana*, ends with *mānta*, the word *śrī*, and *bhadrapāṇi*.
Vikrama, Pulaha, Dhūmaketana, Sūrinandana,
Huṅkṛti, Vaidhara, Bhānu, Vighneśa, Madhusūdana,
Kharvadeha, Sabandhu, Pīta, and likewise Bhallāyudha.
Mādhava, Varuṇa, Bhadrahasta, Sargiṇa, O Lotus-born One, Pavitra, Sūdana, and then Vairāja and Samīraṇa;
Oṃkāra-ādi, Jaya, Pīta, Sūdana, and again Vidhura.
Śrīdhara, Māṇibhadra, Dvirada, and likewise Vikrama; Vakratuṇḍadhara, Bindu, Pīyūṣa, and Rāmaśīrṣaka; Atri, Sūdana, Yānta, Mandara, and Daravaidhara.
The two [are] Vasuśiras, Śaṅkha, Kumbha, Vikramamastaka,
Pūrṇaphuṭa, Sadhruva, Vaidhara, and Caturgati;
[and] Śukla, Phuṭa, Vahnipara, Vaidhara, and Madhudviṣ.
One should utter twice these seed-syllables: Subhadra, Madhuvidveṣa, Sarasīruhasambhava, Kapilākṣa, Hutavaha, and Nṛsiṃha; [the syllables] being white, yellow, and the final one. 31.415–31.416.
Śīrṣa, Gopana, Caṇḍa, and the western Jayatattara;
Bhallāyudha, Māruta, Sargin, O Four-faced One;
Kṛpākara, Śarīra, and likewise Vasutatśiras.
Subhadra, the Lord of the Upper World, Vijaya, Samprasāraṇa;
Subhadra, the Self of Puruṣa, Kalānta, Phaṭkṛti; likewise Nigamādi, Śaśadhara, Mādhava, and Vasumādhava.
Bhallāyudha, Sarga, Phaṭkṛti, Dakṣa, Akṣara,
Gopati, Gopana, Kumbha, Vikrama, Krodharūpin,
Pracaṇḍa, Amṛta, Mādhava, and Ghaṭavikrama.
Ugrātman, as well as Kumbha, Kamala, Dvividhuntuda,
Datta, Bhadra, Sūdana, Dakṣāntaka, and Humphaḍantaka—
ending with Svāhā— such is the great mantra of Viṣvaksena.
Then, one should extract its seed-syllable, the *tāra* (Om), the *kumbha*, and the *dhruva* mantra;
with these very [syllables], the expert in mantras should fashion the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*). Drupada beheld this; its meter is called *aticchandas*.
Furthermore, one should recite the mantra of Viṣvaksena, the deity, three hundred thousand times.
O Brahmin, for one who recites this great mantra with the desire for success,
all fear from all gods and asuras shall perish.
Now I shall explain the ritual for his propitiation:
having fashioned a great lotus endowed with twelve petals,
one should properly worship the Commander of the Army seated upon its pericarp.
O Viṣvaksena, salutations be unto you; salutations to the one who brings fear to death!
Salutations to the lord of the attendants, salutations to the leader of the worlds!
You are the origin of all things moving and unmoving; for you, neither birth nor destruction exists.
Having placed the burden of the worlds upon you alone, O Supreme Person,
he who is the master of bliss lies in his enchanting sleep upon Śeṣa.
[This is so] for those who are single-mindedly devoted, whose karma has been exhausted by the excellence of their austerity and devotion.
Those who perceive you as the gateway for attaining the Blessed One call you Brahmā for the sake of abundance at the beginning of the kalpa; they call you the enemy of Madhu for its protection,
and the Lord of cattle (Paśupati) for the destruction of the world, including all that is stationary.
With your foot you tread upon the earth, with your waist the entire mid-region, and with your head you have ascended to the celestial vault; standing alone, you are the one who pervades the universe.
You are the earth, you are the abode of the waters, you are fire, and you are the wind.
You are space; pervading all, your sovereign power abides within you.
Becoming the sun yourself, you heat the entire world and its inhabitants;
then, becoming the moon, O treasure-house of compassion, you refresh it once again.
Within your form as *sattva*, there are the other two qualities, *rajas* and *tamas*,
just as they exist within the forms of Viṣṇu and the other [deities], like the white color inherent in a white object.
Having first created you, O Blessed One, and then having divided [the world] by means of those causes...

Remembering you, the best of beings later becomes a man who possesses you as his very self. While you, bearing the universe with your own majesty, rest upon Śeṣa, the Grandfather, the Lord of the entire world, sleeps in peace.
With *ṛg* verses they praise you at dawn, with *yajus* formulas at midday,
and with holy *sāman* chants at evening— the twice-born praise you, the very soul of the sun. They know you alone to be the cause of the world's activity and its primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Even the Puruṣa, who is indifferent, the witness of that [universe], and stainless—there is nothing more beautiful than him. Furthermore, this entire world is your domain;
you have no name, yet those who know the Friend call fire by your name.
There is no number to your qualities, nor even to the splendors of the sun;

yet, because they are said to be sixfold, they are designated as the objects of cognition and so forth. You are able [to know], you perceive the universe, you sustain it, and you do not undergo transformation.
You rule and you strike down those who hate; indeed, you alone govern the three worlds.
O Lord, just as you are a seeker of the welfare of your devoted followers who have cast off all sin, so too are you their kinsmen, their very self, and their abundant daily sustenance.
Like the ocean for waters, like the sun for rays of light,
O Lord, you are the source of all branches of knowledge rooted in the Vedas.
Yet, even while you speak, many scriptures do not remain [retained in memory].
And for those whose essence is devotion to you, contemplating auspicious things in this world so full of suffering, they say that you are the goal of yogins,
the support of auspicious waters, and the refuge for travelers and exiles.
Blessed are those in your regions who, seeing no other refuge, you would not otherwise extinguish with the nectar-essence of your sidelong glances;
for living beings composed of earth are being consumed by the forest fires of suffering. (31.447)

I go for refuge to you, who have a broad chest, who are dark-complexioned, whose eyes resemble lotuses, and who possess four arms with the form of a *sāla* tree— just as ruddy geese seek the sun, or as *cātaka* birds seek a rain-cloud.
Like cakora birds longing for the cool-rayed moon, I take refuge in you.
Whoever recites this hymn, established with their ears [attentive],
the Blessed One Senānī will be pleased with them without delay.
And he should bestow all riches, even those difficult to obtain, upon that devotee.

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Extraction of the Mantras of Vighnarāja, Utpatti, Kirīṭa, and Others," in the *Caryāpāda* of the *Pādma-tantra*, within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Thirty-Two:
The Great Majestic Power of the Sudarśana Mantra, Beneficial in This World and the Next,
Spoken by Brahmā.
"O Blessed One, today I wish to hear the entire supreme *saudarśana* mantra, which pertains to both this world and the next, as well as its purifying secret;
it should be granted to me, your devotee who bows before you, exactly as it is."
The Blessed One said: "Indeed, I shall tell you the mantra that accomplishes all aims.
Its name is true to its meaning; therefore, it must not be told to just anyone."
One should first extract the *udgītha*, the primordial moon, the jewel of the sky;
then *ātṛ*, the white-rayed one, *vahni*, the protector, the blazing face, the sibilant (*ūṣman*), the rising hero, the lotus-eyed one, and Viṣṇu as the head. (32.3–32.4)

"Delight of the Heart"—thus, O Four-faced One, is the extraction of the mantra. Having extracted the seed-syllable consisting of the fire [letter], the first vowel, and the nasal *anusvāra*, one should fashion it. Now, the extraction of the six limbs according to the sequence of the syllables is being told.
O Four-faced One, the three limbs were previously revealed by me.
One should employ the word "cakra" in the dative case, followed by "udgītha" and so forth;
immediately after that, the word "sūrya," and then that same word [divided] according to its grammatical case.
The fifth and also the sixth limb consists of the sequence of those respective case-endings;
and [the syllables] beginning with "sahasra" and preceded by "jvālā" and "dhārā" are to be extracted.
Thus, O Brahmin, the six profound limbs have been described to you.

Ahirbudhnya is the seer of the *mantra*; the *virāj* is the meter; and Sudarśana is the deity. Furthermore, O Lotus-born One, the sages for each syllable here are Vyāsa, Kaṇva, Nārada, Vasiṣṭha, and the supreme Bhṛgu. || 32.9–10 ||
In the Atri lineage, there are these six seers; hear now the meters according to their syllables:
Uṣṇih, Bṛhatī, Gāyatrī, Paṅkti, Jagatī, and Virāj.
Their colors are like the hue of the fire of time (Kālāgni), and Time itself is indeed their presiding deity.
Having placed the six syllables on the palms of both hands,

one should place the remaining syllables, beginning with the first and ending with the last, on the joints starting from the thumbs and then on the fingers in due order; thus is the placement of syllables (akṣaranyāsa) described.
The six syllables of the mantra should be placed in sequence upon the body, the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, the knees, and the feet.
[One should employ] the Śrīsudarśana-gāyatrī, the Aparā, and the Aparājitā.
I shall explain its extraction; it is now being stated word by word:
first the word *sudarśana* ending in the dative case, beginning with *udgītha*;
then one should utter another word of manifold meaning, *vetti*, ending in the periphrastic future (*luṭ*). (32.15–16)
The great primordial *cakrapada* arises from its division and is born of manifestation;
meditating upon that foot while uttering it as before, adorned with those [syllables],
that foot is our instruction, and our foot is two-headed.
One should extract the mantra from Manu [the *Mānava-dharma-śāstra*] by taking the word beginning with *pra* and ending with *coda*.
O Four-faced One, its seed-syllable should be understood as previously stated;
having established the mantra in the ten directions with the *taccakra-mudrā*, one should quickly fulfill all hopes.
One should meditate upon oneself situated in the center of that, surrounded by flames of fire,
upon a pure spot on the ground, within a thousand-petaled lotus;
in its pericarp is the wielder of the discus, two-armed and with round eyes.
With a face made terrible by fangs and eyes curved with a frown,
possessing a large belly and a massive body, resembling the color of a hibiscus flower,
adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped headdress, and decorated with red garments.
He bore upon his crest-jewel a discus with the luster of a cloud, complete with hub and rim,
difficult to endure due to its circle of flames;
it was joined with six blazing spokes and possessed a radiance equal to ten thousand suns.
One should meditate on a lotus situated thus in that very extensive navel.
Therein is the deity who presides over the wheel, a two-armed male standing upright,
wearing red garments, red in color, and smeared with red sandalwood paste.
Adorned with a crown and a jeweled casket, and embellished with all ornaments,
his face was formidable with fangs and his countenance was furrowed by a scowling brow;
he vomited forth fire from his claws, which were driven by the wind.
Emitting from his thousand forms of will many unbearable sparks of fire, he possessed a voice like the roar of the clouds at the dissolution of the world,
and in his right hand he bore a threatening gesture with his left forefinger.
As if striking a terrifying enemy whose fingers are being crushed,
as if burning with his two eyes, and as if drinking up the great ocean—
having meditated thus, one should worship him with offerings such as the *arghya* without weariness.
For the accomplishment of the king of mantras, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) is as previously described:
in the appropriate place and time, the form and number of the mantra are as before;
one should subsist on vegetables, tubers, fruits, milk, barley-meal, or balls of rice.
One should perform libations with water and offer oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks and other materials;
for one who acts in this manner according to the rule, the mantra becomes perfected.
Furthermore, success indicates itself to him through auspicious visions in dreams.
Then one should employ the mantra in rites such as those for pacification (śāntika).
One should construct a sacrificial pavilion provided with sixteen pillars,
and there one should duly place twenty-five water-pots (kumbha).
O Lotus-born One, one should wrap auspicious objects in threads, cloth, and so forth, and having gathered these materials, place them upon heaps of grain.
Immediately thereafter, [one should place] ghee, warm water, a jewel, and fruit-water.
One should pour into these nine jars, in sequence, iron-water, cleansing water, scented water, and water with unbroken grains; likewise,
water with barley, water for the feet, molasses-water, curd, and sugarcane juice.
Then unboiled coconut water and milk, followed by water containing all medicinal herbs, as well as the ācamana water, auspicious water,
honey-foremost water, pacifying water, and subsequently the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
O Four-faced One, one should pour root-water, decoction-water,
and flower-water into these jars situated outside;
and for each, one should consecrate it a hundred times with the mantra alone.
Having placed the ritual substances in the pitcher, one should then fashion a lotus-wheel;
in its center, one should worship that Sudarśana with the King of Mantras.
And in a circular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, food, and so forth, in due order.

Having offered oblations at night, and having worshipped the King of Weapons (Hetirāja) with arghya and other offerings in due order at dawn, and having offered fuel-sticks and other materials into the fire,
one should draw the wheel— complete with its hub and rim— upon a birch leaf.

Having written a six-spoked [wheel] there, with the six syllables in the order starting from the east, and having written the beginning of the meters and the name of the practitioner (sādhya) in its center,
one should write it with a golden needle using substances mixed with sandalwood and so forth.
Then, with fragrant substances such as the two types of sandalwood, saffron, gorocana, and agallochum, well-ground together, one should fashion that birch-bark leaf into a pill;
and that pill [should be placed] upon heaps of śāli rice.
Having accepted [the request] and bathed her daily with jars according to the ritual procedure,
the knower of mantras should bind that [amulet] upon the mother’s body with this mantra.
By the mere binding of the pill, a person is liberated from diseases and other afflictions.
He quickly becomes radiant, like a snake freed from its skin.
For one who is burning, there shall be peace through flowers produced from the *nimba* tree,
and by sprinkling sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and mango leaves with honey, milk, and ghee.
One should, without weariness, offer oblations into the fire for seven nights,
ten thousand times each day, in the presence of the sick person;
likewise, one should consecrate the patient with water-jars using the Cakra-vidyā.
Having formed the pill, the practitioner should release the fevered person from the fever.
Thereafter, he should satisfy the practitioner with gifts such as cattle, land, gold, and clothing;
and he should give cows, blankets, and so forth to the Brahmins according to his ability.
For the pacification of men afflicted by spirits, grahas, piśācas,
and the like, one should offer oblations into the fire with three thousand fuel-sticks made of *kiṃśuka* wood for three days; thereafter, their topknots should be bound.
Having fumigated those afflicted by the *grahas* with incense made from *guggulu*,
one should strike them with a staff or even a creeper over which a mantra has been recited. Then the *piśāca* or other spirit, being tormented, will say, "I release [him]."
Having caused him to take an oath, one should loosen the binding of his topknot.
Then, with the consecrated jars, one should bathe the person afflicted by the planets using the mantra;
furthermore, one should bind a consecrated medicinal pellet (gulikā) upon him.
Then one is liberated from disease and from the afflictions of mind and speech.
By the power of the mantra, one becomes radiant and attains a lifespan of a hundred years.
And a woman who is unfortunate shall become fortunate by wearing the wheel.
A barren woman shall immediately become pregnant; one who has given birth to a stillborn child shall give birth to a healthy offspring;
she who is past her fertile season shall become fertile, and she whose face is averted shall become fair of countenance.
Within a short time, she who is separated from her husband shall be reunited with him.
Whether she has given birth to daughters or sons, and whether her breasts are dry or adorned with milk,
by means of the rites prescribed for the affliction of children by Kumāra and the birds, she is released from suffering and attains supreme peace.
Even in the palace of the lord of men, when the planets with mouths like those of Brahma-rākṣasas had entered,
he unweariedly placed jars filled with jewels in their midst as before, using sacrificial fuel and other offerings.
O Lotus-seated One, the practitioner of mantra, being composed, should offer oblations with the mantra for twelve days, ten thousand times for each [day]. Furthermore,
having drawn a wheel upon a copper plate or a stone slab...
Having placed [the substances] upon heaps of grain, one who has risen in the morning should bury them,
consecrated with mantras, at the door of the palace and in the eight directions.
One should then sprinkle the entire house, without exception, with water from the pitcher.
All the planets flee far away from every direction;
they certainly do not remain in that kingdom at any time. All those dwelling in the palace live free from affliction.
There shall be an abundance of wealth and grain, as if in the house of Kubera;
yet there will be damage from clothes, beds, seats, and so forth, caused by gadflies, mice, and the like,
as well as by the sight of blood and bones, and likewise by the burning of hair.
When there is a sudden fire of gate-towers and the like, or when struck by lightning; when Indra’s bow (a rainbow) appears at night; when a sacred tree (*caityabhūruha*) breaks in a windless place;
when an anthill arises; or upon having a bad dream or other such [omens]. || 32.69–70 ||

Upon such ill omens as these, one should perform a rite of pacification (śānti) by means of this [mantra]. O Lotus-Seated One, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with fuel-sticks from sacrificial trees according to the previously mentioned number, and effect pacification through rites for prosperity (puṣṭi) and so forth.
These are described in many ways; they do not differ in essence despite their differences.
One should have all rites for worldly prosperity performed in square pits, nourishing rites in lotus-shaped pits, and peace-bringing rites in circular pits.

The rite of killing (māraṇa) is performed in a triangular fire-pit (kuṇḍa), while the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) is performed in one shaped like a bow; for the accomplishment of the Yakṣakanyā, it is in a five-cornered pit. The rite of paralyzing (stambhana) is in a six-sided pit, and the rite of enchanting (mohana) occurs in a seven-sided one.
In a nine-cornered [pit], there is the rite of inciting enmity; in an eight-cornered one, the procedure for killing.
In an eleven-cornered one, one should perform the subjugation of Brahmā and others;
in a ten-cornered pit, the procedure for pleasing the deities such as Paśupati.

One should perform the rite for seeing the Puruṣa Vaikuṇṭha on a twelve-sided [altar]; for the sake of marriage or for a maiden, O Lotus-seated One, it should be in the shape of a womb (yoni). The measurement of its width and length should be twenty-four finger-breadths.
The excavation in the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) should be exactly that much; now hear the rule for the surrounding area:
having left two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) on all sides, there should be three altars (*vedikās*) outside, each measuring half of that, or a quarter, or even just four finger-breadths.
And their width should be made four finger-breadths;
O Brahmin, the height of the *kuṇḍa* should likewise be that much. Furthermore, for the bow-shaped [altar], it is ninety-six finger-breadths, and the string is thirty-six finger-breadths.

Having fixed a peg in the center of that [space], one should rotate a thread ten finger-breadths long all around it; thus the pit (kuṇḍa) takes the form of a circle. One should divide the side of a square pit into five parts.
Two parts, one arm (bhuja), and thirty or five finger-breadths (aṅgula)—
this is recorded as the bhuja for a triangular mark (trikoṇāṅka).
In a hexagonal fire-pit (ṣaḍaśra kuṇḍa), the arms are eight, eight, and eleven finger-breadths.
One arm in the pentagonal [fire-pit] measures twenty finger-breadths;
furthermore, in the heptagonal [pit], the length of the arm is six barley-corns more than that, and three fingers more in the octagonal pit. (32.84–85)

Twelve or ten finger-breadths on the ground are declared to be ten *aṅgulas*; the length of the arm is said to be one part of the *nala* and the shoulder. In the case of nine-cornered sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*), the length of the arm is five *yavas* in a five-cornered pit.
O Four-faced One, ten finger-breadths are prescribed for the ten-cornered [pit],
while the length of the arm is five barley-corns and nine finger-breadths;
however, in the eleven-cornered pit, it is accompanied by eight barley-corns.
In a twelve-sided (dodecagonal) pit, the length of the arms is said to be eight finger-breadths;
in the case of yoni-shaped pits, O Lotus-born One, the lengths are eighteen finger-breadths,
and they should be forty-eight finger-breadths.
The womb [of the fire-pit] is like the lip of an elephant or like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.
Now, having described the types of pits, the rites for pacification and so forth are prescribed:
whichever pit has been specified for a particular rite such as pacification, that one should be used for it.
Having inscribed the wheel-mechanism according to the rules upon copper, wood, or other materials in the stables for horses and elephants, one should consecrate it during the night; thereafter,
a fire-oblation (homa) must be performed one thousand times in an auspicious sacrificial pit.

One should establish the consecrated pitcher with sacrificial fuel-sticks suitable for the sacrifice. Then, at dawn, one should dig a pit for the machine in the ground within the hall and sprinkle the elephants and horses individually with water from the pitcher.
Likewise, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) with the *Saudarśana* mantra;
O Four-faced One, their diseases will perish, and the strength of those elephants and horses will become superior— thus one should perform this for seven days.
One should give wealth to the Brahmins and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
O Brahmin, then powerful elephants and horses will be born in great numbers;
likewise, there should be a daily fire-oblation (homa) performed with the Sudarśana-vidyā.
In this manner, the knower of mantras should perform the protection of cows, buffaloes, and other animals.
Now, O Brahmin, I shall explain the protection of the city exactly as it is:
[it should be] provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass.
Having established a water-shed in the center of the city,
one should again offer oblations of clarified butter with fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood for nineteen days—
likewise in the eight directions and in the center of the city, O Lotus-Seated One.
One should dig [a pit] and quickly place the *saudarśana* machine and the water-pot;
the wise man should sprinkle the city with water using the *cakravidyā* and the praised *pāvamānī* verses in their proper order.
In city gates, palaces, and pavilions of kings,
one should everywhere bury the discus and perform oblations with sacrificial fuel (samidh) and other materials.
Furthermore, death, disease, famine, fever, and other ailments [shall cease].
The inhabitants of the city shall perish [from other afflictions] and become powerful,
O Four-faced One, throughout the center of the village as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should bury the Lord of Weapons at all the crossroads.

Planets, vetālas, and rākṣasas, as well as chronic diseases, fevers, and the like, do not afflict the city or the village; likewise, epilepsy and other such ailments do not trouble it. There is no fear of thieves whatsoever, nor is there untimely death.
Men shall possess the full span of life and be endowed with grain and wealth;
there shall be good fortune, peace, health, as well as the increase of their lineages and the splendor of Vedic knowledge for the Brahmins. (32.107)
The cows will become full of milk, with swelling udders;
likewise, there will be only prosperity for the people in that kingdom.
Now, O Brahmin, I shall describe to you the means for warding off the serpents.
In a temple, on a riverbank, or in Nandana groves,
one should construct a sacrificial pavilion (homamaṇḍapa) provided with four pillars, adorned with four archways (toraṇas),
and beautified on all sides with garlands of darbha grass.
Having prepared nine new jars and placed nine others [therein],
one should again construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) on the eastern altar according to the previously mentioned characteristics.
One should then worship the nine forms (mūrtis) in these jars in their proper sequence.
Having offered milk-rice (*pāyasa*) to them, he should thereafter take up a serpent measuring one *tāla* in length with a copper vessel into the fire within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Then,
O Grandfather, having fashioned it [into form] with the *Śeṣa-mantra*, he should install it.
Upon it, one should draw a wheel; in its center, again, the figure of a fish.
Then Garuḍa, Śaṅkhapāla, and the Kṛṣṇa-mantra as an encircling border.
That nāga-yantra [should be bathed] with milk, ghee, and honey.
One should bathe [the deity] with curd and even with the juice of cow dung while reciting the Cakra-vidyā,
as well as with other services such as flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth.
Having worshipped the Nāga with its own mantra and the Cakra with the Cakra-vidyā, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, the wise man should dig a serpent-mechanism (nāgayantra) in the middle of the pit.
Having placed the fire upon that [mechanism] which is turned face upwards,
he should [offer oblations] with curd, ghee, milk, and honey.
One skilled in mantras should offer oblations with the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of the *brahmavṛkṣa* tree, repeating each [mantra] one thousand times; then,
for seven days, one should offer portions of wild rice (*nīvāra*), even by the tens of thousands, sprinkled with cow’s milk.
The supreme practitioner should offer oblations with the mantra beginning "apānas tu.
When three days have passed, Parjanya, whose vehicle is the clouds,
shall cause the entire earth to flow once more with the rising of waters.
O Four-faced One, I shall explain the pacification of excessive rain: the knower of mantras, adorned by the mantra, should meditate upon himself as having the form of Piṅgala, permeated by nectar,
and bearing a trident and a vajra.
One should offer oblations of parched grain, mustard seeds, and salt, sprinkled with oil and clarified butter.

One should offer ten thousand oblations into the blazing fire while reciting the two words "stambhaya" (stop) preceded by the word "vṛṣṭiśabdam" (the sound of rain), [performed] seven times over the ocean.
O Brahmin, this should be employed at the end of the mantra by one who knows the mantras;
then that great rain is pacified by means of the Great Wheel-vidyā.
Now, listen likewise to the pacification of disturbances in kingdoms, cities, and so forth.
Then, having installed a wooden wheel according to the prescribed ritual, one should dig within the city and the kingdom and likewise offer oblations with that wood; thus,
the multitude of horses and elephants will suddenly fall into agitation.
O Brahmin, the kingdom will become agitated and unstable if he should again withdraw the Wheel and set his mind upon peace;
therefore, one should bathe the Blessed One with the waters of a thousand jars.
Evil shall be instantly pacified for both the city and the kingdom.
O Four-faced One, I shall now describe to you the attainment of a kingdom and other such blessings:
it consists of a six-petalled lotus within a circle, complete with a pericarp and filaments.
O Kamalāsana, one should fashion a lotus-wheel on pure ground;
outside of that, one should draw a navel-ring and a six-spoked wheel,
and outside of that, a rim-ring endowed with garlands of flames.
Outside of that, one should fashion a pedestal adorned with four gates;
having constructed such a mandala, complete with primary and secondary ornaments,
O Brahmin, one should worship Sudarśana therein according to the prescribed rite.

Having offered oblations with fuel-sticks, food, and clarified butter, one should recite this purifying verse at the conclusion of the chanting while making this prayer: "May the mantra be propitious! [Grant] a horn, a wheel, a kingdom for the body, and likewise wealth for the kingdom of the body. (32.134) Thus he should recite it.

Then he bestows upon him a city, a kingdom, and a district as his wheel. (32.135) Now, O Brahmin, I shall explain to you the means by which the wheel-lore may restore the prosperity of men who have been deprived of their kingdoms, according to their former glory. (32.136)
For the lotus situated within, there may be four petals;
then, O Brahmin, eight, twelve, sixteen, and then four;
twenty, and likewise thirty—these are the outer petals in sequence.
Thus, upon the pericarp of the six-petalled [lotus] is Sudarśana.
Then, upon those six types of petals, in due order,
are first the four Mūrtis, and likewise ten [Mūrtis] increased by eighteen [i.e., twenty-two].
Then, O Grandfather, sixteen thousand and twenty,
and then thirty-two— these are the ornaments in the six intermediate spaces respectively, beginning with the Śrīvatsa.
One who knows the ritual application of mantras should worship the eight Śaktis together with Śrī, the Cakrādi [deities], the homamaṇḍala,
the seven plus five Ravis, and subsequently Kumuda and the others,
as well as Indra and the other guardians of the directions.
With fuel-sticks in the form of *bilva* wood, with sesame seeds, lotuses, and likewise with clarified butter,
one should offer oblations a thousand times for each, using the *cakravidyā*.
When seven nights have thus passed, the knower of mantras, having risen in the morning—
O Brahmin, with twenty-five jars placed there, filled with ghee and other substances, consecrated by the *cakravidyā*, and provided with seats made of rice—
[one may restore] one fallen from his kingdom, deprived of counsel, and oppressed by bandits.
One who knows the ritual procedure, while recollecting the Discus (Cakra), should consecrate a king, a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, or anyone else afflicted by misfortune, using its mantra.
Likewise, he should fashion a yantra and cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the preceptor.
O Four-faced One, when this is performed, there shall be good fortune and the attainment of a kingdom;
through the splendor of the Sudarśana [mantra], there will be the destruction of bandits and prosperity.
Furthermore, O Brahmin, at the beginning and at the end, it should be accompanied by the Haṃsa-mantra.
One may destroy all poison, whether stationary or mobile, by means of the *cakra* mantra.
Now, O Lotus-seated One, I shall describe the victory in battle regarding the sword,
the javelin, the spear, the arrows, and likewise the armlet.
Likewise, having inscribed the wheel-mandala upon other weapons, on the foreheads of horses and elephants, and on the ends of banner-cloths,
one may enter the terrible battle that causes the hair of enemies to stand on end.
By the neighing of the horses, the trumpeting of the horned beasts,
the shouts of joy of the warriors, and likewise by the sounds of chariot rims;
and by the clouds of dust raised from the earth trampled by the hooves of the steeds— 32.152.
The sky was obscured, resembling the abode of Death;
it was agitated by the flow of blood, with pairs of *vaitāla* demons rising up,
and crowded with thousands of hawks swooping down to seize flesh.

Meditating upon a wheel composed of garlands of flames, and having conquered even his enemies with the weapons of Akṣa and Nāga, he may advance to the front of the army. Alternatively, at the boundaries of his kingdom, he should plant stakes made of khadira wood.
One should place them, sprinkled with the remains of the oblation and clarified butter, using the Cakra-mantra.
They take on the form of blazing fire and cannot be looked upon by others.
O Brahmin, at the time of entry, there is trembling due to the power of the Cakra-vidyā.
Wherever there is fear for men,
there let that fear arise [only] when they meditate on themselves as standing in the center of the discus and with an angry mind—
whether on a mountain ascent, in a forest, or during a sea voyage and the like.
Traveling on a desolate path beset by tigers, lions, boars, and the like, one who recites this mantra of the Cakra incurs no fear;
weapons do not cut him, nor does fire burn him.
And the waters do not moisten him in whose heart this mantra resides,
O Lotus-Seated One— whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra,
or one born of the inverse or natural order; such a wise man shall effect his own integration.
With fuel-sticks from the trees of sacred knowledge— the *aśvattha* and the *vaṭa*,

as well as those born of the *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, and *jāti*— one should perform the fire-oblation for the sake of liberation in the sacrificial fire; one should do so according to the respective order, as well as for women of those same classes.
A Brahmin attains prosperity by means of oblations of white lotuses;
[he attains it] for a king with red lotuses, and for a Vaiśya with white *pāṭala* flowers.
By performing an offering with *śrīphala* fruits, one becomes the sovereign of a kingdom.

Whatever woman a man touches with a limb upon which the mantra has been placed, she comes under his control and follows him even in death. I shall now describe the conquest of untimely death; listen attentively as it truly is.
Having properly taken the fire into the sacrificial pit located in the *homa* hall,
and having invoked Hetīśa therein, one should offer oblations with pieces of wood soaked in ghee,
using ten million mantras or otherwise according to one's capacity.
Thus, with his senses restrained, he should protect the fire for two months.
At the conclusion of the *homa*, if the king should perform the weighing on the scales (*tulārohaṇa*),
or else whatever other property he possesses, he should give it away to the Brahmins.
One should bathe [the deity] with twenty-five jars using the Cakra-vidyā.
When this is done, O Four-faced One, a person shall conquer timely death.
How could there be untimely death for him? There is no doubt regarding his victory over it.

Alternatively, O Grandfather, let the means for conquering Death at his appointed time be understood. Having fashioned [an image] out of a thousand *niṣkas* of gold, in the form of a two-armed man with eyes furrowed by a frown; || 32.171–32.172 ||
[He visualizes the deity] with a face formidable with fangs, eyes like those of a boar,
holding a staff in his right hand and a noose in his left;
having thus purified [the vessel] with the five products of the cow and likewise with the five Upaniṣads.
Then, having sprinkled [the grain] with fresh water, one should deposit it upon heaps of grain.
Having invoked [the deity], recited the *vyāhṛtis*, and worshipped [him] with their respective names,
one should perform an oblation in the fire with sacrificial wood, boiled rice, and clarified butter.

Then, at dawn, he gave that golden man to a pure brāhmaṇa who was devoted to the Lord and observed the five daily rites, using verses containing the signs of the end of time as well as the Brahma-vyāhṛtis.
Or, having conquered Time and Death, he shall attain the state of long life. Now, O Four-faced One, listen to this procedure for killing:
one who knows the ritual rules should construct a sacrificial hall in a secluded place.
In the midst of that, the preceptor should fashion a sacrificial pit facing south, O Brahmā,
having taken a board for the axle two cubits in length,
half that in width, and four finger-breadths in thickness.
Having drawn the form of the hated person upon it, as if it were before one's eyes,
one should perform the rite of death— especially during the dark fortnight and under unfavorable constellations or when the enemy is in the eighth house.
Then, on the eastern side of the pit, one should draw a six-spoked wheel;
having adorned it with black threads, the wheel is established therein.
One should worship it with black perfumes, black flowers, and black waters.
O Lotus-Seated One, one should fetch earth from a cremation ground, a deserted dwelling, or an anthill; having mixed that with the dust from the feet of an enemy,
one should grind it with donkey urine mixed with the juice of the *unmatta* plant.
On the Viṣṭi or Mṛdu lunar day,
the knower of mantras, having established the vital breaths of his enemy within that [image] by means of this mantra,
[should perform the rite for] the immeasurable Udgītha, as well as Mandara and Bhuvana.
Krodhānila facing west, Hutāśa Madhusūdana;
Pracaṇḍa and Gopana, Rāma, and Bhāskara facing west; with the word "amuṣya" (of him) following the pair of Gopanas in the middle.
The living beings situated here [perceive] the sound, as well as Viṣṇu, Dakṣa, and Udaya;
Krodharūpa performing austerities, Sarvaśabda, Anantara,
Vikrama, Vighnarāja, Atri, Vahni, Bandhu, and Gopana.

One should extract the mantra beginning with "Oṃ," ending with "svāhā," and containing the words "vanamālādharaṃ rāmaṃ" as well as "vāṅmanaḥkāyai," followed by the imperative form "atha māyātṛtīyāntam" and "yāni yanmukham. (32.189–190)

And one should bury that Prāṇavatī in the pit lying on her back, O Grandfather, having plastered over her form as it rests upon a wooden plank with the previously mentioned clay; thereafter, one should restore life to the living being by means of the science of vital breaths (prāṇavidyā).
With his heart stepped upon by the foot and his remaining eyes bloodshot,
the knower of mantras should recite the mantra of the discus a thousand times;
[he should then pierce] the eyes and the heart with a stake grown from a poisonous tree.
The wise practitioner should perform piercing on the hands, feet, private parts, ears, nose, and belly, as well as on other limbs;
when this is done, each respective limb of the enemy will become impaired.
Then, O Grandfather, one should place the cremation fire in the sacrificial pit;
one should spread *darbha* grass upon the altar facing south-west,
having likewise scattered the enclosing sticks and performed protection for oneself.
When the sixteen officiating priests had performed the recitation at the gates,
he gave wealth to the Brahmins and, recollecting Hetirāja,
[offered] according to the rule with a *sruk* and *sruva* ladle fashioned from wood and seeds.
One should offer a thousand fuel-sticks of Akṣa wood daily, prepared with black snakes, black mustard seeds, and long pepper, moistened with blood, and combined with the eight kinds of grain.
The knower of mantras should also offer fuel-sticks from the trees associated with the enemy's birth-star;
at the end of the mantra, he should proclaim the enemy's name, saying "Kill!
Having performed the oblation daily with contempt, it should be offered into the fire.
As long as there is no vision of the Kṛtyā in the fire,
one should offer oblations for twenty-one days in succession;
furthermore, one should fumigate her with the smoke of the burnt offering while she stands upon the altar.
One should burn agarwood and guggulu in the fire for the purpose of incense.
Then, O Grandfather, when seven days have passed,
during those seven days, these fevers occur in their respective order.
There will certainly be harsh abuse, intense pain, and a lack of control over the limbs;
furthermore, there will be hiccupping, the cessation of breath, and the loss of the tongue for the enemy, by the power of the Cakra-mantra. || 32.204-32.205 ||
Thus, when two weeks had passed, on the very next day at midnight, once the fire-oblation (homa) had been performed, the Kṛtyā emerged from that fire with seven hands,
terrifying with tridents, and three feet.
Licking her own mouth with a tongue that dripped blood,
she vomited forth from her two eyes a fire-devouring flame drenched in clarified butter;
wearing a necklace of human bones, she had a girdle fashioned into anklets.
Accompanied by Kapālakuṇḍalā, she laughs a terrifying laugh;
she bears a staff, a bell, a winnowing basket, a broom, a noose, and a circle [of ashes],
with her hair disheveled and hanging down from her two hands.
Mounted upon the shoulder of another, his form resembling darkness,
appearing terrifying with his pride cast off as if standing amidst a circle of sparks,
he rose up, joined his palms in reverence, and said, "What shall I do? (32.210–211)
"Then the Teacher will say, 'Take the life of the enemy.
Having been thus commanded, she will say, 'So be it,' and having slain that enemy of the Great-souled One even though he is standing at a distance, she will return once more to her Guru."
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* together with the officiating priests (*hotṛs*), the knower of mantras should,
on the twenty-second day, recite this six-syllabled mantra one hundred thousand times;
likewise, he should recite the Aparājita mantra and the Nārasiṃha mantra.
Furthermore, one should perform a self-consecration with twenty-five jars filled with ghee and other substances, consecrated by the mantra of the wheel;
thereby one is released from that sin, and likewise peace shall prevail.
O Lotus-Seated One, I shall now duly describe the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*). With the juices of neem and dhattūra leaves mixed with charcoal from a cremation ground,
one should fashion a two-cubit long effigy of a corpse using *akṣa* wood.
One should gradually write within the mandala marked by a six-cornered hub and rim;
having uttered the name of the enemy in the interior,
then [place] the letter *ya* in the south and the letter *jha* in the west, O Brahmin, as well as the world-element (*bhuvana*).

Likewise, in the three remaining corners, there are eight mandalas and so forth. Furthermore, one should [offer] into a bow-shaped fire-pit (kuṇḍa) the enemy mounted upon them, using sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) from the nimba tree as well as from poisonous trees.
One should offer oblations into the fire on all sides, scorching the enemy with nectar;
there one should fix that banner upon a lofty sacred tree (*caityapādapa*).
Within twenty-one days, even a great enemy of his—
Abandoning his own abode along with his wife, sons, and others,
he flees to the ends of the earth and finds no place of rest anywhere.
Now, O Brahmin, listen duly to the rite of causing aversion.
Having fashioned two smooth pieces of wood from *akṣapāda* timber into the shape of the two [individuals],
one should write upon them their respective mantras and their names as well,
joined with the words for "mutual enmity," using the blood of a crow and a jackal.
O Brahmin, [one should do so] for the rat and the cat, as well as for the snake and the peacock;
likewise for other hostile animals and even birds.
Having bound the ropes of illusion to the hair on the heads of a buffalo and a horse, [one should proceed].
Having likewise bound those two figures and joined their faces together, one should cover the mouths of the two with them and recite the six-syllable mantra. Then,
one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of the *mṛtyu* and *bandha* plants.
One should offer oblations into the fire one thousand and eight times with the *sudarśana* mantra.
A duel between two affectionate [opponents], comparable to that of a crow and an owl, shall take place.
Thus, after ten days have passed, that knower of mantras—
It removes the sense of possessiveness between a husband and wife, and even between two friends. They should bathe with milk; their affection will then become as it was before.
Now, O Brahmin, that which is called "stambhana" (the rite of immobilization) shall be explained; listen to it.
Then, O Grandfather, having drawn four sets of four squares upon a stone surface,
and having inscribed within each of them the Vāmana-mantra consisting of four parts ending with *indrakānta*, using leaves and ritual substances; || 32.231–32.232 ||
One should worship that golden-hued [deity] marked with a vajra with flowers;
having established him upon this sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should utter the mantra beginning with "āsikya.
One should also offer oblations of pieces of *arka* wood while reciting the word "stambhaya" (paralyze).

Thus, there shall be an immediate immobilization in marriage and in the attainment of conception. O Brahmin, I shall describe the *tilaka* for disputants in debates, discussions, and polemics, after having written down its effigy.
With equal parts of the limbs of one who is to be hated, mixed with cow-dung and charcoal,
one should draw the mantra— conjoined with its seed-syllable— upon that person's limbs.
Then, the embodied being whose mind harbors hatred shall be rendered devoid of power.

Now I shall describe the method of striking them: with the juice of *dhattūra*, *bhaya*, and *mārī*, O Brahmin, mixed with charcoal from a cremation ground, one should draw the image of a deceased person on a piece of cloth using wood from the *bilva* tree. (32.237–238)
Then, taking a conch-shell peg measuring four finger-breadths,
the knower of mantras should strike his limbs with that peg;
he should constantly perform the recitation of the six-syllable mantra without weariness.
He shall suffer the loss of wealth and other possessions, and at the end of his life, one who knows the mantras will hate him.
O Brahmin, I shall now describe to you the method for subjugating kings,
using kuṣṭha, saffron, white mustard, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should write the wheel upon birch bark using yellow orpiment together with safflower powder; the six-syllable mantra should be placed within the six spokes.
Outside of that, there should be a twelve-spoked wheel, complete with a hub and a rim.
Having drawn a twelve-spoked [wheel], one should then draw outside of that a twelve-syllable [mantra] accompanied by the eight-syllable mantra and the haṃsa-mantra;
outside of that, a twelve-flamed [circle] with two nooses and two goads.

O Brahmin, having marked it internally with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) preceded by the *praṇava*, and immediately thereafter interwoven (*vidarbhitam*) with these sixteen [syllables],
one should then form this into a pill (*gulikā*) and wrap it with a lotus fiber.
Having perfumed the lotus of the wheel and worshipped it with flowers and other offerings,
and having performed a fire sacrifice (*homa*) in a pit (*kuṇḍa*) shaped like a lotus using flowers and clarified butter for twelve days, one should thus accomplish auspicious rites and the like.
Kings and others gaze upon his face as if powerless;
the planetary spirits (grahas), headed by Kūśmāṇḍa, flee from him from afar.
O Four-faced One, I shall describe to you his entry into the subterranean realm (rasātala).
Having obtained wood from the *bilva* tree, the wise knower of mantras should draw a six-spoked wheel with safflower powder; outside of that,
according to the instruction, he should depict Pātāla, teeming with serpents and asuras.
Having drawn [the mandala] again, one should place a fire in that pit,
offer human flesh as oblation, and recite the mantra in its entirety.
After twelve days, those [demons] who dwell in the depths of the netherworld [will appear].
Terrified and tormented by desire, young women will attend upon him;
with bright smiles, they—speaking sweetly and longing for him—will seize him as their husband with hands whose bracelets jingle, crying, "I first! (252–253).
They will give elixirs to that traveler of the netherworld;
by consuming them, he shall possess long life and enjoy himself as he desires with those women in delightful regions, or wherever his fancy may lead him.
O Brahmin, I shall now tell you the method for accomplishing the sword.

Having touched a sword possessing the characteristics prescribed in the treatises and covered by a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, one should recite the six-syllable mantra while meditating upon the Sudarśana.
Then, if the sword should become heated, one will conquer the yakṣas and other such beings;
when it begins to smoke, one becomes the lord of the gandharvas.
When its mouth is ablaze, O Brahmin, one becomes the sovereign of the vidyādharas.
Having taken up that sword again, one shall attain the world as desired.
Then, O Grandfather, having smeared a deserted house with cow dung and having drawn a wheel adorned with white flowers and *sumanas* blossoms; || 32.258–259 ||
Upon that [altar], having placed the corpse of a Brahmin or a king— free from wounds—
with its head facing east, one who is alone and of undistracted mind should smear its feet with buffalo ghee while reciting the mantra.
Having placed his foot upon his chest, he should mutter this king of mantras.
Every day he should offer oblations into the fire with fuel-sticks of the *vetra* tree;
O Grandfather, he should recite the mantra a fixed number of times through these recitations and burnt offerings.
At midnight, the corpse will rise as a living being with hands joined in reverence;
it will speak of a divine elixir to that practitioner who has mastered the mantra,
and it will bestow, as desired, magical sandals, collyrium, or a sword.
If that meat were to be taken away after being struck by that sword,
O Four-faced One, one shall obtain knowledge of the entire realm of the three worlds;
and being free from wrinkles and grey hair, one shall achieve immortality.
He perceives even other hidden treasures as if they were before his eyes.
Having prepared mercury, he should inscribe the six-syllable mantra upon stone;
having placed the mercury in a crucible and bound it with appropriate substances.
O Brahmin, having consecrated it with the Cakra-mantra according to the ritual manual,
the wise man should employ it and also mutter the six-syllabled mantra;
[he shall obtain] health, strength, sovereignty, and the transcendence of death in due time.
"Oratorical skill, intelligence, physical form and strength, youth,
and even the power to travel through the sky as if he were Garuḍa himself—
such qualities as these will belong to him, without a doubt. (32.269)
Listen to how there may be no fatigue for the feet even after traveling a great distance:
taking *kākajaṅghā* combined with *kokilekṣaṇa*, along with *balā*, *moṭā*, and *rasa*, together with the juices of their arrow-shafts (*śarapuṅkha*). 32.270–271.
Having smeared a wheel with mustard oil mixed [with other substances] and consecrated it with the Cakra-mantra,
and having placed that wheel upon his feet on a great forest path,
one shall not experience fatigue for two thousand yojanas.
I shall proclaim the accomplishment of the Yakṣī; one should write it upon a linen cloth.
Having meditated upon that Yakṣī-mantra at the foot of a banyan tree, the wise man should recite it while honoring her with incense made from guggulu, O Lotus-Seated One.
One should offer oblations into the fire using fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree, as well as those of the *aśoka* and *karañja*,
along with red lotuses and sesame seeds.
At the end of twenty-one nights, that *vaṭa* tree trembles repeatedly.
Furthermore, the wise one of firm intellect should likewise mutter this mantra.
Then that yakṣī, possessing auspicious marks, appeared before him in visible form;
like a loving mother, she granted him the success he desired.
By this very procedure, the Yakṣas, Vaiśravaṇa and the others,
appearing in person, shall grant the boon chosen by the practitioner.
O Lotus-born One, the more extensive the fire-oblation or the recitation, [the greater the result].
For this wheel-mantra, for every five crores [of recitations] performed in successive order,
these very words cause one's sins to be shaken off,
even those belonging to the Ādityas, the Moon, the Vasus, and the Maruts.
By the power of the Cakra-mantra, [the gods] of the Aśvins, of Vāsava, of Manu and the other ascetics, of the Rudras, and even of Brahmā—
through a thousand times ten million oblations and recitations— [attained their goals].
Through most intense austerity, one indeed attains the state of Viṣṇu.
What is the use of further prattling? Whatever is desired shall come to pass; by that very means he obtains it and is liberated even from sins.

Thus, O Brahmin, has the time for the great six-syllable mantra been told in summary form; it is a secret that bestows all perfections. Thus ends [the section on] Sudarśana in the Caryāpāda of the Padma Tantra within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
The thirty-second chapter, titled "The Great Splendor of Mantras.
The thirty-third chapter:
"The Extraction of the Mantra for the Limbs of Propitiation."
"Brahmā,
O Blessed One, I wish to hear the ritual mantras by which,
when employed, great delight shall arise for you. (33.1)
O Brahman, listen attentively to the mantras that constitute the limbs of worship for the Blessed Lord,
which the exponents of Brahman hear within the portions of the Upanishads. (33.2)
Placing Bandhukosa at the front, followed by Kakubha, Brahmamastaka, Vairaja, Devara, Ekanetra, and Rigeśvara;
and also Pavitrabhuvana and Brahmacaṇḍavanālaya.
Hutāśa, Vāmana, Padmagopa, Vinatātmaja,
Vighneśa, Mandara, Kānta, Kalātmā, Jaya, Ajaya,
Pīyūṣarāma, Śrīkumbha, Sūkṣma, and Gopanapaścima.
Varuṇa ending with Bhadrahasta, Vighneśa who is fond of the *pāṭala* flower,
Aniruddha, Jaya and Īśa, Śukla, Jaya, and then Udaya;

Having made *kakubha* the last, one should utter *manu*, conquered by you;

Now I shall tell you the five mantras of the Upaniṣads:

as well as Āmnāyādi, Krodha-rūpa, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Gajānana.
Dakṣa, Aniruddha, Pāpaghna, Vahni, Gopana, and Māruta;

At the end, one should utter Vighneśa, Mādhava, and Parameṣṭhin. Its seer is named Āditya, its meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and its deity is Sadāviṣṇu; one should recite it twelve hundred thousand times.

"Pāvaka, Bhuvana, Śakra, Dāhaka,
Gopana, Jayada, Dakṣa, Bhadrapāṇi, Devadatta, and likewise the last two"—

They say the seer for this is Nārada, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
Vāsudeva is the deity; hear what follows regarding the universe.
