"Pavitra, Vahni, and the other deities; Śaṅkha, Varuṇa, and Vikrama;
Śrīvatsa, Kumbha, Vijaya, Mandara, Vighna, and Mādhava"—thus is the Viśvamantra declared. Furthermore, Bhṛgu was the seer (draṣṭā) of the Manu-mantra.
Its meter is Gāyatra, and it should be recited by the one named Saṅkarṣaṇa.
The two deities Udgītha and Kumbha, the two-headed Vighneśa,
Mandara, Varuṇa, Pāpahanana, Vahni, Gopana,
Vāyu, Vighneśvara, Rāma, Pīyūṣa, and Vasumastaka.
Ekanetra, Vāyu, Ādi, the gods, Vairāja, Mandara, Manuṣyeśa, Mṛgeśāna, Nivṛtti, and Anu are proclaimed [as the deities]. The seer is Nārada, and the meter Gāyatrī has been stated previously.
Through this [mantra], Pradyumna is the deity; by it a person attains Nivṛtti.
[One should meditate on] the Praṇava, shining with a yellow hue, Gopana, the Lord of Men (Mānuṣeśvara), Mādhavī, Sargin, Pāpahanana, Vahni, and Gopana.
One should extract the four-faced [mantra] from the four states of existence, the essence of the arts, Kumbha, Pāvaka, and Gopana.
Having extracted Vairāja and Mandara, O Four-faced One,
one should fashion the entire mantra beginning with Gajāsya and ending with Devadatta.
Furthermore, its meter is the *uṣṇih*, its seer is Nīlalohita, and its deity is Aniruddha; these five are proclaimed as the *manavas*. O Four-faced One, these are the five meritorious *upaniṣads*.
These [practices] destroy great sins and bestow fruits such as the *parāka* penance.
I consider those two who properly study either these [verses] or the entire Vedānta to be equal; or perhaps the one who has mastered the five elements is even more highly praised.

One should employ these [mantras], which destroy all sins, in due order during expiatory rites, fire offerings, consecrations, sprinklings, and so forth. Hereafter, I shall proclaim the fourfold mantra for pacification.
[He praised] Praṇava, Madhuhantṛ, Pavana, Madhusūdana,
Bhāskara, Puruṣātman, Gadi, Vighneśa, Mādhava,
Bhallāyudha, Hṛṣīkeśa, Agni, and Bhallāyudhodaya.
One should utter the mantra: "Kumbha, Mṛgāṅka, Pīyūṣa, Kamalānana, Antima, Śukla, Kumbha, Madhuśatru, Bhāskara, and Gopana. Brahman is the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra, and Manu is its deity.

Udgītha, Vijaya, Kumbha, Vighneśa, Atri, Mṛgeśvara, Pīyūṣa, Gopana, Bhadra, Hastagopana, Yaṣṭi, [33.37]

Pavitra, Bhuvana, Krodha, Paścimānana, and Gopana.

Furthermore, one should employ the *jitaṃ te* mantra when offering handfuls of flowers.

The mantra beginning with "subhadra vāyūttadeha" and ending with "natyanta" has been proclaimed;

Caturgatimacāmādi, Māhendra, Viṣṇu, and Pannaga; Mandara, Vāmana, Paścāt, Paścima, Vijaya, and Anila;
Devadatta, Śrī, Vahni, Mahāmāyā, and Mahābalā.
One should repeatedly recite this seed-mantra: Hṛṣīkeśa, Dhruva, Pavitra, Anila, Caṇḍa, Gopana, Dvināyaka, Vaidhara, Madhuhantṛ, Vijaya, and Mandara. (33.86)
One should utter the mantra ending in *ṭha-ṭha*: "Bhadrahasta mṛgeśa.
Sindhudvīpa is the seer of this mantra; Virāṭ is declared to be its meter;
and the Supreme Person is its deity, the lord of dreams.
The knower of mantras should utter the sacrificial mantra for Hṛṣīkeśa;
its meter is Uṣṇik, and its deity is Hari, the Man-Lion.
Next, they proclaim the names of the Aṅgirasas and their respective mantras.
Having touched this Aśvattha tree, whose branches and trunk are unbroken, one who has restrained the senses should recite this [mantra]; within seven days, he shall transcend death.
Now, O Lotus-born One, hear the mantras that are to be accomplished with little effort.
The pervasive Self of Puruṣa, Vāsudeva, along with Paścima;
Rāma, Vighneśvara, and Māyā, excluding Udgītha—these [nine];
Dakṣa, Īśāna, and the other gods; and the well-established lotus of Māyā.

One should extract the syllables *vāyuṃ*, *padmaṃ*, *madhoḥ śatruṃ*, *śaṅkhaṃ*, as well as *vahnidhruvān*, *hutāntaṃ*, and *gobhitaṃ*— this is the supreme mantra. Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times.
On the twelfth day as well, one should fashion a woman with uplifted breasts;
having invoked the Yoginī into her, offered oblations, and worshipped her,
one should present the *bali* offering at midnight and cut down that effigy.
The Yoginī will declare to him the past, the present, and the future:
the source of the tradition (āmnāya), the Ordainer, Pracaṇḍa, Vasumastaka,
the Western One, Vikrama, Lakṣmī, Gopana, and Khaḍgadhārin.
With valorous stride, he beheld a jar, fire, a lotus, and its elephant-faced [emanation];
then a water-born lotus, the western quarter,
another fire, nectar, and likewise the wealth of cattle.
Jhaṣa, Guhālaya, Śaṅkha, Vahni, Mandara,
Śrīdhara, Padmavairāja, Gopana, Sūkṣmalocana, Vahni, Pracaṇḍa, Vighneśa, Rāma, Mandara, and Pāvaka. (33.99–33.100)
Pītādideva, Pulaha, Yaṣṭi, Padmaguhāntika,
Ekanetra, Śrī, Vahni, Vāmana, Vahnimādhava,
Mṛgeśabhāvasadbandhu, and likewise Viṅghopahatika.
Svacchanda, Vijaya, Vahni, Vīrasena, and Saroruha; Ādideva, as well as Candra, Ravi, Dṛṣṭi, and Śubhaprada;
Vahni, Vināyaka, Rāma, twice Dakṣa, and Caturānana. (33.102–33.103)
Pracaṇḍa, Pāvaka, Yaṣṭi, and the two fires of the western face;
together with Pīyūṣa and Rāma, these grant auspiciousness, as do Vāyu and Gopana;
Vijaya, Pañcabindu, Vairāja, and Madhusūdana.
Behind Gaṇeśa and Gopana, [he saw] Gadin, Vijaya, and Ghaṭa;
likewise Ekadṛṣṭi, Vahni, Mandara, and Madhusūdana;
and Kuñjarānana and Viṣṇuvant, as well as Vighneśa and Bandhumastaka.
One should formulate this mantra: "Kakubham, candradhavalam, gopanām, paścimānanam, caturgatim, ṭhaṭhopāntam.
Reciting this without weariness beneath the Netra tree, one should practice.
By the grace of this [mantra], one knows the lost, the stolen, and even thoughts;
having first fashioned the seven-syllable [mantra]: Varuṇa, Gopana, Dara, Pīyūṣa, Mādhava, Dakṣa, Dṛṣṭi, Vahni, and two Daras. (33.108–109)
Having twice conceived these four— Sūrya and Rāma, yellow and reddish-brown— who have arisen within the fire with their faces turned toward the west;
[and] Śukla, Yaṣṭi, and Vivasvat, ending with Vahni and Svāhā.
O Lotus-seated One, one should fashion this mantra for the immobilization of women:
beginning with the *praṇava*, [the name of] Vāsudeva, the auspicious pair of lotuses, followed by *māyā* (hrīṃ), then the slayer [ha], Pulaha, the moon [sa], and Jaya [svāhā]. (33.111–112)
One should bow deeply to Yaṣṭi, Bhallāyudha, Vighneśa, and Rāmamastaka,
and recite the mantra for the water-stambhana (stopping of water) as prescribed by the mantra rules.
With the aforementioned mantra, one may move about within the standing water.
To the north, however, one should perform the rite for the immobilization of the currents of the Sindhu rivers.
I shall tell you, exactly as it is, the mantra for the immobilization of fire:
the seven-syllabled [mantra] consisting of Kumbha, Vahni, Bhuvana, and Vanamālin.
"Gopana, Puruṣātman, Trivahni, Śaśalāñchita,
Vairāja, Bindu, Hrasvānta, Caturgati, and then Ṭha-Ṭha"—
by reciting this mantra for the suppression of fire ten thousand times, a person shall achieve success.
Having touched these seven— iron, oil, ghee, milk, an axe, water, and likewise fire— he shall become cool;
he may sit at ease within the heat as if in the interior of a lotus.
O Four-faced One, [one should worship] the seven-syllable name ending in the dative case,
the word "Viṣṇu," the pure Śrī Hṛṣīkeśa, Vighneśa, and Madhusūdana.
One should utter the mantra ending with *ṭha ṭha*, beginning with "Pradyumna, the destroyer of sin, Vijaya, Vāyu, and Mādhava, [grant] sight [after] the fall of Mount Mandara.
By means of this, one may bring cows and buffaloes under one's control.
First, there are four syllables of four colors, followed by Dhanaprada and Guhālaya;
then Pavitravahnikamala, Sumukha, Vahnigopana, and Vāyuṣṭhaṭhānta—this is the mantra beginning with Vyāla and ending with Damana. (33.121–122)
In the *praṇava*, the sixth syllable and so forth, ending in the vocative case like a *piśāca*;
the slaying of the Lord of the Upper World (*ūrdhvalokeśa*), with *ṭhaṭha* upon stones—this is the mantra.
Indeed, one should strike the head of the enemy while reciting this mantra.
Piśācarūpa, Pratyakṣa, Pāṣāṇa, Asthi, Śava,

Śrīkumbha, Gopana, Kumbha, Śaśāṅka, Brahmasādhana, Mandara (twice), Madhuśatru, Subhadra, Bandhumastaka,
Pīta, Krodhana, Māyāma, Vijaya, Gopana, and Dhruva.
One should thus construct the mantra: Brahmā, Mānuṣeśāna, Vāyu, Gopanama-staka, Bindu, Pavitra, Anala, Māruta, Pretanāyaka, and ending with Svāhā; this is the Gandharva mantra.
Then Pinākin beheld this Atharvaṇa mantra situated upon his head,
while [the Lord] himself sat upon a golden lion-throne beneath the Pārijāta tree,
his chest adorned with long, divine garlands.
His limbs were anointed with sandalwood and aloe, and he was adorned with divine ornaments.
He was constantly attended by women of sixteen years, endowed with beauty and youth, holding yak-tail fans in their hands, and possessing eyes as lovely as blue lotuses.
By women born of noble lineage, their forms unsteady with intoxication, possessing wondrous playfulness of the eyebrows and voices of song dear to the ear;
with garments slightly slipping and their head-dresses disarrayed over one shoulder.
It was attended by young maidens whose necklaces swayed upon their breasts, whose thighs were as beautiful as plantain trees, and who wore garlands of curling locks;
they listened again and again with rapt attention to the songs of the *kiṃnarīs*.
Meditating upon the lord of the Gandharvas, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times;
then excellent women of noble family will attend upon him, [attracted] by the command of the king of the Gandharvas, as he is endowed with beauty and youth. (33.135)
Now I shall describe to you the essential form of the Indra-jāla mantra:
Brahmā, Kumbha, Vīrasena, Krodha, Sumukha, Vāruṇa, Rāma, Dakṣa, the enemy of Madhu, Caturgati, and Mṛgeśvara.
Then, bewildering the forms, he displays his head twice;
he utters the syllable *huṃ* four times, as well as *brahman*, *kilikili*,
the two seasons (*ṛtu*), Kumbha and Rāma, and the pure fires Vāmana and others.
Having placed *vijayā* upon the eyes and *bhadra* on the head of Vāmana,
one should mentally construct the mantra twice with the two forms of *māyā*.
Through a recitation numbering one hundred thousand, *māyā* becomes manifest before one's eyes.
Whatever is desired by the practitioner, that he shall accomplish at that very moment;
he shall cause all the deities beginning with Brahmā, who reside in the sky, to appear.
He may turn the sky into the earth, and likewise turn night into day.
A living being cast into the waters, yet possessing breath; likewise a corpse;
water in a desert region; a reservoir of milk that is drying up;
and lands where the six flavors appear in their opposite form—these he perceived as being contrary to reality.
He struck his body with stones, likewise plucked out his eyes and other organs,
caused the growth of hair on his head when it was shorn, and likewise brought about old age in the young; he turned men into women, women into men, and a eunuch into both.
Or the eunuch nature of those two is strange, due to the reversal of beard and breast; likewise,
Śukla sang the Gītā with a different emotional state,
perceiving a non-pregnant woman as pregnant, and a pregnant woman as non-pregnant.
The joining together of broken feet and other limbs, the production of celestial flowers from the sky, the unexpected falling of mountains at will,
as well as the appearance of horns on humans and other beings, and likewise the ascent into the heavens; 33.147.
The untimely onset of battle, as well as the dragging away of images;
the liquefaction of hard things and the solidification of liquid things; even today, the states of dissolution and the rising and sinking [of worlds]. (33.148–149)
He brought about the non-breaking [of weapons] by swords and other arms, as well as the mobility of the immobile and the stability of the mobile;
he bestowed consciousness upon the insentient and the absence of consciousness upon the sentient;
he granted the sight of forms to the blind and sweet speech to the mute.
Even for the deaf there was hearing, and for the lame, walking— this was marvelous.
There was the appearance of celestial chariots on the earth, the orbs of the sun and moon,
a most terrible rain of stones, and an eclipse by Rāhu outside of the proper season.
The fourteen worlds, which had been situated in a single place,
were thrown into a tumultuous mutual conflict; there was a falling from one's seat,
the reversal of the ocean's course, and the taking of one's seat upon the sacrificial fire.
At that moment, there was the sprouting of leaves and fruit on trees that had never grown before;
the sprinkling of fire with water and the blazing of water with fire;
moonlight at midday, and the confusion of the quarters caused by a whirlwind. (33.154–155)
The agitation of the elements such as consciousness, the non-perception of even that which is directly present,
